en: The River of Kings | First Wave
Oṃ, may there be well-being! Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa!

Salutations to the one who has cast off all attachments, who is like a great tree for the sake of Śiva, and who is beautiful with the silken garments shimmering from the jewels on the hoods of the serpents that serve as his ornaments.
Bearing a forehead marked by a crest of flames, wearing above his ear a large, playful serpent-earring, and possessing the luster of a neck as white as the moon born from the ocean; KRT_1_0002ab
May that left or right shoulder of yours, which bears the mark of a bull and is adorned with the bodice-like skin of a serpent while half-joined with a woman, lead to glory.
Some indescribable quality of the good poet is to be revered, for it overflows with nectar;
by means of it, the body of fame attains stability for both oneself and others.

Who else but a poet, the lord of creation, endowed with the skill of beautiful composition, would be capable of bringing the past that has transcended time into direct perception— were it not for his intuition,
which perceives all things as if they were present to the senses?
What, then, serves as proof for the poet’s possession of divine vision other than this?
Even though variety has not been elaborated here out of regard for the length of the narrative,
there is indeed some substance herein that brings joy to the virtuous.

He alone is praiseworthy and truly virtuous, who is free from hatred toward snakes and whose speech remains steady when recounting the facts of reality. I shall now compose anew the narrative material already established by my predecessors.
It is not fitting for the virtuous to turn away upon hearing the purpose [of a work].
For those who have passed away after witnessing the deeds of kings again and again,
the accounts are filled in their compositions by those born in more recent times.
Therefore, how much skill is there in this description of things as they truly are?

My effort is directed toward providing a comprehensive remedy for every kind of error. (A pair of verses) The earlier treatises are extensive; I am condensing my words for the sake of easy memorization. (KRT 1.011ab)

By the power of Suvrata, those discourses based on royal legends have been severed; even that renown which once spread abroad does not reach him when it comes to the illumination of what is to be expressed. The speech of Suvrata possesses a proficiency that is intense and surpasses the learning of the wicked.
Due to some inadvertence, even though poetic works exist,
there is not a single part free from fault in this *Nṛpāvalī* of Kṣemendra.
The compositions of former masters concerning royal narratives have come within the range of my vision.
"However, eleven [years] have passed for me, according to the opinion of the sage Nīla as well.
Having seen the inscriptions on monuments and edicts established by former sovereigns,
as well as panegyrics and treatises, my confusion and fatigue have been entirely stilled."

Fifty-two kings, beginning with Gonanda, were not remembered by those [historians] due to the loss of the traditional accounts; however, from the *Nīlamata*, the sequence of four kings starting with Gonanda is seen. Thus, the lineage of kings has been composed in twelve thousand verses.

Previously, the twice-born Helārāja, who was a practitioner of the Great Vow (Mahāvratin), having observed that doctrine here, placed eight kings beginning with Aṣka— starting from Lava and so forth— within his own work. (This is a pair of verses.)
Śrī Śavillāka said that among those fifty-two kings beginning with Aśoka,
this verse of his is as follows:
"The five kings who were declared [to have ruled] from Abhimanyu down to the end of the verses."
These fifty-two [verses] were obtained from the very middle by the ancients.
This narrative, which serves as a medicine and corresponds to reality, is appropriately employed for the rise or fall of kings, as well as for [the conditions of] place and time.

Whose heart, being well-disposed, would not be moved by such a composition that transmits the infinite traditions of the past? Or rather, when one reflects upon the flickering existence of living beings, which is subject to momentary destruction— [The verse continues: ...in this world that is as fleeting as a flash of lightning, who would not find such a work captivating?
Let the consecration of the essence of tranquility be considered here.
O dear one, let this [work], beautiful with the flow of its abundant rasa,
be clearly drunk by the shells of your ears, like the River of Silver (Jāhnavī).
In ancient times, from the beginning of the Kalpa until now, the earth remained within the womb of the Himavat mountain, filled with its dust for six Manvantaras. Then,
when this Vaivasvata Manvantara arrived, [he gathered] the gods...
Having caused [the demon] to descend through Kaśyapa— the progenitor of beings who was himself brought down by Druhiṇa, Upendra, Rudra,
and others— and having had that water-born one slain within it, he fashioned that lake upon the earth as the region known as Kaśmīra. (A pair of verses.)
[The city] which is protected by Nīla, the sovereign of all serpents, whose parasol is the staff emerging from his uplifted hood;
[the city] which possesses a luster like that of a cow whose milk-dust has been drunk by the mouths of serpents turned toward her calf.
Where Gaurī, though having become the Vitastā river, does not abandon her inherent dignity;
and which city is attended by serpents with faces like conchs and lotuses, resplendent with various jewels, as if by the treasures of Kubera.
To protect the serpents who had arrived out of fear of Tārkṣya,
he surely extended his arms across his back in the manner of a mountain rampart;
[I bow to] the Lord of Umā in the form of wood, from whom the attainment of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation is secured.
Within the Pāpasūdana Tīrtha, where it shall be for those who touch [the water];
on that waterless mountain where the goddess Sandhyā holds the water;
[therein lies] the vision of merit and sin through their positive and negative concomitance.
Where the Self-Existent One, emerging from the womb of the earth as the consumer of oblations,
accepts the sacrificial offering with the forests of his flame-arms;
where the Goddess herself, on the peak of Mount Bheḍa, pure with the source of the Gaṅgā— *Kṛtyakalpataru* 1.0034ab–cd, 1.0035ab.
There, Sarasvatī is seen in the form of a swan;
in the temple that is the abode of Hara at Nandikṣetra,
even today the drops of sandalwood paste from the offerings made by celestial beings are still manifest there.
Where, upon beholding the goddess Śāradā, one instantly attains the Madhumatī river and speech cultivated by poets.
Adorned by Viṣṇu, the Lord of Victory, and others such as Īśāna,
there is not even a sesame seed’s worth of land therein that has been excluded from sacred fords (tīrtha).
That [land] is conquered by the power of merit rather than by the forces of those bearing weapons.

In that place, fear of the next world was the greatest for those who dwelt there. There, the rivers were free from danger and devoid of aquatic creatures; they served as houses for steam-baths in the cold and provided secure landing-stairs during the rains.
Knowing that it was not subject to heat because it was built by his father, the sun, as if out of respect, maintains its lack of intensity even in summer. Furthermore,
the lofty halls of learning here possess saffron and water cool with snow.

Where there exists the grape, a fruit rare even in the celestial realms—that land is praiseworthy as a source of jewels within the three worlds; and therein lies the quarter of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera).
Even there, the mountain that is the father of Gaurī stands; and upon that very mountain lies the region [of Kashmir].
In that Kali age, they remember only fifty-two kings, beginning from Gonanda, who were born at the same time as the Kauravas and the sons of Kuntī; for at that time,
it was certain that due to the misdeeds of those rulers of the earth, [the land] became barren.
The creators of the body of fame for the Architect of Poetry did not exist.

(KRT_1.0045cd) Having resorted to the shade of the forest-trees of the arms of those of great majesty, this earth, girt by the ocean, became free from fear from any quarter. (KRT_1.0046ab) To that work of poetry, which is great by its very nature, we offer our salutation—that without whose favor even kings do not enter into one's memory. (KRT_1.0046cd)

Those whose feet rested upon ivory couches, those who attained sovereign glory, and in whose houses young women once dwelt like moonlight by day—even this world regards those ornaments of the world as if they had never existed even in a dream. O brother, what is the use of hundreds of praises for you? A blind world will not perceive you through them alone.
Twenty-two hundred and sixty-eight kings [have passed].

Gonanda and the others ruled over Kaśmīra during the Kali age; however, at the end of the Dvāpara age, they were deprived of their joy by the report that Bhārata had become [the land]. Some of them declared this calculation of time to be false. (A pair of verses. KRT_1_0048cd–KRT_1_0049ab–KRT_1_0049cd.

Having calculated the years of the kings whose sovereign status has been established, there remains no period of the Kali age from the time elapsed; thus, [the calculation] is devoid of that [Kali period]. On this earth, when six hundred and three and a half [years] have passed— KRT_1_0050ab–0051ab.
In the Kali age, the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas came into being.
Now, in the twenty-fourth year of the common era of the Śaka period,
one thousand and seventy years have passed.
At that time, approximately two thousand three hundred and thirty autumns had passed since the beginning of the third *go-nanda*,
[making] twelve hundred and sixty-six years.
It is held that for kings, the calculation of time is based on fifty-two of those [years].
When one asterism passes to another in a hundred years among the Citraśikhaṇḍins,
the authors of the *Saṃhitās* have thus provided this determination regarding its movement.
While King Yudhiṣṭhira, under whom the sages presided during the Maghā asterism, ruled the earth,
the Śaka era was diminished by six, two, five, and two [years] from the duration of his reign.
The powerful Gonanda, lord of Kaśmīra, was attended by the direction [of the north], which laughs with Mount Kailāsa and wears the flowing Gaṅgā as its silken garment;
as if out of fear of being embraced by the venom of the serpent Śeṣa, that direction had abandoned its own body.
The earth took its place upon his arm, which was marked with the jewel of the *gārutmata* gem.
Summoned by his kinsman Jarāsaṃdha to provide assistance,
he besieged Mathurā with vast forces against the enemy of Kaṃsa.
Then, while establishing his camp along the banks of the Kālindī,
he adorned the fame of his warriors with the laughter of the Yādavas.
Once, when his forces were broken on all sides, he prepared to protect his own army.
The plow-bannered one (Balarāma) hemmed in that warrior in the conflict.
For a long time, as those two of equal vigor fought, the Goddess of Victory remained poised in the balance between them; did she perhaps grow weary in her doubt regarding their victory?

Then, on the battlefield, the Kashmiri king embraced the earth with his limbs wounded by weapons, while Yādava embraced the Goddess of Victory. When that excellent kṣatriya had departed for the path easily accessible to great heroes, [the world was left behind].

His son was the illustrious one named Dāmodara, who ruled the earth. Although that king obtained a kingdom enriched by the enjoyment of pleasures, the proud monarch found no peace while brooding over the murder of his father.
Then, at the Svayaṃvara of the daughters of Gāndhāra near the Indus,
where the Vṛṣṇis had been invited, he whose tree-like arms were nourished by pride heard that they had arrived.
Thereupon, out of extreme fury toward those who stood nearby, [he spoke].

In that battle, the expanse of the sky was swallowed by the dust raised by the horses and banners; it was as if a bridegroom’s suitor, eager for a wedding, were slaying her husband-to-be. Indeed, there was a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage) among the Gandharas for the celestial damsels.
Then, having overcome the circle of his enemies in that battle with the discus-weapon,
the steadfast universal monarch went to heaven by the sound of the edge of the discus.
At that time, the scion of the Yadu clan [consoled] his pregnant wife.
In the kingdom, Madhusūdana had the twice-born consecrate her under the name Yaśovatī. At that time, uttering this traditional verse, he dismissed his ministers with indignation.

The Kaśmīras are Pārvatī; the king there should be known as born from a portion of Hara. Even if he is wicked, he must not be despised by a wise man desiring prosperity. Those glances which men cast upon women at a meal, devoid of respect—

They beheld her, the mother of subjects, like some divine being. Then, in the month of childbirth, the queen gave birth to a son, a child endowed with divine marks, who was like a sprout for the family tree that had been consumed by fire.

Together with the rites for his royal consecration and other ceremonies, the birth-rites and subsequent sacraments were performed by the foremost of the twice-born. That infant king, along with the splendor of royalty, attained the status of a ruler.
Thus, in due order, his grandson was named Gonanda after his grandfather. While he was still a child, two nurses were appointed for his upbringing:
one who provided milk, and the other who brought forth all prosperity.
Guarding his unfailing benevolence, the father’s ministers gave wealth even to those standing nearby whenever he smiled without cause;
they continued to act thus, failing to understand the unspoken words of that infant.
The officials considered themselves as if they had committed an offense.
As that young king ascended his father’s throne,
he did not even feel a longing for the footstool, as his feet were already resting upon it.
Having placed that [child] upon the royal throne, with its fly-whisks fluttering like the feathers of a crow,
the ministers listened as he resolved the legal doubts of the subjects;
thus did that king of Kaśmīra conduct himself while still in his childhood.

He was not led away by the Kurus or the Pāṇḍavas to provide assistance in battle. Thereafter, thirty-five kings— their names and deeds lost through the violation of the sacred tradition— sank into the ocean of oblivion.

Then there was a king named Lava, an ornament of the earth, who was the object of the affection of the goddess of victory, whose silken garment was his undulating fame. By the roar of his army, which brought sleeplessness to the world— *Kṛti 1.84ab–85ab*.
It is a marvel that his enemies were sent to the state of eternal sleep.
By him, having constructed ten million stone mansions minus one hundred and sixty thousand,
the city of Lolora was built.
Having bestowed a land-grant upon an assembly of twice-born brahmins at Leda and Levāra,
that long-armed king, whose glory consisted of irreproachable valor, ascended to heaven.
His son was Kuśa, lotus-eyed and skilled in prowess.
Immediately after him, there was a donor of the Kuru-hārā agrahāra.
Then his son, the illustrious Khagendra— the destroyer of the lineage of enemy elephants, a pre-eminent leader, and a refuge of valor— attained the sovereignty of kings.
He was the founder of Khāḍi and Khonamuṣa, and the primary donor of Mukhya and Agrahāra.
Through deeds as white as the laughter of Śiva, he gradually led the worlds [to liberation].
Possessing priceless majesty, he was long excluded from the state of being a donor (maghavat-tva).

Then his son, King Surendra, became a performer of wondrous deeds; though he possessed a hundred-fold wrath, he was one whose anger was pacified. He was a protector of his lineage, yet he surpassed even the Lord of the Gods (Surendra) in that no other Lord of the Gods could serve as his equal.

Having established a city named Soraka near the land of Darad, the illustrious king constructed a monastery called Narendrabhavana. By that man of meritorious deeds, whose fame spread throughout his own realm, [the monastery was built].

A magnificent monastery named Saurasa was constructed there. When that king had passed away and left no lineage, one born of another family named Godhara bore the earth, including its preeminent mountains, in peace.

The noble-minded one of meritorious deeds, having bestowed upon the twice-born the agrahāra named Godharāhastiśālā, ascended to heaven. His son was named Suvarṇa, who became a "Golden River" for those seeking wealth.
He who was the founder of the Suvarṇamaṇikulyā at Karāla had a son named Janaka, who was like a father to his subjects;
he established a monastery, a land grant, and the place called Jālor.

His son was Śacīnara, a lord of the earth who was like a husband to the Earth (Śacī). Then his illustrious son, Kṣamāśīla, protected the world with unassailable commands. He was a maker of royal grants and a destroyer of enemies, both those who were physically weak and those who were fierce.
There was a son of Sobhūta who occupied half of the throne of Sutrāman;
he was the great-grandson of that king Śakuni and the great-nephew of [his] father’s brother. Then his grandson, named Aśoka, who was true to his word, ruled the earth.

The king, who had stilled all afflictions and had taken refuge in the teaching of the Jina, covered the dry earth with circles of stūpas. Within his various monasteries, there arose cities of copper that were like the very abodes of the Dharma.

The illustrious king built the city of Śrīnagarī, a most magnificent city consisting of nine million houses resplendent with wealth, which he had constructed as a caitya whose height was such that its peak could not be seen even by the gaze of those who reached it.
He caused a stone wall to be built for Śrī Vijayeśa, replacing the dilapidated structure made of plaster; he constructed it without hesitation, free from all blemish.
Furthermore, he erected [a hall] in the assembly hall near Vijayeśa.
There were two temples known as Śāntāvasāda and Prāsādāvaśokeśvara.
When the land was overrun by barbarians,
that virtuous king obtained from Bhūteśa— a deity propitiated through his ascetic penance— a son for the purpose of exterminating them.
Thus the mountain became a lord of the waters and a leader of the gods on earth,
who purified the entire circle of the universe with the nectar of his fame.
When the stories of that one of divine power reached the path of his ears—
They surely attain the status of a wondrous teacher even for the dwellers of heaven;
for once that elixir capable of piercing ten million [atoms] was perfected,
he was certainly able to pierce through the hollow of the golden egg by means of offerings of gold.
Having solidified the waters and entered the interior of the serpent lake,
he brought the youthfulness of the serpent maidens to a state fit for enjoyment.
He [was] the conqueror of the host of Buddhist disputants who were then fiercely inflamed with pride.
He became an accomplished Avadhūta who bestowed the instruction of knowledge upon him. During his own worship of Īśvara, Nandīśa, Kṣetrajyeṣṭha, and Īśa,
the promise of that king of truthful speech was always fulfilled.

He prohibited the running of horses stationed in village after village; some elephant, out of friendship, constantly carried him [on its back]. Having expelled the Mlecchas who had obstructed the earth, he of unyielding prowess [reigned].
He conquered the earth, girdled by the oceans, through his victorious expeditions.
Wherever those Mlecchas, who had covered the entire region, were driven out by him,
that place is even today called *Ujjhaṭaḍimba* by the people.
Having conquered the earth beginning with Kanyakubja,
he settled the four castes from those regions in his own country, as well as righteous judges;
and while they had not yet attained proper prosperity through legal proceedings, wealth, and other means, [he established them].
In this realm, the kingdom was indeed like that of a common locality;

for there were seven constituent elements: the Superintendent of Justice, the Superintendent of Wealth, the King as the Superintendent of the Treasury, the Envoy, the Family Priest, and the Astronomer-Priest. (This is a pair of verses.)
By him, who established eighteen righteous offices of state,
the royal order of Yudhiṣṭhira was thereafter maintained.
Through the fortune acquired by his valor and majesty, [he ruled].
The one of exalted intellect established the days of the week, the lunar days, and so forth, as well as agrahāra grants.
In the various locations such as the gates, the circles of the Mothers (mātṛcakra) were fashioned by his wife, the goddess Īśānā, who was fierce in her power and preeminent.
Having heard the Nandipurāṇa, that king, a disciple of Vyāsa,
performed service for his uterine brothers and others out of a desire to rival Nandīśa. By him, who was establishing the preeminence of Jyeṣṭharudra in Śrīnagarī—

Because of that, he did not consider even Nandīśa to be his equal, let alone his own brother. Once, due to being preoccupied with business, he forgot his daily duties; distressed by the failure to obtain water from his distant brother, he remained troubled in mind.

Seeing water suddenly arisen from a place devoid of moisture— possessing qualities such as color and taste that did not differ from those of his own brother— he [performed his ablutions]. Once that sacred bathing-place had appeared, he performed his immersion there.

Out of pride, he entered into a rivalry with Nandirudra and attained mastery [in the art of music]. Once, for the sake of testing him, a golden pitcher with a hollow interior was placed inside his brother's [body] with its mouth covered by a lid.
In one and a half days, having emerged from the waters of the Śrīnagarī river,
he severed the king's doubt:
"Surely this is the Lord of Rivers himself who has descended here to enjoy worldly pleasures."
Otherwise, the accomplishment of actions, whether seen or unseen, would not occur. Once, as that king was proceeding toward Vijayeśvara,
a certain woman encountered him on the road and begged for food.
When he had promised to give her whatever food she desired, she, having become deformed, revealed her longing for human flesh. He,
who was free from harming living beings, gave her flesh from his own body.
When she had thus granted him permission to eat, he then said:
"O protector of the earth, you are a Bodhisattva;
for what great-souled one could possess such firm compassion toward living beings as this?"
Not knowing the Buddhist language, the king, out of his devotion to Maheśvara, said to her:
"O auspicious lady, who is a Bodhisattva that you should know me? She spoke again to the monarch: "My purpose must be heard."

For I have been raised up by the Buddhans, who were provoked to anger by you. We Kṛttikās, dwelling on the slopes of the mountain Lokāloka, are of the nature of darkness; with the Bodhisattva as our sole refuge, we long for the destruction of that darkness.

In this world, starting from the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, there are certain beings who have transcended the afflictions; recognize them as Bodhisattvas. Even when harmed, they do not become angry, and through patience, they benefit others.

They, striving to support the universe, will lead their own enlightenment [to ruin]. Formerly, when you were awakened by the sounds of musical instruments from the monasteries and incited by the wicked, you, out of anger, carried out the destruction of the monastery.

That king, the great Śākya, cannot be thwarted by you; however, O auspicious lady, upon seeing him, the destruction of your darkness will come to pass. At our word, he should be urged to construct a monastery.
Having bestowed your own wealth of gold, you have been defiled by wicked men. If that [act] had not been committed, the calamity of destroying the monastery would not have occurred;
thus, atonement would have been made for both him and those who incited him.

"Enraged, the Buddhists meditated upon you and rushed forth to slay you; but at that time, I was summoned and instructed by the Bodhisattvas. Therefore, this excess of courage in you has been tested under such a pretext. (Kulaka) KRT_1_0144ab–KRT_1_0145ab.

"Your sins have now been exhausted; may it be well with you, I shall depart. When the king had thus given his promise, Queen Kṛtyā, her eyes wide with joy at having accomplished the task, vanished once more.

Then, having constructed a monastery at Kṛtyāśrama, the lord of the earth reunited the goddess Kṛtyā, whose darkness had been dispelled, with that very place. Having built a temple of Śoṣa in Nandikṣetra, the king—
He offered forgiveness to the Lord of Beings and a jewel-encrusted worship with precious vessels.
Having performed penance for a night within the Cīramocana Tīrtha,
he sat upon the seat of Brahmā, his form motionless in meditation.

By the king’s long-accumulated meritorious deeds, the golden rivers were brought to a state of dullness through their longing for the touch of Nandīśa. At the moment of dancing and singing, they rose up to dance due to the arising of joy.
He gave a hundred wives from his own harem to Jyeṣṭharudra.
Having enjoyed sovereign power, at the end he entered Cīramocana;
together with his wife, the king attained union (sāyujya) with the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Then there was a lord of the earth named Dāmodara, born of the Aśoka lineage or perhaps from another noble family, who protected the land.
He was like the crest-jewel of Maheśvara, blazing intensely with great prosperity.
Even today, his power is heard of as a wonder to the world. By him—
who was a vessel for the grace of Śiva, who delighted in virtuous conduct, and who was truly happy— Vaiśravaṇa himself formed a friendship.

Like Kubera, he was the foremost among kings who carried out his commands; having issued orders for a long time, he constructed the Guddasetu. That city which he had built for himself was located at the kitchen of Dāmodara.

With that bridge, he desired to effect a crossing even there for the sake of the moon. Alas, what a pity! Obstacles arise for a noble-souled man who wishes to perform some extraordinary benefit for the world, due to the limited merit of human beings.
For he strove to have the yakṣas construct within his own domain long stone embankments to quell the overflow of the waters;
for the power of asceticism belonging to brahmins of fierce splendor is inconceivable.
Even for such [kings], those who would cause a reversal of their power—
having seen Fortune lost through the strength of heirs and the like, yet risen again; Fortune, once vanished through the king's contempt for Brahmins, never to arise again.

Once, when the king had risen to bathe for the sake of performing his religious duties (*śrāddha*), he was requested by some hungry brahmins for food before his bath. As he was about to depart, he dismissed them while still inside the Vitastā river.
Then, by his power, they diverted that river in front of him.
"Behold this Vitastā; feed us here," he was told by them;
yet, though thus addressed, he did not perceive that the course of the river had been altered by magic.

"O Brahmins, I do not give food to one who has not bathed; depart now! Having been addressed thus by him, they cursed him, saying, "Become a serpent! Having heard your *Rāmāyaṇa* in its entirety in a single day," [he shall become a snake].
"Peace shall come to the curse," they said, having been propitiated. Even today, that Dāmodara is perceived by people as he runs far away with thirst, his breath heated by the curse like smoke.
Then there were three kings in that very place named Huṣka, Juṣka, and Kaniṣka, who established three cities marked with their own names. Among them,
Juṣka was the builder of the monastery (vihāra) and of the city of Juṣkapura.
The pure-minded [king] was also the founder of Jayasvāmipura.
Those kings, though born of the Turuṣka lineage, were patrons of merit;
in regions such as Śuṣkaletra, they constructed monasteries, caityas, and other edifices.
During their extensive period of royal rule, the region of Kaśmīra was for the most part enjoyed by the Buddhists, those renunciants of exalted splendor. At that time,
following the final nirvāṇa of the Blessed One, the Lion of the Śākyas...
Indeed, one hundred and fifty years passed in this world-system;
and in this region, there was a single Bodhisattva who became a lord of the earth.
He was the illustrious Nāgārjuna, who took refuge in the forest of the six Arhats.

Then King Niṣkaṇṭaka, having eradicated all thorns [enemies] and bestowed agrahāras, became fearless and full of valor, like another Śatamanyu (Indra). Having fashioned a crest-jewel marked with his own name and adorned with the moon, he—
The illustrious [king] established the city of Abhimanyu, which possessed supreme splendor.
Having obtained the traditional knowledge (*āgama*) from that region through Candrācārya and others,
he set forth the *Mahābhāṣya* and composed his own grammar.
At that time, the Buddhists attained preeminence in the land,
protected by the wise Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.
Having defeated all the learned disputants in debate, they [prevailed].
Without interrupting the ritual prescribed in the *Nīlamata Purāṇa*, he approached the enemy.
In the sacrificial circle (*maṇḍala*), where the conduct was disrupted and the offerings were interrupted,
the Nāgas, raining down abundant snow, caused the destruction of the people.
As the Buddhist persecution fell upon Himālaya year after year,

the king resided for six months in Dārvābhisāra and other such places during the cold season. At that time, there was a certain power belonging to the one who performed the rites of *bali* and *homa*.

O Brahmins, others perished through his power, and even the Buddhists met their end. Then, a twice-born man named Candra-deva, a descendant of Kaśyapa, performed austerities directed toward Nīla, the lord of the earth and protector of the land.
Having become manifest before him, he warded off the delusion of the blue frost and spoke again of the ancient rule of his own city.
By the first Lord of the Moon, the delusion of the Yakṣas was quelled.
But by the second [king], the subversion of the monks in this land became unbearable.
The third king, Gonanda, obtained the kingdom in the interval between them;
he resumed the processions, sacrifices, and other rites for the *nāgas* as before.
When that king had set in motion the ordinance of the blue-clad [Buddha],
the monks and the evils of the cold season were entirely pacified.
At the proper times, through the merit of the subjects, such rulers of the earth come into being.
Those who carry out the restoration of a kingdom that has been long devastated,
and those who are intent on not oppressing their subjects, shall perish along with their kin; however,
for those who restore what has been lost, prosperity shall follow their lineage.

Having observed these characteristics regarding the history of this region, the wise should discern the auspicious and inauspicious fortune of future rulers. This earth shall belong to the descendants of him who has renovated the land.
Long enjoyed by Siddhas such as Pravarasena and others of meritorious deeds, that king—
like Raghu, the first of the Raghus descended from the lineage of Gonaṇda—
ruled over the earth for thirty-five years.
For sixty years and six months, minus six years,
Vibhīṣaṇa, the delighter of the sons of the earth, protected the land. Indrajit and Rāvaṇa were the two kings, father and son, in succession.
Thirty-five and a half years passed for those two. He,
whose pure splendor of dots and lines foretells future events upon being seen—
he, Vaṭeśvara, shines as a *liṅga* for the sake of worshipping Rāvaṇa.
Within a four-winged monastery (maṭha),
the king bestowed the entire Kaśmīra maṇḍala upon Vaṭeśvara. That mighty-armed ruler enjoyed the earth for thirty-five years.
Vibhīṣaṇa’s son was Sārdhāmanya; then there was one named Kiṃnara, whose prowess was sung by the Kiṃnaras. The son of Vibhīṣaṇa was the king named Nara.

Although that king was always devoted to right conduct, due to the reversal of his subjects' fortune and the defects of his realm, he brought about a succession of great calamities. Dwelling alone in a pleasure grove situated within a settlement of *kiṃnaras*, he—

By the power of his yoga, someone brought his beloved [back] as a mendicant. Out of anger toward him, he burned thousands of monasteries and seized those villages by means of brahmins residing in the central monastery.
With its flourishing marketplaces, royal highways, and boats illuminating the river,

and with its vast gardens of flowers and fruit, it was like another manifestation of heaven. With wealth acquired through the conquest of the quarters, it surpassed the city of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera).

On the banks of the Vitastā, he had a city constructed. [A pair of verses. There, in a certain garden, there was a lake named Suśravas, which served as the dwelling of a nāga, adorned with clear and sweet water.
Once, at midday, when he was weary from a long journey, a young brahmin named Viśākha, seeking shade, entered the marshy bank of that lake; there,
beneath the canopy of shady trees, his fatigue was assuaged by the breezes.

Having slowly touched water for purification, he proceeded to eat the barley meal. Even as he was taking it in his hand, the sound of anklets— which had previously been heard by the swans wandering on the shore— was now perceived by him.

Having emerged from the bower of *mañjarī* creepers, he then beheld before him two maidens with beautiful eyes, dressed in blue veils; they touched [him] with hands that mimicked the playful grace of lotus stalks adorned with *karṇikā* gems and rubies.

With her lovely white cheeks marked by a thin line of collyrium, and with the corners of her eyes—captivating and stirred by the gentle movement of the breeze—adorned upon her two shoulders like the fluttering fronds of a banner of beauty; [this is] the *tilaka* verse. (KRT 1.208cd–209cd)
Seeing them slowly approaching her moon-like face,
she paused from the commencement of her meal, momentarily paralyzed by shame;
while the lotus-eyed one was eating the pods of the *kacchaguñjā* shrubs.
Then, having seen them and casting his gaze forward slightly, the twice-born one thought, "Alas! This food is for such a form!
Meditating thus, moistened with compassion and honoring them, he fed them the barley meal.

When they had attained purity, he offered them water from the lake— clear and cool— for their drink, using cups fashioned from lotus leaves. When they had sipped the water and attained purity, and had taken their seats, [he waited upon them].
Then, fanning them with leaf-fans, he said:
"Ladies, having obtained this audience through some past merits of yours,
this person wishes to ask a question out of the restlessness so common among brahmins."
"Of the two of us who are auspicious, which meritorious birth has been adorned?
Or where has such weary and tasteless food as this been eaten?
One of them said to him: "Know us to be the daughters of this Suśravas."
Why is such delicious food being consumed that has not even been obtained?
I, Irāvatī, was intended by my father to be given to the Lord of the Vidyādharas; and this younger sister of mine is Candralekhā.

The twice-born spoke thus once more: "What poverty do you possess? They replied: "Father, he knows the reason for this; let him be asked. On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, for the sake of the procession of Takṣaka—
"You will certainly know that we have arrived by the stream of water flowing from [her] crest;
you shall see us both then, stationed near her. Having spoken thus, those two daughters of the serpent vanished in an instant.
Then that great festival procession gradually commenced, crowded with actors and wandering minstrels,
and thronged by spectators;
even the twice-born man, drawn by curiosity, quickly wandered through the arena.
He went into the presence of the Naga, who was known by the signs described by the maiden. Then,
having been previously informed by the two maidens standing at his side,
the leader of the Nagas addressed the twice-born man, saying, "Welcome."
Then, during the course of a conversation, when asked about the cause of his misfortunes,
the eater of breaths (the snake) sighed and said to that twice-born man:
"O Brahmin, for those possessed of self-respect who discern between what is right and what is wrong, [misfortune is inevitable]..."
It is indeed fitting that those who are inevitably destined to experience suffering do not reveal it.
When a person of naturally noble character hears of the suffering of another,
they suffer a pang in their heart because of their inability to provide assistance.

The person of limited intellect highly prizes his own livelihood, harbors grief in his heart, openly disparages his own worth with words of feigned compassion, and praises himself. He speaks of resorting to censurable means and describes his misfortune as enduring; upon hearing of another's calamity, he inflicts a piercing pain by expressing his own suffering. For this very reason, it remains in the minds of the discerning for as long as they live.
The fire of the funeral pyre consumes at the end those pleasures and pains that have grown old. Who could perceive the external calamity of those whose nature is profound,
unless it is made manifest by a young child or a servant?
O virtuous one, since this matter has become manifest before you due to our youth, it is not possible for me to conceal it from you; likewise,
by you, whose nature is inherently upright, [it must be told] for the sake of our welfare.
O auspicious lady, if it is possible, let a slight effort be made.
This shaven-headed ascetic with a topknot who is seen at the foot of the tree— by this guardian of the crops, we have been driven to flight.

When the food has not yet been eaten by the mantra-practitioners, it is not consumed by the Nāgas; yet this one eats it, and because of that, we have been struck down by the *samaya*. Even upon seeing the abundance of fruit, he guards the fields while this [other] one is present.
We are not at all able to enjoy it, like hungry ghosts [unable to drink] river water.
Act in such a way that this lifelong ascetic may fall from his vow;
we too know how to provide a fitting retaliation against those who have wronged us.
Having said "So be it" to the Naga, the twice-born man then became intent on his task;
day and night he contemplated how to deceive the grain-guardian,
remaining hidden within a hut situated outside his field.
Then he threw fresh rice into the vessel where the food was being cooked;
while still eating, he took away that abundant abundance of fruit from it in that very instant,
like the Lord of Serpents raining down a lake of water-jars.
And on another day, that king, having transcended poverty, brought that twice-born man— who had rendered him assistance and had come to the shore of a lake— to his own land. There,
at his father’s command, he was honored with the offering of two daughters.

Day after day, he gratified [the snakes] with enjoyments easily obtained even by the immortals. In time, having summoned them all, he prepared to go to his own domain; then Candralekhā entreated the Naga, who had previously granted her a boon.

Though he was unworthy of such an alliance, that serpent, constrained by his sense of gratitude, shared with him both his daughter and his wealth. Thus it was for that twice-born man who had obtained such prosperity through the boon of the excellent Nāga.

In that great city of men, time passed amidst various perpetual festivities. The daughter of the lord of serpents, for her part, devoted to her husband and possessing supreme splendor, gratified her lord with her virtues such as character and conduct.

Once, while she was standing on the top of the palace, a horse, roaming about, began to eat grain that had been left outside the courtyard after the heat of the sun had passed. When the servants summoned to restrain it did not arrive at the house, [she herself went out].
With her tinkling, sweet-sounding anklets, she herself then descended.
With the edge of her garment slipping from her head due to the force exerted by her hand,
she then ran and struck him with her lotus-like hand.
Then, as he was departing after leaving his food, from the touch of the serpent-woman,
a golden hand-mark appeared on the body of the horse.
At that time, King Nara [learned] of that beautiful-eyed woman through his spies.
Having heard [the news] of the brahmin’s wife, his passion had already begun to sprout; he stood there,
and as his elephant-like mind ran wild like a madman,
he lacked the goad of fear of scandal to restrain it by force.
When that king was again overwhelmed by the surging fire of passion,
the behavior of his horse imitated the conduct of a haughty wind. Transgressing all bounds, it acted with its foreleg, which was beautiful with straight fingers.
Like the ocean by the moon marked with a golden hand,
he— freed from the shackles of shame and accompanied by messengers who revealed his intentions—
then delighted Sundarī by wooing her.
And when she could not be won by any means whatsoever, her husband, that Brahmin,
was entreated by that greedy man; for where is there any shame among those blinded by passion?
Then,
despite being repeatedly rebuked by him, the king gave orders to his soldiers to seize her by force;
they leaped upon the front of her house, while she herself went out by another path.
Seeking protection, the twice-born man entered the abode of the Nāgas along with his wife. When they had approached him and informed him of that event,
the lord of the serpents, blinded by rage, emerged from that lake.
Producing a mass of darkness with thundering, dark clouds, he consumed the king along with his city by means of a rain of terrible thunderbolts. A river flowed there,
carrying the fat, blood, and marrow dripping from the limbs of burnt living beings.
The Vitastā became marked with eyes like those of a peacock's tail.
For thousands of embodied beings who had fled in fear to the presence of the Wielder of the Discus for refuge, their bodies were consumed in an instant.
The fat of the creatures being consumed then touched every limb of Madhu and Kaṭabha, just as the discus touches the thighs of the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu).
From a mountain cave came the sister of Suśravas, a Nāga woman named Ramaṇī.

Taking heaps of stones as assistance, she then arrived there. When she learned that her brother had accomplished his task and that the shower of stones had ceased near the village, she abandoned them once the remaining distance of the road was more than a yojana.

Then, for five yojanas, there arose a desolate waste supporting villages; even today, that lovely forest remains, filled with large boulders and caves. Having caused a terrible destruction of people, the serpent, though full of remorse at dawn, [remains].
Despondent due to public censure, he abandoned that place and departed for a distant mountain,
where he created a lake as white as the Ocean of Milk;
even today, it is seen by people during the pilgrimage to Amareśvara.
Even for that twice-born man who had become a nāga through the favor of his father-in-law,
another lake there became renowned as "Jāmātṛ-saras" (the Lake of the Son-in-law). [He was] one who,
under the pretext of protecting the subjects, brought about their destruction without hesitation.
Some such beings appear suddenly as bringers of death.
Even today, passion is considered a fault only by those of limited vision;
for that [passion] has become such [a source of ruin] because it never belonged to anyone anywhere.

In the view of those with limited vision, what indeed is the fault of passion in kings? That very thing occurred for him because of it, which had never happened to anyone, anywhere—even due to the anger of a single virtuous woman, a deity, or a brahmin. (KRT 1.0271–0272ab)
For he had heard the news of the upheaval of even the three worlds:
having ruled the earth for forty years less three months, that bull among kings met his destruction through his own misconduct.
Although its circle of walls and watchtowers had been seen for only a short time,
that city of the Kinnaras came to resemble a city of the Gandharvas.
But his only son, due to the course of his diverse karmas, [fared otherwise].

Led by Svadhātrī to the field of victory, he did not abandon his life-breaths. Then that king named Siddha likewise caused the remaining people to be completely destroyed, just as a rain-cloud revives a mountain scorched by a forest fire.
Thus, this most wonderful account of that high-minded one’s paternal lineage served as an instruction in merit for understanding the worthlessness of saṃsāra.
Even though he was situated in the midst of it, he did not allow himself to be led into defilement by the pursuit of enjoyments.

He could not be defiled by the mud, like the stainless moon reflected in it. While he gazed incessantly upon the one whose crest is the digit of the nectar-born moon in the midst of kings feverish with pride, his own state of health and well-being flourished.
By that virtuous man, who cast away jewels like blades of grass,
his mathematical skill remained unimpaired even in the worship of the crescent-moon ornament;
for it was the royal glory of that very king which followed him into the next world.

The rogue, having ruled the earth for sixty years according to the unfailing dharma, ascended to the worlds of the moon-crested Lord (Śiva) along with his physical body, accompanied by those who had attended upon him.
[12] Servants, by relying upon a man, fall into a state of wretchedness;
but by taking refuge in his son as their lord, they attain a status venerable to the world.

One who relies [upon another] indeed attains in this world either a censurable state, obtainable by those who are themselves relied upon, or a state honored by all people. A blade of grass, having attached itself to a well-drawing mechanism, goes downward; yet a flower, resting upon it, rises to the heights where the heads of gods reach.
"He is perfected! He is perfected!"—thus do the gods in heaven proclaim concerning this one while still in the body.
Beating the drum for seven days, he proclaimed:
"He has attained the renown of 'Utpalākṣa' (Lotus-Eyed) because of his beautiful eyes. His son ruled the earth for thirty-five *varṣas*.
His son was Hiraṇyākṣa, who built a city marked with his own name;
he ruled the earth for thirty-seven years and seven months.
His son was Hiraṇyotsaka, whose lineage was called the Hiraṇyakula.

His son was Vasukula, who ruled for sixty-six years. Then, when the realm was overrun by hordes of Mlecchas, his son Mihirakula became king; he was fierce in his conduct and resembled Time (Death) itself.
Eager to conquer through rivalry the southern quarter that desires peace,
it was as if the weight of the northern region had come near by means of its pretext;
[the mountain] whose presence is surrounded by thousands of slain creatures.
Seeing vultures, crows, and other scavengers before them, people ran away;
he who was once a vampire among kings, surrounded by thousands of slaughtered creatures day and night even within his pleasure palaces— [now wanders thus].
Compassion for the ignorant, tenderness toward women, and respect for the elderly—
these never existed in that cruel man of terrible appearance as he was engaged in slaughter.
Once, [he saw] the queen clad in a bodice of fine Siṃhala cloth...

Seeing her breasts marked with the impression of golden footprints, he burned with indignation. When questioned by the chamberlain— who remarked, "A cloth is being prepared in Siṃhala bearing the king's footprints"— he then gave orders for the expedition.
The southern ocean, where rivers formed by the water poured from the jars of his army met,
attained the joy of being embraced by the Yamunā; he,
together with the lord of Siṃhala, tore [the enemy] apart with fury.
After a long time, the night-stalkers beheld his army from afar through the towers of Laṅkā; perceiving the anger born of seeing their beloved touched by his feet,
and suspecting once again the exertion of Rāghava, they trembled.
Having installed another king there, he of fierce power brought [as tribute] a cloth-painting named Yamuṣadeva, marked with the likeness of the Sun;
and having turned back the kings of Cola, Karṇāṭa, Lāṭa, and others.

Just as a scent-elephant crushes rival elephants with his very scent, he overwhelmed them by his mere presence. As he advanced, the cities— whose girdles of watchtowers were crumbling away— reported his defeat to the lords of men who had arrived there.

Having reached the gateway of Kaśmīra, he heard the cry born of terror from an elephant that had fallen into a chasm; hearing it, his hair stood on end with joy. Then, in his agitation upon hearing that sound, he became joyful, yet his mind was conflicted.
He violently crushed another hundred lordly elephants;
just as physical contact defiles the limbs, so does the mention of sinners defile speech.
Therefore, no other cruelty of his has been described.
Who indeed knows the purpose of those whose actions are wondrous, yet who possess ordinary minds—
even he [the king] undertook that [act] for the sake of attaining merit through righteous conduct.
For in the city of Śrī, that man of evil intellect established the Mihireśvara temple.
In Holaḍā, he [established] the great city named Mihirapura;
thereafter, the Gāndhāra Brāhmaṇas took up the status of agrahāras.
Surely those lowest of the twice-born were of similar character to him.
The arrival of clouds delights the peacock, while the renowned darkness and the clear departure of the clouds delight the swan; indeed,
for both the giver and the receiver, it is only a shared affinity that leads to mutual satisfaction.
Having ruled the earth for seventy years, that Bhairava of the mortal world,
his body afflicted by many diseases, entered the fire.
He is this very Vikoṭihā, who was devoid of compassion even toward his own self.
"Upon the abandonment of the body, a voice shall issue from the sky"—
those who spoke thus [were refuted],
for he himself provided the rebuttal by demonstrating their lack of compassion through acts such as the granting of agrahāras.
When this land was overrun by Dāradas, Bhauṭṭas, and Mlecchas of impure conduct,
and when its dharma had perished, he established people from the Ārya country and performed severe austerities in order to promote virtuous practice.
Having resolved to burn his own body as an act of atonement, he performed that rite. For this very reason, he bestowed a thousand agrahāras upon brahmins born in the Gāndhāra country at Vijayeśvara.
At that time, on a sacrificial altar filled with razors, swords, and butcher knives, and suddenly ablaze with fire at its edge, he cast off his own body. Thus,
within this tradition of people, which is unerring in some respects—

They declared that the cruelty of that lion among men was beyond reproach. The Khāśas who had arrived when the city was being consumed by the serpent in his rage— others related the previously mentioned account of their destruction.
As he was diverting the river named Candrakulyā,
a stone that could not be uprooted appeared in its middle as an obstacle.
Then, having performed penance, that king was addressed by the gods in a dream:
"A powerful yakṣa, a celibate student (brahmacārī), dwells here upon this rock.
If a virtuous woman touches it, he will not be able to restrain her. Then, on the following day, he had that which was spoken in his dream executed upon the rock.
Then, as his efforts with those various noble women proved fruitless,
that great stone was touched by a woman of good family named Candravatī. Consequently,
the king became enraged at that offense and [imposed] thirty million [fines].

He brought about the destruction of the two families, including their wives, brothers, and sons. This fame is not renowned as being based on another's intent; rather, it is known in truth that even when performed for a specific purpose, the injury of living beings is most grievous, even for one who is unworthy.

Thus, even though he was a petty king, he was not slain by the people who gathered together; rather, he was protected by those very gods who caused him to perform his duties. When he finally met his end after a long time due to the intense exhaustion of the merit of his subjects, it was through the rising of their own karma.

Baka, born from him, was consecrated by the citizens as one of virtuous conduct. Even there, because of his previous conditioning, the people felt the same dread as if they were in a cremation ground, though it was the king’s residence, like a pleasure-house.

Born from one who had undergone extreme suffering, he became a source of joy to the people, like a torrent of water from a dark rain cloud on a day when the heat has passed. At that time, the people regarded him as if Dharma itself had arrived from another world.
And Abhaya returned from his exile as if from a dense forest;
having established the city named Lavaṇotsa— possessing supreme splendor— he likewise created the Bakaśva chasm and the river Bakavatī.
There, while ruling the earth, that king spent sixty-three years and thirteen days. Then,
at the onset of night, a certain Yoginī named Bhaṭṭā appeared.
Having assumed the desirable form of his beloved, she waited upon the lord of the people.
With those various captivating words, she dulled his memory;
thus, he was joyfully invited to witness the greatness of the festival of yoga.

Accompanied by his sons and grandsons, he went there in the morning; the emperor was led by her to serve as an offering for the circle of goddesses. By that act, she became perfected, a sign of which was her ability to traverse the sky.
Even today, the two knee-marks of hers can still be seen.
The Lord Śatakapāleśa, the circle of Mothers, and that very stone— these are all there.
Even today, the memory of his fame persists in the monasteries of Khairī.
The root of the royal tree of the Goddess was preserved by Kṣitinandana;
thereafter, his son ruled the earth for thirty years.
His son, named Vasunanda, the author of the renowned *Smaraśāstra*, ruled the earth for fifty-two years and two months.
Nara was his son, and his son was Akṣa; [he ruled] for sixty [years].
The Lord Varṣāṇabhu made the village Yokṣavālaka his capital;
then his son protected the earth with its islands,
manifesting the dawn of the first age through his supervision of the castes and stages of life.
He established agrahāras named Sakholakhāgika, Hāḍigrama, Skandapura, Śamāṅga,
and Āsama;
and having installed Jyeṣṭheśvara on Gopādri, he [settled] those born in the Āryadeśa.
By him, the wise one, were the twice-born made to accept land-grants known as *gopāgrahāras*;
he banished those who ate garlic from the milk-orchard (*bhūkṣīravāṭikā*) and established Brahmins who were devoid of their own proper conduct in Khāsaṭā.
Having brought others from holy regions such as Vañcika and elsewhere,
he established pure Brāhmaṇas in the agrahāras;
for in the panegyrics, the mark [of his reign] was that "this king is the most excellent of the world-protectors."
He who, having attained [sovereignty], endured the loss of cattle even without performing sacrifices—
having protected the earth for sixty-six years plus six days—
he went to the worlds of the virtuous to enjoy the ripening of his merit.
His son was Gokarṇa, who, having established the lord Gokarṇeśvara, ruled the earth for fifty-eight years, less thirty days. His son was Narendrāditya, whose other name was Khiṅkhila.

He was the founder of the Bhūteśvara-pratiṣṭhāna and the maker of the Akṣayinī [well]. His guru, named Ugra, who possessed a form exalted by his spiritual power, performed the installation of Ugreśa and the Mātṛcakra, having received divine grace.

Having ruled as the lord of the earth for thirty-six years and a hundred days, that virtuous man reached through his long-lasting good deeds the stainless worlds. Then, his son became the king named Yudhiṣṭhira.
He whom the people called the "Blind Yudhiṣṭhira" because of his subtle and unimpaired vision,
while ruling the hereditary kingdom with vigilance,
followed for some time the path of former kings.

Then, after some time had passed, due to his misfortune, he— who was intoxicated by prosperity— indulged in whatever whim came to him. He did not favor those worthy of favor, nor did he support the wise.
For those who had ceased their worldly activities, Priyaṃkara was no longer as dear as he once was.
Honored without distinction by the assembly of scholars who were like lamps of innate brilliance, that ill-born man was nevertheless shunned by them along with the assembly of the ignorant.
"Indeed, this equanimity toward all things is a virtue for a yogin;
however, it is a great fault for a lord of the earth, being a cause for infamy.
For by flatterers, faults are turned into virtues and virtues into faults."
With his wit eclipsed, he gradually became like one conquered by women;
his long and constant jesting with rakes, which cut into the very vitals of speech,
and even his play, though unbecoming of a lord, became a source of fear for him.

In his presence, he would falsely seize upon virtues, while behind his back he pointed out faults; thus the king became an object of hatred for those who lived in attendance upon him. As that monarch stumbled even slightly through a moment of inattention— KRT_1_0358ab–KRT_1_0359ab.

In this manner, the stability of the kingdom soon fell into disorder. For one who is neglected by those free from malice and who has not conquered his own self, the treacherous ministers, having gained strength, then conspired for his destruction.
While those who had been restrained by the Lord’s command moved about without restraint,
rival kings, desiring to seize the kingdom, rose up against him.
Animated by that [desire], all those [ministers] who resided in various directions were as agitated as hawks eager to seize sacrificial ghee and meat;
then the king, seized by fear, was unable to maintain his composure.
Like a craftsman setting a stone fallen from a machine,
when that king’s kingdom had long been worn out and thrown into disorder,
not a single means for its stability was found to prevail.
"Having incurred faults, he has reached a position of power and will undoubtedly destroy us.

Thinking thus, his own ministers did not accept conciliation. Then, fully armed with their forces, they besieged the royal palace, which was filled with the cries of people separated by the most terrifying sounds of kettledrums.
The palace rooftops, which obstructed the sun’s rays with the deep shadows of herds of rutting elephants and rendered them shrouded in darkness even by day,

seemed to grant the king space to depart from his own lands as the sun was held back by them. Deprived of his royal splendor within the city, the monarch set out with all his heart along the royal road, which was strewn with grains of parched rice falling from the tears of the citizens agitated at the sight of the departure of the noble horses and their mistresses.

As he departed from his kingdom, his enemies repeatedly seized his retinue, women, treasury, and other possessions—just as boulders on a mountain slope might suddenly carry away the fruits of a tree growing on a peak of that great mountain when it has fallen. Traveling by delightful mountain paths, he took refuge in the shade of trees due to exhaustion; while dozing while seated there, he remembered with great sorrow [his former state].

He was awakened from afar by the cries of the common folk that reached his ears, appearing as if he were sinking into the abyss of his own mind along with the waters of the mountain torrents. Having traversed the forest floor of intense fragrance, filled with various creepers and grasses, and the slippery mountain streams where the rocks were struck by the turbulence of the water,
his exhausted wife— her delicate limbs pale against the shade of the lotus sprouts— fell into a swoon as she threw herself into his lap.

Having gazed for a long time from the edge of the distant mountain slope at the royal ladies' flower-ends as they cast them down to summon the king’s retinue now rapidly shrinking away, even the flocks of birds dwelling in their own nests cried out with agitation from within the mountain caves, their beaks touching their wings spread across the surface of the earth. (3.71) Beholding from afar their own country, with their upper garments slipping from the surface of their breasts and their bodies trembling as they turned their heads back, (3.72ab)

On the road, the water of the mountain streams was surpassed by the tears of the weeping royal women as they placed their hands upon his head. Through the stability of their affection, through consolations offered with appropriate words that brought peace to his grief, and through various sincere acts of service, those virtuous kings of the land eased the king’s sorrow over his fall from the throne as he approached his own territory.
The Second Wave.

Victorious is the Lord’s creation of a body from the female and male portions of his own self— a treasury of diverse and wonderful compositions— constructed with the tips of the horns of a goat and a cow for the bow, and with half the bodies of Naraka and Karati as the two quivers. By that king, the exertion for repeatedly acquiring sovereignty was abandoned.
When old age and the goddess Śamī had reached the root of his ear, he—
exalted by discipline and foremost among those who have mastery over their senses— brought them all equally under his own domain, causing even those five objects of sense to be forgotten.

While he was running through the Durgā-galikā with his own ministers out of a desire for the kingdom, he was captured and imprisoned by some people over time; thus it was reported by certain individuals.
Then, one named Pratāpāditya was brought there by them from another region.
A kinsman of King Vikramāditya was consecrated here;
he was [called] Śakāri-Vikramāditya by those who resorted to error. By others, however, it was written here otherwise—contradictory and distorted.

For some time, this circle of kings, free from internal dissension, remained a source of enjoyment for those rulers through their joy; from that point on, although the earth had never before been ruled by him alone,
it was as if it were indeed possessed by a predecessor.
Like a new bride cherished by a husband who knows her heart, she was thus attended.
After he had enjoyed the earth for thirty-two years and departed for heaven,
his son Jalauka became the ornament of the earth.
He shone together with his father for the sake of prosperity, like the full moon at the equinox shining alongside the sun of scorching rays. Then,
together with the goddess Vākpuṣṭā, who possessed divine power—
Born from them, he enjoyed the earth and delighted his subjects.
This earth was cherished by that couple,
just as the matted hair of Śiva was cherished by the Gaṅgā and the crescent moon.
The two of them established a circle, beautiful with its various colors,
like a rainbow in the clouds of lightning;
and those two highly fortunate ones made it an ornament of the earth’s splendor.
Tuṅgeśvara, the abode of Hara, and the city known as Katika;
in a certain place within the kingdom of Maḍava, blazing with fierce heat,
by its power trees planted at that very moment bore fruit.
That great poet who composed the drama to be witnessed by all people was,
at that time, Candaka, an incarnation of the sage Dvaipāyana.
As if intent on testing the power and majesty of those two, [the Goddess] arose.
An unbearable divine calamity broke out among the subjects. In the month of Bhādrapada, amidst the circles of fields covered with autumn rice ready for harvest, a great mass of snow fell all at once.

In that [time], which was like the laughter of the Destroyer (Kāla) intent upon the destruction of the universe, the rice stalks sank down along with the life-hopes of the people. Then, the land became crowded with the multitudes of the deceased, whose people were emaciated by hunger.

The terrible famine-calamity was like a rampart surrounding hell. Tormented by hunger and intent only on filling their bellies, all the people forgot their affection for their wives, their love for their sons, and their devotion to their fathers.
[17] Hunger and exhaustion cause one to forget shame, pride, and noble lineage; the world, smitten by the egoism of eating and glanced upon by the side-long looks of Fortune, [acts thus].
A father abandoned his son— who was emaciated, whose life-breath had reached his throat, and who was imploring him—
or a son abandoned his father, and each provided nourishment for himself alone.
[This occurred] regarding their own loathsome bodies, which were reduced to mere sinews and bones, yet possessed by those who maintain the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
A battle broke out among those seeking food, like that of hungry ghosts (preta) for a corpse.
Harsh in speech, emaciated by hunger, and terrible, he cast his eyes in every direction;
alone, he sought to nourish himself with the living beings of the world.

In that terrible and great danger, which was exceedingly difficult for living beings to endure, the world-protector’s heart was seen to be moistened with compassion. Having dismissed his attendants, he [entered] with [a hand] resplendent with jewels and medicinal herbs.
By his very sight, he severed the exhaustion of misfortune for the destitute.
Together with his wife, he sustained living beings day and night by providing them with food purchased from his own treasuries and the accumulated stores of his ministers.

In forests, cremation grounds, on streets, and in dwellings, that king— emaciated by hunger— spared no one. Then, seeing the earth with its food exhausted and its wealth entirely depleted, he [reflected].
One night, being thus distressed, he spoke to the queen:
"O Queen, surely due to some transgression of ours, such a calamity has befallen innocent people— a disaster that is certainly difficult to overcome."
"Fie on me, the unfortunate one, before whom this world, afflicted by grief,
perishes— though he is worthy of compassion— he sees the earth without refuge.
These subjects are without protection, abandoned by their kinsmen, and left to one another."

If there is fear for one who does not protect [the world], what is the use of my life? In some way or another, I have diligently passed all these days so that this world has survived entirely and no one has perished.
Her splendor has passed away, oppressed by the tyranny of time;
today the earth has become destitute and stripped of its dignity.
Therefore, she is submerged on all sides in this dreadful ocean of calamity.
What means, then, is capable of uplifting these subjects?
For this world is without light, its sun seized by a dark storm;
it exists as if entirely surrounded by the hordes of the Night of Time.
With their exits blocked by mountains difficult to traverse due to masses of snow,
people are rendered helpless like birds dwelling in nests within closed doors.
Even those beings who are brave, wise, and learned [fall prey to this].
Behold how, through the tyranny of Time, their inherent fitness has been destroyed!

What quarters of the earth are not covered by clusters of golden flower-buds? What region on the surface of the earth is not adorned and made fit for habitation by those worthy ones who rain down the nectar of goodness?
What paths are not filled with those praised for their long-standing and beautiful conduct? Yet here they dwell, their virtues concealed, having been deluded by Time.
Therefore, having abandoned all means [of protection], I offer my body as an oblation into the fire;
for I am unable to witness such a destruction of my subjects. Blessed are those rulers of the earth who sleep peacefully at night.
Seeing his citizens all around him as happy as if they were his own sons,
the lord of the earth, overcome with compassion, said this; then, covering his face with his garment and falling upon his bed, he wept silently.
Then the queen, watching him with lamps steady in the wind as if they were craning their necks out of curiosity, spoke to the lord of the earth:
"O King, what is this perversion of judgment caused by the misdeeds of your subjects?"
By which you desire to act as another would do, according to your own whim.

(KRT_2_0045cd) If you lack the power to sever sufferings that are impossible to overcome, then what is the mark of greatness for the greatness of great men, O Protector of the Earth? (KRT_2_0046ab–cd)

Who is Śakra? Who is the Creator? And who is that wretched Yama, capable of violating the commands of kings devoted to truth? Devotion to the husband is the vow of women; non-betrayal is the vow of ministers.
The protection of the subjects is the sole duty of kings; this is their vow. Arise, O foremost of those who observe vows! Where else could my word be set aside?

"O Protector of Subjects, for you there is no fear of hunger among your subjects. When she had spoken thus with vehemence, he meditated upon the deities; [he saw that] in every house, life was departing, covered by flocks of pigeons.
Seeing this in the morning, the king desisted from his attempt at suicide;
and the subjects sustained their lives by means of the pigeons that arrived every day.
Surely, that virtuous woman must have created some other extraordinary thing.

The pigeons did not become the life-sustenance for the people; for it is impossible anywhere to stain the practice of dharma through violence on the part of those who possess such genuine compassion for living beings.
The sky gradually became stainless along with the queen’s religious rites;
famine, together with the king’s grief, came to rest.
She established a magnificent agrahāra for the twice-born, abounding in prosperity and wealth.

Free from blemish, how many dawns did Satī endure while her husband was afflicted by consumption? When her husband had been stilled by the thirty-six Vaiṣṇava rites, she abandoned the fever born of separation,
casting it into the flames of a fire whose petals were like lotuses.

The place where she of pure conduct followed after her deceased husband is even today called by people the "Forest Nourished by Her Speech. Since that virtuous woman had thus rescued her husband there through her beautiful conduct, [the forest was named].
Even today, it is still consumed by caravans of the destitute who have come from various paths.
Having reflected with certainty that "who has the power to create anything superior to these two?", the Creator, suffering from a loss of appetite, did not produce any offspring for them.

The Creator exerts his utmost effort for those who examine him through the production of the sugarcane’s fruit; therefore, what could arise from it that would surpass the capacity to provide the abundant essence of nectar? Yet, due to its own misconduct, the kingdom has had the sun lost amidst a long and grievous storm of misfortune.
Some say that, having learned this from the foremost of the queens, she performed [the funeral rites] for his body.
Thereafter, King Vijaya, born of another lineage, ruled for eight years;
he established the deity Vijayeśvara, which was surrounded by a city.
The son of that lord of the great earth, Jayendra, was the king; with arms reaching to his knees and vast renown, he then enjoyed the earth,
which was radiant with the fluttering silken garment of his unswerving fame.
For his pillar-like arm bore the statue of the Goddess of Victory. That king had a minister named Saṃdhimati, the best among the wise, adorned with devotion to the Bhava of wondrous deeds.
"There is no means whatsoever in this cycle of existence capable of restraining the unsteady ears of these intoxicated elephants that are kings. Having said this,
he was suspected by the jesters as being possessed of an exceedingly marvelous intellect.
The king harbored hatred toward that minister; thus, [the pair of verses:
"His entry being forbidden, he was then filled with anger at that causeless [act];
having been stripped of all his possessions, he was reduced to poverty for as long as he lived. (KRT 2.0067cd–0068)
The king’s officers did not provide even a word of news to refresh him, who was being withered by the summer heat of his sovereign’s enmity;
for as long as the deep-sounding mountain [the king] held its speech, those standing before it remained silent.
To those who merely repeated what had been said, he was clearly like an echo.
Yet he was not distressed by his poverty or by his opposition to the king; rather, he rejoiced in having attained service to Hara, which was free from all obstacles.
Then, due to the greatness of the future object, the fame that "the kingdom will belong to Saṃdhimati" spread through every house,
even though it had not been heard [before].
Having heard from trustworthy persons that "speech does not proceed unless prompted," the king [reflected].
Then, seized by fear, he cast him into a prison cell. There,
his feet were tormented by cruel shackles as he withered away.

The tenth year of the king's allotted lifespan was completed. Childless, that protector of the earth, facing death, prepared for cremation due to the affliction arising from disease and his own anxiety.
Constantly burning with the fire of enmity,
he felt that there was no way to escape death except by taking his own life;
for the ignorant employ whatever means they can to conceal an inevitable destiny.

That very door, opened by destiny, should be known as such. When a man rolls about in a heap of burning coals, his light flickering slightly, the Creator— desiring to bestow upon that spark of fire an incomparable power— is forcibly creating for him, as he stands nearby wishing to extinguish it, the delusion of a water-jar in a vessel filled with abundant ghee that is melting from the heat.
Then, by the king's command, cruel executioners impaled Sandhimat on a stake at night and put him to death.
When the news of his being impaled on the stake was heard, the king was struck with great apprehension.

First there was the departure of one broken by disease, and afterwards, indeed, the end of life. When thirty-seven years had passed in this lineage-less reign, the earth remained for some days with its protector of the land at peace.
Then, having perceived that the preceptor named Īśāna had been thus slain by Saṃdhimati, even the heart of that self-controlled master became helpless,
like a *śirīṣa* flower in this world, which is easily crushed for those who possess wisdom.
"Alas, only that single stalk of compassion remains, like a solitary stem.
He reached the ground of the cremation ground, as if for a withering, helpless man,
in order to perform for that humble youth the funeral rites appropriate to himself.
And he saw that [corpse], reduced to mere bones, being dragged by force by jackals;
it was rendered motionless by the fragments of bone still bound to the base of the stake,
while the openings of its skull were filled with wind escaping from within.

With sounds that seemed to mourn his such a state, he cried out, "Alas, my child! Today you have come to see me in this condition! And as he spoke thus, the skeleton was then pulled by him from within the interior of the stake.
With his feet encircled by his hair, which was matted and grey with dust, he led Kaṅkala away, warding off the barking dogs and wolves; then,
he prepared to perform for him the hospitality that was his due.
On his forehead, he read this verse inscribed by the Creator:
“Poverty for as long as one lives, ten years of imprisonment,
death upon the point of a spear, and then there shall be a kingdom again.”
The meaning of the first three quarters of the verse was clear to him, like that of a yogin;
yet, filled with curiosity regarding the realization of the meaning of the fourth quarter which remained to be seen, he became agitated and wondered: "How will this come to pass? (KRT 2.0091–2.0092).
And he spoke, reflecting for a long time upon the inconceivable power of destiny (*vidhi*):

"Bound by their dependence on the interplay of various past actions (*karma*), all beings are intent on exerting effort to uproot the stubbornness of their own resolutions. Yet, even therein, the power of destiny arises in a wondrous and most marvelous way; through its majesty, the accomplishment of diverse arrangements proceeds without obstruction."
In the city of Maṇipūra, Vidhi— the treasure-house of all wonders— restored Pārtha to life by the power of the serpent-maiden; likewise,
he revived Parīkṣit in his mother’s womb after he had been consumed by the weapon of Droṇa’s son.
Through the greatness of Kṛṣṇa, the Creator alone is capable of reviving those who have failed in their duties;
for who else but Fate has the power to restore to life Kaca, who was reduced to ashes by the Daityas, or the Nāgas, who were devoured by Tārkṣya?
Having spoken thus, intent on seeing the fulfillment of the future purpose, he took up residence right there and protected that skeleton. Then,
at midnight, remaining sleepless with such wondrous thoughts, he remained as before.
Once, the Lord, accompanied by his host, was perfumed with incense;
he heard a gurgling sound from the fierce resonance of the *ḍamaru* drums, produced by the clashing of masses of bells struck by the forceful blows of his staff.
[20] Having dispelled the mass of darkness,
he then beheld those yoginīs in the forest of the cemetery, situated within a halo of radiant light.
Observing their agitation and seeing Kaṅkāla cast aside, Īśāna, sword in hand, went toward that cremation ground in alarm. Then, concealed by a tree, he saw [him] lying within a ritual circle.
The hosts of yoginīs,

their desire for excellent sexual union inflamed, searched for that skeleton— its every limb being joined together— and having found it, they carried it away, for they were goddesses of wine who longed for the company of heroes.
Then, having set aside each of their own limbs one by one for a moment,
they brought from somewhere the male mark and fashioned him with all his limbs complete.
Then the city-of-eight (the subtle body), wandering and not yet occupying a physical form, [entered].
Having drawn him there by means of yoga, the mistresses of yoga placed him within the womb of their minds.
Then, like one who has awakened from sleep, having been anointed with divine unguents,
that leader of the circle was enjoyed by them according to his desire.
As the night was waning, Īśāna, alarmed by the sound of the goddesses crying out as they were being dismembered,
became apprehensive; yet that steadfast one, roaring for their protection, arrived at that very spot.
And that circle of the Yogīśvarīs quickly vanished from sight.
Then their voices were heard: "O Lord, let there be no fear for you;
there is no loss of our limbs, and since he has been chosen by us, there is no deception."
