By my boon, having been endowed with a divine body, he shall be possessed of great skill in joining [limbs];
and because of his nobility, he shall become renowned on earth as Āryarāja. Then, wearing celestial garments, garlands, and adorned with divine ornaments—
Bowing low, the wise one, having regained his former memory, paid homage to his guru.
Even Īśāna, embracing him—who was difficult to obtain even in dreams—ascended to that state;
who indeed is able to describe it?
As they meditated together upon the essence-less and manifold nature of saṃsāra, a conversation between them proceeded, clarified by their discernment. Then,
having learned this news from somewhere, the inhabitants of the city...
Together with the children and the elderly, and accompanied by his ministers, he went to that very spot.

Then, because the appearance did not correspond to the previous description, the thought occurred to him, "This is not he"; yet, as he questioned everyone who was there, their words were all consistent, and thus his doubt was severed.

Though free from desire, he reluctantly consented to rule the kingdom for the sake of his subjects so that they would not suffer defeat, in accordance with the command of his guru. Having brought him, who was radiant with a divine form, to the edge of the grove, [he spoke].
The twice-born bathed him with consecration waters accompanied by musical instruments.
He did not require instruction in the conduct appropriate for a new king;
having witnessed his past deeds, they performed all the rites free from any flaw.
Clad in royal attire, he entered the city with his army— a city resplendent with the shouts of the citizens' blessings and showers of parched grain falling from the palace towers. While he,
free from passion, ascended the vast throne of kings, Kṛt 2.119ab–2.120ab.

Neither divine nor human offspring entered into decay; day after day, the forest regions— with their women in the form of the earth possessing hips and devoid of the coquettish movements of the heart— captivated his mind, but not [ordinary] women.
He was delighted as he was touched by the hands [of the ascetics], fragrant with the holy scent of contact with forest flowers and scented with camphor incense;
and he beheld the lords of beings: Vardhamāneśa, Vijayeśa, and Īśāna.

He maintained a constant discipline in his royal duties every day. Touched by breezes laden with droplets from the water used for washing the steps of Śiva’s temple, his body became motionless with joy.
When the previous worship was removed, Vijayeśvara— beautiful in his unadorned state—
was seen by him alone as he was being bathed;
the sound of the earth shaking from the agitation of the water from the bathing jars falling upon the pedestal of the *liṅga* [was heard].
Even as he lay there, his beloved became one who was hostile to the lute;
he shone amidst ascetics marked by ashes, rudrākṣa beads, and matted locks.
The assembly of that lord of the earth was like the retinue of Maheśvara;
in the performance of the rite for the consecration of a thousand Śiva-liṅgas by that sovereign,
his daily vow was never once thwarted.

When that [task] failed to be completed due to negligence, he had a stone carved; the *sahasraliṅgī* (the thousand-linga monument) fashioned by his servants is seen even today everywhere. In various ponds, he installed [the lingas] under the pretext of being lingas.

He spent his time observing, from place to place, the succession of births of his own lotus-like merits; and he adorned the rivers with numerous Śiva-liṅgas installed within the water, so that they took on the appearance of the Narmadā’s waves.
By him, great villages were bestowed according to each [deity's] emblem;
today, the enjoyment of those by the assemblies has vanished with the passage of time.
He constructed [shrines] with great palaces, great emblems, and great bulls.
Having fashioned the great earth with great tridents,
Mahāmāheśvara established Saṃdhīśvara in the Pitṛkānana grove for the purpose of joining his body; and by the name of his guru Īśāna, he established Hara as Īśeśvara.
Then, at every step, he brought Bhīmādevī and other regions to a state of great value through monasteries, statues, liṅgas, and palaces; and,
adorned with devotion, he purified them with self-manifested images and sacred fords.
That very wise man alone knew how to enjoy the Kaśmīra maṇḍala. For that king,
as he bathed in the waters of mountain torrents and engaged in the festivals of worshipping the *puṣpaliṅga*,
a month passed while he wandered through the forest lands during the flowering season.
And that exceedingly delightful Kaśmīra summer, difficult to find even in the celestial realms,
attained its purpose at the edges of the forests through the worship of the snowy peaks.
Reaching the shores of lotus ponds whose quarters were blocked by clusters of blooming lotuses, [he found fulfillment].

Accompanied by Lakṣmī, he became intent on meditating upon the one who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel. Having plunged into ponds filled with blue lotuses, which had become free of poison at the rising of Agastya, he spent the autumn season performing worship to Hara.
As he enjoyed festivals of wakefulness together with those various ascetics rich in austerity, the Māgha nights of that lord of the earth became fruitful. Thus,
the virtuous king made his attainment of the kingdom truly marvelous and successful.
He passed fifty years, less three, [in this state]. While he was devoted to tranquility and neglected the affairs of state, at that time the subjects fell into dissatisfaction.
The king searched for someone who was heard of as being fit for the kingdom—
a prince, desirous of victory, and illustrious, born in the lineage of Yudhiṣṭhira. Out of a desire to conquer the lord of Kaśmīra, he protected one named Gopāditya.
At that time, the lord of the Gandhāras, while residing there without having yet attained universal sovereignty, obtained in due course a son from Yudhiṣṭhira’s great-grandson—
Meghavāhana, who was unfailing and endowed with divine marks.

There, by his father’s command, he went to the kingdom of the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa— who was born of a lineage devoted to Viṣṇu— to attend a maiden’s svayaṃvara. There, in the presence of the king, that umbrella of Varuṇa [stood] with its shade.
The princess Amṛtaprabhā sent him a magnificent garland;
by that sign, people perceived his approaching prosperity,
just as one perceives the coming rain from the wind blowing from behind a cloud.

For this heat-shield, brought by King Naraka from Varuṇa, produced shade only for one who was not a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). When he had reached his father’s presence, attended by his wife and Fortune (*lakṣmī*), [the king]— Kṛt 2.150ab: For this heat-shield, brought by King Naraka from Varuṇa, Kṛt 2.150cd: produced shade only for one who was not a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
Kṛt 2.151ab: When he had reached his father’s presence, attended by his wife and Fortune (*lakṣmī*)...
The ministers invited him with words appropriate to his lineage.
Then the noble king, perceiving that his own kingdom was shattered by internal dissension, did not accept it; though capable, he remained intent on renouncing it.
And he thought: "The Creator of beings is well-pleased with my truth;
he is now intent on removing the long-standing obstacles to my success.
Yet, when much remains to be accomplished, one might resort to indolence out of weariness."

"By good fortune, like a traveler in the rainy season, I have not been overcome by delusion. By good fortune, I have avoided the shame of being forcibly expelled when Lakṣmī herself, like a disaffected courtesan, abandoned me at her own time."
[22] Like an actor on this stage of kingship, as I have long been performing,
though the bitterness of enmity has been fully brought to its conclusion, by good fortune the spectators have not departed.

"By good fortune, I have always loudly proclaimed my aversion to prosperity; thus, at the moment of renunciation, I am not afraid, like a braggart on the battlefield. Thinking thus within himself, the king turned his face toward the total renunciation of everything.

Like a poor man, he was delighted while indulging in his royal fantasies. On another day, having assembled all the subjects within the assembly hall, he returned to them the kingdom— which he had protected like a trust— just as one would return a deposit.
Having cast it away at his own will, no one was able to persuade him to take it back, even with great effort, just as one cannot force a serpent-king to accept its slough. Then,
taking up a stone image of the deity, he set out facing north.

Wearing washed garments and without a turban, the Lord of Creatures proceeded on foot alone. As the silent Lord went along, his gaze fixed upon his feet, the citizens followed the path behind him, shedding tears in silence.
Having traversed a distance of two leagues, he sat beneath a tree and, consoling them with gentle words, sent each person back home with tears in their eyes.
Having delayed on the paths at the foot of the mountains, he left his small retinue behind as he traveled upward; thus, as he proceeded, he gradually became visible from afar.
Advancing from his own place, filling the dense forests and moving on high like a cloud emerging from the ocean followed by only a few drops of water,
he proceeded. Having completely barred the path within the forest near the village, and having both consoled and dismissed the people with words faltering with tears due to the onset of grief,

he entered the woods— a forest where the cave-dwellings were illuminated by the luster of the crest-jewels of rows of Siddhas and travelers sleeping there, while the rustling wind was hushed by the bark of the trees.

Then, at the end of the day, he made his dwelling beneath a tree on the shore of a forest lake; there, he prepared a high couch from pure leaves, filled with water drawn from the hollows of leaf-bowls and jars. The ground was variegated by shadows cast by white sunshades resting on their peaks, while the earth was carpeted with lush meadows and the floors of blooming, spotless jasmine trees where groups of sleeping women from the cowherd community lay nestled together.

The nearby mountains, with their waterfalls mingled with the humming of bees guarding the forest paths, brought sleep to his weary eyes as they came within his range of vision. As he prepared to depart, he perceived that the night was slipping away through the cries of wild cranes at every step, which vied with the sound of the falling water, and through the hooting of owls.

On another day, having duly worshipped the morning twilight, the protector of the earth, his sleep dispelled, reached the abode of the Lord of Beings (Śiva) at Nandīśa— a place where the waters of the nearby lotus-lake were familiar to him— situated on the shore of the lake. While he stood there in the field of Nandi, facing the Teacher of the Three Worlds, there arose of its own accord that which brings about the attainment of one's desired goal.

Smiling with ashes, his matted locks well-bound and adorned with a sacred thread and marked by *rudrākṣa* beads, he was gazed upon with longing by aged sages. Wandering about, having generated great merit through the vows bestowed by Śrīkaṇṭha, he went from one hermitage to another for the sake of alms; while the female ascetics were busily preparing to give him food, the trees filled his begging bowl with rows of pure fruits and flowers. Thus, even while engaged in the yoga of dispassion, he remained honored, never suffering the humiliation of being refused by others.

Thus ends the second book in the *Rājatarangiṇī*, the composition of Kalhaṇa, son of the illustrious Kaśmīrian minister and lord Caṇṇaka. In this second [book], consisting of two hundred years less eight, six kings of renowned virtues have been described.
The Third Wave.

"Shall I eat his garment, which is fit for the tips of my breasts, from the hollow of his jar? Is collyrium to be accepted by my eyes instead of the fire blazing on his forehead? Thus speaking even as he was being forbidden to join his two halves of the body, may Hara—intent on following his beloved's lead—protect you.
Then they brought Meghavāhana forth, who was receiving great and radiant praise.
Having gone to the region of Gāndhāra, the subjects were governed by his ministers;
for that king who was beloved by his people, the subsequent pleasing of the world was perceived by the people as being like the washing away of bleached linen.

Moreover, that noble-minded one surpassed even the Bodhisattvas who are compassionate toward sentient beings by means of his conduct and exalted deeds. Those authorized ones who held his command were indeed entitled to the consecration itself.
Causing the drums of the boundary against all enemies of the Dharma to resound on every side,
when that righteous king had prohibited the slaughter of living beings within his realm,
the butchers and others were provided with a sinless livelihood from his own treasury.
In the kingdom of that lord who was an enemy of Māra like the Jina,
during the sacrifice, the sacrificial animal consisted of clarified butter and the sacrificial victim consisted of flour;
he established a royal grant named Meghavana.

Then, for the enjoyment of the local monks, Vallabhāsyāmṛtaprabhā had the Megha monastery built by Mayuṣṭagrāmakṛt— the foremost among those who perform meritorious deeds— constructed as a lofty vihāra named Amṛtabhavana.
From a certain region, the father’s elder brother of that [queen] arrived;
he was called Lostonpāstu in her own language, and he acted as a benefactor.
In the Naḍavana forest, he made [a dwelling] for the king’s wife, whose name was Yūkadevī.
Striving in rivalry with her co-wife, she built a monastery of wondrous form;
in one half of it she placed the monks and their rules of training,
while in the other half she placed those censured by householders— her wife, sons, cattle, and female slaves.
Then the queen Indradevī constructed a monastery named Indradravya with four halls, while the king’s other beloved wife built a stūpa;
the others likewise erected structures after their own names, headed by Svādanāsammā.
Many monasteries were built for him by queens.
Although this king arose in recent times,
his period of sovereignty became extraordinary due to accounts that surpassed the legends of ancient kings.
While wandering outside the monastery, he heard from afar the sound of wailing uttered by those terrified of the king: "This is a thief!
A robber! When he was asked in anger, "Who is here? Let the thief be bound!", [he replied: KRT_3_0017ab.

The sound of lamentation was stilled, and no thief was to be seen. After he had departed, two or three days later, two or three women of divine splendor appeared before him, seeking protection from fear.
Having heard those desired words, they were addressed by that compassionate one who had restrained his horse; with their hands joined in añjali at their parted hair, they spoke these words:
"O Lord, by your divine power, you sustain the world."
O treasury of compassion, who could ever have fear of another?
At that time, while you sustained the world through your divine power,
those seeking their own ends falsely feared the sudden fall of a hailstone.
O Lord, the elephants, their minds undisturbed by the protection afforded by the groves of ripened śāli rice, have been reduced to the state of mere ground by the fury of your wrath.
When the King, hearing your husbands’ piteous cries of "Thief! Thief!",
spoke in anger,
saying, "Let them be bound," they fell at that very moment, ensnared by your mere command.
"Let favor be shown to them now out of compassion for us.
[Cakkalakam] Having heard that, the king, his face bright with grace, spoke with a smile: "Let all those elephants be released from their bonds."
Then, by the command of that king, the elephants, their bonds loosened, quickly departed with their attendants after bowing at his feet. Then,
in order to cause the kings to accept the command for the cessation of violence—

He set forth for the conquest of the quarters, practicing the Dharma without artifice. His valor was praiseworthy as he surveyed the people without fear; even the common folk longed for his endeavor toward victory.

Having brought the kings— who had been consecrated in non-violence and other virtues— under his power by means of his majesty, he, free from blemish, reached the vicinity of the Lord of the Waters (the ocean). There, his soldiers rested comfortably in the shade of palm groves.
For a moment, he reflected within himself on the means for crossing over to another island.
Then, from the edge of the coastal forest, the sound of a piteous cry was heard by him:
"Even in the kingdom of Meghavāhana, I am being slain!"
Then, as if pierced within by a red-hot iron spike, he quickly went to that land accompanied by his moving parasol. There,
in front of a temple of Caṇḍikā, he saw someone.

As a man was being struck down face-down by the leader of the Śabaras, the king rebuked him, saying, "Shame on you, ignorant of the Self! Fie upon this evil deed of yours! Terrified, the Śabara addressed the king in this manner:
"O King, this son of mine is a child on the verge of death, afflicted by disease. The gods have declared that this act will bring about even a small portion of his welfare;
otherwise, by the withholding of the offering, he will perish immediately."
Know that this entire circle of kinsmen is the very life of the living.
O King, you protect this helpless child found in the depths of the forest;
how can you neglect him, who is the refuge of many people?
Then that Great-Souled One, rendered helpless by the glances of the one about to be slain and distressed by those words of the Śabara, replied:
"O Kirāta, do not be afraid; you are being protected by me yourself."
This son of yours has many kinsmen, yet he is without kin even while being bound.
Here I offer my own body as a sacrifice to Caṇḍikā;
strike me without hesitation, so that these two people may live.
Astonished by the loftiness of the mind of that wondrous Great Being, with his hair standing on end, the Śabara then addressed him:
"O Lord of the Earth, under the guise of your excessive compassion..."
Some form of mental perversion takes root in the heart—
that which must be protected even at the cost of the life-force of the three worlds as if with mere playfulness. How can you disregard this body, so fortunate in its enjoyment of the earth?

Out of a thirst for their own lives, O kings, they do not protect their pride, nor their fame, nor their wealth, nor their wives, nor their kinsmen, nor their dharma, nor their sons. Therefore, be gracious, O Lord of Subjects; do not commit the act of killing this man.
"May this child and these subjects live while you live. Then that king, wishing to offer himself up and as if honoring Cāmuṇḍā with the grand display of the light from his teeth, spoke:
O forest-dwellers, who are you that you do not savor the nectar of virtuous conduct? Like those dwelling in a desert, you do not know the joy of bathing in the Ganges.
By exchanging this body, which is certain to perish, for imperishable fame—*Kṛtyakalpataru* 3.0047ab–cd. *Kṛtyakalpataru* 3.0048ab.

O fool, this persistent obsession of yours is intended to erase my desire. Do not say anything more, unless you have compassion for striking me; is my own sword not capable of accomplishing what has been set forth?

Having spoken thus, he himself prepared to offer up his body; for the purpose of severing his own head, he drew a weapon from its scabbard. Then, as he was about to strike, [the Sage covered] his head with celestial flowers.
And his hand became obstructed by someone possessing a divine form. Then,
being in such a state, he saw before him a certain being of celestial appearance.

He did not look upon Caṇḍikā, nor the one to be executed, nor the Kirāta, nor the boy. Then that divine being said to him: "O Moon of the Middle World, O Treasure of Compassion, know me, Varuṇa, who have been brought under your power by your virtue."
This very parasol that attends you today was taken away from my city long ago by Mahābala, the son of Bhauma, who was once your father-in-law; he took it from that ancient ornament of Rasātala,
which possessed such great majesty.
Life-threatening calamities beset our citizens at every step. O Compassionate One, desiring to obtain this [kingdom] and to test your magnanimity, I have fashioned such a situation as this.
That son of Vasu’s lineage, who at your command brought forth creatures that were destined for death,
now seems to perform penance for that sin through the burden of supporting the earth—
a task suited to one who inspires both fear and longing.
In his remaining body, darkness and light were like a mass of gems on the hoods of a serpent vomiting poison;
they were like smoke and flame-sprouts on a fire whose radiance had pervaded the quarters of space.
In that circle of radiant beings whose exhaustion was dispelled,

it was a marvel to behold how two individuals— one like the heat of summer and the other like the onset of the rainy season— were born into a single great family, just as the heat and the rain appear together on a day when the clouds have cleared.
[There was] that Lord, the destroyer of the three types of enemies, who is non-violent; [regarding him], there is a *cakkalaka* verse.
Then the submissive Emperor, with palms joined in reverence, performed worship with a hymn and an umbrella for the Lord of Sea Creatures as he spoke thus.
As Varuṇa was accepting it with affectionate warmth,
the Mountain,
foremost among the virtuous, said to him: "The wish-fulfilling trees and the holy ones do not deserve to be placed on an equal footing."
Since some [gifts] bestowed upon those who seek them first bear fruit, while others ripen by themselves;
how could our parasol have been supported [by you],
had you not sought it for the sake of aiding the distressed through the commodity of your merit?
A generous person should bestow full favor upon those worthy of sharing;
even a tree, nourishing with its shade, gives forth its fruits as well.
Thus, impelled by the noble practice of such sharing as prescribed—
"O Blessed One, this person requests a certain supreme boon:
by your grace, this entire earth has been brought under my control;

The blessed Varuṇa, the warder-off of heat, vanished from sight. On the following day, parting the waters with his forces, which were smiling with wonder, he crossed the ocean whose turbulence had been paralyzed by his power.

Out of affection, Vibhīṣaṇa, the sovereign of Laṅkā, attended upon him. That meeting between the king of men and the king of rākṣasas was splendid, filled with the excitement of their first conversation as heard from the bards.
Then the Lord of the Rākṣasas, having led him to Laṅkā, the ornament of the earth,
attended upon him with splendors easily attainable by the immortals. At that time, the name "Rākṣasa" (eaters of raw flesh) of the demons became truly significant.
Then, even as he was being seized, that [tree] attained the status of a conventional term for him;
the Lord of the Rākṣasas bestowed upon him trees whose branches were graced by the heads of demons, which served as substitutes for his own head and indicated his firm submission.
Those who came from across the ocean and even now rule in Kaśmīra—
known as the Pāradhvajas— they march at the head of expeditions.
Thus, he prohibited the slaughter of living beings among the Rākṣasa clans.
The king, having accomplished his purpose, returned toward his own realm.
From that time forward, the command of that sovereign monarch was [established] over the whole earth.
Consisting of abstention from violence, it could not be transgressed by anyone:
neither by base creatures such as snakes in the waters, nor by lions and the like in the forest, nor by hawks and other birds in the sky; for in his kingdom, living beings were never slain.
Then, as time passed, a certain brahmin, overwhelmed with grief,
arrived at the king’s gate carrying his son who was afflicted by disease, and cried out:

The son of one whose lineage is peerless is now perishing from fever.
O Protector of the Earth, if you do not protect him by means of your commitment to non-violence,

Let this decision be given by you alone, who are a weighty authority on the castes:
what difference can there be between the life of a Brahmin and that of a beast?
Even those who were established in asceticism were slain for the sake of obtaining the life-breath of a Brahmin.
"Alas, O Mother Earth! Now those protectors of the people have vanished.
While the twice-born man was speaking thus with reproach, his words harsh with grief, the king, who removes the suffering of the distressed, reflected for a long time in this manner.

"Previously, I established a covenant that living beings are not to be slain. Even for the sake of a Brahmin, how could I violate that vow? If a twice-born man were to perish today by taking me as his cause, [what would become of my promise]?"

Even there, the most extreme evil is the ruin of one's resolve. My mind— swayed by doubt and delusion, clinging to only one side, and fallen into the whirlpool of conflicting thoughts— is like a flower [caught in a torrent].

"By propitiating Durgā with the offering of my own body, it is right for me to protect the lives of both [the king and his son] in accordance with my vow. Having reflected thus for a long time, the king prepared to offer up his body.
Having said, "I shall do what is pleasing for you tomorrow," he dismissed the brahmin. Then,
on that night, Durgā restrained the king who was intent on seizing his own [son], and restored the twice-born man to his natural state.
Thus we feel ashamed as we describe the conduct of this king even in the present day— conduct that would be inconceivable among ordinary people.
Or rather, [it is] through the path of the sages, which is no different from a literary composition.
Having set out, they did not conform to the inclinations of their listeners.
When he had passed away, having enjoyed the earth for thirty-four years,
the world became entirely devoid of light, as if the sun itself had ceased to exist.
Then Śreṣṭhasena, the son of that protector of the earth, ruled the land;
whom people quickly called Pravarasena and Tujjīna.
Upon the jeweled mirror of his sword, which was held fast by the pillar of his arm, [the reflection appeared].
The beauty of the world appeared as if transfixed,
looking upward at him. Having first established the preeminent Lord (Pravareśvara) together with the circle of his mothers,
he performed various meritorious consecrations at the ancient foundation site.
He who, regarding the earth as if it were the courtyard of his own home,
gave the land of Trigarta to the preeminent lord in the midst of a village;
he who was the sovereign of kings, the master of all the fields and households upon the entire surface of the world.
That king remained free from weapons for thirty equal years.
Then he appointed his two sons, named Hiraṇya and Toramāṇa,
as the vessels of universal sovereignty and the status of crown prince, respectively, for the delight of the earth.
Having prevented the excessive and improper killing of animals,
Toramāṇa issued dināras struck in his own name.
Why has this man acted with such arrogance, as if he were a king, showing contempt for me?

Thus his elder brother, the king, being enraged, cast him into prison. While he remained there for a long time, having abandoned all sorrow, the queen named Añjanā— the daughter of the Ikṣvāku king Vajrendra— became pregnant.

With her delivery imminent, she was urged by her husband, who was overcome with shame; having entered a certain potter’s dwelling, she gave birth to a son. Like a female crow to a cuckoo chick, he was raised by the wife of the potter.
The prince, having been adopted as a son, grew up until he reached maturity;
he became known to his mother, his nurse, and his protector.
Like a hidden treasure for the serpent Ratnasūti,
the grandson of Pravarasena and son of the king was proclaimed by his maternal grandmother through her speech,
using his grandfather’s name alone.
As he grew, he could not endure the company of his fellow residents;
like a lotus among the waters, the child was one who delighted in the friendship of the radiant.
He [was surrounded] by boys of noble birth, by those who were brave, and by those who were learned in the sciences.
The people, filled with wonder, beheld him playing together with his own group of boys;
that king of exceeding noble splendor played with them like a lion cub with young deer in the forest.

He shared with others, showed favor, and brought his children under his influence; he never practiced any conduct unbecoming of a king. When lumps of clay were presented by potters for making vessels and the like, [he did not take them].
Having accepted them, he established a succession of Śiva-liṅgas. Thus,
while sporting in his wondrous conduct,
he was once observed by his maternal uncle Jayendra, who greeted him with great respect.
Being told by the children, "This is Jayendra," he looked upon him with the same lack of disdain as he did the princes, as if favoring him; for,
judging him by his steadfastness of character, he recognized him as being born of an extraordinary lineage.
Due to their resemblance, he suspected the nephew to be the brother-in-law;
with haste, driven by the essence of his desire to know the truth,
he followed him and, reaching that house out of eagerness, beheld his sister.
Seeing one another after a long time, those two brothers, filled with mutual grief,
repeatedly shed tears whose heat was doubled by their sighs.
The boy asked his nurse, "Mother, who are these two?"

"Child, this mother of yours and your maternal uncle are not to be spoken against here. Having thus instructed him— who was filled with anger toward his father's kinsman but restrained by his regard for the proper time— Jayendra then departed to attend to the remainder of his duties.
While his brother was distracted by the accidental production of a tuft of hair,
he was released from bondage by the man-eating crocodile and reached the shore;
having been distressed by his mother’s despair, he desisted from his attempt at suicide.
Then Pravarasena departed for another region out of a longing for sacred pilgrimage sites.
Having protected the earth for thirty-one years less ten months,
at that very moment Hiraṇya also passed away, leaving no progeny.

At that time, in Ujjayinī, there was a glorious universal monarch named Vikramāditya, also known as Harṣa, who held sole sovereignty under one umbrella. Fortune, with unrestrained ardor, attended upon that king of wondrous good fortune.
Having abandoned the arms of Hari and the four oceans,
he made Fortune his instrument once his virtues had flourished;
even today, those possessed of fortune and virtue stand with their necks held high.
For Hari, who was about to descend to earth for the destruction of the Mlecchas,
he first lightened the burden of his task by annihilating the Śakas.
He sought a king of noble character, renowned throughout various foreign lands and easily found.

The poet named Mātṛgupta attended upon him while he was present at all the court assemblies. Having grown experienced in various assemblies, he reflected upon and contemplated the most wonderful majesty of that profound sovereign.

This king, who is fond of the virtuous, has been attained through merits; he exists for the sake of attaining the highest excellence, following after that former ruler. In him, the wise scholars who know reality and have accumulated sacred learning were born.
Never is a respectful salutation offered to pride or to mere virtue. When manifesting her own intention through this artful means,
her intellect does not fall into a state devoid of cleverness, just like a woman of noble family.
While this man— who renders the speech of the wicked barren and distinguishes between what is right and wrong—
is being served, let our own virtues not incur the state of being rendered useless by those who,
possessing flawed knowledge, bring about the ruin of their heads through their blameworthy conduct.
The virtuous do not experience life-in-death before them. From this,
the discerning person proceeds according to their conviction.
A gift of affection from high-minded men is not lamented with heaving sighs;
for they accept it according to its merit with hearts full of appropriate appreciation.
This man, who understands the inner thoughts of all, increases their enthusiasm.

The effort expended in generating courtesy toward one who has witnessed one's hardships through service is like the sale of snow on the Himalayas by those servants who do not possess it. A minister who falsely proclaims his own virtues and is fond of quarreling is no true counselor.
This king has no servants who are untruthful in their dealings or unstable;
nor are there any among his attendants who speak indecorously to one another in jest, piercing each other's vital points,
or who cannot endure the intrusion of others and remain united.

This king does not look to the faces of those who follow his whims, who praise their own wisdom, and who are blinded by the conceit of thinking themselves omniscient. A conversation with him has resulted in a vast and noble awakening.
It cannot ever be interrupted by those of low birth or by wicked people.
Thus, for me who serves this king— who is free from all faults—
the attainment of my own goals is not far off, thanks to my merits.

This king is profound, a knower of virtues, and firm in intellect; having abandoned the fear of afflictions, he appears to me as one who should be served. And unlike other kings, he does not take wealth from us once we have been gratified.
"I am wandering upon this earth; another [worthy person] appears to me as one to be served.
Having reflected thus with firm resolve, he did not take pleasure even when standing in the midst of assemblies of virtuous men, as if that assembly were something new.

Seeing him thus displaying his virtues with gentleness, the lord of the people recognized that he was intent upon the propitiation [of the gods] in order to manifest his distinguished fitness; and he thought: "This noble-minded one cannot be merely a man of virtue."
"His profundity declares his worthiness for honor.
Having reflected thus, the king, in order to ascertain the depth of his mind,
did not fail to provide him with appropriate gains and honors for the sake of testing him.

Perceiving that the king possessed such noble intentions through his consistent conduct, the wise man served him with affection, intent on winning him over. Through the wise man’s practice of service, which increased in regularity, [the king was gradually won over].
The king did not feel agitation toward him, as if he were his own body;
neither by an excessively brief nor by an excessively long stay did the king attain clarity, but rather he attained a state of serenity like that of an autumn night.
He was not moved to agitation by the jests of the palace servants, nor by the shifting demeanors of the doorkeepers, nor by the false praises of the parasites;
like a mountain that does not take up a shadow when it encounters pleasant conversation.

As if in rivalry, he grew angry and showed contempt for his lord. He observed the glances of the king’s female slaves, shared seats with those who hated the king, and reported at the appropriate time the low conversation held before the king.
Because of his innate character, neither the king’s men nor his own people who censured the king— those who lived by backbiting— were able to find fault with this lord.
Though they spoke with zeal regarding his steadfastness, it was of no avail for the lord day after day.

He did not allow his enthusiasm to falter when served by those unable to endure his zeal. Even when speaking of the excellence of others in the course of conversation, he remained free from attachment; thus, illuminating his own learning, he became beloved by the hearts of the assembly.
Thus, serving him with the most strenuous effort,
Mātṛgupta passed the six seasons without despondency.
Then, [the king saw] him, whose entire body was emaciated, grey, and clad in worn-out garments.
Once, having gone out abroad, the king saw him and reflected:
"This man is a foreigner, without refuge, virtuous yet abandoned by kinsmen;
wishing to test his fortitude, I have caused him great hardship."
"What is its support? What is its food? Or what are its garments? Alas, such things were not considered by me while I was deluded by power.
Even now, I have not been joined with beauty as if by the springtime.
This tree of a person withers from cold, wind, and heat;
for him who is thus sick and despondent, there is medicine and consolation.
Who could provide the end of fatigue to one who is weary, or prosperity to one who lacks it?
I would not have given him the *cintāmaṇi* jewel, nor would I have served him with nectar,
since he is now being tested by me to such an extent through my own delusion.
"By what kind of service, then, might I attain freedom from debt for his virtues and for the exhaustion of my intense devotion?"—
while the king was thus reflecting regarding that servant, [the following occurred].
No hospitality worthy of his favor was at all manifest.
Then the onset of winter began with wintry breezes carrying flecks of spreading mist, as if burning his very limbs.
Under the guise of continuous darkness,
the quarters of the sky, overcome by intense cold, appeared as if shrouded in blue veils.
Due to the affliction of the cold, the sun and the fire of the earth longed for the heat of a forest conflagration.

The days seemed to hasten toward the ocean and grew short. Then, once in a palace illuminated by lamps and graced by a shimmering, radiant lamp-stand, the king happened by chance to awaken at midnight.
In his palace, he saw lamps slightly shaken by the winter winds that were harsh with loud whistling sounds entering from the front; then,
wishing to command his servants to relight them, he spoke thus.
"Who is clearly standing on guard outside among the watchmen?"—
while everyone was sleeping soundly within the outer courtyard, he heard these words from outside: "O King, here I am, Mātṛgupta."

Then, having been granted permission by the king himself with the words "Enter," he entered that house, which was delightful due to the presence of Lakṣmī, without being questioned by others. Being told, "Light the lamps," he did so with skillful steps.
As he was about to go outside, the king said, "Stay for a moment.
With his cold trembling doubled by fear,
he sat down not too far from the lord, reflecting, "What indeed will he say?"

Then the king asked him, "How much of the night remains? He replied, "O King, one and a half watches of the night still remain. Thereupon the monarch said to him, "How can you know the time of night so precisely?"
"How was it that you did not fall asleep during the night?
Having composed this verse in an instant, he addressed him,
intent on abandoning both hope and dejection through the disclosure of his condition.

For me, who am rubbed by the cold like a bean or a *śimbi* seed, sinking in the ocean of anxiety; whose fire is extinguished as I blow upon my parched lips; and whose throat is emaciated by hunger—sleep has gone far away, abandoning me like a beloved woman slighted, and the night does not diminish, like wealth bestowed upon a worthy recipient.
Having heard this, the protector of the earth [honored] his exertion with words of praise.

Having greeted that lord of poets, he dismissed him to his former place. And he thought: "Shame on me, who, while listening to these words of one whose mind was distressed by worldly qualities and scorched by suffering, have remained thus even now!"
"Perceiving my empty words of praise as if they were mere sophistry,
this man, whose heart remains unknown to me, surely dwells in sorrow outside.
Though I have long reflected with effort upon a fitting mark of respect for him..."
"Nothing worthy of being given appears to me even now. "Or rather, by this very hymn of his, I am reminded now how the lovely land of Kaśmīra exists, devoid of a king."
"Because he is a worthy recipient, this earth is therefore being bestowed upon him by me,
disregarding even great kings who are intent on making requests.
Having thus resolved, the king, during that very night, acted with skill.
He secretly dispatched messengers to the subjects of Kashmir and commanded them:
"Whoever among you shows me this edict,
let that man named Mātṛgupta be consecrated in the kingdom without hesitation."
Then, after the messengers had departed and he had caused his own edict to be written,
the lord of the earth, having accomplished his purpose, passed the remainder of that night.

But Mātṛgupta, reflecting that even a conversation with the king was fruitless, became like one who had cast off his burden through having grasped despair; and he meditated within himself: "That which was to be done has been done; today all doubt is stilled."
"Now, abandoned by the demoness of hope, I shall live in happiness.

Those who feed on air are proclaimed to be "serpents" (*sarīsṛpa*); those who possess coils are called "elephants" because they ward off singing bees with their broad ears; and that tree which undergoes transformation through the heat generated within is called a "shami" by the world—thus, everything has been turned upside down by this man who prattles on without restraint. Or rather, for one possessed of such knowledge, there is no place whatsoever that is inaccessible.
By him, who is beloved by Lakṣmī, the homes of his friends have been made prosperous.
What fault can there be in this generous and stainless lord of the earth? It is my own demerit that is blameworthy, which acts as an obstacle to my welfare.

If the ocean, its waves blazing with jewels, were to scatter them as it was driven by the winds toward its obstructed shore, that would indeed be a fault resulting from the reversal of fortune for the seeker; yet it would not be a fault of the giver’s generosity. For those who covet easily obtained fruits, it is better to live off the king.

But those [deeds] do not bear fruit through the intense afflictions of their owners. Those who indeed remain at the feet of Paśupati quickly obtain nothing other than ashes. But for those who, by attaining the brilliantly shining gold of his bull, have no ill fortune, what days are not auspicious?
Even upon reflection, I do not perceive any fault of my own by which this king, though being served, has become detached. Or rather, he may have attained his proximity while disregarded by another.
Who would seek a connection with the fruit [of their actions] from a Lord who merely follows what has already occurred?

The ocean clearly transforms into precious pearls those countless water droplets that were constantly tumbling within it; having received them as they come with its circling waves, it takes hold of them. Generally, even one who is insignificant is honored by masters when he arrives having been shown respect by another.
Reflecting thus, he became indifferent toward that which was worthy of service; for the intellect of even one who knows the truth becomes perverted when he is distressed.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, the king remained seated in his place.
"Let Mātṛgupta be summoned," he commanded the doorkeeper. Then, as many porters ran forward to enter, he approached the presence of the lord of the earth like one who has abandoned all hope.
To him who had offered his salutation, the king, after only a moment, by a sign of his brow, gave a letter to the bearer of letters;
and he himself said to him: "My dear friend, do you know Kaśmīra?"
"Go there and present this edict to the officials.
He who reads this letter on the road shall be cursed by my body. This agreement must never be forgotten; it must be kept in mind with great care."

Not understanding the king’s intention and fearing it was a mere affliction, he perceived that command as a flame of fire rather than the luster of a sprout of jewels. When Mātṛgupta had departed, saying "As you have commanded, so shall it be," [the king remained].

Free from pride, the king remained as before, conversing with those who had arrived. Then, seeing Mātṛgupta departing—emaciated, unaccustomed to hardship, without provisions for the journey, and without kinsmen—the people censured the king thus: KRT_3_0210cd KRT_3_0211ab KRT_3_0211cd
"Alas, how arbitrary is this conduct of the lord of men! He who appoints an Arhat to a task fit only for an ordinary person—
day and night serving one who harbors evil intentions and is burdened by afflictions."
The ignorant king surely perceived him as one who deserves affliction;
for whatever means a servant employs when serving his master,
one who lacks insight considers that very means to be what is appropriate for him.
Seeking happiness through the pacification of the fear of the serpent-king, Śeṣa, on the contrary, abandoned his service to the enemy of the Asuras after making his body a couch for him;
for by him, having attained the capacity to endure affliction, the endless bearing of the earth's burden was undertaken with ease.

Among those who have acquired these virtues, he, being himself virtuous, perceived that this man possessed superior qualities; thus, with firm conviction, he took refuge in him. Who else, other than one who knows what lies immediately beyond, could demonstrate such superior virtues?
"Who indeed would not perform such worship for this virtuous one?

Even though he delights in various brilliant objects, that peacock—who feels affection even for Indra’s weapon (the rainbow)—what kindness would he not do for me upon seeing my plumage here? Thus thinking, who else but the cloud—leaving aside that peacock who dances when the rows of his feathers are displayed and does not release anything other than rain—is there of such empty intent?
As Mātṛgupta proceeded along his path, free from all dejection,
not the slightest doubt arose in his mind regarding the greatness of his destined future,
due to the auspicious omens that manifested themselves as if competing with one another to proclaim his good fortune.
Having been granted a firm support, as it were, he felt no fatigue.
On the road, he saw a wagtail perched on the tip of the serpent’s hood;
and in a dream, he saw himself ascending a palace and leaping across the ocean.
And the knower of the sciences reflected: "By these auspicious omens, the command of the king will surely bring me good fortune.
Even if my reward in Kashmir were to be very small, it would still be beneficial."
What could that place not surpass by virtue of its priceless greatness? Its paths were easy to traverse, its houses had beloved guests, and for him as he walked, there was hospitality at every step.

Having thus traversed the path, he beheld before him the Himalaya mountain, with its swaying trees and grassy slopes, appearing like a vessel of auspicious curd. It was graced by the streams of *sarala* resin and bore the spray of the Gaṅgā.
The Maruts, praised by the earth, rose up to meet him as he reached that region called Kramavarta;
there,
he who now resides in Śūrapura encountered the drum named Kāmbuva.
Then, in that place crowded with people from various regions, he heard that the great ministers of Kaśmīra were stationed there for some reason. Thereupon,
having discarded his former attire and donned white garments, he [approached them].
He went into their presence to deliver the king’s command again and again.
As he set out, his undertaking signaled by the birds rising up in flight,
certain travelers followed him to witness the fruition of those omens.

Then, having heard that the messenger of Vikramāditya had arrived, the gatekeepers quickly informed the ministers of Kaśmīra that he was near. Then, being told from all sides, "Come! Enter! [he proceeded].
He approached all those vassal kings without obstruction;
having been accorded the appropriate honors by his ministers according to their rank, he then sat upon the most excellent throne indicated to him.

Then, having been honored by the ministers, the king was asked for his command; as if feeling ashamed, he slowly delivered that decree to them. Having saluted their lord’s letter, they then gathered together in secret.
Having untied [the letter] and had it read, they spoke to him with humility:
"Is this praiseworthy name 'Mātṛgupta' truly yours alone?
He too, having offered a smile, said to them, "It is exactly so."
Then this voice was heard from among those standing nearby: "Who is here?
And the equipment for the royal consecration was seen gathered together. Thereupon, the place became crowded with a vast multitude of people, noisy with a great clamor.
In a mere instant, that region became like an agitated ocean. Then,
seated upon a golden *bhadrapīṭha* facing the east,
Mātṛgupta was consecrated by the assembled subjects.
As he rolled about upon his chest, which was as broad as the slopes of the Vindhya mountains, the water of the consecration appeared to flow with a roar like the current of the Revā river. Then,
his limbs bathed and anointed, and all his ornaments cast off from every part of his body—
The subjects petitioned that king who had ascended the royal throne;
[they were petitioned] by King Vikramāditya himself, who desired to protect them.
"You have been designated as our equal; rule this earth.
By means of this [power], mandalas are obtained every moment.
O King, do not think that these mandalas have been obtained by us from our enemies."
Just as parents are the cause for a birth obtained through one's own past actions,
so too are others the cause for the commencement of kingship for monarchs. This being the case, by declaring "I am yours," you [offer yourself] to someone else.

"O King, you should not lead us and yourself to humiliation. Although addressed with this truth by them, King Mātṛgupta, remembering the hospitable treatment he had received from his master, smiled for a moment.
Making that day auspicious through his generosity, he celebrated that very day with great magnificence and splendor. Then,
on another day, he was requested by his ministers to enter the city.
He dispatched a messenger bearing extraordinary gifts to the giver of his kingdom;
perceiving that [the king's] rivalry was in accordance with the greatness of his own country,
he felt ashamed in his master’s mind and considered himself guilty.
Then, having summoned other servants to remind them of their service to the Lord,
he sent them with gifts— though small in value—
as they were suitable to each; his eyes filled with tears as he recalled the king’s extraordinary virtues.
Having written it himself, he sent forth this one verse of his own:

“O King, you do not assume a formal air, nor do you boast; you do not hint at your desire to give, yet you release the fruits of goodness. Like the silent pouring of rain from a cloud, your favor is perceived only through its results. (KRT 3.251cd–252)
Then, having entered the city with his armies filling the quarters of the horizon,
he protected the earth according to tradition, as if it were his hereditary inheritance.
In both renunciation and prowess, that noble-minded king was elevated by his sense of propriety.
Like Tarkuka, the lord of the earth possessed no limited desire;
though he was intent on performing sacrifices with extensive sacrificial fees,
the renunciant king’s heart grew contracted with compassion upon reflecting on the slaughter of animals.
Then, from Amāra up to Īśa, as far as his own kingdom,
he pulverized [the kings] and gave them gold and other wealth as *karambhaka* (grain-offering).
While the *karambhaka* was being scattered by King Mātṛgupta, [the following occurred].
Who indeed did not cultivate that state of contentment which blossoms from freedom from craving?
That king was virtuous, had witnessed the world's hardships, and was generous;
he was more approachable than even Vikramāditya for those seeking auspiciousness.

The playful manifestations of Fortune, made fragrant by his praiseworthy discernment, shone among the wise of that lord of the earth. Before him, Meṇṭha presented a new performance of the *Hayagrīvavadha*.

Until its completion, no word was uttered as to whether it was well or poorly composed. Then, when the book was prepared for binding, he placed a golden vessel beneath it out of fear that its beauty might overflow [and spill].

Having been honored by him with such intimate knowledge, the poet Bhartṛmeṇṭha considered the offering of wealth to be redundant. He composed [the work] called *Madhusūdana*, known as *Mātṛguptasvāmin*.
"By chance, he did not take [the bride] from his father-in-law’s house.
Thus, as that lord of the earth ruled the world having attained sovereignty,
five years passed for him— minus three months and plus one day.
Having caused his ancestors to attain the fulfillment of their purpose through the waters of the sacred fords by means of the son of Añjanā,
he heard of such valor displayed in his own country;
his heart’s dampness from grief for his father was then eclipsed by his wrath.
Like the sprinkling of a drop of night-lotus water upon a tree scorched by the heat of the sun;
at Śrīparvata, the Siddha named Aśvapāda, providing him with roots for food, announced his arrival to him who was dressed in the garb of a Pāśupata ascetic.
Having attained success in another birth, I, as a practitioner, questioned you from above; my desire was for the sake of sovereignty, yet your aspiration arose [for something else].
"In order to fulfill that desire of his without fail, I shall go there. Then the moon-crested Lord commanded me thus:
"This host of mine, who has attained perfection, is to be employed for your sake as a *sādhaka*."

"In another birth, I shall fulfill his desire for sovereignty without fail. Having spoken thus— "The Blessed One, who has granted me a vision, will bring this disposition of yours to fruition"— Bhava vanished from sight.
As he was performing austerities there for one year, desiring universal sovereignty,
Śiva— having regained his memory through the voice of a *siddha*— revealed himself to him. He directed him, who was dressed in the garb of a vow-observer, toward the bestowal of his desired object.

He sought the sovereignty of men, which is ever vigilant in conquering the world. "Disregarding liberation, why do you desire these fleeting pleasures of the earth? Thus was he addressed by Śambhu, who wished to test his inner disposition.
Perceiving you, Śambhu, to be a mendicant in disguise, he spoke to him: "I have spoken this quite plainly;
you are not that God, the Teacher of the World.
For when great beings are entreated, they yield little fruit, whereas those who are not great yield much of their own accord."
With a thirst for giving, that generous one drew forth the ocean of milk for the sake of the seeker. For him,
whose mind was fixed on the attainment of absolute liberation from all deficiencies,
you shall not perceive the humiliation of his lineage, which would cause such piercing pain to the vitals.
The Lord of the World, his affection matured, having made that prayer fruitful,
manifested his form once more and spoke again:
"For you who are immersed in the pleasures of sovereignty, [I shall grant] the messenger for attaining union."
"By my command, Aśvapāda shall regain his consciousness in due time.
Having spoken thus, when the god had vanished, he— having completed his vow—
departed for that Aśvapāda after taking leave of him, and proceeded toward his desired land.
Then, having learned of the situation regarding Mātṛgupta’s military expedition,
he restrained his ministers who had arrived nearby and spoke these words:
"My mind strives to destroy the arrogant Vikramāditya."
Our minds are not inflamed with anger toward Mātṛgupta. What would be gained by crushing those who are disagreeable yet unable to endure suffering?
The desire for victory shines forth only against those who are capable of uprooting him.

What other lotuses are there that envy the rising moon? And what kind of logic is this—that it is the very act of being crushed by the tusks of the elephant who destroys them that makes one disagreeable?

It is a strange thing that those who, having shaken off rivalry with the incomparable in order to manifest their own power, rise high; yet against them, those who were once deeply rooted in resentment clearly give way when they gain the upper hand. Then, having conquered the land of the Trigartas, that king set forth on his journey.

On that day, he heard that Vikramāditya had met his end through the law of time. Sighing incessantly out of grief, the lord of the earth remained with his face cast down, neither bathing, nor eating, nor sleeping.
On the following day, he heard that Mātṛgupta had departed from Kaśmīra and left the earth, having taken up residence not very far away;
he was apprehensive, thinking, "Could it be that he has been exiled by some of my own men?"

Accompanied by a limited retinue, Pravarasena went to his side. Once he had been honored and was seated comfortably, the king, bowing low with humility, then slowly asked him the reason for his renunciation of the kingdom.
Having paused for a moment, he sighed and laughed, and said to him:
"O King, that virtuous man has departed, by whom we kings are surpassed.
As long as the rays of the sun illuminate the quarters of the sky upon his head..."
"In illumination there is nothing else; he is like a sun-stone (tapanopala) for a rock.
Then the king said: "O King, what harm has been done to you?"
"Since you grieve for that Lord out of a desire to retaliate against him," Mātṛgupta then said, his lips whitened by a smile of anger:
"No one, however superior in power, dares to do us harm."
Therefore, let him who knows the difference between us be counted as one who leads us astray;
for ghee poured onto ashes is not an oblation, nor is seed sown in salty soil. Yet those who remember a favor remain subject to the power of gratitude.
Even inanimate objects follow the path of those who do them a favor:
the sun-stone cools after the sun has cooled,
and the moonstone withers as the moon withers.
Having gone to the holy Vārāṇasī, I therefore desire, being intent upon the bliss of tranquility, to perform the renunciation of everything appropriate for a twice-born man— [a state] which,
without that Lord who is like a jewel-lamp, remains shrouded in darkness.
“I am afraid even to look upon the earth; what talk can there be of enjoying its pleasures?

Hearing these words of that treasury of propriety, the steadfast Pravarasena was struck with wonder and spoke words that were fitting: “Hearing these words of that treasury of propriety, the steadfast Pravarasena was struck with wonder and spoke words that were fitting.”
O King, it is true that the goddess Earth is a mine of jewels;
yet she is illuminated by those like you, who are righteous and grateful by nature.
What other ruler of the earth is more praiseworthy than he, who possesses such deep insight into the inner essence of things?
Thus, in this inert world, you alone have known [the truth] exactly as it is.
O steadfast one, the paths of gratitude have indeed long remained desolate;
they will be traversed only by you, were it not for the fact that your movement is not yet visible.

If this ripening is not for my welfare today, then he surely did not bestow it upon me previously; if it were for his own sake, why would he not resort to the wretched and his own kinsmen? "He fears me because of my piercing gaze"—if that is so, would he, being greedy, abandon [me]? Thus does the lowest of men generally reflect when a favor has been done for him. This [gratitude] has been planted by those of merit among those of exceedingly noble qualities.
Even a virtuous deed, however small, branches out into a hundredfold [of merit].
You are the foremost among those possessed of virtue, celebrated by the knowers of reality;
like a gem that has been tested, you are clearly held in high esteem by the wise.
Therefore, show us favor; do not abandon your status as lord of men. Let my own reputation also spread for my partiality toward those possessed of virtue—first by him, and then finally by me as well.
"May Your Majesty make me your devoted wife once again.
Having heard these words of the king, whose conduct was characterized by sincere generosity,
Mātṛgupta smiled and slowly spoke these words.
When there are certain syllables between which the intended meaning cannot be expressed, what recourse is there in employing them without transgressing the bounds of propriety? Therefore,
even something harsh is being said by me today.
Even this sincerity and straightforwardness is disregarded for the sake of profit.
Everyone remembers the former state of everyone else’s insignificance;
however, only one's own self knows its own greatness at the present moment.
My former state and that which was yours, as it dwells within my heart— deluded by these two, we do not recognize each other’s true disposition.
How could one such as I, having become a king, accept riches?
How could all propriety be wiped away in a single stroke?
The extraordinary nobility and greatness of that king—
how could one like me bring it to a state of commonality for the sake of mere enjoyment?
Moreover, O King, if I were one who craved enjoyments while my pride remained intact, by whom could they have been restrained? Since that favor was done for me, it requires no further return.
It is certain that this [old age] now prevails over my limbs.
As I follow the path taken by this king,
let me make manifest the reputation for discerning between worthy and unworthy recipients.
Since this much alone remains to be done, now that he has passed into the state of being remembered only by his fame,
I shall maintain my commitment to truth by renouncing all material enjoyment.
When he had finished speaking and become silent, the Lord of the World said:
"While you are alive, my wealth must not be touched by you;
rather, having gone to Vārāṇasī and having taken up the saffron robes..."
Having renounced everything, the virtuous Mātṛgupta became an ascetic. King Pravarasena, firm in his resolve, also promptly sent the entire account of his own birth in Kaśmīra to Mātṛgupta.

Bestowing upon all supplicants the fortune that had fallen to him by chance, the virtuous king, subsisting on alms, sustained his life for ten years. Among those who were mutually proud yet possessed of mutual propriety—
The waters of the triple-pathed river [Ganges] are the narrative of all three as well.
Then King Pravarasena, bowing down the mountains,
made the quarters of the world easily traversable for his mature fame.
Like Agastya, who crossed the yellow ocean and the mountains,
his majesty, prevailing over the worlds, brought them clarity;
[he brought] the *tamāla* trees to wither and the *tāḍī* leaves to shrivel.
He made the faces of his enemies' wives the shores of that ocean-like army.
He bestowed upon the eastern ocean, whose body was embraced by the Gaṅgā,
the beauty of a confluence with the Yamunā through the flowing ichor from the temples of his military elephants.
With mountain ranges that touched the horizons on the opposite shore of the ocean,
he uprooted the Saurāṣṭras and brought about the destruction of their kingdom; for,
though seeking glory among kings, he was free from both hatred and passion.

The victory of righteousness increased for that Indra among kings. He placed his son Vikramāditya— born of his father’s lineage and known by the other name Śīlāditya— who had been exiled by his enemies, upon the throne through his own prowess.
Then, having cited various reasons for his defeat, he brought back to his own city the lion-throne of his ancestors, which had been seized and taken away by him from the residence of Vikramāditya.
Having conquered King Mummuṇi, he released him after seven rounds.
Then, on the eighth round, when [Mummuṇi] prepared to state his reason out of audacity, the king, filled with rage, said: "Fie upon these beasts! Let him be bound!"
Saying, "O hero, I am not to be slain as a sacrificial animal," he, eager for safety,
danced in the midst of the assembly,
imitating a peacock. Seeing his dance and his cry like that of a peacock, the king [bestowed] wealth upon him.
He bestowed upon him, equal to fearlessness itself, the appropriate role of a court musician (*tālāvacara*).
While his grandson resided in the city of his grandfather after having conquered the quarters,
a desire arose in him to establish a city bearing his own name.
Then, on one occasion, in order to know whether the field and the auspicious moment were divine even at night,
that hero, a noble sun among kings, set out upon his heroic course.
As that lord of the earth was walking, his crown was reflected here in front of him.
The multitude of stars bore the appearance of mustard seeds used for protection.
Then, wandering along the river at the edge of the cemetery, whose trees on the banks were made clearly terrifying by the light from Ananta’s funeral pyre, he reached it.
Then, on the far bank of that river,
before him as he let out a great roar, a massive being of immense power appeared with its arms raised high.
The king was turned ash-gray by the blazing glances of that being.
Clasped by the light of meteors, he shone like a mountain peak;
then, filling the quarters with a terrible echo,
the night-stalker laughed aloud and spoke, causing terror.

Having abandoned Vikramāditya, who is overflowing with courage, and Śūdraka, you too, O protector of the earth, possess sufficient fortitude that is difficult to find elsewhere. O lord of the world, the fulfillment of your desire is ordained for you.
"Having crossed this bridge, which marks the boundary of my side," having thus spoken,
the Rākṣasa extended his own knee from the far shore;
that knee created a partition in the waters of the great river like a bridge.
Having perceived through his own body that a bridge had been constructed by the Rakṣasas,
the hero Pravarasena then drew his sword from its scabbard.

Having cut that flesh with her [claws] and fashioned a series of steps, she crossed over to that place which is called "the power of the razor" (*kṣurikābala*). Having spoken to him who was standing nearby and clinging [to her], she said: "In the morning, let my thread be cast down."
Having seen him, the being said, "Build a city," and then vanished. In the village of Śārīṭaka, presided over by the goddess Śārikā and the yakṣa Aṭṭa, he saw a cord cast down by a vetāla.
Desiring to bring about the installation of the Lord of Pravaras there with devotion,

Jayasvāmin himself broke through the ritual diagram (*yantra*) upon the pedestal and sat down. While the king knew the auspicious moment (*lagna*) had been announced by a *vetāla*, [the ceremony proceeded].

He became renowned by the name of his patron, the architect Jyāka. Out of devotion, so that the city would not be turned away from its proper direction, the Vināyaka Bhīmasvāmin himself changed his orientation from facing west to facing east.
The goddesses, beginning with Śrī, whose nature is goodness, were marked by the word "Śrī" and established in that city by Pañcapañcajana;
that king also caused the Bṛhatsetu to be built across the Vitastā.

From that time forth, such a construction of formidable embankments became renowned. His maternal uncle, Jayendra, built the Śrījayendra-vihāra and the residence for the Great Buddha on behalf of the king.
He who ruled over the islands of Siṃhala and others made them his ministers;
he was named Morāka, and he built the Morāka palace, a wonder of the world. Formerly, that city in Pramathe contained thirty-six hundred thousand houses.
Vardhanasvāmin and Viśvakarman were the lords of its two boundaries. Long ago, on the southern bank of the Vitastā, he indeed constructed a city provided with well-arranged marketplaces.

Having ascended those cloud-touching palaces there, one beholds the world at the end of summer, glistening with rain, and in the month of Caitra, covered in blossoms. Without that city, where on earth can such purifying sights be so easily found?
The confluences of rivers are auspicious in the pleasure-parks and along the streets;
elsewhere, a pleasure-grove is seen, but never in the middle of a city,
for the splendor of all inhabitants is as clearly visible there as if from the path of the sky.
Where else but there can one find water as deep as a span, filled with large flakes of ice,
on a scorching summer day, other than from the tops of one’s own houses?
For in every temple, treasuries have been deposited by kings for that very purpose.
By whom the earth, clothed by the oceans, could be purchased for thousands;
for that king, the creator of his subjects, as he dwelt in that city,
sixty years passed gradually while he sought the attainment of imperial sovereignty.

On his forehead, marked with the trident-syllable (śūlamudrā), his hair was white with age; it bore the likeness of the waters of the Gaṅgā as they swirl around Śambhu. Then, at the command of Īśāna, Aśvapāda arrived there in that very instant.
A certain Brahmin from Kashmir named Jayanta was appointed as his attendant. [The king said:
"O traveler, you are weary; there is no other place than this country where your desire might be fulfilled. Let this letter be presented to King Pravarasena."

Having spoken thus and handed over the letter, he said: "I am unable to travel long distances; I am exhausted by this journey and have just now set out. "First, you must bathe today, for I, a twice-born man, have been touched by a *kāpālika*."
Having spoken thus, he was thrown by him into the nearby water of the pond.
Suddenly opening his eyes, he saw himself risen from his own country,
while the king’s servants stood busily engaged in offering worship and fetching water.
While he was being led by the river to the presence of the king to announce himself,
he then cast a letter— unwaveringly— into a bathing pitcher;
as the lord of the excellent [city] was being bathed, it fell again from that pitcher.
The king, having read the letter, sent Jayanta into his presence:
"The great task has been accomplished, wealth has been bestowed, enjoyments have been experienced, and life has passed away.
What else remains for you to do? If you will, go to the abode of Śiva."
Then, having fulfilled their appointment and gratified him by bestowing what he desired,
he shattered that stone palace and entered the stainless sky.
As he traveled toward the quarter adorned by Mount Kailāsa, he was watched by the people.
While he was creating the appearance of a second sun rising in the clear sky,
Jayanta attained great prosperity through that wondrous event.
They were rendered pure through deeds such as the granting of agrahāras marked with his own name.
Having thus enjoyed sovereignty over the worlds, that best of kings,
in this very body, entered the assembly hall of the Lord of Beings (Śiva).
In the palace of the Lord of the Earth at Siddhikṣetra,
even today the gate that rivals the Gate of Heaven (Svargadvāra) is still visible.
From him and Queen Ratnaprabhā was born King Yudhiṣṭhira.
For forty-nine years,

he ruled the earth. His excellent ministers, whose names were marked by the title "Jayaskandagupta" and who possessed all jewels, occupied themselves with the construction of monasteries, shrines, and other such works.
He who established the village named Bhavaccheda, which was worthy of praise due to the perfection of its shrines and other monuments—
his minister Vajrendra, born of Jayendra,
was like a mountain of diamonds; he painted the faces of the women of the quarters with the sandalwood-paste of his fame.
Āsaṅku, Mārasena, and others were his chief ministers.
From him, a son named Narendrāditya was born in Padmāvatī;
he, also known by the name Laṅkhaṇa, installed Narendrasvāmin [as king].
He whose two ministers were Vajrendratanaya and Vajrakanaka, who were like well-fashioned tusks of ivory,
and whose queen was Vimalaprabhā—
he, having established a court for the purpose of recording his decrees...
The mighty-armed one ascended to heaven after thirteen years.
His younger brother was Dharaṇibhṛdraṇāditya,
whom people directly called by the other name Tuñjīna.
His head, marked with the conch-emblem, was unlike anything else in the world;
it bore the splendor of the sun vanished within the night of an unprecedented moon.
His sword-blade, falling like a rain-cloud, lay amidst the forest-like throats of his enemies.
The abundance of water was maintained by the wells that were the eyes of his wives;
for when the unprecedented fire of his majesty entered the earth of his enemies,
it deposited waves of water into the eyes of their women and sprouts of grass into the houses [which had become like ponds].
When his sword came into the embrace of his hand,
he performed a dance unlike any other among the headless trunks in the enemy host;
the beloved queen of that godlike being of unassailable majesty—

The power of Viṣṇu, having reached the earth, became known by the name Raṇārambha. Indeed, it is said that in a previous birth he was a gambler; once, having lost his entire fortune to cheats, he attained a state of world-weariness.
Even as he was prepared to cast off his body, he remained reflecting upon something yet to be attained;
for gamblers do not neglect the means to achieve their own ends even at the very end.
[He learned of] the goddess Bhramaravāsinī on the Vindhya mountains, whose sight is never in vain.

Desiring to see [him], the wretched one longed for it, regardless even of his own life. For as a living being is being torn apart by bees such as those with thorn-like tails, the five-yojana distance to that abode is indeed difficult to traverse.

The wise one, considering that their counter-measures— consisting of adamantine spikes and tails— were difficult to overcome, resolved to abandon his body when it was inevitably to be cast off. First he covered his body with the hide of a goat, and thereafter with the hide of a buffalo.
While covering it, he then applied a coating of clay mixed with cow dung. Then,
his body smeared repeatedly with dried coatings of clay,
like a moving clod of earth, he set out with a cruel resolve.
Abandoning the straight path along with his longing for life, he then plunged into that cave, terrifying with its dense darkness. Then,
from the chasms, there rose up dreadful swarms of bees.
Striking at him with words of censure like the sounds of the drums of Death,
they suddenly did not even approach him to strike, though they sought to harm him, for their eyes were irritated by the dust from parched clay and mud.
The bees, their vision obscured by the dust, turned back;
yet others, breaking through the coating of mud, fell down one after another.
As he traveled for three *yojanas*, they fell upon him with fierce force as he proceeded.
Gradually, his armor of clay was worn away on the path. Then,
as they struck repeatedly at the buffalo-hide shield,
a terrible and terrifying *caṭacaṭā* sound arose.
Having traversed half of the fourth league, he perceived those bees,
which were falling upon his armor with a humming sound.

Running with extreme speed, though stung by bees, he cast off his weapons and armor; yet his mind was not released from its steadfastness. Possessing fortitude, he drew near to the goddess’s abode, which was but two *gavyūtis* away.
Shaking [the bees] with his two hands, that man of steady intellect ran after the honey-bees. Then, his body reduced to mere sinews and bones with its flesh torn away by the six-legged insects,
he reached the temple of the Goddess, protecting his eyes with both hands.
When the falling of the stones had subsided, he looked around clearly;
with his life-breath wandering, he fell at the feet of the goddess.
Then, in order to comfort him whose remaining breath was but slight, the goddess—

Having made his body beautiful, he touched [the prince] on his limbs with his hand. By that divine touch of the hand, which rained down nectar, his health was quickly restored, and he cast his eyes in all directions.

As soon as he had entered, at the edge of the lion-thicket, he beheld that goddess of terrible form; yet he did not see her there again. He saw her once more, sporting in a bower of creepers in the garden.
She stood on the bank of the lotus pond, dark-complexioned and with eyes like lotuses; she held a handful of pearls as an offering, her full breasts joined together in a gesture of reverence,
her limbs honored by the beauty of her youth and by most precious, lovely flowers.
She bore feet that had become dark from subsisting on barley and were emaciated by the practice of austerities;
her face was concealed by her breasts as if she were performing penance day after day to behold [him].
She possessed lips like the radiant orb of the sun, black hair, and a face bright as the moon.
Having meditated upon her— who was like Śivā in form, with a waist like that of Hari, and as if composed of all the gods—
that woman of faultless limbs, exalted by her youth,
was brought into subjection by Kāma, who acted as his own adversary in solitude.

Displaying a form whose invincibility was concealed by a flood of beauty and sweetness, that Apsaras appeared before him; for she, not some celestial deity, dwelt within his mind. Softened by compassion, she said to him: "You have been distressed on this road for a long time."
"O gentle one, having rested for a moment, let a suitable boon be requested.
He said to her: "My fatigue has been stilled by the sight of you;
however, O lady, how can you be capable of granting a boon?"
The queen said to him, "O gentle one, what is this delusion in your mind?
Whether I am a queen or not a queen, you two would be able to choose me.
Having thus caused him to give his promise for the attainment of his desired object, she—
Having transgressed all bounds, he begged for union with her.
She said to him, "O evil-minded one, what is this improper conduct?
Ask for something else, for I am a dweller among the bees."
Even though he knew her to be the goddess, his mind was not attentive. By whom can the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) that bind one to future births be restrained?
He said to her: "O Goddess, if you truly desire your own mountain..."

Make my words your authority; I desire nothing else. For even before living beings are born, their dwelling place is already established, and like that of sesame seeds, it does not perish even at the end.

Though she was the Great Goddess, being fearful of contact with a mortal, she deluded him with her *māyā* and never touched him at any time. She created for the king upon his bed a woman made of *māyā* who resembled herself.

Having constructed two divine temples for himself and for the Goddess,

In the consecration of Raṇeśvara, just as he was previously prepared,

Having fully understood their divine foundation, he established it in secret. Recognizing the Lord of Battle through his conduct, he installed him in the conflict and,

And slowly, Kauśika, Vīrabhāgya,

"Union with wanton women, pleasures, youth, the father’s house,
