By the constant practice of seeing him, he gradually entered her mind."
Anaṅgalekhā was united with the minister Khaṅkha;
her modesty, fear, and agitation lost through the practice of the pleasure of secret love,
she attained a state of absorption in him as she grew bolder day by day.
Having won over his attendants with gifts and honors,
that minister sported at will in the inner apartments together with her;
and he gradually perceived in her a lapse from virtuous conduct.
The wise Durlabhavardhana, manifesting signs of dispassion,
[beheld her] in the midst of her friends, smiling in private but turning pale at the sight of her husband; then, having suddenly departed, she looked back at him from the road with a smile.
She showed her disregard for her husband’s anger through the movements of her eyebrows, eyes, and chin;
when he spoke words unpleasant to her, she cast her gaze upon him with a smile;
she became despondent at praise for those possessing qualities equal to his, yet took delight in the praise of his enemies.
Perceiving his desire for dalliance, she engaged in conversation with her friends;
when he kissed her, she bent her neck; in his embrace, she relaxed her limbs; during their union, she abandoned all joy; and upon his bed, she feigned sleep.
For a woman’s heart is generally sold by love, as she reveals the deformity caused by the possession of the demon of immoral conduct;
thereafter, her body becomes emaciated from brooding over the hidden wickedness of her husband. (A Kulaka)
Durlabhavardhana never entered the inner apartments at night; however,
one night he beheld his beloved, overcome by the exhaustion of amorous play and rendered helpless by sleep,
as if she were inlaid within the limbs of her adulterous lover.
With sighs whose force had not yet subsided, shaking her budding breasts,
she announced that very moment the conclusion of their love-making;
yet, she once again manifested an impatience that served as a cause for another’s anger.

Seeing her standing thus, he blazed with fury. Desiring to strike her out of rage, he was restrained by his own reflection; he felt as though he had turned back after having struck her again and again.

Then, that ocean of the onset of agitation and fury, though of such a nature, was forcibly calmed by the tide of his reflection. Homage to him! Who else, then, can be counted at the forefront of those who have mastery over themselves?
By which the cholera of the poison of envy, once fully developed, is digested.
He thought: "Alas, how painful are these activities that follow after passion! Devoid of discernment, men are quickly cast down by them."

If it does not appear to me that this [disgust] is to be cultivated because it produces agitation,

even the very name of passion has been destroyed in half a moment.
"Having perceived this with divine vision, one should prescribe the remedy for those possessed by passion:

Astonished by his elegance and such splendor,
he remained right there for two or three days, having been duly honored.
One day, he beheld a woman of graceful form who had entered that place.

Seeing me, whose limbs were faultless, wandering fearlessly in the palace because it was deserted, he touched me with desire. She too,
her face slightly turned away as indicated by her friends, [looked at him].

She beheld the beloved of Kāśyapa with a gaze that rested upon her ears. Whether due to the bond of affection from a previous birth or by the command of the god of love, she made his mind partial toward her by her very look.

Having her limbs concealed by the pillars of the palace for a moment, she departed,
turning her face back to look at that king again and again.
By that alone, the lord of the earth had already captured the heart of the slender woman.

With eyes downcast in thought, he proceeded slowly toward the royal capital. There, as his gaze was fixed in meditation upon that form [of the Buddha], his body attained a state of emaciation equal to the longing felt for the inner apartments.

He thought: "Alas, what a tragedy! This poisonous tree named 'passion,' which brings about misfortune, has taken root here in the garden of my mind. Oh, how fortunate is the state of passion, having conquered the mind!"

He has cast far away discernment and the like, which are his true friends, while embracing those who stand as his adversaries. For a virtuous king who ought to be afraid of public scandal, what is this intolerable reversal of proper conduct on my part?

One who knows his duty, whose mind is not agitated by the wheel of worldly existence,

Even his own faction, like that of Garuḍa out of fear of the thunderbolt,

This utterance, which restricts [the description] by proclaiming his virtues,

Her wife, known as Prakāśadevī, who was radiant with the splendor of light and space, became the patroness who caused the monastery of Prakāśikā to be built through her meritorious deeds. Her teacher, named Mihiradatta, possessed exalted virtues.
The city magistrate named Chalitaka, who was the creator of instability for all administrative offices and the destroyer of the stability of Viśvaṃbhara’s lord known as Gambhīra,
appointed [his own man] as the lord of that city.
Once, while the king was seated and being questioned by his judicial officers, a certain Brāhmaṇa woman who had sat down in a fast unto death spoke to him:
"While you rule the earth, O great one, in the eradication of reproach..."
"The life of my husband, who was sleeping peacefully, has been taken away by someone. This alone is a great shame for a king of virtuous conduct:
that untimely death touches his subjects."

If, due to the power of this Kali age, even someone like you perceives that [fault], how can one remain indifferent toward such a sin, which is more sinful than sin itself? Even though I reflect upon it, I do not perceive anyone who is an adversary to my husband.

For him who was free from fault, all directions were cool on every side. He was free from malice, devoid of pride, pleasant of speech, and devoted to virtue; he was the first to speak, free from passion, and indeed not hateful to anyone.

A Brahmin residing in Mākṣikasvāmin, who was of equal age to him and had been his fellow student since childhood, was suspected of being an expert in malevolent magic (abhicāra). He was one of those petty men,
devoid of virtue and destitute, who are sleepless with envy toward those possessed of skill.
Out of envy for those who are famous, these fools are oppressed by their own barren efforts.
(KRT 4.0089cd) One who is unchaste is not [to be trusted], nor one of bad character, nor one who is treacherous and constantly suspicious;
nor one who is talkative and a speaker of falsehoods, nor one who is inactive and possesses an ungrateful mind. (KRT 4.0090)
One who is not born of a noble family, who is greedy, who is not free from envy, who is perpetually miserable;
one who is not conquered by women, who is a laughingstock to all, who is not aged, yet speaks with affection;
one who is not of non-human origin, who hates his father, who is devoid of passion, and who is shameless—[such a person is not fit for this].
"One who possesses no meager learning is not a sinner"—this is a summary of the true state of affairs.
[Tilaka] When the Brahmin woman had spoken thus, the lord of the earth summoned the twice-born man, who was the abode of that suspicion, and said to him, "Be purified. [KRT 4.0092cd–0093]

The Brahmin, renowned for his knowledge of the *khārkhoda* spell, spoke to him again. "O King, I am undisturbed; I shall paralyze this divine ritual. Then the lord of the earth, as if with a withered face, said to her:
What can we do here regarding one whose fault is unseen? We have no authority in this matter. Nor should there be any application of punishment even toward another when their guilt is certain;
how much less so for a Brāhmaṇa, who is not to be punished with death even for a fault?
When he had finished speaking and paused, the wife of the twice-born spoke again:
"O King, four nights have passed for me in fasting.
I did not follow my husband in order to retaliate against his killer."
"Therefore, since no punishment has been prescribed for this, I shall give up my life by means of fasting.
While the Brāhmaṇī remained thus resolved, having undertaken the fast unto death (*prāyopaveśana*),
he himself performed [the rite] dedicated to the Lord of the Three Worlds.
There, at the end of the night, the supreme dreamer Satyavāhana spoke these words of truth to the king, who had fasted for three nights:
"O King, such a search for the truth is not appropriate in the Kali age."
"At midnight, who has the power to cut through the sky?
This [task] is performed but once, in accordance with your power.
Let rice-powder be scattered here in this courtyard of my palace."
If, while he is performing circumambulation three times,
the footprint of the murder of a Brahmin is seen following after his own footprints,
[then it is so].

Therefore, having become a slayer, he deserves a corresponding punishment. This rule should be applied at night; by day, the Sun is the remover of sin. Then, having caused that [act] to be performed, he [should punish] the twice-born man who has been seen committing the offense.

The wielder of the rod imposed a punishment that excluded death because of his status as a twice-born. When that executioner had been punished by the lord of the earth for killing his master, the wife of the twice-born man, having offered her blessing, then spoke this:
"O Lord of the Earth, in this entire creation of mountains, has any secret punishment for evil ever been seen— either that of Kārtavīrya or yours? While you,
O King, are the wielder of the rod of justice and rule over this earth,"
"Who, failing to reach the further shore of enmity and affection, would despair?

(KRT 4.108cd) Thus, by means of these accounts of righteous conduct, which were worthy of being meditated upon in the Kṛta Yuga, even his very brief period of kingship was fully completed. (KRT 4.109ab–cd)
I know that through contact with the Creator’s lotus-throne, dullness became unrestrained and established a dense presence in his intellect;
otherwise, how could such a thing have occurred to him, whose beauty of complexion was so clearly distinguished?
Having caused that brahmin, fierce in his wrath and intent on malevolent magic, to perform a rite that made Indra’s bow appear and vanish like a flash of lightning,
Tārāpīḍa’s younger brother reduced him to a mere remnant of fame.

Wicked men, seeking to enjoy the fruits of their ill-fated misdeeds, trample upon those exalted in virtue, just as young camels trample upon *ketaka* flowers in their attempt to reach thorns. From that time forward, toward the preceptors of kings who desire sovereignty—

Evil practices such as malevolent incantations have been set in motion in this kingdom. To whom does the memory of the final act of forgiveness by the illustrious King Candrāpīḍa not cause their bodies to bristle with horripilation?

Though he was on the verge of death, having encountered that twice-born man who had inflicted such agony upon him, he did not slay him, thinking, "What fault is there in this wretch who was incited by another? Today,
the Creator has forgotten that king in the midst of the assembly of monarchs.
Having surely left his mark like a crow’s foot upon the lineage of kings,
he ruled the earth for eight years and eight months; then, having brought it under his control, that self-mastered one entered heaven and the hearts of the virtuous.
Then that fierce Tārāpīḍa, formidable through the majesty of his enemies who had betrayed their brothers and friends, bore the circle of the earth;
he plundered the fame of his foes as if it were a vessel full of wealth.
When the infant Pratāpa was born, he caused headless trunks (kabandhas) to dance;
for that man of exceedingly wicked conduct, his fortune, though blazing on all sides,
became a source of terror, like the radiance of a funeral pyre.
Thinking that the presence and power of the gods are brought about by the twice-born through mantras,
that hater of the gods imposed a punishment upon them;
for one month, their lifespan was brought to an end by the twice-born through secret malevolent rites.
He flourished until his store of merit was exhausted by the sprouting of his betrayal of his guru.
Then, with the destruction of his lifespan brought about by the brahmins through secret malevolent rites,
he attained a peace similar to that of his brother, but not the final goal.

Whatever means one devises for the purpose of harming another, by that very means his destruction shall surely come about. Just as a cloud, having become fire, emits smoke that causes blindness to the eyes, yet becomes that very same cloud and quenches it with its waters;
so too did King Śrī Lalitāditya become a sovereign ruler over the whole earth.
Beyond the scope of the intellect of Brahmā, the creator of local lords,
he— who by means of the massed rays of his majesty’s luster, which shared the nature of fine perfumed powders,
performed the adornment of Jambudvīpa, that lordly elephant.
When kings joined their palms in supplication during his military expedition for victory,
the monarch, whose prowess was vast, released his anger in battle;
he let it go as a multitude of people, out of fear, release fetuses from their wombs.
Upon hearing the drum of his assault,
the dwellings of his enemies were filled with faces whose eyes were like trembling tilaka-ornaments and which shed tears.

He caused funeral offerings of handfuls of rice to be made for his enemies. For that lord of the earth, who desired victory, his life passed away almost entirely in military expeditions, as if he were the sun circumambulating the earth.
Taking tribute from the eastern direction in the presence of the fire of his majesty,
the great king shone in Antarvedi with the crest-jewel of his own fame. There,
in Gadhipura, the Wind-god had once caused the hunchbacked deformity of maidens.
In that very place, he was to be praised by men;
for King Lalitāditya, momentarily making himself a distinguishing feature of the river flowing from Mount Yaśovarman, attained the height of majesty.
The wise lord of Kanyakubja, who understood the nature of services to be rendered, shone brightly; for, having bestowed upon those who had requested it the illustrious Lalitāditya, he served him.
Even more so than that, his proud companions were devoted to him according to their desire.
The sandalwood breeze was more fragrant than even the springtime; yet,
during the treaty of Śrī Yaśovarman, Mitrasharman did not tolerate the conduct of the minister of peace and war, who failed to apply restraint in the drafting of the agreement.
Thus there was a reconciliation between Yaśovarman and Lalitāditya.

Knowing the Lord’s unworthiness [to rule] because of the mention of [his predecessor] Adinirdeśa by Likhita, [the people] were incensed by the generals who had not pacified their very long-standing hostilities. (A pair of verses. KRT_4_0138cd–KRT_4_0139ab.
The king highly esteemed his regard for propriety;
pleased, he established him as the recipient of the five great titles,
while he uprooted King Yaśovarman along with his very foundations.
Beyond the eighteen [offices], the established ones of old attained their status through five subsequent departments of action arising from them; namely,
the Great Chamberlain, the Pīḍa, and that Great Minister of Peace and War.

The great horse-stable and the great treasury as the fifth; the great department of implements— these were the designations adopted by those [officials] in whom the sovereign lords appointed their chief ministers as superintendents.
Served by poets such as Vākpatirāja and Śrī Bhavabhūti, Yaśovarman attained the state of being praised for his virtues;
that Yamunā river, whose banks were bent low by the weight of its mud, lay on this side of him.

The shore of the Akālika ocean came under his control as if it were the courtyard of his own house. Having bypassed Yaśovarman, his army entered the eastern ocean with its ships, just as the Gaṅgā flows over the Himalayas.
As they watched, the elephants from Kaliṅga— scorned by those who looked upon the land of their birth with eyes full of envy—
somehow managed to set out on the road.
It was as if they had come there from the very presence of the elephant that serves as the couch for the Goddess of Fortune.
All the elephants from the Gauḍa region took refuge with him.
As he advanced, the eastern ocean appeared before his vanguard, its waves stirred by the trunks of the masses of elephants on his flank, as if it were being seized by the hair.
With his sword, dark as a line of forest trees, he set out along the shore of the ocean toward the quarter marked by Yama; meanwhile,
the Karṇāṭas with their hair tied in high topknots gazed upon him as they offered their salutations.

In that context, having abandoned the *suvarṇaketakī* flower and his own prowess for the sake of being an ornament, the king of great fortune became the ruler of the southern region, while a woman from Karṇāṭa named Raṭṭā, with tremulous eyes,
remained there.
The paths of the Vindhya mountains were rendered free of obstacles by that goddess of boundless power, as if by an impenetrable fortress;
[they were reflected] in the mirror-like orb of the toenails of her lotus-feet, beginning with the *lalitā* step.
Beholding her own reflection transferred [upon the surface], she too bowed down and was filled with joy.
[KRT 4.0154cd] The waves of the Nārīkera river, whose waters were cooled at the foot of palm trees, [KRT 4.0155ab]
The breezes from the banks of the Kāverī caused his warriors to cast off their fatigue. Then,
under the guise of snakes falling out of fear of being attacked by the sandalwood mountain,
[the serpents] fell like a multitude of sword-blades from the arms of the sandalwood trees.

Having cast his foot upon the islands as if upon the northern stones without obstacle, he performed a coming and going across the ocean as easily as over a small stream. By that [action], the auspicious sounds of victory were sung forth by the roar of the ocean waves.
The foremost among those who desire victory set out toward the western quarter.
Having traversed the seven Kramukas and the seven Kauṇkaṇas,
his majesty spread abroad like the rays of the sun across the Tāpya region.
From the western ocean, with its waves dispersed by the wind,
there appeared Dvārakā, which inspired eagerness for entry in his armies.
The Vindhya mountain, its sky covered by the dust of minerals crushed by that force, [loomed before them].

Rising up as if copper-red with rage, he seemed to have cast aside all bounds of propriety. In the land of Avanti, the rows of three hundred tusks of his elephants were shattered by the moonlight from the Mahākāla mountain, which served as their crest-jewel.
Having surveyed all directions and seeing that the kings had been for the most part conquered, he entered the vast northern region by an untrodden path. There,
fierce battles took place at every step between him and those formidable kings.
The horse-stables of the Kambojas became deserted of horses, as if by the mountains of his lineage— which had once reached out to strike at Indra’s wings—
being blocked by buffaloes acting as enemies under the guise of darkness.

The Tukhāras, abandoning their horse-drawn chariots, fled toward the rows of mountain peaks; yet, upon seeing those with horse-faces, they were reduced to a state of paralysis, as if their longing for those [mountains] had been fulfilled.
Having defeated him three times in battle, he considered Mummuṇi already conquered.

For the heroes consider a single victory over the enemy to be like the accidental carving of a syllable by a wood-boring insect. No anxiety is seen on the faces of the Bhūtas, which are naturally pale; nor is there anger on their faces, which are naturally tawny like forest-dwellers.

His majesty could not endure the Daradas, just as the morning sun, risen like the luster of medicinal herbs from within mountain caves, cannot endure the night-blooming lotus. He was one who touched the musk deer and shook off the filaments of saffron.
The northern wind groomed his army as if it were a woman.
In the empty city of Prāgjyotiṣa, he beheld smoke rising from incense— superior even to that from a forest of black aloe-wood consumed by fire.
In that ocean of sand, where the delusion of a sea was projected by a mirage,
the great elephants there became equal to a multitude of massive crocodiles. He reduced those warriors, their fortitude dissolved, to the status of women in the kingdom of women.
Placing their high breasts forward, yet not those of the jar-like women of the door-panels;
seeing before her the Queen of the Realm of Women undergo such transformations as trembling and the like,
no one could determine whether it was fear or longing.
Fleeing from that fear, the inhabitants of the Northern Kurus abandoned their birthplaces,
like great serpents retreating to their holes out of terror of the Destroyer of Serpents (Garuḍa). Then, having acquired wealth through his victories, he entered his own realm.
With his hands full of pearls from slain elephants, like a lion [seizing] a mountain,
he made Jālandhara, Lohara,
and other territories submissive, and established his sovereignty over his dependents.

In order to manifest his defeat, the kings were made to adopt various emblems by him through force; even today, they carry them without pride. Furthermore, at his command, their five arms were bound behind their backs for the purpose of branding them with the seal of captivity.
The Turuṣkas clearly wear their heads half-shaven;
he made the tail of the southern kings touch the ground, while they wore only a loincloth, in order to signify their animal nature.
There was no city, no village, no river, and no ocean, nor was there any island where he did not establish his presence.

In some places he adopted conduct appropriate to his actions, and in others he followed established conventions; for the most part, that proud man established himself among the settlements. Having resolved upon the conquest of the quarters, the Sage made Citrapura his base.
Full of pride, the king constructed Darpitapura;
he built Kṛtakeśava while gathering fruit, Phalapura while collecting fruits, and Parṇotsa while gathering leaves;
and sporting about, he established Krīḍārāmavihāra.

Leading one jewel of a policy upward and pulling down another, he bound them together and established Nṛhari in a kingdom of women, free from external support. While that king was ruling over the ends of the earth, it is said that he performed such deeds.

Having established a city named after him, he experienced the fruit of that anger. In that city called Lalitā, the king— exalted by his own pride— bestowed upon Āditya the land of Kanyakubja together with its villages.

By that noble-souled king, the illustrious Muktasvāmin was established in Huṣkapura; he constructed a great monastery (vihāra) along with a stūpa. Having taken one crore [of gold], he set out for the conquest of the quarters.

He arrived with eleven crores for the sake of purification and gave them to the Lord of Beings (Bhūteśa). There, the lord of the earth performed the construction of a stone temple for Jyeṣṭharudra and made a gift of land and villages.
By him, the wielder of the discus, the crossing of the waters of the Vitastā was accomplished; having constructed rows of water-wheels (*ārghaṭṭa*),
he bestowed various villages [upon the people],
and he built palaces within [the city] whose stone ramparts were unbroken.
The donor of the wondrous city of Mārtaṇḍa and the flourishing town of Drākṣā,
having established a city at Lokapuṇya with a multitude of various implements, that victorious one, Jiṣṇu, bestowed it upon Viṣṇu along with villages.
Thereafter, the lord of the earth, who was by nature fond of jesting, established the city of Parīhāsapura, laughing at the abode of Vāsava. There,
the divine Lord Śrī-Parīhāsakeśava shone resplendently in silver.
As if smeared with the rays of pearls from his sleep in the ocean of jewels,
and as if colored by the mass of filaments of the lotus at his navel,
the golden Śrīmuktākeśava Hari shone resplendently.
The Great Boar shone, wearing his golden armor,
like the sun bearing its rays to destroy the darkness in the netherworld (pātāla). The Lord, who bears Mount Govardhana, was made to appear resplendent by him.
He who attained a whiteness like the floods of the milk of Gokula;
having raised up fifty-four great stones,
Garuḍa was placed by him at the tip of the banner of the enemy of the sons of Diti.

The stainless king constructed the Rājavihāra, which was vast, adorned with four halls, great shrines, and large Jina images, and was built with constant effort. He [weighed] it at more than four thousand *tolakas*.
He deposited eighty *palas* of gold in the image of Mukta-Keśava;
with an equal amount of silver *palas*,
that man of pure intellect commissioned Śrīparīhāsa-Keśava after making the necessary arrangements.
With exactly that many thousands of *rīti* measures of earth,
he fashioned the glorious, great Buddha with a body pervading the sky;
and with the same amount, he constructed a four-winged temple (*caitya*).

By means of wealth alone, he created five equal emanations; in some places he fashioned deities of silver, and in others, of gold. Beside the principal deities stood his attendants, who resembled the Lord of Wealth (Dhanada).
Who is capable of measuring by their extent the jewels, the villages, and the surrounding territories that he bestowed there?
[He was accompanied] by his harem, ministers, servants, and subordinate kings.
There, hundreds of foundations were established, wonders of the world.
His queen was Kamalavatī, who made the lotus market flourish.

The minister Mitraśarman fashioned a silver image of Keśava in the form of Tripurāri; the minister also made an image of Hara as Mitreśvara. King Kayya, a Lāṭa by name, fashioned an image of Śrī Kayyasvāmin.
The illustrious and wonderful Kayyavihāra was also established by him;
there, the monk Sarvajñamitra became like a Jina in due course.
Tuḥkhāra and Caṅkuṇa built the Caṅkuṇavihāra.
The king erected a lofty stūpa for the Jina, as well as others made of gold;
his queen, Īśānadevī, offered water from the excavated well,
which was as clear as the essence of nectar and brought health to the sick.
Cakramardikā was the beloved of King Lalitāditya;
there she established Cakrapura with seven thousand dwellings.
The teacher named Bhappaṭa constructed the temple of Bhappaṭeśvara.
Many others as well, such as Rakṣaṭeśa and so forth, were constructed by many [people]. Furthermore,
even here at another location, a magnificent monastery (vihāra) together with a shrine (caitya) was erected by Caṅkuṇa, though he was not a minister.
The physician named Īśānacandra, the brother-in-law of the minister Caṅkuṇa,
built a monastery after obtaining wealth through the favor of Takṣaka. Thus, that lord of the land made the earth as if it were composed of gold.

By his virtues, such as magnanimity and heroism, he surpassed even Indra. Never was the command of that lord of the earth ever transgressed, even by the gods, for it issued from his mouth with effortless ease.
For instance, once while living with his family on the shore of the eastern ocean,
he would occasionally command, "Let the wood-apples be brought!
while his attendants stood before him, bewildered as to what they should do.
A certain man brought two wood-apples (*kapittha*) before him.
Accepting the gift from his hand, the Lord signaled with his brow that he was ready for an audience;
then the doorkeeper stepped forward and asked him, "Who are you?"
Having given those wood-apples to the king, he said:
"Today Mahendra has dispatched a guardian of the Nandana grove.
He has a certain message from Mahendra that must be told to me in private."
Having heard this, he had the chamberlain clear the assembly hall of all people.
Then a divine being spoke: "O King, Śakra tells you:
'Out of kindness, you must forgive these harsh words, even though they are for your own benefit.'"
O protector of the earth, even in this fourth age we are those very guardians of the quarters who, having bowed down, carry out his command; hear now the reason for this.
Long ago, there was a certain householder living in a village who possessed vast wealth.
It is said that in another birth you were a plowman, a laborer.
Once, during the summer, after you had driven his great oxen [to work],
the day was nearly spent for him as he grew weary in the waterless wilderness.
Then, someone came from his own home to your presence, exhausted by hunger and thirst,
carrying a water-pot and a cake;
having washed your hands and feet, you then prepared to eat.

He saw before him a Brahmin guest whose life-breath had reached his throat. He said to you: "Do not eat; for me, who am afflicted by famine, my life-breaths, desiring to depart, remain in my throat without food."

Even though you were restrained by one standing at your side, you affectionately gave him half a cake and a water-jar while speaking pleasant words. By that gift at the proper time to a worthy recipient with a serene mind, for you—
In the celestial realm, there were a hundred unimpeded commands;
by that merit of bestowing water, even when merely a wish is expressed,
rivers of excellent flavor appear even upon desert paths.

Planted in a fertile field, its trench of endearing words well-tended, and its watering performed with the faultless water of mental clarity— the tree of giving belonging to the donor, O King, even in its infancy, bears fruit according to whatever is desired at the proper time; it thus triumphs even over the wish-fulfilling trees and the like.

O King, those commands of yours now remain with but little left, since you have disregarded them here and there without reflection, transgressing your own word. Even so, for a great man such as you, [this conduct] is easily accessible even to other kings.
Why does the emptiness of deliberation take root even in your heart?
Those few days that occur in Kashmir during the onset of the rains become fruits in the eastern ocean; how could they arise in the winter?

Whichever direction you enter, there too the effort of its lord to receive your command proceeds by the power of his former generosity. Even now, though you have resorted to the quarter of Indra, your command is still but slight.
This [woman] was somehow seized by Śakra, whose power remains unbroken. Therefore, O King,
you must never again issue such a command for no primary purpose,
since such women as she are rare indeed.
When he had spoken thus and vanished, the king of vast intent,
reflecting upon the greatness of giving, was struck with supreme wonder.
From that time forth, he remained yearning for the attainment of such worthy recipients.
In Parihāsapura, he established a firm and grand festival,
renowned as the "Thousand-fold Feast," at which one hundred and one thousand alms-bowls were provided with sacrificial gifts.

With that very intention, he established towns in the desert wastes so that anyone afflicted by thirst might drink water whenever they wished. He recruited various men from different regions who were skilled in local knowledge.
Like the wind [bearing] clusters of blossoming *aśoka* flowers from the trees,
he brought from the land of Bhuḥkhāra one named Caṅkuṇa, who was exalted by his virtues and was the brother of Rasasiddha, the master of the *kaṅkaṇa* rain.
Bestowing a wealth of gold within his treasury through his aesthetic excellence,
he became a bringer of auspiciousness to the mountain-like king, like a lotus-pond to a lotus.
Once, however, he was blocked at Pañcanada by the difficult-to-cross confluences of the Sindhu rivers.

The king, having halted his army on the bank, was lost in thought for a moment. Then, while standing on the shore with his troops, Caṅkuṇa threw a jewel into the unfathomable waters of the river as a means for crossing.
By its power, the river water split in two; accompanied by his army, the king quickly crossed over and reached the opposite shore.
And with the jewel Maṇimantha, Caṅkuṇa also drew him across.
In an instant, the water of the rivers returned to its former state.
Having marveled at that wonder, the king, his face bright with praise,
affectionately requested from Caṅkuṇa the pair of jewels.
Laughing, he said to him: "Karma, these two jewels perform their functions;
what beauty could they possess among various superior objects?
It is only among common things that such an object attains the reputation of excellence."
What splendor does he possess among great beings or amidst various superior things?
(KRT 4.0254cd) They count the oozing of a moonstone only so long as it remains on a single spot of the ocean’s shore;
if it is taken up by that ocean, then its flow, though shimmering, is no longer perceived within its waters. (KRT 4.0255ab–cd)
When he had finished speaking, the king said with a smile:
"Do you consider any jewel of mine to be superior to these two? Or do you see anything whatsoever that is even more excellent than this?"
"Taking that, give me these two jewels as their price. Then Caṅkuṇa said, "This is a great favor," and added:
"The jewels belong to the master's own control; however, let whatever you desire be given to me."

Having mounted this [image] upon the back of an elephant and brought it from the Magadhas, let this image of the Sugata be given so that these people may be favored. Let the King take up the jewel, which is the means for crossing over the flood.
"May the Sugata, the means for crossing over saṃsāra, be granted to me.
Thus requested by him with reason, the king gave him an image of the Jina.
Whose speech could obstruct the words of the eloquent?
Then the Blessed One was settled by him in his own dwelling,
he who shines with tawny splendors as if with saffron robes.
Even today, he is seen encircled by iron bracelets;
his throne was once supported upon the shoulders of elephants.
According to one's disposition, he reveals what is pleasing.
"Aha! The earth belongs to kings of great power. Being himself an expert in the science of horses, he once led the horse untrained into the forest alone to tame it.

From afar, in that desolate place, he beheld a woman of graceful form; one was singing while another was dancing. In an instant, those two deer-eyed women brought their singing and dancing to a close.

Seeing them bowing slightly as they departed while restraining the horse, he mounted that steed and went there day after day. Having seen them doing exactly the same, he went and asked them in astonishment: "O lovely ones, why do you go thus every day?"
Those two dancers, residing in a temple, said to him:
"In this village where Śūravardhana lives, that is our home.
[We have come] according to the instruction of our mothers, who live here subsisting on alms."
"In our family, a dance is invariably performed here.
This tradition, handed down through generations, is established in our house. Whether it be we two or anyone else, no one is capable of knowing the reason for this."

Having heard these words of theirs, the king was filled with wonder; on the following day, at their suggestion, he had the entire earth excavated by artisans. When the earth had been removed to a great distance, he then beheld what was reported to him by them.
The king saw two ancient temple structures with their doors closed,
which were revealed by the syllables *udghāṭitāri* carved upon the pedestals;
there he beheld two Keśavas fashioned by Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having set aside the stone temple from the side of Parihāsa-Hari,
that illustrious [king] performed the consecration ceremony for Rāmasvāmin.
Likewise, Deva also, having entreated the king, [performed the consecration] for Lakṣmaṇasvāmin.
Placed beside the Lord of the Wheel by means of the Cakramārgikā rite,
a certain man who had recently completed his conquest of the quarters threw himself before the king as he sat mounted upon his elephant, having just finished suppressing his enemies.
Seeing him with wounds on his hands, feet, nose, and other parts from which blood was flowing,
seeking protection, the compassionate king asked him for his story.
He [the man] told it to him [the king], who was staying near the river of sand (Sikatāsindhu).
The famous [minister] spoke to his well-wishing counselor:
"Let a prostration be made before King Lalitāditya.
This was said by him who, while speaking what was beneficial for himself, [faced] restraint from the king; [this is] a *yugma*.
And then the king vowed to subdue their master;
and he was honored by those who had been treated with kindness, though they were tormented by the pain of wounds that had already healed.
Then that minister, having performed the rites of hospitality, prepared him for the expedition.
On one occasion, Vihana spoke thus to the lord of the earth:
"O King, regarding the protection of such a body as this,
the hope for the purification of enmity therein is a mockery."

Having offered handfuls of water with tears for both my sorrow and my joy, I shall surely cast off these life-breaths, which have been struck down by humiliation. Having inflicted excessive harm upon the enemy, one should conquer him with measured retaliation.
Like a mountain echoing the roar of one who cries out, [the earth] resounds deeply.
How can this ground, which is to be traversed in three months from here, be reached quickly? Or rather, once the enemy is reached, why should one remain right there?
Therefore, I shall point out to you a path that can be traversed in half a month;
however, having reached there, you will find water for the army, yet it will be without water further on.
My kinsmen born in that land will not report your arrival.
"The king, along with his ministers and the women of the inner apartments, will be captured by this stratagem.
Having said this, he caused his entry into the sea of sand.
When the lunar fortnight had waned, the camp became devoid of water.
Even there, the king remained for two or three days, moving about;
then, seeing his army distressed by thirst, he spoke to that minister:
"How many more days beyond the time already mentioned have been spent on the road?
How much of that path remains for the army, which is dying of thirst?
Then, laughing, he said: "O seeker of victory, as for the remainder of the journey..."
"What do you ask concerning the enemy's kingdom or the realm of Yama?
For it was for the sake of your master alone, disregarding your own life,
that I have skillfully entered the jaws of death along with your army."
"This is not merely a desert land; this is a terrifying ocean of sand.
Nowhere here can water be found; who will be your protector today, O King?
Having heard this, the entire army lost its composure.
Like a field of rice where the stalks remain after the fruit has been shattered by hailstones;
[hearing] the sound of the wailing of cowards who had abandoned all hope for life,
the king then raised his arm and spoke to quieten them.

"Minister, because of your deed, we who desire the welfare of our lord are thrilled; though here in this desert, we are as if bristling with joy like those afflicted by cold. Yet, even toward me, whose essence is unbreakable, such [affection] of yours is clearly manifest."

Your effort will come to naught, like iron striking a diamond. Like those who, mistaking it for a gem, grasp at a spark of fire and burn their fingers, you will surely lament today when your falsely severed limbs have been lost.
"Behold, by my command alone, O milk-producer, the earth today yields water,
just as the land of Vaiḍūrya produces gems at the roar of a cloud. Having said this, he tore open the earth with his spear to draw forth the water.
Desiring to lift up the waters of the Vitastā, as if with a trident, the three-eyed Lord Śiva [acted];
then, with the luster of the playful smile of the Fortune of the netherworld (Pātāla),
the river emerged from the subterranean realm along with the armies, out of hope for their lives.

That army dispelled the fatigue of his soldiers and fulfilled the desire of that minister, whose body had been wasted in vain. With his limbs mangled, that minister’s efforts rendered fruitless, he who had hoped for auspicious success— [The text continues: ...was reduced to such a state. His hopes for prosperity were shattered, and his labors proved to be in vain.
First, Yama entered the city of his own master; thereafter,
that king of crooked conduct, having seized the lord of the earth,
was reduced to the same state as his own minister.
Employed according to their utility, they were set in motion by him in various places;
even today, the rivers carrying spears (Kuntavāhinī) flow in the Northern Region (Uttarāpatha).
Although thousands of other wonders of the world continue to arise, [they do not equal his].

To avoid excessive prolixity, their specific histories have not been recounted. (KRT 4.0307cd) That even the great rivers of noble lineage are seen to have waters silent [and still] in regions harsh with solid rock and clouds, yet to emit terrifying roars; and that they appear clear during the proper season, yet become corrupted by turbidity when the sky is clouded—this is the truth: these two, direction and time, cause even the great to engage in conduct consistent with their own nature. (KRT 4.0308)

Is this the power of Kali, or perhaps of the throne of the lord of men, that he displayed such terrifying and wicked activities? (A *yugma*). The king, accompanied by his harem, remained in the city of Parihāsa.
Once, like a woman with intoxicating eyes, he thus commanded his ministers:
"If you consider the splendor of my city to be as it is, then burn down this excellent city which was built by Pravarasena."

Having heard this command of the king, whose authority was terrible and unassailable, they went to the heaps of horse fodder and set them ablaze in the windless enclosure. Watching from the top of the palace, [the king] saw his face illuminated by the flames of that fire.
He became like a fire-mouthed demon (ulkāmukha), fierce with the white laughter of joy.
(KRT 4.0313cd) To one who possesses such distortions as hatred, another appears falsely and strangely more intense, even though [the object] is clear by nature.
Indeed, the eye afflicted by the defect of darkness sees the moon and other luminous objects before it as doubled. (KRT 4.0314ab–cd)
If it were not so, how could he— who was the creator of countless cities— have known even a single city of that preeminent king to be superior? (A *yugma*) [KRT 4.315cd]
Then, his fatigue exhausted, he contemplated the sin of burning the city; with a sighing friend— his own internal fire of remorse— he touched that which,
though hidden within its hollows, produces a soundless crackling and leads to inexhaustible ruin.
They burn like withered trees containing fire within their hollows. Then,
seeing him grieving in the morning and filled with sorrow, the ministers spoke to turn away his anxiety, saying that the burning of the city was merely a falsehood.
When the city was destroyed upon hearing the news, the lord of the earth became free from sorrow,
like one who has awakened to find his son standing there after having been lost in a dream. "That word which is spoken by me when intoxicated must never be acted upon."
Praising those ministers who acted as they were told, he said:

"Fie on those servants who seek only the pleasure of their own livelihood and delight the king in what is pleasing yet improper—such as the sight of women and gambling. Blessed is this land by those great-souled ones who, disregarding even their own lives, forcibly protect the king when he has gone astray."
Even as that king presided over a majesty that surpassed Indra,
another fault arose, one characteristic of other monarchs:
namely, that although he had granted Śrīparīhāsakeśava to a neutral party, [he later seized it].

With fierce men, he struck down the Gauḍa king at Triśagrāma. At that time, the courage of those who lived under the Gauḍa was truly extraordinary: those steadfast men abandoned their lives for the sake of their lord, even though he was out of sight.
Under the pretext of visiting Śāradā, they entered Kaśmīra;
having gathered together, they surrounded the temple of Madhyasthadeva. Seeing that those who wished to enter were there while the king was staying in another region, [they acted].
The worshippers made the enemy-enclosing Lord Parīhāsa-Hari their own;
having obtained Rāma-Svāmin, they— exalted by their valor—
mistook him for Parīhāsa-Hari and, raising dust, treated him as such.
Having reduced him to pieces as small as sesame seeds, they scattered them in every direction;
being struck at every step by the armies that had marched out from the city,
those dark-complexioned men, drenched in blood, fell dead upon the earth.
Like fragments of the rock of Añjana Mountain, radiant with flowing minerals,
this earth was made brilliant by the showers of his blood; blessed indeed is this Vasuṃdharā, possessing such extraordinary devotion to her lord.

Fear caused by a thunderbolt ceases because of a diamond; from a ruby, prosperity arises; and poison is neutralized in various ways by the *gāruḍa* stone. Each of these is employed as a specific action according to its established power among gems. But what cannot be accomplished by the "jewels" of supreme men, who are exalted by immeasurable majesty? Where is the long path to be traversed, and where is devotion toward the Tranquil Lord?
That which was then performed by the Gauḍas was impossible even for the Creator;
at every step, such were the jewels among servants of kings, whose power derived from their extraordinary devotion to their master.

During the upheaval caused by the Gauḍa Rākṣasa, Śrī Parīhāsakeśava was protected as a favorite of the king through the sacrifice of Rāmasvāmin. Even today, the site of the city of Rāmasvāmin is seen empty.
The universe was once again brought under the auspicious sovereignty of the Gauda heroes through their fame.
In this way, the days of the king passed with various kinds of news:
sparse in his own city, but abundant throughout the ends of the earth.
Curious to behold the earth untraversed by others,
he then entered once more the northern region, which is boundless,
having been dispatched by Kubera and the other gods to test his power.
Then those various encounters of his with the Nairṛtas occurred;
even today, I believe that no part of the earth has been seen even by the rays of the sun where the king’s command did not roam at its own will.
Then, having been sent by the ministers who had long been unaware of his whereabouts, the messenger returned from his presence and spoke to them thus:
"Thus does your master command you: 'What is this delusion of yours that you wait for my return when I have entered this earth? Day by day, abandon the pursuit of ever-new victories.'"
"What business have you with me, now that I have entered my own kingdom?
For those who emerge from their own domain like rivers flowing toward the ocean,
there is never seen any limit to their sincere desire for victory."

Therefore, I shall declare to you the essence of conduct appropriate to your own sphere; O sinless ones, rule your kingdom without obstacle in accordance with it. While remaining here, always maintain your distinct identity as powerful lords.
For these people, like the Cārvākas, have no fear of the next world.
Even without any offense, those who dwell in mountain fastnesses are to be punished here;
for they would possess accumulated wealth and, taking refuge in fortresses, would be difficult to overcome.

The grains to be consumed for a year are commensurate with the extent of their fields; the oxen of the villagers do not exceed what is required for their work, yet they repeatedly provide more than enough, for by the end of the year their wealth has indeed increased greatly.

They would become fierce and cruel, capable of transgressing the king’s commands. When villagers ever obtain garments, women, rugs, food, ornaments, horses, and houses that are fit for city-dwellers— KRT_4_0349ab–cd.
When kings, out of pride, neglect their fortresses that ought to be protected;
when their immediate knowledge regarding their servants is observed to be lacking;
and when the livelihood of those bearing arms has become rooted in only one particular region.
If the scribes (*kāyastha*) are united through mutual marriage alliances,
and when kings look upon their offices of business as if they were mere scribes,
then it should be known without doubt that there is a reversal of the people's fortune. (This is a *cakralaka* [crossed] verse.)
Having inferred the consciousness of his hidden intention by following his outward gestures, I said: "The inner workings of those who possess the seed of kingship must be kept within the heart.

Just as the wind [infers] the proximity of a rutting elephant by the scent of its ichor, or as lightning with its manifested radiance [foretells] the thundering and rising of a cloud; || KRT_4_0354ab ||
"Action clearly reveals the steady mental disposition of a being that has been familiarized in another birth, a truth to be inferred by the skill of the wise.
My two sons, Kuvalayāditya and Vajrāditya, are equal to me;
yet the intellects of these two brothers, born of different mothers, differ according to their distinct characters."
"The elder brother must be consecrated in the kingdom whenever he becomes capable; at that time, you must by all means obey his command. That king may even renounce both his life and his kingdom."

Remember these words of mine: no one should ever grieve for him. Even if the younger brother is not made king due to negligence, his command must not be transgressed, and he must be protected even if he is difficult to manage.
"Among my grandsons, let this youngest boy, Jayāpīḍa, always be told: 'May you become equal to your grandfather.
Having bowed to her with a meaningful gesture, she [spoke] to her who had lost all hope for her husband.
They offered their final obeisance, shedding tears that fell like drops of water.
Then Caṅkuṇa, having assembled all his subjects, spoke,
drenching with his tears the earth that was scorched by the fire of separation from her husband.
"Let Prince Kuvalayāpīḍa be consecrated in the kingdom;
that virtuous king, whose name was Sugṛhīta, has gone to heaven.
By the gods, for the sake of increasing his treasury, [the moon] was created for that skillful one."
Since that success in alchemy has suddenly come to an end for me,
it is clear that even though that king was far away, by some power of destiny he remained effortlessly accomplishing tasks that were otherwise difficult to achieve.
Even when obscured by thick clouds, the sun causes the lotuses to bloom; even from afar, the rain-cloud brings a most cooling touch to the heat.

There exists an indestructible power in the great that acts at will; indeed, by the force of their majesty, even the most distant tasks are accomplished without restraint. For thirty-six years, seven months, and eleven days...
Having thus gladdened the earth, that moon among subjects departed for his home; meanwhile,
thick showers of frost fell upon him unexpectedly.
Some said that he perished in the region called Āryāṇaka; others said that,
in order to consume the long-accumulated wealth entrusted to him by the king,
he entered a fire somewhere in a place of distress.
According to the view of some, however, the mountain-dweller entered the northern region of the earth—
which is easily accessible to mortals— accompanied by his army;
indeed, his most wondrous deeds have been heard [of].
Likewise, the misfortune of his lord was heard to be even more extraordinary.

When the sun had set, some say he entered the waters of the ocean; others say he entered fire; and by still others, it is reported that he departed for another world. Oh, how marvelous! Even in the face of calamity, the reports concerning great men—who possess such incomparable modes of departure—betoken a greatness that is truly peerless.
Then Kuvalayāpīḍa,
who was born of Kamaladevī like the glorious Śakra from Aditi, assumed the sovereignty over the earth; by his generosity, he made the royal fortune both pure and devoted to him.
Like a mahoraga shedding its skin, though naturally dark,
he— his luster for a time eclipsed by his brother of equal power—
shone no more, like a lamp overcome by the heat of a fire.
Like bees following out of greed for ichor, moving in turn,
the royal fortune remained between those two, as if between the temples of two rutting elephants.
Then, together with the circle of servants who were to receive the wealth of both, [he departed].
King Kuvalayāpīḍa swiftly crushed his younger brother.

Having rendered the kingdom free of thorns, the king, having acquired power and possessing a victorious stride through his conquest of the quarters, then became one who had gathered all the necessary means for war.
At that moment, one minister transgressed his command—
either out of remembering his father’s words or through the agitation of pride. Then,
when night had arrived, the king, agitated with anger upon his bed, [reflected].

Bearing that transgression against his command, he did not go to sleep even for a moment. Thus, as he was eager to slay the one who had committed the offense, many who were worthy of death appeared to him as he roused his wrath.

The great ocean of his mind, churned by the churning-stick of reflection, subsequently produced the nectar of tranquility after the poison of anger had been destroyed. Then, his anger having subsided, he reflected: "The destruction of living beings has increased."
"For whose sake indeed should such a thing as this have appeared to me?
Having exhausted oneself in improper acts and even having committed the acquisition of sin, for whose benefit is this body maintained? To whom does it truly belong?"
For the sake of this ungrateful body, whose memory does not fail,
whose paths should be destroyed? Alas,
living beings do not perceive their own selves as they truly are.
Seeing that very same condition brought about by the Reaper of Time moment by moment—
[the face] which yesterday was like the bud of a lotus, white with a causeless smile, and now today is harsh with the growth of a beard and possesses the luster of heated copper;
[and which tomorrow morning will be] disfigured by withered, grey hair, resembling the head of an old goat— surely this face is being mocked by long-lived spirits.

Thus, having found no delight in the peace and happiness derived from contemplating such impermanence, he abandoned his kingdom and went to the forest of Plakṣaprasravaṇa. "Go, my good man, to the forest itself; let your mind be devoted to ascetic practice."
"Such prosperities are fraught with danger and are subject to momentary destruction. By thus renouncing his kingdom while remaining seated upon his own throne,
he indicated through this verse the fullness of his cultivation of dispassion.

The lord of men, who had attained perfection through unbroken tranquility and spiritual urgency, is even today seen by the fortunate on Śrīparvata and other such places. When his son had thus departed, Mitraśarman was overcome with grief.
At the confluence of the Vitastā and the Sindhu, that lord of the earth, together with his wife, gave up his life. Having ruled the kingdom for five and a half years,
that wise sovereign attained perfection, reaching the ladder that leads to the attainment of the supreme good.
Vajrāditya, Bappiyaka, and also Lalitāditya—
renowned as such, there was a king whose mother was Cakramardikā.
That man of cruel conduct was surely as ill-suited to his brother— who brought him joy—
as Durvāsas is to the moon;
[he took] from Parihāsapura the various collection of paternal implements.
That man of evil conduct, enslaved by greed for land, carried her off. To the passionate king, those various wives of others became as dear as mares are to a stallion eager for seed.
By selling many men to the Mlecchas,
he introduced the Mleccha-customary practice of trade within his realm.
Having enjoyed the earth for seven years, through the passion born of excessive indulgence—
That sinful king met his destruction through a wasting disease. From him was born to Queen Mañjarikā a king who brought an end to his subjects; thereafter, Pṛthivyāpīḍa reigned for four full years.

One born in the lineage called Mamma did not shine at all in the kingdom; then, having produced one named Saṃgrāmāpīḍa, he became king. Having obtained those two brothers, the kingdom did not shine at all.

Then, once the oppression of war had been stilled, like the orb of the sun having reached the seasons of late autumn and early winter, the illustrious King Jayāpīḍa— the younger son of Bappiya— attained the kingdom in due succession.

Remembering the words of his minister, "May he become equal to the Grandfather (Brahmā)," he set forth for the conquest of the quarters, having gathered his forces and desiring victory. Together with kings who had been brought under his control from their own lands by means of statecraft, he departed.
As he was departing, he questioned the elders in the vicinity of the Kashmiri gate:
"Tell me today, as you set out on your expeditions, how many soldiers were there in our grandfather’s army as it marched forth?"
Smiling, they said to him: "O Lord, what is the use of this question?
One is no longer able to imitate a thing that has already passed.
That ruler possessed one hundred and twenty-five thousand palanquins."
"Eighty thousand [soldiers] are with the god today for the exertion of victory.
Hearing this, Jayāpīḍa did not consider victory to be far off,
due to the power of Time as the earth rapidly shrinks.

Observing such a disposition in that king who desired victory, the elders displayed their knowledge of human nature toward King Lalitāditya. When he had marched far away, his brother-in-law named Jajja forcibly [seized power].

Having seized Kaśmīra through treachery, he himself took possession of the royal throne. Day after day, the soldiers from the king’s army, who were mindful of their own country, then turned back, facing forward with devotion to their sovereign.
Intending to proclaim his own power even without an army,
Jayāpīḍa entered into a certain agreement that was appropriate;
for the self-respect of that wise man remained unshakable.

By means of these [horses], he surpassed even the perverse ways ordained by the Creator. Having abandoned his own respective lands, he went to Prayāga together with his own limited forces, which were as swift as thought.
There, having collected the remaining horses swift as thought,

he bestowed ninety-nine thousand of them upon the twice-born, providing abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Another person who might give a full hundred thousand horses here— [the merit of these two would be equal].

Having uttered, "Let this seal of mine be a barrier," he gave the seal of the waters of the Gaṅgā to the illustrious King Jayāpīḍa, marked with the syllables [of his name] and intended for those traveling to various regions and directions.
Even today, having drunk the pure water of the Gaṅgā marked with his seal,
the heat of anguish increases in the hearts of proud kings.
He [granted] permission for the army to return to its own country through the mouth of a trusted messenger.
Having given [the gift], he departed alone for another camp during the night.
Like the sun among circles of clouds, he [passed] through the circles of kings,
reaching the secret refuge of the Gauḍa king, which was protected by the monarch named Jayanta.
Then he entered, in due course, the city of Pauṇḍravardhana,
which was delightful through its excellent governance and in which he took pleasure in the prosperity of the citizens.

Desiring to witness the *lāsya* dance, he entered the temple of Kārttikeya; accompanied by Bharata and observing the rules, he was well-versed in the sciences of dance, song, and so forth. Then, for a moment, he sat upon a stone at the entrance of the divine shrine.
[avoided by people who were startled by his extraordinary brilliance],
a dancer named Kamalā beheld him, who was full of splendor.

Filled with wonder, she beheld that man of extraordinary form running along with his hand resting here and there upon the back of his shoulder. Then she thought to herself: "He must be moving through this land in secret disguise."
Whether a king or a prince born of a noble lineage,
he thus practiced the art of wielding [the sword];
for with his hand shining, he carried these leaf-wraps upon his back and shoulder at every moment.

"Even an elephant with its ear-holes twitching in agitation does not turn back to look at a lion, though the danger from the attacking bees has passed; even when the threat from a herd of elephants is behind him, a lion casts a backward glance. Even when the clouds have ceased to appear, the peacock does not stop its loud cries, for the persistence of these behaviors remains long due to habit, even after the cause has vanished.
Thinking thus within herself, she transferred her consciousness [to the statue].
She sent her friend, whose heart was undivided [from hers], to his presence.
When her hand had moved away as before,
Jayāpīḍa turned back, looked at her, and saw the pieces of betel nut offered by her in her mouth.
"Whose are you?"— when the fair-browed woman was thus questioned by him with a sign of her eyebrows,
he learned her story as she offered him a betel-roll.
Through those various sweet words of hers, which produced such courtesy, [he gained further knowledge].

When her friend had finished her dance, she was led slowly to her dwelling. There, that graceful woman, whose speech was refined and charming, attended upon him with such supreme splendor that he too was filled with wonder.
Then, when the onset of night had become white with the moon,
she took the protector of the earth by the hand and entered the bedchamber.
Thereupon, lying upon a golden couch, intoxicated by wine—
Even though he was thus entreated, he did not loosen his lower garment.
Then, drawing her toward his broad chest,
the long-armed one embraced her— who was filled with shame— and spoke these words softly.
"O lotus-petal-eyed one, you do not captivate my heart;
rather, it is the constraint of time that makes me appear at fault.
O auspicious lady, I am your slave, purchased by your genuine virtues."

"Once you have learned the news shortly thereafter, you will surely show me courtesy. O proud lady, know me to be ready for some small task yet unfinished, and one who has resolved not to enjoy any pleasures."
Having spoken thus to her, he sighed as if sounding a lute with his hand adorned with a ring, and while seated cross-legged, he recited this verse:
"What concern for women can there be for a high-minded man who has not yet achieved his desire for victory?"
"The sun does not enter its twilight phase without having traversed the entire world.
By that verse recited from his own heart by the king,
she, who was skilled in the arts, recognized him as someone truly great.
And when that king desired to depart in the morning, his beloved wife,
having entreated him for a long time, earnestly requested that he not set out.
Once, having gone to the bank of a river to perform the twilight worship, he [departed].
Having arrived at her house, he saw her extremely distressed.
When he asked, "What is this?", she, with a smile on her face, said to him:
"A very large lion descends here at night and attacks living beings."
Day after day, he carried out the slaughter of men, serpents, and horses;
while you were long away, we were overwhelmed with fear of him.
Kings and princes alike were paralyzed by that dread.
"When the moment of leisure has turned into a moment of no-leisure, they do not even emerge from their homes here.
Having thus rebuked the innocent girl who was speaking this way, and having laughed,
Jayāpīḍa passed that night with her as if they were sharing a common nest.
On the following day, at the close of the day, having departed from within the city,
he waited for the arrival of Siṃha beneath a great banyan tree.
Then, from afar, Aṭṭahāsa was seen, possessing the hue of a blossoming *bakula* tree,
like the lord of beasts wandering as the messenger of Death;
he was traveling by another path, moving with a slow gait.
The lion-king challenged the lion with ease.
With ears pricked up, mouth wide open, whiskers trembling, and eyes blazing,
the son of the Creator rushed toward him with his forequarters raised.
As he was falling with his elbow placed in the opening of his mouth in a fit of rage,
Jayāpīḍa, acting with swift resolve, pierced his chest with a razor-edged dagger.
He released blood that resembled the vermilion on the temples of an elephant whose scent had been tasted [by other elephants].
His life was not abandoned by him, even though he had been split by a single blow.
Having bound a bandage over his wound and then concealing his elbow,
he entered the dancer’s house and slept at night as before.

When the night had turned to dawn, having heard that the lion was slain, the king, filled with joy, went out in person out of curiosity to see Jayantī. He beheld that massive-bodied creature, destroyed by a single blow.

Filled with wonder, he certainly considered the striker to be superhuman. Then, with astonishment, he beheld an armlet that had fallen from between the striker's teeth and been placed at his side, bearing the name Śrī Jayāpīḍa.
When the king asked, "Where could he be here?", the city became agitated with fear, suspecting the arrival of Jayāpīḍa. Then,
after reflecting thus upon the citizens, King Jayanta said:
O fools, why does fear arise in you at a time of great joy?
For it is heard that King Jayāpīḍa, powerful through the strength of his arms,
was wandering alone in a distant region for some reason.

"This prince named Kallaṭa is Kalyāṇadevī; she was designated by me, being childless at the time, to be given to him. If he, seeking that jewel, has come here of his own accord, he must be sought out."
"For one intending to set out for the Island of Jewels, the acquisition of treasures occurs from his own home; therefore, that ruler of the world must remain in this very city.
Having searched for him, you should say to him: 'Whoever would give me what I desire...'"

The citizens, placing their trust in the word of the truthful king, searched for him and reported his whereabouts as he resided within the abode of Kamalā. Then, the ministers and the women of the inner apartments approached him and, with great effort, sought to win his favor.

Then the king, having celebrated a festival, led her to his own palace. Thereupon, by that Kalyāṇadevī, who was intent upon auspiciousness, he was grasped by the hand as if she were the Royal Fortune (Rājalakṣmī) herself, now that she had been cast aside.
Manifesting his power there even without a complete array of forces,
he conquered the five lords of Gauḍa and their sovereign, his father-in-law; then,
remaining there, he escorted the remainder of the army that had been abandoned by its master.
Then Devaśarman, the minister and son of Mitraśarman, approached him;
requested by him, he then set out toward his own country,
placing the Goddess of Victory before him and Sulocanā behind.

Having conquered in battle the lion-throne of the King of Kanyakubja, that king of noble prowess seized the very crest-ornament of sovereignty. When he, whose formidable valor was bursting forth, had entered his own realm...
Accompanied by his armies ready for battle, Jajja went forth to fight. A most terrible conflict took place between him and Jayāpīḍa in the village named Śuṣkaletra for many days.
The king, who was beloved by his subjects, being unable to endure the decay of his kingdom,
was pursued in battle by bands of village and forest-dwellers. Śrīdeva, the outcaste of the village, reached the battlefield together with the villagers.
Wandering about and asking the warriors everywhere, "Where is Jajja?",
they saw him from afar in the midst of the battle, mounted on his horse, afflicted by thirst as he drank water from a golden ewer.
Whirling a stone to be thrown, he then hurled it into his mouth;
crying out, "Jajja has been killed by me! he released the sacrificial offering.
Having said, "I am going to assist the king," and having requested food from his laughing mother, he made a vow regarding the slaughter of Jajja and departed.
He saw him fallen from his horse, about to die, with a terrifying mouth crushed by a stone.

Leaving Jajja writhing upon the earth, his own [kinsmen] departed. Constantly distressed by anxiety over the potential fall of those capable of causing harm, he was deprived of the kingdom acquired through treachery within three years.

The prosperity of kings is indeed unstable, arising from the embezzlement of merchants' deposits, the deceptive seduction of courtesans, and treachery. When Jajja was slain, Jayāpīḍa returned and reclaimed his own royal fortune.

With his arm he bore the burden of the earth, and with his righteous deeds, the hearts of the virtuous. In that land where that king attained prosperity through the slaughter of his enemies, there was a city named Kalyāṇapura, and there dwelt the queen Kalyāṇadevī.
The king established a city named Vipulakeśava for Malhāṇa; Kamalā, for her part, founded a city called Kamlā after her own name. Having assumed the office of chief chamberlain, he—

Out of courtesy toward Queen Kalyāṇadevī, he brought about even greater prosperity. Just as the river Vitastā was brought down by the learned Kaśyapa to his own birthplace, this [learning] was introduced by him into this land, though it had remained far, far away.

To someone who clearly said, "This man is a fool with words," the lord of the earth summoned from other lands all those devoted to learning who were expounding [the scriptures], and he established a circle that bestowed all forms of knowledge.
He caused the interrupted *Mahābhāṣya* to be propagated within his own realm. Having acquired extensive learning from the teacher of grammar named Kṣīra,
that scholar Jayāpīḍa grew in excellence together with the wise.
He could not tolerate anyone vying with him for the status of a lord of the earth;
however, being pure-minded, he highly esteemed those wise men who vied with him for that status.
To such an extent did the reputation of the word "scholar" (paṇḍita) spread, even surpassing the reputation of the word "king" (rājan).

Despite those various faults, he did not succumb to despondency as time passed. While the king remained under the influence of the learned, the houses of the scholars were filled with kings who had arrived seeking his patronage and desiring the favor of the sovereign.
Having thus searched for them, the king gathered all those wise men together,
so that there was a famine of scholars in the realm of other kings as well. The superintendent of the minister Śukradanta’s kitchen—
By him, [the king] named Thakkia, having accepted [him] on account of his learning, he was promoted;
the learned Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa became the presiding officer of the assembly for that lord of the earth, receiving a daily salary of one hundred thousand dīnāras.
He appointed the poet named Dāmodaragupta, the author of the *Kuṭṭanīmata*, as his chief minister of statecraft, just as Bali did for the sage Kavi. Furthermore,
there were Manoratha, Śaṅkhadanta, Caṭaka, and Saṃdhimat.
Kavirāja and Vāmana were his poets, and others were his ministers.
In a dream, perceiving the rising of the sun in the western quarter,
he rightly rejoiced at the arrival of Dharmottarācārya in his land.

Possessing consciousness, that king became one who could distinguish between familiarity and solitude; he discerned the internal flavors of the objects being enjoyed. He perceived those things of great relish through his refined discrimination of taste, which others were unable to see.
What object of knowledge is there other than food for kings who are like blind oxen?

For one who has ascended the funeral pyre, whose memory is utterly destroyed by a violent great delusion from drinking the juice of red sugarcane, the company of beloved women who have made the effort to follow him in death is [the only thing known].

Just as the fragrance of garlands, ornaments, and bracelets may be absent from objects, so too is the auspicious majesty of intrinsic nature absent in the mindless [unconscious] world. His two powers— mantra and valor— were like two mirrors,
in which his single reflected form attained a thousandfold magnification.
Once, when five Rākṣasas had disobeyed the command of the Lord of Laṅkā,
a messenger stood before him and was told by him, "Bring them here.
Then that minister of peace and war, while departing, fell from his boat into the ocean.

Having torn out the *timi* fish that was swallowing the *timi*, he reached the further shore. Out of devotion to Rāma, Vibhīṣaṇa, who was beloved by mortals, sent the one who had delivered the king’s command back to his own country along with the demons he had given him.
Having filled the moat with wealth and Rākṣasas,
the king constructed the fortress of Jayapura, which was equal to Triviṣṭapa.
Having established a monastery containing three large Buddha images, he—
That man of meritorious deeds established the goddess Jayādevī within the city.
And in that city, Keśava— both as the fourfold Self and as Śeṣaśāyin—
surely establishes his presence, abandoning his station in the world of Viṣṇu.
Some relate that, having commissioned the other work, he had the Rākṣasas themselves construct the water by means of artisans;
for it is said that in a dream he was told, "Build Dvāravatī within the water."
Thus addressed by the enemy of Kaṃsa, he constructed such a city:
the external fortress was the seat of Śrī Dvāravatī,
while the inner city is even today called Jayapura by all people.

The minister Jayadatta, the son-in-law of Pramoda, the royal chamberlain and lord of Mathurā, constructed a monastery in that fortress-city of Jayapura, which was a vessel for the five great sounds of the earth-protector.
The pure Ācābhidha fashioned a garland for Hara, the Lord of the Night.
Again, having gathered all the necessary provisions, he set forth for the conquest of the quarters,
causing the great mountains on the shores of the ocean to tremble with his vast forces and massive elephants.

Though she had already entered the eastern ocean, the army following him shone like the Gaṅgā of Bhagīratha, which remains unbroken even as it flows over the Himālayas. Wandering outside the camp together with fierce Caṇḍālas...
On the night before his departure, kings headed by Mummuṇi waited upon him. Proclaiming his own name as Aṭṭinayāditya, the king adorned the eastern quarter with the city of Vinayādityapura.
Through excessive pride and great audacity, Fortune may ascend even the highest of mountains for those intent on reckless deeds. He [ascended] the fortress of the eastern lord named Bhīmasena.
He, bearing the marks of an ascetic, entered silently along with other vow-observers.
Having recognized him there as one seeking a vulnerability,
Jajja’s brother, named Siddha, who had been waiting for a long time, went and informed the king.
Then Bhīmasena suddenly bound that king,
just as the serpent Nahuṣa once bound Bhīma of terrible prowess;
while that hero, the leader among those who act with human effort, was thus held captive.
"I know that fate, which hates human effort, has raised its head.
Jayāpīḍa, however, remained undeluded even in the midst of most terrible calamity;
reflecting upon various means, he remained intent on his future success.
In the meantime, O Lord of Men, a most difficult-to-overcome calamity caused by the disease of spider-poison arose within the kingdom of the citizens.
Disease spreads through contact and is contagious therein;
therefore, due to the defect of the location, a person afflicted by a spider is avoided.
Having heard this, Jayāpīḍa applied his mind to the means for a remedy.
In private, he brought back various substances that had been used by his own servants.

Having consumed those things which provoked an excess of bile, the fire of his bile flared up and produced a fever; then, having poured the sap of the *vajravṛkṣa* tree over his body, he became covered with pustules.

Hearing from the mouths of the guards that he was covered in scorpions, Tripakṣa thought, "He will certainly perish," and banished him from the country. Thus, by the greatness of his own intelligence, he crossed over the ocean of calamity.

His fame, having pervaded the sky, seized the fortress of his enemies. (KRT 4.0529cd) That tree of the scriptures, which is constantly mocked by the ignorant because it never puts forth even roots or sprouts, truly bears fruit for a man during calamities and cuts away misfortune in a single stroke. (KRT 4.0530ab–cd)
Endowed with both learning and prowess,
a king named Māyāvyarāmuḍi, the protector of Nepāla, desired to deceive him. When [the Buddha] had entered his own territory, that king did not offer him a respectful greeting.

He marched with his army along a road that extended very far from the front. For him who was thus desirous of victory, the successive conquests of various kings required no separate effort as he pursued them.
Seeking his enemy here and there, now in a great place and now in a visible spot in every region—
like a hawk pursuing a pigeon within its own enclosure— he went forth.
Then, having completely eliminated all adversaries, he continued his conquest of the quarters.
He caused his army to encamp on the shore of the ocean near its edge. Then,
after two or three days, he set out toward the eastern sea,
leading an army whose banners were fluttering from the fatigue of being struck by the coastal breezes.
Then, on that southern bank of the river belonging to the lord of the earth,
Aṛamuḍi stood with his army, displaying its own royal umbrella;
beholding that powerful force resounding with the clamor of many kettledrums, [he was struck with wonder].

Jayāpīḍa blazed like a fire fed with clarified butter. Seeing the water of the river before him up to his knees and free from obstacles, he— being ignorant of the ground due to its unprecedented nature— plunged in angrily to cross it.

When the king had reached the middle [of the river], the tide began to rise; out of season, the river flowing near the ocean became bottomless with its waters. Likewise, the army of the lord of the earth, abounding in men, elephants, and horses—

Being overwhelmed by the surging [flood], it was destroyed in an instant. The king, his ornaments and garments cast away by the clash of the waves, was carried far off by the waters as he tried to ward off the billows with his arms.
The quarters of the sky became tumultuous with the piteous cries of one army and the roars of the other,
as well as the sounds of the river’s waves.
Acting with speed, [the soldiers] crossed the river from within its waters with their maces ready and armored.

And having drawn Jayāpīḍa [toward him], he bound him, having performed a festival; for there is no fixed rule whatsoever regarding the favorability of either destiny or the rain-cloud.
