For destiny, manifesting an intense pleasure for a living being, brings about an unpleasantness in an instant—just as that which, having quickly manifested the extinguishing of the heat of suffering from the calamity of long summer days, produces a discharge of lightning upon a tree.
He cast Jayāpīḍa into the hands of trusted guards within a very high stone chamber situated on the bank of the Kālagaṇḍikā;
thus once again the King of Kaśmīra was plunged into calamity.
Confused as to what ought to be done, he burned inwardly with grief.
Just as neither the moon among the arts nor the sun among luminous bodies could see him, so did that wise king protect him.
Not seeing anything, he went out with his eyes fixed upon some light; then, reflecting on means of escape, he came upon a nearby river.
There, verses composed by the king that revealed his state of mind were woven together; even today, they are remembered by the wise with moistened hearts.
For instance, while he remained there, the proud Devaśarman alone among the ministers [was not so affected].
Constantly reflecting on his master’s distress, he burned with grief;
intent on performing what was beneficial for his lord by sacrificing his own body,
he was enticed by messengers with sweet words and great efforts.

"Along with the glory of Jayāpīḍa, I shall grant you the kingdom in the Kaśmīra region"—thus was he informed by messengers. Then, when the counter-messengers had arrived and the agreement was fulfilled, KRT_4_0553ab–cd; KRT_4_0554ab.
Having taken up his camp, the minister went to the territory of Nepal.
Having established his camp on the bank of the Kālagaṇḍikā river, on this side of the ocean,
he crossed to the further shore with a limited retinue.

When he had been ushered into that assembly by the vassal kings who had arrived at the head of the procession, Aramuḍi, having honored him, seated the humble man upon a throne. Because he was exhausted from the journey, he was soon released by the lord of the earth.
Having been provided with hospitality by him, he spent the day in that man’s residence. On another day,
the king and the wandering mendicant, both having drunk from the same vessel and having reached a mutual understanding regarding their purpose,
sat together in a secluded place, firm in their resolve on what was to be done.

The minister said to the king: "The wealth acquired by Jayāpīḍa exists in the army; it is known to his trusted men, or perhaps to him. By giving it away, your liberation will come"—having spoken thus, he deluded him.
Therefore, I wish to ask him: "Where has the wealth been deposited?
For this very reason, I have kept my army gathered and have not allowed it to enter;
for those who hold a deposit cannot be bound while they remain in the midst of such a crowd.

Therefore, having summoned them one by one and bound them, the soldiers— whose hearts were unknown [to him] and who desired to speak— will not depart in anger. Thus, from that deluded man, the wise one obtained permission.
He went to the side of King Jayāpīḍa while he was still bound. Concealing the grief born of seeing him, that ocean of fortitude quickly made the house empty and questioned the king.
"Moreover, have you not lost your own innate splendor, which serves as the very wall [upon which things are depicted]? For when that exists, the conceptualizations of daring deeds are accomplished.
He spoke to him: "O counselor, I am thus situated, though unarmed."

"What wondrous deed could I perform with your splendor still remaining? The minister said to him: "O King, if your splendor has not yet departed, know that in this very instant you have crossed the ocean of calamity."
"Are you capable of leaping from this window into the waters of the river to reach the opposite bank? For the army would be torn asunder by such a long fall.
The king said to him, "One who has fallen from here cannot rise out of the water."
Without a messenger, even a leather bag here would burst from being thrown too far.
Therefore, this is not the right means here; nor indeed has he been insulted. I consider the abandonment of one's body by an enemy who has been thoroughly crushed to be highly praiseworthy.
Then, having made his decision, Soma said to the king:
"O Lord of the Earth, by some means or other, you must spend two *nālikās* outside the fire-pit;
then, having entered alone, you shall see that which has been prepared by me."
Having heard that this means of crossing the river must be practiced without hesitation,
he departed; having gone to the room for washing his feet,
he lingered there until the time specified by her had passed outside.
Then, having entered alone, he saw him fallen upon the ground, deceased,
having hanged himself by his neck with a firm strip of cloth.
With my body just slain, my frame filled with breath, I am now invulnerable;
mount me, O firm one, as I cross the river.
For the binding of the thighs of the rider, let the turban-band serve as the strap for your own thighs.

"Having entered him, I shall bind him and quickly cast him into the water"— seeing this inscription, which spoke of his body being torn by my nails and smeared with blood, she read it upon the sprout-like cloth tied around his neck. (Tilaka 4.577)
Alternately overcome by wonder and affection,
the king fell into the current of the river and reached the further shore.
Having regained his army, he entered [the city] and in a mere moment brought [the matter] to a conclusion.
He brought that entire assembly guard and the territory of Nepal to destruction;
even before the guards realized he had escaped from confinement,
he reduced them to nothing but a tale.
With dancing headless trunks and the sound of musical instruments mingling with the garlands cast off by celestial nymphs,
there was a festival of battle upon the king’s release from captivity.
Just as in the summer heat, mountains are far more to be avoided than the earth scorched by a raging forest fire.
It is a marvel that on that very same spot, having thoroughly enjoyed the snowy mountain— moist with the melting of dense frost—
it became, in an instant, a place of slaughter for the Jajjās and others who were their enemies; yet it was there that the skillful minister Devaśarman achieved his wondrous success.
Indeed, that son was not equal to his father Mitraśarman,
just as Saturn is not equal to the radiant sun;
for when that minister, who was like a protective jewel, had departed, [the king was left unprotected].

The king regarded the sovereignty he had attained as if it were merely the greenery of a forest. At the conclusion of his world-conquest, the withering of his pride departed from that lord of the earth, just as the minister’s service emerged once more from Lake Mānasa.

The kings greatly admired that great circle of women’s kingdoms conquered by Citra, as they considered it a victory over the entire collection of his own senses. Having donned the ear-ornament of glory taken from the conquered realm of women, [he shone].
And he established an office for judicial affairs known as the Dharmādhikaraṇa;
he also created a second office for administrative business called Calagañja,
which was utilized when his own treasury was located at a distance during military expeditions.
What else could it be? For the Goddess of Victory, who dwelt upon his arms, the four oceans became the jeweled mirrors for her playful charms.
Then, surrounded by kings, he entered Kaśmīra once again.

For a long time, the king enjoyed the prosperity acquired through victory. Once, in a dream, a certain person of divine form addressed that monarch— who was exalted by his conquest of all quarters— with palms joined in reverence.
"O King, I have been living happily in your realm along with my kinsmen.
I am Mahāpadma, a lord of the nāgas, and I have come to you for refuge.
A certain Dravidian mantra-practitioner is intent on leading me away from here."

If you desire water, I shall show you a mountain in your own country whose soil contains gold ore— a source of abundant benefit— to sell in the desert region. Therefore, if you would protect me, I shall point out that mountain to you.
Having heard this in a dream, the king dispatched spies in all directions;
having brought her from somewhere, he questioned her about what she intended to do.
Granted immunity from fear, she related everything exactly as the Naga had told her.
Filled with wonder, the lord of the earth himself asked once more:
"How was that serpent, preeminent in power, able to be extracted by you from within the lake that extends for many yojanas?"
He informed him: "O King, the powers of mantras are inconceivable.
If you wish to see them, come quickly and behold this marvel.
Then, followed by the king, he reached the vicinity of the lake.
With arrows discharged after being consecrated with mantras, he dried up the water;
then the king saw a creature with a human face wallowing in the mud.

"O King, I shall seize this serpent that extends for the distance of a *vitasti*, though it is surrounded by many smaller snakes, once it has been contracted by my mantra," he said; having spoken thus, he was forbidden by the king with the words, "Do not seize it!"

Then, by the king’s command and through the power of the mantra, that [lake] was quickly restored; it returned to its former state as a lake, once more pervading the horizons. Having bestowed Dravidian wealth upon him and dismissed him, the king reflected:
"Even now that Nāga has not yet given you the mountain in the form of gold. While he was thus reflecting, the serpent spoke to him in a dream:
"By what service may this mountain, a mine of gold, be shown to you?"

The habitual attachment to staying [in one place] is what, through positive and negative concomitance, activates the notion in an embodied being that "this is my own country" and "that is a foreign land. Yet,
out of fear of humiliation, I have come to you once again for refuge.
That very thing has been demonstrated by you yourself, who are the true refuge.
Like the ocean, a lord is known by those who have sought his protection as one who cannot be shaken;
what other shame could there be greater than that he is overcome even in their presence?
When I am overcome by those other women and unable to protect myself from their gaze, with what pride shall I look upon the faces of those women,
who share the same nature as the cause of my own confusion? (4.609–4.610ab)

We are being made to act like common folk for the sake of sport. Or rather, what is so wonderful about kings who, blinded by the intoxication of power, act without foresight and do whatever comes to mind?
Kings consider the humiliation of the exalted to be a mere sport;
yet they know that for them, such humiliation is death with breath still remaining as long as life lasts. For kings, honor is disregarded when it serves their own purpose.
Yet, even at the cost of their own lives, those of noble mind place [the teacher] on the side of what is to be accepted;
they esteem the great and strive to serve them even when treated with contempt. By what can their profound knowledge of the true nature of the mind be inferred?
"Just as with you, we shall not show you that place in vain;
rather, that mountain of yours, from which flows a stream of copper ore, will be shown to you.
Having spoken thus, he gave her to him in a dream.
Just as one awakened at dawn reaches the mountain of copper ore, he,
drawing out copper from that place known as Kramarājya,
fashioned ninety-nine crores of dīnāras engraved with his own name.

"Whoever could perform a full hundred million [verses] would defeat me"— thus the king established a rule to humble the pride of monarchs. Like a poetic riddle (*samasyā*), that lord of the earth remained with his deeds yet to be completed.
He hurled it [at him] because of his inability to match [the king's] supernatural powers, as was the case with the other mountain-dwellers.
Then, O protector of the earth, due to the reversal of the people's fortune,
the king suddenly abandoned the path of his grandfather and proceeded by the way of his father.

"What is the use of the hardships of world conquest and the like? Let wealth be acquired from one's own country. Being thus entreated by the scribes (*kāyastha*), he punished his own province with fines for the sake of the greedy officials in charge of the treasury, such as Śivadāsa and others.

His desire for wealth increased, and he fell under the sway of greed. From that time forward, kings became dependent on the facial expressions of the scribes (kāyasthas), as these individuals arose among the Kashmiris to obstruct their own commands.
Whatever counsel that king had when he was seized by various monarchs,
that very same counsel became his firm resolve when he was occupied with the thought of binding his subjects.
That which brought tranquility to the virtuous, he taught to the wicked.
Jayāpīḍa’s scholarship and his proficiency in oppressing the subjects—
like Saudāsa, he was one who took away the lives of many people;
he never, even in a dream, reached satiety in performing deeds unworthy of praise.
"Let us commit this very sin, keeping it in our hearts"—thinking thus out of curiosity, wanton women and kings would, alas, act with fickleness and cruelty even once.
Then, their minds overcome by evil, they do not suffer as those low-born people do who feel remorse even when merely touching others; nor do they feel shame like those who kill their own parents.

Through the practice of greed, he likewise became cruel for three years; together with his share of the harvest, he took the autumn fruit as it was gathered. With his intellect destroyed by greed, the king [seized] those who gave only small fragments of wealth.

He regarded the *kāyastha*s—who seize all one's possessions—as benefactors. (KRT 4.0629cd) Timid sea-monsters and certain kings are alike: those who, having taken from their own waters, recognize as "giving" only when they relinquish drops of wealth; and alas, others—even those of the wicked *kāyastha* caste—who, having openly plundered everything, consider themselves "hidden benefactors" only when they bestow mere fragments. (KRT 4.0630ab–cd)
Oh, how unshakable was the fortitude of the Brahmins at all times! Though they had been adversaries even to that sword,
those who remained after others had fled to foreign lands eventually desisted.
Though they cried out, neither death nor the king could prevent it;
ninety-nine Brahmins perished in a single day.
Then the king, overcome by cruelty, declared, "This must be reported."
Thus, even by the wise, this perversion of praise has been applied in poetic works to that cruel king of perverted conduct, who,
having already fully accomplished his purpose, brings about the increase of virtues [in others].
What difference is there between the illustrious King Jayāpīḍa and Pāṇini?
During the occasion of explaining the *Bhāṣya*, he was surpassed by verses that displayed his profound expertise;
thus was this reversal brought about by the wise themselves.
What difference is there between the illustrious Yaśodharman— who caused harm to Brahmins yet established the finality of the elements—
and Pāṇini?
And [what difference is there] between one who stands on the bank of the Candrabhāgā and steals the value of cotton?
He heard that ninety-nine brahmins had died in those waters;
consequently, he ceased his seizing of planets [and other assets] immediately,
yet he did not relinquish the land belonging to the inhabitants entirely.
Then, at the time of the announcement, certain twice-born men, who were like cotton-wool in their insignificance, suddenly cried out before him when struck by the doorkeeper:
"Manu, Māndhātṛ, Rāma, and others were preeminent kings."

Even in the presence of others, the Brāhmaṇas must not be treated with contempt. For when provoked to anger, Brāhmaṇas are indeed capable of incinerating in a single moment heaven along with Indra, the earth with its mountains, and the subterranean realm with its lordly serpents.
Hearing that, the lord of the earth, his back no longer turned by his vassals,
raised a single eyebrow and spoke these words out of pride:
"What is this fever of arrogance in you, deceitful mendicants who subsist on mere crumbs?"
"By which you speak words proclaiming your own power like sages.
Then, while they stood silent, terrified by his formidable frown,
a twice-born man named Iṭṭila, a treasury of Brahmanic luster, spoke to him.

"Since the sages follow the presence or absence [of dharma] according to the nature of each age and act in accordance with the ruler's conduct, why should we not do the same? Did Viśvāmitra, or Vasiṣṭha—that treasure-house of asceticism—not say so? (Kṛt 4.0646–0647ab)
"Are you Agastya, or could it be someone else?"— with such pride the king spoke to him.
Then, blazing as it were, his form difficult to behold due to its flashing splendor, he hissed like a snake with upraised hood,
and gasping with anger, he said to the king:
"Wherever Hariścandra, Triśaṅku, or even Nahuṣa existed, I alone was capable of becoming like them through the agency of Viśvāmitra and others.
Laughing, the king spoke to him out of anger toward Viśvāmitra and the rest.
"Hariścandra and others have perished; what might happen if you were to become angry?
Striking the earth with his hand, the twice-born man then spoke in anger:
"If I am enraged, would not the staff of Brahmā fall in an instant?"

Hearing that, the king laughed and said to the Brahmin in anger: "Let this Brahmā-daṇḍa fall; why does it still delay? When the Brahmin then replied, "Indeed, it has already fallen upon this wretch," [the king was struck].
The king’s golden staff fell, having slipped from the canopy;
wounded in that limb by it, his body was drenched with the moisture of the crushing impact.

Swarming with multitudes of wriggling worms, he was tormented by saws being driven [into his flesh]. Having been made to experience this agony, which served as a description of the future sufferings of hell, his life-breaths, longing for release, abandoned him after seven nights.

Having endured the punishment inflicted by the Brahma-staff, the lord of the wielders of the staff— who had himself unleashed that sudden punishment— then approached the presence of the wielder of the staff. For thirty years, he remained there with his mind unsettled.
Thus, the enjoyment of the earth by the king became full of such fierce heat.

Likewise, the kings—like fish whose thirst is stirred by the turbid waters of wealth—abandoning their own stability, follow the path of evil. Indeed, they are caught by the multitudes of fishermen who are the followers of the God of Death (Kārtānta), for they are devoted to the net of the eternal hell.
Aiming for that man whose sins were burnt away and who had perished, Amṛtaprabhā,
his mother, fashioned an image of Amṛtakeśava for the sake of his resurrection from death. Thereafter, the lord of the earth was named Lalitāpīḍa.
He who was born from Queen Durgā, known by the name Jayāpīḍa,
came to rule a kingdom corrupted by misconduct, which became a source of enjoyment for courtesans while he himself remained impassioned and neglected his royal duties.
Wealth acquired through evil deeds by a father destined for hell— he who, bestowing it upon the wandering minstrels and others, made expenditures appropriate to them; those who,
through their kinship with the paramour, obtained refuge in the royal palace.

The libertines made him an insider among the arts of courtesans. Deprived of his crown and bracelets, he considered the ornaments of his body to be hair bitten by women’s teeth and a chest marked by their fingernails.

Whosoever was skilled in the talk of courtesans and whosoever was clever in jesting, each one attained his favor; neither the hero nor the scholar did so. That king, possessing fierce passion, remained unsatiated even with few women.
He considered Jayāpīḍa— who had emerged from the kingdom of women— to be dull-witted compared to himself, who was victorious;
he laughed at the former kings who were addicted to world conquest, while he himself,
enjoying the pleasures of courtesans, remained in the midst of his contemporaries.
By warding off with humorous remarks the elders who were causing him to shrink back,
the company of jesters received rewards from him, who was well-pleased;
they were like the attendants at a festival, clearly skilled in the art of ridicule.
Accompanied by courtesans, he shamelessly brought the elder ministers to the assembly hall;
that man of wicked conduct made those worthy of respect wear beautiful garments and other finery marked with the footprints of unchaste women, as if they were mere painted pictures.
The proud minister Manoratha abandoned him completely,
being unable to subdue him and turning his back on the path of compromise;
[he recognized] his evil deeds, his lack of spiritual discipline, his despondency, and his treacherous conduct.
... For a ruler of evil conduct, there is no remedy other than avoidance.
Bestowing Suvarṇapārśva and likewise Phalapura upon the Brahmins, that lordly king, the sovereign, remained thus for twelve years with Locanotsa.
Born of Queen Kalyāṇadevī to King Jayāpīḍa,
he then became the lord of the earth named Saṃgrāmāpīḍa;
that monarch also bore another name, Pṛthivyāpīḍa.
He brought his empire to completion within seven years. That king, bearing another name, Śrī Cippaṭajayāpīḍa, was then succeeded by King Lalitāpīḍaja, who was still a mere child.
To King Lalitāpīḍa, who was seized by the demon of passion,
she— who was born from Jayādevī as the courtesan Kalyapālī— was given;
that daughter of Uppa, the keeper of the tavern at the village of Akhuvagrāma, [he took].

For that king had imprisoned him, lusting after his beauty. Protected by his maternal uncles— the Padma, Utpala, and Kalyāṇa— who were skilled in their own duties and shared in the enjoyment of the earth, he remained a child.
His maternal uncles took up for him the five great sounds as his superior arts; others took up various other fields of activity.

Jayeśvara was appointed by Jayādevī, the mother of kings, whose command was honored by her brothers who had brought the empire under their control. As for the wealth of kings that is defiled by the entry of the meager riches of the wretched, [it is not like his].

Before long, that [wealth] was led to its destruction by certain unprecedented means. For whatever wealth had been expended by the son of Jayāpīḍa, all of that property was subsequently seized in succession by his sons-in-law.
Those who possess fortune have been made to cry out for those fickle enjoyments by means of riches arising from the good fortune of their sisters' hips;
yet, having gradually cast off their childhood, they act with unrestrained impulse.
Those base-born men plotted for the destruction of their royal sister's sons.
Then, having consulted together through malevolent rites out of a desire for the kingdom, those wicked men killed both the sister's sons and that king, their master.
When he had been killed in that manner, those twelve years passed while they ruled over the earth;
yet, being full of mutual pride, they did not wish for the kingdom to belong to any one of them alone. For those kings whose territories were overrun by them, there remained only their names.
A mutual conflict arose between them as they strove to perform various extraordinary deeds.
Then, a son was born to King Bappiya by Queen Meghāvatī;
although he was the eldest, he was excluded from the kingdom because he lacked political acumen.
This Tribhuvanāpīḍa begot upon Jayādevī a son, King Ajitāpīḍa; Ut pala forcibly made him [the ruler].
(Yugma) To that king, [Ut pala] offered those [revenues] arising from the overflow of the treasury of Śeḍā and other such places. (KRT_4_0691ab)
From the fifth stage of calculation, they gave [him] food and clothing;
yet, as he grew weary from speaking with only one person day after day,
the king, who was dependent on him, did not desire those other five who were equal in appearance.
Those kings, who had seized the kingdom and removed its sovereign,
performed the rites of consecration for cities, temples, and other such structures;
accompanied by their offspring, they enjoyed the kingdom that was now bereft of a master.
Like two wolves full of mutual envy toward a peaceful buffalo in a desolate place,
so did Utpalasvāmin establish Utpalapura with an *utpala* lotus,
and likewise Padmasvāmin established Padmapura as the handiwork of a *padma* lotus.
The queen Guṇojjvalā, resplendent with virtue,
established one monastery at Adhiṣṭhāna and a second at Vijayeśvara. Dharma, striving for righteousness, was the cause for the construction of [the temple] by Dharmasvāmin.
Kalyāṇavarman, a man of virtuous deeds,
being wise and possessed of great wealth, provided five thousand dīnāras and various implements for each of his cows, which were dedicated to the illustrious Lord Keśava.
Having bestowed eighty-five thousand cows as a gift,
he who provided the materials for the consecration of the water-jars for Mammasvāmin—
among the total of that one person alone, who is capable of calculating the number?
How much more so, then, for those brothers who possess abundant wealth?
Whether that fortune was acquired through treachery or earned through virtuous deeds,
it is surely to be envied by all because of their generosity with it.
Temples were built by them beside those abodes of other Asuras;
they attained a resemblance to young elephants standing near the elephants of the quarters.
When his sister’s son had attained peace in the eighty-ninth year, [the king]—
They enjoyed their wealth without obstacles until the end of twenty-six years. Then,
a fierce battle broke out between Mamma and Utpalaka,
in which the Vitastā river had its flow obstructed by slain great warriors.
The poet named Śaṅku, who is the moon for the ocean of the minds of the wise,
composed the poem titled *Bhuvanābhyudaya* with reference to him.
Yaśovarman, the son of Mamma, slew him in battle,
just as Āryaman [the Sun] seizes the splendor of the stars.
Then, having uprooted Ajitāpīḍa, he who was born from the conflict known as Saṃgrāmāpīḍa—
The king was given the name Anaṅgāpīḍana because he was tormented by love and the like.
Due to his inability to endure the passion of love, he manifested a transformation of indignation. His enemy, Sukhavarma—the son of Utpala—ruled over his kingdom.
Then, after three years had passed since Utpalaka’s arrival,
he made Utpalāpīḍa the king born from Ajitāpīḍa;
among those kings who were like the full moons of the month of Āśvayuja.

Even among servants, some who were successful attained great prosperity. At that time, his minister of peace and war, named Ratna, was a possessor of such wealth that he even constructed a temple for the Lord Ratneśvara.
Having uprooted the lands of Bhehura,
Dārvābhisāra, and others, the Vimalāśvas became lords of the earth; the village-dwellers, men of business,
and others [ruled] until the lineage of the kings of the Kārkoṭa dynasty had almost entirely perished.

The lineage of the Utpalakulyas attained great expansion upon the earth. Then Sukhavarman, who had nearly attained the status of a king through his own capability, met his end due to hostility with his own kinsman named Śuṣka.
Then the minister named Śūra, the son of Sukhavarman,
placed his trust in Antivarmā— who possessed all virtuous qualities— thinking, "He is fit for the kingdom.
Then, in his thirty-first year, for the sake of pacifying the upheaval among the subjects, he [installed him].
Having repelled Utpalāpīḍa, he made that very king [his own];
that success which had rendered his father and grandfather’s efforts fruitless was attained with ease by his grandson of meritorious deeds.
Those jars which were said to constantly carry out the futile labor of drawing water from the ocean— how wonderful that,
by the production of this single [son], they displayed here in an instant the sport of drinking up the entire sea!
Thereafter, he was placed upon the head, where the inaugural turban had been bound by the side-glances of Royal Fortune.
King Avantivarman, as the ninefold consecration from the mouths of golden jars suddenly descended upon him,
bore it upon his two ears like the newly established system of statecraft taught by the kings born of his own lineage— those who were like the moon and the sun.
Under the guise of two jeweled earrings and the pretext of a clear royal parasol, the king shone, casting a radiance formed by the lotuses that serve as the throne of Lakṣmī.
The Fifth Wave.

May that Lord protect you—he whose tongue, though vibrating separately, speaks such words to one another in their fresh union: words that have different meanings yet identical syllables, as if there were some longing for these [words] in the hair of serpents, like that of a male cuckoo; and as if his throat were delighted by the rays of the sun before his eyes, O observer with eyes and ears!
Having attained sovereignty, Avantivarman has cleared away all thorns.
By his wondrous deeds, he caused the bodies of the virtuous to bristle with joy.
As for those two— the king and the minister— they were both equally sovereign in issuing commands to one another, yet servants in receiving them.

Grateful, patient, a supporter of the earth, a minister, devoted, and free from pride— such an unbreakable alliance is seen only rarely through the power of past merits. Having attained sovereignty, that king, a discerning ruler, beheld the splendor of royalty.
With his mindfulness unimpaired, the wise one thought within himself as follows:
"The Fortune of the lords of the earth is cherished in the embrace of elephants;
yet she, having aroused desire, brings defilement even to those of exalted soul."
There is no one at all who, having first displayed favor,
is not later tormented by her, as if by the affection of a low-born woman.
This [affection] has increased in the ocean along with the fickle celestial courtesans.
Whence did she learn the conduct of those who wander alone? For though she was well-acquainted with them for a very long time, this woman, devoid of affection,
did not follow any of the kings— who were her travelers on the road to the next world— as they departed, for they were strangers to her.

Why do those kings who have passed to the other world not act as masters over this gold, the dining vessels, and the rest that were accumulated in the treasury? Having eaten from these vessels which are the leftovers of others, those lords of the earth [have gone].

Why did they not feel shame, or why did they not care about purity? Upon seeing the names of the King of the Dead (Pretabhūpāla) engraved upon large silver platters and bowls, who would not be filled with apprehension?
Torn from the throats of those wishing to die once the noose of Time has entered them—
whose hearts would such necklaces captivate? They are ill-omened and impure,
having been cast off by former men who, tormented by tears hot with grief, were themselves about to die.

Who would not feel a sense of shrinking upon touching these ornaments? Fortune, who remains perpetually sullied even by her constant proximity to the waters within the ocean, attains purity when bestowed upon worthy recipients who share the lot of the destitute, just as a doe becomes pure through the cleansing fire.
Having thus resolved, the king reduced gold and other treasures to powder and,
with his own joined palms, offered it as *karambha* to the twice-born.
When it was said, "Excellent, O King," the twice-born man, out of joy, spoke without reserve;
saying, "Excellent, O Avantivarman," another offered many salutations with joined palms.
Having bestowed his entire fortune upon supplicants, the virtuous Avantivarman—*Kṛtī* 5.0017ab–5.0018ab.

His royal splendor was reduced until only the fly-whisk and the parasol remained. Yet, during his youth, the majesty of kingship— which is difficult to withstand— belonged to him, even amidst the widespread ruin of his vast kinsmen who possessed infinite wealth.

Having conquered his brothers and rivals who were overwhelmed in battle, he ruled for many years a kingdom free from all thorns. Then, having successfully established the kingdom without obstacles, he, tender with affection, [proceeded].

Having divided his royal fortune among his kinsmen and dependents, the king enjoyed it. His half-brother, named Śūravarmā, who was deeply devoted to him and beloved by his relatives, was consecrated as the heir apparent in that vast kingdom.
He who, having demolished the two embankments known as Khādhūya and Hastikarṇa,
constructed Śūravarmasvāmin and Gokula— [he],
complete [in merit], a temple for the immortal greatness of Pūrṇamahiman.
The other brother of the king, named Samara, who was skilled in virtuous deeds, established a monastery measuring five cubits on the wheel [of the earth],
and likewise installed the fourfold Keśava as Samarasvāmin.
Two others, the two younger brothers of Śūra, named Dhīra and Vinnapa, became lords of the Gaṇas by their own names;
these two wise ones established themselves on earth as dwellings for the learned,
while their power and experience remained concealed under the guise of madness.
The two Haras, having assumed physical forms, attained the status of the foremost members of the assembly.
(Yugma) The illustrious Mahodaya was the royal doorkeeper of Śūra;
he was the one who established the sovereignty of the lord Mahodaya. (KRT_5_0028ab–cd)
In that celestial temple, he appointed as the reciter (vyākhyātṛ) one named Rāmaṭa, a teacher renowned for his exertion in grammar;
[this was done] by the minister of the lord of the earth, Śrī Prabhākaravarman.

He built a temple for Viṣṇu named Prabhākarasvāmin. Having arrived together with parrots, he gave [the birds] to the domestic parrot; once they were released during the consecration ceremony, he created a famous row of parrots known as Śukāvalī.
The science, whose flow had been interrupted, was once again introduced into this land by the heroic minister,
having honored both the learned and the courtiers. Possessing great splendor, it was carried forward by the suitable yoked teams of the kings.
The wise men, for whom honor had increased, entered the assembly of the king.
Muktākaṇa, Śivasvāmin, the poet Ānandavardhana,
and Ratnākara attained renown during the reign of Avantivarman.
The bard Māndāra acted appropriately toward the heroic minister when he recited this noble verse (*āryā*) in order to instill in him a sense of resolve and mindfulness:
"This is the occasion for doing good, while this prosperity— fickle by nature— still remains."
When prosperity is ever-present, what opportunity is there to offer further assistance? By him,
who constructed many dwellings upon the site of the Lord of the Gods, that temple of Śiva and Śivā was established in its enduring state.

Having established Śūreśvara in his own lofty residence as it were, the wise king built the Śūramaṭha for the ascetic’s enjoyment. In that excellent city named Śūrapura, which he had himself founded, [he established it].
Stationed at the site of Kramavarta, he established the temple of Ḍhakkā;
and from the eastern courtyard of Sureśvarī, he built the shrine of Hara, the Lord of Beings (Bhūteśvara). Furthermore, Śūrajā Ratnavardhana constructed a monastery within the Śūramaṭha.
The wife of Śūra, named Kāvyadevī, of pure lineage,
gave birth to Sadāśiva by Sureśvarī; he was known as Kāvyadevīśvara.
The modest Avantivarman bestowed upon his brothers a share of the royal prerogatives, and he granted the full honors of a king to the heroic [Bhāravi] along with his son;
for the monarch followed the will of his minister as if he were a deity.
From his childhood, though a Vaiṣṇava, he displayed himself as a Śaiva.
In the sacred field named Viśvaikasāra, which grants liberation to those who die there,
that king founded a city that became a seat of abundant enjoyments.

There, having first installed Avantīsvāmin before his attainment of sovereignty, the successful king, once he had secured imperial rule, then established Antīśvara. By the king, [shrines were likewise established] at Tripureśvara, Bhūteśa, and Vijayeśa.
With that silver bathing tub, he fashioned three thrones.
Even for Śūra, as he meditated upon that king as his own tutelary deity,
dharma, life-breath, and even his son were disregarded for the sake of pleasing him.
And so, once when the king had gone to worship the Lord of Beings (Śiva),
and his own offerings for worship had been presented according to his means,
he saw [a certain object] prepared by the attendants upon the deity’s pedestal.
There stood a wild bitter vegetable known as utpalaśāka.
The king questioned those stationed there regarding the reason for its presence; they then informed him, with their knees placed upon the ground and palms joined in reverence.
In the region of Laharī, there is a powerful man named Dhanva,
a servant of King Śūra who is like a son to his minister. By him,
whose power was unrestrained, the villages were seized.
This very offering is presented to this Lord of Beings.
The King, describing the agony produced by a sudden colic, made what he had heard as if unheard; then, having abandoned his worship, he went forth.
Abandoning the worship and perceiving the Lord’s sudden departure and his spear as having a cause, the hero became an investigator of the circumstances. Then,
having understood the truth, he quickly [proceeded] to the presence of the Lord of Beings (Bhūteśa).
Enraged at his circle of mothers, Bhairava entered his house;
having thinned out his retinue because of the excessive number of people who had been forbidden,
he then sent messengers again and again to bring Dhanyā.
Making the earth tremble with the trampling of his infantry host,
that cruel man, whose own body was unshakable, slowly approached the presence of the hero. As soon as that armed man had entered, those urged on by the hero—
They severed the head of the living man right before Bhairava;
having thrown that blood-spouting body into the nearby lake,
the steadfast hero, his resentment washed away, emerged from the king's presence.

Hearing that his head had been severed by the minister— as if it were his own son’s— the lord of the earth’s anger subsided, and he became filled with a sense of shame. Then Śūra, having inquired after his welfare, addressed him who said, "I am slain."
Having raised the Lord from his bed, he performed the remainder of the worship.
Thus, in all his duties, that [servant], knowing the inner disposition of the lord of the earth,
accomplished each beneficial task even without being told, even at the cost of his own life.

Those two royal ministers were seen, and not merely heard of, as being free from mutual resentment, malice, or corruption; such others as they have never been seen before. They were like Śrī Meghavāhana and Antivarmā in their imperial sovereignty.

This plague-free period lasted for ten years for all living beings. During that time, the autumn heat was experienced on their backs by the *pāṭhīna* fish, who, free from fear from any quarter, left the water and came to the banks in the cool season.

For the sake of favoring the worlds, Bhaṭṭa Śrī Kallaṭa and others, having attained perfection, descended to earth during the time of Avantivarman; for while their life stories are many things to be told, even the account of a single one among them is purifying.
This incidental account shall now be described:
This region, variegated by the waters of the great Padma lake and by rivers with abundant currents,
was always one where harvests were meager.
By the powerful exertion of King Lalitāditya,
the waters were drawn out somewhat; thus, it attained its origin there to a small degree.
When Jayāpīḍa had passed away in due course and the kings possessed little power,
the earth was once again overwhelmed by floods of water;
the tax of one thousand and fifty dināras became the standard.
When the land was afflicted by famine and the cause for purchasing grain had arisen,
the illustrious Suyya, the Lord of Food himself, descended to earth through the merits of Avantivarman in order to sustain living beings.
The fact that he was not born from a womb was certain even at the fourth stage of life for that wise man, whose origins were unknown,
as evidenced by his deeds which were wonders to the world.
Long ago, while she was sweeping away a heap of dust from the street as if it were a covering...
A Caṇḍālī woman named Sūryā obtained a new earthenware vessel.
Having removed the lid from it, she saw lying within a child with eyes like lotus petals, sucking his own fingers.
"By what mother has this handsome boy been abandoned? Alas for my misfortune!"—thinking thus, her breasts overflowed with milk out of affection.
While she was not censuring the touch [of the child] in the house of the Śūdra woman who was his nurse, Kṛṣṇa grew.

Provided with a livelihood by her, that child was brought to maturity. That intelligent boy named Sūrya, having grown up and been taught the alphabet, became a teacher of children in the house of a certain householder.

In social gatherings, clever men surrounded him— who was pleasing to the hearts of the virtuous due to his observances such as the vow-bath— and who possessed clear discernment. While they were engaged in their discourses, they censured the deluge of the waters.

"I am wise, but my purpose is gone; what shall I do? he said. Hearing those words from the spies of the king—who spoke like one deranged—due to his self-restraint, the monarch remained for a long time filled with wonder.
Then the king, having summoned him, asked, "What do you say?

He, being steadfast, spoke even before the king, "I am [the one]," and so forth, remaining unperturbed. Even when his own people told the lord of the earth, "This man is a madman," he remained undisturbed.

Desiring to see his own intellect, he entrusted his personal wealth to it. Having easily taken many vessels for crossing from the treasury, he boarded a boat and departed swiftly for the kingdom of Maḍava.
In that village named Nandaka, which was submerged by rising waters,
the king deposited her alone and became intent on searching for her whereabouts.
"He is truly a madman," they said, even as those in the assembly spoke.
Having heard that report, the king became intent on searching for its conclusion.
Having reached the kingdom of Krama in the region named Yakṣadara,
he cast two dināras into the midst of the water with both hands joined in reverence.
There, rocks rolled down from mountains resting on both banks squeezed out the water so that it flowed back upstream; at that time,
villagers afflicted by famine were searching for coins.
Having extracted stones from the current, they thoroughly cleared the Vitastā. Thus, for two or three days, having skillfully drawn out the water,
the laborers bound it on one side away from its place.
By means of a stone dam constructed by Sūrya of wondrous deeds,
the entire river Nīlajā was blocked for seven days;
having cleared the downward flow and remedied the rolling stones, [the water was released].
Having broken through the embankment of stone barriers that had been constructed,
she rushed toward the ocean as if longing for it after a long period of confinement;
then, that river flowing to the sea began to flow swiftly.
The earth, though drained of its waters, shone like a pond adorned with mud and shimmering fish;
it appeared like the vault of the sky when free of clouds, yet clearly marked by its blackness and the stars.
Wherever he perceived the traces of the flood from the deluge, [he recognized the former state of the world].
In various places, she created new channels from the current of the Vitastā;
with many streams forcefully ejected from her primary source,
the river shone like a black female serpent whose single body supports many hoods.
To the left flows the Sindhu with its three branches, while the Vitastā flows to the right; those two rivers,
which met in the presence of the ancient King Vainya, continue their course today,
for even at the end of a kalpa, their flow does not cease.
Their meeting took place at the edge of the city,
beginning with the Sun; even today, they remain stationed there, as if standing before the laughter of the City of Fruit (Phalapura).
Viṣṇusvāmī is at the confluence, and Vainyasvāmī is on the two banks.
But today, for him who has reached the vicinity of Sundarī’s abode,
Hṛṣīkeśa, reclining in yoga, is worshipped on the bank of the Sūryā.

Even today, withered trees growing on the banks of rivers’ former courses can still be seen, marked by lines of reeds pulled down by hunters. With tongues of shimmering waves, he seized those rivers as his path.
Like a mantra-master binding female serpents according to his will,
he constructed stone embankments extending seven yojanas from Vitastā;
thus he made the waters of the Mahāpadma lake restrained.
By whom the Great Lotus Lake was joined with the Kuṇḍa,
flowing out through the path of the bow-mechanism and other structures,
like water from a machine; having thus lifted the earth from the waters, like the Primeval Boar.
He established various villages crowded with many people;
by damming the waters with embankments, he created places resembling basins (*kuṇḍa*),
which the people call "Kuṇḍalas," all of them abundant in every kind of grain.
Even now, the rivers, emaciated by autumn, reveal clusters of uprooted pilings that,
through their watery scent, resemble the binding posts for elephants;
for he had not discarded those miserable vessels within the depths of the unfathomable waters.

When the water had receded at Nandikā, that [land] was obtained from the edge of the dry ground. Having inspected various regions consisting of villages not dependent on rain for their water, he distributed them with water divided by means of rivers.
And he sprinkled the villages with water and brought earth;
as each [patch] dried up in a certain moment, he applied that much [earth] to his heart.
Considering in due time that each village was ready for the sprinkling, he poured forth streams of water.
Having conceived its dimensions and divisions, he cast it away;
and with rivers such as the Anūpā and others, he filled all directions.
It possessed the splendor of an abundance of noble fields yielding excellent fruit. (Tilaka)
Neither was it done by Kaśyapa, nor by Saṃkarṣaṇa; rather,
this lifting of the earth from the waters and its restoration to the field of the twice-born was accomplished with ease by that virtuous Sūrya within this very circle.
The building of the bridge with stones, the subduing of Kāliya in the water—
those deeds which were accomplished by Viṣṇu over the course of four births, were achieved by Sūrya through a single birth alone from his mass of merit. (A pair of verses.)
In that land of great abundance, where formerly— since the beginning of creation— a sum of two hundred *dīnāras* was the cause for obtaining a single *khārī* of grain;
from that time onwards, a marvel occurred right there in the realm of Kaśmīra.
The purchase price was declared to be thirty-six *dīnnāras* of grain and salt.
On the bank of the Vitastā— which, having emerged from the waters of the Mahāpadma lake, resembles heaven itself—
he established a city marked with his own name.
By him, a boundary was established in the lake that pervades the horizons—
a boundary for the fish and birds that shall remain as long as the world endures.
Having made the village named Sūryakuṇḍala the property of the twice-born, [he gave it].
In honor of Sūryā, he constructed the Sūryā-setu in her name.
By him, thousands of villages were established on the lands reclaimed from the waters;
these were founded by Avantivarman and others, with Jayasthala as their foremost site.
Through such accounts of righteous conduct,
his majesty having been fully established, Avantideva protected the earth like Māndhātṛ.
Then, seized by a disease that made him eager for the departure of life, he departed.

That field is situated at Jyeṣṭheśvara on the Tripureśa mountain. There, at the end of his life, the hero, with palms joined in reverence, revealed his Vaiṣṇava nature, having long concealed his own misfortune.
Thus, at the end, while listening to the Bhagavadgītā with a purified soul and meditating upon the abode of Viṣṇu, he was liberated from his life.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha,
in his fifty-ninth year, that lord of the earth reached his end;
when he had passed away, the minds of those whose hearts were swollen with individual wealth [fell into despair].

The desire for sovereignty was equally strong among the many members of the Utpala lineage. Then, with great effort, the chamberlain Ratnavardhana installed Śaṅkaravarman, the son of the king of Avanti, as the monarch.
The minister Karṇapa, out of enmity toward him, appointed the son of Śūravarmā, named Sukhavarman, to the position of crown prince. Consequently,
a feud arose between those two, the king and the crown prince.
In every moment, the kingdom was as if mounted upon a swing; for there,
the heroes such as Śiva and Śakti, having abandoned their lives for the sake of their master’s work,
obtained the opportunity to test their own fortitude.
Although their masters promised them gifts and honors,
those enemies did not submit to compliance because of their singular focus on virtue;
having abandoned all desire for material gain, they were never taught by egoism.
So long did they not live the life of dogs, subsisting upon the darkness of ignorance.
Then, having somehow conquered the highly resplendent crown prince,
Śaṅkaravarman made his own victory resound with a mighty roar.
Having repeatedly engaged in battle with Samrāṭ Samaravarman and others,
he experienced a fame that was united with the sovereignty he had attained.
Then, having conquered his rivals and acquired royal fortune, the lord of the earth—

The illustrious Jiṣṇu was full of great resolve to undertake the conquest of the quarters. Due to the force of time, in that region where the wealth of the people had dwindled, nine hundred thousand foot soldiers emerged from his gate.

He whose commands were once resisted even on the outskirts of his own city now imposed his orders upon the crest-jewels of kings. As he proceeded toward the quarters of the world, he became the living tradition for the uninterrupted transmission of the sacred scriptures.
Led by his own wisdom by King Śaṅkaravarman,
that army of his increased at every step through the forces of other lords of men,
just as a river increases by the small streams entering it from all sides.
The mountain valleys, sought out by the terrified King of Dārvābhisāra,
did not provide any refuge for his armies, as they were overwhelmed by the roar of his host.
In an instant, he seized the monkey host with his own formidable troops of monkeys.

He made that fortress, which had never before been reached, a guest of another fortress. Nine hundred thousand elephants and three hundred thousand horses, along with a hundred thousand cavalry, formed the vanguard of his army.
That conqueror of Gurjara brought the King of Trigarta, Pṛthivīcandra— who was apprehensive of his own defeat— to the state of a laughingstock in the darkness [of exile].
He had already previously bestowed upon him his son, named Bhuvanacandra, as a hostage.
For he had indeed approached his presence to pay his respects. Then,
seeing that army approaching toward him like a surging great ocean, with its many leaders moving in vast circles, [he was struck with wonder].

Because he feared his own bondage at the end of their union, he fled far away, his vital energy expanded by *nirvāṇa*. Thus say those who know the past even today of him whose beauty was without equal. (Tilaka) KRT_5_0147–KRT_5_0148ab.
The terrified kings beheld him as if he were the fierce God of Death himself.
In battle, he uprooted the long-established fortune of Alakhāna, the king of Gurjara, and in an instant instilled in him a sorrow that would endure for ages.
Having given him the region of Ṭakka like a finger out of humility, the lord of Gurjara withdrew from the circle [of vassals] as if it were his own body. He bestowed that empire,
which had been seized by the sovereign of the Bhojas, upon him.
When the descendants of the Thakkīyaka lineage had become servants as doorkeepers for the lords of Darad and Turuṣka—
who were like lions and boars— the wealth of those two was [appropriated].
Between the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains, there was a region like Āryāvarta;
in Udabhaṇḍapura, kings dwelt free from fear,
like mountains in the great ocean terrified by the agony of having their wings clipped.
Just as among the stars, just as in the sky, and just as in the Northern Region,
his fame alone was vast, like the orb of the sun.
That illustrious Śāhi Lalliya, who took refuge with Alakhāna, was filled with wrath.
He did not obtain service from that emperor who was intent on repelling [his advances].
Having thus completed his conquest of the quarters, he returned to his own realm;
in the region known as Pañcasatra, he established cities named after himself.

The beloved wife of that King Śrīsvāmirāja, the lord of the sea routes, was named Sugandhā, just as the full moon is the beloved of the night-maker. Together with her in that preeminent city, the king resembled the sovereign of the gods.
In that place, he constructed Śaṅkara and Gaurīśa, as well as Sugandheśa.
Among those two temples of Gaurīśa and Surasadman, the twice-born man named Nāyaka—
learned in the four Vedas— built by him a temple for Vāgdevī, the abode of the lineage of the Goddess of Speech.
In this present age, poets nourish their own compositions by plundering the works of others, and lords do so by seizing the property of others. Such a king,
being of little strength, [acts] for the sake of proclaiming his own city.
He carried away the very essence of that city of jests:
the wearing of turbans, the sale of livestock, and so forth—
whatever was characteristic of that town came to exist in that [new] city.
By the minister Ratnavardhana, who was devoted to his sovereign, O King,
the auspicious Sadāśiva was established under the name Śrīratnavardhaneśa.
It is a marvel that the elephants of the king’s fame, their forms purified by cascades of glory, [have become so white].

They become stained by the dust of addiction to calamities. Then, in due course, through excessive habituation to greed, the king’s mind became so occupied that he grew skilled in oppressing his subjects.
With his treasury depleted by numerous vices he had undertaken, from moment to moment,
he seized the entire wealth of the gods and others through methods of harassment;
he plundered the wealth of the workshops, cities, houses, villages, and so forth.
When he had established what was called the "Eightfold Division" housework,
he took wealth from the temples arising from the sale of incense, sandalwood oil, and so forth,
under the pretext of a small fraction of the purchase price.
Having assigned the supervision to appointed officials,
he swiftly plundered sixty-four temples of the gods;
that king [levied] taxes from the villages belonging to those temples.
Having personally accepted the land, he established its cultivation like a farmer.
Having fixed a scale for the annual tribute that was three-quarters less than the full amount, he gave more to the assembly under the pretext of the value of blankets for use and other such items.

Those villagers who, staying in distant regions, had not yet arrived with their loads, he fined for one year at half the value of the load for that region. In the following year, he fined all those who had still not arrived the full value of the load.
By that very same reckoning, he punished the villagers village by village.
Thus, he first cast down this burden-bearing [institution],
which stood in thirteen forms as the messenger of poverty for the villages.
By means of collecting taxes from villages such as Skandaka, including levies on liquor and trade,

and through various other exertions such as the infliction of punishments, he stripped the villages of their wealth. By means of collecting fines for theft, weights-fraud, and village-offenses, [he further impoverished them].
Thus, he established this administrative system for domestic affairs.
When those duties were divided, he appointed five secretaries;
likewise, as the sixth, he appointed the excellent treasurer named Lavaṭa, who was as capable as Śakra.
Having accepted his own descent into hell as a favor,
that fool committed sins against future kings or their officials.
In this circle,

there is no one other than Śaṅkaravarman who disregards those possessed of learning, nor when the majesty of kings declines. When a king who is the foremost among the virtuous suffers a loss of wealth, his reputation is likewise lost.
By that fool by whom the *kāyasthas*— the sons of slave-girls— were set in motion,
so too, through his oversight, the earth became the food of the *kāyasthas*,
just as a change of color arises from the plundering of kings.
While that terrible suffering of the subjects was occurring, his son, named Gopālavarman, moved by compassion, once spoke thus to the lord of the earth:
"O Father, there remains a deposit previously entrusted to you as a giver."
That boon which belongs to one true to his promise is now being sought by me.
(Kṛt 5.183cd) Due to the instigation of the scribe, these [demons] have been set in motion today by the God;
because of their exertion, the vital functions of embodied beings now consist of nothing but breath. (Kṛt 5.184)
Indeed, there is not even the slightest benefit for my father, appropriate for both worlds,
to be gained by this oppression of the people.
Who can explain the profound matter concerning the realm of the unseen?

Even when undesirable things are seen, nothing other than the result of this [king's] action is perceived. On one hand, all calamities, foremost among them disease and famine, are seen; on the other hand, there is the singular greed of the lord of the earth toward his subjects.
The prosperity of a king who has conquered greed is not welcomed by some, just as the expectation of fruit is abandoned in the case of an out-of-season flower. Yet,
for a lord, generosity, truthful speech, and eloquent discourse are the means of winning over all.

Greed is the first and most strenuous effort toward the destruction of those two [valor and policy]. Just as a cloud reduces the majesty, future prospects, and splendor of a winter day to mere memory, so too does greed reduce the majesty, future prospects, and splendor of kings to mere memory.

Heirs become arrogant toward one who has begun an undertaking out of fear of expenditure; no servants will do what is pleasing to one whose mind is anxious for a return favor. When their master’s life is constantly endangered by a hoard of wealth, his own kinsmen would strive against him as if he were an enemy; what unpleasant thing, then, might not be done through greed? This labor of serving the king is a new hardship, bringing no friendship to people.
"Therefore, O Lord of Creatures, let this which originates from greed be restrained.
Having heard these words of the prince, radiant with benevolence,
the king, his lower lip cleansed by a smile, slowly spoke these words:
In this matter, these words— consistent with reality and tender with kindness—
now cause me to recall my former state of mind. Formerly,
in my youth, when my inner self was as moist with affection as yours, [I felt thus].

O child, his affection for his offspring increased until it was fully developed. Thus, when it was hot, I was made to wear a heavy cloak, and in the cold, a fine silken garment; on foot and without footwear, I was led about by my father.

Seeing me wandering with my horses in the hunt for deer, wounded by thorns and with tears welling within, those who were walking ahead grumbled at him. He said to them: "Having been an ordinary man, I have obtained this kingdom."

From time to time, he understands the toil of service endured by his attendants; having experienced such suffering himself, he will certainly understand the pain of others. Otherwise, having attained sovereign power, he would become deluded by the thought that he is a master even within the womb.

By such means as these, I was well-trained by my father; yet even by me, having obtained the kingdom, the subjects have been thus oppressed. Just as one who has been born into a body forgets the pain of dwelling in the womb, so too [have I forgotten].
Likewise, once you have attained the kingdom, you must certainly reflect upon what was previously considered. Therefore, let a single boon be granted to me today:
having obtained the kingdom, do not cause excessive oppression to the subjects.
When he was addressed by him with words full of envy, the prince, his face cast down in shame, was watched by the king’s attendants and the libertines who exchanged smiles with one another; for,
out of fear of being parted from his wealth, he had turned his back on the company of the virtuous.
The poets Bhallaṭa and others practiced inferior modes of livelihood; however,
the poet Bhārīka was without wages,
yet through his favor, Lavaṭa became one whose salary was two thousand dīnāras.
His birth in a family of cowherds was validated by that very fact:
because of his speech, which was as appropriate for milk as it was free from corruption, he did not possess divine speech.
With his beard wrapped [around his head] and a turban on, the minister of King Sukha held his forefinger at the tip of his nose; he thought:
"This attire, which is appropriate for a nobleman, is ill-suited for a lord who indulges in misconduct."

By following his whims, he suffered a humiliation like that of an actor. (Yugma) Together with his followers, out of fear of treachery, he treacherously slew the brave lord of Dārvābhisāra, Naravāhana, during the night. (KRT 5.208cd–209ab)
When the curse of his subjects fell upon the king who had strayed onto the wrong path, his thirty and twenty sons perished without any disease. For kings,
lineage, fortune, life, wife, and even their very name [depend on the favor of their subjects].
"In an instant, the destruction of those who act against the welfare of their subjects occurs.
This has been said, and will be stated further on; let this be clearly reflected upon. Just as even his name perished through his cruel deed.
He made his own city famous by the name Pattana; for who else, like Śaṅkaravarman, could cause such a name to vanish?
He appointed the nephew of Sukharāja as the governor of the gateway.
In the place called Vīrānaka, he killed an attendant through negligence.
Out of anger at that, the king himself, emboldened by liquor and having granted him leave to depart,
uprooted Vīrānaka and entered the Northern Region (Uttarāpatha).

Having conquered vast regions situated along the banks of the Indus, he then returned after being saluted with prostrations by the kings who were overcome with fear. As he entered the city of Uraśā, he was joined by the inhabitants of Uraśā.
For the sake of a dwelling, a conflict suddenly broke out among the soldiers.
A Śvapāka, perched upon a mountain peak, struck him;
by his own negligence, the swift-flying arrow entered his throat.

Desirous of dying, he said to his trusted attendants, "Take the camp and protect it," and having spoken thus, he mounted a palanquin and departed from that place. Perceiving that his capacity for vision was failing, he spoke slowly with a low voice.
Embracing the body of his wife as she wept, he spoke in a feeble voice:
"Having entrusted for protection the son named Gopālavarman—
who is like a mere infant and has no kinsmen— to the Great Queen Sugandhā..."
In the seventy-seventh year, on the seventh day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, while his arrow was being extracted, Mārga himself perished. Tilaka.
While Sukharāja and others were guarding the army in foreign lands, KRT_5_0223ab.
Concealing him with various tales, they proceeded as if they were going toward the Lord of the Earth.
With mechanical strings that produced the effect of bowing and rising from their heads,
they caused the subordinate kings who arrived at each salutation to perform the same.

When six days had passed and he had reached his own residence named Bolyāsaka, they, freed from fear, performed his funeral rites there. Then the three queens, Surendravatī and the others, followed after the king.
Velāvitta, Kṛtajña, and the skillful Jayasiṃhādvaya—
these two, along with Loḍa and Vajrasāra, followed him as his servants.
Thus, by these six who had mounted the funeral pyre, he was suddenly consumed by fire.
Then Gopālavarman,
radiant in his righteousness and true to his word, protected the earth while being guarded by Sugandhā;
even though he lived in the midst of the wicked, such as Lālitaka and others.
Although he had not yet passed beyond childhood, he did not succumb to those evil influences. The queen mother, intoxicated by pleasures even more so because of her widowhood,
desired the minister named Prabhākaradeva.
Thus, out of intense delight in their mutual enjoyment, he was marked by the treasurer—
who had plundered the wealth of that passionate woman— with the three circles of the crest-jewel of the erotic sentiment, the very seat of good fortune.
In Udabhāṇḍapura, he conquered the kingdom of the Śāhi.
Having subjected those who transgressed his commands to the name of "Kamaluka," the Śāhi—
He bestowed the kingdom upon Toramāṇa, the son of Lalliya; then,
having returned, he entered the city, exultant in his victory,
full of pride in his own person which was the abode of the intoxication of valor.

That paramour of the king’s mother, filled with egoism from his victories, daily inflicted humiliation upon the honor of the heroes through his insults; just as a base lover does in the house of a courtesan, so did he act in the king’s palace.
"Let there be no entry for anyone else while he is there;
for one who has gradually learned the news, he will be a plunderer of wealth and honor. Thus, he became exceedingly influential at the court of King Gopālavarmā.

"Whatever is not found in the treasury has all gone to the war with the Śāhis," he said to the king, who was intent on counting the treasury. Then the treasurer, having become the king's confidant, [spoke] to the one who knew the Khārkhoda [treasury].

He caused a malevolent ritual (*abhicāra*) to be performed against his kinsman named Rāmadeva. By that act of sorcery, King Gopālavarmā— having enjoyed the earth for two years— perished, consumed by a sudden fever.

His evil deeds having become manifest, that sinful Rāmadeva, agitated by the fear of royal punishment, himself destroyed his own body. Then Saṃkaṭa, the brother of Gopālavarman, was seized in the street.
Having obtained the kingdom, he became lifeless after ten days. Then, when the extinction of King Śaṅkaravarman’s lineage had occurred,
Sugandhā herself assumed the sovereignty at the request of the subjects.
He established Gopālapura, Gopālamaṭha, and Gopālakeśava;
he also founded a city marked with his own name for the increase of dharma. Nandā, born of an irreproachable lineage, was the wife of Gopālavarman.

Even as an infant, she became the bearer of the lineage of Nandāmaṭhaka. At that moment, her mother-in-law, desiring progeny, placed her hopes in Jayalakṣmī, the wife of Gopālavarman, who was acting as a mediator within [the family].

When her children had perished at the end of her pregnancy, she became exceedingly distressed; she was intent on bestowing the kingdom upon some member of her lineage. At that time, [he who was] capable of protecting the earth and exercising restraint and favor—

There, the lineage of the *tantrin* foot-soldiers became united through their concerted efforts. Then, for two years, Sugandhā herself, having taken refuge with a single division, governed the kingdom as a friend to the *tantrins*.

Once, indeed, intending to bestow the empire upon a worthy recipient, she presented the ministers and vassals— who were dependent on her alone— to her counselor. At the end of the lineage of Avantivarman, [she installed] the grandson of Śūravarmā.
Gaggā’s own wife conceived a son by Sukhavarmaṇ.

[Thinking], "He shall be devoted to me solely out of affection for his kinsman," the desire arose in her mind to have him named Nirjitavarman upon the kingdom. (A yugma). KRT_5_0251cd–KRT_5_0252ab–KRT_5_0252cd.
Because of his addiction to sensual objects, he was told that by her;
for while he remained awake at night, he slept during the day, corrupted by a lack of exertion. He received the name "the Lame One"—what fitness does he have for sovereignty?
When some ministers had spoken thus and were about to strike him down,
the son of Varma was defeated by the infantry of Tantri— who had emerged from their ranks and joined together—
and the Pārtha was made king at the age of ten. (Tilaka)

They considered that by uprooting Sugandha, they had performed an act of atonement for those who caused the loss of their honor, according to the words of the Lord of the Treasury. Deprived of their imperial sovereignty, they departed from the capital city.
With tears falling that seemed like offerings made for her necklace,
she perceived each servant who had come to her by hereditary succession as a refuge;
as she departed, she saw each one of them joined with her enemies.
In the eighty-ninth year, having assembled, the soldiers of a single division went and brought back from Sugandhā the one who resided in Puṣkapura.

Hearing that [army] was approaching out of pride, all the stringed-instruments players (*tantriṇaḥ*), intent on battle, set forth at the end of Caitra to show favor to the son of Pṛthā. Having defeated those who were broken in their cohesion in the month of Vaiśākha after ninety years, they—
They bound her as she fled, having formed a compact group with their ranks drawn up in a single file. Bound by them within a monastery that was without a guardian, she perished.
The rise and fall of beings are unstable; the workings of fortune are manifold.
Then,
in that preeminent circle of vassals, a succession of calamities arose from every direction, caused by the depletion of both wealth and men.
King Janaka, having become the protector of the young monarch, was himself crippled.
Even the ministers oppressed the people,
being intent on seizing bribes; like village scribes under a king, they engaged in mutual strife, providing excessive bribes through their service to the administration.
In that region, such as Kanyakubja and others, which had been granted by kings,
the livelihood of the administrators arose from the issuance of *huṇḍikās* (tax receipts) by the monarchs.
Formerly, at Purāṇādhiṣṭhāna, Viṣṇu [was appointed] by the minister Meruvardhana.
He who established the one named Śrī Meruvardhanasvāmin—

at that very moment, his sons, who were like cogs in the wheel of profound treachery and who secretly desired the kingdom, brought about the ruin of the subjects through their own efforts. (A *yugma*).
Together with Sugandhāditya, Śaṅkaravardhana’s eldest son, who was secretly bound in friendship with them, plundered the royal palace. At that moment,
when the subjects were diminished, it was like the application of caustic to a wound.
The autumn rice, which had flooded the entire land, flourished like a reservoir.
(KRT_5_0270cd) When a *khārī* could be purchased for a thousand coins, food became difficult to obtain;
in the terrible ninety-third year, there was a destruction of people due to famine. (KRT_5_0271ab–cd)

The Vitastā river became difficult to discern in its waters, as it was entirely covered on all sides by corpses whose bodies had swollen from being long submerged in the water. When the entire circle of the earth had thus become composed of bones, one could no longer distinguish between land and water.

Even out of fear of all living beings, a unity arose in the cremation grounds. The ministers of the king, having acquired wealth through the sale of vast stores of precious grain, and those who were protectors [of the people], likewise attained great opulence.
That minister, whom the king had appointed over such subjects,
would sell them and carry away the money from the tax-collectors (*tantriṇaḥ*) as promissory notes (*huṇḍikā*).
When there was a downpour in the forest, he would [flee] while being harassed by wind and rain.
Just as someone who has reached a cool palace looks upon all the people outside [with indifference],
so too the base man, seeing the people in distress while remaining long in the capital like a cripple, highly esteemed his own happiness. (A pair of verses)
The subjects, who were dear to protectors of the people such as Tuñjina and Candrāpīḍa, were thus brought to destruction at that moment by the king-demons. At that time,
no kings anywhere attained long-term stability.
Like bubbles produced by the falling of rain on a stormy day,
Pārtha was sometimes born from his father himself,
and sometimes he brought him forth and then existed through the cycle of the wheel of worldly activity.
The youth gratified the circle of harem women, who were like mares lame from old age, by means of the practice of sexual union; he, whose seed was like the fragrant sun,
[gratified] Queen Bappaṭadevī with merciless festivals of love.

She, too, allayed his itching desire for wealth with riches. The sons of Meruvardhana themselves gave that woman of lovely limbs to the cripple, their kingdom being bound by the fortune of their sister’s beauty.
Out of longing for Sugandhāditya, Queen Mṛgāvatī herself, desiring her beloved, entreated him and enjoyed his company. In turn, he became their servant for the sake of increasing their pleasure.
Like a single eating bowl used daily by two poor women,
[the kingdom was shared] by the two sons, out of rivalry, for the sake of obtaining the sovereignty, with their own minister.
Faith in amorous dalliance was bestowed along with wealth and ritual fees.
Then, having produced Pārtha, his father became dependent on a cripple;
in the ninety-seventh year, he was consecrated by the three Tantris in the month of Pauṣa.

In the ninety-eighth year of the Māgha era, having consecrated his young son named Cakravarman upon the throne, he passed away, his merit exhausted. While Pārtha desired the paternal kingdom, the followers of [Cakravarman] obstructed him.

There, the cavalrymen engaged in battle with those who had but a single limb. For some time, that infant king was protected by his mother, Bappaṭadevī; for ten years, he was protected by his maternal grandmother, Kṣillikā.

Because their misconduct was unmanifest due to their youth, the protection of those two by him was faultless, resembling the caressing of a serpent that has cast its slough while on its perch. Then, in the ninth year, a son was born to Mṛgāvatī from the three strings.

Having established Cakravarmāṇa, King Śūravarmā was deposed. Devoid of affection and intent on their own self-interest, the maternal uncles and ministers departed, failing to provide what was due to the councilors, which became the cause of his overthrow.
Although that king was of good conduct, he did not become dear to the courtesans and the musicians without the payment of abundant fees, just as a virtuous man is not beloved by them.
When a year had passed, having produced him [the son], they perceived the king through the sight of his birth.
Furthermore, those who had shaken off the triple fetters bestowed many benefits upon Pārtha. There was a courtesan named Sāmbavatī, who established the temple of Sāmbeśvara;
she was dear to Pārtha and was well-versed in the circles of the *tantras* and the assembly of adepts (*cakrikā*).
Kālāpekṣī and Cakravarman desired even more wealth than that;
in the month of Āṣāḍha, when he was eleven years old, it was again produced by those three.
Having brought forth Pārtha and the others, it was formerly enjoyed by them through the cycle of the wheel.
And by those various means, they obtained their livelihood from him;
by whom his father and brother were uprooted from the kingdom; and even by those kinsmen who, having given him a daughter in marriage, wronged him in return.
That man of ruined intellect bestowed the office upon those very sons of Meruvardhana who had committed visible offenses.
Śaṅkaravardhana, having been made lord of the department of oxen (the *ukṣapaṭala*) by him, [ruled].

Even in his domestic affairs, he was disrespectful, hypocritical, and a hoarder of wealth for Śambhu. In the month of Pauṣa of that very year, due to a lack of funds, he fled in a state of panic, fearing that the officials would demand payment from him on their *huṇḍikā* (promissory notes).
While Maḍavarāja was still in power, Śaṅkaravardhana,
desiring the kingdom, dispatched Śambhuvardhana as an envoy to the ministers. He [the envoy] won over all of them by means of discussions regarding excessive bribes.
Having deceived his elder brother, they consecrated themselves alone in the kingdom.
A crane dwelling at a sacred ford devours its own kin while remaining silent; having approached a timi fish, it lives in the forest depths.
Yet the hunter kills the crane; such are the various powers of those whose cleverness lies in successive deception.

Once at night, Cakravarman, his royal fortune lost, entered the house of the preeminent Dāmara Śridhaka, a resident of Ḍhakva. Recognizing him by his exceptional splendor, he [the Dāmara] joined his palms in reverence.
Having prostrated, he hurriedly offered him his own seat.
After relating the account of his fall from the kingdom and requesting assistance,
the humble Ḍāmara reflected upon that man, who was tender toward misfortune, and spoke.
O King, what account can there be in battle of mere blades of grass?
In what task do I lack the capacity to serve you?
Having regained my vigor, I shall slay none other than us once again.
For kings, once their purpose has been accomplished, forget the assistance rendered to them;
like an axe-wielder intent on descending who cuts down the very tree-trunk that served as his support for climbing upward.
A king who is assisted by someone through the excellence of their wisdom, fortitude, and other virtues,
once he has attained his rise, suspects that very person who helped him.
Thinking, "While he was present, misfortune befell us," the foolish lords, desiring auspiciousness, shun the one who served them in times of calamity.
O kings, you have forgotten the assistance rendered by him who was your companion in both prosperity and adversity.
They take to heart any lapse caused by negligence that arises within them.
Having observed the physical distortions resulting from illness, pain, grief for a son, hunger, and so forth,
kings— who have attained their rise through modesty and fear— strike down those who follow them.

Even though he is a king, there is no confidence in him whose ears are like those of an elephant; those of impure nature hum like bees. By his presence during the day, the instigation of sycophants reaches the lord.
O King, if even a wanton woman can be guarded by a jealous husband,
then it is impossible for those who are not omniscient to remain awake and vigilant there, where the royal preceptor teaches the Queen in secret.
Somehow, during the day, wholesome instruction has been instilled in the heart; yet at night, it is forgotten by the king, as if by a donkey.
