Who would not give rise to greed through their long, smooth tongue?
Like ants devoured by predators or like small lizards by snakes, they are seized by kings. A king who knows how to strike down his enemy when he is nearby, but not when he is far away,
is truly one crane among many other rulers whose conduct is treacherous.
One should not allow crookedness to become apparent simply because one is covered in thorns;
a lord of the earth, mindful of the right time, is like a mongoose regarding its own body.
Even a lion may kill while bowing down, and a serpent may strike even while embracing.
Whether laughing like a Vetāla or praising like a lord of the earth,
if you always regard us with a disposition free from malice,
then I shall go before you tomorrow morning at the head of my army.
Hearing this, the king, his lips whitened by a smile of shame, said:
"You, who have previously done me favors, are as worthy of my protection as my own self.
Then, having placed his foot upon the blood-stained sheepskin, he spoke.

The two kings, both fierce and armed with swords, sheathed their weapons for one another. Then, at dawn, Cakravarman— surrounded by a circle of countless, fierce, and formidable warriors— set out on his expedition toward the city.
At that moment, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the cavalry and infantry marched forth to fight, placing Śaṅkaravardhana at their head;
they were disguised to follow the times and devoid of any ostentation.
He hastened to display his own prowess before Cakravarman.
Then, as the terrible battle commenced outside Padmapura, he,
having urged on his horses, first struck down Śaṅkaravardhana.
When their commander was slain there,
that army fled in a hundred directions like a ship on the ocean driven by the force of the wind;
the king, intent on pursuing them from behind, struck them down.
As he moved through the battle with the speed of a horse, his head was severed by a sword; Bhima then saw the fluttering ends of the hero’s turbans spinning about,
resembling the thick mane of a lion-king wearing a circular armor.
What more need be said? On the field of battle, five thousand arm-seats of the lute-players fell in an instant, slain there;
the lute-players lay upon the surface of the earth, utterly exhausted by the fury of the combat.
Lying in the shade provided by the wings of vultures,
the hero Śaṅkaravardhana, together with those of pure lineage who were virtuous, slain, and had sought refuge with him, adorned the bed of heroes.
To whom would these rulers not be an object of longing, seeing that they attain their rise only in union and their destruction likewise only in union?

he abandoned his body there due to his lack of wealth.
Thus, having lost all my possessions and being long held back by people as they grieved for me, a certain man who had resolved upon a daring act said to me:
"What will you give to me, who has been made to pay back the wealth? (KRT 6.0049cd–6.0050cd)
Overwhelmed, I said to him: "Who am I to be the master of that matter?
Whatever pleases you, let that be given by you to me. Then, having descended from the coins, he gave me two.
He gave [the number] quite clearly, but he accepted ninety-eight.
Legal proceedings among kings who seek glory consist essentially of words;
thus, he was censured by the people who said, "I have been humiliated by that legal decision."

"Having been deprived of my wages by one who has used deceit under the guise of courtesy and simplicity, I shall give up my life at the door of you, who treat me so poorly. Then the king asked that man his name and his lineage.
"I have only the recognition of your face," he replied.
Having been promised by the king, "I shall provide you with clothing in the morning," he was somehow made to take his meal at the king's side.
Then, on another day, that twice-born man, standing within the city of the people who were summoned as messengers from the salt-ocean,
showed himself to the king.
When questioned by the king, he replied to the brahmin exactly as he had been told.
Declaring that all speech is established upon convention, he uttered this discourse:
"Failing to perceive the difference between the reality of things and the dependence on truthful words,
people watched the earth with minds agitated like a swing."
Then the king, seated upon the Dharma-throne, spoke regarding the images:
"One [image] is for the Brahmin who is the recipient of ninety-eight [coins], and another two are for the other [Brahmin].
He also addressed the interrogators, saying, "The [intentions] of that Great-Souled One are difficult to conceive."
The movement of Dharma as it rushes to strike down the upsurging unrighteousness is such that,
entering the evening fire and the watery lunar orb,
it shares its own brilliance with the lamps and the moonlight.

Just as the sun, having risen, dispels the thick darkness, so too this dharma, when practiced with undivided attention, removes unrighteousness. (Yugma) Yet, this dharma is difficult to perceive; it suppresses unrighteousness directly.
"Remaining ever-present for the sake of the unworthy, like fire to wood that is to be consumed—
whatever you give to one who has abandoned [the world], saying 'it is given,' and so forth;
at that time, these words of his, such as 'it pleases you,' issued forth."
Ninety-eight [coins] became pleasing to him;
he did not take that which was pleasing to him, giving instead two coins.
Thus, through such subtle observation, he discerned the distinction between dharma and adharma.
Devoted to discernment, the king brought about the dawn of the Kṛta Yuga.

Thus, while he was disciplining his people, he became an object of ridicule because of his own misconduct— like a physician who prescribes wholesome medicine to another but himself consumes unwholesome food and thereby contracts a disease.

Even by him, though he was a learned brahmin (*śrotriya*) and devoted to purification with clay and water, his servants did not abandon his side, for they fed upon the leftovers of the *ḍomba*s. Thus,
those who had sought refuge with him followed one after another, each falling behind the next in a succession of dependents.

The four city officials carried out the seizure of his wealth. From that act of true execution, the foot-soldiers met their death, even at the hands of the Lord who had placed his sword upon the foremost seat of Raṇeśvara.

When his elder brother died, he remained joyful for a long time; it was from him that the wise first observed the offering of aesthetic flavor (*rasārpaṇa*) in that context. He was appointed by the king as the governor of the coastal region (*velāvitta*).
The queen adopted the "elephant's blink" toward him as he desired her;
she placed him upon the very head of the beautiful women of the inner apartments. A courtesan named Lallā became his mistress, bringing him into a state of total subjection.
"There is no room within the hearts of women for those of virtuous conduct"—
as if thinking thus, the Creator fashioned her breasts outside, well-rounded.
Knowing that even when associated with the highest or the lowest, women of pure exterior maintain a uniform conduct, Fate has ordained the state of being a woman for them. Thus,
though she was cherished by the king, that Lalitā-locanā remained as Lalitā.
A couple [engaged] in union during the nights in the dwellings of Caṇḍālas, guards, and Nāgas. (Yugma) Something that brings good fortune occurred for a young Caṇḍāla:
that even the king’s queen, rendered helpless by his power, resorted to him. (KRT_6_0078)

Whether she was born of a Caṇḍāla family or whether she was skilled in the arts of sorcery— otherwise, how could such an improbable union have come to pass? In what manner did he become united with her?
Thus this account reached no one’s ears;
only the mutual affection of those two sinners remained apparent.
However, it was soon revealed through the observation of the movements of the eyes of the official named Hāḍi.
Then the king, having examined that matter with truth through his reflections,
and being purified by the performance of penance, donned the black antelope skin.
Even though he was provoked to anger, he did not slay her, for he was deluded by passion.

Because of that very thing, he became a vessel for the anxiety of foreboding misfortune. Through association with the followers of the *ḍomba* who eat the leftovers of others, impurity was transferred to his glorious reputation;
and through contact with a leper, it became like the suffering of leprosy itself.
Reflecting that he had obtained sovereignty through certain auspicious deeds similar to his own, performed generally in other previous births,
the king, desiring sovereignty even in future lives, [proceeded].

By means of sound reasoning, he bestowed the secure royal fortune upon a twice-born man. By that king, who was exuberant in his generosity, a monastery was established on his father’s ancestral site for students from the noble lands who were seekers of knowledge.

There, he bestowed upon the lord of the monastery the royal splendor of a sovereign— complete with parasols and chowries, yet devoid of laughter and the inner apartments of the harem. On the banks of the Vitastā, the king [bestowed] those provided with various implements.

He bestowed fifty-five agrahāras upon the Brahmins. Then, having developed the disease of dropsy, he realized, "This one is not born of my marrow," and knowing this, he set aside his own son named Saṃgrāmadeva.
Having handed over the ministers, the single-limbed [officers], and the vassals, he consecrated Varṇa—
the son of Rāmadeva and the grandson of his paternal great-uncle— in the kingdom. For it would have been possible to remove the child from the throne had he not been consecrated.
Then those who desired to seize the kingdom became despondent. Though he was on the verge of rising to power through the machinations of Parvaga and Kauṭilya,
on that day his time for fruition seemed as if it were about to turn toward ruin.

Although Varṇaṭa was residing in the capital and bestowing the kingdom [upon him], he remained one who did not even look after the dying man, despite news of his health. Then the king, filled with remorse and tormented, was urged on by his ministers.
In order to give the kingdom to Saṃgrāmadeva, by means of those who offered consolation,
Varṇaṭa was released in the morning from the palace courtyard, which had its gates bolted from the outside and where the pillars were bound by the king’s command for one night.
Out of fear or perhaps due to the vigilance of his discerning servants,
that assembly hall was reduced by them to the state of a place for washing the feet.
On a certain day, a royal officer [placed] that sword at Vijayeśvara.
Out of shame, the prince named Devaprasāda surrendered himself.
Then, his agony intensifying, he consecrated Saṃgrāmadeva,
departed from the capital, and went to his own soldier to die.
The thought of shaving off hair and beard, the discarding of the head-cloth,
the distress at accepting the ochre robe, and the taking up of the renunciation of weapons—
these were promised by the king’s servants when his destruction was certain.
He truly lives, though he is devoid of those things that manifest gratitude. (A pair of verses.
Two thousand and five hundred pieces of gold were tied to the hem of his garment. (KRT_6_0101cd–0102ab)

The king who had departed from his own palace, desiring to die, was robbed of his life while still alive by five ministers, Parvagupta and the others; they divided it among themselves right before his eyes. (A *yugma* couplet).

Tossing about on his bed, his inner being consumed by disease, the king remained within a small hut in the courtyard of the monastery, shrouded in blinding darkness. With his consciousness failing him in its onset, he saw his own people intent on doing him harm.
When he was not released from his life-breaths for two or three days,
then his friends, kinsmen, servants, and those seeking wealth, acting with haste and desiring to seize the empire, caused him to perish by administering poison.
From the midst of the women of the harem, that virtuous lady followed her husband,
like the Goddess of the Three Worlds alone following Virocana, or like one's own radiance following the sun.
The lord of the earth, having girded his loins for the protection of the castes and stages of life, [proceeded].
Having observed that the twice-born ascetic named Cakrabhānu had committed a grave transgression at the *cakramelaka*, the king, who was a proponent of the lineage of Dharma,
suppressed him by striking the surface of his forehead with his own foot.

Then, out of anger at that, his maternal uncle, the yogin Vīranātha, who served as the minister of peace and war, restrained him by means of his own power alone. Through the influence of his former teachers, he imposed his own greatness [upon him].
When it is said by the teachers that [the deceased] is liberated "through faith" while they proclaim this,

the sacred tradition (śruti) states that he is indeed proclaimed as having perished after seven days. How could there be any logical justification for that [liberation] if he has been struck down by a long-term illness?
If it is argued that this news was merely a rumor even during his illness,
then let the curse of Varṇatā and others also serve as the cause here;
for he had enjoyed sovereign power for nine years when he passed away in his twenty-fourth year.

On the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, he perished. Having slain his paternal grandmother and the other [relatives] by force, the powerful Parvagupta then came forward together with five [others], including Bhūbhaṭa and his companions.

In due course, having slain those others along with his grandmother, that powerful one alone thus ascended to the position of king. Flashing with an activity that blended the status of a monarch and the role of a minister, he shone forth.
Thus he formed a mixed perception, thinking, "He is a king, and he is a prince.
While personally serving the young king with offerings of food and other attentions,
Parvagupta appeared to the upright as one who was free from malice.

Those whom he, the bringer of glory, had honored and shared his wealth with, thinking them incapable of treachery— when it came to the extermination of his own sons, they became the very instruments of that end.
Like a king, their beards were tawny like the hair on the trunk of a young elephant.

He applied a coating of saffron paste upon his own body, which was spread over the green grass. Fearing that [the child] might tear him apart limb by limb, yet unable to manifest the power to actually uproot him, he employed a malevolent rite (*abhicārika-karman*) against the infant for the purpose of killing him.
"The kingdom rightfully belongs to you and your lineage on this day of Caitra and others;
otherwise, for one who acts contrary to this, there will swiftly come the destruction of both his dynasty and his life.
Thus he heard these words of a being during this very night.
Reflecting upon the fruitlessness of his malevolent magic,
he became increasingly apprehensive; trembling with agitation at every single limb, his consciousness stolen by anxiety, he burned with distress day and night.
Just as on a day rendered motionless by a great falling of snow,
he suddenly gathered his forces and besieged the capital;
having recognized the one who acted as an adversary, together with his son named Buddha—
Having slain the minister Rāmavardhana, who was free from malice in battle,
he took the tribute that had been brought as a gift by his father, the master of the coastal regions.
Having tied a garland of flowers around his neck, he caused the king’s throne to fall;
having cast him down at night within the Vitastā with a stone bound to his neck, he sent him to another world in a battle where his feet were turned back.

On the tenth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna in his twenty-fourth year, the wicked man, clad in armor and bearing a sword, sat upon the royal throne. [Cakkalakam] From the newly bestowed title of the son of the Divirapati, he was known as Pāreviśoka. KRT_6_0130ab
The son of Saṃgrāmagupta then became the king. Those who had previously vowed to oppose him all bowed down at dawn, terrified of him.
Due to fear of him, among the provincial governors, feudatories, ministers, scribes, and secretaries— who were otherwise prone to treachery— only the non-duality of their enmity was visible.
At that time, in his court, there was only one Sūryābhijana by birth.
Through negligence and intoxication, the drum named Āditya was split asunder.
Having been humiliated by the enraged king who stripped him of his garment,
he had his hair and beard shorn and became an ascetic.

Furthermore, even today, those born of noble lineage continue to dwell in Tripureśvara as the descendants of that very man who had become the son of his friend. While King Parvagupta was engaged in the acquisition of wealth, [the following occurred].
The diseases of the subjects, having been brought back to renewed vigor by the officials,
he likewise established Parvaga-Īśvara near the grounds of the Skanda monastery with wealth acquired through his own efforts.
The queen, pure-minded as Gaurī, severed the scandal concerning the harem of King Śrīyaśaskara,
she who had long since cultivated affection for Parvagupta.
A virtuous woman, seeking her husband’s welfare, skillfully employed a deception appropriate to the occasion;
having abandoned this half-finished temple of the Lord Yaśaskāra for her deceased husband, she completed the construction.
"By my ascetic discipline, I shall make your desire fruitful.
Thus was he, while still attempting to entice her, addressed by that fair-browed woman. Then, with his pride greatly increased, in just a few days—

That king brought the celestial abode to its fullness. In the sacrificial fire, where clarified butter was being poured, that virtuous queen suddenly offered her body as an oblation along with the *pūrṇāhuti*.

While showers of flowers fell profusely above her as she was being cast down, words that were harsh and devoid of color fell [upon him], for he was longing for her. He was withered by the intensity of his anxiety regarding the undertaking of that very long and reckless deed.

He became a guest on the path consisting of craving, previously guarded [against it]. (KRT 6.145cd) Even though they know that their condition is unstable, fools—deluded by the splendor of malice, greed, and delusion—do not abandon their deep-rooted attachments through the exhaustion of efforts to pacify the lord of diseases. (KRT 6.146ab–cd)
Fearing that even one with such devotion might be harmed, some who had attained auspicious states pierced him with sharp arrows; thus, in the field of the Queen of the Gods (Śrīparvata),
he passed away on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha in his twenty-sixth year.

That king was deprived of his kingdom acquired through treachery. (KRT 6.148cd) If indeed destruction were not seen immediately in this very world—foretelling the ripening of intense tears and misfortune regarding the course of the next life, which transcends the senses—who would not strive for prosperity by avoiding evil deeds? (KRT 6.149ab–cd)

Then his son, named Kṣemagupta, became king; he was consumed by the fever of wealth and youth, which were swollen by the indulgence in intoxicants. Due to his reliance on wicked men, he became exceedingly ill-behaved by nature.
Like a terrifying darkness caused by fierce clouds on a night of the dark fortnight, he was a source of fear;
[he was] adorned with dress and ornaments equal to his own. A hundred pampered favorites, including Arjuna and others of wicked conduct, attended upon that king.
Even when addicted to gambling, wine, and the company of women, and even though he was being plundered by parasites, that king was never deprived of his fortune.
He who is passionate, full of sweet affection, and whose gaze is fixed upon her, who forms a friendship with those whose essence is the wealth of honey,
and who finds attachment even for a mere day in the lotus— what is there in that which would not be a source of wonder if Fortune herself were present there? Or rather,
the rogues born of Viṣṇu, such as Vāmana and others, have entered his heart.

They made that which was impure pleasing to him, as if he were a *piśāca*. Skilled at mocking others, fond of dalliance with the wives of others, his mind dependent on others, the king remained intent solely on worldly gain.

Spittle was discharged upon their beards and mustaches, and saliva flowed from their ears; by that [act], the *ṭakkara* blows were directed into the skulls of those waiting [for them]. With the clashing of their hips, the women became like deer-hunters wandering through the forest.
And the parasites gained his favor with their lewd chatter.
The royal assembly became so filled with harlots, scoundrels, fools, children, and traitors that it was unfit for the entrance of high-minded men.
Was the son of the king— not yet a sovereign— by the sons of Jiṣṇu, namely Kṣemagupta and Kṣamābhṛt,
not made to dance by those rogues, drawn by his quality of being a *cāraṇa*?
Having bestowed upon him the name Kaṅkaṇavarṣa...
Being repeatedly satisfied, they made their arms the recipients of bracelets.
They obtained the king’s favor for pointing out faults where none existed, for revealing new matters, and for establishing invincible *ṭakkas*.
Having placed his own wives before him, their breasts and armpits clearly visible,

the king— though full of passion— was led away from his home at dice and stripped of all his wealth. They vied with one another, each desiring to preserve her good fortune through continued enjoyment.
Having enjoyed them, he was urged, "Tell us the difference.
He was made by those shameless men to enjoy his own wives;
and at the end of their dalliance, he—who bestowed desired wealth—was asked, "Which one was pleasing? (a pair).
While his pampered children remained ignorant of the pursuit of sensual enjoyment, Viṣṇu and Śiva—
out of a desire to protect their mothers' virtue— were reduced to the status of beggars.
Women, having cast aside their own pride and abandoned their families out of a sense of purity, now take pleasure in their own bodies by making them the subject of jesting talk.

I know that they destroy happiness through attachment to long-term service for the sake of which they undergo toil; having renounced that very thing, what is sought by the vulgar through service? Although Bhaṭṭaphalguṇa was a minister who brought him fame, he became his subordinate; fie on the latent tendency toward the habitual pursuit of enjoyments!
The king repeatedly mocked that man in private for his role in establishing the shrines of Phalguna-svāmin and others;
subsequently, seeking to kill him out of enmity, he forcibly seized him along with Ṭakkura and his companions.
The aged Rakka, the lord of Kampana, found himself in the midst of a wicked assembly. Having entered the fierce battle-ground to slay those who had launched sharp insults,
that pitiless man set fire to the Śrī Jayendra monastery.
Having destroyed the images of the Sugata and having gathered a heap of stones from all the milk-drinking [temples],
from ruined temples,
and from elsewhere— that fool, seeking the stability of his own fame through the consecration of a god, [acted thus].
Within the market streets of the city, he established the temple of Kṣemagaurīśvara.

(KRT 6.173cd) One man goes to his end, while another, having forcibly seized his wealth, carries it away with great joy. He does not realize that at his own death, it will pass into the treasury of another. Fie upon this desire, which creates a blinding darkness through incomparable delusion! (KRT 6.174)
By Tyāgin, who was protected by Kṣepa, thirty-six villages were offered to the King of Khaśa for the sake of his sustenance, after he had destroyed the burnt monasteries. He,
a ruler of fortresses such as Lohara and others, was like Indra, the lord of a hundred sacrifices.
The king named Siṃharāja gave his own daughter to him. With his mind attached to that Diddā, the granddaughter of Śāhi, the king became known by the shameful name "Diddākṣema."
By her maternal grandfather,
the illustrious King Bhīma Śāhi, a noble palace named Bhīmakeśava was constructed for that daughter-in-law of the lord of the earth.
Diddā became envious of Phalguna, the gatekeeper, who had given the maiden named Candralekhā to the king. [She thought:
"The instruction from my teacher was very great, as was the labor in the art of the spear."
Because of that ignoble conclusion, the king fell into ridicule. For,
though his spears were unfailing in their descent and fit for the business of battle,
he considered them inferior to his devotion to the hunt for jackals.
People constantly saw him wandering about together with dogs, surrounded by bands of hunters, foresters, and Ḍombas carrying snares.
[He was seen] in Dāmodara’s forest, at Lalyāna, Śimikā, and other such places.

In places where he delighted in hunting jackals, his age passed away. Then, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, while the king was engaged in the hunt, he saw a flame issuing from the mouth of a howling female jackal.
Then, trembling with terror born from that sight, he was seized by a fever of spider-bites, which became the cause of his death. He went to die at Vārāhakṣetra, where the Creator resides.
Near Dhruṣkapura, at the monasteries of Śrīkaṇṭha and Kṣema,
his body became soaked by spiders as large as split lentils;
he died on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa in his thirty-fourth year.
From him was born King Abhimanyu, the son of Kṣemagupta,
who was protected by Queen Diddā, who followed the conduct of a lioness.
He appointed officials for the primary duties of peace and war, as well as for the inner apartments.
They brought no fear to the royal bride, whose bed was never barren.
While Abhimanyu was protecting the earth,
a terrible fire suddenly burst forth from the vicinity of the lofty temple of Īśvara.
He burned down the great houses situated within the range of the Vetāla-sūtra, extending from the side of Vardhanasvāmin as far as the nuns' quarters—
houses defiled by contact with the king who had been touched by a *ḍomba* and a *caṇḍāla*.

Having burned down the great houses, the fire seemed to perform a purification of the earth. The king’s mother, his protector, her intellect deluded by the nature of women, did not touch upon the investigation of what was essential and what was trivial, for her ears were distracted [by idle talk].
Since she had previously remained with her husband due to her devotion to the king’s son,
she was like a devoted wife (*pativratā*) together with Phalguna, the chief minister; for,
seeing that the wives of those whose husbands had died followed them in death, she [resolved to do the same].

He quickly consented to her desire to die through deception; however, out of compassion, the minister Naravāhana forbade her from death as she stood by the funeral pyre, filled with remorse for her persistence.
Therefore, his innate suspicion, corrupted by anger,
seized upon the queen’s apprehension that Arjuna might seize the kingdom;
for he perceived her disposition to be treacherous through bodily signs indicative of disaffection.
Even Phalguna remained apprehensive toward Samyu, along with all his ministers;
for he, holding every office of authority, was present before the eyes of everyone,
shining intensely with qualities such as counsel, heroism, and energy.
Having taken the bones of Kṣemagupta and gone to the Ganges,
his son named Kardamarāja, accompanied by powerful forces,
prepared to remain at Parṇotsa until his return.
Lacking trust in the king’s palace and apprehensive of his enemies,
Arjuna departed from the city with his treasury-keeper and soldiers;
by the time he reached the vicinity of the wooden enclosure, he was pursued by Rakta and the others.

Perceiving this, Diddā quickly abandoned her prayers and entreaties; instead, she dispatched a staff-bearer from behind to strike him down. Distressed by this fresh insult, he assembled an infinite army.
Turning back from there, the proud king arrived at the field of Vārāha.
Hearing that he had returned with his army, the majestic Diddā,
along with her ministers, trembled, fearing an assault.
Having gone to that field and lamented for his master, who had passed away peacefully, for a long time,
he surrendered his weapon near the feet of Varāha.

By laying down his weapons, the minister wiped away the sin of having entertained such a thought, as well as the fear of the queen mother. Service to one whose mind is beyond the discernment of what is proper or improper is indeed a great calamity; yet, to retaliate against him when he is enraged brings about deep-seated enmity and the reproach of treachery.

For a discerning person, it is most appropriate to feel supreme indignation toward one who serves as an instrument for those of inferior virtue, whether that person be a weapon or even a sword. When Arjuna had slowly departed with his army like a mere leaf, the ministers rejoiced like children whose teacher has gone, being left without a guide.

Although Kṣemagupta was the chief minister, he remained constantly awake himself, thinking of security and prosperity while personally clearing away all obstacles. Parvaga and Kośapīthin were the two ministers who coveted the kingdom.
Previously, he had taken the hands of his two daughters, Choja and Bhūbhaṭa.
From them were born two sons, renowned as Mahīpa and Pāṭala,
who grew up in the royal palace like princes.

While remaining there at that time, longing for the kingdom, the two of them consulted together and joined forces with the powerful Himyaka and others. Those two strong men were then expelled from the royal residence by the weak queen.
The two queens remained in their own quarters until they had completed their coming and going; meanwhile, she,
manifesting her deformity, provided staff-bearers for the expulsion of his majesty as he departed from behind.

Knowing this, he entered the residence of his father-in-law named Śaktisena; they too fled from that place. When the staff-bearers had been pacified by Śaktisena and did not move, [he proceeded further].
Then he clearly granted refuge to the frightened son-in-law;
Himmaka and Mukula likewise obtained that refuge,
as did the one named Antaka, who had previously resided in Parihāsa.
The illustrious one named Udayagupta, the son of Amṛtākara, and those led by Yaśodhara, all born in the city of Lalitādityapura—
each of them individually, with their mutual armies, caused a trembling of the world.
Having united, they established a dual sovereignty, having taken sides with Mahima.
Amidst that great danger, the minister, along with his kinsmen, alone remained on the side of Diddā;
Naravāhana, however, did not abandon her, for he was free from malice.
Then, their armies swelling and intent on battle, the enemies approached Padmasvāmin with their weapons gleaming. Thereupon,
in the Śūramaṭha, the agitated Diddā dispatched her son.
He reflected upon various means for pacifying the calamities;
having quickly won over the twice-born residents of Lalitādityapura with abundant gold,
he brought about a division among the enemy hosts.

Those who argued that all should show their anger when a single person is insulted— those whose treasury of majesty had been plundered— concluded a peace treaty with the Queen. No one could even perceive her power to leap over a cow’s footprint.
That cripple acted like the Son of the Wind in crossing the ocean of the Saṃgha.
Homage be to that Wealth of wondrous power, by whose relinquishment the gathering of jewels and great medicinal herbs brings an end to all calamities.
Even when accepting gold as a bribe, they consider it a great service;
thus, Diddā bestowed the office of *kampana* upon Yaśodharā and others.
Within a few days, she also performed a malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) against Mahima.
The widow’s ignorance regarding the drawing of the mandala manifested itself.
Once, out of anger toward the Shahi ruler named Itthakan,
the Lord of Kampana set out on an expedition together with his own kinsmen.
As he entered that region, a fortress consisting of the Nimangā mountain, with unimpeded power and speed, he forcibly seized Thakkana.
Having received his prostration, she took the hand of that king and once again nourished the creeper of his fortune with the waters of consecration. At that time,
the wicked Rakta and others gained entrance.

By the foolish queen, hatred was fiercely grasped toward the Lord of Kampana. Within the heart of a lord of the earth, of a crystal stone, and of a woman’s heart devoid of character, the influence of another gains entrance due to the constant absence of those who are ever-present.

Speaking words that accord with their own desires, rogues gain entry into the minds of commoners, courtesans, libertines, and even the inner circles of lords. This betrayer is a protector of his master; he is a taker of wealth—thus they spread slander.
She herself believed that his self-proclamation was indeed true. Then,
when the Lord of Kampana had arrived at his own residence, victorious and exultant, the wise [queen],
clearly intent on his banishment, dispatched her staff-bearers.
Having heard that challenge,
Himmakaira, Manta, and the others remembered the bestower of the treasury and underwent a transformation as before;
however, those known as the Naravāhanas did not abandon the side of the Rākṣīpaka.
Thus, as before, he brought about a division within his own army.
Then, when Śubhakarāditya and the others had entered [the city] out of anger,
Diddā again dispatched [troops] to the monastery of Bhaṭṭāraka.

Deluded by fate, those fools did not open the king’s palace— which was bolted shut— at that very moment while she remained there without her son. On the very next day, the people gathered around the queen.
By the power of which, she then displayed a certain degree of steadfastness. Then,
as the enemy forces spread out from the vicinity of Jayābhaṭṭārikā up to the borders of the Śūramaṭha, the battle commenced.
When the royal army had entered the capital and fled in terror,
the single-limbed warriors displayed a solid phalanx at the main gate;
disregarding their own bodies, they steadied that frightened force.
The army of his enemies fled, and some of the foes retreated.
At that moment, the royal courtier arrived,
shattering the enemy host with the sounds of musical instruments and gladdening his own.
When he arrived, the perishable army of his enemies was destroyed;
for the deities of weapons never tolerate malice or lack of discipline. [They think: "It rends iron bonds and shatters stones."
Himmaka, of terrifying prowess, who had brought about a reputation for truthfulness— by the sword of that [king], which fell upon half the body of the royal commander Bhaṭṭa,
not even a mere piece of leather was torn from his impenetrable armor.

Beholding that incredible wretchedness that had taken hold of the army, Himmaka, the upholder of fame, was emboldened by his warriors to strike at the sins [of his enemies]. Nevertheless, he remained for a moment in the battle, quivering like the Destroyer himself.
With his sword shattered and fallen from his mount, he was captured alive. That illustrious kinsman of the king, whom they could not slay in battle,
Udayagupta, fled somewhere, abandoning the great fray.
Thus, having achieved victory, the queen immediately seized Yaśodhara,
Śubhadhara, and Mukula along with their kinsmen in a rage—
those who had been destroyers of the offerings and fees for the ancestral rites of the Kashmiris at Gayā.
That brave Sopyeramantaka, who took refuge in mockery,
had a great stone tied around his neck and was cast into the waters of the Vitastā;
he experienced the fruit of his own misconduct through the divine wrath of the Goddess.
From King Gopāla up until Abhimanyu, there were sixteen sovereigns who ruled for seven times seven years, from seventy-seven years ago.
Those ministers, whose conduct was hostile and who had brought about the destruction of power, life, and fortune for sixty years— all of them, along with their lineages and followers,
were swiftly [destroyed] by Queen Diddā through her mere wrathful knitting of her terrible brows.

Like great asuras brought to the end by a fortress, they were reduced to nothingness. Having seized those highly arrogant men, the queen appointed Rakta and others as officials in charge of duties such as the Kampana.
In this manner, that preeminent minister,
Naravāhana, who was free from malice, made that widow— who resembled Indra— possess an unbroken circle [of sovereignty].
And she too, out of a sense of gratitude, [acted] within the assembly of ministers.
The king himself summoned that man, who was free from malice, under the name of Rājānaka. When he had fallen asleep, she herself slept; when he had finished his meal, she ate.
When he was joyful, she rejoiced; when he was despondent, she became despondent, acting in accordance with his disposition.
He found no satisfaction in him until he had inquired after his health, requested his instruction, and offered him his own possessions while he was at home.
In former times, there were two sons of a cart-driver named Kuyya.

Of those two who were both *sindhubhuj* (sea-rulers), Sindhulalitaka was indeed the elder. Having entered the service of Parvagaṇa’s household, he gradually attained the position of treasurer (*gañjādhyakṣa*), and subsequently, he slowly rose to the office of steward (*gañjādhikāritva*) for that queen.
By that very title, Gañjeśa causes no further exertion;
he is the founder of the administrative office known as Sindhugañja.
Naravāhana, whose kingdom has for the most part been seized, remains there.

Thus the evil-minded one spoke to the queen, whose intellect was to be led astray. She said, "So be it," and while she was still speaking, the minister, out of affection, once requested her to come to his own house for a meal.

"He will surely capture you there along with your followers," said the Ocean; thus addressed, she, overwhelmed by fear, asked what was to be done. Without saying a word, she set out for the capital city, remaining unobserved.

"I have become subject to the menses," she later sent out this report. When the queen had thus departed along that path, having already begun her customary observances, the minister's affection and his secret agreement perished with her.
From that moment on, their mutual affection was extracted by the wheelers [of fate],
who rendered them as utterly harsh as sesame oil-cakes and dregs;
for the thunderbolt is the destroyer of all metals, and stone dams are the destroyers of waters.
The deceptive appearances of the wicked are not perceived at all;
yet those who are more deluded than a child, even though they are wiser than the Teacher of the Gods— for them,
we do not know what the atoms of their own creations may be.
A crow, its mind devoid of discernment, regards other chicks as its own; a swan, skilled in separating milk from water, fears the insubstantial cloud.

A king, whose intellect is sharpened by observing the world, recognizes the truth in the words of the wicked—fie upon the Creator’s decree, touched by such a confusion of cleverness and delusion! That [speech] is foolish, footless, and excluded from the Vedas.
She became as contemptible as the nature of a foolish Brahmin. Constantly tormented by her, that man-borne king,
heated by such humiliation, himself gave up his life.
For those whose hearts are scorched by their own splendor when provoked by one who cannot be remedied, what refuge is there other than death for those who seek glory?
Like a night without the moon, like the speech of Sarasvatī abandoned by Truth.
The royal splendor did not shine, being deprived of its rider, Naravāhana.
Cruel from her habitual practice of violence,
she contemplated how to slay the sons of Ḍāmara, who stood nearby and were intent on their martial prowess.

Fleeing out of fear of him, they raised their own cries of "Help! and put to death the gatekeepers, warders, and others who were engaged in their duties. Abandoning shame and modesty, the queen, driven by her agitation, [acted].
They attained their positions through great effort; for how could there be self-respect in those who seek only their own interests?
Sthāneśvara and the others, along with the chief Ḍāmaras and the rest, [were thus established].
Terrified, they returned before her and yawned once more. Then, when Rakka had met his death, the queen, fearing him and desiring a hero, brought Phalguna back again into her presence.

While performing royal duties, he took up arms once again; for even though he had laid down his weapons, it is true that the latent desire for enjoyment is difficult to abandon. This was the final manifestation of the majesty of him who had conquered Rajapura and other cities.
It was a marvel that he became like one imprisoned by an old harlot.
He was the very dear brother-in-law of King Udayarāja,
a wicked-minded man named Jayagupta, who served as his assistant in the department of elephants.
On another day, other officials of cruel disposition, joined by him,
carried out a plundering raid in Kaśmīra through the evil deeds they had accumulated. And [the king], though possessed of good character, was distressed by the sins of his mother.
At that moment, Abhimanyu was seized by consumption.
The wise Puṇḍarīkākṣa, adorned by the sons of the learned,
shone with both erudition and youth.
Thus, for him whose nature was so pure, the encounter with evil deeds became a cause of withering, like the heat of the sun upon a *śirīṣa* flower. While being thus oppressed,
that moon among subjects, in the third month of Kārtika, [attained his end].
In his forty-first year, Śukla was seized by Niyati-Rāhu.
His son, Nandigupta, though still a child, ascended his own throne;
meanwhile, the aged [Śukla], casting from his heart the sorrow for his son, [passed away].
With her cruelty shrouded by grief, she remained cooled by tranquility,
like a sun-gem needle whose heat and distortion have been covered by darkness.
From that time forward, through her wondrous practices of dharma, [she became renowned].
Even though Fortune had been brought low by evil deeds, she attained a state of purity. Furthermore,
the lord of the city, Sindhubhrātṛ, who was of auspicious intent,
became a nurturer of her righteous conduct.
Having been freed from sin by him, she gave birth to a son who was free from passion;
from that time forth, the queen became esteemed by the whole world.
That minister of the king, whose cruelty had vanished, was truly difficult to find.
She made [the city] pleasant to dwell in, like the winter season does for the sun;
she was the creator of the ruined son’s prosperity through her virtuous deeds,
and she became the mistress of both Abhimanyu and the city of Abhimanyupura.
Then Diddāsvāmin, accompanied by Diddāpura, was established by her;
and a monastery (*maṭha*) was founded for the sake of increasing the excellence of the religious merit of her husband Kaṅkaṇavarṣa, providing shelter for those from Madhyadeśa, Lāṭa, Śauḍa, and Oḍra.
The beautiful Rāmaṇī built Kaṅkaṇapura, which rained down gold;
she also constructed another [city], Diddāsvāmin, made of white stone,
as if it were whitened by the immersion of the waters of the Gaṅgā rising from her feet.
She established a refuge for the Kashmiri Vaiśikas,
a monastery with four very lofty halls and beautiful splendor;
she [named it] after her father, the illustrious Siṃharāja, as Śrī-Siṃhasvāmin.
She established a monastery for the residence of the twice-born spiritual teachers.
Through her own works, such as the consecration of the monastery and the construction of Vaikuṇṭha,
she made the confluence of the Vitastā and the Sindhu exceedingly pure.
What is the use of speaking at length regarding those various places?
Tradition holds that she established sixty-four such shrines.
By the Goddess, who undertook the restoration of ruined sites, the circles of ramparts were set ablaze.

Almost all the temples of the gods were constructed with stone ramparts. The Queen’s army, though physically impaired by her being lame, moved about for pleasure and recreation; the woman named Valgā, who carried burdens, had a stable for horses built.

The crocodile, though resorting to sacred fords and observing silence, remains attached to eating its own kin; the peacock, though eating only wind daily and subsisting on mere rainwater from the clouds, devours birds of confidence; and the heron, though manifesting meditation, eats aquatic creatures. There is no conviction among the wicked regarding the transformation of their faults, even when they perform virtuous deeds.
In just one year, that land of *carṣaṇī* became free from sorrow.
When that grandson, who was devoted to sensual pleasures, committed adultery,
he met his end in the forty-ninth year, during the bright fortnight.
On the twelfth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, while she was distracted by no other path,
her grandson named Tribhuvana was likewise slain by her on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, in his fifty-first year.
Then, at that time, the youngest grandson, named Bhīmagupta, was placed at will by that cruel woman upon the path of death called "kingdom.
At that very moment, the aged Phalguna also passed away.
She who had previously remained hidden due to her cruelty, wickedness, and so forth, out of respect for him,
now became manifest with hundreds of her most violent and evil deeds;
like a fierce elephant in rut, she was formidable with her face and veil cast aside.

Alas! Fie upon those born of noble lineage; by their very nature, the conduct of women follows the downward slope, just like that of rivers. Having attained sovereignty over the currents and shining brightly, they give birth to the ocean, yet remain dwellings for but a small amount of water.

When the lotuses in the lake had come into bloom, even women of noble lineage became incessantly attached to them, becoming the objects of enjoyment for the low-born. Then Tuṅga, the son of Bāṇa— who was born in the village of Parṇotsarga in the district of Baddivāsa— entered the service as a buffalo-herder for Khaśa.
Once, having entered Kaśmīra for the purpose of delivering a letter,
he was in the presence of the Minister of Peace and War together with five brothers: Sugandhi, Siṃha, Prakaṭa, Nāgaṭṭayika, and Ṣaṇmukha.

Having come within the range of the Goddess's vision, he became the captivator of her heart. [Tilaka] Led into private by the female messenger through the power of his destined fate, that youth became beloved even to her, though she had already enjoyed many paramours. [Kṛt 6.0320cd–6.0321]

Then the sinful queen, who was passionately attached to Tuṅga and devoid of shame, caused him to be killed by administering poison out of sheer malice. Fie upon those thoughtless and wicked kings whose minds are so unjust!
Praise that yields no fruit brings satisfaction when there is fault, yet results in the loss of life and wealth.
By her, the god’s water-jar was made into a source of income for the shore;
a shameless lecher practiced the role of a village headman in the office of the lord.

Even those heroes such as Kardamarāja and others, who were gatekeepers and leaders, resorted to thievery; what need is there to mention others? The child remained in the king's palace for four or five years.
As Bhīmagupta’s intellect gradually matured,
he perceived that the administration of the kingdom and the conduct of his grandmother were ill-ordered; these matters remained fixed in his mind as things yet to be rectified.
Because she was devoid of the conduct of her station, merciless, and prone to loose speech,
he became an object of suspicion for her, whose mind was not to be trusted;
for Abhimanyu’s widow had caused him to enter in secret.
Therefore, he became such a son born of a noble lineage. Then,
having been given the mantra by Devakalaśa, she, though apprehensive,
cast aside her shame and clearly bound Bhīmagupta.
The doubt that had arisen among the people regarding the secret plot of Nandigupta and others was likewise dispelled by him through his manifest actions.
Having cast Bhīmagupta down with various such tortures, she—
In his fifty-sixth year, having himself ascended the throne, King Tuṅga—
favored day by day by the Queen, whose passion had grown intense— became the supreme authority,
surpassing all others.

The former ministers, who had grown estranged, conspired with the haughty Tuṅga and his brothers; being disaffected, they strove to bring about the ruin of the kingdom. Having deliberated together, they brought from Kaśmīra a man of cruel prowess.
He [the king] approached Ugra, known as Vigraharāja, the son of Diddā’s brother,
in order to bring about the ruin of the kingdom by seizing the principal agrahāras. The wise [Ugra], for his part, quickly summoned the twice-born for the purpose of fasting unto death (prāyopaveśa).
When the Brahmins who uphold the three Vedas were in discord, the entire world fell into ruin;
day after day, it sought out the exalted ones here and there with the intent to slay them.
In a certain house with its doors closed, having concealed her lofty [form], she remained there for some days, fearing an assault.
Likewise, by the gift of gold, Sumanas, Mantaka, and the others—

The Brahmins were then assembled, and consequently [the conflict] mostly ceased. Thus, when that great provocation had been averted by such generosity, Vigraharāja departed as he had come, his power broken.
Then, having secured Dārdya, the powerful leaders such as Tuṅga and others gradually overthrew King Kardama and his followers, who had instigated the rebellion. Sulakṣaṇa,
the son of Rakka, and other chief ministers likewise [acted].

Banished from the country by those who were angry, they were welcomed back by those who were pleased. However, as their enmity increased, the Brahmins were once again made to choose death by fasting by Vigraharāja, through secret emissaries dispatched [by him].
O Brahmins, those who sought to cause vomiting through the administration of emetics were, in turn,
struck down by the lofty [king] once he had attained firm stability.
While dwelling secretly among them, one named Āditya escaped.
The beloved commander of the camp for Vigraharāja was slain; furthermore,
the doorkeeper named Vatsarāja, wounded by weapons, was captured alive as he fled on horseback with Nyanka, Utaka, and others.
Those Brahmins, Svarṇāgrāhin, Sumana, Mantaka, and the others—
all of them were bound by Tuṅga and cast into prison. Then,
the two lords of Rājapura became arrogant due to the destruction of Phalguna.
An attack was launched against her by all the ministers who were enraged.
Then the hero named Pṛthvīpāla, having fallen into a perilous situation,
that king of Rājapurī brought about the destruction of the Kashmiri forces.
The two ministers, Śipāṭaka and Haṃsarāja, perished there;
Candrādya and others saw misfortune, for where death is the remedy.
Then, by another path, Tuṅga suddenly [arrived] together with his brothers.
Having suddenly entered the entire royal city, the hero consumed it with fire. By that means, the king who protected the earth perished;
however, the army of the remaining ministers attained liberation from the peril.
Being weak, that king paid tribute to Tuṅga;
thus was the restoration of his lost wealth accomplished by him at that time.
Then Tuṅga, having taken possession of Kampana, entered the city.

He of lion-like prowess brought about the destruction of the village of Ḍāmara. Diddā, moreover, without hesitation, appointed the tested son of her brother Udayarāja as the crown prince, known by the name Saṃgrāmarāja.
To test all her brothers' sons who stood before her— most of whom were still children— she first released a string of *pālevata* fruits,
saying, "Who here is capable of reaching how many of these fruits? (Kṛt 6.356–357ab).
That became the cause of quarrel among those princes. And he saw them receiving blows while seizing only small fruits, whereas King Saṃgrāma, having enjoyed the fruits for himself, remained unhurt.
When asked with wonder about the cause for attaining infinite fruit and remaining unhurt, he then spoke to her thus:
"Having made these people preoccupied with mutual quarrels, I dwell apart from them."

I gathered the fruits therein and remained unharmed. For those who have not entered into calamity, who remain steadfast and vigilant, and who are free from affliction— what successes of their own goals do they not achieve?
Having heard these words of his, which served as a messenger of vigilance, she—
timid by the very nature of women— considered herself fit for sovereignty;
for just as valor is attained by the brave through valor, so too is it attained by the timid through timidity.
For an effect indeed manifests within [the mind], and it could not be otherwise.

Even wood abandoned by fire serves to cool the monkeys' fur; water purifies the hair of the *agniśauca* goat; and fire purifies the *eṇaka* deer. Just as the dispositions of a living being bring about the accomplishment of their destined effects, there is in reality no inherent essence in them whatsoever.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada in his seventy-ninth year,
when the Queen had ascended to heaven, the King became the crown prince.

This third chapter, a wonder to the world concerning the royal lineages through their connections with women, now proceeds in this circle. When the family of thorns had been destroyed, the illustrious Sātavāhana dynasty attained preeminence on this earth through its wealth of treasures.

He grew like a mango sprout in a pleasure grove, watered by the rain from clouds, after its trunk had been scorched by a forest fire. Then, with gentleness concealing the majesty of his inner fortitude, that king of battles placed the entire earth easily upon his arm, just as the lord of serpents, whose vital strength is hidden by a beauty resembling a cluster of lotuses, supports the multitude of hoods.
The Seventh Wave.

O Mother, you were born from a stainless womb in a praiseworthy paternal lineage; you are the body praised by the Creator, the twilight who brings the presence of the gods, and you sport upon the breast of the Lord of the Earth (Śiva).
May that Lord of Gaurī, who bows even to the Twilight with such clever words of praise—words that provoke the jealousy of Pārvatī while she performs her own twilight worship—delight the entire world.
The lord of the earth, bearing forgiveness both in his mind and in his arm...
In both depth and power, he conquered the commander of the army.
At that time, a defeat occurred for all those [enemies] upon the destruction of the queen,
just as a lover experiences the end of his union with the twilight at the close of the day’s beauty.

On the contrary, by the crushing of the arrogance of each respective opponent, his own rise was constantly observed by them; for who knows the course of the Creator? Thus, the brave and powerful [hero], having become a kinsman through the king, [was established].
Then, due to his fitness for all offices, Candrākaraka met with destruction; meanwhile,
other sons of the village official Bhīmatika, who possessed great wealth and were the sons of Puṇyākara, attained peace through their heroism.
Due to the absence of capable ministers, though unwilling,
the lord of the earth was led by fate— having been deprived of all other courses— to take refuge with those of high rank.
Queen Devī caused Saṃgrāmarāja, Tuṅga, and others to drink from the treasury.
Previously, they had remained together without mutual malice, as if intending to die; however,
the king, unable to endure hardship, even due to the demands of his duties,
became weary of enjoyments and entrusted the affairs of the subjects to his ministers.

His cowardice was sufficient; what more need be revealed? He tolerated the loss of his reputation through unequal matrimonial alliances, since he gave away his daughter—who was esteemed for her beauty and valor—to one who sought only her assistance.
He gave Loṭhikā to Preman, the lord of the Diddā-maṭha. (KRT 7.0011cd) Where is a princess, fit for a king who strives to support the world?
And where is a Brahmin of meager mind, his hands moistened by the water of receiving gifts? (KRT 7.0012ab–cd)

Then, in order to bring about the downfall of Tuṅga and the others, the Brahmin ministers caused a Brahmin assembly to be convened in Parihāsapura. That upheaval of the king was carried out through the consensus of the Brahmin ministers.
The unbearable Pavamāna became like a conflagration.
Even though the twice-born, prepared to uproot the king, were somehow entreated,
their minds were set on his lofty expulsion rather than on an offering of patience.
While this was being promised to them by the king, Tuṅga, and the others,
those men of deceitful intellect began to request something else:
"This Brahmin who died in the house of Tuṅga’s brother-in-law— we [must have his property]."
Saying, "Let us burn him," a certain corpse was moved from the well by those deceitful men; when they had lifted it up and brought it toward the lofty houses,
a *kṛtyā* (demoness) that had been raised from the hair and filth became manifest.
When the Kali age had arisen for the destruction of the twice-born who were devoid of purity and had turned their backs [on dharma], suddenly becoming weaponless,
the Brahmins fled; he who was among them the giver of mantras— *tilaka* (verse-end marker) KRT_7_0019ab–cd, KRT_7_0020ab.
The royal pitcher entered that house in secret out of fear. Having manifested his crookedness, he engaged in battle for a very long time;
meanwhile, those brahmins fled through side doors and went to their own homes.
When the royal pitcher was won, the twice-born were to perform the ritual together;
however, seven ministers, the sons of Śrīdhara, arrived and waged war.

Having performed that great feat, they reached the conclusion of the battle; having pierced the sevenfold circle, they swiftly departed like the seven-horsed sun. When they had been stilled in the conflict, Sugandhasimha was victorious.

Then, having been bound, Rājakalasa was brought to the house by Tuṅga. As he was being led away, he was quickly placed upon Skanda; wounded along the way, his weapons were snatched away as he was made to dance by Tuṅga’s draft animals.

Another minister named Bhūtikalaśa was also defeated by the son of King Kāka; together with him, he went to Śūramaṭha. Then, through compassion, he was gradually released by Sugandhi, Siṃha, and the others.

That good son, tormented by the fire of his own dishonor, departed for another land. Thus, the upheaval that had arisen in the city of Parihāsa-pura actually turned out to be for the welfare of Tuṅga through the power of destiny.
Then, when King Guṇadeva had been propitiated by the minister,
Bhūtikalaśa arrived, having performed his ablutions in the Gaṅgā;
he slowly gained a slight foothold once again in that royal palace.
Secret messengers were dispatched by the king to slay Tuṅga; however,
when that matter was revealed by Tuṅga after he had learned of the news,
Bhūtikalaśa, along with his son, was once again exiled by the king.

The son of Candrāka slowly regained a slight degree of composure; even he, who was like Death itself toward me, passed away at that moment. Having become for a brief instant the recipient of the princess’s embrace—
The illustrious Premā, who had rendered service to the king, also met his death.
All others who were dear to the monarch, such as Gaṅgā and the rest, perished; however, the exalted Tuṅga, together with his brother, alone remained for the sake of enjoyment.

Thus, whatever event was feared as leading to his destruction, that very thing, through the favor of destiny, instead became more intense. A tree on a riverbank, its supporting ground eroded by the passage of time and remaining rooted only in its own base, [is swept away] by the floods of the river's waters.
Indeed, the firmness of his foundation would have been secured by those very people who, fearing he might fall, had bestowed earth upon him.
While he conducted himself with the brilliance of political science (*nīti*) and was intent on pleasing his subjects,
he— once lofty— gradually became one whose mind faltered due to the exhaustion of his prior merit.
He took up a low birth to deprive him of his own good fortune,
and for the sake of assistance, he employed a lowly scribe named Bhadreśvara;
[he also engaged in] the trade of excrement, the slaughter of animals, and the selling of wood, and so forth.
The park-keeper, whose duty was appropriate to his lineage,
then went toward the food-offering with his back rubbed by a woolen blanket;
and he who carried the bellows and the ink-pots followed behind the officials.

Exhausted by anxieties concerning the affairs of state and other matters, Tuṅga appointed him as his assistant; yet, through that association, he did not perceive the exhaustion of his own fortune. Because of him, Dharmārka was kept away from the righteous among those of noble mind.
That evildoer was appointed to the office of domestic affairs.
That wicked-minded man brought about untimely death for gods, cows, Brahmins, the helpless, guests, and those who depend upon the king, and he cut off their means of livelihood.

Even the cruel Kāpālika Śavājīva nourishes his own kin; but Bhadreśvara was a sinner who even robbed his own people of their lives. When the lord Bhadreśvara had been constructed everywhere by Tuṅga in the month of Caitra, [the following occurred].

Sugandhisiṃha met his end in the month of Āṣāḍha. When he, the source of support for all beings, had passed away to the other world, Tuṅga— deprived of his head and filled with wretchedness— considered himself as one whose life was lost.
Then, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the king dispatched Śrī Trilocanapāla, who was seeking the assistance of the Shāhi, to that country;
he was accompanied by a continuous retinue of princes, high ministers, feudatories, and others.
A vast army, capable of shaking the world, followed him.
Having been received with honors by the Shāh who had come forward to meet him, he was accompanied by his son.

When he remained in that place for five or six days, intoxicated by his obsession with staying awake, performing *nyāsa* rituals, and practicing weapons, the Śāhi, observing him engaged in such exertion, spoke these two verses: “... [he was] habituated to staying awake, performing *nyāsa*, and practicing weapons; seeing him thus intent on application, the Śāhi then said: (Yugma) KRT_7_0049cd–KRT_7_0050ab–KRT_7_0050cd.
"As long as you have not resolved to engage in battle with the Turuṣkas,
remain here on this mountain slope, overcome by indolence.
Thus spoke Trilocana, yet he did not accept that beneficial advice.

He stood there, perfectly equanimous amidst his troops, eager for battle out of pride. Then, a small portion of the army was dispatched by him across the Sītā river to scout the enemy; having crossed it with those limited forces, he then struck them down.

Then the Shāh, who knew the true nature of battle, spoke again and again to him— who was filled with pride— the very same proposal as mentioned before. But he, being subject to his eagerness for combat, did not accept his words.

Instruction is useless for those whose destruction is imminent. Then, at dawn, the leader of the Turkish army himself, skilled in treacherous combat, marched forth with a full-scale assault out of anger.
Then the ridge of Tuṅga suddenly met with defeat;
for a moment, the Śāhi army appeared to form a firm alliance.
Even when the Śāhi army had departed, Jayasiṃha remained resplendent on the battlefield.
Śrīvardhana, Sāṃgrāmivibhramārka, and Ḍāmara—
by these three warriors striking in that terrible tumult of horses,
their own fame was preserved in the field of heroes within their own land.

Even countless enemies were unable to defeat him in battle; the three-eyed Lord, raining down streams of blood, shone resplendent in the fight. KRT_7_0060ab–KRT_7_0061ab. Only the Lord is capable of describing the majesty of Kartrilocanapāla. KRT_7_0060cd. Even countless enemies were unable to defeat him in battle. KRT_7_0060cd. The three-eyed one, raining down streams of blood, shone resplendent in the fight. KRT_7_0061ab.
Like the three-eyed Lord Śiva with his spreading radiance like the fire at the end of an eon,
he— having fought in battle against millions of armored warriors—
emerged alone from the peril of the enemy, for he was one who understood the vital points of action.
When Trilocana had gone far away across the entire circle of the earth,
which was being shrouded by the shadow of the locust-like army of fierce Caṇḍālas,
Hammīra, though victorious in battle, could not even draw a breath.
Recalling the superhuman valor of Śrī Trilocanapāla,
even Trilocana, having fallen from his own position and relying upon a force of elephants,
became filled with great energy and strove with effort to recover the goddess of victory.

Just as the very name of the glory of the Śāhis has quickly perished, so too has it been described here incidentally and not in detail. That which was impossible even in a dream, wherein all desires were shattered—

For one who performs such deeds with ease, nothing remains unachievable for Fate. Even that slight extent of the territory belonging to King Śaṅkaravarman has already been made manifest here in the previous description of events.
Now it is being considered whether that Śāhi kingdom, along with its ministers, its rulers, and its retinue,
existed or did not exist;
for the Turuṣkas have established their descent upon the entire surface of the earth.

Having suffered defeat, Tuṅga then slowly entered his own country. The king, whose disposition was consistent with his fortitude, did not direct his anger toward Tuṅga for that offense, even though he had been defeated like a jackal.
However, the dependence upon his lofty lord became a source of distress;
for even the mind of a beast suffers when it is subject to another.
Though he was the son of Tuṅgā, Kandarpasiṃha was proud of his royal valor.

As he conducted the royal affairs, his mind became filled with anxiety. At that moment, his brother Vigraharāja, seeking a vulnerability in the king through secret letters, dispatched Tuṅga for the purpose of assassination.

Then the king, his mind long wavering due to the recollection of the *Kośa* and other treatises, and distressed by their constant urging, spoke to those who were inciting him: KRT_7_0075ab: "The king, his intellect for a long time oscillating because of the recollection of the *Kośa* and so forth; KRT_7_0075cd: being vexed by their repeated instigation, he then addressed the instigators.
That excellent son is always our sole refuge;
if he should fall at this very moment, what shall we do when we see it?
Otherwise, being surely provoked, he would surely slay us by force.
Having spoken thus for the purpose of passing the time, the king became silent.
Taking those very words, which served as a seed, to heart,
they made an effort to bring Tuṅga to that same state.
Within six months, Tuṅga was summoned from his home by the king;
though he had seen a bad dream, he went forth with his son due to the power of fate.
Having entered the royal assembly hall, he stood before the king for a moment.
Accompanied by five or six servants, he entered the sacrificial pavilion.
Thereafter, Parva, Śarkaraka, and others entered;
even without addressing the protector of the earth, they struck down Tuṅga with their weapons.
The minister of Śaṅkaravarman, named Mahāratha,
had a descendant in the line of Tuṅgabhr̥tya, namely Siṃharatha, who was highly praiseworthy. At that moment, though unarmed, he desired to provide protection.

He cast his own body upon the back of the lofty elephant as it was being struck. At the first blow dealt to the lofty one, the king’s breath was stifled by fear; when that [elephant] became breathless, the king regained his breath.

Near the court Brahmin named Dharma was a son who was a doer of evil: Pārtha, Tuṅga, and the wicked-minded Kaṅka. For the sake of protection from those two impure companions, [he placed] his own finger in his mouth.
There, like animals, they dropped their weapons out of fear as they were being hurled about.
And those who had been his high-ranking ministers, such as Caṅga and others,
though armed with weapons, sat silent like women, overcome with terror.
In that tumultuous situation, where death was imminent and its timing unknown, the king,
fearing that his servants might set fire to the place or engage in battle,
swiftly cut [the branches] with his sword to reassure his own men.
He struck off the head of Tuṅga, along with his son, outside [the city].
Seeing their master’s head severed and the army fleeing in dejection,
a few of Tuṅga’s servants, however, displayed true devotion as servants.
A feudatory named Bhujaṅga, the lord of twice-born men, arrived at his house; he made Saṃgrāmarāja flee from house to house,
breaking down the barred doors with a golden staff.
That king slew twenty warriors in the assembly hall;
the treasury official named Trailokyaraja was killed in battle, as were the hero Kayya, the foster-son of Antaka, and the one named Abhinava.
Thirty-one heroic Aṅgas, who lived by their height, formed a line; though slain, they became a ladder for the path to heaven. Having fought a battle, the one named Padmarāja emerged unscarred.
By resorting to sacred fords, he cast off the torment of the fire of grief caused by his master’s death;
whereas others, abandoning their weapons— the friends that protect one in both worlds— on the field of battle, were deprived of both fame and life.
The one named Canda, who considered himself a great warrior, the guide called Arjuna,
Helācakra, and Ḍāmara— having cast aside their weapons, they were slain by their enemies. The lofty palace was overturned and its wealth plundered by the king.

On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the story was brought to its conclusion. When the king— who had acted without malice— was slain along with his high-born son, those who were mostly wicked flourished, having attained their rise in the sovereign’s domain.
He who, by the act of secret slander, defiled the king’s mind and became the cause of the ruin of both brother and nephew— burnt away by malicious rumors,
that serpent was the destroyer of his own kin.
Then Tuṅga’s brother was made the commander-in-chief by the king.
[Couplet] Kṣemā, the most excellent wife of Kandarpasiṃha,
united with Nāga, like the dark night with a *rākṣasa*.
When the tumult had subsided, after four days, the virtuous Bimbā,
the noble daughter-in-law and daughter of the Shāh, entered the fire.
While this Kandarpa was held captive by Mammāyāja for as long as he lived,
Maṅkhanā, the beloved of Tuṅga, took those two famous sons, Vicitrasiṃha and Mātṛsiṃha,
as well as that daughter-in-law.
Driven out from his country, the wretched man took up residence in Rājapurī. (Yugma) Then, at a prominent post, the wicked Bhardeśvara was appointed by the king;
he plundered the treasury and other assets of Bhūteśvara and the other deities. (KRT 7.0105cd–7.0106)
How great is the deficiency in the discernment of this king,
that he made even such men as Pārtha and others his superiors!
For Pārtha was of supreme dull-wittedness, notorious for having lived with his brother’s wife.
Through diligent and dispassionate effort, he was appointed as the city magistrate. By Pārtha, whose mind had abandoned all concern for the sin of killing and other evils,
the sacred stage-platform of the Supreme Lord was set in motion.

In former times, there was a son of the ocean named Devamukha, who served as the chief scribe (divira) for a greedy king; he was the foremost among the miserly and was skilled at oppressing the subjects in order to increase the treasury. Mataṅga, the son of that scribe, became [the minister].
The son of the courtesan Āpūlikā was named Candramukha.
Having obtained the favor of the king through his reliance on the minister Tuṅga,
he accumulated a hoard of wealth starting from a single cowrie up to tens of millions.

In the midst of his wealth, the greedy man, having presented other offerings as tributes, engaged in the sale of cakes to his own servants— an act unbecoming of his lineage. Having recovered his prosperity once more, he became possessed of abundant fire and free from disease.
He who had a weak digestion and was afflicted by disease was mocked by the people as he stood there;
yet at the moment of his death, he alone possessed a single meritorious deed:
that he had given one-third of a *koṭi* [of gold] at the shrine of Śrī Raṇeśvara.
Then, three sons— Nānābhāga, Nandin, and Mukha— were appointed by the king as lords of the army's division, living off their high positions. Yet,
the king’s appointment of them to such lofty ranks became a source of ridicule.
It was like the sudden binding of a child in place of gold. In that battle against the Turuṣkas, while the king and the ruler Kṣāntiśīla were present,
some of the Darad, Divira, and Āmara tribes fell into a state of extreme agitation.
While the ministers were thus unqualified and the king was characterized by patience and virtue,
certain [ministers] such as Darad, Divira, and Ḍāmara attained a state of arrogance.
Loṭhikā, the daughter of the king, having established a monastery (maṭha) named after herself, [became its head].

He established another monastery for Tilottamā, named after her mother. Even among the sinful, there exists some latent impression of virtuous deeds, since Bhadreśvara also constructed a monastery resplendent with merit.
Truly, Saṃgrāmarāja, the discerning one,
having declared his own wealth to be acquired through what is right and not through what is unjust, does not bestow it nor does he withhold it.
Śrīlekhā, the wife of the king, is the daughter of Śrīyaśomaṅgala.

When her husband’s power had become feeble, she indulged in wantonness. He who was born to Sugandhisīha by Jayalakṣmī became the queen’s most beloved; he surpassed even the three worlds in his charm for her.

He, possessed of exceedingly sharp intellect, was the creator of the Jayākaragañja and other treasuries; Jayākara became his son, who likewise provided assistance to the treasury. His son was Jāra, who was intent on accumulating wealth by managing the Mayagrāma village treasury and other such holdings.
By her husband’s grace, she became fortunate and possessed of great splendor, like the earth itself.
On the first day of the fourth month of Āṣāḍha, that lord of the earth,
having consecrated his son named Harirāja, passed away.
Served by the well-disposed and illuminating all directions without exception,
he brought joy to everyone like the festival of spring. By him,
whose commands were never in vain, this earth was made free of thieves.
On the night market, the closing of the gates was forbidden;
that command of the king, whose rising was unexpected,
became venerable among the monarchs like the crescent of the new moon.
Having ruled the earth for twenty-two great years, that lord of the earth,
of pure fame, met his end on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śuci.
Like the splendor of shining stars upon a living being in an instant,
or like the heat of summer nights, this prosperity brings about destruction;
it is like the conduct of a wanton woman toward her own son when she is filled with passion.

There was an uncontradicted popular rumor that she had performed a malevolent spell against him. While the regalia for the coronation were being prepared, the queen mother Ślīlekhā herself, desiring the kingdom, arrived after having bathed.

Then, with his body parts joined together by his brother and his foster-brother named Sāgara, that son was made king as the infant Ananta. (Yugma) When another person, desiring to seize the treasure, took it away from there, [Ananta] caused him to be put to death. (KRT 7.135cd–136ab)

Just as it was surely for the evil of a greedy man who stole the guards, so too did the destruction of the son occur for the queen mother who was greedy for the kingdom; when the kingdom was seized by another, it resulted only in her own ruin. (A pair of verses)

Her heart so distressed by that deprivation of the kingdom, she forgot her affection for her son; fie on the latent tendencies produced by the habitual pursuit of sensual enjoyments! Then there arrived an elderly paternal uncle of the young king.
Vigraharāja, whose prowess was far-reaching, set out from Lohara to seize the kingdom; having unexpectedly burnt the gate,
he entered the city with haste in two and a half days.
The armies dispatched by Śrīlekhā entered Loṭikā’s monastery;
having set it ablaze, they slaughtered him along with his followers.
Then, having established two monasteries—one for himself and one for his son—...
The queen remained constantly engaged in acts of treason against the kingdom.
Then the king, his childhood gradually fading,
became addicted to excessive extravagance due to his status as the lord of the womb [the treasury].

He had as his most beloved sons the Śāhis, beginning with Rudrapāla; they seized vast wealth and stripped him of his sovereignty. Yet, the king maintained his daily sustenance with only half a lakh [of gold].

Rudrapāla never abandoned his state of poverty even for a moment. Diddāpāla, however, though he possessed eighty thousand [gold pieces] daily bestowed by the protector of the earth, did not sleep peacefully at night in his own home.
Anaṅgapālavetāla, who was cherished by the king,
set his mind constantly upon the shattering of statues of the gods made of gold.
Rudrapāla became a wandering mendicant [to escape] those who seize one's wealth, life, and other possessions.
And he became an adamantine cage for those who were mostly thieves and outcastes.
The scribes, having obtained Rudrapāla as their patron, caused oppression to the subjects;
the illustrious one named Utpala, who was their leader, established a monastery for the blind.
Let it be told what other mark of royal favor he possessed:
the lord of Jālandhara, Inducandra, himself married the daughter of Indumukha, who was like the moon-faced goddess herself,
because of her exquisite beauty, as if she were the personification of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
He founded a monastery at Tripureśvara under his own name; then,
he married the goddess Sūryamatī, the younger sister of that [queen], who was slightly less than two years his junior.

By Rudra, his friend who brought delight to his ears, that lord of the earth was made a vessel for wicked deeds, just as Suyodhana was by Karṇa. At that moment, the powerful Tribhuvana became the lord of Kampana.

He arrived, having prepared a formidable force, to seize the kingdom from the king. When he had approached to fight, having drawn in his entire army (*kaṭaka*), those who were loyal to the king— even if they were single-handed or accompanied only by their horses— did not abandon his side.
Leaping over spears with his sword, Anantadeva, whose prowess was praiseworthy, himself struck down the three worlds in battle. His body,
