though protected by armor, was tormented by those firm blows.
He fled, vomiting blood from his mouth as if it were his own prowess;
that king, whose heroism was concealed by discipline and who was like a mere child,
having seen that inconceivable force, had abandoned the battle and departed.
[111] Ślūvyavikrama rendered Moghavikrama’s valor futile by striking down with spears the one named Abhinava, who was slaying Śamālāḍāmara at the site of the hall.
In the midst of the battle, Khaḍga, who had become like a pillar due to being enveloped in flesh and blood,
became Bhairava, the lord of infinite beings, causing the world to tremble.
Seeing bodies with limbs severed by blows at every step, he—
Then, as the offerings were being presented with the recitation of their names preceded by the finest [ingredients],
the King,
having manifested courtesy toward that which was offered, forbade the restlessness of the single-limbed [deities] from the records of the accountants. (A *yugma* couplet).
Thus, being grateful, he bestowed upon his servants a gift of ninety-six crores of dināras in succession.
(Yugma) When the king returned from battle, the sword in his hand was cleansed by showers of milk. (KRT 7.164ab)
"It is popular rumor that he was dragged away after a long time by a firm and steady grip.
"Oh, the greatness of the lord of the earth! Having arrived from another land in a single day, he, free from anger, shared out such a portion of the three worlds!"
He appointed his kinsman named Brahmarāja as the governor of the treasury;
but having become estranged due to his hatred for Rudrapāla, he departed in disillusionment. Joining with seven Mleccha kings, he became a formidable leader of a confederacy.

By him, King Darad, whose auspiciousness was as immovable as a mountain, was brought [as a captive] with great effort. When he reached the village named Kṣīrapṛṣṭha, eager for battle, Rudrapāla, exultant in his prowess, went forth to meet him at the head of the host.
When the battle had been arranged for the following day,
the lord of the Darads went to play at the abode of the nāga named Piṇḍāraka. Although he was restrained there by those standing nearby due to his improper conduct, he did not desist.
He struck the spear into the body of a leaping fish.
Then, a serpent emerged from the pit in the form of a jackal;
and the lord of Darada pursued it out of a desire for hunting.
Beholding him approaching,
the king’s army, intent on uprooting him and fearing an assault, went forth for battle.
Then there arose a mass of fire produced by the friction of the clashing weapons.
In that festival of battle for heroes, where the arms of celestial nymphs were won,
amidst the tumult of the great warriors, the severed head of the Lord of Darad caused the fierce glory of Rudra, possessed of terrible splendor, to grow anew.

In battle, the Mleccha kings suffered slaughter, captivity, and the like; conversely, the King of Kaśmīra obtained gold, jewels, and other riches. His crest-jewels, pearls, and so forth, were washed by the splashing water of his trembling garlands.
Rudrapāla brought the head of the Darada king to his master.
His brothers Udayana and Vatsa, as well as the twice-born who had performed the funeral rites,
and other such people from abroad became his attendants.
Then, when Rudrapāla had met his death through a disease of the glands,
the other sons of Śāhi also quickly went to their destruction. Upon the disappearance of the blindness caused by affection for Pāla, he came to possess a pure disposition.

Queen Sūryamatī was reflected in her husband as if in a mirror. Known by the other name Subhaṭā, she, who established the shrine of Gaurīśvara, constructed the Subhaṭāmaṭha on the bank of the Vitastā as a meritorious work.
Through gifts of gold, horses, jewels, and other valuables, she rendered many brahmins non-poor during the consecration of Sadāśiva. [She was the younger sister] of Kallana,
who was also known as Āśācandra.

Out of affection, she established a monastery named Sāgrahāra; and that virtuous woman also had two monasteries constructed beside the temples of Vijayeśa and Amareśa, using the names of her brother, who was called Sillana, and of her husband.
At Śrī Vijayeśvara, he bestowed one hundred and eight agrahāras,
a source of great merit, upon learned Brāhmaṇas; likewise,
he granted agrahāras at Amareśvara under the name of his lord.
He also established tridents, arrows, liṅgas, and other such objects.
When the king known as Rājarāja died, his son and wife performed these rites for him.

Having abandoned their royal residence in the vicinity of Sadāśiva, those two took up their abode there. From that time forward, the kings, abandoning the traditional customs of their former dynasties, established their dwellings in that very place according to such custom.

The attendants of the king’s stable, being fond of horses, became dear to him; through his favors and by plundering the countryside, they attained equality with him in every respect. Being a favorite of his lord due to his mastery over the inner apartments, he was skilled in providing amusement.
A guide named Ḍallaka was constantly plundering the subjects;
Bhoja, the lord of Mālava, having sent heaps of gold,
caused him to construct a wall around Kapaṭeśvara.

A vow had been made by King Bhoja to perform daily face-washings with the waters produced at the Pāpasūdana Tīrtha. He who, from the very beginning of his religious observances, fulfilled that vow which was otherwise difficult to accomplish—
With clusters of glass jars sent to him filled with that water,
he— named Padmarāja, a teacher who provided leaves— became dear to that generous man who was habituated to betel. (Cakkalaka)
Then that seller of leaf-plates and such items was made by the king to pay almost his entire wealth, produced from his native land;
[he received] from the king a seat upon an elephant-throne marked with the beauty of five moons.

When that creditor was to receive his due wealth, he took even more for the sake of bondage. Every half-month, every month, and every day, there arrived from his palace the royal insignia used for the court assembly.
Then Queen Sūryamatī, having given her own accumulated treasury,
prevented the distress of the land arising from King Padma;
and at that time, the fear caused by the *ḍallaka* thieves and others in the horse-stables was pacified.
Once again, conditions conducive to stability prevailed in the land.
From that time forward, the queen alone became intent upon the affairs of state;
the king, having abandoned talk of valor, remained instead as the executor of those duties.
A woman’s submissiveness to her husband and likewise the husband’s victory over his wife— through their stainless character, neither fell into mutual reproach.
Through qualities such as devotion to existence, observance of vows, ritual bathing, renunciation, and virtuous conduct, [they flourished].

Even the sages were utterly conquered by the accomplished Anantadeva. During the long reign of that lord of the earth, Royal Fortune, ever seeking new objects of her desire, attended upon his various servants like a bride choosing her husband.
Named Kṣema, he was a fulfiller of the royal treasury and a crusher of fools;
offering wealth in various forms such as the twelve-fold share, he acted [as minister].
Thereafter, there was a virtuous minister from Trigarta, the brahmin Keśava.
By whom the king was adorned as if by moonlight upon a palace;
yet that very man, wandering alone and deprived of his fortune, was seen by the people. For whose prosperity are dense clouds of the waters of luck? (A pair of verses).
Reflecting that wealth depends on fortune, this pride of family and prowess among those of deluded intellect is truly in vain regarding its vastness.
[This was said] by Prāsādapālaka, the Vaiśya, at the temple of Gaurī, the abode of the gods.
Bhūti’s sons were Haladhara, Vajra, and Varāha.
Among them, Haladhara, who had been served by Sūryamatī,
attained preeminence over all as he grew day by day.
As he brought those who were next to him in rank under his command through the application of his intellect,
the lord of the earth became his subordinate, looking to his face for guidance along with his wife.
The one of exalted intelligence had previously drafted, with great care, a plan that was both comprehensive and detailed.
He made the office of the treasury manifest as the bearer of the burden for all other departments.
Whatever recording of the value of gold and other matters was under the king's authority,
which revealed the accumulation of wealth for the people, [was handled by him].
Knowing that future kings would [suffer], he prevented that [practice];
for the wise man understands that the accumulation of wealth causes the hardship of punishments and the like.

Having slain some who had plundered the wealth and wives of those whose horses were kept in his stables, he brought peace to the world's turmoil. By him, the city was led away from its former weariness and restored with shimmering golden temples that served as abodes for the gods.
The confluence of the Vitastā and the Sindhu was graced by monasteries and palatial residences;
his brothers and sons, intoxicated by their familiarity with fortune, never displayed a fondness for giving, remaining like elephants that withhold their ichor.

His nephew, the illustrious and heroic Bimba, born of Varāha, served as the official in charge of the gate; he was a rain-cloud for the cessation of [the flow of] gifts. He became the untimely death to the lineage of the Ḍāmaras, having few followers.
In his own kingdom, he gave up his life, turning his back on flight. Having uprooted King Śāla in Campā, King Ananta, victorious over various kings, installed a new ruler of the earth.

In foreign lands, the king— who lacked the power of counsel— repeatedly fell into distress as he attempted forceful invasions through mere valor. When the son of Tukka, Kalaśa, began his enterprise, the army became exhausted.

The wielder of power liberated him from Vallāpura through strategic means. And the lord of Kampana, having cleared the paths for him who had entered the city of Uraśā— his way blocked by enemies— provided an exit.
In the midst of the perilous conflict with his enemies, during the time of that great lord of the earth,
various acts of daring broke forth moment by moment.
The illustrious Rājeśvara, the gatekeeper and son of Bhadreśvara—
Who enjoys freedom from humiliation in the royal palace while surrounded by *ḍāmaras*?
Even one who conducts himself with fear after seeing what must be done by those with eyes like thunderbolts—
who enjoys freedom from humiliation in the service of the royal palace?
Having become the object of malicious rumors due to his intense devotion to the Goddess,
even Haladhara was bound by the enraged Āśā, Candra, and others;
with all his wealth confiscated by the king, he endured the suffering of imprisonment.

When fortune is devoid of power, how can there be a face that is exclusively radiant? Fortune, released from imprisonment by the king, returned once more and embraced him, her white face bright with a smile born of shame at the white royal parasol.

Through his affection for the queen, which was like that of the rainy season, he experienced from moment to moment the alternating appearance of clouds and suns— the manifestations of her anger and favor. Then,
in due course, [the state of] straightforwardness arose within him.
The king’s state of being conquered by his wife was on the verge of yielding a bitter fruit;
though he was being restrained by wise men such as Haladhara and others, who pointed out that by renouncing his office he would incur no further blame.
Constantly urged by his wife, who was deluded by affection for her son,
he became intent on giving the kingdom to his son Kalaśa. Even though he was made to speak thus, O King, you will later feel regret.
By him, the chamberlain named Raṇāditya prepared the consecration.
On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, in his thirty-ninth year, the son was consecrated by the king.
Then, stationing the princes in an improper place for battle, Raṇāditya—
reflecting on the majesty of sovereignty and being harsh in his conduct—
spoke these words: "This prince is Ananta, O King."

With his hand placed upon the back of his neck, he announced himself to the protector of the earth. Turned around and looked at by the enraged king, he, clearly smiling and firm in statecraft, spoke to him thus: *He, with his hand resting on the back of his neck, announced himself to the protector of the earth. Turned around and looked at by the enraged lord of the earth, he, having smiled in this manner, spoke to him plainly, being resolute in policy.*
Since kings such as those of Kānyakubja and other lands are reported to be in this state,
what other course of action could there be for you, whose kingdom has already been made manifest?
Day after day, you will surely be filled with remorse.

"Even for a sage, it is not possible to completely abandon pride. Having heard those words of the minister, which were deeply moving to those who see far into the future, the king became unable to offer a reply.
On another day, he saw the new king being served by a circle of monarchs, while the former king was accompanied only by a limited number of attendants.
The wise Haradhara, out of resentment, rebuked Lakṣmī with these words by means of logic;
thus reproaching her, he brought him back again.
Having made his young son devoid of happiness by entrusting the burden of the kingdom to him, [he departed].
Why, out of regard for your own pleasure, do you not feel shame in this old age?
You yourself must take up the burden of the king’s affairs;
let this son of yours be filled with the enjoyments of youth.

Having spoken thus, he once again assumed his royal office; and by means of a mere fraction [of his power], he rendered King Kalaśadeva utterly powerless through his stratagems. Even while constantly attending upon his parents for matters such as food and other necessities, he remained in their presence.
Then there was a king named Kalaśa, whose sovereignty was merely nominal.
In all the arrangements for the worship of sacred sites and weapons appropriate for a monarch,
he acted as if performing the duties of a domestic priest, serving as an assistant to his father.
For those who are firm in signlessness and do not regret the signless,
there is no wavering of mind anywhere, unlike the uncertainty found among animals.
Having thus compelled her husband to hand over the kingdom through such persistence, [she departed].
The queen became filled with remorse as if she were a pauper;
envious of the excellence of her daughters-in-law, which was worthy of a king’s pleasure-woman, she,
with a harsh heart, could not endure their finery, ornaments, and the like.

She constantly compelled her sons and queens to perform the duties of female slaves, so that they showed no aversion even to the smearing of the house. Then there was the son of Vigraharāja, named Kṣitirāja.
Once, a brother born of the king’s paternal uncle came into his presence.
He reported to him his distress, which was a torment to his mind,
concerning his son named Bhuvanarāja, who had become utterly ruined despite having obtained the kingdom.
For his son, having taken refuge in the kingdom of Nīlapura,
became intent on exerting effort to counteract his father’s undertaking by means of those forces;
and he established for his father the name of the venerable Bhāgavatas.

To dogs that had been given the sacred thread, the king of the earth, whose mind was pure, felt impurity; and toward his own wife, who had acted contrary to him, he—possessing a purified intellect—felt aversion. Thus, to remove the torment of his mind, he conceived a longing for the nectar of total renunciation.
Having swiftly bestowed the kingdom upon his son by Queen Rāmalekhā— who was born immediately after his elder brother and was named Utkarṣa— even though he was still a suckling infant, he [departed].

The royal sage, together with the gods, performed pilgrimages to sacred fords. Having enjoyed the great happiness of tranquility for many years, that wise and supreme devotee of Viṣṇu attained union with the Wielder of the Discus.

Both that lord of food and the king were renowned for their excellence in generosity; at that moment, those two wise ones were equal as friends of poets. [He was born] from the paternal uncle of his father, by King Ananta.

The infant grandson was placed as a trust upon the lap of the King of Tanvaṅga. Having brought both that kingdom and the child to maturity, Tanvaṅga returned once more to Kaśmīra and departed for the Setting Mountain (Asta).
Among the descendants of King Indu, whose enjoyments had become common to all,
there arose here a lineage stained by treachery.
From Indurāja’s son, Buddharāja, came Siddharāja.
He begot a heroic son named Madanarāja. That son of his, exceedingly arrogant, marched forth from the circle of kings while the king was in distress, remaining unbroken due to his excess of valor.
At that time, a man named Jindurāja, having been brought to his own home by the queen— who was distressed by the excesses of the Ḍāmaras— was made to accept the role of counselor. Through him,
a one-eyed man named Śobha, who caused intense anxiety to the lord, [was removed].
Then Ḍāmara, residing in Degrāma, was struck down after being granted an *askanda* [military escort].
Having bestowed the lordship over Kampana upon that powerful man, [the king departed].
The king made Yājapura and other regions pay tribute.
When King Anantabhūbhuj was in danger due to various lapses in his reign, Haladhara went to his destruction, like one who has lost his support.
To that King standing at his side, who was accompanied by his kinsmen and seeking instruction, the wheel-bearer, who was about to die, spoke as follows: "Do not,
out of impulsive rashness, undertake ventures against the kingdoms of others."

By means of logic, I have dispelled your distress regarding Vallāpura and other places. This Jindurāja, having attained supreme prosperity, is to be suspected; Jayānanda will cause a rift between you and your son.

Having remembered that which was told by him, the wise King bound the highly powerful Jindurāja, having deprived him of his weapons. Then, in the course of time, King Kalaśa became corrupted in his intentions.
While on the road, that wicked man was led into intimacy with his servants.
His favorites were Vijja, Pittha, Rāja, Pāja, and others—
four arrogant princes born of the Śāhi lineage.
The son of Gañjapati, named Nāga, was his close attendant;
he too, Jayānanda, became his teacher of Kauṭilya.
When the lord of the twice-born, Amarakaṇṭha, had attained equality with Śiva, [the king]— KRT_7_0275ab–cd / KRT_7_0276ab.

The king became a pupil of that Pramadakaṇṭha, who was by nature ill-behaved; he [the king] became his instructor in what ought not to be done. The teacher became one who avoided any consideration of what should or should not be approached.
What else can be said of that Guru who has transcended all conceptual constructs— he who,
having cast aside all hesitation, engaged even in sexual union with his own daughter?
By those who were skilled in moving through the great ritual commitments (*mahāsamaya*), he was approached without fear.
Even Bhairava is not counted as fearless by those who are fierce through their own power. My disciples,
having fallen with broken knees out of terror,
were restored to health by the cat-merchant through the offering of his head and hands.

Long ago, out of fear of my feet, cats fell with their knees broken; thus, that foolish cat-merchant assumed the name "Viḍālavaṇig" (Cat-Merchant) as a means of not forgetting himself. That fool, arrogant in his succession of being a physician and a teacher, maintained this pretense.
He attained the status of a guru to artisans such as poets, painters,
and royal craftsmen. Placing the healthy Bhaṭṭapādas upon his head,
he [the merchant] offered a handful of asafoetida whose pungent fragrance was intense, like a flood of cat-dung.

Thus, though they were by nature devoid of essence, those heavy [men] led him daily into blindness as thundering clouds lead the day into darkness. Those who stay awake for long periods at night and indulge in excessive eating—
Their necks are perpetually foul-smelling from the belching up of undigested flesh;
resembling drains for refuse, they quickly discharge a torrent of honey from their backs, as if it were a stream of cleansing water cast down by those following the lower path.
At night, having performed service together with them through sacrifices involving musical instruments, the *cāraṇa*—
who was skilled in playing the flute—
forcefully overpowered the women while the son of Haladhara was enraged at the one named Kanaka, who was overflowing with pride.
Having been tied to a pillar by his servants, he was made noseless;
that rogue named Camaka, who had his fingers cut off,
gradually regained the favor of the new king through his skill as a poultry-keeper.
With his wealth consisting of the favor of the king, even amidst the ministers,
that dog among men attained a firm footing and acquired the name *Ṭakkura*. Having easily shattered the bamboo staff— a cause for shame— as he gained notoriety, he [proceeded].
He considered the breaking of his nose even more [unbearable] than that.
Thus, incited to such depravity and cast off all shame, he did what was done;
although the account is unspeakable, it is told here because it falls within the middle [section].
The king’s sister, named Kallanā, and his daughter, named Nāgā,
were not spared for him to enjoy, as he was already addicted to the wives of others.
Having heard that news together with his wife, the aged king did not contradict it out of shame;
he remained there, suppressing his distress.
A certain twice-born man, born in a village near the forest, was begging for handfuls of grain.
There was also a foolish astrologer named Loṣṭaka;
by the grace of the village field-guardian, he would wander at night and,
through his knowledge of objects held in closed fists, became known as Muṣṭiloṣṭaka.

Having attained supreme renown as the beloved of the passionate new king, he was dear to his consort due to his gravity, integrity, and skill as an astrologer. [Tilaka] The venerable Maṭhādhīśa, the ascetic Vyomaśiva, was a holy man with matted hair. [KRT 7.298ab]
In the legal dispute known as the Khurkhuṭā,
he who had undertaken fixed vows [took] from the blind musician named Mamman— a servant of his own worship—
the garment of a twice-born man from Avanti who was being seized by the hand.

He who had previously received that which was lost through being cherished— by him, whose garment was made of thread intended for breaking hopes, the king was now restrained. Having been sent away, he was made to gather flowers and brought into the presence of the monarch.
[Madana], talkative by name, attained the status of an intimate confidant, gradually finding his place within the secret gatherings of the harem. (Cakkalaka)
Quickly deluded by those and other sycophantic courtiers,
Kalasha, being rendered turbid, mistook faults for virtues.
Joking that causes shame, speech that is improper, the oppression of subjects as a duty, audacity as brilliance, and intimacy with women accessible through passion— these were his traits.
Their essence is indeed the endurance of verbal abuse from the vulgar; in their presence, no action—whether good or evil—is considered a fault, for it is known and abandoned [as insignificant].
And a king, wandering from house to house out of an eager passion for thievery, found no pleasure during the nights in the embrace of his own wife.
With a boundless love for dependence on others, delighting in the wives of others,
and offering oblations into the blazing fire of desire for those possessed by passion—
the king once placed five or six such profligates at the forefront.

Desiring to commit theft, he went to the house of Jindurāja at night. There was Jindurāja’s daughter-in-law, an exceedingly unchaste woman, who had been given a secret signal by King Kalaśa for that very night at her own home.
As he entered, announced by barking dogs, the Caṇḍālas, armed with swords and suspecting him of being a thief, rushed toward the house door;
seeing them prepared to strike, he fell to the ground out of fear.
His followers protected him as he stood with his body cast upon their backs.
Though they were dealing him blows from their fists and other injuries, it was with great difficulty that he was made to desist by his own people, who said, "Do not do this; this is the god Kalaśa."
That he placed one deprived of his sense of smell at the head and pursued a woman—
surely that was an ill omen for that lustful man. He departed from his home, rendered helpless by the side-long glances of his beloved.
On the road, he did not meet his destruction by the glance of Kālī’s eye, due to fate;
yet, through the transgression of policy caused by the offense of his own mind,
even the king suffered humiliation from those who were untouchable.

By those very senses by which even the gods, such as Indra and Candra, were made to bristle with pride, how could a mortal possibly maintain unfading humility? First, a most perilous ill-repute blossoms; thereafter, a censurable longing arises; then, righteousness first goes to ruin; and finally, the praiseworthy course of self-respect perishes.

First one’s noble lineage falls into doubt, and then, upon the loss of the wish-fulfilling jewel of character, does one’s very life not likewise meet with reversal? When the ill-behaved king reached the capital, his parents learned of that news during the night itself.
Having wept for a long time, filled with affection for their son, shame, and grief, the two of them made a resolution regarding the imprisonment of that guilty man.
[They did so] to their eldest grandson, Bappika’s son, who was a treasury of all sciences.
And wishing to celebrate her enthronement, they passed those nights in joy. Then, in the morning, King Kalaśa was summoned by them.
Vijaya and Ānanda said, "We have apprehension; there is fear from Janaka.
With their permission, Jayānanda, having somehow taken Vijaya by the hand, entered his parents' house while being followed by Vijaya.
As soon as he had entered, his father gave him a slap on the face and said, "O you who share in misfortune, cast away that knife! Then,
supporting with his hand the joints of his limbs which were loosened by terror, [he stood there].

Touching his weapon with firm resolve, Vijja said to the king: "O King, though you are the foremost among men, how is it that you do not know that for the proud, the great passion for honor is something never to be abandoned?"
"How can I, having accepted my wages, abandon my master while he lives in this peril, even though I am armed by this prince?
O Lord of the Earth, you are the father and this boy is your son; how could I forsake you for a mere moment?"
"While I am absent, let that which is appropriate for him be done.
Having deluded the king with words that were both affectionate and harsh,
Bijja took his master and departed from his presence.
The wise honored the superhuman fortitude of Anantadeva as he thus displayed his prowess even in the presence of the king;
for the king’s wife, Caṇḍī, was [steadfast] by the power of the inevitable destiny.
At that moment, she remained observing a vow of absolute silence.
Had she been intent on speaking then, neither of those two things would have occurred:
either the certain destruction of everything, or the imprisonment of the jar.
Then, with the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the jar was swiftly brought into the residence of his beloved wife named Trasyandinī. Having said,
"A headache has come upon him," she made her husband appear terrified.

That wise woman, having learned the circumstances, had her husband’s head anointed with oil by them; under that pretext, she forbade everyone from entering and protected her husband by appointing Bijja to guard the door.

Then the queen, rising from her meditative absorption, rebuked the king and went into the presence of her son under the pretext of seeking his welfare. When the king likewise set out with the intent to seize him, [the son said: KRT_7_0334ab–cd; KRT_7_0335ab.
Having been granted entrance by the seed-syllable (*bīja*), he then became all alone;
because his followers were forbidden from following him, the lord of the earth (the king) became enraged,
and in his anger, he set out impetuously to go to the field of victory (*vijayakṣetra*).
As he was traveling with his wife and had reached the vicinity of Padmapura,
the brahmins Viśvāvaṭṭa and others, who were staying there, approached him and said:
"O King, why do you follow [this path] after having yourself renounced your office?"
Remorse is appropriate for what has been done, but not for that which exists nor even for that which does not exist.
"These subjects have not been abandoned by me through wicked intent"— having reflected thus, it is fitting to address the reproach due to your son's misconduct.

For a king possesses no power whatsoever like that of a mechanical puppet; rather, he becomes either virtuous or otherwise according to the good and evil deeds of his subjects. Indeed, it is the clouds that release the waters, or else the lightning.
That is the fruit of the ripening of the good and evil deeds of the lords of the forest (trees).
As for your desire to live in comfort by abandoning a son who has strayed from the path— how can that be appropriate for you, who have set out having abandoned your own treasury?
"Even one who has attained the height of power, who is worthy and pure,
by whom can such a man be touched when his treasury is exhausted, like a sword?
Having heard this, the discerning king desired to return until he could reflect further.
Then, having been appeased by his son who approached him together with his wife,
he entered the city; but with his anger still unappeased, he took the royal splendor that had been bestowed upon him from the palace and departed once more.
Having personally taken up his horse, weapons, armor, and other gear, he departed; then,
waiting for the queen, he stood for a moment on the bank of the river.

Having loaded various kinds of treasures onto their vehicles, the king’s women did not leave even the iron spikes [used for securing the wagons] behind in the house as they departed; meanwhile, the people remained silent,
unaware of the news prior to his departure.
Then, having learned the news, the people’s faces became resonant with wailing;
as they offered handfuls of flowers to those two in the city,
they seemed to cast out long, priceless pearls under the guise of teardrops.
"Alas, mother! Alas, father! Where are you going?"—from such lamentations as these, no other sound was heard on the roads at that time.
In the intervals between the cries on the paths, the sound of mountain torrents was heard.

A sound like the hissing sighs of grief from the mountains was heard. Their ears, which had long since become accustomed to those two through their constant cries on the road, seemed to hear their lamentation repeatedly even though it was empty space.
Seeing those two [trees] on the path of the tree-dwellers being struck by the *putrāghāta* (son-slaying) [wind],
people even censured the nurturing of fledglings by birds.
For Vijayeśvara, whose mind was tormented by the thought of his two sons’ departure, [the trees appeared thus].
Upon being seen, he brought peace to the mind, like a kind kinsman. There,
that day passed while the two were occupied with the distribution of storehouses, horses, servants, and dwellings,
as well as with the performance of various arrangements.
In that region, which was filled with herds of cattle laden with stores of wealth and implements, the market stalls appeared as if their streets were covered by heaps of fuel; there,
the princes— sons of the king and of high-born kinsmen such as Tanvaṅga and Rājatuṅga— resided.
Sūryavarman, Candra, and others followed that Ḍāmara.
Having stationed the Ḍāmaras, Kṣīrabhūpa, and others in their respective places such as Naunagara and elsewhere, the king remained guarded and secure.
For the illustrious King Ananta, whose mind was entirely at rest,
the days passed in festivities during the month of Vaiśākha;
[he was accompanied] by circles of princes, horsemen, charioteers, and groups of warriors.
He remained in the presence of the aged king, bound by all [his duties].
In his fifty-fifth year, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, he departed;
having reached the field of victory, he experienced the bliss of heaven.
When the king had departed, Kalaśa obtained a kingdom that was devoid of wealth; yet,
like a treasure-earth moving after its protector has left,
he made an effort even though empty, in order to illuminate his own realm.
Having consulted with Bijja and others, he appointed those who were esteemed as officials.
By him, Jayānanda was appointed to all offices;
and Varāhadeva, born in Trapura on the Vitastā, was placed at the gate.
For he who had been the minister of Ambara during the reign of Jindurāja was appointed by the king as the governor of Kampana;
having assigned others to their respective offices, [the king] established the various officials.
He zealously began to deliberate on matters of state regarding his father’s conflict;
Jayānanda, eager to assemble a body of infantry,
was likewise zealous in his father’s conflict, even taking jewels from those who were unworthy.
Having accepted the challenge, accompanied by the groups of princes such as Pattinbijja,
he then reached the city of Avanti to fight King Vṛddhi. Having been requested by the king, he was made to wait at the shore after being released from prison.
Jindurāja went forth to fight by way of Śimikāvartman.
Hearing of their exertion, the enraged [forces] of the elder kings—
namely, their own Ḍāmaras, cavalrymen, and others— assailed them with fury.

In Vijayeśvara, the entire forest of battle became impassable with weapons, where circles of horses were seen playing with discarded balls. Then Sūryamatī [sought] a husband from Ratna, who was exceedingly wrathful.
Out of affection for her son, she requested that there be no battle for two days. Then,
having dismissed at night the most trusted Brahmins led by Maya, she—
Out of extreme affection for him, she spoke these words in private to her son:
"O son, what is this reversal of judgment of yours that forebodes your destruction? For today you wish to fight with your father, who possesses such fierce valor."
By the mere knitting of whose eyebrows kings such as Darada and others were destroyed—
why do you wish to act like a moth in the fire of his wrath? For this king,
who is equal to Vītihotra (Agni), has now ascended the throne.
Who among those bearing weapons could be the savior of your grass-like men?
By which army divisions, by what valor, and with what riches do you, the foremost of the powerful, rush forth to fight him? (KRT 7.0376cd–7.0377)
"Enjoy this unbroken kingdom, which has been abandoned by him through fate.
What harm was done to you by your father while he sat at a sacred ford? He was struck down by the enemy while desiring a state of duality in this most dreadful calamity."

In just a few days, though already empty, you will become utterly destitute. Lead the armies; there is no fear for you so long as I am alive. Furthermore, lead this upright man with gentle and conciliatory words.
Thus, having been secretly entreated by his mother through the mouths of messengers, the son brought the army from all directions into his own presence during the night itself. And the messenger,
having heard of the retreat of the troops, was appeased.
The bold and beloved queen reproached her husband at dawn;
thus, although their mutual accusations had been quelled,
their minds fell into turbidity moment by moment due to the instigation of the slanderer.
For this very nature of enmity repeatedly undergoes division;
even when being reconciled, it is like a garment that remains damp within.
Having heard news of his son from the outer palace and elsewhere, the king’s heart was filled with anguish.
Having entered his home, he became dull-witted by the bold words of women.
Thus, though tormented day after day, he abandoned that torment night after night; with a pure heart, he attained a state comparable to a shallow pond in autumn.
The son brought about the destruction of the houses and other property belonging to his father’s faction;
but the father, being under the sway of his wife, did nothing for those on his son’s side.
Thus were they oppressed by the wife, who was blinded by affection for her son, and by the followers who had been incited against them.
Constantly tormented by harsh words, the king remained in a state of distress;
desiring to seize the kingdom from his son and perceiving that force to be devoid of heroes, he regarded King Jiendu as possessing only a slight measure of manliness.

Desirous of seizing the kingdom from his son, he then entreated those women who delighted in slender-limbed beauties, though they were averse to the undertaking of the kingship. At that time, fearing for the welfare of her own kin, she urged him on during the night.

The queen sent messengers to summon the king in order to bring him joy. Summoned by the messengers of his two grandfathers, he, eager for the daring deed, went out to the outer courtyard, even though he was being guarded by prepared guards.

Striking the horse's haunch with his heel, he crossed five yojanas in half a moment on that steed of mind-like speed, whose vigor remained unbroken. Those who were striving to follow the horse, which had surpassed all practice, [were left behind].
Many weary horses of the army, distressed on the road, were traveling along.
As he arrived and fell at his feet, his two grandfathers performed for him a consecration with the flowing streams of their tears of joy.

When his son arrived near him, the wise Kalaśa sent him away; wishing to reconcile with his parents, he turned back from performing what was displeasing to them. From that city, the wise man sent messengers to his side.
He ensured that his own internal dissension remained undisclosed while the kingdom was in turmoil.
Thus, even as the enmity continued to grow, King Kalaśa remained for some time, as it were, somewhat compliant with his mother's will.
The lord of Kampana, who was about to depart from Khaśālā for Kalasa and other regions,
was made to abandon his path by her as she caused him to falter.
In the meantime, [the king] set out to pacify the enmity that had caused the destruction of the country.
Aiming for those two, father and son, the twice-born performed the rite of fasting unto death (prāya). Then,
when the joints of his body had become rigid, out of deference to him, they acted accordingly.
The couple remained together in that city for two months. Then,
perceiving through their intellect that their son was intent on binding him out of joy at his sacrifice,
they departed again in distress and went to Vijayeśvara.

At night, his son set fire to the stables of horses; he also caused the destruction of foot soldiers by means of poison, weapons, fire, and various stratagems. Thus, even as the hostility continued to increase, he restrained the truth.

Overwhelmed by maternal affection, the queen, her mind subservient to him, desired to retaliate against her husband. At that time, there was a fisherman’s harlot named Luḍḍā, whose intellect was under his control,
and a wicked paramour of hers named Thakkaḍāmara.

That evil-minded one, with his face brightened by a playful smile, constantly heard his parents being addressed by their very names by those standing nearby. (Yugma) Furthermore, that couple had once again given a pair of golden *tulāpuruṣa* offerings. (KRT 7.0406–0407ab)
Through various virtuous practices, they cast off the torment of their minds.
But when, due to their initial intensity, the steadfastness of those two did not diminish,
then that wicked son, filled with envy, set fire to the house at night.
By that fire, along with all the belongings of the lord of the earth,
the city of Vijayeśvara was reduced to nothing but ashes. Distraught by the grief of this total destruction, the queen prepared to die.
With the help of Tanvaṅga’s sons, he somehow dragged [the king] out from his burning house.
Having abandoned their garments upon their beds at night, as they rose from sleep,
that entire royal army became clad only in the directions (naked).

Beholding this from the top of the palace in his capital, King Kalaśa danced with joy, as if together with the blazing flames that reached toward the sky. Having lost all his possessions, that king crossed to the far shore of the river.
She sank down into the difficult-to-cross ocean of grief.
Having arrived, she first gave food and garments to her attendants;
having obtained in the morning that unblemished jewel-liṅga, the king’s wife—

He sold [the property] for seventy lakhs of ṭākās to those who approached him; with that wealth, he purified even the dwellings that had been consumed by fire. Meanwhile, the king recovered gold and other treasures from the surface of the ash-covered ground.
Indeed, even a mere story now arouses such curiosity! There,
in that city which had become a desolate wilderness, the king dwelt with his followers in what was covered by a canopy made of woven reed-stalks.
Even though he possessed such power over the matter, his desire to build that new city was not accomplished by the aged king without the command appropriate for a monarch. The new king,
having never before experienced defeat and being favored by his mother, [proceeded].

He constantly caused distress for his father with various ill tidings. Then, because of his persistence, the father was repeatedly told by messengers that his son, eager for exile, was about to depart for the forest of leaves.
When his wife, who was exerting herself, was being urged again and again with reproaches for the accomplishment of that very task, then once,
while a certain slender-limbed woman stood nearby in private—
He spoke these words, never before uttered, to that very man:
"Self-importance, fame, heroism, sovereignty, vigor, wisdom, and wealth—
alas, what has not been lost by me, who am subject to my wife?"
People count women as mere instruments for their own pleasure;
yet in the end, men become the playthings of women.
This occurs through the manifestation of hatred from those who were once attached, now turned away by envy.
Who indeed here has not been made a guest of Death by their splendors?
Some women stole away the men's beauty, some their strength, some their wisdom, and some, through their charms, their virility and even their very lives.
With their sons who have gone over to other herds, they carry away the earth like pressing-stones;
intoxicated by the height of their breasts, these women are like rivers. "What is the use of such worn-out ones at the end? [he says], regarding their wages.
Women nourish their sons but wither their husbands; yet,
although I have recognized these faults committed by women at all times, I have not rejected this one out of deference to her conduct.
Having destroyed these worldly riches of pleasure, this powerful [passion] is now intent on destroying even my hope for happiness in the next world.
For me, who am possessed of wrinkles and grey hair and whose death is now near, where would it be fitting for me to go, having abandoned this field of victory?
[Only here] is there that which is capable of destroying sin, belonging to the one who wears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel.
How could my longing, nurtured by constant attendance at the threshold of the door, ever be dulled?
Whose other son could be such a savior of both worlds,
who, while sending me away from the sacred ford, desires me dead on the wrong path?
This report appears clearly in my mind today:
that he has been ushered in by this woman, having been brought here from another family. He is inconsistent in his appearance and conduct, and he opposes his own kinsmen.
Speaking thus,
her husband struck at her vital spots, as he spoke these words while she, having long since revealed her intention, was abandoning the restraint of her life-breaths.

For she was the daughter of one named Praśasta, who belonged to the same lineage; having heard those unpleasant words, she became exceedingly ashamed. For she was the daughter of one named Praśasta, who belonged to the most noble family.

There was a popular saying that [the wife] had been taken [as a bride] when the auspicious conditions for offspring had failed. Women who had mastered their husbands knew that the husband’s arrogant speech was like the striking of a head with a foot.

Therefore, with words harshened by the impressions of her intense maturity, she spoke aloud in anger to her husband like a common woman: "He who was once a destitute ascetic and had no garment even before— "

"This fool does not know that he has grown old in vain, nor what ought to be said. "The world knows that for this man, who rose from his bath without any covering as before, nothing was lost upon encountering me; why then do you lament?"
"Speak to me whatever is appropriate for a woman of your own family;
why should this time not be used for the performance of penance?
I am no longer fit for action, my years have passed, and I have been restrained from the country by my son."

"I am indeed afraid of this scandal that my wife has also abandoned me. When the king remained silent, pained by her words which were full of reproach and contained within them allusions to his family's faults and conduct, [the minister spoke].
Then, emerging from the edge of his seat and flowing outward,
a stream of blood was clearly seen issuing from him whose appearance remained unaltered. Thereupon, as the queen became agitated, Thakkana saw it and wept.
Then, as the king had angrily inserted a cow-tongue-shaped dagger into his anus,
the exceedingly steadfast king himself, overcome with shame, commanded him:
"Let it be said outside that the king has suffered from a severe hemorrhage."

Kings whose entire wealth is entrusted to their sons become submissive to women; when it comes to servants, they are impelled by a sudden surge of misplaced confidence. By recklessly treating the *ghumārin* (the female elephant) as a mere subordinate through forceful advances, these kings soon meet their destruction.
Or, like a king who has exhausted his horses and is weary from the heat of autumn, [he perishes].

Thirsting, he drank the water of the grain and became one born from blood that had flowed out. (KRT 7.0450cd) The royal officers conducted their inquiries so deeply that no outsider at all perceived this occurrence. (KRT 7.0451ab) [This is a *yugma* couplet. (KRT 7.0451cd)
In his fifty-seventh year, on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika,
the king was deprived of his life before the Lord Vijayeśa.
Abandoned by the distress caused by his wife and son, the king, though accustomed to comfort, passed away.

Having stretched out his legs, he at last found the opportunity to sleep after a long time. He did not become angry with anyone, nor did anyone become angry with him; high-minded and free from resentment, he became happy through death.

An heir to the kingdom of battle, he was not dear to anyone; covered in fine garments, he lay upon the ground like one who is helpless. He felt no affection for the lamentations of his loved ones, nor did he feel anger at their harsh words.
The king, having renounced everything, entered the state of one who knows the taste of eternal sleep. Abandoning his life-breaths as if to perform penance for transgressing his sense of courtesy,
he was then restored to the state of having a protector by his grateful wife.
[122] From the prince down to the outcaste, she gave daily wages;
she did so to her own servants as well, in order to make her husband free from debt.
All the servants who had received their wages were personally made to drink from the treasury by her in the presence of Vijayeśa, the grandson of Kṣema;
with his head bowed at her feet, the grandson wept as she offered him the treasury.
Having smelled her on the crown of her head, he said, "Do not trust my father. Then,
rising up and herself taking hold of a creeper,
she performed a miracle for her husband while having him adorned with the final ornaments.
Having assigned a hundred horsemen to guard her grandson right there,
she then had her husband, who was mounted upon a palanquin, set forth.
Having remained thus for half a day at a solitary watering place, she whose deity was her husband—

Having bowed to Vijayeśāna, she set her husband forth mounted upon a vehicle. As the two were departing, the quarters of the sky seemed shattered by the tumultuous wailing of the people, mingled with the swelling sounds of the funeral drums.
Reflected in the ornaments of the banner-adorned celestial chariot,
the subjects shone in the presence of the king as if they were striving to follow him.
The winds tossed the hair upon the shoulders of the kings who had been granted passage.
While the king was seated in his celestial chariot, they bore the splendor of chowries for him.
Beholding from afar the service rendered by the troops,
the king’s beloved entered the cremation ground as the day was longing for its setting.
Whether out of maternal affection for her son born in the dust, or for some other reason,
at that moment she became eager to look upon her child;
though she was aware of the dust raised by the wind and stirred up by the army.
She became anxious and longing with the hope of Kalaśa’s arrival.
At that moment, some people arrived by way of the city road;
she herself asked them, "O sirs, has Kalaśa arrived?"
But at that moment, that son, wishing to go to his mother’s side,
was detained by those who created obstacles through various terrifying displays.
Then the queen, having lost all hope regarding the sight of her son, [fell into despair].
Having requested the water of the Vaitasta, she then recited this verse:
"Those who have died with the water of the Vaitasta within their bellies shall undoubtedly attain liberation, just like those who expound upon Brahman."
Having drunk the water of the Vitastā brought to her and performed the ritual rinsing of her mouth,
she then uttered this curse upon those malicious ones who had caused the destruction of our affection by instigating a life-threatening enmity between us and our son.
May their destruction, along with their descendants, come within a limited number of days.
Because of her unfailing curse,
Jayānanda, Jindu, Rāja, and the others quickly perished.

The virtuous woman, having made the next world her stake, skillfully took an oath to quell the rumors arising from Haladhara’s infidelity; thus did she of the pure smile manifest her stainless character.
He leaped from his chariot onto the blazing fire.
Then the sky was born as if encircled by a garland of flames,
appearing as though the gods had applied vermilion powder for the festival of his arrival.
The fire was perceived by the people as if it were painted in a supreme picture: it did not crackle with those who cried out, nor was it hot for those consumed by grief.
Gaṅgādhara, Ṣṭakkibuddha, and Daṇḍaka, the driver of the carriage—*Kṛti*, 7.480ab–cd; *Kṛti*, 7.481ab.
Tāvu and Ddānonikā, as well as Valgā, were the female slaves who followed them at that time.
Both Senaṭa and Kṣemaṭa, the kinsmen of Bappaṭa and Udbhaṭa, were favorites of the king; out of world-weariness, they both resided at Vijayeśvara.

All things are exceedingly fragile by their very nature and do not endure for long; yet this one quality of that heart, which is like a jar of glass, is enduring: the water of the celestial Gaṅgā in the form of wondrous speech, once placed within it and grown deep, does not leak away, nor does it wither, nor does it suffer decay. Having surpassed sixty-one years of his life, the king—
Accompanied by his wife, he attained union with Gaurī, the enemy of Tripura. Then,
on the fourth day, having gathered the bones of those two...
All the sons of Tanvaṅga set out for the Gaṅgā.
Accompanied by his grandfather’s treasury and retinue,
Harṣa, however, incurred enmity with his father at Vijayeśvara.

In the excellent city of Śrīvijayeśvara, the father was [residing]; there, the son was also present, while the father remained near the outskirts of the city. Then, the father—though poor and possessed of wisdom—[confronted] the son who was excessively wasteful.
Fearing misfortune, he entreated them for peace through messengers. Inflated by those who arrived repeatedly and spoke persuasively,
the prince somehow brought about a reconciliation with his father.
Having received his wages in return, Janaka pledged protection for the treasure of the Grandfather (Brahmā) and for the body of his own son; meanwhile,
[messengers] entered Vijayeśvara to bring back the king’s son.

His reputation was scorched by the burnt houses, and his learning was consumed by the reproach of the people. Taking his son along with the treasury, he entered the city; having placed the treasury under seal marked with the king's name, he secured it.

In the meantime, there arose in that king a righteous resolve, a virtuous disposition toward wealth that cuts through poverty on all sides; and he had a son named Naya, the ruler of the city of Selyapura.
A householder named Jayyaka gradually attained a state of great prosperity. Born on dry land, he sold grain from various regions and countries through his trade;
having accumulated wealth, he slowly became so greedy that he vied with the Lord of Riches himself.
Having dug a trench one *krośa* deep, he constantly sowed many grains of rice upon the surface of the earth, which was filled with heaps of *dīnāra* coins; and every night,
he had his servants place those *dīnāras* [upon the grain].

Many were secretly struck down by him, who was afraid of a schism. While he was seeking to obtain Bhāṅgila, his horse suddenly bolted away; with his horse obstructed by a grapevine, he was killed by some foot soldier.
With the wealth he had acquired from the surface of the earth,
the king did not abandon poverty for as long as he lived;
even as his coins were being washed away day and night in battles.
For many months, that water remained turbid.
Deprived of both giving and enjoyment, and with great hardship at that time,
those greedy yet noble-minded men wondrously guarded their wealth for the sake of others.

Having drunk the winds, he sustains his life-breaths; he lies in a hole blinded by darkness; in the enjoyment of food, he desires what is given by another; in the interval between shame and nakedness, he spreads out his garment—thus the serpent displays its miserliness for the sake of another. There is no one else more mature in acts of service to others than this greedy one. And through many other paths, [the wealth] entered him as rivers enter the ocean.
Those various perfections of wealth [attend] a fortunate king.
When fortune rises, riches enter a person of their own accord by the hundreds,
like birds returning from all directions to a tree in the evening.

The streams, having gained strength, nourish the earth at their roots; from the sky above, water falls, and the green fields release it through the mouths of irrigation channels. Thus, when the lake is parched, it is filled from all sides during the rainy season. When good fortune arises, through whose hundreds of doors do riches not enter?
Therefore, in his skill at protecting the people, he was like a father day after day.
The mind of Kalaśa became skilled through the arising of his subjects' merits;
though he was himself as adept at calculating wealth as a merchant,
he remained discerning in avoiding the path of the wicked and was always open-handed in generosity.
Personally observing both his income and expenditures as they were being managed,
the official did not abandon the birch bark, chalk, and other supplies that were kept nearby.
He himself purchased gems and other goods at their true value.
No sellers were able to deceive him.
Devoting himself to the three aims of life while dividing his time appropriately, he lived happily;
after midday, he became invisible to all those with business.
But while he was thus investigating the affairs of both his own people and those of others through spies,
the conduct of his subjects remained unknown to him, as if it were a dream.
As he meditated upon his own domain and the [Buddha’s] mandala,
no person whatsoever in the countryside ever experienced misery. The king, wary of public scandal, carried out the clearing away of thorns [from his realm].

He never, even for a moment, openly abandoned the rod of punishment against thieves. No property whatsoever was lost to him; he employed ministers to recover it. Furthermore, he ensured that the ministers restored whatever wealth had been lost.
In his kingdom, the people were seen to be constantly joyful and free from misery, their lives filled with hundreds of great festivals such as weddings, sacrifices, and processions. By that king,
who was skilled in statecraft, all neighboring rulers were brought under his sway.
Even while eating, they remained vigilant, their senses accompanied by watchfulness;
they [encountered] the three sons of Tanvaṅga— Kvan and the others— who had arrived from another region,
as well as the Gūṅgas, headed by Malla, who had spent one younger brother [in ransom].
He gratified his kinsmen and servants with auspicious riches,
just as the moon gratifies the gods and ancestors with its digits moistened by nectar.
(Yugma) Although the king had reached full maturity, he was not corrupted by misconduct.
Abandoning the wicked conduct taught by his evil preceptor,
Ṭakka, who was known as Bullī, brought home young maidens;
he purchased from the Turuṣkas girls originating from various regions and countries.
Out of greed for their beauty, he presented those women— along with the wives of others whom they had brought him— with his own harem ladies, numbering seventy-two,
to the many women he desired day after day.

His nourishment did not diminish even through fish broth and other aphrodisiacs. Engaged in the worship of the Great Samaya together with his teachers, he abandoned conventional morality and partook of the food of great sacrificial carus.
Thus, by that Śabala, the city was renovated;
yet, in the field of Vijaya which had been consumed by fire, the stone temple of the Trident-bearer remained.
Above the stone temple of Vijayeśa, he placed a parasol.
The king constructed a golden pinnacle that kissed the sky;
he established an imperishable foundation for the Lord of Tripura,
and he built a temple for the wielder of the Pināka bow with a central core of pure gold.
Then, skilled in virtuous deeds, he constructed for Kalaśeśvara a stone temple marked by a multitude of countless golden jars;
[he built it] desiring to place a gilded parasol over Kalaśeśa.
A craftsman born in the land of the Turuṣkas approached the presence of the king,
proclaiming his skill in the accomplishment of a parasol by means of many thousands of pieces of gold;
he was covering his own copper with the application of gold.
For some days he remained there, receiving the king’s hospitality; then, having inferred [the truth] through his exceedingly sharp intelligence, the minister named Nona—
who was skilled in the arts— departed as he had come, feeling embarrassed.
And that parasol attained perfection with very little gold. The king, whose majesty surpassed even that of Śakra, performed various consecrations for the Bāṇaliṅga named Ananteśa and other [deities].
When King Sahajapāla had passed away,
his son named Saṃgrāmapāla was then consecrated in Rāhapurī;
he was the paternal uncle of that young king and desired to seize the kingdom.

Afterwards, he dispatched Jayānanda along with the heroic Vijja and others. Out of fear, [the enemy] sought refuge with the king, seeking his assistance; so too did the sister of Saṃgrāmapāla and the nobleman (ṭakkura) Jassarāja.
The king, having shown his favor, gave them assistance;
thereafter, he gave Jayānanda along with the brave Vijja and others.
There, having put his enemies to flight, he shone forth, having overrun the entire territory.
At the conclusion of their business, the ministers of Saṃgrāmapāla became suspicious;
desiring his departure, they offered various threats and sought to instill fear in him,
yet that hero did not waver.
Suspecting that he had given this counsel to the people of Rājapurī, Bijja then summoned his wrath.

Then, entreated by them who had offered him wealth there, the high-minded one stationed his own army under the pretext of providing protection and turned back. Thus, when he had taken possession of Rājapurī and arrived in its vicinity—

The wise King Kalaśa, who understood the core of political affairs, was gratified. Then, as Bijja and others were successively ascending to the throne, Jayānanda was struck by illness due to the power of fate, which became the cause of his death.

To inquire after his health, the king came to his house; in the course of conversation, he said, "There is something to be told in private. Then, when everyone had departed, he did not say anything at all.
Then, under the pretext of wishing to leave the betel grove,
the fisherman went out. Although addressed by the king— "Why are you going out?"—
and by the minister, that wise man, having been told "Wait," lingered outside the palace grounds.
Having told the story of Rājapurī, Jayānanda said to the king:
"It is evident that your kingdom no longer exists at all now that Bijja has grown powerful;
for even from the wages due for your affairs, they are being seized by Bijja."
He presented a detailed account of great value to the king.
Then the king, having fallen into a state of dejection, departed for his own home;
he was asked for permission to leave by Bijjana, who was skilled in discerning gestures.

As if forbidding his persistent entreaties out of a mere trace of courtesy, the lord of the earth, inwardly delighted, gave him permission to depart. Having received this command, he went home along with all his belongings.
Having dispatched his brothers ahead, he went to inquire after the king. At that moment,
between the master and the two servants, Krūra and Rājavarmabhīru,
there occurred a certain action that was truly marvelous.

That the lord did not turn back from his departure for the sake of his beloved servant, and that the servant, filled with indignation, did not reproach his beloved lord— having risen together, they walked only a few steps with the king.
After speaking for a long time, Bijja departed with a suppressed laugh.
Just as Haladhara had caused Jindurāja— who was about to die— to fall from his position by slandering him,
so did Yajñānanda cause Bijja to be deposed from his rank.
"Let him depart after reducing the earth to nothing more than its great splendor";
the king did not accept this advice from his ministers, namely that Bijja had been deprived of his wealth.
"The lord of the earth will certainly turn back upon his departure."

With this intention, the entire populace followed Bijja, with the exception of the king. Suspecting an attack from the powerful Bijja, the king remained awake for five nights, trembling even at the rustling of a blade of grass.
When he had departed for Śūrapura and his followers had turned back,
he, free from suspicion, revealed that very suspicion to his ministers.
Having heard that, they then deliberated on the counsel regarding the seizure of the wealth of Bijja.
When he did not appoint him [to office], the ministers considered this a sign that the king was ignorant of statesmanship.
But Bijja and the others, free from malice, wherever they took up residence,
there they attained honor, like jewels.
Though he had grown powerful, Bijjodhika remained as devoted as a worshipper to a deity;
Satyaṅkara was always at the feet of the god Kalaśadeva.
Thus, having exiled Bijja and the others, he attained sovereign power.

The joy born from the defeat of Sūryamatī’s curse quickly came to an end. At that very moment, Jindurāja, who had spoken of the king’s hostility and the infallibility of the curse, also met his death.
Those [princes], Bījja and the others, having swiftly attained their prosperity, all met with death in the Gauḍa region— a fate worthy of their curse. Then,
following that sudden death, Bījja himself met his end.
Even his younger brothers fell into long-lasting suffering in bondage;
when they had fled from prison, the cook was killed by a tiger,
while his remaining younger brothers, freed from their afflictions, met their end.
Two or three of those who split that [empire]—Madana and the others—will not perish;
by them, through their misdeeds, it will come to pass in no long time.
Then Jayānanda, with his companions, protecting his sons, [will rule].
The king appointed a man named Vāmana as his chief minister;
though he was not very learned, his various administrative acts were wonderful to behold.
Even today, those advanced in years recount this in the assemblies of the wise.
Having seized villages that were the enjoyments of Avantīsvāmin and others, the king of greedy intellect established a royal workshop known as Kalaśagañja.

He gave the minister Nonaka, who knew how to generate wealth, even the tip of his foot; yet he, who was skilled in protecting the people, did not give it to Krauryavasta. The children of the king’s jar-like ministers attained an extremely intimate position.

Praśastakalaśa and others held positions at the side of the king; however, his sons—helpless due to their own lack of self-restraint—were thieves who took refuge in the twilight hours and other such times. The king, having bound them to their specific duties, kept them under control through clever stratagems.
When Madanapāla had again seized the lord of Rājapurī,
the king dispatched Bappaṭa as commander-in-chief to provide assistance. By that mere fraction of his service, the king was conquered through his own majesties.
Having bound Madanapāla as well, he was sent into Kaśmīra. The king made the heroic brother of Varājadeva, named Kandarpa, the governor of the gate, and he carried out the suppression of the Ḍāmaras.

Trained in both statesmanship and valor by Jindurāja, his commands were touched by the crowns of neighboring vassal kings. Victorious over Rājapurī and other cities, he was exceedingly wrathful; he [attacked] the gate.
Being appeased by the king who said "moment by moment," Madana was personally granted [the title] by the protector of the earth; having attained the lordship over Kampana,
he slew many fierce Īḍāmaras who had gained great power.
Subdued by his service, he made Vijayasimha the lord of the city, having destroyed all the thieves; and once,
when Loḥara was attacked by Kandarpa, Upodayasiṃha, and others.
The king carried out the complete expulsion of Bhuvanarāja. Having obtained the daughter of Nīlapuraprabhu, named Bhuvanamati, the son of Kīrtirāja, he became free from the ailment of his enemy.
Having seized Vijayasiṃha and others,
the son of Guṅga, that wrestler, was then made the lord of the city by the king and appointed as the gatekeeper for the undertaking of receiving the royal business.

He established his own majesty upon the crest-jewel position of kings. (Yugma) The valor of Pārtha, when unaided during the seizure of the northern cattle, was heard of; or rather, the valor of the proud wrestler [Cāṇūra] at the time of entering the chest [of Kṛṣṇa].
(KRT 7.584cd–585ab) [The valor] of the proud wrestler was heard of at the time of not entering the chest. (KRT 7.585cd)

For with fifty horses he crossed the Kṛṣṇā river and seized the kingdom of the king named Abhaya, along with his multitude of steeds. Thus was the sovereignty won by that monarch, who knew the ways of policy and had brought the earth under his control.
At that very same time, eight kings entered the city with sixty-three [others].
Kīrtinnyabbapura’s lord was the king Āmyeya,
and Tukka’s son Kalaśa was the sovereign of Ballāpura.

The king named Saṃgrāmapāla was the lord of Rājapurī; Utkarṣa was the ruler of Lohara, and Aurvaśa was the king born of the Muṅga lineage; Gāmbhīrasīha was the sovereign of the Kāṇḍa region, and [there was] the lord of the earth at Kāṣṭhavāṭa.

The illustrious and supreme kings also attended upon the King. (Tilaka) Although the royal assembly was vast, it appeared within the forest as if it were part of the countryside; like the flood of a monsoon river when it enters the ocean, it became indistinguishable. (KRT_7_0590cd–0591ab / KRT_7_0591cd)
At that moment, in the waters of the Vitastā which had turned to stone,
the kings experienced a happiness that was not diminished even by the cold;
for those monarchs did not think of anything at all, even with their minds.
Seeing that very city already occupied by Vāmana,
the skill of that minister shone forth, a quality difficult for others to attain;
unperturbed, he carried out that event as if it were an ordinary occurrence.

Then, when the kings had departed and the Malla king was averse to his duty, Kandarpa was once again granted entrance by the protector of the earth. The minister, whose only wealth was his self-respect, began his undertaking with his own resources.
By a clever stratagem, he took up a difficult disguise known as that of a sleeper, which was hard to detect.
Though he had entered the city, for some reason he remained despondent; and even when entreated by the king, he would not undertake any business at all.
At that time, Praśastakalaśa, constantly performing the role of a messenger,
was tormented by his own arrogant speech and touched upon the state of self-conceit.
Having gathered numerous armed men through his own exceedingly great splendor,

he caused his own brother to be placed upon that throne like a jar of jewels. Although he was famous for having purchased [his position] with wealth, he was never equal to Kandarpa in beauty anywhere.
Can a lion painted on a canvas ever perform the actions of a real lion?
Thereupon, by degrees, that jewel among servants was somehow granted the office of royal steward in the city by the lord of the earth.

When the thief perished from excessive beating, he was overcome with compassion; abandoning even that office, dejected, he went to the Ganges. Having struck the hand of his lord, he concealed it within the hem of his garment.
Having departed for another country out of anger, the king remained full of resentment toward him;
though he was extremely distressed when the man was brought back again into his presence,
the monarch prepared himself to strip him of his pride, but not of his life.

Thus that lord of the earth, possessing firm fortitude and being an expert in the inner nuances, displayed the ascent and descent of these lions among men. He was devoted to the art of *upāṅga-gīta* and took great care in gathering female dancers.
The king had already established there what was appropriate for other lands; therefore,
the lord of the people began to construct a city named after himself, consisting of vast houses built continuously on the outskirts of Jayavana.
Successions of monasteries, landed estates, palaces, and great mansions,
along with waterworks and groves, attained perfection there in their thousands.
In the meantime, the prince Harṣa, possessed of preeminent prowess—
Through qualities difficult for other kings to attain, he achieved renown.
Knowing the languages of all regions and being a true poet in every tongue,
that treasury of all sciences attained fame even in foreign lands.
Abandoned by their greedy father, people who had arrived from various directions—
resplendent with virtue and heroism— were recruited by him and provided with wages. Even when the wages provided by their fathers were insufficient, they remained devoted to their expenditures.
The food of that renunciant became provided at intervals of one day.
Like a singer clearly delighting his father with songs,
he supported those who were to be maintained by means of the rewards granted by him.
Once, while the Udgātṛ was singing before him and the members of the assembly were being entertained, the king rose to perform his purification rites and went out.
By that interruption of the discourse, the wise [king], whose splendor was like that of fire, felt his vital energy diminished.

Agitated by both embarrassment and anger, the prince gazed upon the earth. "A lord devoid of patience, a most treacherous friend, a wife of harsh speech, a son swollen with pride, and a retinue that offers insolent replies—surely such a circle of people, burning the heart, can be endured; but not one who, with a sidelong glance, insults the listener."
Then a servant of his father, a rogue named Viśvāvaṭṭa,
said to him, "Rule the kingdom after having slain this man, as if he were a mere phantom.
Insulting him in his rage, the king replied, "Nothing improper was ever spoken by this man."
Thus spoke Dhammaṭa, who was standing nearby and smiling: "Prostitutes,
like female companions of lovers, will first show affection toward the prince's attendants— those who are hidden by their desire for enjoyment— and then win them over."

Having re-entered the assembly hall, his father gratified him with various gifts of affection and with words of praise from those who were honorable. On another day, however, having eaten at his father’s side, he went to his own home.
Having approached, Viśvāvaṭṭa spoke those very same words to him in private. After he had repeatedly stated what was appropriate and tried to dissuade him,
[the king] struck him with his hand even as he persisted in his entreaty out of anger.
Seeing him vomiting blood from his nostrils due to the blow to his vital organ, that prince, ever devoted to courtesy, was filled with compassion;
he had his servants wash away the blood, thinking, "May such an evil as this not befall him."
Saying, "Even though it has been said," he smiled and had garments brought;
by that act of giving, his desire was inferred even though he was one who had no desire.
The immoral woman felt a desire for him merely from his smile.
After making repeated efforts over a long period of time,
he then urged him toward that task by winning over Dharmaṭa in their midst.

Afflicted by the evil born of his resolve to commit patricide, he wept; having consulted with his father, he dispatched fierce men in every direction to kill him. Yet, he was constantly within the range of those who were touched by a fragment of affection for him.
He was neither slain by his son, nor was the subject of him ever avoided;
for when he had attained the status of a trusted confidant among the group of harsh ministers out of fear of being exposed,
Viśvāvaṭṭa quickly reported that news to the king.
On that day, Prince Buddhavān, having become afraid,
did not come to his father’s side to eat, even though he had been entreated by messengers. When he did not arrive for that purpose, the king’s doubts were pacified.

On that day, due to mental anguish, he did not eat along with his retinue. When his brother arrived in the morning, he informed him of his suffering; resting his head for a long time on Thakkana’s lap, he wept aloud.
Having related the news of Dharma, he spoke to him with various turns of eloquent phrasing: "Make arrangements for his delivery and bind him. Then, addressing him, he said:
"We two have not yet mastered this task."
The two slender-limbed delights spoke again for the sake of their brother:

"O King, by the power of your grace, we two are consecrated to protect those who have come to us for refuge; therefore, for the sake of his entry, we shall keep the gates open even during the nights."

O Protector of the Earth, how could it be that when the moment of death has arrived, the younger brother—whether blameless or guilty—is abandoned by those two? For by protecting him, there would certainly be the reproach of treachery toward one's master. (A pair of verses)
"Abandoning that [land], there is no other refuge for us two than leaving the country.
Having reflected thus, as the two placed their heads at his feet,
the king wept and with some difficulty granted them permission to depart.

"Someone might kill him on the road," he thought, making him the target; thus, according to the law, those two departed from that place with their armies and vehicles once all living beings had been removed. When the slender-limbed daughters had gone, the palace was made solitary.

Having summoned him, the king spoke these words in a consoling manner: "Throughout the entire course of worldly existence, in this world, it is by Janaka alone— whose fame is renowned everywhere— that the knowledge of the One to be Born is produced for all people."
"O son, because of you— a virtuous son whose fame is proclaimed throughout the quarters and continents like that of the cool-rayed moon— every person knows me. You,
being the foremost among the virtuous and possessing unrestrained glory, have become such."
Tell me, why do you pursue this path frequented by the wicked?
You should not harbor resentment without first hearing the reason why I did not bestow upon you my paternal inheritance or my own wealth.
"O King, a ruler who is depleted of his own people as well as those of others meets with defeat;
it is with this in mind that I am now undertaking the protection of the treasury.
Having established the city and entrusted the burden of the kingdom to you,"

"I shall go to Vārāṇasī, or perhaps to Nandikṣetra. "Before long you will become the master of that kingdom and its treasury; why then, with such excessive persistence, do you strive for what is unbecoming of a noble man?"

Do not disregard what has been reported to you by the wicked; therefore, let this scandal be dispelled by speaking the truth. Let him perform a formal confession (*apratiśrava*) for the sake of purifying his own deed.

Desiring to win him over through affection and other means, the king spoke these words with a specific intention. He wished to lead [the prince] toward the mere use of words that conceal [his true intent],
for he was eager for patience in order to convince the people.
Harṣa, however, having honored his father’s speech with cries of "Well said," said, "I shall declare the truth from the mouth of a reliable authority," and went outside. He spoke thus:
"This desire to act arose from a general impulse."
Ashamed, he went to his own dwelling after the messenger sent by his father had departed.
Seeing the messenger with a dejected face, he beat his head with both hands.
Crying out, "Alas, my son!", the king caused his shoulder to be offered.
When the Lord had spoken, saying, "I would cut off my own head on this very spot," the teachers remained surrounding that palace by the command of the Master.
But the fierce men, having blocked the gates and surrounded the prince,
spoke these very harsh words, for they were certain of his death:
"This compassionate man, though negligent, has practiced a hostile deception toward us."
"O you of evil conduct, having caused [him] to be slain, where do you wish to remain alive?
That father will protect his son, and he was protected by you;
