there is kinship between the two of you, yet we ourselves have been slain once again."
"Fight as one who stands among us; otherwise, we shall slay you.
Thus, in every way, it is evident that there is no life for you.
Having heard this report, he stood before the king who was deeply agitated.
The chief minister named Daṇḍaka went into the presence of Harṣa.
Having gained entry through his own sharp wit, that intelligent man approached the prince and spoke thus, utterly bewildering everyone.
O son of a Kṣatriya, even after living for many, indeed countless, eons, one must inevitably submit to the power of destiny, regardless of the reasons. Therefore,
since this death is so near and unfailing—

Protect that honor for which the sword is grasped. You are one who has completed his studies, renowned for your fame, a youth, and a noble kṣatriya; why then do you perceive any purpose in delaying the battle?
With these as your excellent allies and me now at your head, O majestic one, whether it be calamity or victory, it befits you.
Arise! Quickly cause the sheaths of your claws to be extended for a yojana.
"Even while binding the hero’s turban, he binds the garland for his marriage to a celestial woman.

and others were bound by Harṣadeva and cast into prison. Thus, in a single day, such a reversal of royal fortune occurred.

And this most wonderful deed was performed by Harṣadeva as if by destiny itself. (KRT 7.0867cd) In some way or another, many rulers of the earth have passed away; alas, a path difficult to comprehend has now been entered. (KRT 7.0868ab–cd)

She is the field of water for all enthusiasm, the messenger who brings joy to all; she is the mother who gives birth to all established orders and the one who dispels all improper conduct. She is the manifestation of the exalted teaching and the ground where exalted commands are never exhausted.
Abounding in the perfection of generosity, yet possessing an abundance of seizing and grasping;
lovely through the overflow of compassion, yet terrifying through the excess of violence.
Adorned with the excellence of the true lineage yet marred by the arrogance of sin;
desirable and yet to be avoided, venerable and yet to be censured in every respect; beyond reproach yet an object of ridicule, both desired and subject to purification by the wise.

To be desired, to be shunned by ill-repute, to be remembered, and to be cast out from the mind—the discourse concerning the king Harṣa will now be described. [Kulaka] Surely he was created from atoms consisting solely of light. [KRT_7_0874ab]
Otherwise, how could he be so difficult to behold even for the great?
Neither among mortals nor among gods is his appearance seen anywhere;
it is only among the lords of the Dānavas that he is perceived as supreme by the wise.
Adorned with earrings blazing according to the proportions of his face,
his head encircled by a broad *uṣṇīṣa* bound within a towering crown;
he gazes with the serene glance of a lion, his beard and mustache finely trimmed.

With shoulders like a bull, mighty-armed, his body dark-red in hue; with broad-chested limbs, a slender waist, and a voice as terrifying as the roar of clouds; he was one who brought about the shattering of the splendor even of the gods and men. (Tilaka)
At the lion-gate, he hung great bells in the four directions so that those who had arrived with petitions might be known by the sound of those instruments;
and having heard their cries of distress, he provided for the quelling of their thirst.
Like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season, he acted for the sake of the cātakas;
yet in the royal palace, no one was seen who lacked colorful garments, gold ornaments, or modest attendants, nor anyone who appeared devoid of splendor.
At the king’s main gate, which was crowded with various people,
the glories of all the provinces sat as if heaped together without ceasing—
countless in number, and adorned with golden chains and bracelets.
The chief ministers and doorkeepers roamed about in the king’s palace.
Thus, that king, radiant with his new sovereignty,
remained steadfast in the counsel of his elder, Vijayamalla, as if he were his preceptor.
As he spoke, the assembly of that king became crowded with servants, for the monarch was grateful;
disregarding his own servants, he protected the integrity of the established order.
He entrusted the offices of authority to his paternal ministers;
he appointed Kandarpa at the gate and Madana at Kampana;
and he assigned Vijayasiṃha and others to their respective duties.

By him, whose anger was pacified, Praśastakalaśa and the others were released from bondage and appointed to their own respective duties. However, the minister Nonaka, remembering his many past injuries, [acted] further...
He was impaled on a stake out of anger by his brother, the son of his wet-nurse. Yet,
from time to time, when faced with difficult matters requiring great wisdom,
he would remember that devoted servant and be touched by remorse.
Even one who has committed an injury may sometimes be useful;
the fire that set the house ablaze became a refuge for the preparation of food.
Having displayed before his own wife the severing of her ears and nose—
Viśvābhaṭṭa was impaled upon a stake by the king’s servants. At the dawn [of his reign], he distributed among his servants those taxes that had emerged from the treasury,
just as a tree in full bloom in spring distributes nectar to the bees emerging from the hollows of its branches.
That grandson of Rākka and Kṣema, Vajrāja,
along with his younger brother Sunna, was appointed by the king to the position of chief among all ministers.
At every step during the king’s expeditions and other occasions, for those who were spectators—
The minister, becoming one with each [of them], caused confusion among the kings;
he was appointed to the head of the entire assembly of doorkeepers.
Jayarāja’s younger brother became even more dear to him than his own life.
The sister of Jāhnavīyātraya was Anuśaṃsyā;
he too, Dharmaṭa, went forth with those sons of his brothers as companions.
Having honored that king— who had lost his eldest brother for his sake— he always looked upon him, along with his brothers and sons, as no different from himself. Yet,
while he was thus dividing and administering the kingdom, he was incited by wicked men.

Then Vijayamalla, desiring to seize [the throne], gradually underwent a transformation of character. When he was told by wicked men, "Did you not grant the kingdom to another after conquering [him]?", he, wishing to obtain it, plotted the murder of his first-born son.
Having deliberated, "I shall kill him in a secluded temple," the king,
under the pretext of performing a sacrifice, invited him to come.
When the king's counsel became known, he (the minister) then became apprehensive of Skanda.
He swiftly commanded his troops to prepare for battle. When the king’s army had thus equipped itself, Vijayamalla quickly emerged from the monarch's stables and seized the horses.
Gathering his horses together, striking at the king’s army,
and waging a great battle, the hero hastened to depart from the city.
Accompanied by his wife, who stood embracing his back as he went, he proceeded on his way.
Mounted upon his horse, he waged a superhuman battle. At that moment,
with torrents of arrows released at unseasonable times,
the earth appeared as if overturned on every side.
In that battle, amidst the roar of many kettledrums and the sound of the whistling wind,
the prince was being covered by a downpour of arrows; yet,
as his army was wasting away, those [enemies] prepared themselves to slay him as he advanced.

The sons of Caṇḍaka did not abandon their ordinary duties. Having dismounted from his horse, he, along with his attendants, crossed the confluence of the Vitastā and the Sindhu— where the bridge had been broken by the force of the waters— by grasping it with both arms.
The courageous man caused his wife to bathe amidst the peril of the enemy;
having crossed the swollen river, even the horse followed him.
Having come within the range of vision of his foes, he mounted that steed.
The hero set out toward the land of Darad by way of Lahara;
his path obstructed on all sides by Kandarpadvārapati,
he crossed over the mountains and entered the mountain-fortified city of Daratpura.
There, some of his own attendants, led by the noble Vidyādhara, slowly approached him as he was being honored by the Daradas.
Hearing that he was being accepted [as their king] amidst the tumultuous clamor of the Ḍāmaras and others, they arrived.
The mountain-like king, becoming anxious day after day, employed various stratagems;
when these proved fruitless, he spent the winter season in the city of Darat.
Then, receiving a message sent by the Ḍāmaras, he set out on his expedition in the month of Caitra with great enthusiasm.
Having crossed over the perils and standing within a cloth pavilion at the end of the path,
he suddenly became proud, his life struck down by a mass of snow.
That great agitation which is spread forth by the steadfast for the sake of his exultation— [it has now been turned against him].

Fate destroys one's purpose with even a very slight matter. (KRT 7.917cd) The Creator, enraged by an elephant, uproots with a single trunk those lotuses which the sun must laboriously open with thousands of rays. (KRT 7.918ab–cd)
For a short time, the kingdom of King Harṣa remained contracted due to the fear of a dual sovereignty; thereafter, it was once again firmly established through his majesty.
At that time, the title of "King" could not be imposed anywhere else.
Because of his extreme excellence, he caused graceful gestures that bestowed great beauty upon the circle of other kings through their contrast with him;
the king, free from envy, was like the spring season in a forest.
Formerly, having abandoned their single sovereign, embodied beings here became free from sheaths, devoid of turbans, and stripped of ornaments. In this place,
where Madana is the lord of trembling, [there occurs] the braiding of the hair-tuft.
Jayānanda, the foremost of ministers, because he wore a variegated lower garment,
experienced the king’s wrath throughout the entire circle of vassal states without distinction.

Therefore, the king adopted there the attire appropriate for royalty. (A pair. Free from envy, he caused the *ārātrika* ceremony to be performed by his own maidservants for certain ministers who were radiant with the splendor of their festive finery.

The graceful movements of the women from the South became the beloved of that playful man; consequently, he introduced the *ṭaṅka* style, which is suited to the Karṇāṭaka region. [His attendants] were beautiful with thick sandalwood pastes applied as marks and with *tālī* leaves worn as ornaments.
Then the people in that place shone, bearing praiseworthy long swords;
their matted locks were adorned with hanging, radiant garlands marked by golden *ketaka* petals, and they were embraced by flickering *atila* flowers clinging to the sprouts of their tilaka marks.
With lines of collyrium forming a junction between their outer corners of the eyes and ears,
with golden sacred threads fastened to the ends of their hair from which the unguents had been washed away,
and with the trailing hems of their lower garments kissing the ground; KRT_7_0929ab–KRT_7_0930ab.
With the curves of their arms half-concealed by their breasts,

their nipples appearing like camphor-dust, and their brows arched like the bow of the god of love, these tawny women, dressed in the attire of men, wander about under the guise of the dolphin-marked banner. (Cakkalaka)
Seekers attained a state of being supported by him through their desire for his wealth,
just as clouds attain the state of nourishing the entire world through their affection for the ocean. By the favors of that generous king, who showered gold, [the people were sustained].
The entire assemblies of singers rivaled the king himself.
That monarch, the crest-jewel of the learned, made those scholars adorned with jewels his bearers for palanquins, horses, and carriages.
While Vidyāpati was departing from Kaśmīra for the kingdom of King Kalaśa,
the Karṇāṭa king Paramāḍi made him his own;
as he advanced through the midst of the Karṇāṭa army accompanied by elephants.
In Rājyogre, he beheld a lofty sunshade belonging to that very [king].
Having heard that Harṣadeva was a generous patron and a friend to good poets,
Bilhaṇa considered even such great prosperity to be a deception.

The royal capitals of the lord of the earth, such as Sauvarṇa and Amalasārā, shone forth as wonders of the world, with palaces that scraped the clouds and were easy to traverse. They did not establish their residence among the trees in his Nandana grove.
By him, through his renunciation, the wish-fulfilling trees alone were surpassed.
By him, the lake named Pampā was made to pervade the expanse of the quarters, filled with various kinds of water-birds and deer, and abounding in water.
He knew all the sciences, even their names being certain;
clearly, there was no capacity to describe them even for Vācaspati himself.
Even today, the song of that composer is still heard.
Even with tears rolling from the tips of his eyelashes due to his adversaries,
that voluptuous man— who had always slept through two watches of the day—
now experienced wakefulness throughout the nights, for he had been granted a place [of exile].

While he was seated in the assembly pavilion marked by a thousand lamps, the nights passed in the course of learned discourses, songs, and dances. At the conclusion of the conversation, there was heard from that place a great sound produced by the chewing of leaves.
And there was the rustling sound produced by the *śephālī* flowers from the braided hair of lovely women and by the *triṭija* grass.
With its canopies, it was as if accompanied by clouds; with its lamps, as if with fire and Brahmins;
with its golden ornaments, as if with lightning; and with its circles of swords, as if with smoke.
Like an Apsaras with lovely women, like the night with its stars, like a gathering of sages with the gods, and like a place with Gandharvas and singers;
it was the eternal dwelling-place of the rendezvous for Kubera and Yama.
The forest for his dwelling was one; his [only] fear was of giving.
The night-station of that king, whose splendor surpassed that of Śakra—by whose speech, even that of Vācaspati, could it be described in its entirety? (A *cakralaka* verse).

At that time, there was a dense circulation of gold and silver coins throughout the realm; however, copper *dīnāras* were rare. Having attained the position of *daṇḍanāyaka*, Sunna enjoyed the highest prosperity.
At that time, however, there was a base man named Muṣṭipaca who was exceedingly greedy.
In his own Jayavana, at Sūryāmūla and Vijayeśvara,
the monasteries proclaim his greed for the sake of maintaining their own expenditures.
The royal fortune of Paṭṭa attained its fulfillment most clearly by removing the suffering of the hungry, the diseased, the helpless, the wretched, and others in distress.

Having spent seven days every year at Nandikṣetra, Cappaka made his wealth— accumulated over all his years— fruitful. By means of gifts such as black antelope skins and cows with faces turned in both directions, the king [honored] the foremost [sages].
The king named Vasantalekhā, beloved of the Śāhi dynasty, made the Brahmins free from poverty by completely severing the suffering of those who sought her aid;
she established monasteries and agrahāras in the city and at the venerable Tripureśvara.
Thus, a certain woman, embodying the power of Maheśvarī, rose up like a flame; yet they do not call that kingdom one of noble conduct. Then, the nine new ministers gradually attained full influence.
They brought about a delusion of mind in the king, who was hostile toward his former ministers.

A peacock with two feet afflicted by leprosy runs to seize a many-footed snake; the sun, possessing a thousand rays, moves step by step with its body. That even the strong are deceived by those of slight strength, and that those of perfect conduct are led astray by those lacking power—this is the playful sport of destiny.
Though he was a sovereign of the people, mature in his mastery of all the sciences,
he acted with a mind deluded by ministers who were themselves as ignorant as children—
driven by the desire to avenge his deceased father’s enmity.
He demolished the monasteries and other structures bearing the names of royal capitals. Being a spendthrift, he squandered that treasury here and there, and gave the greedy man the name Pāpasena.
In the inner apartments of those of pure conduct,
that king of deluded mind presented three hundred and sixty women;
having stationed such women as they were there, he remained watchful night and day.

Only the women of the *ḍomba* and *janaṅgama* castes were not captured. In the meantime, Bhuvanarāja— his mind greedy for the acquisition of Laharā— returned, secretly filling himself with troops and foot soldiers.

Having reached Darpitapura, he heard that Kandarpadvāra-nāyaka had come forth to fight; he departed once more and became invisible. Even in that situation, the king, the lord of Rājapurī, remained arrogant.
For some reason, Saṃgrāmapāla underwent a transformation.
While he was intent on gathering the Koṭabhṛtya troops who had been divided against Kandarpa,
the king, becoming enraged, dispatched the commander-in-chief toward Rājapurī.
Traveling along the iron road with his vast armies, he,
being impatient, lingered for a month among the marshy thickets;
this was due to the proximity of the summer heat and the prowess of his enemies.
Trembling during his journey, he could not even form a resolve;
remaining inactive due to his lack of discernment toward his master,
Kandarpa then became nothing more than a mere object of reproach.

Having made a vow for the conquest of Rājapurī by means of fasting, he then remained immovable even though deprived of his retinue, being tormented by reproaches. While Kandarpa dwelt in the mountain cave without food, [the gods]...
On the sixth day, the royal city lay more than a *yojana* away.
Having struck down his enemies with his arrows like a plowman, he entered the forest like a lion crushing the tender leaves of plantain trees, felling the weapons of his foes as they fell.
Only one followed him from among the army commanders:
the general named Kularāja, born of the family of Buddharāja. In the outer enclosure of Rājapurī, he slew countless enemies.

Having slain Kandarpa— who bore the mark of a white parasol— they believed him to be dead. But at midday, that powerful Kandarpa himself entered Rājadhanī from Rājapurī, accompanied by twenty or thirty warriors.
Thirty thousand enemies, warriors who never retreat, besieged him at the front of Rājapurī with three hundred foot soldiers. There,
two hundred of the Kashmiris were slain in battle.
Four hundred Khaśas lay prostrate upon the earth.
When the enemy force was shattered, they cremated the slain with countless funeral pyres,
acting as the kitchen staff for Death’s great feast.
Thus, that vampire of a reproach against his master,
having been impetuously offered by the hero in the cremation ground of battle, was quelled with flesh and blood.
When only one watch of the day remained, those enemies, once again united and burning with the heat of their humiliation, went forth to battle Kandarpa. Then,
in that conflict, he discharged iron arrows at them.
Those by whom the directions were set ablaze with arrows pierced with medicinal oil—
those fools, filled with apprehension, thought, "He knows the fiery weapon," and they fled far away in fear, disparaging their own return.
Boldness, quick-wittedness, vigor, skill in application,
and composure— these qualities of high-minded men do not abandon their intellect, which is bound by fortitude even in the most dire straits.
Having entered the capital while the sun was longing for its setting, [he...]

Once more he saw the outer line of the camp shrouded by dense forces; desiring to go forth to battle, he heard that the commander-in-chief had arrived. Having beheld the terrible forest of war, his soldiers stood still out of fear.

Some exult greatly in battle at their own visible wounds, while others tremble at those of the enemy; who knows the inner state of embodied beings? Then, having been brought out, he was submerged once again in that very same fear.
Like a crow competing with a swan in the ocean, who else but a fool would enter another's kingdom—
whose subjects are devoted, whose army is gone, who is undivided, and who possesses abundant treasure—
relying solely on his own prowess?
Then, having taken tribute from the prostrate lord of Rājapurī,
Kandarpa returned once more to earth in just a single month;
he was honored by the king with welcoming ceremonies and other marks of respect.

He brought about headaches for the chief magistrate and others. While serving as a city guard in Parihāsapura, that man of cruel intellect gained notoriety among the assembly there under the name Vātagaṇḍa.

Corrupted by the influence of ministers who had been bribed with abundant gifts, the king dismissed Vāmana and appointed Ānanda to the office of *icchādvāra* (the gatekeeper of royal pleasure), assigning him to positions such as the footmen. At that very moment, Ānanda attained that authority.
He was highly esteemed by the ministers who were hostile to Kandarpa. Then, urged by them, the king sent Kandarpa to drink [the waters] of Lohara, which had been devastated by enemies,
after bestowing upon him the status of a regional ruler (*maṇḍaleśvara*).

Endowed with the prowess of his spells, he was driven away from the presence of that beast of a king by wicked servants seeking their own advancement, using that very power. Having abandoned the eloquent and wise man from his side, thinking "he is fit for the role of a messenger," and having cast him out as one who steals words and causes separation from kinsmen, [the king] sent him to another land.

Thinking, "This hero shall seize the kingdom," she abandoned all reflection; thus, impelled by rogues, that ignorant beast of a king did not meet his destruction for a long time. Though firmly established in her heart, her love for Kandarpa vanished over time due to the king's absence, like sand from a closed fist.

Taking Utkarṣa’s son and desiring to exercise lordship over Loḥara, the ministers said to the king, "Kandarpa is at hand. Saying "So be it," the king then swiftly seized his kinsman in order to kill him.
He dispatched Paṭṭa with his army, as well as Ṭakka, who was known as Asidhara.
When those two arrived, learning of the news through the exchange of letters,
he became averted and terrified in spirit, like Kandarpa repeatedly [overcome by fear].
At the moment of the dice throw, as he was rubbing his hand before him like Devaka, a sword-wielder then rose up to seize him. Then,
having drawn back his own hand, he [seized] that man’s hand with the tip of his thumb.

Because he had been rubbed with *amṛdgā* and other substances, his skin was stripped away and he became as moist as a bird; consequently, the king, ignorant of what had happened, censured both himself and the man who had sought refuge with him. Distressed, the royal attendant spoke thus: [The king] was reproached by the distressed [attendant], and the sash was likewise addressed.

"Let the king, whose intention is to be led astray, send away my family; having entrusted the fortress to them, I shall then depart for another region. Having brought back the kinsmen given by them, I shall take them with me, free from malice."
Then that minister, having fulfilled his office, went to Vārāṇasī.
Having slain a local chieftain at Gayā and installed another in his place,
he abolished the tax on funeral offerings for the Kashmiris.
Having slain the leader of the bandits along with his army on that difficult mountain path,
he cleared the eastern direction of all thorns for those traveling the road.
By slaying the fierce beast, the tiger, and expelling him from Vārāṇasī,
that king adorned the eastern quarter with monasteries built by those skilled in virtuous deeds.
Because of his expulsion, those wicked ministers finally attained their mark.

Then, out of mutual envy, the kings struck down one another’s undertakings. Where, with their heavy pride aroused by eating at will, their minds clouded by irresistible jealousy, and driven by evil counsel, they strike each other for the sake of scratching the itch of their horns; in that kingdom, the total collapse of the monarch—who stands like a central pillar—occurs within only a few calculated days.
As time passed, Vangīśa, desiring the kingship and wishing to see [the king] slain, applied himself to the destruction of the monarch. He thought:
"If this kingdom were again to fall under the charge of treason and scandal..."

"He will surely come to me, thinking that because I am the son of a Vaiśya, I am unworthy [of this position]. Having deliberated thus for a very long time, Jayarāja was incited by that crooked-minded man to slay the king. (A *yugma* couplet).
O King, having dispatched fierce men born in the village of Vilāva to commit treason,
he made two or three women from the royal harem fall into their midst.
When that mission was gradually on the verge of success, the king [proceeded] toward the royal city.
Out of great respect, he once dispatched Dhammaṭa as an envoy;
while he was staying in the auspicious chamber, awaiting a favorable day,
Jayarāja arrived, anxious about the failure of his mission.
While those two were deliberating over that matter hidden within the pavilion,
a certain follower of Prayāga, concealed by a wall, overheard it. Then,
having been informed of that news from Prayāga, he related the story of it from there.
Having understood this, the king turned back from his journey to Dharmaṭa;
remaining there out of fear for the destruction of his lineage, he was slow to take action against it, and day by day he remained anxious,
protecting only himself.

But Jayarāja, seeing through his messengers that the two heroes Śamāla and Ḍāmara were in his presence, dispatched the two named Vāgapāja and Pāja. They set out with their own servants who had emerged to create a rift, as was reported to him.

Having heard this during the night, the King dispatched guards in all directions. Under the pretext of setting out on a journey, he prepared himself; then at dawn, the rogue Vaṅgiṇ brought Jayarāja before him for worship in the quadrangle.
Then, while the king remained in his palace with its bolts fastened, he entered the sacrificial enclosure together with his brother’s son, Dharmaṭa. Thereupon,
by the king’s command, Prayāga stationed the guards outside.
"Bind Jayarāja! he commanded Dhammaṭa in a low voice.
(KRT 7.1026cd) Trusting in Dhammaṭa, Jayarāja would certainly lay down his weapons;
by this command, Dhammaṭa knew both what was known and what was unknown to himself. (KRT 7.1027ab–cd)
"In a battle between two, or even one of them, their death would be for our benefit; moreover,
the slaying of those whose unity has been made manifest is not censured even in the world"—
as Brahmā thus reflected constantly without contradiction, [the following occurred].
The king’s wisdom shone forth, and his counsel was most appropriate.
[Tilaka] "The king certainly did not perceive me, for he was confident that they were Angiras," [he thought].
Then, approaching Jayarāja, he spoke these words with boldness. [Kṛt 7.1029cd–1030ab/cd]
If the king is not well-disposed toward you because he is certain that you are treacherous, then,
for the sake of your own purification, you must quickly hand over your dagger.
Or perhaps he has been deluded by fate, or else he has abandoned you out of misplaced trust.
Though being provoked, he who was skilled in weapons and missiles drew his weapon as if it were another's; then,
out of envy upon seeing that display of agitation, the son of the daughter of Tanvaṅga, known as Ṛṣṭi, spoke these harsh words to the son of Jaka.
O you who are devoid of courage, you were not born for the sake of performing deeds by King Kalaśa;
surely your father was some mere eunuch,
one who did not understand the ultimate transformation of the practice of fortitude.

Having been addressed with "So be it," he became like a well refreshed by the sprinkling of cool water. (A pair of verses) When questioned about the news of his offense, the steadfast man—even though tormented by the agony of the torture—spoke only of himself, and not of Dhammaṭa. (KRT 7.1036)
Having rendered the consumption of poison futile through the power of the obstacle-averting mantra,
he pressed down on the front of the neck with a rope; then, in the night, [the victim] was destroyed.

Jayyaka, the *pratīhāra*, having cut off [his] head, abandoned it and departed; that body was cast into the waters of the Bhaṭṭāranaṅgalā to be devoured by fish. In the seventy-first year, in the month of Bhādrapada, the king—
Deep in heart, he even contemplated the slaughter of Dhammaṭa. Then,
for the sake of accomplishing that, he secretly commanded the best of weapon-bearers,
the heroic Ṭhakkura named Kalaśarāja, who was based at Lohara.
When he dispatched a messenger, he said to him,
"This must be accomplished by you at Prayāga," having treated him with great honor;
for that messenger from Prayāga was taking his own man with him out of fear of failure.

"Having consulted together, let this be done," he said to the king in anger. While the king was thus deliberating, the five chief ministers were summoned; then Vāmana, having cast off his body at the bolted door, spoke these words: *saṃmantrya kriyatāmetadityūce kupito nṛpam ||* *rājñi mantrayamāṇetha pañcānīyāgryamantriṇaḥ |* *vāmanaḥ sārgale dvāre tyaktadehobravīdvacaḥ ||*
If it is argued that "as long as these mantras and the reciters have not yet gone outside,
the ritual action has not occurred," this does not prevent misfortunes from diminishing.
Then, by the king's command and through the performance [of the rite], the messenger was dispatched.

The fierce one named Kalaśarāja went along with his two sons. On that occasion, the Lord of Vaṅga remained within the capital city together with only two or three attendants, providing shade for them under a *śyena* tree.
As soon as she saw that king of jars in front and her two sons behind, she cried out in alarm; at that very moment, he was seized by his own servants.
To him who was saying, "Though I am capable of drawing my sword, [I will not]," Dharmaṭa—though capable of drawing his blade—[remained silent].
Just as he raised his hand with a weapon to strike the King of Kalaśa,
he was struck from the front by him and from behind by the king's two sons;
while still rising from his seat, he was swiftly deprived of life.

By him, who was about to die, the elder brother born of Kalasara was wounded; yet, due to the defectiveness of his weapons, he did not become repeatedly pierced. Indeed, through the force of his own misfortune, during those very days, the armed men—
His own sword snapped, and thus he became "one whose weapon is ill-fated" (Abhadrāyudha). Having been struck down, he was cast from their backs like a bird by hunters;
at the king's command, he was abandoned to be devoured by dogs by the outcasts.
The king himself came and protected Ralhaṇa and Malhaṇa, the two grandsons of Tanvaṅga,
having cast aside his sword in the courtyard.
But Ṭulla and the others, eager for battle and full of fury, were struck down by Āskanda.
Deceived by the hypocrite Udayasiṃha who approached you with illusions, you—
desiring life— did not cast away your weapons because of the trust you placed in that righteous man when he said, "You are my sons."
"Let the king's purification be performed; come to his side"—this was their word. Having assembled, they took the path toward Rājagṛha.
He who had been reared from childhood on the remnants of food from the houses of slender-limbed women...
Then, laughing, the umbrella-bearer said this:
"O grandson of Tanvaṅgana, what you previously said to Jayarāja—
'You, O one lacking courage, are not fit for trade'— that has been forgotten by you."
This very same moment of crisis has now come upon you.
O fool, why do you resort to despondency at a time that demands fortitude?
Therefore, you were surely born from the leftover handful of food of my parents.

"But I [shall be purified] by that hero, your father, who shares in glory. Having said this, he, the proud one, fell in battle while seizing the water from the edge of his sword's blade, as if washing away the impurity of his birth.
Having then resolved, "We shall go into the presence of the king," the royal officers cast Tulla and the others into prison; they,
intoxicated by the fullness of their youth, were like springtime trees.
Out of compassion, the kings appeared as those who ought to be protected.
But a wicked man named Bimbiya, the *ṭakka*, having observed the king,
seized them by their necks at night, casting nooses around them.
Ṭulla, Vijayarāja, Bullo, Gulla, and Teluṭhan—
these four grandsons of Tanvaṅga were slain on the execution ground.

Even now, the beauty of those who have been slain is described by elders in the course of conversation, as they shed tears that darken the air like a stormy day; their teeth, worn away by constant chewing of betel, have fallen out, leaving gaps where their tooth-sprouts once were.

The execution ground became like a long-strewn garland of blood-red stones. Then, although the king had promoted both the son and the minister to high positions, a man named Ḍomba, acting as a secret agent, measured out the destruction of the family through covert punishments.

Regarding the infant Jayamalla— the son of Vijayamalla— as a mere spark amidst a blazing mass of fire, he slew him. Having killed his own kinsmen who were his protectors, he intended to devour [the kingdom] for the sake of some single individual.

Kings struck by fate rule a kingdom free from thorns. A foolish person, unable to easily remove a well-established honeycomb from the dense thicket of high branches belonging to some fortunate soul, becomes helpless with trembling at the instigation of fate; having violently struck down the bees that protect it with blows of his leaves, he destroys the holy fig tree.

Then the king, his intellect destroyed by the great sin of betraying his kinsmen, met with a fate even children could not have imagined— becoming food for his enemies. Kṣema, the son of Vāmana, [deposed] that Janaka-hater, Jāja.
The Lord of Kalaśa urged [his horse] toward the golden parasol atop the temple;
his devotee Prayāgaka skillfully cut off that desire of his,
just as a steady driver restrains an elephant rushing toward the edge of a precipice.
He who was skilled at entering the interiors of kings— who were constantly devoid of activity like corpses— acted like a *vetāla* (vampire).
Then there was a libertine named Loṣṭadhara, the grandson of Haladhara.
Once, in a secluded place, he spoke to the king out of a desire to please him:
"Let the gold and other riches belonging to the temple of Kalaśeśvara be taken;
with the stones from that temple, I shall build for you a bridge across the Vitastā. (Yugma)

"I shall paint a picture in the sky, weave a garment with lotus fibers, bring back the gold seen in a dream, and bind a rampart with snow"—though such things have been clearly stated, only one of dull intellect would take them as true. A king who, out of shame, does not speak in such a manner has lost his maturity and is utterly deceived. Yet, O Lord, he even forbade the King's desire to go to Prayāga.
Like a patient’s entreaty for suitable attendants and medicine;
then, on an occasion for laughter, Loṣṭadhara addressed the king: "O Lord, let there be a release for one who is bound."
Smiling and asking him, "What is this?", he [the king] informed him:
"In the city of Udabhāṇḍapura, there was formerly a king named Bhīmaśāhi.
Due to a conflict with his courtiers, Bhīmakeśava was created by him..."

In the kingdom of Kalaśadeva, the gates remained closed for a long time. But when those enmities had been pacified by them, and the enemy was made fully exposed, then he was seen wearing a coat of mail that had been stripped of its color by thieves.

Furthermore, out of fear of him, he [the king] made himself a partaker in the power of the treasury; from that time until today, it is clear that his gates and so forth have remained firmly closed. Therefore, let his treasury, which brings fear to thieves, be seized.

"May he too be released from bondage and partake of enjoyments such as flowers and lamps. Thus urged by him, the king acted accordingly; thereafter, the treasury became filled to overflowing with jewels, gold, and other riches.

And he thought: "If such a thing as this exists in a place that is but a hollow abode for gods, what then might it be like in those other, primary celestial mansions? Then the king was largely attended by the courtiers from that place.
A ransom was extorted from him by means of an elephant that had grown accustomed to carrying heavy loads.
Gradually, his mind became intent on seizing the wealth of the gods due to his obsession with the expenses and calamities of the army's front-line divisions, as well as through such presumptions.
Then, with a greedy mind, he plundered from all the dwellings of the gods the treasuries dedicated by former kings, which were wonders of the world.

In order to bring even the images of the gods from hostile treasuries, he appointed one named King Udaya as the leader for the uprooting of the deities. And with the mouths [of his agents] being naked ascetics whose noses, feet, and hands were withered...
To destroy the forms of the gods, he cast their excrement, urine, and other filth [upon them].
The figures of the deities, fashioned from gold, silver, and other materials,
rolled about even in the rubbish heaps like piles of firewood on the roads.
They fashioned images of the gods, their ankles drawn up by girdles;
these were covered with flowers and the sound of hissing, while the broken and naked actors and others [were cast down].
In the village, the town, or the city, there was no palace whatsoever [that remained standing].
He whom even the Turuṣka king Harṣa could not render peerless—
of him there were two supreme, powerful protectors, invincible to gods:
Śrī Raṇasvāmin in the city, like Mārtāṇḍa among the towns.
Two [beings] protected the image of the Buddha from within a great statue. Once, in the context of giving, having requested that generous king,
[he was born] on earth in the city of Parihāsa with the name Kanaka.
The singer Kuśalaśrī and the ascetic [were seen] within the city.

(KRT 7.1098cd) Indeed, for those who desire the acquisition of wealth, there is no cessation of evil deeds even after they have attained a prosperity that is a wonder to the world. (KRT 7.1099ab) For even an elephant, though he is the dwelling place of the goddess Lakṣmī, commits the sin of uprooting lotus ponds in order to obtain her. (KRT 7.1099cd)

By means of the wealth inherited from his grandfather and father, as well as through his desire to govern the kingdom, that king— who had augmented his treasury by seizing the riches of Lohara— appropriated the funds of the former kings even though he was [otherwise] righteous. He plundered the two treasuries for the sake of the wealth of his predecessors.
"Alas, even he desired the acquisition of wealth through the oppression of his own subjects! (Yugma)" Then,
having received merely his command, those wicked ministers appointed various leaders,
each marked with a new seat and a new name.
Fie, fie upon those who live off the king, who are devoted only to following the whims of the times!
For even the minister there, though of mature age and of virtuous conduct, is a mere buffoon.
His only vow is the plundering of all the gods' temples and the entire property of the villages.

By accepting [the title], she even assumed the role of her husband’s patroness. (Yugma) The attendant Samarasvāmin, who was a companion of King Vijayamalla, became an object of the king’s hatred because he had been trusted with the temple of the god Sahelaka. (KRT 7.1105ab–cd)

By granting double the increase [in his salary], he attained the position of leader over all matters; having gained an opportunity before the king, he gradually became a high-ranking minister. What else could be said? By him, who surpassed all other leaders, all objectives were seized.
The leader of the city was also appointed for the acquisition of wealth;
by virtue of his power, which concealed his dullness under the guise of the title "Śrīgarbha" (Womb of Fortune),
he ensured that the treasury thus amassed was spent in a fitting manner.
To purchase the rarity of deer-eyed women, the endurance of horses' breath, the ability of parasites to tolerate foul speech, and the boastfulness of bards,
kings squander their fortune;
[and they do so] through the anger and favor of their beloveds, and by seeking news of horses and other such matters.

Through service to their attendants and stories of the hunt, the time of kings passes like that of children; whether they be wicked or virtuous, the entire class of rulers performs all activities— amusement, laughter, sitting, walking, giving, drinking, eating, and so forth— as mere imitations of others, like a shadow.

Thinking that their superhuman status as sovereigns of men is made real by the praises of the *viṭas*, and believing "my third eye is superior" or "my two arms [are supreme]," they do not perceive death.
For those whose wives prevail during the nights, while during the days their ministers hold fixed authority—
Oh, what a delusion of one's own, that even these kings perceive their own sovereign power here!
She eats what is delicious only with a sense of propriety, yet she spits out even those things that have been spat upon.

Terrified, both the king and the child suddenly fell into a state of fear; they were of equal condition. Whatever slight dullness or other such traits were observed in kings, all of that was rendered insignificant by the dullness of Harṣadeva.
Pleased by the playing of the drum, he, who was skilled in delightful musical instruments, gave an elephant together with its mate to one named Bhāmanāyaka. Then,
through him, his own disciple Kanaka became that man's singer.
Cappakāvaraja, out of weariness, made an effort to practice the *Gītā*;
and by him, whose mind was unshaken and who desired to dispel that weariness,
a hundred thousand gold dinars were bestowed upon him as a gift.

Seeing the beautiful woman named Caṇḍalā, painted in a portrait, belonging to the lord of Karṇāṭa, Parmaṇḍi, he became wounded by the flower-weaponed god [of love]. In rivalry, jesters provoke those of dull wit with laughter.
Constantly inciting those of vulgar disposition like dogs,
that shameless man, instigated by the courtiers,
made a vow within the assembly to obtain Cāṇḍālā and to churn the ocean of Pārtha’s wealth.
Having vowed to renounce all refined and artificial camphor, the wandering bards thus mocked him under the guise of praise:
"By the excellence of your particular dialect, you have been identified as a traveler from the South; for even by its scent, it is discerned that there is a piece of camphor in your hand."

O King Harṣa, if this [fruit] is ripe, prepare it as an offering for us; if not, let it remain within the hollow of this coconut for now. From the time of the slaughter of the Lord of the Karṇāṭa land, until the embrace of Candra, until the ritual entry into Kalyāṇapura, and until the sight of Pimmala—from the curiosity regarding the vast wealth at the edge of the forest that is the king’s refuge—the Lord of radiant splendor has forbidden the chewing of betel.
Madana, the lord of Kampanā, having propitiated the king,
obtained the status of a high official for her whose form was depicted in a painting,
as well as a salary for providing her with clothing and ornaments.
She constantly received gifts from the king in order to appease his jealousy; thus,
the sequence of Madana’s stories served as a touchstone for his lack of shame in his role as a libertine and for the king’s own fickleness and infatuation.
"This is my mother; she did not bring her from another land," said some as they showed him an old woman, while he was being robbed by other profligates.
Others, saying "These are slave-girls and deities," caused him to enter [the house]. (KRT 7.1128–1129ab)

Abandoning both his exaltation and his prosperity, he was mocked by the people as he bowed down. His female servants, instructed by parasites who sketched out amorous conversations and secret spells, brought about the delusion of his mind.

Among them, some, desiring sexual union with the mountain-king appropriate to the season, deprived him of his good fortune by touching their own limbs. To him who desired long life and wished for a prolonged existence— (Kṛt 7.1131–1132ab)

They granted those [elixirs] for a lifespan of hundreds of years to that dull-witted man. By some *ḍomba* seeking the attainment of the physical body (*piṇḍasiddhi*), he was made to drink some [substance], having been told, "This elixir brings about the attainment of the physical body."
What was the use of telling him of other youthful follies, he who, when entreated by libertines,
brought about the expenditure of even his life as if it were wealth already in hand?
Desiring strength and beauty, he resorted to other means.
Who would speak of such conduct, which is even more shameful than that?
Thus, with his intellect deluded by his own stupidity and by wicked ministers of evil birth, he is cast into the blinding darkness (andhatāmisra) for eternal years.

Just as there were some of small intellect whose minds were shaken by doubt regarding the world-transcending deeds of the leaders of the cloud-vehicles, so too are there some today who, while this difficult deed— which brings about wonder— is being described, remain wavering in their resolve.
Surely, in the course of time, people will undoubtedly become distrustful;

for in a kingdom full of deceit, he was likewise afflicted by such wicked policy that in the remainder of his life, he did not remain under the control of his enemies who were seeking his vulnerabilities.
While teaching the female dancers here, he himself rose up to perform a dramatic gesture;
as he stood in a chamber illuminated by lamps, he was [seen] from afar by a certain enemy.
That even one with an arrow shot at him was neither slain nor wounded was the fruit of the remaining lifespan of those subjects, or perhaps of their own misdeeds. Then,
a messenger from the king arrived at the inner apartments.
From that treasury of all impurity, the corruption of women’s conduct emerged.
Those youths, intoxicated with passion, and those women, maddened by youth,
became the cause of Harṣadeva’s destruction at that very moment.
Out of anger, he imprisoned some women along with their paramours; others, however, were dragged from the inner apartments by their lovers and carried away to distant lands.
Due to the fault of his own immoral conduct, everyone became filled with suspicion.
His servants desired ill fortune for him and strove for his destruction;
meanwhile, his deficiency in character spread everywhere until it reached King Kalaśa, from whom he was born.
Those very mothers by whom he was reared in childhood after climbing onto their laps— embracing them and placing them on his own lap, he enjoyed them constantly,
performing sexual acts upon the group of his sisters with an indescribable and fierce passion.

The daughter of his father’s sister was both imprisoned and enjoyed by him. That evil-minded man, constantly nourishing the lords of hundreds of Turuṣkas with wealth until their death, devoured village pigs.
Then, at one time, the king, provoked by the success of his service,
that dull-witted man marched with an assault against the royal city;
and on the way, he beheld a military array such as was peerless.
The kings suspected him of possessing the power to conquer the three worlds. But he, seeing that the mountain was a fortress on earth and intent on seizing it,
did not enter the royal city, but sat down at its base.
Oppressed by him for more than a month,
the guards of the fortress found their stores of food and other supplies exhausted.
To protect them, the lord of the earth, Saṃgrāmapāla, took up the cause.
Fearing how much tax he might have to pay, and seeing how many other arrangements there were,
the king— his resolve having become firm— refused to accept that [bribe]. Thereupon, by means of a gift of a bribe, he took control of the greedy chief of the police.
While the king remained unsuspecting, she incited armed men in secret to seek a large reward for exile; when those men,
who were mostly commoners, had made their boastful declarations, [the plot was set in motion].

While the king’s treasury was situated at a distance, his camp fell into agitation. Just as the commander-in-chief (daṇḍanāyaka) was attempting to stabilize it, he presented another terrifying threat arising from the Turuṣkas and the Āskandas.

Then the king, lacking in fortitude, rose up and departed with his army; out of fear on the roads, he took the entirety of his treasury along with him. An unexamined servant, when favored by his masters in a time of extreme peril, [acts as follows].
Like a low-born elephant in battle, he brought about a calamitous downfall.
By him— himself unfit and unwilling to allow others who were fit—
the royal fortune was defiled, just as a stable is defiled by a base horse.
From that time forth, the title "Emperor by Valor" (*pratāpacakravartin*) completely faded away for King Nirvāṇapratāpa;
for what he had not accomplished with his own face cast down in dejection, his servants and all others likewise failed to achieve.
He held Kandarpa in high esteem for having performed that deed. However,
while that foolish king was desiring to bring him back,
the commander-in-chief alone thwarted his wish through the act of slander.

Then the king, out of resentment toward his kinsman, imprisoned the commander-in-chief; yet he did not seize him out of sheer anger, but rather out of consideration for his past service. Although his life was precarious while dwelling in that fortress, he continued to accumulate wealth.

Deluded by fate, the greedy king accepted betel, garments, and other gifts sent by his servants and kinsmen, which resulted in the total ruin of himself; instead of honoring him as one worthy of increase, the monarch restored him to his former position.
The court jesters further inflamed the king with their flatteries,
praising his victory with hymns, just as Karṇa and others once did for the Kaurava.

A debater defeated in debate who insults his opponent with abusive words; a woman whose eightfold vow of chastity is ruined who terrifies her husband with quarrels; and a scribe who, having seized all the wealth and power, brings the king to distress—each of these provides further support for their own impending downfall. A high official, fearing that the wealth he has consumed must be repaid, treats him with contemptuous ease.
A man skilled in his own self-interest, inciting the lord of the earth toward evil deeds,
sought out his kinsman Darada along with the Lavanyas and Lāharas,
and urged him to seize the fortress known as Durgaghāta.
For in the past, when the protector named Lakṣmaṇacandra was slain by Janaka, the gatekeeper, at the command of King Ānanta,
his wife also surrendered herself at the gate while sitting in a fast unto death.
The king reached Dāra, where King Kalaśa had arranged for him to be ignored; yet,
because that region was overrun by the forces of Dāra in its endless villages,
both the king and his minister then resolved to take action.

The snow that had been gathered there in the lake for the sustenance of its guardians was, at that very moment, brought to total exhaustion by the drought. Having observed that vulnerability through their spies, the great darkness prepared to seize it.

Constantly urging the king, he made an effort in that regard; and by the king's command, Cappaka, who was stationed at the gate, desired to deceive Vātagaṇḍa as he was about to set out on that mission.
Having been barred from the gate by the king, he was elevated to the status of a provincial ruler;
for he shared the gate with all those officials in charge of the gateway. Even when his army was routed by him, that gatekeeper [remained steadfast].

Having crossed the honey-sweet Sindhu river, he surrounded that inaccessible place with his troops. Sending out all the vassal lords himself in every direction, the king remained resolute even when separated from Koṭa by only a single march.

Abandoning their boulder-like fortifications and other inaccessible strongholds that were difficult to overcome, the Kashmiris engaged in battle with the Darada troops. Residing at the site of the assault known as Prājimaṭhikā, he [the king] waged war.
The wrestler Guṅgaja, together with his son, [endured] intolerable agitations;
while his two sons, the heroes Uccala and Sussala, whose attainment of the kingdom had been predicted by an astrologer, increased their pride through his favor.

The elder of those two, though exceedingly haughty and even an enemy, occupied the royal throne due to the power of destiny; he set out on that expedition. Dried up by drought and by the majesty of the king’s prowess—

In some manner or other, the soldiers with their wives guarded that fortress. Then, as if by the decree of fate, a great rain fell, obstructing both joy and distress, and merging water and land into one.
The entire peak of Durgā was surrounded by impenetrable snows,
as if by defensive armor deployed by a favorable fate;
it caused some to fall as they rose and others to rise as they fell.
May the Creator indeed cause the illusion of playing with a ball to sprout anew.
Then, remembering their homes and distressed by the rain,
those wicked ministers again caused the king’s camp to be fouled with excrement as before.
Like a *timi* fish whose mouth is struck by a rock and forced to swim upstream against the current,
the king, turning his back on old age, turned away from that [kingdom] as well. With his pearl-market closed, his treasury depleted, abandoned by prosperity, and his weapons fallen away, he departed.
The entire camp became intent on flight.
As the royal soldiers fled by various paths with cries of distress, the long river on their route swallowed up the enemies who were pursuing them from behind.

With linen garments it was like a lake with rows of swans; with shields it was like a pond with clusters of lotuses; with a multitude of swords it was as if covered in moss; with horses it was as if filled with stones;
and with golden and silver vessels it was as if possessed of aquatic plants.

The river became honey-sweet with the corpses abandoned by the people, as if covered in foam. There was no counting the embodied beings who were led away, slain, or carried off by the rivers by the Daradas, who had exerted themselves to the utmost.
Though alone with his younger brother, the proud Mālliruccala made an effort to protect the army that had become like one who is helpless; yet he did not waver.
Rushing forth like an ocean of Dārada forces, intent on a universal conquest,
he was completely checked by those two as if by the coastal mountains;
having protected them, they attained strength and reached incomparable fame.
The royal fortune attended him with its visible splendor, as if he were a bridegroom chosen by her own will.
From that time forth, this was the thought of all the world:
"These two proud men are worthy of the kingdom; this one, however, is a eunuch, not a king."
Even after acting thus, because they avoided showing themselves to the king,
people concluded that the two were averse to bestowing gifts of affection; therefore,
the king entered the city with his fear of enemies allayed.
The prowess of the two sons of the king of the Mallas spread throughout the quarters.
At that time, everyone said, "These two are Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa";
for when a king resembles Rāvaṇa, his speech accords with the destined outcome.

But that king, devoid of shame and dull-witted, began once more— without weariness— to oppress the circle [of vassals], as if it were his daily duty. A base man slays one standing at his side even for a slight offense, but does not strike an enemy from afar even if he has committed no wrong.

A dog with fierce rage bites a stone that falls near him, but not one that is far away and has abandoned him. Then, having entered joyfully after being granted protection through his service, he heard Madana speaking freely about his own defeat.
Out of anger, desiring to kill him, he seized that other man,
who had incurred the offense of transgressing the written command issued by the queen;
having been deprived of an audience with the king, he was brought from the kingdom of Maḍava.
Terrified, he went to the palace of Lakṣmīdhara, the minister of Ṭakka.
Although the king was being propitiated by another minister acting on his behalf,
he had him executed along with his son, while his troops looked on with smiles.

The king’s smile of anger is like an untimely flower on a tree, or the loud laughter of a *vetāla*; it is not pacified in this way alone. Those who, having cultivated a great pride of deep affection, serve their lord without hesitation— [they are truly devoted].

In their haste to attach themselves to mantras, they go to their destruction even while proclaiming their friendship with the lord of serpents. The curse of Queen Sūryamatī, which extended her arms [in threat], remained within the family of informers until the dissolution of Madana.

Trembling at the sight of his prowess, the lord of the earth cast that King Kalaśa into the residence of Lakṣmīdhara after having him bound; under the pretext of requiring instruction for one so hostile and imprisoned, the king [dealt with him].
He dispatched his minister named Udaya to destroy [the king's] splendor.
Seeing him blazing with beauty,
that high-minded man, having obtained a small knife from someone, slew him on the spot in a fit of rage.
Then, having fallen upon him, his servants, filled with rage, slaughtered that [minister];
thus did the servants of that evil-minded king perish,
like a region scarred by the wound of royal punishment.
A succession of miseries arose, resembling the falling of caustic lye.
Thieves who had even carried away golden platters from the king’s palace— such were the people who, though their actions brought no laughter, struck at the virtuous.
As the plague increased, the sound of the wailing of the dead,
filled with the resonance of funeral instruments, did not cease day or night;
this occurred in the year seventy-five, when villages were submerged by rising waters.
A famine broke out, leaving all provisions in short supply.
A khārī of grain could be obtained for five hundred dīnāras,
while two palas of grape wine could be purchased for a single dīnāra.
The purchase of a single tuft of wool was accomplished with six dināras;
even the names of salt, pepper, asafoetida, and other such items became difficult to obtain.
The rivers became filled with water consisting of corpses whose bodies had swollen from immersion in the liquid.

With its waters hidden by trees fallen from the mountains, it was as if covered by forests of felled timber. Thinking, "The royal capital, obscured by this, cannot be seen from afar," the king ordered the cutting down of trees on all sides.
[150] Trees laden with flowers and fruit were felled like householders;
they were lamented at every step by swarms of bees, as if by kinsmen.
Even toward a person in distress, the king inflicted a life-taking heavy punishment,
like a massive boulder hurled at a broken old bull;
having oppressed the people through the administration of severe fines by means of scribes.

In cities, villages, and elsewhere, not even a trace of earth was left behind. Then, as if enraged like the wielder of the staff (Yama) to slay all the most terrifying demons who had reached a state of extreme excess, he commanded the lord of the maṇḍala.
Formerly, on the earth of King Maḍava, he [Śrīkaṇṭha] struck down those Ḍāmaras at Holaḍānta like birds in a nest with his sharp intellect; and while slaying the Lavanayas,
he displayed a formidable form with his matted hair tied up.
Because of that, even a brahmin was cast out from within the kingdom of Jīvanmṛḍa. Then, with the thought that they were beautiful, stakes were driven into the ground by passers-by;
thus the earth became terrifying in form, like the kitchen of Bhairava.
While one Lavanīya was cruelly impaling his bride upon a stake,
all the other Lavanīyas fled in every direction, terrified of the lord of the mandala.
Some of them devoured their own beef in the lands of the Mlecchas.
Some who had been dragged away by water-wheels, mills, and the like,
returned. The lord of the circle [of vassals], whose head was adorned with a garland of severed heads of low-caste men, sent a profuse gift to King Bhairava.
Circular archways were seen everywhere at the royal gates,
filled with the skulls of *ḍāmaras* as if with water-jars;
and at the entrance of the king’s palace, bracelets, garments, and other items were hanging down.
Some leader of the *ḍāmara* outcasts indeed sat down;
having reached wide archways to feast upon the heads of the *ḍāmaras*,
the vultures, herons, and other scavengers attended at the royal gate.
Wherever the king was stationed,
there the people hung garlands of arches made from the fierce heads of the Lavaneyas.
Their sense of smell was assailed by a foul stench, and their ears by the terrifying howls of jackals.

He felt no distress in that circle, which was strewn with corpses like a cremation ground. The lord of the circle established a single-file line extending from the edge of Balarāja’s water-shed to the very limit of the world’s merit, using the *ḍāmaras* impaled upon stakes.

Having thus brought the kingdom of Maḍava under control, with its *ḍāmaras* eliminated, he rushed across the earth to establish that very same path for the kings of Krama. Having resolved, "We shall certainly no longer exist," the *ḍāmaras* [fled].

They made preparations for the army of the kingdom of Kramarāja at Laulāha. With all of them having given battle and causing great carnage, the Maṇḍaleśvara remained there besieged for a very long time.
What else could it be? Some Rākṣasa, desiring to destroy this circle of kings worshipped by the sages of Surātīrtha, descended under the pretext of joy.
Exultation at night, sleep during the day, cruelty, and ferocity—these were his traits.
"An aversion to speech, a delight in performing tasks suited to the right hand"—
such were some of his qualities, appropriate for a night-stalker (*naktaṃcara*).
For indeed, they were proclaimed by wise men as the favorites of that era.
In the meantime, the youngest son of the Malla, intoxicated by his youth,
became the delighter of the heart of Lakṣmīdhara’s wife;
for she was already infatuated with that prince, their neighbor.

She did not feel affection for her own husband, whose form was like that of a monkey. O King, why did you not slay these two arrogant men, Uccala and Sussala— who, though possessing the marks of those worthy of sovereignty, failed to destroy their countless kinsmen?

Although the king was thus addressed by Lakṣmīdhara out of envy and anger, he did not become enraged; for he had already experienced the agony of remorse due to the slaughter of his kinsmen in the past. Thereafter, he was repeatedly urged by him, both personally and through the mouths of others.
Reflecting upon that agitation caused by the slaughter, he summoned his composure; then,
forgetting out of affection for his kinsmen and other ties,
he consulted with his ministers and made a resolution appropriate to the situation.
Then the woman standing nearby, named Thakkana,
made the king’s wicked intention known to their ears.
Their doubts severed regarding that matter by their friend Darśanapāla, the two of them departed during the night together with two or three followers. Then,
in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, when they were sixty-seven years old, they went forth from the city.
Upon reaching Unnāsavasa, he received the instruction of Ḍāmara.
King Praśasta, desiring to seize his own younger brother Sillarāja, conspired with him;
thus, those two Lavanyas were led away to another region.
Then the elder brother set out for Rājapurī, the capital of King Kalha;
the younger brother went to the presence of the lord of Kaliñjara.
Once those two had departed, no one placed any trust in the kingdom.
The King himself, who was skilled in interpreting omens, became suspicious because of ill omens;
through Lakṣmīdhara’s mouth, he made Saṃgrāmapāla— who had been eager to reject the request— accept wealth and then [proceeded].
But he, showing respect to the son of Malla who had arrived uninvited,
felt an even greater weight of suspicion toward his enemy because of that; for,
impelled by fate, one hates an enemy whose prosperity is imminent.
By manifesting suspicion, he would bring [the matter] in the world to a state of public rumor.
Since the people of Rājapurī are by their very nature desirous of wealth from Kaśmīra,
what could be said regarding the wheel of intrigue when a powerful enemy has arrived?
Then Ucchala, exerting himself, caused some of the Dāmaras who were mostly treacherous and stationed at his side to go back and forth;
the highly energetic Dāmaras, for their part, dispatched him to bring [the enemy] back.
The son of Sūryavarman, named Janaka, increased the enthusiasm of that king— who had been treated with contempt by the monarch— by means of many envoys sent with gifts,
dispatched through illusory messengers.

Seeing those messengers of the *ḍāmara*, Uccala cast off his fear of the king; clearly, Saṃgrāmapāla brought him [to safety] through his greatness. Bowing low out of respect for the gravity of the task, he placed camphor powder upon his head.
Having done this, he desired to release him for the sake of his safety;
just then, a chief official named Kalasarāja,
who had been bribed by Harṣadeva, approached him in a secluded place and said:

Abandoning the propitiation of the king, you— who desire only your own welfare— have cast aside the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) and seized hold of the neck of a goat. What is this obsession of the kings of Kaśmīra, and what power does this wretched ascetic possess?
By propitiating that king, act so as to remain free from fear.
Then let this monarch be established on the inaccessible Rājagiri mountain;
thus he shall be a friend who always showers desired boons like a rain-cloud.
"Ten" was the name by which that lord of the Khaśas, who was of limited intellect, was known;
terrified of him and greedy for his own interests, he agreed, saying, "So be it.
And he said to him, "I am not able to bind this man while he is prepared [for battle]."
"Let him be bound by you alone while we look on; he has been sent into our presence.
Having said this, he dismissed him to his own dwelling and spoke to Uccala:
"In the morning, you must go into the presence of King Kalaśa."
"In this matter, he is the chief minister; therefore, you shall remain free from harm. Consequently, for the sake of destroying the enemy faction, I shall release you along with your followers.
Then, on another day, Uccala set out to go to his residence.
Having been alerted by portents previously occurring that indicated this deed had been committed,
and hearing that he had withdrawn once the conspiracy was betrayed,
King Kalaśa then marched forth with his army ready for battle, full of wrath toward the presence of the Khaśa king.
Knowing that he had arrived for an assault, that best of weapon-bearers,
accompanied by his own servants, desired to go out to battle.
When the agitation had begun, the lord of the Khaśas, having consoled him—

Standing there, he was led by the King of Kalasa to his own assembly hall. That treasury of prowess, having forcefully cast off the servants who attempted to restrain him, entered that gathering of the Khaśas with his lower lip trembling in anger.
No one was able to look upon him, who was as fierce as the sun at the end of an aeon,
like the enraged King of the Vases or a king who is a treasury of splendors.
In a secluded chamber, [he saw] the Lord of Khaśa together with his ministers.
To him who was thus consoling him, the one of great splendor spoke with words harsh with anger:
"In former times, O King, there was a man named Bhāradvāja, a ruler of the Dārvābhisāras."
His son, named Naravāhana, fathered Phulla;
from him came Sātavāhana, and his two sons were Gopāla and Siṃharāja. Candurāja also obtained [the throne].
The lion-king Bahvātmaja gave his daughter named Diddā to King Kṣemagupta; Sāvīrā gave her son, who delighted his brothers,
named Saṃgrāmarāja, to the kingdom as the son of Udayarāja.
Her brother, Kāntirāja, begot Jassarāja.
Saṃgrāma was the father of Ananta and of Jassa, whose limbs were as slender as the Gaṅgā. From Ananta, Kalaśakṣmābhṛt was born, and from Guṅga, Malla was also born.

"From the jar [Kalaśa] were born Gharṣa, Deva, and the others; likewise, we are born from Malla. How can those fools say, 'Who is this? and so forth, in such a sequence? Or rather, what use is there for a lineage on this earth that is to be enjoyed by heroes? (KRT 7.1287ab–1288ab)

And who could be a better companion for a hero than his own two arms? By good fortune, by placing my hand, as it were, upon the heads of those worthy of compassion, I have not become a disgrace to the lineage of the kings of Kaśmīra.
Having said, "Therefore, you shall see my power," he departed from there; followed by a hundred foot soldiers, he advanced for victory. Someone arrived before him, carrying the slain hare.
By that auspicious omen, he considered the fortune of his enemy already captured.
As he departed, the Ḍāmaras, Vāṭṭadeva, and others, having abandoned their water-wheels, mills,
and other agricultural implements, came out and attended upon him.
The queens of that king, having learned from a messenger stationed at the camp of Saṃgrāmapāla that he had arrived nearby, led him from his state of distress to a state of cheerfulness.
Having eaten there, he departed for his own residence at the close of day.

The army of King Kalaśa was forced outside by those who had provided him with support. When the queens emerged and blocked the gate, preventing their exit, his soldiers were slain in the battle with clods of earth, water-jars, and other such objects.

Having entered the center when the leaders had been neutralized in that battle, he— though already possessing a small army— became one with a truly meager force. By the end of the full moon of Caitra, he had experienced great hardship.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, his mind free from fear, he organized a procession;
having dismissed the Vāṭṭa deities and others so that they might depart by their own paths,
he himself took up the desire for entry by way of the royal road of the Krama.
He released that Kapila, the son of Kṣemaja, who had been stationed by King Udayasiṃha at the edge of the earth; as he entered [the city],
the king himself went ahead of them all, bearing sword and shield.
In his flight, he stationed his former disciples as soldiers at Parṇotsa.
Having bound the gatekeeper named Sujjaka, who was sitting there without suspicion, he,
desiring meat, swooped down upon Kaśmīra swiftly like a hawk.
Then some Ḍamas and Khāśikas, who dwelt in the mountains,
surrounded that royal elephant from all sides as soon as it arrived—
[the elephant] which was like one fallen from the sky or risen from the very womb of the earth.
Hearing that he had arrived unexpectedly, King Harṣa trembled. He thought:
"Let it not be that this man has taken firm root; let him not slay the lord of the province who resides within his own kingdom. Thus he remained constantly anxious.
While the general, with his army fully equipped, was lingering,
he quickly dispatched a royal turban, accompanied by countless leaders;
for [the enemy] was either one whose prowess was struck down by fate or one overcome by thoughts of treachery.
Abandoning his hostile intent, he instead lingered on the road. Furthermore,
whatever other kings, such as Tilakarāja and others, the monarch dispatched,
they all, upon reaching the royal insignia (the *paṭṭa*), did not allow their passage to proceed further.
When the chief commander of the army had been dismissed by the king,
Uccala fell into a state of confusion;
yet, as he entered the base of the Varāha mountain, he found refuge from the force of his enemies.

He mounted a horse endowed with auspicious marks, like the very Fortune of Kings; and it fell upon his head, which was adorned with a garland on the crest of its great boar-like snout, as if offered by the Earth herself, who had not yet settled upon him, to choose him as her husband.
His path blocked by warriors born of the families of physicians such as the Kākas,
he abandoned Huṣkapura and proceeded toward Kramarājya.
In the meantime, hearing that he was approaching,
the lord of the district (maṇḍaleśvara), filled with arrogance, was driven toward flight by the ḍāmaras;
for he had already been brought to defeat by them after they had slain great warriors.
He proceeded toward many kings headed by Yaśorāja, whose valor had become diminished;
then, slowly withdrawing, he reached Tārasūlaka.
Those enemies stationed on high ground also pursued him from there.
Held there for a long time by him with his infinite army assembled, he was like the eastern wind that precedes a cloud at the end of the world. There,
for the sake of the female elephant of the Goddess of Victory belonging to both armies, [the battle raged].

A fierce struggle ensued, like that between two elephants filled with mutual envy. Then Ānanda, the maternal uncle of Bhaṭṭavarāja, rose up in a tumultuous surge and, having intensified the violence, launched a fierce attack.
Upon its collapse, multitudes of rebels surged forth by the thousands from every direction and region,
like bees emerging from their holes at the end of winter.
At that very moment, he fell through the door like one whose fortune has been exhausted.
The great minister, who had been a companion to the king during his tremors of agitation, became full of pride;
having frequently engaged in battles and being emboldened by joy,
he did not abandon the kingdom of Maḍava, for that [pride] had become excessive at that time.
Then, having surrounded the great army with his wondrous prowess,
Bhaṇḍaleśvara, together with his troops, was captured in battle by Uccala;
we do not know what happened to the warriors at that time, for they were indeed unconscious of it.
"Equipped with swords, horses, and armor, it is clear that we are bound.
Even though he was thus bound, that noble man meditated upon what would benefit his master;
for the devotion of the proud does not falter even at the very end.
Then, repeatedly saying, "There is no other moment for trust," he urged Uccala to enter the city quickly. As he was entering,
many people plundered the city and its villages.
Thinking, "By this deed,
let there be public scandal concerning her," he was then ushered by him into Parihāsapura—
a place from which exit is extremely difficult due to pits, water, and precipices.

There, in the four-winged palace, he urged his own people to burn themselves during the night; but those who desired his welfare did not do so. For if his body were as capable of such rashness as his mind, it would have been so.

What desired goal could not be accomplished by one who is indifferent to his own self? A tortoise dwells with its body concealed by skin that cannot be cut away, yet it is defenseless; while a lion, possessing great enthusiasm for the daring feats of battle, is always without armor. Fie on Fate, which, impetuous in its partiality toward the base, strikes the bodies of heroes on all sides with the arrows of mutilation!
Then he commanded the king: "Having dragged this man before me, let him be executed immediately like a jackal that was cast away by you.
Thereupon, accompanied by the entire host of his vassals and armies, [he set out].
Having resolved that today would be either death or victory, the king went forth. At that moment of mortal peril, he ordered the cessation of all exertion;
by the proclamation of the drum, he was followed by everyone.
Reaching the vanguard of Bharata’s army and slaughtering the hostile host,
the king’s servants traversed the road in an instant on noble steeds.
When the royal army had arrived like a turbulent ocean, it overwhelmed the enemy force.

The Lord of the Mandala himself, having entered within, destroyed them. When the army of Ucchala was thus broken, some of the swift-footed fled; others, being exhausted, entered the royal monastery (*rājavihāra*), as did some of the *ḍāmaras*.
Seeing the fierce warrior named Trillasena enter among the enemies,
they mistook him for Uccala and set fire to that monastery. Meanwhile,
the one named Somapāla, the slayer of his foes, remained for a long time amidst the enemy cavalry.
Engaging in combat with the paternal uncle of Darśanapāla,
the proud warrior was with great effort turned back from the battle by Janakacandra and others;
he departed from the city of Parihāsa as if fleeing from the jaws of death.
Having crossed the Vitastā at Gaurikābālagrāma with his horses,
he set out once more for Tāramūlaka accompanied by the Ḍāmaras.
Intoxicated by that mere victory like a petty gambler,
the king returned to the capital, praising his joy;
for even upon hearing that his enemy was still alive, he did not turn back.
By that means, even the formidable rebels, though suffering defeat, were brought to a state of near-recovery.
In the month of Jyeṣṭhāmūlīya, Uccala, remaining steadfast in mind, desired to rally once again from all sides those who had fled.
For that proud man, who relied solely on his own arms yet was dependent on others,
that great effort undertaken during the famine became a source of distress.
Even though he was extremely poor, he protected whatever he had obtained in the midst of it.
Having produced that [sound], King Anavatapta caused Śrī Parīhāsakeśava to emerge.
When that [city] was shattered, the dust, grey like the wings of a pigeon,
covered heaven and earth, reaching as far as the cutting off of the heads of those exulting.

Previously, even during the day, darkness had spread throughout this land, as it was rumored among the people that "the light of the day belongs to the Rūpikas. But when Parīhāsa-Keśava was installed, that [darkness] subsided.
Once he had been uprooted, for another month and a half, [the kingdom] remained blooming.
When the king had recovered somewhat from his faintness due to the enemy's slight advance,
Sussala then appeared from the direction of Śūrapura.

For while he was living at Avanti, he was drawn away from indifference by the messages sent by his father, who was intent on reproaching him for not honoring his elder brother. He took with him some horses given by the King of Kalha.
After a long time, he abandoned his royal courtesy and persisted with it;
