from the very beginning until its conclusion, even while remaining in a cruel state of enmity,
he employed conciliation— which brings about delusion— against the enemy who was a treasure-house of deceit.

Having defeated in battle the army commander named Māṇikya, he obtained from the town of Śūrapura both the glory of sovereignty and abundant wealth. By means of that prosperity which he had thus attained, he became a worthy recipient of further advancement.

The entire period of his undertaking became one of wondrous power. Then the king dispatched Sussala, who acted with haste, to fight against Maṇḍaleśvara, Paṭṭa, and others, whose movements were inconceivable.
By him, who was distinguished by valor, the warriors in Śūrapura were broken;
many met their destruction, submerged in the waters of the Vaitaraṇī river.
There, the body of Darśanapāla, who had committed treason against his master, [was seen].
As he strode forth, it was as if the Goddess of Victory herself had touched him, yet remained weary.
On the following day, the remainder of that royal army, having been slaughtered,
fled and approached the presence of Sahela, who dwelt amidst the merit of the world.
Suspecting that the end of the conversation was near, he entered the city together with those various broken forces, accompanied by his companions. Thus,
when the king had been approached and thrown into disorder by Sussala—

Standing at the base of Mount Tāra, Uccala regained his footing once more. Terrified by the cavalry, he was led back through the mountain fortress by the infantry-led Ḍāmaras along the path of the river Lohara.

The king, having again appointed the one named Udayarāja as the gatekeeper, dispatched Uccala to conquer Lahara, the lord of the province. Then, when [Uccala] had reached Padmapura, the maternal uncle of the two born of the Malla lineage—
No minister, overcome with fear, took up the trembling of the king. Then,
as the lord of the earth sighed, "Who is there for me?",
Candrarāja seized the garland of office from his hand.
Death lies in wait for those who offer no blessing; he was born into their lineage. He established the propriety of the illustrious Jindurāja and others.
Like the son of Droṇa when his time had passed away, he was appointed as the commander-in-chief.
Having emerged from that city of Padmapura, he warded off the enemy army.
That opponent, the lord of Kampana, was slain by him as he gradually advanced across the earth,
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas, within the city of Avanti.
For he, having been deprived of his own army by those engaged in battle near Govardhana-dhara, listened to the song accompanied by only a limited number of followers.
Having entered by way of the path along the banks of the Vitastā with his enemy-slaying horses, he suddenly met his death; for how can there be prosperity for those who are heedless?
Seeing that head sent by King Candra, the lord of the earth—

Perceiving the favorability of destiny, he further raised his hopes for victory. Destiny, which creates the illusion of a return by turning back with glances like a lion, might cause one who is departing in opposition to turn toward him through its intervening favors.
Then King Candra, having gained strength, entered with diminished effort the field of victory,
drawing his army in ten and eight divisions.
Like a merchant on a scale, the Creator could not endure the breaking of the balance.
Then, like the two pans of a balance scale,
the army of the lord of the maṇḍala was overwhelmed on the third day by the waves rendered helpless by an untimely rain.
Struck by the cold wind, the warriors sank into the mud of the irrigation channels; their horses quickly cast off their black armor and other gear as if they were slithering away like snakes.
Then, although he was being protected by Uccala with a compassionate heart, [the enemy]— KRT_7_1374ab–KRT_7_1375ab.

Janakacandra and others slew the lord of the province who had arrived; while the circle of King Harṣa’s servants was filled with apprehension regarding treachery, that very minister purchased fame through the sacrifice of his own body.
Surely Devaśarman and those others are worthy of praise for competing with him;
otherwise, no one would have proclaimed the fault in his reversal [of fortune].
[For him,] there were the uprooting of the Lavanya, the enemy’s great array, the bewildering of them, and so forth.

When the fruit is understood to be dependent on ritual action, whose actions would not be worthy of praise? Does the moon not destroy the darkness of the underworld? Does water not cause fear to one who swallows poison? Is Dhanvantari not the destroyer of the internal fire (of disease) for one who drinks it? Everywhere, a single word becomes fruitless when addressed to a fool; yet the ocean is not to be called such. For those who reflect upon the fact that success is subject to destiny, true knowledge of things is found in praise alone.
Let there be honor for women who are praiseworthy for their exertion in the service of their husbands; let his mother, the elephant-lady, bow down to her own lack of discernment,
since that king committed such a rash act toward her son.
As he was being led away, she, deluded by affection, said to the king:
"O Lord, this is my only son, belonging to a lineage with no others;
do not employ him in any matter where his life might be in jeopardy."
He told her how he had [acted] toward another’s lineage;
she thought that this was the same as toward another’s servant, for he was the sole support of his own master. She then perceived that devotion and honor shown by her husband toward his own kinsman.
At that moment, when her established status was secured, the proud and virtuous woman considered her purpose fulfilled;
then, the local brahmins assembled and conferred upon Uccala— the son of Hiraṇyapura— the royal consecration.
In that situation, the king is utterly helpless; there are many ministers with him—go with them to that mountain of iron and stone.
Thus, the subjects will have their longing for a new king pacified.
"They will bring you here before long, or you yourself shall come within a few days. He replied:
"I cannot bear to depart immediately, leaving behind my harem, women, treasury, lion-throne, and other such things that are not shared by others."

Furthermore, speaking again, he said: "The trusted ones, mounting swift horses, shall carry [the king] on their backs and lead him into the treasury and the women's quarters. Even if there were one who was a lover of a dog-cooker (outcaste woman), or even another such person in that place—"
"If he were to ascend the lion-throne, his pride would then be shattered. Let this be; now speak the mantra, they were urged. Then, once more, they spoke with great agitation to the king.
For those who rule the earth while placing the duty of a warrior (kṣatradharma) foremost,
what room is there for dejection, since death in battle is their blessing? Furthermore,
lack of exertion, shame, fear, and duplicity belong to the minister.
When the calamities of kings flourish, their enemies are not those born of the same lineage.
He who is lazy and does not perceive his duty himself, having entrusted all tasks to his servants—
like one whose sight is lost and who relies on a staff, he surely meets with disaster at every step.
Thinking with contempt that his enemy is so insignificant, he himself takes up the weapon;
thus, indeed, one of short-sighted intellect, deluded by shame, brings about his own growth.
In time, even Mahendra becomes a worm, and a worm may attain the state of Mahendra. To think "this one is great" and "that one is unstable" is an arrogance unworthy of final truth.
For one who desires to live, fear that brings about defeat is more harmful than a defect in every limb.

By whomsoever one is attacked, he comes to be struck by deficiency even if he is full of every prosperity. (KRT 7.1397cd) The attacker, having secured his position as a vessel of abundant wealth, becomes wretched, subsisting on the alms of others. (KRT 7.1398ab) How indeed could there be defeat in the first case? If there were fear here, that state would not exist there. (KRT 7.1398cd)

The failure of even the slightest undertaking is seen to result from discord among ministers, just as when two farmers pull at a rope in the month of Vaiśākha by taking turns. Even for a king who has overcome his enemies, if he possesses complete power, yet acts alone... [the undertaking fails].

Even though he is an enemy deprived of all his limbs, he will still diminish your kingdom and your lifespan. Go wherever that enemy is; once you have conquered the earth, you who seek dominion will soon regain your victory.
Even when fate is adverse, fame is attained through the renown of kings who, surrounded by thousands of heroes, fall in battle; [a fame] where severed necks dance as lofty actors,
where the bowstrings resound like lutes, and where the flames from the mouths of Śiva’s emerging fire-sprouts serve as budding lamps.

Blessed are certain [kṣatriyas] who, having attained the hero’s bed, lie down with their bodies praised for being cleared of the fever of pride, and whose affectionate blessings have been made fruitful. Like gamblers reflecting on the final roll of the dice, these kṣatriyas, playing for their kingdom, embrace the state of being devoid of fear.
Having set aside even that which was consecrated by mantra,
they addressed him with harsh words suited to the occasion after sighing:
"In this crisis, you are capable of casting off your life along with your pride."
"Otherwise, you will incur something improper and harmful that you have not intended. He said to them: "I am not able to kill myself;
therefore, you yourselves must strike me with poison when I have approached [the edge]."
With tears in their eyes and lamenting, they spoke again to the Lord these words, which were like the feeble utterance of a coward overcome by impotence:
"If we, who are struck down by fate, lack the power to provide a remedy for ourselves..."
On the contrary, how could taxes be levied for such a purpose?
That king surely nourished those who were cattle in human form;
for those who fell into such wretchedness were dug up by him with great difficulty.

Even after living through the end of an eon, the body is inevitably subject to destruction; fie on the wretchedness of those who live as dependents, for whom liberation is achieved merely by abandoning it! Even women enter the fire, yet one might fall into forgetfulness by merely meditating upon that [body].
Even among men, who else is more base than he who lacks affection for his master?
This earth— though it possesses sacred pilgrimage sites— is not purified by those who, like actors, display no change of emotion such as grief, fear, or dejection toward their master.

Whose son is emaciated by hunger, whose daughter-in-law is dejected as a servant in another's house, whose friend is impoverished, whose cow bellows piteously for lack of fodder, whose parents are near death due to lack of nourishment, and whose master has been defeated by an enemy—he shall experience no further unpleasantness in hell. Then that king spoke again to those human beasts: [The verse continues: "O you who have seen your son emaciated by hunger, your daughter-in-law languishing as a servant in another's home, your friend ruined, your cow lowing in distress for want of food, your parents on the verge of death from lack of sustenance, and your master vanquished by an enemy—for such a person, there remains nothing more painful to endure in the depths of hell. Then that king spoke once more to those human beasts: [KRT_7_1415ab]

Though performing noble deeds, he was as if deluded by spirits entering him. "In this final period, I know that this vast kingdom which I have enjoyed will not be enjoyed by another in such a manner, due to my extensive desire."
"Yama and Kubera stand at the tips of the lips of kings"—
in this Kali age, fame has become my sole refuge in this regard.
When destiny has arrived— the path by which Rudra, Upendra, Mahendra, and the other gods have departed— what cause for grief is there for a mortal? Yet,
I grieve because this earth, having become like a virtuous wife, [is now widowed].

Like a low-born servant-girl, she has been brought under the power of force due to my own fault. From this point forward, whoever— knowing that this kingdom has lost its luster and can be accomplished by mere intrigue alone— shall harbor hope for it, [will meet his end].
When something extraordinary is undertaken, if it is seen to be devoid of fruit,
those of little strength who have attained their rise will surely mock it out of pride;
for people generally begin an undertaking only after observing a flash of success.

One is not censured by those who calculate what is inconsistent. When the churning was completed, why did some blame even Mount Mandara—the support for the sun at the end of the fortnights and the eye of the ocean—for its death in the milk, by examining it as a cause of failure? (7.1422cd–1423)
Although he was well-versed in the compositions of the scriptures, his very essence was [filled with] the splendor of Śrī;
yet, that which he displayed for the sake of the people's livelihood resulted in the establishment of his own dullness.
Even when performing a noble deed, Uccala acted with a mind as lofty as the tip of his hand.
They will display their darkened teeth and mock me;
therefore, neither out of contempt nor out of fear,
I now desire such a death as this, even though I am currently distressed by my inability to defend myself.
If he were not slain by his own [actions], who else could take away the earth from him?
It is for this reason that I desire to protect the fame I have acquired.
In former times, King Muktāpīḍa, having blazed at the heads of all kings...
Having found a vulnerability, his enemies forced him into a state of wretched supplication.

For he, with his army hemmed in by various routes in the northern region, found his path blocked by those with limited followers who were well-concealed; thus, on that difficult road, he was obstructed in his stronghold.

King Śalya made a vow to his kinsman, who was helpless due to the lack of harmony among the assembly, that he would provide him with eight hundred thousand horses. His mind became despondent from reflecting on the failure of the means beginning with conciliation.

He questioned the chief minister regarding the matter called Bhavasvāmin. After reflecting upon that calamity as incurable and having determined its inevitability through legal reasoning, he replied to him concerning what must be done.

When a task has been addressed with skillful means and a response given by those who pride themselves on their reputation, the eloquence of such people becomes utterly devoid of composure, for their hearts have been shaken by greed. One who knows what must be done must perform that duty, guarding the fame they have already attained.
The acquisition of universal sovereignty is merely a secondary consequence of your activity.
Even when reduced to mere ashes through the dissolution of the body,
a living being is inferred by its fame, just as camphor is known by its fragrance even after it has vanished.

The abode of life for two who are at peace is a marvel among marvels: the side-long glance of a woman for the bodiless Love, and the tongue of a devotee for the illustrious one. Indeed, the preservation of one's reputation is a creature’s endurance unto the end of an eon.
The entire collection of atoms of his body of fame remains intact. Wise men, being attentive toward his adversaries, should contemplate the course of fate—
that which daily exerts itself to destroy their rising wealth and status.

The Creator, addicted to the vice of violent destruction, brings about such humiliation through the falling of the elephant’s trunk upon the lotus cluster— born from his own source and belonging to the noble family of the lotus— even though its sovereign, the sun, has already set and is devoid of purity. Those who fall by the Creator's violent decree find their intellect brought down to infamy.
They neglect [their duty] to protect; what indeed has been protected by them?

(KRT 7.1440cd) Birth on the mountain [of royalty], by virtue of its dependence on a noble lineage, kindles this fame and prestige—yet who here are but mere *vetra* sprouts, having abandoned their own bodies?

Alas, those who know how to protect themselves have been made to undergo the humiliation of coming and going at the gate of the king, driven there by the gatekeepers acting under the command of an angry sovereign. (KRT 7.1441ab–cd)
"O King, having understood that these desired enjoyments are mostly devoid of liberation,
you should now exert yourself for the sake of stability, excellence, and protection."

"Let the sudden onset of this disease known as *daṇḍakālasaka*, which acts so swiftly, be disclosed today under the pretext of some other matter. Tomorrow I shall speak of the remedy capable of neutralizing its calamity. (KRT 7.1443–1444ab)
Having spoken thus, that great minister departed from his own house and went to Daṇḍakālasaka. Then, bearing a staff under the pretext of being an attendant,
he wailed like one distraught, rolling on the ground with motionless eyes.

"By means of treatments such as fomentation, massage, oleation, and emetics, [the physician] rendered him free from looseness and pain; therefore, people said of him, 'He is about to die. Then, by one who announced the certainty of her husband's death,"
The minister, demonstrating his gratitude by entering the fire,
praised the king from within even as he stood before him, refusing to mention the remainder of his duties out of courtesy,
and having spoken harsh words with a clever artifice.
Saying, "I am unable to endure such intense agony," the proud king, lacking any other recourse, then cast off his body;
thus that high-minded man, disregarding his life-breaths, attained another form.

A staircase has been constructed for ascending upwards, not merely for the sake of self-praise. Thus, the remedy for those who are brought low by fate and remain unrecognized is reached by wise men through their own intellect or the counsel of ministers.

Having spoken thus, the son of Bhoja ceased speaking for the sake of preserving the seed of his lineage; "Let Koṭa be released," he said to his ministers. Then, as that prince had departed at the conclusion of the auspicious rites for his journey—
Deluded by the commander-in-chief, he turned back once more.
That wisdom, that undertaking of daring, and that steadfastness in adversity—
all were lost at once for him when the time of destruction had arrived.

Fortune is his lightning-streak, fame his crane, valor his thunder, and majesty the rainbow following the cloud of his destiny. At this time of fortune, by virtue of his wisdom, heroism, and other qualities, it is conceivable that no one could have prevented this sole king from having once made an assault upon Indra himself. (Kṛt 7.1455–1456ab)
Thinking, "How indeed can he proceed on the earth when his footsteps have been blocked by that [enemy], as if he were a cripple, a fool, or a blind man due to the rise of misfortune?"—
the army was dispatched by the king to oppose the adversary;
yet even while remaining in the city, it plundered the wealth of the exile.

All the king’s servants took refuge with the heirs; those who were in the house of the deceased did so merely by means of their bodies. Only two or three, intent on depending on others, did not form even a mental resolve [to stay].
Or what is the use of those praises for those who, like women, did not long retain their lives? There was a certain dancer in the lineage of the *kāṇḍaśrāvatī* dancers,
who adopted as her daughter a girl born somewhere else named Jayamati.
Having become a young woman who had taken a maiden’s vow,
yet possessed of restless passion, you were detained by one greedy for wealth and wedded to the lord of the Maṇḍala.
When he was slain, at that very moment, you became overwhelmed by shame and fled in haste.

By that very stroke of fate, she shall become the principal queen (*paṭṭadevī*). [Tilaka] The royal servants, their fear dispelled even at the sight of the king, formed a row for the discussion and took refuge in the exalted one. [KRT 7.1463ab–cd]
Honored by all who have received their wages as one who imparts instruction,
he robs the soldiers of their confidence in battle by proclaiming greed and contempt;
having attained a state of diminished prowess, he pierces their vital spots with mocking speech.

At the moment of taking food and other such acts, acting as the agent for the sake of the ritual process, he was exceedingly skilled in proclaiming the greatness of the Lord’s gifts and other virtues during the Kali age. Alone, this warrior brought about the total disintegration of the enemy armies. (A *yugma*).

The son of Vyaḍḍamaṅgala, who was the grandson of Śrīlekhā’s brother, was attacked and killed by the king out of anger toward the Mallas. His maternal uncle’s daughter became the wife of those two Mallas.

She died by setting fire to her own dwelling together with her mother-in-law. A wrestler who is an extreme hypocrite, whose cruelty is concealed by observances such as the vow of silence, acts like Death itself by causing those within his fold to fall into dissension.
At that moment, the daughters of the Śāhis said to the king, "Let this enemy, who desires the kingdom for his son, be executed without fear. KRT_7_1470ab–cd [p.

He himself granted him an immediate entry as he stood before the gate; and for the sake of fulfilling the desire of that man who sought his life, the wrestler went forth. For even though he had been requested by his two sons, who were prepared for a dual kingship, [he did so].
Observing the vows of a sage and not abandoning the king out of regard for his virtuous conduct,
he lived in the palace, having given a dowry to Salhaṇa and others— the half-brothers of the two future kings— to inspire confidence in them.
Then that king, whose death was imminent, became enraged at him who had attained the state of a sage and who had not yet satisfied the sacrificial fire; for he,
while performing the worship of the gods, had been summoned by his enemies.
He set out for battle in that very same attire;
with his sacred thread, his hand marked by a rosary, and his fingers radiant with *darbha* grass,
he bore a mark of ash upon his forehead like another son of Jamadagni.
With the grace of his dark, wet, and white hair hanging down from his head-dress after bathing,
he seemed to bear the waters of Prayāga upon his head at the moment of casting off his body;
wearing a turban, a hero’s cloth-band, and a shield to ward off the heat.

Carrying a staff, he shone with his sword like a traveler on the path to the Sosidhārā holy ford. Some of his servants, who had previously gone out to enjoy pleasures, were now the first to partake even in the enjoyment of immortal women.
The two, Rayyāvaṭṭa and Vijaya, the two twice-born men (dvijas), as well as Paurogava,
Koṣṭhaka, and the warrior named Sajjaka, appeared slain in battle. Furthermore,
the chamberlain (kṣattṛ) named Udayarāja, though wounded, [endured] through the power of his life-force and fortitude.
In that battle, not even a single person among those who had come under his command was deprived of life.
Seeing the entrance completely blocked on all sides by hostile warriors, he,
free from trembling, leaped right onto their heads.
Like a royal swan wandering amidst mossy swords and shields as if they were lotuses, he appeared white with age;
and in an instant, he was seen covered by hundreds of sharp arrows and spikes.
A pre-eminent hero, sleeping on a hero’s bed like a second Bhīṣma—
why did such a man not become an object of pity for the king whose life had ended, he who,
out of derision, cut off the head [of his opponent] while whirling a horse around behind him?
The queen named Kumudalekhā and Mallālā, the beloved of the Malla king,
offered their bodies as oblations into the fires maintained within their homes.
The two wives of the kings Avakalya and Salhaṇaralha likewise [performed the same] while their children were still young.
I praise the peerless Sahajanyā of Malla, who followed Agnisikha into the fire;
all the attendants of the women in his harem, sharing in all his enjoyments, perished in the flames right there.
He stayed on the left bank of the Vitastā, whose waters were heated by the scorching heat of a great house-fire and by the hot tears of grief; he remained there while his mother,
unable to look upon him because her breast milk had increased, [offered him water].
In that other [existence],

while staying within her own inner apartments on that very bank, Nandā— born of an irreproachable lineage— will be the mother of two future kings, together with her daughter named Cāndrī, during the funeral offerings being presented by her nurse.
Having observed the two sons by the smoke of the kitchen fire,
he looked longingly toward the northern and southern peaks of the mountain from his palace and said:
"In just a few days, my sons, let the camp of the enemy— the father who hates us— be destroyed."
The virtuous woman cursed the king, saying, "May the lineage act like that of Jamadagni! Without even sitting down, she consumed herself in the blazing fire within her own home,
surrounded by flames as if by dancing female companions.
But when the king arrived for his execution, Darśanapāla was protected by the remainder of his lifespan through most extraordinary obstacles occurring at every moment; or rather,
he was protected from harm because only one year of his life remained.
For the consumption of the pus of his own sleep and the disease born of it;
having heard of that slaughter of his father on the ninth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada,
the grief of the two sons of the Malla was swallowed up by anger.
Then one day, blazing with the fire of his wrath, Sussala set out from the villages of Āvahnipura toward the field of victory;
then Candrarāja emerged to meet him as he was rushing forward to fight.
He was surrounded by Paṭṭadarśana, Pālā, and others, together with their armies; yet,
though neglected by his own people, he waged a long and difficult struggle there against his enemy who possessed a vast host, even though he himself had but a small force.
In that battle, Akṣoṭamalla and the wrestler Cācari,
both servants of the king, attained the state of sharing in the enjoyments of celestial women.

When the moon-king was slain— embraced by the parasol that shone like a moon amidst the darkness of night— the moon-king’s followers, the celestial women, were also destroyed. When that hero too had been killed, King Harṣa established [his own power] over the earth.
Fate has utterly crushed the root-tuber of the lotus-pond that is hope.
Then, out of fear, Paṭṭa and the others entered the courtyard of Vijayeśa;
once Susssala had entered the region, they bolted the door.
The courtier named Padma was killed outside after fighting;
Lakṣmīdhara, desiring to die, was bound and led away by the Ḍāmaras.
Then Sussala ascended the great palace at the treasury of Vijayeśvara.
He looked down upon them all, who were as agitated with fear as cattle;
that rogue, standing amidst those who had been given [as witnesses], laughed and brought back again two of their own,
the keeper and the overseer of the silken cloths, to his presence.

Because there was no ladder, they were unable to climb; with their hands bound by the followers of Sussala and suspended from ropes, they appeared as if dead. As they were about to depart for a foreign land, they felt ashamed before their own people.
Having given his word, the wise Sussala wiped away their dejection with affectionate speech and the enjoyment of fine meats and other delicacies in their presence.
On that very day, he removed their lethargy and their longing for foreign lands.
Whatever that Sussala accomplished the following day, presided over by some [divine power],
I know that even the memory of it causes the hair on the body of the Creator himself to stand on end.
King Jāsaṭa was the son of the maternal uncle of King Harṣadeva.
And there were other kings, such as Umādhara and others, where three [of them] resided; in that place,
there was no counting at all among the eighteen armies consisting of a multitude of princes, horsemen, ministers, and vassals.
Having forced open the door of those stationed at the courtyard of Vijayeśa, he entered alone, sword in hand and speaking harsh words with a threatening gesture. There,
the patient [hero] made Vijayeśvara his witness.
Having granted a promise of safety to those who had prostrated themselves, he departed.
Then, having ascended the roof of the palace once more, he had all of them— those who had surrendered their weapons and whose hands were bound with ropes— brought into his presence by his servants.

Adorned with a multitude of weapons having hilts of gold and silver, the ground where Sussala stood became like a place strewn with offerings of flowers. Having placed those [enemies] there like cattle among herdsmen, he [levied] taxes upon them.
He remained there for three days to protect the *ḍāmaras*.
Then, having reached the village of Suvarṇasānūra from his bonds,
he sent Paṭṭa and Darśanapāla away toward another region.

Paṭṭa reached Śūrapura with his wife who had come from home; though he was treated with honor, that man of little fortitude forgot his own native land. Even that slight measure of propriety, characterized by an inclination toward one's own country—[he lacked it].
The treacherous [Sussala] was torn asunder by the bond of friendship with Darśanapāla.
Then Sussala, desiring to seize the kingdom through a scramble for priority,
sought to deceive his elder brother by attacking the city.
Between those two, who were of similar disposition and age and always unrestrained,
there existed no seniority or juniority, as they were devoid of formal protocol.
When two or three days had passed, the powerful one, traversing various regions of the earth, [proceeded].
Sussala himself rose up from the very vicinity of the capital.
To burn down Kalasa, the king’s son Bhojadeva— also known by the name Buppā— set out to fight.
Fearing that the princes might become corrupt, as if fearing for his own self,
the father— who was always deprived of his vigor by the power of the destined future—
then rendered him unrestrained, as there was no other recourse.
In which battles did he not stand as the leader of warriors?
If he had been nurtured from the very beginning, being equal to his great-grandfather,
would he not— endowed with such energy— have made the quarters of the world devoid of heirs?
No application whatsoever is lost for one who knows the rules; every weapon is obtained, yet one who knows the specific targets is difficult to find.

That prince became the conqueror of his enemy of unrestrained prowess, just as the *timiṃgila* fish devours the *timitiṅgila*. When the father has met his death, his offspring does not deserve reproach for the state of being a slayer of the dead.
If it is already lime, why discard the oil? Has the fragrance of flowers not been imparted to the oil? (KRT 7.1531cd) Pittha, the son of Deveśvara, received great honor from the king;
yet, though he was promoted, he became wicked by taking refuge with his enemies. (KRT 7.1532ab–cd)
Then, at that time, when King Sussala had set out for battle, his son Milla,
being offered a horse by the king, was looked upon with disdain due to his fatigue; saying, "O King,
you shall know my difference [from others] today," he departed.
The proud man washed away his dejection in battle with the waters from the edge of a sword.
Having said, "O King, my sorrow arose from the total destruction [of my kin]," he departed;
yet because he did not understand what had happened in the interim, it was even greater for that grateful man.

Kings who are perpetually deluded by their riches do not recognize the difference [between them and others], only when they are treated with honor through mere empty words. Having been defeated by Bhoja, Sussala fled from the battlefield.
Having fled from the salt ocean, he made two trips back and forth;
then the Bhoja king, tormented by the intense heat,
returned and repeatedly cast his body upon a couch within the garden together with his father.
Then, from the opposite side of the river, a great clamor arose from the royal palace:
"The son of Malladeva has arrived; let the bridge be cut!
Sussala has seized the kingdom; if you do not come quickly today, [it will be lost]."
He had been thus commanded by that wicked commander-in-chief;
therefore, being swift, he first entered and slew in battle Devanāyaka,
who was devoted to Narendreśvaradeva.

Then, from his position, he set out with a formation of cavalry; the elephant Nagas, accompanied by a vast force of soldiers, emerged at the head of the city commandant. There, the king took up his stand within that preeminent army.
Having emerged from the fire of Sussala’s sacrifice, he did not entertain any suspicion of treachery;
for as long as the son of Malla, possessing only a small force, feared him, so long did he— his helmet of policy removed—
pay him homage.
Not trusting his enemy, though he was dear to him like a lord of the mandala,
he said, "Go to your own home," and that wicked man did so.
The fruit of his treachery was seen in this very birth.
Having begged for alms from no one else in the circle [of the city], he gave up his life.
Then the king reached the riverbank and beheld the *ḍāmaras* at the edge of the bridge,
dark and deformed like trees scorched by a forest fire.

In their midst, the body of Balakṣavārabāṇa shone like the supreme moon of Janaka amidst the darkness, or like Venus in the midst of the night. A great bridge was constructed by the king using boats for his own success.

By the power of destiny, they were finally brought to the success of their enemies. Then, desiring to die, the queens, including the daughters of the Shāhi, took fire and ascended a four-pillared pavilion on the roof of the palace, which had a hundred doors.
The world, having become indifferent, witnessed that foremost of men, together with his kinsmen, making a solemn vow like the Aśvayujī-lāgī rite;
and while victory was yet incomplete, those dear ones were intent on offering oblations into the fire.

Constantly warding [the enemy], the king took up the battle at the front of the bridge. Then, with arrows, Janaka, Candra, and others, led by the foremost, struck the elephant of the royal army which had its armor fastened, as it stood at the head of the bridge.
Pierced in his vital organs by arrows, that elephant, trumpeting and vomiting, turned back and crushed his own army with his feet; thus was it brought to ruin by the elephant,
like by adverse fate.
The army became one from which the riders of the infantry and cavalry were falling away.
Then, having crossed the bridge, the king was turned back by the enemy soldiers;
terrified, he entered the courtyard of the hundred-gated palace together with his horsemen.
He was not seen even in secret, devoid of his noble attire; nor was the seal of his mouth ever perceived, even while he was eating.
His body drenched with sweat from the rays of the sun, which seemed doubled by his fear, his armor and flesh repeatedly slipping as he was tossed about by his own [horses],
he mounted a steed whose hooves were unsettled by the shifting impact of its heels.
Repeatedly pulling back his hand—

which had lost its grip on the reins— in order to restrain [the horse], he brought the clusters of locks of hair hanging down to the edge of his bald head to the vicinity of his ear with his hand, from which the sword had slipped.
Under the guise of his dangling, unadorned ear-creepers swaying to and fro,
he appeared as if his withered cavernous mouth were encircled by a black serpent;
and because he was without betel, his lips were parched, looking like two pieces of lac that had been sucked dry.
Lifting his lips with difficulty, agitated and licking them with his tongue,
he turned his thin and dusty face upward— his pupils fixed on the hands [of those behind him]— and, standing at the rear, gazed longingly at his beloveds with a dejected mind.
Wandering among the women, he was seen by the people in a state of terror;
and as he was warding off those who were intent on setting fire [to the palace] with hand gestures,
he reached the residence of the King of the Mallas, which was situated near the capital.
Having crossed [the river], Janakacandra caused a fire to be set there.
Seeing the blazing fire approaching toward the capital,
Bhoja fled, realizing his kingdom was lost.

Having burst through the gate— which was obscured by the enemy's terrifying spears as if by reeds— he emerged from the courtyard on horseback. Accompanied by five or six cavalrymen, he set his sights upon Lohara.
Having crossed the bridge, he set out toward the monastery of Siṃharāja;
shedding tears as he gazed at the direction from which his son’s sight had vanished,
the king, accompanied by horsemen, wandered outside the houses.

In the meantime, certain queens who desired to die in order to save [him] were struck with stones by his attendants; the couch was thus broken. Not knowing this, the sons of the Shahis fell upon him, thinking he was their enemy.
Then, thinking [this was the time], they kindled a fire at the corners of the quadrangular platform.
Thereupon, the local *ḍāmaras*, with weapons raised,
began slaughtering one another and plundered the treasury and other goods from the blazing palace of the king.
Some there met with death, while others abandoned their calamity;
for some, the attainment of an unseen object became a source of laughter.
One person, saying "This is white sugar," threw down camphor.
Then, with his face scorched, he cast those goods into the river.
Some commoners, desiring to seize gold, burned the garments adorned with gold; others diligently gathered the ashes.
In some places, masses of unpolished pearls have been ground in mortars by rustic women, mistaking them for white rice grains.
Such people dwell in this invisible land, having suffered such humiliation.
Thus mocked, Fortune was not seen anywhere again.
Cruel bandits were seen at every step, carrying away the beautiful wives of kings who were dressed in noble attire like Vidyādharīs.
There, the queens, headed by Vasantalekhā, together with their daughters-in-law—
seventeen in all— cast their remaining bodies into the fire.
And from the burning houses, the crackling sound of *caṭat* was heard.
Causing the sound of the ocean to be perceived as the roar of clouds boiling with intense heat,
the king saw him standing by the side of the Śrīpadmaśrī water-station;
remembering this verse of the Ṛṣis out of grief, he recited it again and again.
The fire of wrath, born from the suffering caused by the oppression of the subjects, does not turn back until it has consumed the king’s lineage, his fortune, and his very life. Then,
having burnt that royal capital, Añcala, accompanied by the Ḍāmaras, departed.

Seeing his enemy’s army still unyielding, he crossed over once more to the further shore. Then, desiring to die after fighting, the king brought about the destruction of his own side through the high and low fluctuations of the infantry's minds from moment to moment.
As he went along, thinking himself to be a prince such as Anaṅgapāla,
he was stopped at every step by the words of the commander-in-chief;
and Caṇṇaka said to him, "Either fight or go to Lohara."
The latter position appeared as the response to the formal argument, but not the former.
[163] Not having learned the news of his son, the king became deeply distressed;
he said to Caṇṇaka, "Go on the track of Bhojadeva."
"O King, by merely following [me] to Prayāga, you will attain perfection in an instant.
Sighing, he said to him, "Therefore, do not abandon even me.
With tears welling within, he replied to him, "You are called one who is free from malice."
Why, then, do you too disregard his words at this very moment?
Without my son, I cannot see the quarters of the sky, even on a day when the sun is shining. You ought not to harbor resentment toward him, who was raised upon your own lap.
On those very days, a quarrel arose on account of a horse between that proud prince and his minister; the minister was then reproached by the lord with words pregnant with insinuation.
With his face bowed down by shame, he followed after the prince.
Together with fifty horsemen, along with his brothers, servants, and others, he crossed to the further shore of the river; including himself, there were five of them.
When his two brothers and the groom had been killed on the road by the son of Śeṣarāja, he wandered about accompanied only by Dhanaka;
not having obtained any news of the prince, he continued to travel along the path.
On the sixth day, he reached the confluence of the Vitastā and the Sindhu.
Thus the king dispatched other trusted men to search for his son;
others as well, seizing that opportunity, moved toward him.

Because of the one who took bribes, the army was made to depart from the royal city and other locations during the conflict; the camp was rendered leaderless by the ministers’ inability to endure their duties. Furthermore, the king caused an obstacle for his son’s departure to Lohara.

The enemy was ushered into the city amidst the clamor of battle for the kingdom; he who had destroyed all his possessions became the very lord of the king, even as the commander-in-chief remained there to restrain him from performing what was appropriate. (Tilaka)
While the king was completely despondent and listening to much deliberation, those of unsteady intellect did not find a firm footing anywhere in what ought to be done;
for just as a flute is filled by everyone through all its holes, it certainly does not reject the sound.
It is said that through such various accumulations of many paths, counsel is fashioned; yet it never attains certainty.
Even a common person, when his fortune is exhausted, exhibits this very sign:
that he would brazenly offer counsel suited to his own heart, even when unasked.
As the charioteer named Trailokya was praising the commander-in-chief while restraining the bridle,
the king, intent on battle, spoke again:
"Your grandfather once conquered with a single division consisting of horsemen."
Therefore, let us go to the vicinity of the edge of the Liberation-chapter with the desire to grasp it;

let us slay those enemies who are gathered together with their armies consisting mostly of foot-soldiers, and then, swooping down upon them like hawks upon birds, we shall strike them down along with them.
Then, as if wishing to move, that royal camp filled the quarters of the sky;
like spectators at a theatrical performance, it gathered with a downpour of rain.
To those who had arrived on the banks of the Vitastā for the sake of provisions for their offspring, [the camp appeared]...
He gave the jeweled necklaces and other ornaments to those born of the Śreya family;
when those royal insignia had been taken away by the gardeners as if in an instant,
the people saw the king— once so exalted by his radiant majesty— as one whose glory had departed.
At every step, as the masses of elephants and other troops were falling away,
he wandered through various places, yet no one feared that his calamity was at hand.
Then, seeking refuge, he wandered through the houses of the ministers in the evening.

And no one granted him entrance as he stood at the gate. Those who are experts in fasting unto death are capable of nothing else in the end; for those pseudo-Brahmins are merely objects of kings' false esteem.
Wandering through the houses of whoever lived in that country out of curiosity,
and desiring to enter their dwellings, he reached the home of the minister named Kapila. While he was staying there at Loharakoṭṭa, he was requested by the minister’s wife to remain.
Deluded by fate, he was unable to enter Koṭṭa even by means of ships.
While he was thus distressed, his sons, who had committed treachery against him like enemies toward a father, [acted].
Like a pauper whose own property has been hidden by creditors,
he realized for himself that "I am at fault" as he heard his own censure;
at that very moment, all his duties had been concealed long ago by wicked ministers.

Having renounced all worldly attachments and placing no trust even in his own kinsmen, he became exceedingly solitary, with only Pradyumna remaining as his follower. Those who proclaimed their birth among the thirty-six clans—

Even those who are radiant and brilliant do not endure being placed in a position higher than themselves. Though they were as hot as fire, the princes, beginning with Anantapāla, did not abandon him; for even when the darkness becomes dense, horses that have been blinded by it continue to move step by step.
Having reached the vicinity of the Vāhanājohila monastery, he alighted;
he was then left there by the commander-in-chief along with his kinsmen.
"This is the residence of our father-in-law; we shall stay here for this night."
Having said, "I shall come to your place once I have seen [him]," he departed under a pretext.
To his younger brother, who was about to depart, the man from Prayāga asked for provisions for the journey;
he gave him some barley meal (*saktu*), but not that [other thing].

Then the king became one whose royal splendor was reduced to a single garment, or rather, one whose life was reduced to its very last breath; he was accompanied by no one except Prayāga. At that moment, he was attended by a cook named Jelaka, who had only a few servants remaining.
Having reached the presence of the king, he was released and attained the status of a trusted confidant.

As they were wandering over ground that was difficult to traverse due to trenches dug by Udayana, a certain woman from within a cave spoke to them: *udīpavihitaiḥ khātair agre duḥsaṃcarā kṣitiḥ |* *bhrāmyatas tān uvāca iti nārī kācid guhāntarāt ||* "The ground ahead is impassable because of the trenches dug by Udayana; as you wander, a certain woman spoke thus from within a cave."
Then, while he was seated on the bank of the Vitastā at Prayāgaka,
he summoned the boatmen to go to the fortress of Jayapura;
for he had previously made an agreement with the soldiers stationed there.
To lead the king to take refuge with his beloved at the palace of Bhīmādeva,
he was addressed by that Bhīmādeva, who had already taken up residence there:
"I shall follow as the king's attendant once he has entered the assembly hall."

The king did not board the boat brought by the sailors; being on the verge of destruction, he was agitated by the fear of their approaching gaze. His lamp of intelligence seemed extinguished by the sight of the serpent held in the hand of Death as he approached.
At the time of destruction, embodied beings quickly turn toward their own pacification. Yet,
even amidst that abundance of malice,
the man of noble character maintained the vow of a virtuous wife, his gaze fixed on no other.

Then that man named Bimba, a follower of Nīlāśva, joined by the Ḍāmaras and their allies, was likewise forgotten by the king as he sought refuge with them. (Yugalaka) Thereupon, the host of clouds began to release its water. (KRT 7.1631–1632ab)
As if to wash away the earth defiled by the touch of treachery—was there anything that did not cause him suffering?
The earth became desolate, the falling rain was shrouded in darkness, his companionship became unbearable, and there was constant fear of enemies. What indeed did he not endure as misery?
Thus, out of regard for the narrative flow: "Fie upon those who perform evil deeds!
Even that name which should not be remembered shall now be clearly proclaimed.

“I am born alone, without provisions for the journey, rolling about and subsisting on alms, O lady!”—contemplating each of these points one by one, he perceived no end to his suffering; for even in conversation, he found no one like himself who had not fallen into despondency and was grieving. Since he did not utter even a single word against his enemy, even when reporting unpleasant news,

He grieved for his son, thinking of the restraints he had imposed upon him in his youth for the sake of political discipline.

Beholding pearl necklaces upon his son’s limbs and upon his chest, which was broad with youth, he became distraught with mental constructions regarding himself, while pronouncing blessings: "The boy must be protected; the old man is already as good as dead. Thus [he spoke] regarding his own life.
Thinking, "I shall protect [him] lest he be disgraced by improper conduct," he,

Having fulfilled his purpose, he who had dispelled sorrow from his mind did not form even a mental resolve to go to the Lord’s monastery at Prayāga during the night. She,

"Who else would be able to contemplate this entire universe, wondering how it could possibly endure after being deprived of me?

This secret discourse, fit only for the guest of a very small heart, is like the nectar of the ocean; it is extremely difficult for those of little fortitude to digest. There was a Brahmin living in the forest named Manoratha, who was a member of a noble lineage.

He learned that story from that well-behaved ascetic. Having said, "Let us show ourselves as heirs to the king so that we may become vessels of prosperity," that base ascetic was led away by him with treacherous intent.
He was born as a servant by some low-born man of contemptible status;

however,

Mounted upon the shoulders of a dog-cooker (*śvapāka*) and having suffered various humiliations,

Harṣadeva, however, tormented by hunger and repeatedly entreated through [magical] means, [was released].

"Though skilled in martial exercises on the ground, he did not slay him with a sword-stroke;

Even that universal monarch met such a death within his own palace.
No other king in this age was seen to possess such prosperity as he;

Or rather, by that single act of turning away from battle, his majesty—

Or perhaps his only fault was his inclination toward a forced interpretation [of the situation].

Like King Duryodhana, desiring the destruction of his own lineage, he brought about the ruin of his family through the configuration of his birth. For him, Mars and Saturn were present, as were Jupiter, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, and the Moon.

As the head of that lord of the earth was being severed, the earth, together with its oceans, trembled; though cloudless, the sky released a great rain.

By that curse, he became subject to fierce and long-lasting calamities.

"Alas! What a tragedy—that such a universal monarch should be treated like a common thief!"
Without the king’s command, the funeral rites for his body were not performed.
Abandoned by his servants and with his lineage destroyed, he was reduced to ashes by a certain man named Gauraka, a wood-gatherer,
like a naked beggar.

This long account of King Harṣa is something truly wondrous; it is certainly in the style of either the Rāmāyaṇa or the Mahābhārata. Prosperities are as flickering as lightning from the clouds of fortune, and that state of being forcibly exalted is bitter at its conclusion.

Even there, alas, this pride in the experience of power does not find peace for those whose hearts are struck by delusion. (KRT 7.1729cd) Even with such a retinue of harem women, not a single one cried out; even among his followers, no one followed him, nor did anyone remain at the sacred ford.

Nothing exists at the beginning, and that which is certain does not exist at the end; in the middle, a certain being suddenly brings about a state of well-being. Prosperity, having brought splendor to the Sātavāhana dynasty and established itself in the lineage of Kāntirāja, now abandons its standing in the family of Udayarāja.
Leaving behind the peak of the Himālaya, which is devoid of snow, she [the river] rests upon its divine bank like the splendor of day upon the celestial mountain.

Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Rājatarangiṇī*, the composition of the poet Kalhaṇa, son of the great minister Caṇpaka of Kaśmīra. For some time, the new king remained with his anger concealed and his favor manifest, like the ocean before its churning, when neither poison nor nectar has yet been revealed. His brother and a host of turbulent men became exceedingly intoxicated with power.

Like the onset of wind and rain before a cloud, they were both captivating and obstructive. Whatever misdeeds that brother, intoxicated by youth, might have committed, they brought hardship upon the king who was otherwise full of affection.
Indeed, as he wandered about mounted upon his elephant with sword unsheathed, that slayer of enemies made the earth—its essence extracted and its moisture drunk up—like the sun.

"Let the *ḍāmaras* be provoked against him because they cannot endure his equal zeal; or rather, let this man of pure intent become their dwelling place due to the excessive honors he receives. Having reflected thus, he proclaimed his desire to give [the kingdom] to him at the gateway.
Just as Bhīma, Deva, and all the others underwent transformation,
so too did their envy reach its full intensity.
Then the servants, relying on one another and eager for battle, made a wager. Desirous of witnessing their mutual combat on the back of the causeway, the king,

Then his followers, as if by force, dragged the king with their two arms and entered the door of the pavilion, which they bolted shut. Janaka, Candra, and the others, out of great respect for Bhīma, even laid down their weapons.

There, in that tumultuous fray, Bhīmādevānu pierced the body of Janakacandra with a sharp blade; Arjuna, the son of Kālapāśa, was fierce.
Perceiving his own injury and knowing that treachery had been employed by the king,
he struck out with kicks at the gate of the royal palace out of anger. While those [kicks] remained unbroken, he fled in terror into the interior of the bath-house.
Bhīmādeva, wielding a drawn sword, rushed forward with the intent to kill.
Seeing this, the householder of that residence, who was concealed by a pillar,
split the belly of Janakacandra in two with his blade.
When he was slain, his two younger brothers, Garga and Śaṅkha, rushed forward;
he, however, rendered them unconscious and wounded with his sword.
Just as a thunderbolt, having shattered a tree, does not remain there for long, [so did he pass away].
And that man of vigorous action, having slain his exceedingly haughty enemy,
was himself killed in that year of Dvibhadra, immediately after the joyous conclusion of the festival,
by no more and no less than three fortnights.

Because he committed an injury against his benefactor and his master, that sin of his quickly went to destruction due to his extreme agitation. While [the king] manifested feigned anger and grief within a heart filled with genuine joy, KRT_8_0036ab–cd; KRT_8_0037ab.

King Bhīma fled, while Gagga took heart upon the king’s departure. When Gagga was dispatched to Lohara to heal his own wound, the other *ḍāmara* chieftains, terrified by him, were driven from their own lands.

Having obtained the kingdom— which had been abandoned by the bandits through their own stratagems— King Uccala thus gradually regained his firm footing. Then, having secured his stability, he, desiring victory, [proceeded] in just a few days.

The Ḍāmaras were deprived of their successive kingdoms, horses, armies, and so forth. Then, having set out for the kingdom of Maḍava, he bound the Ḍāmaras led by Kāliya— who had previously done him harm— and executed them on stakes.
Illārāja, who had gradually conquered the earth with his forces,
was in turn slain by a sudden assault within the city itself by that powerful [king],
either due to the latent impressions of affection from a previous birth or because of [the king's] insight into his inner nature.
His affection for Garga increased like that for a son; the king,
who was so fond of his subjects that he could not endure even the mere mention of thorns,
never once grew angry with Garga, even when he had committed an offense.
When King Bhīmādeva, intent on beginning his reign, had spoken these two auspicious instructions, the wise one remembered them as if they were a mantra.
Having gone out from the palace early in the morning for the sake of worldly affairs according to the first [instruction], he...

He moved about the outer precincts until the end of the day, directing his attention toward the outside; by his habit of rising at other times and even hearing the name of an enemy at midnight, he brought an end to disturbances through his expeditions.
Even for that high-minded king, whose fortitude remained unshaken in the midst of other monarchs,
his conduct was never stained by the wretchedness of supplication;
for today, by immersing himself in the waters of the Ganges in the form of his ever-ascending noble conduct, [he has purified himself].
The sin arising from the proclamation of a false king shall be removed by his voice; by him,
whose limbs are not yet fully developed, the masses of darkness that destroy sight will for the most part be warded off, just as by Anūru (the Sun), who likewise dispels the accumulations of gloom.
When those who had sat down in a fast unto death were about to pass away by virtue of their vow to renounce the body,
he did not have the overseers of dharma investigate the matter.
Hearing that piteous cry of distress from the one who had done him harm,
even his own self became ungraspable to that great-souled one. Or rather, it was because of the fault of the litigant that the cry of distress arose.

When he became enraged, that [calamity] was quelled by the wailing of his own kinsmen. While that king was intent on showing favor to the weak, the strong remained as mere residents, whereas the weak held positions of authority.
Wandering alone on horseback, he was addressed by people who did not recognize him as "O King.
Whatever fault of his own he heard mentioned, he would immediately abandon it.
By whatever means possible, the king reached [his destination].
His sight was never in vain; he was like a wish-fulfilling tree to those who sought his aid.
Showering nectar through the gifts of his affectionate speech, he was beloved by the people; even in his private chambers, he could not bear to dismiss his attendants.

By those who performed his service with praiseworthy efforts at every moment, he was seen even three or four times during the nights. Being served with constant courtesy, he bestows fruit in an instant.

Whose [sorrows] did he not uproot like a tree planted by magicians? Having heard the distress of the inhabitants, he— having abandoned all other activities— performed the warding off of the Daityas for them, just as a father does for his sons.
By selling his own stored rice for a small price, that one who is compassionate toward his people destroyed the very onset of famine. And,
moist with pity, he even restrained the thieves from their practice of robbery.
Appointing treasury officials, he ensured their livelihoods were beyond reproach.
Constantly occupied with anxiety, he would investigate one by one through spies, asking: "Who in this realm deserves a share of wealth? Whose misfortunes ought to be dispelled?"
Even that single great virtue of his, known as disinterestedness toward wealth,

became further developed when it was joined with those various other virtues of the king. Punishing those deserving of punishment for the sake of maintaining order, he took no wealth out of fear of being embraced by sin.

He did not withhold good deeds from them, but rather caused them to perform those acts for the sake of purification. If his faith in giving reached its fullness by bestowing a single object upon a petitioner for what was at hand, it would reach its peak by bestowing a thousand such objects.
Just as the petitioner was heard saying to me, "Give! Give the cow!", so too the donor was heard saying to him, "Give! Give!
[But] that [gift] was uttered in a low tone, given at an improper time, its number exhausted, and offered without respect.

The half [of the kingdom] led away by leaders, envoys, and others was not seen as being given by him. At festivals, in humble petitions, in efforts to please, and in the accomplishment of tasks, he did not yield the fruit of his favor, like a tree depicted in a painting.
On festivals such as Śivarātri and others, he drenched the people with wealth,
just as Mahendra drenches the earth with floods of water during the planetary conjunctions.
He was likewise addicted to the distribution of betel and possessed a supreme passion for festivals.
Even for King Gharṣa, there was not such [generosity] as that which belonged to him;
even when nothing remained but a mere clod of earth, once he had attained the rank of king,
he bestowed gifts and honors upon others that would have been difficult even for Kubera to perform.
Even though he was a Kashmiri, he did not acquire wealth through the constant sale of horses, the casting of images, or the burning of incense; rather,
on every journey, he [attained it] through yoga and the placement of the vital breaths (prāṇa).
He became one who knew how to accomplish every task, like the inner self (*antarātman*) within embodied beings. O brahmins, those afflicted by disease received royal luxuries from him as medicine;
and those lacking a livelihood received wages from him.
To pacify ill omens such as an eclipse of the moon (pitryoparāga) or the appearance of a comet (ketu),
he honored the twice-born with gifts consisting of thousands of cows, horses, gold, and other riches.
The entire city in the region of Nandī was consumed by a fire of portents.

By him, a new kingdom was established with qualities exceeding those of the past. That man of virtuous deeds, devoted to the restoration of what was decayed, performed the consecration of the shrines of Śrī Cakradhara, Yogeśa, and Svayaṃbhū.
That new king established in Parihāsapura the Śrīparīhāsakeśava image which had been brought there by Harṣadeva.
Adorned with the previously described rows of parrots by Harṣanīti,
that king, free from greed, [ruled] as the lord of the three worlds. By him,
the wealth seized from Jayāpīḍa was consumed by fire during the uprooting of Harṣa.
That king established a new lion-throne, the preeminent symbol of sovereignty;
and having obtained the exceedingly rare privilege of sharing half of it with her husband out of love,
Jayamati’s status as queen was not diminished, even though she was of common birth.

For she was distinguished by her auspicious qualities—both those pertaining to the future and those pertaining to the past—such as benevolence, sweetness, generosity, truthfulness, amiability, and policy; and by her preeminent protection of the distressed and the helpless.
Having won the favor of the kings, she did not seek wealth from the subjects through anger.
Even those women who were charming with beauty were like female demons for the purpose of breaking [his resolve].
This was another quality of that king who cherished his subjects— a quality that stood at the head of all virtues—
and it belonged to that lord of lofty fortune who was characterized by a lack of desire for wealth.

Desirous of killing, evil-minded, and intent on seizing the property of others— those known as the *rakṣas* (demons)— from them he must always protect these subjects by means of the policy based on traditional history (*itihāsa*), with full conviction.
By him who recited this verse, the uprooting of the scribe was accomplished. Indeed,
other than those [causes], it is the diseases of the subjects— those swift-acting officials— who strike down the entire world through cholera, colic, and forced abandonment.

attained the state of a favorite to the earth-lord after her marriage was performed.
When King Saṃgrāmapāla had died at that time,
his son, named Somapāla, assumed his father’s kingdom.
Having imprisoned his elder brother, who was worthy of the throne, he was consecrated by the Ākrikas.
Thus King Aśvapati became enraged toward the royal city;
he took the hand of his daughter, who was the surety for the stability of his fortune. [He gave her] to the son of the king of Kāśī, who was like a second Indra.

As that wish-fulfilling gem of a king delighted all his subjects, that final great festival shone with various expenditures. When the son-in-law had departed, the circle of kings appointed officials over the entire administration.

Becoming somewhat enraged at those who were intent on destruction, he dispatched the *dudhrukṣūs*. At that time, Bhogasena, having been forbidden from entering Dvārakā by the king who was filled with wrath, became full of enmity.
For he was valiant, established in his duty, and had conquered all the *ḍāmaras*;
he set out from the city of Lohara to conquer King Sussala,
though he was restrained by the king with a mixture of affection and enmity.
He spoke ill of him and, having approached, became enraged at that;
causing those with mouths like *raḍḍacchuḍḍ* to enter another time,
he [spoke] of that hero, his former friend, who had then been insulted by the king.
Though they were humiliated, possessed of vast desires, united, and their livelihoods destroyed—
yet they were not cast out by him who sought to conquer the realm of Yama. To them, whose true nature was entrusted to Bhogasena, he, being of crooked intent—
Knowing his inner sincerity, Śaḍḍha did not reproach him for his heroism; rather, he said:
"Even at the cost of our lives this very day, let the king be slain, otherwise Bhogasena, whose intentions are inscrutable, will cause a rift."

What Bhogasena said was not true; desiring to cause a rift, he told the king, "I have something to say in private. But the king, saying, "What will you say? I shall not grant you an audience," refused him.
Disregarding him, he treated with contempt that which sought the friendship of the *dudhrukṣu* birds;
for one who is devoted to destiny hates those who provide awakening,
just as a creature whose memory has vanished at the end of sleep on a summer day hates the heat of the sun.
Having become night-watchmen of the state, they then entered during their own turn; united with their own troops clad in armor, they gathered at the capital and declared,
"Whomever we kill in this night, him you shall kill!"

They caused the Caṇḍālas, who bore their identifying marks, to enter the interior of the pavilion. While the King remained seated after his meal, those standing in the outer pavilion spoke thus and, with great anger, carried out the dismissal of the attendants.

And the king, desiring to go to Vijjalā’s dwelling, emerged from within the pavilion, illuminated by lamps and languid with passion. When he had reached the middle pavilion with his few attendants, [he entered].
The Śūdra, having blocked that abandoned pavilion, obstructed the other people. When the gateway was also blocked by others, all of them,
desiring to kill, rose up and surrounded the king.
As he sat before him, obstructed by a single man who was a mere pretender of learning,
that twice-born man— whose splendor had been snatched away— pierced him with a blade.
Then his sword-blades, golden-hued like the limbs of that [beast], entered into her many times, as if entering the peaks of Mount Sumeru;
he, crying out "Treachery! Treachery! while releasing the hair he had been pulling.
Sujanākara, a servant carrying a *kaṭṭāraka* (cleaver), bit with his teeth the clenched fist of Krīḍāśatru as he struck at him while his enemies were attacking. He then fled from his presence.

Therefore, he drew that small dagger suited for a child; it emerged from its scabbard with difficulty, as it was gripped by his fist. With his intestines protruding and his hair disheveled by his enemies, he seized him.
Then, thrusting that dagger between his two knees, Dhammilla roared and struck;
though he possessed such valor,
he became like one whose vital organs have been pierced, falling to the ground.
Then, as Raḍḍa struck him from behind, he roared like a lion; turning back, he tore Vyaḍḍa apart. He also felled another armed man, who was clad in armor.

While writhing, he was soon deprived of his life-breaths. When he had found an opening and was running toward his exile, the pavilion— failing to realize that this was the king— was bolted shut by the guards.

As he was advancing toward another door, he was struck by sword-strokes from Chuḍḍa, who, blocking his path while shouting, "Where are you going?", had his way obstructed. Then he saw Bhogasena standing at the edge of the gateway.
To him who was speaking thus— "Why do you look on with indifference at this man who, with his back turned, is scratching the wall with a wooden stick?"—
he, clearly embarrassed, spoke to him as he ran away.

Rayyāvaṭṭa, the island-dweller, standing there unarmed, engaged in battle with a torch as his weapon; wounded by them, he fell. Cāmpeya, the prince named Somapāla, having struck down his enemies, [fell].
Though reduced to a state of distress by the blows, he did not fall into ignoble conduct. The grandson of Śrī Śūrapāla, Ajñaka, a scion of royalty,
fled like a dog, concealing his sword as if it were the twitching of a tail.
Then, rushing forward and desiring to mount Pragrīva, the lord of the earth had his knees severed by the Caṇḍālas and embraced the earth. Wrecked by their blows,
he cast his own body upon its back.

The scribe named Śṛṅgāra, who was free from malice, was restrained by his enemies. As he desired to rise up again, all the enemy’s rows of weapons were transformed by Kālī into a garland of choice blue lotuses.
At times, he remained like one who had perished, though he was unharmed;
with his neck hanging down, he himself cut off his own head, saying,
"I am he by whom the theft of the foot was committed."

Having cut off his fingers, he even dragged away the row of rings marked with jewels. Standing on one foot, with his hair— adorned with garlands— falling from his slipper, his face covered, that long-armed man was seen sleeping upon the ground.
At the conclusion of his heroic conduct, which was fully sufficient for that man of great majesty, his sword attained a state of flawlessness toward people. Then,
a servant named Śūraṭa cried out loudly, "I am an enemy!"

Having gone out, he was struck down outside by Bhogasena in a fit of rage. As the lord of the earth set out for his beloved’s dwelling, as if under the influence of a loss of direction, Kālī seized him at her abode on the path.

In the garden of sovereignty, the bees that are kings—restless for the filaments of enjoyment and delighting their minds with rows of flowers that are various garments—are suddenly seen and lost, as if struck down by the creeper of destiny, tossed by the wind of fate; alas, what a tragedy! (Kṛt 8.334) The Lord of Laṅkā, who had humiliated the inhabitants of the three worlds, suffered defeat at the hands of mere animals; and the Kuru king, the best among all monarchs, received a kick on his head. (Kṛt 8.335)

Thus, at the end, everyone suffers the humiliation of their hearts being filled with great respect for him; thinking, "Who indeed could be as great as I?", he maintains his egoism. Seeing that lord—who had been honored by those who possessed the highest life-force—now abandoned like one who is helpless, naked, and delivered to the flames, they looked on with eyes that were clear yet grasping.
One seized his arms at the neck, while the other grasped his feet with both hands;
he was bent at the neck, with disheveled locks of hair and drenched in blood.
They dragged the king, who was like a helpless man with a wound hissing with pain,
out from the capital and laid him down in the ancestral grove on a plot of land that had become an island at the confluence of the waters of the great river Vitastā.
Terrified of him, they quickly performed the ritual of cremation for him;
yet he was seen by no one as being slain or even consumed by fire. Having flown away as it were, he swiftly departed beyond the range of sight.
When his lifespan of forty-one years had passed,
he departed from this world on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa in the year eighty-seven.
Then Raḍḍa, adorned with blood, composed verses in the Sāsika meter.
Like a *vetāla* upon a funeral-pyre stone, he placed his foot upon the throne;
[that act] did not shine for those ancient ones who were firmly rooted.
As he was descending from his throne to fight in the battle,
his kinsmen and servants, displaying their prowess, adorned the battlefield.
Having fought for a long time, two of his kinsmen named Vaṭṭa and Paṭṭa perished.

And warriors such as Kaṭṭasūrya and others fell, slain at the lion-gate. Like a dancer performing on the stage of battle within the courtyard of the royal palace, Raḍḍa shone as he brandished his sword and shield, cutting down his enemies.

In every moment, dispelling the doubt regarding victory over his enemies, he struck many blows and fell in battle after a long time. Even though he was slain, he received a punishment appropriate for one who had committed treason against the king.

Garga, having abandoned all bounds of decency in his fury, caused a massacre. Near the Diddā-maṭha, Vyaḍḍa was struck down by the citizens, who rained down ashes and stones; with his face submerged within a drain for refuse, he was cast away.

Dragged by their ankle-ropes here and there, those traitors against their lord at that very moment received the contemptuous jeers of the people, a fitting honor for their deeds. Haṃsaratha and the others fled and went away somewhere, accompanied by their followers.
Bhogasena,
seeing Garga defeated and knowing his younger brother had perished,
heard that news which was like a cosmic dissolution, as he resolved to endure for a short time the agony of calamity that exceeded even death.
Turning back, desiring to counter-attack while seeing his soldiers fleeing, he went elsewhere with a few of his own men out of fear. Thus was that host of traitors, their leaders slain and scattered.
She was accomplished by Garga-candra, who had nothing but his own arm as a companion.
I have never heard in any of the Itihāsas of such courage and success in daring as that which belonged to this powerful man.

Having ruled for one watch of the night and one watch of the day, he attained the state known as King Śaṅkha, which is the destination of evildoers. Birth in the family of Yaśaskara was thus proven by those traitors.

For one who does not abandon a kingdom subject to momentary destruction, it comes to an end like that of Varṇaka-deva. (KRT 8.0357cd) In the forest, hunters who slaughter lions and other beasts by means of forest fires, incendiary devices, and mechanical traps, meet their end through the sudden falling of boulders. (KRT 8.0358ab) Indeed, every person runs along the single path of death; yet, alas, I am struck down while this other man, grasping at distinctions, thinks his time is measured. (KRT 8.0358cd)

Those joyous men by whom the auspicious sounds of the throngs of women at their own wedding were heard, hear at that very moment the rising lamentation of their beloveds when they have become wretched.
Even one who kills an enemy rejoices; another, seeing his own kinsman killed, exults in the end. Alas, fie upon this delusion, which proclaims blindness!
What was contemplated in the evening bears fruit at night, or on another day.

That tree of violence was one that yielded a bitter fruit for his enemies. Then, at the conclusion of the business within the lion-throne, having laid aside his physical form and washed away his resentment, Garga lamented for his master for a long time.

While he was weeping, the entire body of citizens, casting aside their fear and finding the opportunity, lamented before the king who is so compassionate toward the world. Desiring life for themselves, they offered up their treasuries in order to arouse his compassion.
Then Jayamati, who was of deceitful character, said this:
"Make a compact with me; let him be one composed of pure essence."
Having understood that discourse on their nature, he perceived the consciousness [of women] to be inconceivable:

The curliness found in the mass of their hair, the extreme flickeringness of their eyes, and likewise the hardness of their jar-like breasts—these very qualities reside within their hearts as a single mass; thus, these women are recognized by no one as being "deep-hearted."

Even while practicing immorality and even while causing the death of their beloveds, they enter the fire with ease; there is no trust whatsoever in women. While she was traveling mounted upon a carriage, she lingered for a moment on the road.

Then Bijjalā, having gone out from before [the king], entered the funeral pyre. As she was ascending the pyre, while she was being plundered by robbers seeking her ornaments, a spreading exhaustion manifested over her limbs.
Beholding the king being cremated with his parasol and fly-whisks,
the entire world cried out in lamentation, as if it were a rain of burning embers.
And by that act, he then brought propriety to its ultimate purity.

Although he was sought by all, he did not sit upon the royal throne. Some of those [princes] wished to diligently seek out the son of Uccaladeva, a mere child, in order to place him on his lap and consecrate him in the kingdom.
Today, when the world beholds the true nature of certain things, it smiles;
I know that it does not at all recognize its own fitness even for wandering about to beg for alms.
Those sons of the wrestler-king who were born of the queen named Śvetā—
When the middle one had previously perished, there remained three, Salhaṇa and the others;
[then] the two remaining ones, Salhaṇa and Loṭhana, sought to kill the elder and the youngest brothers. Searched for by King Śaṅkha, they fled out of fear to the Navamaṭha monastery.
Having abandoned the treacherous enemies who had been slain by the shameless [rebels], he was brought back by the ministers, who were charioteers and horsemen, acting as spies. Then,
seeing that neither of those two [sons] was worthy of the kingdom, he looked for someone else of senior status.

Out of impetuosity, Garga consecrated Salhaṇa in the kingdom. Alas, what a pity! Within the span of four watches of the night, there were three kings; yet during those three watches, the one who was visible for the duration of a man's life was a woman.
Those royal servants who had attended upon the king in the evening to escort him away reached Salhaṇa at midday when they were seen. Then,
while staying at Loharakaṭṭa, half a day passed for the king.
Upon hearing of his brother’s death, Sussala’s mind was utterly distraught. A messenger sent by Garga arrived, wailing and throwing himself upon the ground;
he then brought relief to the king, who had been lamenting in distress, removing all his doubt.

From the beginning up to the account of Salhaṇa, he heard no story at all; from the messenger Garga, he heard only of his brother’s slaughter and his own summons. Disbelieving that difficult and swift severance of the enemy, he [acted].
Garga, whom he had dispatched from his palace to summon him,
returned with a cry of lamentation; and at the break of dawn that night,
