though his forces were not yet fully assembled, he set out on a journey toward Kashmir.
Then, on the road, Gargadūta encountered him and said:
"Having reported the entire situation, [the king] has certainly commanded that you must not come;
for once the enemies have been swiftly slain, if you are not present, your younger brother [will take your place]."
"King Salhaṇa has already been dealt with; what purpose is served by your coming?

Having heard this message from Garga, the king, unable to endure it out of anger, laughed at his servants who were unwilling to march and spoke these words: KRT_8_0385cd KRT_8_0386ab KRT_8_0386cd KRT_8_0386cd

"Our kingdom is not ancestral if the younger brother is the heir; furthermore, this has been won back by my own arms and those of my elder brother. While we two were reclaiming the kingdom, there was no other giver for us."
"Where has that same method gone now, by which this was previously brought about?
Having said this, he proceeded with expeditions by means of his own forces alone,
and dispatched many messengers to the side of Garga to win him over.
He reached the wooden enclosure of Salhaṇa, who was seeking his welfare;
having gone out with Gargacandra, he established himself in the city of Huṣkapura.
When night had set in, messengers were sent back and forth.
Even though Garga had accepted her as his own, he was accused of treachery;
nevertheless, the king, being occupied with his duties, then sent her away.
At that very moment, Bhogasena, deluded by fate, arrived near Garga with his brother named Hitahita;
having placed the *khāśaka* fruits grown in the Bilva forest between them, he came into the presence of the king.
Having dispatched the king’s horseman named Karṇabhūti— who was near at hand— to Garga with the message, "I shall go on the full moon day of Jyeṣṭhā," he became intent on seducing him;
and disregarding even the need for the right time, he sought to kill that betrayer of his brother.
Seeking a suitable pretext, the wicked man learned [of his whereabouts] from the people:
"How is it that you have taken refuge at the side of one who betrays his own brother? Garga also reproached him, sending messengers with such instructions as these.

But he, having fled from the path and delayed thinking "it is dark," was attacked at the end of the night and slain along with his followers. Falling in battle, Karṇabhūti shone with the conduct of a hero.
His half-brother Tejaḥsena was also not lacking in splendor.
By the king’s command,
however, Marica, the son of Lava and also the son of Aśvapati, was impaled upon the tip of a stake.

By means of his steadfastness, the king became capable of restraining and suppressing [his enemies]; such was his strength that he did not even need to take a stand in order to remain seated. Although he had been placed in front, the king today has made him walk behind as a light-bearer.
Then Sañjayapāla approached him, bringing horses with him.
When they had arrived, that army gained a certain degree of stability;
meanwhile, the commander Garga, known as Sūrya, arrived with a small force.

Desiring to seize [the horse], the king was observed by his attendants and mounted upon it; though his mind was arrogant and deceitful, he was with great difficulty made to put on his armor. Then, making the sky appear as if covered by locusts, he swooped down.
The torrent of arrows from the enemy force, its continuity severed on all sides,
produced the sound of the syllable *oṃ* through the whizzing of shafts; thus, difficult to endure,
it struck all the enemies in the royal camp with every kind of weapon.

His army slaughtered, wounded, and scattered, the reckless king fled alone with speed, having emerged from the midst of his enemies. He could not be overtaken, for he was protected by the immense height of a trumpeting elephant and a chariot that moved without ceasing.
With that [horse] and his steed, he became a bridge difficult to cross even for winged creatures.
Only two or three, such as Sañjaya, Pāla, and others, were able to follow him,
keeping close behind and checking the enemies at every station.
That hero entered the settlement of the Khaśas called Vīrāṇaka,
accompanied by thirty or twenty servants who were like his own limbs;
he remained there together with a few others who were naked and without food.
Having entered Citra there, he punished the Khaśas without fear;
and by a stroke of fortune, he proceeded safely once more toward Lohara, traversing the perilous path where the fall of snow makes passage difficult.
At every step he encountered death, yet he was preserved by the remainder of his lifespan;

nevertheless, he remained constantly brooding over the prospect of reaching Kaśmīra. Out of anger, the group [of ministers] drove that wretched man away from the gateway of the bridge at Dvārasetu, even though he was most beneficial.
Confused in his mind, he threw [the man] into the Vitastā with his hands and feet bound.
As that man was being thrown in, wishing for safety, his own servant named Kṣema threw himself down before him; thus, even in falling to the depths, he attained a high station.

Then Garga, who had destroyed his enemies and bestowed sovereignty upon him, arrived in his presence; he attained a particularly exalted lordship over King Saḷhaṇa. Devoid of the prowess of ministers, that king obtained the kingdom.
With his mind wandering in every direction, he saw [the world] as if it were a whirling circle.
For him there was neither mantra nor valor, neither guile nor straightforwardness; neither generosity nor greed—nothing at all remained predominant.
In that kingdom, even within the capital at midday, thieves would plunder the people;
what need is there to mention travel on other roads?
Even a cripple could pass the time by walking about there.
There, that man too became uncertain as to whether his understanding was right or wrong. Loṭhana enjoyed that same woman whom Sahlaṇa had enjoyed today;
thus, for those two, the enjoyment of the kingdom became a common property, like a pit.
For one who lacks knowledge of other persons and is negligent,
every action of his is ridiculed by those who understand the system.

Loṭhana’s father-in-law, Ojasūha, was appointed by him at the gate; he was fit for assemblies of ascetics, yet harsh in his valor. Accepting the destruction of Sussala upon his approach, he [acted] when that [ruler] arrived.
Through the recitation of his own mantra one hundred thousand times, he brought about success from the moments of the mantra.
At the command of Garga, the crooked king caused that which was displeasing [to him] to fall: Bimba and Nīlāśvaḍāmara, with stones tied to them, were cast into the Vitastā.
Garga, the king’s benefactor, while slaying various enemies—
the numerous Hālāhaṇḍāmaras— had them executed after providing them with food.
In the administration of the kingdom, their life and death were dependent upon Garga.
Whether external or internal, near or far, small or even great—
once Garga had entered the presence of the king,
the entire population of the city was agitated and overwhelmed with fear.
For then news spread that Garga, having impaled [his enemies] upon stakes on ships,
had arrived in a rage to slay all those who had taken refuge with the king;
such was the terrifying report that caused the miscarriage of the fetus in a pregnant woman.
For two or three days, it was experienced by all people like a fever; then,
disregarding the king’s command, Tilaka, Siṃha, and others, out of impetuosity, suddenly launched an assault on Garga’s residence.
The entire region, exceedingly turbulent, rushed forward bearing weapons;
Garga-candra, however, remained unperturbed and received them all.
Dilha-bhaṭṭa, Arala, Lakka, and others, devoid of shame, [advanced] on horseback.
Wandering there, they were seen in the streets of Garga’s residence;
the king did not restrain them,
but rather dispatched them for the sake of rousing those whose power was blunted, so that they might attack.

By those warriors, although the path to Garga’s temple was blocked, the temple itself was neither obstructed nor was it possible to burn it down by setting fire to it. In the Loṭhikā monastery, there was an archer named Keśava who was the master of that monastery.

He struck down the enemy warriors with iron arrows, slaughtering them utterly. As the world of kings gradually became sparse along with the daylight, Garga, mounted on a horse and accompanied by his followers, went forth at evening.
Unimpeded by his enemies, he marched toward Laṅkā; having bound Ojaḥsūha— who was sitting dejected at the lord of Tripura—
he released him the next day, saying, "What is the use of this ascetic?"
Even though he was pierced by that spear, it did not split the king asunder.
From that moment on, at every instant,
the entire region became such that the houses were barred by citizens terrified of Garga’s arrival.
Then, as the distressed lord of the earth desired a reconciliation with Garga,
the Great Darkness appeared, acting as a messenger with ease.
By him, Garga was somehow persuaded to accept the offering of his daughter.
The servants, however, did not desire an alliance with that deceased king.
Then he entered into an alliance with Sussaladeva;
yet, even though subsequently entreated, he did not establish a matrimonial bond.
When the army had thus been shattered in the battle, the king slew Ṣaḍḍa,
Haṃsaratha, and Nonaratha, who had been discovered by his scouts;
he caused those men to be slain by having needles and other sharp objects like sparks of fire thrust into them.
Without abandoning his life-breaths, he experienced a terrible state;
that king had permitted the wrestlers to seize the limbs of Bhogasena’s body, for she,
dwelling there in disguise, had acted rightly by following her husband in secret.
Even upon seeing such a state of distress, the king, apprehensive within himself,
tested him further by offering him a gift of wealth;
yet he was neither one of royal lineage nor possessed of fierce valor.
Since that sinner had been subdued by secret punishment,
his own daughter then reviled him for having failed in his manly duty;
by her entering the fire, the intensity of her pride was proven.
Thus the reign of Śolpopi became as unbearable as an elephant in rut;
it was like a long nightmare perceived during a long night.
Though he had formed an alliance with Garga, Susala, who understood the times, remained fearful.
Then, he first appointed Sañjapāla, who was intent upon the interests of Kaśmīra;
likewise,
Lakkaka, having been granted wealth by King Salha, was sent along with Dvāra.
Having somehow obtained the root of the *varāha* plant and applying it as a departure-remedy,
Garga, remembering the ambush, approached from behind and,
together with the *varāha* root, plundered his army.

He fled, yet he was embraced by those warriors who had been slain; for while the earthly bodies lay upon the ground, the host of celestial nymphs [embraced him] with their divine forms. When the leader had perished, the earth [was left] with those of pure conduct born of noble lineage.
Adorned with pearls that had fallen from discarded ornaments, as it were;
Lakkaka, his fear dispelled by the approaching Sajjapāla,
being without support, sought refuge at the side of King Sussala.

Then, when the protector of the earth had departed far away after his enemies had been routed, he was urged by the citizens who had arrived as messengers and came into the presence [of the enemy]. "I shall conclude a peace treaty there with King Sussala."
Having spoken thus to Salhaṇa, he, accompanied by Helaka, proceeded toward his presence,
which was desired for its rising prosperity by the citizens like clouds by cātakas. All, with the exception of the king, took refuge with Uccala’s younger brother.
Then Garga’s wife, named Chuḍḍā,
arrived in his presence bringing two young girls to be married;
the king himself married the one of them named Rājalakṣmī.
He accepted Guṇalekhā, the younger sister of that [prince], as his daughter-in-law.
While Sañjapāla approached Salhaṇa along with his younger brothers and surrounded him,
the king also arrived at the main gate of the royal assembly hall.

The gate was knocked down by a single servant who was an open adversary; yet it proved futile, failing to reach him along with the enemy's desires. While the foe stood at the royal palace with his army after the gates had been shattered, [the king remained unshaken].

The army of Sussala became alarmed, fearing Garga; even though he had been given his daughter in marriage, they did not trust the royal troops. They remained where they were, fearing even the rustling of a blade of grass, thinking it might be an ambush.
On the eighth day of the waning moon, when the army had been similarly exhausted by the heat, the king,
out of affection, burned his enemies who were stationed within their impenetrable dwellings;
having entered through a gateway bent by a massive stone and shrouded in darkness.

Having opened the gate, the gatekeeper stationed in the courtyard seized the army. Having determined that the enemy host was primarily subsisting on the sun’s rays [i.e., that it was composed of celestial beings], a foot-soldier named Lakka made his way inside.

In the act of seizing [the enemy] and in the struggle through the narrow passages of the wooden enclosure, there was no warrior who resembled him; he became like his very reflection. Both Keśava and the head of the monastery followed after him.
Like Māruti [Hanumān] seeking Śaineya [Aṅgada], or Pārtha [Arjuna] seeking the King of Sindhu,
the resolute king himself emerged from the pavilion with difficulty, his limbs struck by those blows, and entered through the opened gate of the courtyard.
While the battle between the two armies was proceeding without distinction, many armed men met their death there on the battlefield.
Among them was a Brahmin minister of King Salha, born in the village of Pataṅga.
In battle, one named Ājaka attained the privilege of enjoying the company of celestial women.
Even Rudra, though a *kāyastha*, having obtained the office of *gañjādhipati* (treasurer),
brought the favor of his master to fruition by casting off his body in combat.
Just as a lord of the forest, when birds perched upon it have been stirred at evening,
becomes silent once a stone has entered and the birds have flown away,
so too did that battlefield, having become vocal, become like a scene depicted in a painting.
Thus, while King Sussala was threatening from his horse, a sound arose from within the palace where the women had not yet mounted the throne;
and the beating of kettledrums was heard, proclaiming: "Victory to Sussala!"
Such a state had never arisen for anyone else in the capital of the Mallas;
Salhaṇa and Loṭhana fell into such a state of despondency there that Sussala,
having donned his armor and mounted his horse, embraced them.
Calling them "children" and "youths," the rogue made them lay down their weapons;
having assigned their quarters in another pavilion and bound them there,
the king, having secured his kingdom, then entered the assembly pavilion.
He imprisoned him after he had enjoyed the kingdom for four months less three days,
on the third day of the month of Vaiśākha in his eighty-eighth year.
When he ascended that lion-throne, like the sun across the firmament,
the entire world in an instant abandoned its agitation, as if it were the ocean;
for [the people] had always been agitated by the sight of his hostile intent with their weapons unsheathed.
In the world of hunters, he became like a lion with a gaping mouth;
seeking out and repeatedly carrying out the extermination of those who betrayed their brothers,
that master of statecraft did not leave even the children remaining.

Observing the wickedness of the people, he maintained an appearance of unassailability; yet, out of consideration for his duty, he never displayed any softness toward those who had done him harm. In reality, however, his heart was tender as he sought to subdue the cruel folk.
Because of its terrifying nature, he treated that [treasure] as unreal, like a serpent on a wall.
He was a knower of time, one who sacrificed at the right moment, bold, possessed of creative genius, a reader of gestures, and far-sighted; he alone existed, and no other such person was found.

Whether it was some quality that was superior, some that was inferior, or some that was equal— whether it was a virtue or a fault— it was observed in his elder brother, even though their natures were identical. Even when the anger was the same, he imitated the behavior of his predecessor.
He purchased that venomous *viṣamālarka* snake for its honey;
yet, out of malice toward his own household and others, he did not display it. Furthermore, out of fear of disrupting the established order, he did not tolerate the arrogance of his dependents.

He did not desire the slaughter of the proud through the engagement in duels and the like; yet, when that [slaughter] was carried out through negligence, the first king became overwhelmed with compassion for your side, and there arose in him an unbearable distress caused by harsh words.
His [generosity] consisted primarily of affectionate gifts and was free from the injury of taking what is not given; yet,
because he was greedy for wealth, his acquisition of riches remained great,
while his renunciation became limited due to his lack of detachment from sense objects and time.

In that king, who was fond of new works and a multitude of horses, the artisans and the regional horse-dealers abandoned their poverty. When the onset of unbearable calamities occurred for the conqueror who desired tranquility— *KRT_8_0493ab*, *KRT_8_0493cd*, *KRT_8_0494ab*.

For that showerer of wealth, there was nothing whatsoever that could not be given away. Just as the festival of Indradvādaśī shone for that king— who bestowed vast and most precious garments— so did it shine for no one else.
Just as King Prāguccala was easily accessible and fond of his attendants,
so too did [King] Uccala become difficult for his servants to behold because of their great numbers.
No one other than Uccala suffered from the vice of horse-riding.
No one other than King Sussala was renowned for his skill in that regard.
Uccala brought every famine that arose to an end;
such a thing was not seen even in dreams during the reign of Sussaladeva.
What else could he have been, endowed with all virtues, other than superior even to his elder brother?
Having abandoned only the states of being a renouncer, being free from desire, and being easily attainable,
Pālaka— the son of Uccali and Garga— desired to install him in the kingdom.
Out of anger, he banished Sahasramangala.
While Bhadrāvakāśa was staying there, his son, named Prāsaka,
together with the Dāmaras, began to levy a tax on gold.
Not abandoning the child Uccala, who had been requested by his paternal uncle,
Garga also displayed opposition on that occasion;
he treated the teachers sent by the king like blades of grass.
There was the destruction of countless [warriors] consumed by the forest fire that was Garga.
Vijaya, the son of Garga born from the divine lake,
wrought a slaughter of the kings' armies in a backward direction.
When barely more than a month had passed since the attainment of the kingdom,
the mind of that steadfast king was not agitated by the tumultuous roar of the ocean as it surged against the shores of the earth, the domain of the lord of the gods.
By Garga,
those two ministers, Śṛṅgāraka and Kapila, who were eager for carnage among the royal armies, were slain in the tumultuous battle;
as were the two brothers, Karṇa and Śūdraka, who were both officials.
Even for those who were distinguished by having slain vast multitudes of excellent warriors within [the enemy ranks],
no one possessed the skill to extract them [alive].
Harṣamitra, the lord of Kampana and the son of the king’s maternal uncle, [acted thus].
Vijaya, having destroyed the enemy army, established [himself] at Vijayeśvara.
Tilha, the son of Maṅgalarāja, was a king born of another lineage.
There, the followers of the Triśūlabhāra sect and the Tantrikas were struck down.
In the king's army, Sañjayapāla was the most eminent of great heroes,
he who, though possessing only a small force, was conquered by Garga with his vast host.

Having steadied himself on the field of victory by means of the arrows discharged by Lakka and others, the resolute king went personally toward Garga, whose army had been broken. Having searched for the many slain warriors piled up in heaps by Garga, he [proceeded].
On another day, he caused it to be burned by means of countless funeral pyres.
Garga, being gradually oppressed by the powerful king,
then set fire to his own dwellings and turned toward the Halāha mountain.

There he took refuge in a mountain fastness called Ratnavarṣa; his horses having been seized by his followers, he was abandoned by the king and besieged from nearby. Even there, he was hemmed in by Sañjaya, who had mounted his horse alongside him.

He sought refuge at the feet of the king and offered him his own son. While the prince stood nearby, Garga, having quickly restrained Mallakoṣṭhaka— who was born from the ear-cavity of the king and had acted in opposition— restored his confidence.
Having received his submission when Vijaya and the others had perished,
the king, with his calamities stilled, slowly entered the city. Then,
having gone to Lohara and having bound Salhaṇa and Loṭhana, he stationed them there.
He took his pleasure with Kalha, Soma, Pāla, and others, attended by kings who excelled all others;
having entered Kaśmīra once more,
he caused Garga to flourish with ever-increasing favors.
While he was like the summer sun,
the Great Queen and the prince refreshed him with cool breezes and the shade of trees.
Then there were two *ḍāmara* warriors, born from the celestial lake, belonging to the lineage of Vijaya.
Bṛhaṭṭikika and Sūkṣmaṭikka likewise set a time limit;
desiring the king's patronage,
they entered the city and stood together with their weeping followers upon that ground which was meritorious for the world.
In Vijaya, because of his connection with Garga, the king— who was always hospitable—
abandoned proper conduct and had those two beaten by his staff-bearers.
Then his servants, drawing their weapons, struck them both.
Attacking with great violence against the king’s vast army,
the one known as Śvapāka-bhogadeva struck the monarch with a sword;
and the steadfast one named Gajjaka struck him from behind with a scimitar.

Because the king’s life was not yet exhausted, his enemies’ blows went to waste; however, the horse that drew the chariot perished. Shielding the king from the enemy’s blow, the son of the Bāṇa lineage [fell].
There, Śṛṅgārasīha was slain along with his horse and attendants;
by those soldiers, Bṛhaṭṭikka, Ābhoga, Deva, and others were killed,
while Sūkṣmaṭikka escaped— he who was the cause of the future upheaval.

Those who had resorted to treachery, such as Gajjaka and others, were impaled on stakes; the king, having become suspicious of them all, came to rely upon the favor of Garga. Even with the fall of a thunderbolt, no calamity could occur without [the astrological] timing.
Even a flower destroys the life of a living being once its allotted time has come. Those very pearls,
which do not even wither when touched by the flames of the submarine fire in the midst of the ocean,
surely go to their destruction when touched by the mere heat of youthful passion on the breasts of beautiful women.
Even forgetting his former service, the king— unable to endure the arrogance of others— banished from the realm Sañjapāla and others. Thereupon,
a relative of the descendants of Kakutstha named Yaśorāja [was appointed].

The king went into exile near Sahasramangala. Having attained prosperity and established his own position, he desired to launch a counter-attack against the king and those others who had been expelled from the country.
His son, seeking to enter by way of a secret path, was encountered by the king’s soldiers;
when Yaśorāja was wounded, he turned back and fled in fear.
Then, even though the other servants had been dismissed by the king, he [remained].
He learned the truth of the matter exactly as it was among the soldiers. When a new eclipse had occurred, three kings from the mountains were prepared for battle.
Cāmpeya, Jāsaṭa, Vajradhara, and Babbāpurādhipa; King Sahajapāla, the sovereign of Vartula;
and the two crown princes of Trivarta and the lord of Urvīvallāpura.
Somewhere, Balha, Ānandarāja, and the others— five in total— having made a pact for the sake of setting out, arrived at Kurukṣetra. Meanwhile,
[the army] of Naravarman approached, having been summoned from as far as the boundary.

They obtained alms from him, who had provided them with gold for their provisions on the journey. (Kulaka) Having been honored by Jāsaṭa out of affection for his kinsman, and having been escorted by other kings who had become famous, he then arrived at Ballāpura. (KRT_8_0542)

When that [king], whose fame had increased through the images led by Bimba who had departed from his country, arrived, the consecration of a thousand [images] became a minor matter. Then [it was said]: "This is the grandson of Harṣadeva; who are these kings? KRT_8_0543ab–KRT_8_0544ab.
Having spoken thus and abandoned those who numbered in the thousands and more, the people took refuge in him alone.
Abandoning his sense of gratitude and deluded by affection for his kinsmen,
Prince Dāryaka went to him even though he had been banished by the king.
That son of Kumārapāla’s father’s maternal uncle was formerly raised like a son by Sussaladeva; and,
urged by the crown prince Jāsaṭa, [he was sent] for the maiden.

Then that Padmaka, the lord of Vallāpura, gave [the land] to the mendicants. Thereafter, the local chieftain (ṭhakkura) of that region, named Gayapāla, having assembled all the kings, desired to appoint him to his ancestral position.
When the king heard that news, he became deeply distressed;
at that very moment, the powerful Gayapāla was slain by his kinsmen through a stratagem.
Then, having gone to Padmaka to fight them in the midst of the battle...
Even Daryaka, the leader of the host of mendicants, perished.
With that chief destroyed, the mendicant then departed,
rendered powerless like a cloud held back by a drought.
When Āsamati had departed and the gold for provisions was exhausted, even her father-in-law gradually fell into a state of diminished means. Having stayed in Jāsaṭa’s house for four or five years—
He then obtained from that hardship only enough food and clothing;
then the local lord Deṅgapāla, residing on the banks of the Candrabhāgā,
gave him his daughter named Bappikā and brought him to his own presence.

Having attained happiness and dwelling there for some time, free from fear, that scion of royalty abandoned his wretchedness and childhood. In the meantime, a reckless spear-thrower, intoxicated by his own violence, [appeared].
Moving back and forth, he incited the king’s fury;
seeking to enter the path of the perfected ones (siddhas), yet intent on ruin,
he was bound by his own wicked servants and delivered to the lord of the earth.
In that place, the supreme courage of Sañjayāla became renowned;
for even though he was exhausted, he turned away from malice and departed for another land.
What more need be said of him when he was such a hero and of noble birth? He [fled] to the ends of the earth.

That Yaśorāja spread abroad through his very valor— that indeed was a marvel. Then the king, having dismissed Ādya, Sahela, and the other high officials, appointed the *kāyastha* named Gauraka to the position of supreme authority over all matters.
That relative of an ascetic attained the favor of a certain man residing at Lohara in Vijayeśvara through his service; subsequently,
he gradually subdued the group stationed in Pūrvakāya.

Having been appointed to the office of supreme authority, he established a different state of affairs. Having prohibited the livelihoods of those who subsisted on the king from all offices of state action, he ensured the constant replenishment of the treasury for his lord.

Because of his gentleness, people did not perceive the cruelty of that sinner, just as the life-destroying power of poison is not recognized due to its sweetness. He deposited the wealth of the wretched, thereby causing the destruction of what had been previously accumulated.
O King, when the treasury is pure, it is like snow falling upon snow from a cloud;
for a treasury defiled by the wealth of the miserly, once entered,
is plundered by thieves or by the waters [of calamity] belonging to the protectors of the earth.
[189] Again,
through the habitual practice of greed, he remained day after day on the Iron Mountain, piling up his treasury while casting away all his wealth.
By the officials, such as the Vaṭṭāñjaka and others,
who were dependent on the illustrious king, the realm was rendered devoid of substance, like the earth devastated by great portents,
once that high-sovereign king— who was like a stone placed upon the crown of the world— had passed away.
Furthermore, the officials oppressed the people like hunters.
After Praśastakalaśa, his brother’s son,
a scribe named Kanaka, achieved highly praiseworthy prosperity.
By him, through an uninterrupted sacrificial session (*sattra*), the people who had fallen into famine and arrived from various distant regions were made free from calamity and disease.
(KRT 8.0571) At the conclusion of Uccala’s reign, there arose among them an investigation into the ultimate truth (*tattva*). (KRT 8.0572)
Those very men were appointed as officials by the negligent king.
At the gate, Tilakasimha was made such [an official] by him;
and Janaka, his one-eyed brother, was placed in the royal council.

The king’s fierce majesty pervaded the entire circle of the earth; he, moreover, took from the lord of the mountain (the Himālaya) that which had been seized by the lord of the gate (the Ocean). And Tilaka of the Kāka lineage, having been granted the title "Trembler" (Kampana) by the monarch—
Like a wind that makes trees tremble, he drove away those whose great lands shook;
even though he was a village official bearing weapons and a subordinate officer of the king’s treasury,
he conquered those who were themselves deprived of royal majesty.

By the wise Aṭṭamelaka, who had gained access to the royal court through his reliance on the lineage of the Kākas, even though he was but a servant, the desired counsel was obtained by disregarding his own sense of self-importance and looking instead toward the merits of the minister. Thus it is with a counselor who has abandoned the expectation of personal ego.
While performing various [tasks], he passed some time; then,
on the bank of the Vitastā, he began to construct three lofty temples in honor of himself,
his mother-in-law, and his wife.
Burning with a fire of calamity that bestowed countless riches, he caused even this monastery to attain a state of newness. Once,
as he was proceeding toward the city of Aṭṭilī, those standing nearby—
The king was incited by trustworthy men such as Kalha and others to destroy the Gargas;
however, the radiant Gārgi, named Kalyāṇacandra, disregarded them and,
upon seeing them at a moment of hunting and the like, aroused their indignation.

Having reported to you that he possessed superior power over all and was to be suppressed, Garga brought about a change of heart in the king through constant secret instigations. Then [he said]: "The king desires to bind you and cast you into the Lohara fortress."
Garga suspected [the plot], but was convinced by one servant and the king;
then, having fled from there with his son, he went to his own land. After some days, the king also arrived and entered his own kingdom.
Through mutual suspicion, the two royal Gargas fell into division;
by means of spies moving about, their enmity was brought to maturity. Bound by the remnants of his affection for Garga’s brother-in-law, Vijaya— [The verse continues: ...was made to serve him.
As the king departed from his presence, he was touched by remorse. At that time,
Mallakoṣṭaka— who had previously been cast into prison by him as an enemy of Garga—
was released from his bonds.
Having forced him into a formal alliance with other *ḍāmaras*, the king, filled with indignation, reduced him to the status of a tributary. Then,
as before, when the royal army had slowly marched out for battle...
Garga wrought a slaughter of the warriors while the Lord of Men was present;
there, Śamālāḍāmara, who took refuge with the king, attained supreme renown upon the earth for his heroic conduct that surpassed all others.
In the battle, when the Lord of the Gate (Dvārapati) was defeated by Garga and fled,
Tilakasimha’s valor became an object of universal ridicule.
The surviving soldiers were wounded, deprived of their weapons, garments, and other belongings.

Some of his followers were saved out of compassion by Gargacandra. While the bodies of the heroes were being consumed by fire on all sides, there was no counting the number of funeral pyres in the king's army.
Then Garga, his palace set ablaze by King Kṛṣṭasainya,
abandoned Lahara and fled to the mountain named Dhudāvana. There,
he sat at the foot of the mountain together with the king’s soldiers.
He constantly waged war upon those various mountain paths,
afflicting the king’s army every night with ambuscades and deceptive tactics.
In battle, he slew the practitioners of Tantra, headed by Trailokyarāja and others.
In the month of Phalguna, amidst the terrifying mass of snow, though accompanied by only a few followers,
that steadfast man was not deprived of his courage even when his queen became his enemy.
The courageous Tilaka, a scion of the Kāka lineage and lord of Kampana,
was able to rush toward him as he stood upon the peak of a mountain.
Being thus harassed by him, Tilaka sent his own wife and son to [the enemy's] presence.

They brought the king, whose anger was veiled by his favor, into a state of compliance. With his resentment hidden, the king made peace and departed from there; yet he led Mallakoṣṭhaka to further growth, rather than to tranquility.

While King Aviśada was suppressing two or three waves [of rebellion] for two or three months, Mallaka suffered the unbearable humiliation of being treated as an inferior. Observing this, the king secretly sowed dissension within his forces.

He appointed his own servants, such as Karṇa and others, who brought about his welfare. Then, distressed by being treated as an equal by those low-born kinsmen, he was urged by them and entered the presence of the king together with his wife and son.
Once, while he was engaged in bathing, standing upon the edge of the bathing tub,
the king made him cast away a weapon that had been hurled at him. Who else, when his manliness is disregarded, would maintain such steadfastness in the face of provocation?

Even he, at the time of his downfall, displayed such cowardice like a timid man. Where indeed is that pride of one who has uprooted and replaced kings? And where is this livelihood, which shares in wretchedness and is common to other people? Rather, it is the will of the Creator alone that here makes a living being dance helplessly, like a row of strings on a mechanical puppet.

Those rogues who were unable even to look at him in battle— those very same ones, now favorites of the king, tied his arms with knots. While the king himself was staying in a palace near the Śrī-Saṃgrāma monastery, they performed this act.
When he had entered the courtyard from the battle, Kalyāṇa and the others desisted.
Hearing that his father was alive, Garganandana, the King of Videha—
who had been pacified by the king himself— reluctantly surrendered his weapon.
Garga, along with his wife and son, was treated with hospitality by the king at Rājagṛha out of courtesy, being bound by gifts appropriate for himself;
yet Gārgya had already fled from his own palace to Catuṣka.
Having been seen by Karṇa, who was full of blame, he was delivered to the king. Of that monarch, whose anger was concealed beneath a settled appearance of favor,
there was no certainty— just as with a wound that lacks internal purity.

When Maṇidhara, the king of Darad, arrived desiring an audience, the monarch went out to meet him and had Garga executed by his servants. Having spent two or three months in the condition of a prisoner at night, [he was released].
Together with his three sons, he was cast down by the king’s attendants, his neck bound with a rope; just as they had brought those kings to their end by means of Bimba’s mouth, so too was he,
with a stone tied to his neck, thrown into the water along with his sons.
In the ninety-fourth year, in the month of Bhādrapada, the king—
who desired happiness— instead encountered suffering as a catastrophe arose;
for Kalha, the lord of Kāliñjara, and his mother, the chief queen.
When the one named Malla was slain, he (Somapāla) then became deeply distressed.
In the meantime, the one named Nāgapāla, the uterine brother of Somapāla,
killed his elder half-brother named Pratāpapāla.
Apprehensive, he killed the minister who was his slayer and fled;
abandoning his own country, he sought refuge with King Sussala.
Enraged by that cause, the king [Sussala] disregarded the affection of one who was once submissive.
Having resolved upon an expedition against Somapāla,
and having determined that the king was an adversary incapable of being overcome by any means,
he brought his enemy from Vallāpura to act as a mendicant for him.
Having heard that he had no heir, the king, agitated by wrath and with his fierce energy unleashed,
then marched upon Rājapurī. After Somapāla had fled and Nāgapāla had been installed on the throne, [the king attacked].
He remained there for seven months, subduing various enemies;
he was like a wielder of the thunderbolt among kings, a king equal to Vajradhara himself.
By granting him the opportunity for service, he became overcome with grace.
As his troops roamed everywhere along the banks of the Candrabhāgā and other rivers,
even the enemies were unable to catch a glimpse of their vanguard.
Tilaka, the lord of Kampana, became his vanguard;
Pṛthvīhara and the Ḍāmara were consecrated to guard the route.
That righteous king [reached] Brahmapurī and the temples of the gods.
Protecting his realm from enemies, he attained the fundamental fruit [of sovereignty].
How much more can be said of the other abundance of that Indra-like majesty?
Even fodder for his horses came to him from within his own domain.
In that situation, Sujanavardhana,

who was present there, incited Gauraka— who was staying at a distance— to direct his wrath toward [the enemy]. He had been appointed by the king himself to his own district for the protection of the realm.
The one whose intellect was impure due to malice discovered the entire matter;
having reported it, he reviled his father, the lord of the city,
and thereby agitated the mind of his brother, Manastilakasimha.
Then, having seized his office, the enraged [king] appointed Ananda, the son of Ananta born of Parṇotsa, as the governor of the gate. At that time,
Somapāla and others became the praiseworthy ministers.

Even though the king remained thus, those [women] did not come into his presence. Then, in the ninety-fifth year, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, he entered his own realm; Nāgapāla, who had been deprived of his kingdom, followed after him.
Then, agitated by greed— a messenger of unbearable affliction—
he punished the residents unjustly and reduced his expenditures.
Having diverted Gauraka from his duty, he [punished] those who had relied upon him.

As he was thus punishing them, all his ministers became disaffected. Because legal cases were suddenly overturned, he became deeply impoverished due to the lack of experience on the part of the new ministers.

Having fashioned bricks of gold, he sent them within the iron enclosure; he presented heaps of gold resembling the golden mountain [Meru]. Then, in order to punish Garga’s servants, he appointed an official over the rod of punishment.

Lahara killed Garga’s minister named Gajjaka. Then, having been sought out by Garga’s servants who were afraid of punishment, Mallakoṣṭhaka, becoming enraged, treacherously murdered him while he was unsuspecting.
When the kingdom was overwhelmed by the waves [of rebellion], the king then bound his elder half-brother named Arjuna, the son of Mallakoṣṭha, who was stationed nearby;
and he also bound the son of Saḍvacandra, though he was of the same lineage.
Having bound him, he appointed his brother named Bahika as his minister for his own benefit.
Recalling their former enmity, he— acting in defiance of political ethics— bound Sūrya along with his sons, as well as Ānanda, Candra, and others.
When the Malla had fled from the Mallakoṣṭhaka,
he was then placed upon a stake in the Arjunakoṣṭha and executed out of anger.
Having stationed his army there, they then departed as he entered the city.
All the Ḍāmaras bore enmity toward him, the slayer of those who trusted him.
Then, though he was angry even with Pṛthvīhara, he was served by his ministers; subsequently, at the command of the lords of Kampana and others, they instigated a sudden assault.
In some way or other, the king, having traveled across the vast territory of the inhabitants of Jayantī,
entered the residence of his kinsman named Kṣīra;
he did so by passing through the interior of those ancient cities such as Indrapura and others.
Some enemies were unable to afflict the great Vidhura;
that act of causing his distress became the very cause of the destruction of his subjects,
resembling the raising of an enraged Vetāla by a king through negligence.
Then the aged Kṣīra, possessed of sharp intellect, together with Pṛthvīhara,
presented eighteen Ḍāmaras who were beloved by the women of Śamāṅga.
To conquer those whose alliances were unbreakable, he set out for Vijayeśvara.

The king, becoming agitated, dispatched Tilaka, the lord of Kampana. Possessing incomparable valor, he shattered those enemies into pieces in battle and drove them away with his swift charges, just as a headwind disperses the clouds.
On the occasion of honoring him for having returned victorious after conquering the Ḍāmaras,
the king, instead, denied him entry, acting with contempt.
Once the king had entered the city with his pride shattered,

he remained in his own quarters, dejected and devoid of effort regarding his master's business. Those who had attained equality in status with their peers, whose rise had been blocked by those of similar rank, were placed at the forefront in enmity toward their foes, yet were relegated to the outside in times of peace.

Servants abandon a master who, having touched upon dispassion, shows contempt for their skill in performing extraordinary tasks at the completion of his work, just as householders quickly flee a house infested with snakes. When he abandoned the pursuit of his duties, those turbulent subjects brought about the ruin of all his accumulated wealth, like farmers whose crops are destroyed by a blight.

In city after city, the brahmins, terrified by the danger, mostly abandoned their homes; as they fled into the fire with their sacred fires, a terrible infamy arose. By that calamity, both horses and young camels perished.
They announced a great danger imminent for the circle [of the city].
The people, facing misfortune at hand, trembled with fear,
like a row of trees before a wind when the fall of a thunderbolt is near.

Then, at the beginning of his ninety-sixth year, the *Ḍāmarāvali* became like a mass of snow touched by warmth, on the verge of falling away. First [there was] the expansion of the *vilpa* from Devasaras, and after that—
His face, like a boil bringing pain, showed signs of suppuration.
Having brought Tikka and the other kinsmen into a single purpose, the powerful Vijaya approached King Sthāmastha and surrounded his army.
There, even his son Kāyasthaputra, the commander-in-chief known as Nāgavaṭṭa, withstood his fury for a long time in battle. Then,
at last, the lord of Kampana was entreated by the king in some way.
He departed, his composure loosened by the memory of his master’s treachery.
In that battle, as victory took firm root for him,
both his life-force and the goddess of victory repeatedly passed from him into his enemy’s hands.
Even as the rainy season increased,
reaching its peak in the month of Vaiśākha, the king set out for the village named Thalyoraka; meanwhile,
his soldiers were kept wandering there by their enemies during the nights.

Like those about to die, they were brought to despair by terrible dreams. By him, the best among all who possess power, even King Harṣa was cast into distress, though he had nothing but his own arm as an aid.
He who by his prowess conquered this earth many times over— or rather, for whom there was no counting of his heroic deeds— was that son of Jamadagni,
whose valor had been constrained by the overwhelming power of Time.
There, Bhagna was suddenly deprived of his glory of victory. When he had fled, Pṛthvīhara, arriving unexpectedly while Sajjaka was stationed in Hāḍigrāma, brought that hero to defeat.
While he was fleeing and being pursued,
that cruel and powerful man, having set fire to a temple of Nāga near the city, departed.
Then he and other cruel Ḍāmaras began searching for him everywhere.
From the prisons of the king and those dependent on the king, he seized horses;
then the monarch, resorting to a fierce anger,
took to a wicked path suited for those sharing in ill fortune.
Then, having seized the girdle of Pṛthvīhara along with the Ḍāmaramanika,
he cast them behind him like food at night.
Having likewise dispatched his brother Hamba to Viddaka, he—
Distraught, he sent others to the side of his brothers and sons;
having cut off the ears and noses of the mother of the one named Jayyaka, who lived in the village of Siphinnāgra, he brought her before him and dispatched her.
Having impaled Sūryaka along with his son upon a stake in the city, he—
overcome by rage— struck down many others, both those who deserved execution and those who did not.
Then, everyone became suspicious of him, as if he were the personification of a fierce and all-consuming Time.
Both those within and those without attained dispassion. Although he censured that very path of injustice by which King Harṣa had been defeated, he himself adopted it while governing the kingdom.
He who, when those who have entered the fray of battle, who are devoted to the craft of poets, who are intent on gambling, or who are discharging the burdens of kingship,
repeatedly falter in their speech due to neutrality, is himself never subject to deficiency in his own performance.
The king, exerting intense effort and making diligent endeavors even there, caused the wrestlers,
Koṣṭha, and the others to lose some of their formidable prowess.
Then Vijaya slowly led them away by way of Viṣalaṭā.
Then, as he was about to enter the Devasaras lake, that grandson of Harṣadeva— who had been living as a mendicant—
was driven back by the lord of Kampana;
fleeing from the edge of the abyss, he fell to the ground.
Then, having recognized him as slain, that victor sent his head to the presence of the king,
like the fruit of the tree of victory.
Yet even that most wondrous deed brought ingratitude upon the king.

But he was not pleased with him; he did not praise him, nor did he show him honor. Disdainfully, Kampanāpati, known as Śvabhra, struck him down and commanded him: "Why do you display such arrogance there?"
Recognizing the king to be ungrateful in every respect, Tilaka then became disillusioned and resolved to turn toward treachery. For if one should turn away from the virtuous, they cannot be blamed.

But because of her desire to do him harm, she attained the name "Ungraspable" (Agrayāhyā). Let those who love policy cite at every step the examples of those whose intentions were to be guided, or those who performed their duties after being observed;
for the virtuous, though exalted in pride and honored with praise, strive for the welfare of others even at the cost of their own lives.
A wise man who abandons a cloth scorched by contact with fire, the skin of a snake bitten by a serpent, a mantra that has reached the ears of an enemy, a house in ruins,

a king who is ignorant of service, or a friend who turns away from misfortune, finds no peace, for his own greatness is destroyed by his failure to rise to the occasion. Thus, those who abandon the proper means when their lord is provoked to anger—

Those who harm them are said to be at the forefront of the most wicked. While parents provide benefit in this single life and a master provides it everywhere, those who betray their master are more sinful than those who kill their parents.
When Vijaya had been slain and the others as well had lost their power to pacify,
no one— though their inner self was a knower of reality— could find composure.
For even that which approaches for a moment becomes a source of fierce torment.
The spread of the upheaval was perceived by all to be like that of a frenzied wild boar.
Then Mallakoṣṭha, wishing to bring back the mendicant once more,
dispatched his army toward Viṣalāṭā at his side.
Then the Lord of Kampana, though himself a traitor, informed the king that [the prince] was approaching;
he was thus forbidden by the king, and the following instruction was given:
"Leave him on the road where there is no obstruction, and then I shall kill him."
Like a jackal that had preceded him into the midst of a hunt, he was pursued by his horses;
though he knew the vital secrets of the dual sovereignty,
that king, impelled by fate, resorted to deceit regarding what was to be done there.

Having thus received [the news] from the mouth of Marmarāja himself, the betrayer then had the *Ḍāmaras* cause the mountain paths to be marked with signs for the arrival of the mendicants. Consequently,
word-of-mouth reports reached him at every stage.

That which causes fame among people but brings fear to kings—such a thing a stone does not do. A stone does not speak unless it is consecrated; it does not pierce ten targets with a single arrow; nor does it travel tirelessly back and forth, moving across a hundred *yojanas*.

By this praise of the mendicant’s such majesty, the common folk—even those with grey hair, white hair, and long beards—were filled with curiosity. He was like one destined to be the sole heir to half of a future empire. (A *yugma* couplet).
And even though he did not engage in worldly affairs, he sought out news of the mendicant’s well-being.
In the bathhouse by the river, the elderly officials whose duties had ceased were bathing;
in the royal palace, the sons of kings were no longer counted, being mere names.
Some by nature are wicked, while others are warriors longing for high horses;
even teachers cause their pupils to scratch their buttocks with their nails.
The elders, the courtesans of the gods' assembly, the guardians of the celestial palaces, the merchants who had deposited their wealth for use, those devoted to books and sacred learning,
and the twice-born members of the assembly skilled in the practice of fasting unto death.
Armed with weapons, consisting mostly of farmers, and turbulent on the outskirts of the city, they bring some measure of comfort to themselves and others through their tumultuous news;
for the most part, these people in this land are fond of upheaval against the king. (A family verse)
As the news of the arrival of the mendicants spread, the people became trembling with fear, and the king fell into deep anxiety. Then,
Pṛthvīhara, dwelling in a mountain glen shrouded by mist, [remained there].

Having emerged [from his position], he of incomparable prowess shattered the king’s army in battle. He made Ananta, Kāka, and Urvaśya the commanders of the gates of Ānanda, and he turned Tilaka and Siṃha— along with three ministers— into fugitives.

When Vijaya had been slain on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, the king, having met with defeat in Āṣāḍha, became once again helpless. [This was indicated] by the cows uprooting trees and by the snakes climbing to their tops.
Just as a colony of ants is rained upon when their eggs are being transferred,
so too did that king, perceiving through ill omens that a calamity was imminent, reflect upon it and undertake the appropriate action to be taken against the approaching danger. (A pair of verses).
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śuci, the capable king dispatched his son,
the queen, and the rest of the family to Koṭa Lohara.
As he was following them, they were swept away by the collapse of a bridge.
The twice-born Brāhmaṇas of Loṣṭha perished in the Vitastā river. Distressed by that ill omen, he followed after them for two or three days near Huṣkapura and then re-entered the city.
Then, deprived of his son and his queen, he fell into a state as if abandoned by both majesty and fortune. By virtue of that [mantra],
the auspicious counsel manifested itself to him during his calamity.
Even during an internal rebellion, he partook in every kind of prosperity;
though he himself had provoked calamities, like King Harṣa,
he and his lineage continue even today to enjoy imperial sovereignty through that same policy.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, having been brought by the soldiers of Lāhara,
the mendicant was handed over to the powerful Ḍāmaras of the Maḍava kingdom; and they,
like suitors, [welcomed him] as if to a bridegroom’s residence resembling that of their father-in-law.
Following him, they escorted Lahara along with his army.
Having honored those leaders of the wrestlers' quarters,
the immensely wealthy [princes] dismissed them to crush the lord of Kampana.

When the enemy’s army was attacking from all sides, the king, whose expenditures were beyond compare, set about recruiting foot soldiers. While that king, who showered wealth everywhere, was thus immersed in that disastrous vice,
Even the artisans and cart-drivers took up weapons;
in the city, the army commanders stationed themselves along every road,
their horses equipped with armor and eager for the exercise of battle.
The Lāharas arrived and engaged in battle with the royal troops stationed at Mayagrāma, who were residents of Bhikṣāvamara and Īśvara; by them,
a continuous war was commenced on the outskirts of Hiraṇyapura.
The illustrious Vināyaka, Deva, and the other commanders of the royal army were slain.
At the very outset of the battle, having encountered the enemy's royal host,
those two [heroes] arrived on excellent horses and considered themselves to have attained the glory of kingship.
On the bank of the river named Kṣiptikā near the capital city,
King Pṛthvīhara brought about the destruction of the remaining brave warriors.
Even while Vijayeśa was at Tilaka, the Ḍāmaras arrived and seized him.
On the banks of the great river, Khaḍga, Vīhola, and Ḍauka waged war;
besieging the city, they set fires here and there and carried out looting, shouting day and night at the inhabitants.
With armies retreating while sounding their trumpets, and those entering [the fray] wounded by weapons; with throngs of beloved ones crying out as they were slain, and broken soldiers fleeing;
with crowds of onlookers spreading abroad, and swift-coursing messengers carrying news.
With their armor being shifted about and their horses being dragged along,
the dust incessantly spread forth as the nearby crush of the crowd subsided.
Day after day, the royal roads were free from the disturbances of enemies. [Verse 8.737cd: As the enemies arrived at every dawn with all their efforts, it was recognized each day:
"Surely, the King has been conquered today."
Who other than the steadfast Suśśala was there who,
even with great difficulty, could not be dragged away from his own kingdom by his fortitude when faced by adversaries?
[He provided] bandages for wounds, extraction of arrows, and the bestowing of wholesome wealth.
He was seen constantly attending to those wounded by weapons; through the distribution of travel allowances, wages, gifts of affection, and medicines,
the king’s expenditure of wealth among the world of warriors became incalculable.
In battle, as well as in their own homes when they were wounded or fallen,
thousands of men and horses constantly met their destruction. Then, being struck by the king’s forces which abounded in cavalry, [the enemy perished].
Lāharā, Mallakoṣṭha, and the others fell into a state of extreme agitation.
Having received counsel from their own divided inner circle,
those men, eager for battle, led the mendicant along that path with a small force toward the Queen of the Gods.
With a bridge on its very narrow side, the lake was filled with archers;
they achieved victory in battle and were freed from the fear of their horses.
Then that treacherous Lord of Kampana, residing in Vijayeśvara, [acted].
In the throbbing battle, he brought the enemy forces to a state of exhaustion and extreme agitation.
Thinking, "Let not the world of Lavanya perceive my weakness as I retreat;
let him not strike me from behind," he proceeded.
In order to display his power, having reached Vijayeśvara,
he turned back from the army of King Ajja and set out; there,
he also slew two hundred and fifty of his warriors.

Abandoning the field of victory, he went to the city of Drohakṛt. On the road, the Ḍāmaras did not follow him anywhere out of fear; shouting as they mounted the mountain peaks, they abandoned all his paths.
Having abandoned the kingdom of Maḍava, he entered [the city] while the king was afflicted by calamity;

remembering his former conduct, he laughed at the monarch who had been honored with hospitable rites. Then, remaining in his position like any other minister, he did not act as was appropriate for himself.
In the battle, he displayed [his prowess] as if standing there merely as a witness. Then,
from the kingdom of Maḍava, all the Ḍāmaras together approached and took up their positions on that bank of the great river.
The diplomatic expedients, such as conciliation and sowing dissension, which were employed against the circle of enemies,
proved fruitless for the king once they were disclosed by his trusted agents abroad.
Even though that monarch had already traversed the circles of various other kings, [his efforts failed].
The foremost fruit of the prowess of his arms was the protection of the city.
At Amareśa, the gatekeeper stood together with the princes;
near the royal garden were the ministers of state.

Like those who have arrived from distant islands, they accepted from the king abundant wealth for their journey and did not fight anywhere. All the armies of the enemies experienced victory and defeat in turn.
They obtained victory, but Pṛthvīhara never did. By him,
intoxicated with wine and leaping about in battle like a *vetāla*,
almost all the excellent warriors of the king’s army were devoured.
In that single battle, the valor of Udayasiṃha— who was born of the Icchaṭi clan, appeared like a youth,
and was the sole lord of the earth— was spread abroad as he challenged his opponent to a duel.
The sword-blade, like a creeping vine, struck with the hand whose hair was pulled out;
while the battle raged near the outskirts of the city,
even women, children, and others met their death through negligence when struck by arrows.

Thus, as that terrible destruction of people increased, something extraordinary occurred: the king, out of despondency, was unable even to leave his palace. While movement was thus restricted, Somapāla took advantage of that interval.
Having found an opening, he plundered the watchtower and set it on fire.
While the lion was preoccupied with the elephant battle, occupying the mouth of that cave, what other manly effort could there be for the village jackal? It was simply the right time.
[196] By the destruction of two kingdoms, that king became peerless; yet,
constrained by shame, he was unable even to look upon himself.
A certain time ensued for him— one thick with every impropriety, unbearable with every calamity, and consisting entirely of suffering; yet,
while he remained unswerving, that [time] robbed him of his welfare under the guise of being beneficial.
The king was mostly surrounded by forest-dwelling Brahmins who were free from passion.
Your ministers, standing aside during the battle, entreated him:
"Having seized these [treasures], let them be surrendered to them on Mount Lohara."
If, when this calamity had reached such a state that it seemed all-pervasive,
who would not have offered up the ripening fruit of autumn, now brought near by others? That the king did not strike back while remaining neutral was due to his regard for the proper time.

When that [plot] was revealed by them, all the ministers felt apprehension. At that time, the king— who possessed power sufficient to bend even a blade of grass— was led by deceitful brahmins who sought their own ends into a state where his administration fell into disorder.
Crowded with officials who subsisted on their posts and fierce courtiers,
it grew from his side like another army of enemies;
yet at the moment of his consolation, it vanished due to various lapses that arose.

The country fell into turmoil, hardship, and fierce plundering. Since no kings were seen in their positions, those who were deceitful and non-functional spoke to the king, who was in a precarious state, consoling him with various unpleasant words.
Due to the king's loss of beauty, a greater calamity arose for him,
bringing intense suffering like a disease of the throat resulting from a disease of the feet.
Through the giving of gold as a bribe, he [dealt with] the chief intermediary among them.

Having taken some [prisoners], he somehow managed to release them by means of fasting. Vijaya, a descendant of the Śastra lineage such as Varṇa and Soma, was slain by horsemen while forcibly entering the city with his army of mendicants.

Because he entered the city with such excessive haste, having broken through the guard posts, the overthrow of the kingdom was effectively accomplished at that moment. Even though the king’s majesty was somewhat diminished, it remained sufficient even regarding matters of mere pleasure.

Pṛthvīhara’s desire for peace was made manifest to one who sought discord. While that leader of those desiring victory was seeking peace with the king, the soldiers on both sides considered the upheaval to have been stilled.
Then, he treacherously killed three highly trusted ministers whom the king had dispatched to bring [the elephant] to the vicinity of Nāgamaṭha:
Mammaka, the foster-son of the king; Guṅga; and Rāma Vārika, a Brahmin.

Of those, three servants were killed at the side of Tilakasiṃha. Nīvi was given away, but Gauraka was killed while remembering Bhūtapati. While his beloved was crying out, the enemies struck him with pitiless blows.

Upon hearing of that catastrophe, the entire land became filled with world-weariness; within the royal capital, the king was made to utter harsh words. On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, his circle of vassals was overturned.
The day was difficult for the lord of the earth to pass. Then,
overcome with despondency and reflecting that "this [world] does not exist," the king asked even those unworthy of his regard, "What is to be done?"
For him who was thus situated in adversity, there was no one at all who laughed at him from within, nor anyone who did not feel satisfaction [at his plight]. Then,
as he endured even that onset of calamity, [the king]—
In due course, the servants took refuge with the enemy.
Bimba, the half-brother of the Lord of Kampana,
abandoned his own people and sought refuge with Dvārakārya, accepting the position granted by him.
While Janaka-siṃha was secretly and incessantly dispatching messengers,
the promise of his daughter to the mendicant was revoked;
having given swords, horses, armor, and other gifts to the mendicant, [he sent him away].
Horsemen were seen departing every day;
what else could it be? Clearly, those who had been residing by the king's side during the day were now seen before the mendicant at night, devoid of shame.
"The world goes from here and comes from there, clearly disregarding authority"— when the king’s commands had thus become ineffective, a certain upheaval began to unfold.
When the autumn harvest had been carried away in every direction by the Ḍāmaras,
the entire world became terrified and fled, abandoned by its wealth and people. When King Sussala had departed, leaving this earth filled with gold, [the Ḍāmaras] seized it.
"The monk must have committed a falsehood"—such was the world's conviction.
"Where has the renunciation of a monk ever been seen? Whence could he possess such wealth? Thus did the people, following the crowd, falsely speculate.

A streak that was not the new crescent of the moon itself appeared for a long time surrounded by clouds; people seeking the sky paid homage to it—shame on that greed which causes one to abandon the discernment between the real and the unreal!
In the victory of the royal faction, [the enemy] became like one with his neck bent down.
When the faction of the monks was victorious, the world rejoiced without restraint. Then,
the relationship between the king and the *ḍāmara* host— which resembled that between a dog and the daughter of a brahmin—
flourished as their mutual enmity fell away due to fear of one another.
Due to internal dissension among the king's inner circle and the king’s own steadfastness, his enemies,
fearing him and unaware of each other’s intentions, desired to flee. The king, however, remained distrustful even of his kinsmen, knowing them to be intent on doing him harm.

I have no faith in my own life, whether in its preservation or its passing away. When he was dwelling in great calamity, those who had already received wealth did not rejoice in the showering of gold, jewels, and other treasures; rather, the armed men censured him excessively.

Hearing from people who were speaking out of fear, "This man is lost; he will not survive," the sick man suffered as if hearing the words of a physician who had abandoned him. Even when someone brought him something that was right before him, he offered it back according to that [fatal] instruction.
The crowd of followers gazed at him with playful charm and pride; yet,
in that very moment,
even he who was so audacious became, alas, paralyzed by fear, unable even to leave his own house.

Just as the throngs of *ḍāmaras* intended to move against the king by means of schism in the monastic community, the monarch was brought to utter disorder by his own weapons. Drawing their swords, they blocked the gates of the royal palace.
When wealth from abroad was to be received, they observed a fast at every step. Though the king, possessing the splendor of the Lord of Wealth, gave them even more than what was due,
he did not meet with their approval, for they were intent on seeking humiliation.
Desiring to die at a sacred ford, like a debtor burdened by his obligations,

he was restrained by all those who were owed [revenue] and, stripped of shame, was forced to pay what was due. Even the local officials (*sthānapāla*), acting as extortionists, assailed him and compelled him to pay.
Having pulverized wealth such as golden vessels and other goods,
the city— along with its old and young— became agitated from moment to moment;
like a surging ocean, it was impossible to restore to order.
Once, at the very dawn, with the gates blocked by his own soldiers, he beheld the city being thrown into turmoil on all sides. Then,
in order to quell that agitation, [he approached] Janaka, the lord of the city.

Having ordered the city to be cleared for his march, he waited for a moment; and though he had with some difficulty won over those armed men by means of gifts and honors, he set out from the capital, fully equipped and accompanied by the women of the inner apartments.
Before he had even emerged from the city gate mounted on his horse,
plundering was commenced by thieves within the capital. Some wailed loudly, others cried out, and some were looted.

Abandoning the kingdom, his servants followed him, armed with weapons, as he plundered. On the road, the king was followed by five or six thousand armed men who, free from restraint, were devoid of shame and fear.

In the ninety-sixth year, on the sixth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, when only one watch of the day remained, he departed, overwhelmed by treachery and accompanied by his servants. At every step, he was being abandoned by his own men as they seized his horses and other belongings.
With a small force, he reached Pratāpapura during the night;
having gone before Tilaka and reaching the presence of the one who had arrived,
he there shed tears for a long time like a kinsman, overwhelmed by grief.
Thinking, "I must not commit treachery," he quickly reflected thus; and on the following day, he himself entered his residence in the city of Huṣkapura.

Out of respect for him, he performed his ablutions and other rites, desiring to assemble an army; having entered the kingdom of Krama, he was once again eager for victory. Then [he encountered] the Dāmaras, such as Kalyāṇavāḍa and others, who were secretly seeking battle.
Having brought him before him, he caused him to lose his composure.
By that stratagem, he was drawn out from his house and departed from there,
like one who accepts gold while subduing bandits who oppose him on the road.
As he was departing, his paternal half-brother Tilaka abandoned him;
yet, out of courtesy, Ānanda followed him for one stage of the journey.
Abandoned by his servants through his generosity and his prowess, he [confronted] the thieves.
Protected by the remainder of his lifespan, he traveled along the path, pacifying [his enemies].

(KRT 8.0827cd) Even for those lions whose claws are the refuge of trees, mountains, and thickets in the remote forest, the passing of time might occur gradually merely by the support of a child’s throat. (KRT 8.0828ab) Even those tusks of elephants which serve as weapons in battle would receive but the strikes of hands from those playing in sport; nowhere is the firmness of heroism ever established. (KRT 8.0828cd)
In this world, whose nature is manifold, virtues such as valor, renunciation, fame, and wisdom would not remain unshakable among living beings.
Even the sun, day after day, undergoes various states of intensity and mildness.
Such various states come upon living beings; what certainty can there be regarding their powers?
Unable to bear to look at Aṭṭalikā, which was scorched by fire, he ascended Mount Lohara with an army that was silent out of indignation.
Unable to even look upon his own wife there due to extreme shame,
he, with his limbs cast upon the bed, tormented himself day and night; for even during the daytime,
he would not leave the inner chamber because of the lamp that had been lit.
Out of courtesy, he granted an audience to his servants at the time of their meal;
he did not touch ointments, nor did he mount horses;
he did not look upon singing, dancing, and the like, nor did he engage in pleasant conversation.
Fainting, he pointed out their indifference, harshness, cruelty, malice, and so forth;
remembering each one by name, he reported them to the Goddess.
"They have gone after me, abandoning their own lands; they have followed me," he said.
He, possessed of most excellent glory, attained great prosperity through the bestowal of wealth out of courtesy.
When he had departed for Kashmir, all the ministers immediately assembled with their armies before the ancient capital.
And among the ministers, the city governor Janakasiṃha was the leader, esteemed by the vassals, neighboring lords, councilors, citizens,
and others. Through trusted men such as Mallaka and Koṣṭha, who made frequent trips back and forth, he [communicated] with the monk.

To inspire confidence, he had his son and brother’s son handed over as hostages. Then, in a city filled with women, children, and others fleeing in fear, the night began, kingless and terrifying to all living beings.

In that city, some were slain by the enemies, some were plundered, and some had their houses burnt; the weak were left destitute in a realm devoid of a king. On the following day, all the paths and directions were blocked by the clamorous armies.
Standing in the midst of a circle of horse-riders whose forehead-marks were as red as vermilion,
his form was difficult to discern amidst the grove of unsheathed weapons that resembled plantain trees;
like a lion, he inspired both fear and wonder in the world.
He was adorned on his back by locks of hair that were disheveled, intensified by youth, clinging to the silk cloth of a hero’s turban,
and serving as fetters for the binding of the Goddess of Victory;
[he was further graced] by a pair of eyes that were smooth, white, and long, shining like earrings.
With a face whose fresh beard was beautified by the traces of lovely sandalwood paste,
and whose copper-red lips possessed an exceeding luster through the presence of Śrī.
With his horse prancing, he fanned the royal splendor residing within his inner treasury with the mass of its mane,
as if with a chowrie; and at every step, he was attended by subordinate kings who had turned their horses back to follow him.

Accepting the offerings, the monk then entered the city. (A *kulaka*. Like a nurse for that child, the small bowl held behind him acted as the advisor in all matters for the modest youth. (KRT_8_0849ab–cd)
"This man was dear to your father; you were reared in his lap. Thus he pointed out each one, showing that this man was the very root of the kingdom.
He entered the house of Janaka-siṃha in order to obtain his daughter; thereafter,
he went to the capital to attain royal fortune,
by which the long-extinct lineage was once again made to flourish.

A woman who is intensely attached to her unborn child in the womb does not incur ridicule; likewise, those seeking victory do not become objects of derision even when their enemies are depicted in paintings, provided they act with such conduct toward them as a mendicant would show toward those who have rained upon him.
The splendors of King Sussala, the lord of wealth, began to flow forth;
the remnants of the treasury were used for the amusements of the new king.
They distributed the royal fortune, which consisted mostly of horses, armor, and swords.
Released from the constraints of the king’s oppressive plunderers and ministers,

the villagers enjoyed the pleasures of the senses as if they were in heaven within the city; meanwhile, the bandits, who deserved only the spoils of the countryside, remained like Piśācas in their mountain caves.
Dwelling everywhere among the villagers, the mountain-dweller did not shine out of place,
together with those whose ornaments and garments consisted mostly of long hanging blankets.
[He attained] renown for the unexpected appearance of this mendicant.
Others proclaimed that this was an incarnation of Ḍāmarā. He became bewildered regarding the duties of a kingdom to which he had no prior experience,
like a physician who has never seen a patient's condition at every step of the course of treatment.
Having been granted his sister’s son as a hostage by Janaka-siṃha, who had slowly made the surrender of his brother’s son,
the lord of Kampana, though he had given his daughter in marriage, sought refuge with him. Juṅga was the commander of the royal camp for the king of Rājapurī.
The one appointed to the forepart of his feet perceived only his own interest, and not that of his lord. Royal Fortune took refuge in him as her supreme sovereign;
yet he, though a mendicant, became the sole worthy recipient of the title "King."

Though his sovereignty was held in the grip of courtesans and he was full of vulgar conduct, he became a partial reflection of both the virtuous and the wicked, as an intimate friend of them all. He was the son of two mothers, the brother of Daryaka, and a field for wondrous valor.

Even Jyeṣṭhapāla took refuge in the status of being the foremost among the king’s inner circle. His ministers— both those from his own time and those inherited from his ancestors— flourished as many others did, like bees upon the lotus-pond of royal fortune.
O innocent queen, while the ministers were negligent and the fierce bandits were active,
that kingdom, though in its youth, was struck down by a lack of exertion.
Delighted by ever-new women and abundant foods, [the king remained complacent].

The monk, deluded by the experience of pleasure, did not perceive what ought to be done. Blinded by the sleep of the monsoon season of sensual enjoyment, urged by his own [followers] in the midst of the assembly, he, languid with intoxication, desired to sleep during the effort for victory.
Out of pride, he would speak of compassion even to one who was painted with a picture;

yet that simpleton did not become angry, but rather felt affection for her as if she were his own mother. He was attended by those without standing, like a vulgar man served by the leftovers of courtesans.
His actions, which were worthy of a slave girl, were incited by parasites to be pursued;
all affectionate men abandoned the service of that man whose words were unreliable and whose stability was like a line drawn in water.

The king did not speak back to those ministers who had spoken thus; he disregarded the words of his affectionate friend, which were hollow within. Led by the ministers to their own homes and provided with food, that man of deluded intellect—

Like a wealthy man whose father has perished, he was plundered by rogues. In the house of Bimba, the woman Bimbanitambinī snatched away handfuls of food from him, just as a mare in heat seizes the fodder of a passionate horse.

By her smiling as she showed her husband her eyes while deceiving him with glances toward her breasts and armpits, his fortitude was stripped away. Pṛthvīhara and Mallakoṣṭha were filled with mutual envy for one another.

Enraged, the two of them caused agitation in the capital moment by moment. Although the king himself went to their houses and had the marriage of his son performed, those two, intoxicated with prowess, did not heed one another nor did they let go of their resentment.
Then,
after his marriage had been performed, the king himself was clearly abandoned by Mallakoṣṭha, who had become filled with resentment;
though Janaka, though one-eyed, was also cast off because he was plotting harm, he was spared out of regard for their kinship.
He led the Brahmin ministers to states of dispassion, vigor, joy, and so forth.
Standing on the shore, his mind was subject to servants who were mostly treacherous and of poor intellect.

The king fell into disrepute and became an object of reproach. When the world was ruled by Ḍāmarasvāmin, what calamity did not prevail? Therein, even the wives of Brahmins suffered insults from outcasts.
Then, in that realm which was either without a king or possessed many kings,
the established path for all legal transactions clearly came to an end.
In that kingdom of beggars, the ancient dinars ceased to circulate.
