For a hundred of those [coins], eighty new ones were purchased. Then the king, intoxicated with power, dispatched the army along the royal road to Lohara to crush the arrogant force of Sussala.

Accompanied by Somapāla, he brought the Turuṣka army to assist Sallāra, who had become filled with wonder and attained friendship [with the king]. "By showing him this noose, I shall bind Suśśala and have him executed," [he said].
Thus one by one, a single horseman among the Turks boasted. (KRT 8.886cd) A clash occurred between the warriors of Kashmir, the Khaśas, and the Mlecchas;
indeed, for whom was their skill in uprooting the entire universe not conceivable? (KRT 8.887ab–cd)
When Bimba had departed, the mendicant wandered on, his restraint dissolved;
the fool found no place among the various unsettled conditions. He was then invited by Bimbāvaruddhā and led to her own home.

She was satisfied by the granting of enjoyments and pleasures through her boldness; even in the company of the minister’s wife, he had no regard for his own interests. What talk can there be of fear of public scandal for one whose downfall is imminent?

There, he partook of food suited to his physical needs and listened to the sounding of clay drums and brass cymbals; yet, practicing his discipline, he did not feel shame like an ordinary man of desire. Then, as the king’s pride gradually faded away, [his resolve]...

Even food to be eaten at the proper time was no longer obtainable for him whose wealth had vanished. Sussala, who had previously been censured by the world for being overcome by such greed, cruelty, and other vices, now became an object of public acclaim.
Those subjects, who had become detached due to the loss of wealth, honor,
and the like, now felt a deep longing and desired his very return.
Even today, we who have witnessed it with our own eyes remain filled with wonder at this.
By whom were those subjects provoked, and by whom were they further appeased?
In one moment they turn away, and in another moment they turn toward [the ruler];
these common folk, who are like beasts, perceive no underlying cause whatsoever.
Then Mallakoṣṭha, Janaka, and the others, dispatched by messengers, incited the king—
who had previously renounced his kingdom— to once again exert himself for victory. Thereafter,
Akṣauhuṃ was plundered by the people of Agrahāra and Lokaiṣṭika.
The Brahmins residing there generally made vows directed toward the king.
Along with those and other agrahāras, the city of Vijayeśvara became filled with dependents; it was as if the entire Rājñānavāṭikā had settled within that town.
Then, urged on by the preeminent brahmins such as Ojānanda and others,
the assemblies of the inhabitants of the celestial abode likewise observed a fast even in Gokula.
[They did so] with vehicles adorned with white umbrellas, garments, and chowries.
Its courtyards were covered on all sides by throngs resembling the gods;
with the quarters of the sky agitated by musical instruments such as the kāhala, kamsya,
and tāla, that assembly of the retinue was seen, never before beheld.

Being thus consoled by the king’s messengers, those who spoke with arrogance uttered these words: "There is no way out for us except with our beards hanging down. With that casual remark regarding their long beards, they [addressed] King Sussala.
Pointing him out, they considered him to be like a toy puppet. Day after day, as the citizens came together to behold the prince,
what regulation did that assembly of people not deliberate upon?

Terrified by the fear of the king’s assault, the courtiers and citizens repeatedly fell into agitation and prepared fiercely for battle; yet that city remained submissive to Janaka-siṃha, acting according to his will.
Everything was made ready for the complete capture of Sussala.
The king first set out to restrain the brahmins of Agrahāra;
he proceeded to the field of Vijaya, but there his efforts were frustrated.
In their midst, Tilaka said to all those Ḍāmaras,
"Kill him! But he, with his mind one-pointedly focused on the being, did not accept that.
Having learned this from the king’s own mouth, the Lavaṇas placed their trust in him;
meanwhile, those led by Pṛthvīhara took refuge with Tilaka.
[The king then dispatched] the nephew of Prayāga, a chamberlain named Lakṣmaka.

The king, desiring an affectionate kinsman, went instead to Sussala. Then, having entered the city and assembled all the people, he granted an audience to the citizens who were disaffected without cause.

Although he spoke what was logical there, his words were treated as a lie by those of deceitful intellect; the citizens made him [the object of their scorn], for indeed there is no medicine for those touched by calamity.
In the meantime, Somapāla and others [saw] [him] stationed at Lohara.
They all assembled at Parṇotsa to fight against King Sussala.
And a king named Padmaratha, the lord of Kāliñjara and born of that same lineage,
arrived along with Kalha and others, mindful of his friendship.
Then, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha,
King Sussala, full of pride, engaged in battle together with those powerful [opponents].
Even today, that battle near Parṇotsa is described by spectators.
The first moment of that extraordinary fire’s cleansing was like a sudden arrival from somewhere;
from that point on,
it made the king’s own vast domain once again full of life, just as a lion makes a forest teeming with creatures.
In an instant, he of abundant prowess brought about the meeting of those whose fetters were slipping due to fear with the nooses of Death;
the powerful one made Somapāla’s maternal uncle a morsel for his prey.

In that battle on the bank of the Vitostā river, he—like a Vetāla unleashed by his wrath—reduced even those many [enemies] to such a state that his opponents were slain, fled, or destroyed; what else could he do, being as he was with only a small force?
Did the people of Kashmir not possess the sense of propriety that they gave [tribute] to their own lord?
Those who fled from battle with one man brought ill repute upon the other. When Somapāla marched against the Turuṣkas, they were devoid of shame.
Having abandoned their pride, the women of Kaśmīra sought refuge in the presence of the king. With wondrous dispositions, they who yesterday bent bows now bend their heads;
clearly, in the presence of the lord of the lineage, those formerly audacious women felt ashamed.
Then, accompanied by the citizens and the *ḍāmaras* who were arriving,
the king set out once more toward Kaśmīra after two or three days.
Prince Kalhaṇa, the son of Sāhadevi, [entered] as his lord was entering.
Having gathered those established in the kingdom of the Ḍāmaras, he became their leader. Bimba,
who was the very first to seek refuge with the mendicant from the royal army,
abandoned that king and came to him as well.
Other ministers and counselors, esteemed by Janaka-siṃha,
were seen coming out to meet the king, shameless as they were. Sulakṣaṇa, a swordsman born in the village named Kāṇḍiletra, was there.

In the empty Bhāṅgilā, there was a certain monk who had taken up a seat after walking about. At that moment, Pṛthvīhara set out together with him to conquer the people on the path leading toward Sussala, who were already on their way.

Having conquered that desire to strike down Sussala, who was intent on killing him, he subdued Janakasimha out of anger; and he learned that news from the city-dweller. Then, by means of that man stationed in the city, he [learned] of the citizens who had mounted their horses.
Having assembled all [the people], he seized the opposition of the mendicant;
by him, the kingdom was occupied. Then the king, wandering as a beggar, followed by Pṛthvīhara, suddenly entered the city.
At the bridge situated before Sadāśiva,
Janaka-siṃha, though being pacified and honored,
engaged in battle with his armies; the prowess of Janaka-siṃha’s warriors was seen as they leaped about in their intoxication.
Without fearing defeat, he acted like a great warrior for a moment; then Hara,
together with Alaka,
crossed over by means of his brother’s son as another bridge and destroyed his army.
When the charioteers, horsemen, and citizens had fled along with their kinsmen,
Janaka-siṃha then escaped at night and went to Lahara.
In the morning, the monk Bhikṣupṛthvīhara was intent on seizing his [the king's] back;
following him, the fearless cavalrymen and others once again took refuge [with him].
Out of fear, those who were like gods quickly cast [their weapons] into their own armpits.
Those attendants, led by the Brahmins, fled after abandoning their fasts;
some, guarding the empty chariots of the gods,
were not harmed by the monk when they said, "We have turned back from our fast."

Yesterday, at Janaka’s [sacrifice], we beheld in the army horses leaping with pride and mounted by cavalrymen; even now we remain filled with wonder. [Yet] it was illuminated for a moment by the lamp of the mendicant-king, which is itself subject to instantaneous decay.

By virtue of his paternal uncle’s authority, Tilakasiṃha became the king’s brother-in-law. When Janakasiṃha had passed away, the mendicant-king obtained the power to carry out the destruction of the palace and other such acts against those who followed the enemy faction.
In the meantime, while Tilaka and the others had been taken to Huṣkapura,
they were defeated by Sulhaṇa, Siṃba, and others, together with an endless host of soldiers who had arrived ahead of them,
including Mallakoṣṭha, Janaka, and their troops.
Followed by other vassals who possessed great military strength, he conquered the entire realm in two or three days; yet,
on the path to Viṃśalla, he was struck down by his enemies before they were even noticed.
At that very moment, casting aside all fear, he [beheld] the treacherous warriors who had arrived before him from within the city streets and market avenues, riding upon horses;
with his face framed by a curled beard and knit with a frown, he [confronted them].
With pupils trembling in rage and touching his flared nostrils,
he threatened some, censured others, and likewise broke others;
with a body darkened by the intense heat, he was like a fierce God of Death himself, gasping for breath.
With eyes cast down in disdain upon the guilds of city-dwellers who had previously wronged him— men who raised shouts of benediction and rained down flowers—
he nonchalantly bore his armor placed upon his shoulders.
He bore the hair of horses emerging from the ends of their manes,
grey with dust; and he wore the eyelashes of those steeds as they leaped about,
while his sword remained sheathed amidst the rows of drawn blades.

With lion-roars that were unrestrained and filled with the booming of kettledrums, Sussala entered the city, his forces filling the quarters of the horizon. (A Kulaka) On the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, after twelve days and six months [had passed]. KRT_8_0953ab–KRT_8_0954ab.
In his ninety-seventh year, he returned once more.
Without yet having entered the capital, while searching for the monk who had previously fled, he beheld him on the bank of the Kṣiptikā, clad in bark garments.

When his enemy reached the opposite bank of the river, he departed taking the earth with him; however, on the way, he turned back together with other Lavaneyas who had joined him. Having routed him in battle and bound him—wounded by blows—the king [took him captive].

Then Siṃha entered the capital, Pṛthvīhara’s kinsman. To that proud man, who had departed at that time, she— who was marked by the enjoyments of his rival— became a source of distress, like a courtesan.
The monk, having abandoned Kaśmīra along with Pṛthvīhara and the others,
went to the village named Puṣyāṇanāḍa, which was the refuge of Somapāla. When he had departed, the king, having subdued all the Ḍāmaras, established [his own rule].
In Kheryā, [he slew] Vaṭṭātmaja Malla and Harṣamitra in Kampana;
remembering former injuries, he acted without regard for place or time. [The rest of the verse follows].
Unable even to endure the fragrance arising from contact with the monks,
he cut the throne into pieces and gave it to his servants out of hatred. The Dāmaras, unable to abandon the royal fortune they had acquired through such misconduct, [remained there].

Fearing the king, the two generals did not abandon their efforts to cause an upheaval. But Bhikṣu, though deprived of his kingdom, while living in the territory of his friend, restored the enthusiasm of Somapāla through gifts and honors.
Bimba, seeking assistance, went into the presence of Vismaya;

while he was being held captive by his enemies in battle, the steadfast one abandoned his body. Wandering as a mendicant and devoid of Bimba, he took refuge with those who were vessels of wicked conduct.
Free from shame, he brought that beloved woman from Avaruddha;
then, though possessing only a small force, the powerful one descended upon Śūrapura.

Having conquered Pṛthvīhara, he put the son of Baṭṭa to flight from the battle. When that [ruler] had fled, he brought back the monk once more and entered the land of the Maḍava kings with the intention of subduing the bandits.
Accompanied by the Maṅkhas, Jayya, and others who had joined him from that region,
he went to the field of battle to conquer Kampanāpati. In that conflict,
Harṣamitra’s own soldiers were slain.

Abandoning Vijayeśvara, he fled in fear to Avantipura. Then, the people born in the fields of Vijaya, as well as those originating from various cities and villages, entered the presence of the Wielder of the Discus out of fear.
That place was filled with women, children, cattle, rice, and wealth,
as well as by the king’s soldiers who were armed and mounted on horses;
and it was clearly crowded with those who had climbed aboard, eager to plunder the world.
They were surrounded by a multitude of beggars whose bracelets filled the quarters of the sky;
yet, while those enemies stood in the courtyard of the enemy’s palace— which was protected by a gateway and a rampart of wooden planks— the gods were unable either to kill or to bind them.
In order to burn that camphor-like enemy situated within him, a certain wicked and meritless *ḍāmara* named Janakaraja— born in the village of Katisthalī— ignited a fire there with a pair of bellows.
Such a fool was merciless in his slaughter of endless living beings. Seeing that blazing fire approaching from all sides, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the multitude of creatures.

As if out of fear of being carried away by the current of Death, people were struck down by horses whose traces had snapped and who wandered about with such speed that not even a needle could pass between them. The army was shrouded by masses of smoke, terrifying with their blazing flames.

The sky, with its nets of tawny hair-like flames, appeared as if filled with night-stalkers; the spreading tongues of the smokeless fire bore the illusion of waves of gold from a mass of golden clouds melted by the heat.
Falling from the crowns of the sky-dwellers who were fleeing in terror from the heat, the flickering fragments of flame wandered through the women of the sky like red turbans; meanwhile,
the crackling sound produced by the snapping of long wooden joints resounded.
It rose up like the roar of the celestial Gaṅgā being violently boiled by the heat;
with sparks resembling the very life-breath of creatures terrified by the scorching flames,
it seized the frantic whirling of the path through the dense firmament.

The sky was filled with birds crying out in grief at the movement of corpses, while the earth resounded with the sounds of men burning [the dead]. Overwhelmed by lamentation, they embraced their brothers, husbands, fathers, and sons.
The women, their eyes closed in fear, were consumed by fire. Those reckless men who emerged from within that [fire] were slain outside by cruel,
terrifying beings impelled by Death.

At that moment, so many creatures perished there, even those who were merely scorched and not burnt by that fire. When all within had been stilled and the slayers without were likewise stilled— Kṛt 8.987ab–988ab.
In an instant, that place became silent;
nothing more was heard than the crackling sound of the fire whose flames had diminished,
and the hissing noise of the mass of corpses as they steamed.
The outpourings of blood, fat, and marrow flowed through hundreds of channels;
and a foul stench spread for many yojanas. One [disaster] arose from the wrath of Suśravas, and the second from the plundering of the Dasyus.
Such was the terrible affliction by fire that befell the wielder of the discus;
it was like the destruction of the multitude of beings by the fire at the time of universal dissolution (*saṃvarta*),
or as it occurred during the burning of Tripura or at Khāṇḍava.

On the auspicious twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas, that monk committed a great evil deed; he abandoned both royal fortune and his merits. At that time, when the householders along with their families were consumed by fire...
In thousands of cities and villages, houses fell into desolation.
A rogue named Maṅkha, who lived by scavenging corpses from ships and cities,
arrived like a *kāpālika* ascetic, having obtained great joy through the wealth belonging to him.
Then,
having descended into the field of victory,
that sinful man wandered as a beggar; having encountered Nāgeśvara, he was tormented by agonizing pains.
What blameworthy act was not committed by him in his ancestral land? Yet, the slaying of that betrayer of his father brought joy to all.
When Harṣamitra’s wife fled after her husband had abandoned her, [she was seized].
Pṛthvīhara obtained [the queen] from within the inner apartments of Vijayeśa.
Such a slaughter and destruction of his subjects served as a portent;
then King Sussala, reproaching himself, went forth to fight.

Out of a sense of spiritual urgency regarding his evil deeds, King Janaka quickly arrived near the city of Avantī to undergo the torments of hell; for it is on account of such actions that one performs deeds which bring an end to the happiness of the next world.

It is a marvel that this body, which is easily brought to ruin by fools, is not taken into account. Having made Simba the lord of Kampana, the king drew [him] from Vijayakṣetra and even from elsewhere into the tumultuous circle.
Pṛthvīhara marched against Śamālā from the kingdom of Maḍava;
having been defeated by Mallakoṣṭha, he was forced to abandon his own territory.
Some were cast into the Vitastā, and others into the Cakradharāṅganā.

Many corpses were rendered incapable of being cremated by fire; they were merely wailed over. Then, in Kramarājya, Rilhaṇa conquered Kalyāṇavāḍa and other territories. Thereupon, Ānanda, born of Ananta, became the lord of the gateway (dvārādhipa).

Carrying the lion that had been impaled on a stake, the powerful Pṛthvīhara fought together with Janakasiṃha and others on the bank of the Kṣiptikā. On this day, while the holy sites were being established, there was a place here where bones of those who had perished remained.

In the month of Bhādrapada, that [battle] was carried out by all throughout the days of the earth-shaking conflict, within the interior of the city which resounded with the wailing of widowed heroes and whose paths were overwhelmed by the cries of the helpless women. (A *yugma*).
Then Śūra, the brother of Yaśorāja, arrived from a distant region;
he was made a *śrīvaka* by the king and appointed to the office of *kherī*.
He did nothing unpleasant to the Lavaṇyas, nor did they act against him.
But they spent their time with one another, their mutual friendship remaining hidden.
Then, in the month of Āśvayuja, the king marched out from Śamālā;
however, he was defeated in battle by his enemies at the village of Manīmuṣa.

Having attained excellence through constant practice in battles, the monk— the leader of all heroes— displayed there that same prowess he had previously shown. Tukka, the twice-born, and other principal figures were [confronted] by Bhikṣu, Pṛthvīhara, and others.
In that army led by Sausala,

which was overwhelmed by the downpour and onset of arrows and its foremost heroes slain, there was no one at all in either of the two contending forces who could behold the face of that hero as he moved through the battle like a mendicant.
In a battle lasting many years between Pṛthvīhara and the monk [Rāmapāla],
two horses named Kādambarī and Patākā— yellowish-white and most marvelous— were lost,
by which many other steeds were destroyed.
There was no failure amidst the blows, nor did exhaustion ever overcome you.
In the midst of the army's distress, there was protection through tirelessness and the absence of boastfulness. There was no hero anywhere other than the mendicant who could endure such hardship.

In that army of warriors engaged in hand-to-hand combat, there was no one at all to provide protection during the rout; thus, these many were slain in various ways. Some soldiers from the fresh Ḍāmara forces [perished] during the breakouts.
Like young elephants protected by the lordly elephant who wanders for alms,
no one else was seen at that time to possess such a habit of rising [for the sake of others] as he who, having taken possession of the earth,
himself remained awake every night at the door for alms.
From that time forward, he was always a protector both in front and behind,
like the Viśvedevas at a *śrāddha* ceremony; in battle, the mendicant became a great warrior,
and displaying audacity in combat, he protected his own men on all sides.
Thus,

maintaining unswerving steadfastness and not abandoning my resolve, this effort of mine is not for the sake of a kingdom; rather, it is sufficient to dispel the ill-repute that seeks to thwart the undertaking of my ancestors.
At the moment of their destruction, those protectors of the people were like those without a protector;
having realized their lineage was ruined, they surely came to envy those who possess protectors.
Thinking thus, he acts with firm resolve, enduring hardships;
"I am suffering day by day, bringing grief to my kinsmen.
He knows that for one whose time has not yet come, no calamity can exist.
Who that seeks fame would turn away from rashness?
What is the use of speaking of the devious ways of political action, or how they are carried out?
Having ourselves promised to abide by the path of the sages, we do not speak otherwise.
The *ḍāmaras* did not suspect the monk because of his self-exaltation and prowess;
therefore, they never deprived him of his inheritance. Before he attained sovereignty, other kings who were of royal lineage [did not suspect him].
By reflecting on worldly affairs, they gradually attain proficiency.
Yet, neither in his father nor in his grandfather was anything [of such a nature] seen by him;
for this very reason, he fell into delusion when he previously obtained the kingdom.
If he were to obtain her once again, what talk could there be of rending [her apart]? I know that even Fate was unable to look upon him with indifference. [This is a *cakkalaka* (quatrain).
Knowing the crookedness of women, he was slain through negligence by his own well-wisher.

Holding fast to the hope, "May I obtain the kingdom," he passed the days. King Sussala considered the opinion of the bandits to be for his own benefit; desiring to conquer, he sought an opening by employing both policy and valor.
Remembering his enmity toward his own people during the battle, he did not protect them; they, for their part, did not place their trust in him. For this reason, he did not achieve victory.
Thus, he was disregarded by various factions and their opposing sides due to their differing opinions.

The entire kingdom fell into a state of universal lamentation. For because of their connection with him, even the multitude of trees experienced an indescribable suffering from the fire set by wild hunters intent on capturing them. Alas, what a tragedy! Even that elephant, who was intent on destroying them while in rut, could not find any means of securing their welfare—neither through fate’s adversity, nor from others, nor even from himself.
Thus, when a state of dual sovereignty prevailed due to an unexpected fall of snow,
the army of the Śākya monks defeated the helpless King Sussala.
When the monk-king Harirāja departed once more for Puṣyānanāḍa...
Other lords of the earth, having offered tribute with their hands, performed prostrations before him.
Even Simba, the lord of Kampana, who had previously vanquished Damara,
that hero, brought the entire territory of the Madava kingdom under his sway, having quelled all disturbances.
Having attained a state of coolness through the pacification of his adversaries to that extent,
the king then manifested ancient enmity toward his own kinsmen.
When he was reported to the king as being intent on murder, Ulhaṇa fled.

Mallakoṣṭha was also banished from the kingdom by the king out of anger. Having imprisoned Ānanda, the son of Ananta, as the superintendent of the gates, he appointed the Saindhava named Prajji as the heir-apparent (rājabījina).

Then, accompanied by Śimba, he went to the field of victory and entered that city; having bound its inhabitants while they were unsuspecting, he cast them into prison. His fire of indignation was fanned by the great whirlwind of recollection.

He quenched the water of forgiveness for one who desired to burn his servants. Having impaled Simba upon a stake, he— his intellect overwhelmed by a fit of rage— had him killed along with his two younger brothers, Siṃha and Thakkana-siṃha.

In Kampana, he made Śrīvaṅka the minister; Sujji, the brother of Prajji, having been bound along with Janakasiṃha, was appointed to the position of *rājasthāna*. Furthermore, his ministers were then all foreigners (*vaideśika*).

He was a native of his own country who had followed him while he was staying at Lohara. Then, all of them, filled with apprehension, abandoned him and sought refuge with the enemies. Only one man in a hundred remained in the capital, having taken up a position with the king.

Therefore, even when the calamity has subsided, it cannot be remedied; for the misfortune thus provoked did not return to peace. Where even the servants become apprehensive at the mere mention of another's name, [there the danger is great].
In such an offense, only the punishment of a wise king is praised. Then,
having been summoned by Māgha, Mallakoṣṭha, and others,
Bhikṣu, Pṛthvīdhara, Hara, and the rest returned once more by way of Śūrapura.
"This earth, encircled by the moat of the Vitastā, is inaccessible to my enemies"—
thinking thus, the king abandoned Navamaṭha and proceeded to Rājagṛha.
In the year [of the cycle] *iṣṭānavarta*, during the month of Caitra, while the *ḍāmara*s were eager for battle,
Mallakoṣṭha approached and first seized him in combat.
Together with his cavalry, he engaged in battle within the city.
Then, watched with agitation from the tops of the palaces by the ladies of the royal harem,
the mendicant encamped his army at Kṣiptikārīra.
The *ḍāmaras* carried trees from the king’s gardens to the kitchen for fuel, and they took sprouts of *dūrvā* grass from the stables for the fodder of the horses. Meanwhile,
Pṛthvīhara was rounding up the bandits born in the kingdom of Maḍava.
While he was still making preparations for his camp in the field of victory,
the king,
intent on daring deeds, dispatched an assault force toward Prājji in the month of Vaiśākha to engage in a wrestling match at Koṣṭha.
When that [bridge] suddenly collapsed, those who were wounded and deprived of their support somehow crossed the remaining part of the bridge and fled; meanwhile,
Prajñā entered the city of Mallakoṣṭhāgrya.
The younger brother of Pṛthvīhara, that lord of men, having defeated Sujji,
was unable to reach the further bank of the Vitastā because the bridge had been destroyed;
having burned his houses on this side of the river, he then proceeded to Kṣiptikā.
Thinking that Lavaṇa had reached the city, King Sussala,
agitated, raised his army and came from Vijayakṣetra,
accompanied by his own forces who were eager for the honor of being first and distressed by the fear of the enemy.

Afflicted by him, his deep bridge across the Indus broke apart. On the sixth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, his countless hosts of troops perished there in the water just as they had been consumed by fire under the protection of the Wielder of the Discus (Kṛṣṇa).
Raising his arm to quell the agitation of his troops,
the king fell into the middle of a river, terrified and fallen from his mount;
having been repeatedly rebuked by those unpracticed in crossing waters, he was embraced [by them].
With his body pierced by the weapons of the Tarads, he somehow managed to cross over;
leaving behind the army that had not yet crossed, he proceeded followed by a thousandth part of the troops who had reached the far shore, which was crowded with vassal kings.

Although he had abandoned his infinite army, that king, full of steadfastness, entered the city and captured Mallakoṣṭha and the other leaders in battle. Then Vijaya’s mother, named Sillā, [beheld] her husband abandoned.
He led that army from Vijayeśvara to Devasaras.
Then, having arrived there at the assembly, he was struck down by Pṛthvīhara;
likewise, Ṭikka and Datta were killed, and that royal army was put to flight.
When his entire army had fled, having been routed by those skilled in the science of martial exertion, the Brahmin named Kalyāṇarāja was slain while facing the enemy in battle;
he fell before the force of Sussala’s troops, which was crowded with ministers and *ḍāmara* chieftains.

Pṛthvīhara seized and bound multitudes of armed men. He followed them as far as the banks of the Vitastā; having forcibly pursued those who had fled, he bound the Ojas, Ānanda, the twice-born, and others, and put them to death upon stakes.
The ministers, headed by Janakaśrīvaka, as well as the sons of the king,
having crossed the mountain at Viṣalāṭā, sought refuge with the Khaśas.
Thus Pṛthvīhara, having achieved victory, took the Ḍāmaras captive.

Desirous of victory, he went to the outskirts of the city together with a mendicant. Once again, a battle broke out as before against the king who was besieged in the city, while [the mendicant] from all sides withdrew the flood of men and horses.
By this path, Nirnirōdha became the leader of the army of the Maḍava kingdoms in the royal residence; he was himself a fierce commander who seized the earth from the various vassal clans,
along with Kāśmīra warriors and heroes born of those various lineages.
The entire Ḍāmarakula became invincible on all sides.
Thousands of the Kāśmīrakas, beginning with Śobhaka and belonging to the lineage of Kāka,
as well as others such as Ratna, shone forth, renowned in the Bhaikṣava faction.
While listening with wide-open eyes to the tumultuous sound of musical instruments being played by his own troops,
Pṛthvīhara, out of curiosity, counted the musical instruments; then,
leaving behind the drums and other large instruments, that curious man proceeded to count them one by one.
He destroyed twelve hundred dogs, cooks, drums, and vessels;
likewise, although his army was destroyed, he was accompanied by thirty or twenty princes.
Sussala received the enemies with men of his own country who were of measured strength.
The two kings born of the Avicchaṭa and Kula lineages,
Udayadhaunya and Udayabrahmajajjala, were the lords of Campā and Vallāpura respectively.
The Ojo, Malhaṇa, and Haṃsa [lineages], the Dhurya, Hari, and Haḍauka;
likewise the Kṣatrika, Abhiñjika, Sthāna, Savya, Rāja, and others;
the Biḍālaputra, Nīla, and so forth, born of the Bhāvuka lineage.
Rāmapāla was his natural-born son, and Nandana was his [son];
other kings of various lineages, intent on the fervor of fierce battle,
surrounded their enemies on all sides as they stood prepared to besiege the city.
The king’s own son,
Rilhaṇa, especially took the lead at the front of the battle, as did Vijaya and other horsemen;
while the king himself, exerting his efforts, held his two arms like a suit of armor.
Sujji and Prajji became protectors, skilled in the arts of war.
Sharing with them the foundation of the kingdom,
the lord of the earth properly bore the burden during that great calamity.
His partisans— Bhāgika, Śaradbhāsi, Mummuṇi, Muṅgaṭa,
Kalaśa, and others— were skilled in agitating the enemy factions.
In the territory of King Ṭakka, the son of Lavarāja [ruled] over the earth.
And Kamaliya was the leader of the vanguard for his lord.
The horsemen could not withstand the blows of that powerful warrior, who was adorned with a chowrie and a banner, any more than they could endure the assault of a rutting elephant.
His younger brother Saṅgika, and Pṛthvīpāla, the son of his [Saṅgika’s] brother,
took up the role of flank-guards like the Pañcālas for Phalguna;
with such jewels among servants, he was victorious even when his own kingdom was provoked to rebellion.
With horses acquired through the offering of abundant gold, that lord of the earth,
the king, roamed here and there in battle without any agitation,
like a householder himself at every pavilion during a festival.

For at the outset, his calamity was a cause of terror; yet for that wise man, it became a source of fortitude once it had reached its full extent. The fear that causes weakness at the first onset is not so great when one has reached the middle of the ordeal.
Just as water thrown into the cold does not become cool by immersion, so too [the enemy's army was not cooled];
wherever the darkness of the enemy host advanced, there the king’s army emerged like moonlight— white and black in its various parts.
Once, having made a pact for a simultaneous encounter in battle,
the Ḍāmaras crossed the great river and descended upon the city.
The king, whose military camp was divided between the regions of Asīma and Nagara, [was there].

With only a limited number of horsemen, he himself rushed toward those who were entering. The army of Jaḍḍāmara did not withstand him; driven by him, it fled like a heap of leaves scattered by the winter wind.
Tryānanda, born of the lineage of Kāka, Loṣṭa, Śāhya, Anala,
and others— famous warriors in the army of Ḍāmara— were slain by the king’s soldiers.
Having been brought before the cruel king’s eyes after being struck down by the impact of his spear, [they were executed].
Like outcasts living off the king's bounty, they slaughtered many;
then other monks, having climbed a mountain out of fear,
found themselves surrounded by the enemy's encampments and were on the verge of death.
On that path which was difficult even for a bird to traverse,
the proud monk urged his horses forward to protect them.
Somehow, with his neck pierced by a bird, he repeatedly seized hold of it.
Pṛthvīhara was on his side, as were two or three other great warriors.
When the enemy force was blocked by them— like upsurging coastal mountains against the ocean—
they abandoned Gopācala and ascended other hills.
Then, O King, Nikumbha’s army rose up on the left,
its infantry and horses agitating the entire horizon;
it was devoid of its own forces, which remained occupied with seizing the enemy's rear.
Then, everyone recognized him without doubt, crying out, "The king has been killed!
While King Sussala was still unable to withstand the initial assault,
Prajji arrived at the field of battle accompanied by his younger brothers.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, that assembly of horsemen produced a great sound from the clashing of their own weapons and the shouts of "Well done! [p. 208] KRT_8_1111ab–cd.
When the battle had been quelled by those two, he— along with his son and the Wind-god—
was like a forest fire extinguished by showers of rain from the months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada.
In that time of intense conflict, no other such [encounter] had ever occurred.
Such was that day, a touchstone for the grit of heroic valor. That wave of armies arrived with such delay that there was no joining of hands among those who desired to uproot [the enemy].
On that critical day, each came to know the other’s power—
the king’s power over the monk, and the monk’s power over the king.
Consequently, they were shown right there how to fight against those kings of Maḍava.
Having encountered a battle on the banks of the Kṣiptikā,
Pṛthvīhara was captured by the king Yaśorāja, who had arrived from a distant region and,
desiring to subdue his enemies, raised him to the status of a provincial ruler (maṇḍaleśvara).

In former times, upon seeing his face in battles where his valor had been displayed by Lavaṇa during the task of [subduing] Khara, hundreds trembled with fear. He was the one who bestowed saffron unguents, parasols, horses, and other honors.
The king brought that state of being worthy of universal acclaim to himself, as if it were his own. Though long afflicted by calamity, people, desiring health,
fixed their hopes upon him, like a sick man upon a new physician.
The king appointed the eldest of the remaining sons born of Garga, named Pañcacandra,
to act as a counterweight against Mallakoṣṭha.
Protected by his mother under the name Śiśuśuṇḍa, he grew up gradually.

Supported by his paternal kinsmen as followers, he attained some degree of renown. In the battle, those defeated by King Yaśorāja— some of whom were commoners and others were *ḍāmaras*— took refuge in his faction.
The monk Pṛthvīhara proceeded to his own dwelling;
the king, facing the wrestling arena, went out to meet the Lord of the Immortals.
In the meantime, the master of the wrestling arena dismissed the thieves at night.
He set fire to the empty capital in the presence of Sadāśiva. When Pṛthvīhara came again and again to fight, Prajji, Sujja,
and others waged war on the bank of the Kṣiptikā.
Again and again that handsome one, burning down houses in the city,
brought about the state of desolation almost everywhere along the excellent banks of the Vitastā,
creating battles here and there that put lives in peril.
Then the king attacked Lahara with vast forces.

As they crossed the river without a bridge, some of his followers—such as Mandira, Kandara, and others—fell into the water due to the breaking of their footing; yet those who were like Yama himself remained steadfast.
Mallakoṣṭha, having been dismissed by the king, went to the land of Darad;
though accompanied by his son, Śuḍḍā took refuge in a wave amidst the surging waters.
They were brought into the presence of the king by Jyayyaka, the Lavanya.
Then Janaka, Śrīvaka, and the others emerged from within the poison-vine;
at the arrival of autumn, when the heat had been overcome by the onset of the waves,
the king, accompanied by Yaśorāja, then went forth to the forest retreat.
Protecting his army, which had been broken out of fear of Pṛthvīhara,
the son of Sajja, named Ḍomba— a prince who stole the minds of men—
was slain in battle at Suvarṇasānu, Uraga, Grāmaśūra, Purā, and other places.
Constantly engaged in this way, the king experienced victory and defeat in turn.
When the city of Śrī-Kalyāṇapura was brought to ruin by Pṛthvīhara and others,
Nāgavaṭṭa and his followers met their deaths in battle at Śrī-Vakre.
In the month of Pauṣa, Tikkā, desiring to destroy her mother’s end, dispatched Devasaras against Suvarṇasānu, the beloved of Garga;
accompanied by the king’s own army, she, who had conquered her enemies, [proceeded].
Suddenly, having fallen upon him with a *ṭikka* weapon, he was struck down in battle. That protector committed a second murder of a woman, being utterly merciless.
What indeed is the difference between animals, barbarians, thieves, and *rākṣasas*?
Having abandoned their mistress, a woman who was being slaughtered, they fled; it is a marvel that these men, though resembling cattle, took up their weapons once again.

Realizing that Maḍava had once again returned to his bed from which he had only slightly departed, the king set out for Vijayeśvara. To the sons of the Malla king, their own tongue was like a wicked person.
In matters of sovereign power, calamity became the harbinger of misfortune. Moreover,
in this present age,
servants who have adopted harsh conduct display only the chaff of faults, having cast aside the essential core.

From childhood, Yaśorāja had been accustomed to the use of indecent and harsh speech; devoid of respect, O Queen, he grew weary of him. That man of base birth, accompanied by a great army, remained stationed at Avantipura.
Rising from his state of discomfiture, he sought refuge with the opposing faction;
when that [enemy] had joined the side of the foe, the lord of the earth, overwhelmed, fled from the field of victory along with all his finest forces.

Fie on this kingdom for whose sake even he endured that he should have his life taken away while being insulted on the road by those who were like thieves and outcasts, plundering him! Having fled from Māgha, he entered the city named Vaya.
He suspected even his own sons of treachery toward his servant;
then, utterly despairing, the lord of the earth, when the king of Kaśmīra had perished,
placed his head upon the lap of the enemy’s faction.
The fame of former kings such as Rudrapāla and others was eclipsed by the Prāgjyotiṣa king, who surpassed them with his virtues of valor, generosity, statesmanship,
and loyalty; and it was by that very man of pure renown that [the lineage] was further increased in this land.
The authority over both weapons and scriptures has been overturned by the tyranny of Time. Yaśorāja, having met with the monk, consulted with him:
"The Ḍāmaras, fearing your prowess, do not wish for your kingdom."

"Having once again raised a tumult, we, by the power of our incantations, shall either seize the kingdom ourselves or depart for another region. When they had thus deliberated, [the king] heard that Chuḍḍā had been killed at Daratpura.
Having arrived, Mallakoṣṭha also entered his own dwelling.
Then a rain, difficult to endure and known by the number ninety-nine,
began to fall— a most terrible phenomenon that brought about the end of all beings in the world.
In the spring, all the *ḍāmaras*, returning once more by their respective ancient routes, besieged the king who was stationed in the city. Meanwhile,
the resolute Sussaladeva remained there day and night.
He was the vessel for the intense fury of beginning boundless series of battles;
by those violent men, skilled in the arts of burning, plundering, and fighting,
a calamity was brought about that exceeded even previous upheavals.
Desiring to enter the city,
Yaśas, Rājabhikṣu, Pṛthvīhara, and the others stood upon the great highway, which was free from obstruction.
Then, after several days of battle had passed in that conflict...
Yaśorāja was slain by Kayya’s son,
Vijaya, through a mistake for someone else; indeed, while displaying his prowess in battle against Sussala, he was struck down along with the cavalryman named Vijaya.
Deceived by his own men—who, seeing that he possessed horses and armor of the same color as their own—those unrestrained men armed with spears struck him with blows from their spears.
[They thought: "This mendicant is capable of giving us the kingdom, and therefore he shall also kill us."
It is heard that he was killed by those very Ḍāmaras out of fear;
just as his trusting master had been deceived by him through treachery,
so too did he, being trusted, meet his death swiftly in battle.

Having fought the Ḍāmaras here and there, Pṛthvīhara then returned once more to the bank of the Kṣiptikā and engaged them in battle. There, he encountered soldiers stationed by command who lived off the alms of monks.
Manly valor was displayed, which humbled both oneself and others,
through calamities such as arson and the slaughter of great warriors;
every single day during that time was fraught with terror.
The earth, scorched by the fierce heat of the sun, trembled incessantly;
great destructive winds blew, shattering trees and mountains.
The sky was filled with heaps of dust raised by the wind, like the rutting elephants of pride.
When the sky was rent asunder by thunderclaps that shattered the very pillars supporting it,
the great battle then commenced on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
In a single house, they set fire to wood, stones, and *ḍāmaras*; that fire,
fanned by the wind or even arising from lightning,
blazed forth unrestrainedly upon a single spot, consuming the entire city.
At that time, it was seen approaching like a vast array of elephants;
the smoke rising from the Great Bridge (Bṛhatsetu) belonging to the Lord of the Bees (Mākṣikasvāmin) suddenly reached the pleasure garden of Indradevī’s palace.

Then, in an instant, the entire city appeared ablaze. Neither the earth, nor the quarters, nor the sky could be discerned amidst the darkness of smoke. The sun became visible and invisible by turns, appearing like the hide on the face of a *huḍukka* drum.
Then the houses, shrouded in smoke and darkness, were repeatedly revealed by the blazing fire as if for the sake of never being seen again;
the Vitastā appeared with its two banks embraced by the flaming dwellings.
It was like the sword-blade of Kṛtānta, smeared with blood on both edges.
Due to its contact with the upper door-panel of the cosmic egg,
the clusters of flames— falling and rising as they grew— were transformed into a forest of golden umbrellas.
Resembling a mountain of gold with its high and low peaks of flame,
the fire bore a row of clouds upon its crest under the guise of smoke.
From within its flames, houses repeatedly emerged as they appeared.

"The houses have fallen into the Vitastā, its waters heated by the blazing [fire]; thus did the river perceive the suffering caused by the agony of Aurva’s heat, thinking, 'These people are unburnt'— the hope of the deluded householders."
The garden groves, their young shoots ablaze, took flight into the sky along with birds whose wings were set on fire.
The white palaces of the gods, enveloped in flames, appeared as if they were melting away.

The rivers within the city also attained a state of desolation, as they were abandoned by the crowds of people who, fearing the conflagration, fled along with their bathing-places, dwellings, boats, and bridges— creating the illusion of the peaks of the Himalayas embraced by the twilight clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
What more need be said? Devoid of monasteries, temples, houses, towers, and the like, the city was reduced in a mere moment to a burnt forest.
When the city was nothing but heaps of clods of earth, [the king], dark with smoke, remained without a refuge.
A certain tall and large-bodied man was seen, resembling a scorched tree.
Then, as the armies moved toward their blazing dwellings for protection,
the king became joined by about a hundred warriors.

Unable to cross the Vitastā because its bridge was broken, he was surrounded by his endless enemies who had found their opportunity to strike him down. He reflected upon the city that had been burnt, his own ruined state, and his lost subjects.

The king, perceiving that death was near, felt profound despondency. Then, suspecting that he who was about to depart had fled toward the west, Kamalīyā was alerted by others and spoke these words: "O Lord, where have you gone?"
Turning his face, which was radiant with a passionate smile and marked by the scent of sandalwood paste,
that resolute man, having restrained his horse, addressed him:
"Therefore, for the sake of the earth, I shall today [perform] this encounter with Hammīra."
The king acted as did his proud grandfather, Abhijit.
"From where has this heir come, that he is our brother, or that I am his?
That Harṣadeva, seeing us, has fled while there was still work remaining."
"Who indeed, having entered the ranks of the proud, would abandon his own land—
unwatered yet drenched with the blood of his own limbs— just as a tiger leaves behind its bloody skin?
Having spoken thus, he pulled up the reins and raised the horse’s head with its face turned upward.
Desiring to touch [it], he raised his sword with both hands. Then, seizing the horse by its bridle, the son of the salt-merchant king said:
"While servants are present before me, kings are not worthy of entry."
Standing there, overwhelmed by the blows, one man approached from his house toward the king,
Pṛthvīpāla, who was in that very crisis;
out of affection for him, the monarch praised the son of the Kaula woman.
He considered the service he had rendered as a favor bestowed upon himself in exchange for his own liberation.
Then,
those enemies, stationed in three battle arrays, began discharging arrows.
All those warriors, intoxicated by their mounts, were slain by his left hand. As he urged on his horse, by fate such was his state that even many thousands of adversaries were struck down.
With a small army, reflected in the circle of his enemies' swords,
the king appeared like Viśvarūpa come to his aid;
like a hawk toward sparrows, or a lion toward deer.

King Sussala alone put many enemies to flight. As the foot soldiers who were blocking him fell, the horsemen— whose momentum was checked by the formation— struck even at the tips of the horses' hooves.

All those great warriors, whose tongues of flame were reflected [in their armor], were to be slain; they were struck down like red streams of blood from a severed vein. Having wrought a slaughter of his enemies, he returned at the end of the day.
The city, abandoned by the eater of oblations (Agni), was filled with rising tears; yet,
even though that unconquered one had fallen into such a state, the enemy’s regard for victory remained firm, while he himself,
due to the destruction of his beloved city, cast away all regard for life.
Whether waking, sleeping, moving, standing, bathing, eating,
or even departing, he was constantly called out by his enemies as they gazed upon him with tears.
When the entire circle of the kingdom had its store of all foodstuffs consumed by fire, [he remained].

Then, suddenly and all at once, a terrible and unbearable famine arrived. With their stores exhausted by long-standing calamities, the people were besieged by bandits outside; their livelihoods were undermined, their movements restricted, and their houses burnt down.

Unable to obtain wealth from the royal palace, Vidhura departed; O Queen, even the neighboring lords quickly perished there during that famine. Those who longed for food entered dwellings where only the remnants of what had been spat out by fire remained.
The fire, fed by people afflicted by hunger, burned day after day. At that time,
the bridges over the rivers were crossed by people whose bodies were swollen from the sprinkling of water,
while their sense of smell was blocked by foul-smelling corpses.

The white earth, strewn everywhere with heaps of skeletons and fragments of skulls from corpses that had been devoured, bore the appearance of the vow of a *kāpālika* ascetic. The bodies of those moving with great difficulty were emaciated and tall, darkened by the rays of the sun.

Afflicted by hunger, the people appeared like scorched tree stumps. Then, due to continuous fighting, after some days, it spread as a false report that Pṛthvīhara had been wounded by an arrow and was dead.

When he had been rendered helpless by a severe blow and covered over by the people, the king heard that news; he rejoiced and fought with great vigor. Like a clever courtesan, she [the army] captivated him by displaying a feigned eagerness.

The Goddess of Victory, though she tempted him, did not approach him as he was filled with longing. (KRT 8.1215cd) Fate, whose heart is exclusively perverse, feigns favorability and then inflicts persistent suffering.
(KRT 8.1216ab) It utterly blinds one who is traveling through the sky by revealing a blazing thunderbolt for the purpose of identifying a great medicinal herb. (KRT 8.1216cd)

At the end of his long experience of suffering, the king awaited with his heart’s desires the festival of his arrival, as if it were the fruit of his ascetic penance. His love was filled with affection, and his kind words were imbued with respect.
And she who, through her propriety, maintained a courtesy toward him as if he were her own son—
his beloved wife, for whom all royal splendor was but a mere instrument—
Queen Meghamañjarī passed away at that time. (Tilaka)
Perceiving the world as a weary journey devoid of delight,
he saw no purpose whatsoever in life or in sovereignty.
Emaciated by news of her husband’s calamity, she turned her face toward Kashmir.
Out of eagerness, she had set out on her journey and was exhausted near the city of Phullapura;
first, she was a guest of the hope of seeing him, and then, due to that bad news,
the king was touched by an even greater surge of grief.
Because they had not witnessed her harshness, their devotion remained untarnished;
those four excellent women of the retinue followed her. Even though she was no longer visible, they did not abandon their overflowing devotion.
There was a cook named Tejas, who was highly honored among the servants.
On another day, while he was away, his own head—
which had been placed upon a stone by him while lost in thought— was struck by that very stone and fell into the river.
Through the fury of challenges and invocations that cause one to forget grief,
the king’s enemies became his benefactors by virtue of their duties.
Then, with a weary mind and desiring to abdicate the kingdom,
he brought his son— who had passed beyond childhood— from Loharācala;
and he installed his nephew named Bhāgika as the lord of the province (maṇḍaleśvara) among the subjects.

And having led him away, he established a guard over the two regions of the treasury and the harem. Having reached the presence of Varāha, the king, who had come forward to meet his dear son, embraced him and became the object of both joy and sorrow.

After three years, the prince returned to his own realm with his wife; seeing his father in a state of inner distress, he was filled with remorse. With a face bowed by grief, he entered the city, which was reduced to nothing but heaps of earth.
Like a forest consumed by a forest fire, the earth was covered with smoke from funeral pyres.
Then, on the first day of the month of Āṣāḍha, Janaka consecrated him in the kingdom;
having explained the entire system of governance, he spoke to him with a voice faltering with tears.

"O Hero, bear that burden which your deluded fathers and paternal uncles were unable to carry; this weight has been entrusted to you. The King made his son a fit vessel for the mere formalities of imperial sovereignty."

Deluded by fate, he did not entrust you with authority in that matter. At the mere announcement of the prince’s consecration, the calamities— such as sieges of the city, floods, diseases, thieves, and other afflictions— subsided.
And likewise, the goddess Earth became abundant with crops;
the famine duly subsided in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
In the meantime, Siṃhadeva, bringing about the destruction of his enemies in battle—
Informed by whisperers that he was a traitor to his father,
the prince, without reflecting on the truth of the matter, dispatched him out of anger to be bound; however,
the son of Kayyā had already understood that beforehand.
In the presence of him who was fierce with a wrathful smile, he became speechless;
yet, by merely providing protection, he rendered the king’s command not in vain. Out of mental distress, he did not eat, in order to produce confidence in his father.
On another day, he set out to go into his presence along with that son;
thinking that he was impossible to dissuade because he was suspicious, the father, feigning conciliation, diverted him from the paths by means of his ministers.
But he, having entered unobserved, resolved within himself:
"I shall bind him and place him in prison. Thinking thus, he said:
"Fie on this kingdom, for the sake of which fathers and sons [treat] one another..."
Lacking confidence, they do not sleep peacefully anywhere during the nights.
For those whose sons, daughters, friends, and servants are merely a dwelling place for suspicion—
who knows who among kings can truly be a ground of trust for them?
He was the son of a certain cowherd named Sthānaka, who lived near the notorious village called Sāhya;
in his childhood, he had been raised by the sons of Ḍāmaras through the work of tending cattle.
Having taken up arms, he gradually attained the status of a trusted servant to King Ṭikka;
from the first year onwards, one named Utpala became a confidant of the lord of the earth,
who desired the destruction of his enemies.
For he [the sage] said to him, "Go and kill that beggar," while he had already accepted the gift of sovereignty and the task of killing;
and he [the king] promised him regarding that matter, and [the sage] bound him with great supernatural powers.
He attended upon him with gifts and even bestowed upon him the title of "Lord of the Treasury" (Gañjapati).
With his mind swinging like a swing between the desire for enjoyments, fear of his master,
and anxiety, he could not determine whether a particular matter was to be undertaken or avoided.

In that very place, the king’s daughter-in-law gave birth to a child; for her sake, the king sent her various appropriate gifts, just as a father would. She, however, became suspicious of the reason for such excessive hospitality.
She questioned her husband persistently, and he explained it to her:
"One must not commit treachery against one's master;
for this reason, that Sussala would slowly kill you himself, thinking, 'This man is a traitor.'"
It would be better for that very person who inspires trust to be killed there, if such a killing should occur;
thus the master’s family, including his sons and others, would partake in prosperity.
Urged by his wife, he wavered in his resolve; having informed Tika of the situation, he was bound with ropes. Then, as the king went back and forth, desiring to seize him, [Tika intervened].

Deluded by fate, he placed his trust in him as if in a son. For those whose fortune is exhausted, their intellect becomes perverted; they place trust in a son or in one who has taken refuge with an enemy—what indeed is not turned upside down?
Fools, blinded by greed for their own self-interest,
do not consider the arrival of calamity, just as those greedy for honey do not consider the danger from bees;
they are then oppressed by the enemy and by the king, and consequently fall into ruin.
The king then caused his son to take up the *utpaloka* headgear and the *yaṣṭika* staff, as well as the *nīvī*. Having abandoned the conquered Devasaras, O Kārikas,
he went to the village called Vāṣṭaka, situated within the district of Kherī.
In various battles near the vicinity of Kalyāṇapura,
he brought even the great warriors led by Bhikṣukoṣṭheśvara to humiliation; meanwhile,
from the midst of the mendicants and others, Sujji seized the one born of the crow clan.
In battle, he seized the illustrious Mahāvīra alive;
having first brought about the defeat of Vijaya, who belonged to the faction of Bhava,
the king then set fire to his houses located in Kalyāṇapura.
When Vaḍosaka was burnt down, the mendicant, having lost his refuge,
abandoned that land and took up residence in the village of Kākaruha in Śamālā.
Out of fear of Vijaya, the younger brother of Bhavakīya, he [approached] the king...

Having been captured by that fierce man, he was bound and cast into prison. Having stationed Rilhaṇa, who was followed by a vast army, in Śūrapura, the king also placed Rājapurī under siege, fearing an attack.
Thus, by his upright conduct, having shattered the fierce and violent [enemy],
he saw that only a small portion of the task of conquering the foe remained.
The mendicants and the Lavaneyas had reached the exhaustion of their power.
Fearing a powerful enemy, they considered going abroad; for,
due to the manifestation of some ill fortune among those who had joined the faction of mendicants,
their lives, despite being lived, became as if lifeless because of a lack of joy.

Remembering the crookedness of Somapālaka, he turned back, reflecting that at the end of winter he would make the ground of the cremation ground his royal city. For the king, whose disturbances in his own country were now almost entirely stilled—
The perception that he had traversed the very limits of the ocean was conceived [of him].
When the people had been destroyed by the flood, he alone remained as the sole survivor;
year after year, in that kingdom, he regarded each year as being as long as an entire age.
Due to the calamities of unhappiness, fear, poverty, the loss of loved ones, and the like,
that period of his reign brought torment to everyone;
for what can a man achieve through the cruelty and deceitfulness of his prowess?
Since successes depend upon the diverse dispositions of the Creator, [the outcome is uncertain]:
one may pass by a certain person standing before him as if he were darkness, while at another, Hari casts his glance back as if toward a past age;
or, like a frog, one might leap over a nearby king to reach someone further away. Thus, it is clearly seen that the course of destiny is indeed irregular.
Formerly, he lived among those such as Uccala who were slain through misplaced trust;
he was one who constantly kept his weapons unsheathed,
yet having heard from those learned in ancient lore the history of Vidūratha and others, he did not speak of it even during moments of play.
While women were being enjoyed, he cast a gaze clear with confidence upon the lotus; that he trusted it so persistently,
as if it were a kinsman—
who else but Fate could be credited there with such delusion?

When either Ṭikka or Sujji, the lords of the earth, had been slain, they said to Utpala, "We know you to be one who performs deeds equal to theirs. But Sujji did not trust him; he, however, desired to kill the king.
In every instance he was ready, never again allowing the occasion to pass;
for the king, who was filled with resentment due to the delay in the promised [gift],
in order to produce confidence, brought his own son from the celestial lake as a hostage.
"Having taken Vyāghra, Praśastarāja, and others who are fierce yet equal to myself, this task of mine shall be accomplished by them," he said to the king. (KRT 8.1282)

Having repeatedly gathered from his armies three or four hundred infantrymen who were capable of enduring hardship, he once set out together with them. [Tilaka] [He went] toward that slayer who was always nearby, ever seeking an opportunity [to strike]. [Kṛt 8.1283ab–1284ab]
By the gift of beloved food and other such things, [the horse] manifested the effect of inner joy.
The king, who was devoted to horses, in order to restore to health the horse known as Mandurācakravartin who was staying in the city and was unwell— KRT_8_1284cd, KRT_8_1285ab, KRT_8_1285cd.

At that moment, he dismissed his own attendants, headed by the sons of Lakṣmaka and Pratihāraka, leaving himself with only a few followers. Upon hearing from trustworthy messengers that Śṛṅgāra, the son of Lakṣmaka, had arrived, he sent them away.
He brought to the king’s ears that desire to create the *utpala* [poem].

(KRT 8.1287cd) Even when an act of violence has been observed, the perception of kinship may still arise toward one whose end of life is near, just as it does toward a sacrificial animal at the slaughterhouse. (KRT 8.1288ab–cd)

That curse of Gāndhārī, those words spoken by the seer in his wrath, and even those portents revealed his own eye as being non-terrestrial; yet that [eye], unable to save its own lineage, rendered even Vaikuṇṭha powerless. Knowing this, who indeed can alter what is destined to be?
Dismissing it as false, the protector of the earth demonstrated—
With his finger, he pointed to those blue lotuses and others standing right before him and spoke thus:
"This son of mine has become an enemy through [past] association; though unwilling, he seeks my own well-being. Prompted by himself or by others, he points you out as wicked, O Blue Lotus."
Concealing with a smile the transformation caused by fear through their audacity, they spoke thus:
"The Lord says that we must speak.
Then, when they had departed, [he looked at] those who were motionless as if slightly apprehensive.
Through the doorkeeper, he summoned two or three of his chief physicians into his presence. With a distracted mind, sighing deeply as he pondered,
he found no pleasure in witnessing the dances, songs, and other performances, his eyes filled with tears.
Maintaining his delusion, he considered even those who were mostly foreigners to be trustworthy; like a celestial being about to fall from the sky due to the exhaustion of his merit,
he was filled with apprehension as the king’s courtiers became suspicious when their lord was deluded by deceit.
Some, being senseless, cried out for another donor;
this indeed is that grasping by the force of Time,
that living beings, even though they know [the truth], fall into a state of delusion regarding what must be done.
For two days, during every single moment,
the lotuses and other flowers anxiously awaited her gaze;
on the third day, the king, seeking a private moment with them, spoke to them in secret.
"Having bathed at dawn, you all go repeatedly to the house to eat.
Having completed his daily ritual up to the worship of the deities,
he then summoned Utpala by messengers while remaining in private at midday.

Trusting in the success of his mission, he emerged from the royal palace with a sense of urgency; accompanied by his followers, he entered the presence of the king with apprehension, while the gatekeeper barred his way. The king then admitted his younger brother, Vyāghra, who had been detained at the entrance.
He also commanded the remaining servants to stand outside.
As some trusted attendants were lingering, he spoke these words in anger:
"The truth shall arise against him who is a traitor here."
An elderly betel-bearer was left behind by him,
as well as the learned minister of peace and war, Rāhila, who remained close at hand.
Both messengers of Ṭikka, named Arghadeva and Tiṣyavaiśya, were also there.
In that regard, as a consequence, Āsātā and the consciousness of the unknown lotus [will arise].
Vāḍautsa, known as Sukharāja, a Ḍāmara honored by the monks,
shall go to see the feet of the Lord for the sake of accomplishing that task.

Having spoken thus to the king, who was not far away with his army during those days, Utpala created a tumult for the sake of his own protection. And while the king remained there, [Utpala thought], "I have a task to perform with him."

Having addressed that Praśastarāja, he quickly led him into the side chamber. Having entered the secluded outer circle and observed it, he ensured the door was bolted, his own movements remaining unobserved.
With his hair wet from bathing, wrapped in a cloak because of his aversion to the cold,
he had his entire body covered and lay upon a seat with his sword drawn.
Seeing the king seated, [the tiger] said, "Such an occasion as this would not occur;
make a request to the lord of the earth.
By that sign, he was distracted under the pretext of prostrating at the king's feet.
Having approached the queen, he seized her sword which was resting on a seat;
seeing it unsheathed, his eyes rolled in agitation, and the king cried out, "Alas! Woe! What treachery! even as these words were still upon his lips.

First he struck him on the left side; likewise, the king of excellent majesty then struck him on the head. This was a pair [of verses]. Then the tiger’s chest was repeatedly wounded by those two at that time.
He struck there once more, yet the blue-lotus-eyed one did not strike back;
for by that very first blow, which had shattered the chain of his ribs,
he considered him to be one whose entrails were drawn out like strings and whose life had departed.

Having gone to the edge of the darkness, Rāhila, wishing to cry out, was struck twice or thrice on the back by a tiger; yet he did not give up his life-breaths. Leaving behind the betel-bearer and walking along, Jājaka abandoned the *kaṅkola* and other spices.

The wretched man was protected out of compassion by his own people with lotuses alone. When internal agitation arose, a plundering was carried out by those stationed in the outer pavilion, such as the *ṭikkakas* and others, who were seized by malice and raised their weapons.
Realizing that Utpala had been slain by Rājña,
those stationed in the camp then [acted] to reassure their own people being struck down outside;
showing his sword still wet with blood, Utpala, whose body was like a mountain of darkness, [spoke].
"I have slain the king; his army must not be abandoned," he said.
Hearing those words so difficult to bear, the king's servants fled somewhere out of fear; yet those who followed his enmity, finding joy within other women, remained in their positions.
As they were departing, Maṇḍapattrīkṣṇa struck one named Nāgaka,
a follower of the king who had entered through the gate with sword drawn.
He was a servant of Trailokyaka, the guardian of the monarch’s bedchamber.

Reviled and betrayed by the *ṭikkaka*s and others, the sole gatekeeper was cast down; he who was the ornament of the Bhāvuka lineage, running with his staff and sword, stood out as the most excellent among the king’s dependents whose courage had failed.

Having seen him, they departed through the side gate; Tīkṣṇa, however, fell to the ground, wounded by the blows of the prince’s servants. When that host of princes had become a vessel for the turbidity of ill-repute, [the king]— KRT_8_1326ab–KRT_8_1327ab.
The supreme cleansing of his embarrassment was accomplished by his own blood.
Having struck down the body of the Daśika who had spoken in agreement with him,
the wise twice-born man named Nonā, having stepped forward, ascended to the state of royalty through his sharp arguments.
Seeing those sharp arrows flying unimpeded toward the interior of the village, not even a single armed man rushed forward out of fear, as if they were fixed in a painting. Then,
those of royal lineage, who were objects of the king's affection, departed.
Leaving the courtyard empty and their bodies heavy, they remained there, devoid of people;
having repeatedly remembered and recounted those various cowards from the time of Harṣadeva’s report onwards, they felt as if they had taken up a great burden.

Born from contact with evil deeds, we are unable to act out of exhaustion— those who have the audacity to utter the names of the most sinful among sinners. Regarding their ascent to the pavilion as coming from a woman, they consider it a great feat of manliness.
Some of his chief sinners beheld their lord slain,
speaking with a trembling caused by the slight impact of the ritual sprinkling of water,
while biting his lip to express the inner torment of his heart.
With the thought, "How have I been deceived? and "Is this indeed [my beloved]?", he kept his eyes fixed exactly as they were even at the end of his life;
his face darkened with rising tears from the wounds.
With the glow of the lingering smoke from the fire of his inner wrath now extinguished,
the saffron and sandalwood paste on his face had become indistinct,
as if covered by a thick film of water from a recent wound.
With his matted hair clotted with dried blood, naked and fallen upon the ground,
his hands and feet sprawled out, and his neck hanging down from the top of his shoulders.
Seeing him, those lowest of men did not show even the slightest courtesy; they reviled him, saying, "Enjoy the fruit of your lack of modesty!
Having bound him to a horse or a carriage, they did not consign him to the funeral pyre.

Nor was he able to do so by those who fled to save their own lives. Let alone this task, which could only be accomplished with delay, even the wood of the frying pans was reduced to ashes; and though prepared, there was no one who did not consign his own body to the fire.

Having mounted each of their royal horses, they fled; the camp, having been plundered by the *ḍāmaras*, moved through the villages. Neither son protected his father, nor did the father protect his son.
Whether dead, slain, or plundered, as they moved along the road with their kinsmen,
not a single weapon-bearer was seen there who, remembering his pride and dignity on the path,
would abandon both his weapon and his garment even when being dragged away by enemies.
Lavarāja, Yaśorāja, and the twice-born Vyāyāmavedin—
these three, as well as King Kāṇḍa, were slain by heroic conduct; thereafter,
Utpala and the others fled upon seeing the camp not far away.
Having entered, they cut off the head of the lord of the earth and carried it away.
When they had gone to the celestial lake, the king, with his head severed,
became an object of public spectacle for the villagers, like a slain thief.
Thus, on the new moon day of Phālguna in the third year [of his reign], he was killed by treacheries; having lived for fifty-five years,
he passed away while Siṃhadeva was reclining in a pleasure-sleep, according to what was heard.
Having arrived, the one named Prema brought this distressing news to Dhātṛ.
That majestic power which is expected when one is armed upon hearing unpleasant tidings—
even though he had laid down his weapons, he who was devoted to his father experienced it then.
His memory lost through delusion, he regained consciousness after a long time;
with his fortitude shattered by various sorrows, he lamented in broken and indistinct words:
"By making diligent efforts to rid the kingdom of all thorns for my sake..."

O Great King, have you, being base, brought yourself to such a state? Seeing your enemies without cause, you go toward them at the end for the sake of purifying your enmity; yet even as you go, O proud one, my child, you fall from the ground of your own self-respect.

When enmity was restrained by you, your father and brother are now in heaven, free from anger; yet you remain here, ill at ease with rage. You harbor a longing for Anaraṇya, Kṛpa, Droṇa, Jāmadagnya, and others.
Do not harbor even a moment’s resentment toward those whose enmities have been washed away by their noble lineage.
O King, it is your own anger, resting upon you, that is to be pitied; I am merely the one who purifies it. I do not grieve over the fact that the three worlds have fallen under your dominion.
“Your face, which used to be radiant with the thrill of affection and sweet with tender words when you saw me, now seems like that of a stranger to me”—
thus lamenting, and other things as well, his agitation was barely perceptible beneath his profound composure.

He saw his father’s kinsmen standing before him, rendered speechless by shame, grief, and fear; that which anger would have taught them, courtesy restrained. Nevertheless, he addressed them in this manner, somewhat harsh with reproach.
Having observed your noble lineage through your treasuries, you performed acts of hospitality;
yet, fie on you and your weapons, for at my father’s end, you acted with such reversal—
just as those who live on leftovers did when my paternal uncle was slain.
"Alas, fie! Even that success of yours, who are worthy of honor, is not attained even now!
Thus reproaching them, he was restrained by two or three ministers who had approached him, as if they were hearing what ought to be done.
Some said that he had departed for Lohara, abandoning the kingdom;
others spoke of haste there at the end of the night, alleging a danger from mendicants.
Relying upon the son of Garga, Pañcacandra, the king [acted] with his ministers.
Others, for the most part steadfast, spoke against the practice of dual sovereignty: "Indeed,
when a mendicant intends to enter another city as if it were his own home, no one offers opposition— provided there is no Sussala."

Out of self-doubt regarding such ministers, the king, with inner distress, spoke these words: "Tomorrow you shall see what must be done. He remained unsettled by his expectation of time, while the calamity of his paternal uncle’s death was clearly manifest.
Then he gave instructions to the guards, who were consecrated to protection, regarding the treasury and other matters:
"With cries raised and leaping about as they wander here and there..."
The city became resonant with people calling out to one another;
that night-watch became as terrifying to all beings as a row of intoxicated *vetālas* or as the onset of the Night of Doom.
Surrounded by ministers whose thoughts were as steady as lamps flickering in a windless place,
the king, remaining there, reflected thus within himself:
"In this doorless, dark house, fierce with a gale and utterly empty..."
Even my father has been slain while I live helplessly in this void.
Alas! Until this unbearable slaughter is washed away, how shall I be able to look upon the faces of honorable men in social gatherings?
"How will the army commanders come from those regions ruled by enemies,
by paths that are difficult to traverse even with snow and frost?"—
as he was reflecting thus, his mind was seized by intense anxiety.
That terrible night passed with great difficulty for him who was filled with fear. At dawn, having gone out to the quadrangle to reassure the citizens,
he dispatched mounted messengers to search for the lost army camp.
Then the clouds began to embrace the earth, which was devoid of openings due to the movement of the needle-like tips of the arrows; meanwhile,
the clouds with futile armies could not even obtain the name of "army" from afar.
When they had desisted and been restrained, the king reflected for a moment:
"Whatever was seized by each person has now been relinquished by me;
and safety has been granted to those who took refuge with me, even though they were guilty."

Thus he caused his command to circulate throughout the city by means of the sounding of drums. Then the citizens, filled with shouts of blessing, were everywhere delighted there. [Tilaka] Subsequently, by adopting a conduct that was contrary to the customs of former kings, [he established a new way]. [Kṛt 8.1379ab–1380ab]
By that sinless conduct, he experienced the fruit immediately.
Though he remained with attendants numbering fewer than a hundred,
he was at that moment surrounded by people whose hearts were captivated by his affection.
By announcing pleasant words before his lord as a means of offering affection,
Lakṣmaṇa obtained the foremost position of minister among the people.
Thus, through the methods of policy, a wise king brings the kingdom to his bed.

The mendicant, traveling at midday, arrived desiring to enter the city. At that time, a tumultuous military encounter— crowded with *ḍāmaras*, citizens, cavalry, and plunderers, and never seen before— was witnessed by him.
Hearing that his enemy was slain, the king, eager for the kingdom, was proceeding toward the city when he was addressed by Tilaka,
the son of a crow:
"If Sussala has been killed by fate, all his enemies are destroyed."
"How could the subjects abandon their virtuous son?
O King, let there be haste for one day regarding his entry into the city;
come, let us go to Padmapura to block the path of our adversaries."
