The great warriors led by Sujji, their armies destroyed, are either slain or besieged there along with their weapons and mounts as they advance. Therefore, having laid down your arms, you will certainly enter [the city] within two or three days.
The city was filled with citizens who had themselves entreated his arrival;
they cried out, "Enough with these worn-out mantras!
And he, along with Koṣṭheśvara and the others, was made to delay by his own people.

As he was being granted various edicts by those bestowing the kingdom, and as he was swiftly petitioning for this or that, his smiles were met with her disregard. Consequently, his entire army was rendered helpless by the falling of heavy snow.

By that time, he had reached the outskirts of the city according to his agreement. In the interval thus gained, while the king was without troops, Pañcacandra, the son of Garga, arrived at the monarch's side with an army.

Then that hero went forth to fight together with the princes, who desired to wash away their grief by abandoning their slain master. Seeing those battles which were beyond all expectation, the soldiers of the mendicant [army]...
Just as they began to fight,
everything around them suddenly met with defeat in an instant; seeing their own men slain,
they were unable to rally their retreating army.
And those who were the chief commanders of the army, such as Bhikṣu, Pṛthvīhara,
and others— even they experienced a terror never seen before, as if struck by weapons though bearing none.
If they were pursued by the king’s followers for a long distance as they fled,
surely nothing at all would remain of them in an instant.
When they had turned their backs, he finally came face-to-face with them after a long time.
In the city, which was distressed by the power of nine kings,
fate was perceived by the people in one way, yet through the conjunction of destiny, it turned out otherwise.
In this manner, the sequence of victory and defeat unfolded between the two kings.

The Creator brings one person, whose feet are bound by a certain downfall, to ruin in an instant, while leading another, who desires to transcend it, to full growth; he possesses the power of a mind that has no object for its conceptual constructions, like a riverbank against the flood of waters. Then, at the close of day, Sujīrta was relieved of those various causes of fear.
Like a snake emerging from a mountain enveloped by a forest fire, he came forth,
exhausted; having heard that the king was slain while staying in the village of Medhācakrapura, he indeed consulted with his ministers during the night and did not rise, but remained there.

Waiting for Rilhaṇa and the other army commanders stationed at Śūrapura and other locations, he entered the city with them without hindrance. In the darkness, for the sake of recognition, he [placed] their imperishable [signs].
Then he placed lamps burning upon the roofs of his own dwellings. However,
due to the discord among the foot soldiers who had fled in various directions,
they became lost somewhere in the night and did not return to that camp.
Setting out at dawn, followed by those tumultuous pursuers,
he was not left alone for even a moment as they struck him here and there; meanwhile,
the people who had set out with him were mostly elderly women and children.
He went along protecting them, placing them in front like a herdsman with his cattle;
for a short while, he was able to provide protection for them by turning back and standing with fifty of Śiva’s mount-riders.
In the thickets crowded with groves of grapevines, he was harassed by enemies who were not intimidated by the path;
yet, at every step, he looked back toward the world.
[He thought: "My master has been slain, and my master’s son remains in a state of calamity."
For he, desiring freedom from debt, protected his very self therein.
What is the use of those who are like sacrificial animals, who, even while making a firm resolve to sacrifice their own lives, have no regard for the proper time?
To slay him as he approached with his magic power destroyed,
the cruel and merciless Asuras, inhabitants of the Khaḍūvī region,
rose up with a vast army from the village of Kherītalālaśā near Padmapura.
On that occasion, Śrī Vaka arrived there at Vraja by way of the road. Fearing that he might have followers who had not been lost, they fell upon him and,
with their ploughs, put his army to flight.
In that battle, both Meru and the noble Sañjana were slain as cavalrymen;
the wrestler Vaṭṭātmaja was wounded and died after several days. [The army] was in distress due to the water carried away by the chasms created by the rising flames.

At that moment, the place known as Udīpapūrabāla became a battlefield. Having fought again and again, they surged forth from outside Padmapura; there, an arrow struck the throat of Śrīvaka, whose army had been held in check.
Knowing that he was not to be spared because he had been rendered helpless by the blows,
those fierce men looted him and abandoned him out of regard for their former friendship;
they were themselves bowed down by the weight of the treasures they had seized from the plundered army of Śrībaka.

By some of those who had set out, the road to Sujji became free from danger. As a traveler departs, might not the lion, whose life is nearly spent, clear the path by destroying the traps in the forest?

Sujji set out with his army in silence within Padmapura; having reached the vicinity of Udīpaśvabhra, he was discovered by the Ḍāmaras. Seeing them plundering his infantry, treasury, weapons, and other supplies, he took no notice of them.
Having crossed the Avabhra, the king, accompanied by his cavalry, proceeded to the land accessible to horses.
Thenceforth, he threatened his enemies— who had long since ceased to fear him—
from afar with frowns, the brandishing of the index finger, and harsh words.
Terrified, they abandoned it, taking only the parasol, and having fled quickly,
he entered the city and, with tears in his eyes, approached the presence of the king.
When that elder brother arrived at the forefront, the king,
along with tears hot with sorrow, cast off his fear of the enemy's assault;
on that day, there was great joy for the son of Ananta.
In the village of Locanoḍḍāraka, he was attacked by Ḍāmaras while traveling;
because of the unbearable distress caused by their seizing his auspicious staff and other belongings,
he did not fall into such calamity as to become an object of pity for anyone.
Bhāṣābhidha, the loyal servant of Sujji, having fled due to the merit of the people,
arrived exhausted at Avantipura and entered the palace of the Lord of Avanti.
Meanwhile, Kampanodgrāhaka and Kṣemānanda were there as well.
He was surrounded by intolerant ḍāmaras born of the holaḍa clan.
Indurāja, the commander-in-chief born of the Kularāja family,
also took refuge under the pretext of meditation at Dhyānoḍḍāra while being surrounded by Ṭikka.
Many other military commanders as well, such as Piñcadeva and others,
remained within the territories of the Krama kingdom, having surrounded themselves with tumultuous defenses;
they were like young birds fallen from their nest when the great tree collapsed.
Thus were the king’s followers slain and wounded here and there;
many became footless, their feet scorched by the frost, their bodies naked,
emaciated by hunger, and lost their lives along the roads.
At that time, on the roads leading to the city,
no one other than men whose bodies were covered with straw was seen anywhere;
even Citraratha and the others [the Gandharvas] took grass for their bedding and dwellings.
By those great ministers, he will soon be led away.
On the second day as well, the movement of even birds was obstructed;
the clouds, raining down snow, did not cease for even a moment.
Then Dhanya, having stationed the soldiers at Kaṭaka— a village situated to the east of Vanapūrva— entrusted the monk Siṃhadeva to him and took refuge with Siṃhadeva.
Hearing that the king had been honored by his followers, [the people]...
All the mendicants stood facing toward the city, as did the soldiers. Then,
finding their opportunity while the rival’s majesty was diminished,
the four queens set forth to follow the king.
Out of fear of falling over the precipice and because of the cold, the people, rendered helpless,
were unable to carry those bodies to the distant cemetery.
They had their bodies consumed by the fire of funeral pyres near the abode of Skanda.
Then, quickly, not far from those queens and the royal palace,
Queen Campodbhavā entered the fire together with her sister Taralalekhā— she who was the very limit of the Creator’s power to delineate beauty.
Guṇojjvalā, Jajjalā, Mṛtā, and Vallā—all born in Vallāpura—perished;
even Rājalakṣmī, the daughter of Gaggā, vanished into the fire. Perceiving that the obstruction of the kingdom was at an end with the departure of the snow, her own splendors [departed].
They gave the name Himarāja to the new lord of the earth.
Then that monk saw Sussala approaching with his head shaven,
as if burning him with glances kindled by the fire of intense indignation.
Koṣṭheśvara, Jyeṣṭhapāla, and others, intent upon performing rites for him,
were restrained by him as he approached out of enmity;
desiring to fight, he wished to go to the city at the end of the snowfall.
Recognizing that his servants had been drawn away by indifference, he spoke these words:
"If Pṛthvīhara were alive, I might have seized the kingdom by force; but since he has been killed, I am deprived of my inheritance and would not be the lord of the earth."
He thought thus: "This has indeed occurred otherwise by the power of fate;
for when the enemy was slain, my hope for the kingdom has, on the contrary, ceased.
What use have I for a kingdom, or for that which serves merely for sensual enjoyment?"
"To whom else, desiring victory, will it succeed as it has for me?
That very head which he formerly caused to fall on the ground before my ancestors,
that head now rolls about today at my palace gate."
He who for ten months brought about the destruction of the pleasures of those intoxicated by wine and the like—
that very same suffering was experienced by me for ten years.
"Having thus fulfilled my duty, I shall ensure that my purpose is not in vain;
with the fever of my mind stilled, I shall spend the remainder of my life in a state of well-being. Having spoken these and other such words, he went near Tikkā and made him bow down.

Out of affection, he took the golden water-pot, the white parasol, and other royal insignia; yet, driven again by the demoness of hope for the kingdom that arose through his confidence, he approached, seized them, and stood there afflicted by the cold, lost in inward thought.
Furthermore,
it is utterly improper for those who desire to associate with the beautiful that they should entrust the body of a slain king to their guards;
even while taking refuge with an enemy, O Lord, how can such a thing as this be yours?

Reflecting with gratitude on the end of his body’s ten stages, Sajjaka, a city-armed warrior, arrived under the pretext of a desire to see [the king]; having defeated the protectors in battles, he slew Agnisad by means of a *vāṣṭuka* weapon. (Tilaka 8.1459)
From the ninety-fourth year onwards,
possessed by spirits who had attained deceptive powers, he became the instrument for the destruction of his subjects while residing in Triśaṅku;
such is the traditional account, based on the words of those whose bodies were entered and presided over by deities.
He who, through the arising of conviction produced by the correspondence with his own cultivated [knowledge],
is both the one who cuts off and the one who causes delusion by means of that [knowledge] being non-erroneous—
that man has been found, even while this head of his is sleeping or likewise dead. (The Tilaka)

The monk, whose conduct was unworthy of a man and devoid of propriety, cast off his shaven head for the sake of proclaiming his ferocity and went to the enemy’s capital. There, he encountered the queen Uccalātmajā, who was like a streak of good fortune.
While the leaders of Muṇḍa’s uncle were being slain by his followers,
and the royal city was thrown into turmoil, she finally reached the presence of her husband Somapāla, who had been staying far away for a long time. (A *yugma* couplet).
In the case of this king,
who was like a beast— devoid of shame, distracted by the pursuit of honey, wine, and vulgar pleasures, pitiable, and possessed of a leaden intellect—
the members of the assembly there should have reflected upon and performed various appropriate actions.
The elephant-keepers, unrestrained, manifested their own characteristic propriety and impropriety.
But the Naga-guardian, having obtained brotherly affection, remained by his brother's side and could not endure the humiliation of his benefactor, who was now shorn of all but his head.
Even those of far-reaching vision, fearing defeat from the Kaśmīris at the very end, said: "O Lord, this head of yours must by all means be honored,
so that by this act the sovereignty of destiny may be altered."
Where jackals were seen laughing aloud at Hari,
there in that city of cowherds (Gopālapura), his head was brought to its end by the enemies with fire fueled by black aloe, sandalwood, and other woods.
Just as there were various losses of sovereign power, just as there were numerous fluctuations of decline and prosperity on the frontiers of battle,

Who else besides him received the honors of cremation by fire?
In one part of the circle, other limbs were seen; in another, the head alone.
Then, as Tikkaka and the others proceeded toward the city by way of the royal highway, they waited there to kill Bhasa and the others, who had been surrounded from before.
Though they employed efforts involving the kindling of battle-fires and the hurling of stones to cause destruction,
they were unable to conquer him,
as he remained protected within the courtyard of the gods' temple by a great stone wall.

Being struck by them, they were unable either to stand their ground or to retreat. While they were thus delayed, the wise king, having found his opportunity, accepted the *khaḍgaviḍāla* swords as a gift.
Sujji quickly took up his lute and applied it to them;
by means of that, he attained the release of his splendor and so forth, equal to those such as Pañcacandra.
Before he could reach the city of Avanti, [the others] went ahead of him.

Having witnessed the defeat of Kayyātmaja and the others, Ṭikka and his followers fled. Bhasa and the rest, having emerged from the temple of the gods, killed the defeated enemies' pursuers and approached Sujji.
When the Lord of Kampana had entered the city with his prowess restored,
Indurāja also arrived, having abandoned Ṭikka along with his followers.
The king also appointed Citraratha, Śrībhaṭṭa, Ābhāsa, and others as officials in charge of the various administrative departments,
such as the foot-guards and the gatekeepers;
even while remaining ever-vigilant, he did not abandon his previous duties.
What other minister could speak when he must look to the face of the doorkeeper?
Even the doorkeeper, who was highly esteemed by the lawless and fierce village-folk,
fell into a circle of intrigue against him and became an object of the king's watchfulness.
In that array of enemies, there was no one who, incited by him,

did not take refuge with the king, nor anyone who did not become intent on seeking his protection. The king, a master of deception, concealed his true nature through a manifestation resembling that of a sovereign.
Even when he could not obtain food, he did not abandon that resolve. Thus,
stretching out his feet within the city alone,
he remained there, causing the fruit that was near at hand to sprout.
Having assembled all the *ḍāmara* monks at Vijayeśvara,
he then desired to seize eighteen sacred seats (*adhiṣṭhāna*) at the end of winter.
Having seen the previously witnessed unity of his entire military host, the *ḍāmaras*—
Then, perceiving that the kingdom had fallen into the hands of a monk, they became apprehensive.
They observed the intelligence and valor of each one individually, as well as their friends and enemies, wondering:
"Once he has obtained the kingdom, would he not rise up from within his own house to attack us?"
Having deliberated thus, desiring to bestow the kingdom upon Somapāla, they secretly dispatched envoys; he too sent forth an envoy.
By means of his physical appearance, conduct, and agitation, those [envoys] perceived him to be like a beast.

They thought, "Our enjoyment of the kingdom shall be unbroken. However, that which the band of robbers— who had abandoned propriety out of greed for wealth— intended to do in this country, being more sinful than sin itself, did not come to pass by the power of fate.
Let alone the shame of one who is unfit even for servitude, much less for sovereignty;
could such a person protect this land even slightly?
He who treats people of good character like straw effigies, and whose face is scorched by fire through the constant instilling of fear in flocks of sparrows.
Was he not appointed to protect the trees of the forest; would he then fail to act against the wild elephants that were destroying them?
Under the pretext of increasing his fortune, the mendicant accepted the office assigned to him;
thereafter, acting as their messenger, he secretly instigated the *ḍāmaras* who were prepared to offer him gifts.
Then, having commenced his undertaking on the full moon day of Vaiśākha and being filled with a sense of urgency,
Sujji emerged from the city and advanced with great depth of purpose. His resolve to fight was praiseworthy, for he was accompanied by a vast assembly of warriors.

Having thus challenged that many heroes, he went forth alone. It is not surprising that such things happen when one enters into a conflict of reckless deeds; for by the power of fate, a hundred thousand may be conquered by one in battle, or conversely, a single man by a hundred thousand.
While attempting to cross the river that had no bridge,
he saw his enemies on the opposite shore raining down arrows. He remained there for two or three nights on both banks of that river.

The armored warriors, consecrated to watching for one another’s vulnerabilities, were hemmed in. Then, having himself boarded a boat, he crossed over and bound a bridge using the ships brought from the city of Avanti, together with the Śveta and Itaratsuja rivers.
Seeing him crossing over with only a few warriors,
the enemy host became as unsteady as a row of trees on a riverbank buffeted by the wind.
And in just a moment, he was seen having already reached the opposite bank.

The bridge was secured, the warriors crossed over, and the enemies were broken. Neither sword-bearer, nor horseman, nor spear-wielder, nor bowman was able to turn back and look, as they were driven away by the force of the fleeing army.

When the horse’s pace became unsteady due to the loosening of its tether, the riders of the Lord of Koṣṭha hung suspended for a moment in mid-air. Even they, having unfastened their saddles, followed after as the horses galloped behind them.
Like a circle of dust raised by a whirlwind, they quickly vanished.
The adversaries, their armies struck down, plundered, and destroyed,
met their end in fragments in villages such as Dhyānoḍḍāra.
Having crossed the Vitastā-setu at the forefront of Vijayeśa,

Having stayed in the field of Vijaya, when the Lord of Kampana arrived there on another day, the adversaries abandoned their meditative flight and departed. Having remained there for some days, he [the Lord] turned his face toward Devasaras.
Having arrived with the *gotra*-members of Ṭikka who had come forth from [their] divisions,
the two sons of the Bhojas, Jayarāja and Yaśorāja— who were the leaders there—

When he had fled, their ranks were shattered; the monks and others went to Śūrapura, while the lords of Koṣṭha and others went to their own lands. Amidst the great terror, the messenger of Somapāla was censured and fled.

Sent by the son of a slave, he asked, "Where am I? and thus caused distress to his master. For he regarded that [master], who was desirous of rising through the agitation of such a great undertaking, as a jackal overcome by the longing of a lioness.

The blossoming of some occurs through flashes of lightning that are harsh to the eyes, while for others there is the emergence [of fear] through long peals of thunder that are grating to the ears. those who take refuge in him flourish like the sprouts of a wish-fulfilling tree.

The world perceived that the majesty and power of the queen were profound and difficult to fathom; it served those ministers on all sides. But the doorkeeper could not tolerate the excessive influence of those who were not ministers.
As he uprooted all those trees by the side with utter ease, as if they were mere blades of grass,

Having been praised by the king since childhood and being conversant with all legal procedures, he remained entirely unassailable; for his son had reached the prime of youth. Out of pride, that son desired an undivided matrimonial alliance.

For they were of equal age to the king due to their close intimacy with his mother; indeed, during the time of the kingdom, they remained full of pride as the ones who provided him with leisure. Their equipment for horses, baths, meals, and so forth were like those of the king.

In the meantime, while coming from Piñjadeva into a mountain cave,

Having returned from the battle at Puṣyāṇa to create a powder for his own benefit,

Having fallen upon the ground, he encountered an enemy soldier standing at his side.

With his fist like a firm iron bar, he [made] a mallet for the skulls of his enemies;

By the people, the destruction of the enemy was reported even during the very first march.
He was reckoned as one who would utterly eradicate all thorns [of his enemies].
When he had entered the city, some of those who were guilty fled;
others, such as Janakasimha and his followers, were cast into prison.
Some who had fled incited suspicion in the lord of the earth;
consequently, those headed by Koṣṭheśvara turned hostile.
Then, at the end of the month of Kārtika, the illustrious and virtuous king emerged from Śamālā.

In various places, he oppressed the host of his enemies in fierce battles. At Hāḍigrāma, where kings such as Sussala had seen their majesty shattered, Sujji, of formidable prowess, destroyed that place.
Then the mendicant, greedy for the kingdom, was summoned by the Koṣṭhaka and others who were being oppressed by the king; he arrived once more,

He reached the mountain village named Śilikākoṭṭa. That proud man, rushing forward with a desire for victory, took no account of the suffering arising from hunger, thirst, fatigue, enemies, fear, or the confusion of the path.

When fate is adverse, the undertaking of one who desires victory turns away from success, like the silken banner-cloth of a chariot set out against a headwind. Even the mere commencement of some task leads to success for only a few; while another, though intent on great effort, finds their exertion fruitless.

Having obtained the nectar from the ocean by means of Mount Mandara as a churning-stick, he who had long since exerted his power was not surpassed even by the Lord of the Snowy Mountains. The river, having fallen from her dwelling place upon entering the ocean, was tossed about under the influence of the surging waves at the shoreline.
It is merely a false impression that [the effort] has arisen again; for there is no rising up for those whose endeavors have been thwarted by fate.
At the very moment of its emergence, an obstacle to the success of that [effort], which was so harsh due to great exertion, was created by adverse destiny.

Not realizing that he had arrived, at that very moment Pṛthvīhara’s younger brother, whose finger had been cut off and who had suffered defeat, approached the king. And Koṣṭheśvara, having perceived that he had arrived, stood [ready].
Then, like two snakes rendered powerless by a mantra, they were unable to act;
having been deprived of the exertion of their flight by those two, he was made to stop at another place. Departing by way of the road to Kārkoṭadraṅga, he went to Sulharī.
And there was one whose tree-like arms were itching with fierce pride,
burning with the constant thought of invading Kaśmīra;
like the waters of the ocean seeking a weak point, he was ever on the lookout for an opening.

Having entered the city, the king also considered a remedy. Among his ministers, you were without rival; yet the doorkeeper, unable to endure your arrogance, became intent on seeking out pretexts against you.

Then, the elder brother of Dhanya, whose form was purified by immersion in the waters of the Ganges, arrived with confidence and support for the leaping Lord. Thereafter, the king’s foremost ministers, who had long been honored, were praised.
Not obtaining the honors due to them, they were consumed by anxiety;
while he was performing his duties through the ministers of his father,
those men of profound intent inferred his capacity for enduring the wait of time.
The doorkeeper, intent on scrutinizing those who were difficult to discern,
affectionately accepted even those unpleasant things that were useful to the king.
Then, after some months had passed by the turn of fate...
Suddenly the king became afflicted by a severe outbreak of lūtā (smallpox),
accompanied by complications such as boils, swellings, diarrhea, and loss of digestive fire;
while his recovery remained uncertain, the kingdom fell into a state of great agitation.

Thus situated was the powerful enemy, the sole lord and master of the clan; his partisans, the Ḍāmaras, considered the kingdom to be utterly corrupt. Reflecting upon what would be beneficial both for the future and for the present, [he deliberated].
Then, desiring to appoint his own son, the infant Pārmaṇḍi— who was about five years old— as the sovereign Sujji, he consulted with his maternal uncle, Gārgi, regarding King Śrīguṇalekhā’s only son.
Thus, desiring to seize such a one, he, together with his son Sujji,
deliberated throughout the night with Pañcacandra and others by means of stratagem. Having found an opportunity, the doorkeeper and Dhanya and the others, as directed by him, [acted].

Those who know the truth produce curiosity by describing the reality of wondrous things, like the Creator of old;

How could there be well-being for a king whose movements are paralyzed after he has been rendered helpless by beings who have taken up residence in his place of purification or in his private chamber with women, and who—weaponless and having entered his mind through those skilled in deception—are driven to utter helplessness as if by spirits intensely active within the womb? A rogue enters the presence of the lord of the earth, laughing without cause; with eyes wide with feigned affection, the king asks him, "What? What?", though his own intention is anything but pure.
He says something while scratching his hair—which, for those who possess pride, acts with impetuosity like the fall of a thunderbolt upon the very life-force of their honor.
