neither Upendra nor Mahendra was capable of standing against you.

"Whether it be the king who showed you contempt when you were bestowing the kingdom, or whether it be us who act against you while you reside within our territory— we shall deal with both of them. Thus urged by him, [he went] to the presence of Deṅgapāla.
Desiring to go to the presence of the mendicant, he was stopped by Bhāgika;
"It is not fitting for you to perform this act while the bones of your master have not yet been cast into the waters of the Jahnavī," he said, and out of agitation he bit him.
"Having bathed in the celestial river, I shall come to your side"— making this resolve,
he whose sheath was yellow departed for the accomplishment of his task. But the king, having entrusted all burdens to the hands of the doorkeeper...
Because it was being overrun by the dull-witted, he considered the kingdom to be ill-situated.
Whomever indeed he took hold of,
the doorkeeper, standing nearby, would gaze upon him every day as if with favor, after having established a connection with him.
While he was thus acting with arrogance, Udaya, the lord of Kampana, punished him;
under a pretext, he slew the haughty son of Kāliya.
Then Lakṣmaka [dealt with] all those Lavanyas who were notorious for their lack of trust.
He offered a slight conciliation to the Lord of Kampana, who was beyond all bounds:
"I shall bathe in the Gaṅgā until Sujji is rendered powerless;
meanwhile, I am reflecting on how I might lead Kaśmīra."

Having learned from the extent of their respective territories that the *ḍāmaras* were divided, the mendicant-like king entered Viśalāṭā at the onset of winter; but as he sought to enter the interior of that circle, his progress was blocked by the *ḍāmaras*.
The doorkeeper became the restrainer of the winter season.
He had been brought by Ṭikka, an enemy who was singularly hostile due to his treachery against his father;
he was supported by all the Ḍāmaras, who were highly esteemed.

Awaiting the arrival of Sujji as the means to obtain the kingdom, he dwelt in the fortress named Bāṇaśālā— though it was not very high— belonging to Bhāgika, the ruler of the Khaśas and the fearless son-in-law of Tiṣṭhaka.
Through his messengers, he sowed dissension throughout the entire circle of the Dāmaras,
spreading joy among his friends and terror among his enemies. Then, having performed his ablutions in the Ganges, he turned back with a joyful heart.
"Since this monk has previously been an enemy and has now become one who is not to be distinguished [from us],
fear would arise for us just as it does for that king. Having reflected thus, Siṃhadeva, being entreated [by him], adopted a pretext.
While he was striving to secure Sujji’s release, Somapāla was overwhelmed with fear. Sujji reached Jālandhara at dawn and approached a mendicant;
just as he was about to depart for him in the evening, that messenger arrived.
Urged by the eldest brother and restrained by Bhāgika,
he desisted at his word from the obsession of taking refuge with the enemy.

"The king will remit the debt you incurred in another land, and he will grant you authority himself, having been entreated through my mouth. Thus was [the king] addressed daily by Somapāla through the mouth of a messenger.
Having cast off longing for his enemies, he set out toward that region.
Udaya, the lord of Kampana, having crossed over the perils in the month of Vaiśākha,
entered into battle with the mendicant accompanied by the Khaśas.
When the small force had previously stood firm and the great army had subsequently been born [from it],
the monk, having obtained his disguise, entered that interior of the fortress.
Then the king, having marched out to the field of victory, filled it completely.

They dispatched various armies to the camp of the Lord of Kampana; the king's army, stationed in the fortress, fought back against those raining down a shower of machines, stones, arrows, and diverse weapons by discharging a rain of rocks.

Even though it was long, the king’s army was unable to capture the arrows falling from the mendicant— arrows that were neither stones nor marked with his name— for more than a month had passed since they began. Then, after a further period of days, he finally captured them.
Having breached the foundation of the fortress, the fortunate one [the king] filled the trench with water;

those who were difficult to subdue due to their strength, yet desirous of harming that enemy, displayed their intent toward the queen— who was devoted to strategic means— as they became greedy for wealth.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing that matter, the king dispatched the *pratīhāra* along with the sons of the *sāmanta* Ḍāmara and the chief minister.
Koṣṭheśvara, Trillaka, and others [were sent] for the liberation of him who was in a state of distress.
Thinking, "We shall do this for the monk," they followed him.
Seeing from the peak of the narrow mountain below the fortress of moderate height,
the doorkeeper considered his task accomplished upon beholding his own endless armies.
On another day, the gatekeepers and their followers who had been stationed there previously fought against the entire army, which desired to seize the fortress by force;
even though they were so few, they countered them with a shower of stones.
Thinking with certainty that "this cannot be overcome by valor," [the enemies] fell,
struck by stones from the tops of the trees that were the bodies of the heroes;
their heads were like swarms of bees, with flowing blood for honey and the wounds for honeycombs.

In that regard, there was a certain foolishness on the part of Koṣṭheśvara, which brought about the ruin of his own mendicants, of the Lāvaṇyas, and of others. It was for the sake of establishing this reputation: "O hero, there is no one equal to me in this world."
For that [act] of the monk, which resulted in the destruction of lives, was indeed an act of insolence born of non-war.
In that crisis, he displayed fortitude toward the Khashas who desired to seize him;
"I am the Lord of Koṣṭha," he thought, "and the other Ḍāmaras are not distinct from those under my control."
"This vast army that is seen here shall turn out for our benefit"— speaking thus, he perceived it otherwise;
for even that lord of Koṣṭha was an enemy who had become a ground for his [the opponent's] confidence.

"What reliance can there be on others in such a situation?"— thus they reached their conclusion. Then the wise Lakṣmaka, having accepted the office of *Ṭikka* at his own request due to the king’s hostility toward his father, [acted accordingly].

Having won over the lord of the Khaśas by means of his refuge with Mahāgrāma and Svarṇādityāga, [Rājyapāla] made him gird his loins in the desire to milk the mendicants. Ānanda, the brother of the lord of the Khaśas, having been sent back and forth, [was employed].
Having led Ṭikka to the presence of the doorkeeper, he caused him to be executed once again.
Seeing the apparent alliance between the doorkeeper and Ṭikka, the Ḍāmaras,
Koṣṭheśvara, and others concluded without doubt that the monk had been killed.
Enraged, they dispatched messengers to Khaśāntika for his release, along with abundant wealth and promises of gold. But Khaśāntika reflected: "He has been incited by us after we accepted a bribe."
The monk knows that his life is protected by Koṣṭheśvara and others.
Now, Deṅgapāla, having attained the kingdom, is full of wrath; furthermore, Jayasiṃha is far away and might kill me. Therefore, he who is on my side must be protected with great effort.

Thinking thus, they replied to him, and though they spoke to the monk established in purity from their home, saying, "Having become distressed, go out with a wooden plank," they were still addressed as follows:

But he, proud as he was, did not go out, reflecting on the infamy in the world that he had gone by way of the refuse-heap like a dog with his limbs smeared with impurity. Koṣṭheśvara, whose actions were obscure, cast about in his desire to cause a disturbance among the army.
Consoled by the doorkeeper at dawn with harsh words appropriate for the time,
he did not accept the tribute of the Khaśas and others until daybreak; meanwhile,
the chief doorkeepers resolved upon the execution of the mendicant.
Constantly seeking news on the field of victory through messengers going and coming, the king became deeply anxious. For ten years, he engaged in various such battles characterized by great daring.

That which could not be accomplished even by the efforts of an aged monarch became easy for that mendicant; for these [fools] consider the destruction of the king’s followers to be a mere trifle— alas, what has anything to do with anything else?
"Laughing, these Khaśas will arrive and measure out their wealth in an instant;
surely they will depart broken and entirely plundered by the enemy.
This granary here is separate; Trilla is its very kinsman. (KRT 8.1706–1707ab)
These men, nourished by the leavings of beggars, are indeed insiders.
Who has newly arrived here who might accomplish the king’s welfare?
Surely this entire collection [of circumstances] has come together for his very success.
While the people in the camp were still speaking thus,
the fortress was surrounded by the ministers' troops carrying unsheathed weapons;
"He must be slain by all of us together— he is alone, long oppressed, and for his sake [we have come]."
"Alas, shame! An array has been formed by all these shameless warriors!
they cried; and that ocean of an army became silent, its waves of hair and weapons rendered pure, with the shimmering eyes of the combatants as its fish.
The army might fly up into the sky, or leap across like a bounding deer;
or, like a shower from a malignant cloud, it might strike everyone down at once.
At the end, the mendicant, possessing marvelous valor, took up his weapon and accepted [the challenge].
The people were bewildered and terrified, thinking thus within themselves:
"This much had been accomplished by the ministers; now, however, an obstacle has arisen. The pacification of that and the success of the undertaking have come about through the majesty of the king."
While the army, with eyes cast upward, was watching for the arrival of the mendicant,
a single man emerged from the fortress with his weapon drawn.
As he was surrounded by weeping women, they hurled [stones] at him.
On his back, some people— wearing saffron-dyed lower garments that fluttered against their bodies—
cried out, "This is the very monk who was fleeing and has been captured here!
As they spoke with their faces turned upward, the people heard Tika emerge from there.
For he had been prepared for execution during the tumultuous fray in which the monk had committed an offense;
therefore, fearing [harm] from the king’s followers, he departed. And he drew [his bow] to inspire confidence in the people that he was innocent.
With his sword drawn to strike at his belly while being guarded by his own followers, he, along with his attendants,
bypassed the king's army that had blocked the path and sat down not far from the edge of a mountain spring.
Having emerged from the fortress with great relief after long-awaited waters were obtained, he, urged on by the Aṇḍāmaras, began to employ an illusion:
"The sun has become suspended; let it be protected for a moment! (Kṛt 8.1721–1722).
"During the night, the Ḍāmaras will carry off the monk by force.
Hearing these words from the minister, the Khaśas, together with the ministers,
blocked the rocks with their girdles as they sought to climb up— those girdles which were as sharp as swords.
Then, while the warriors made the air resonant with shouts of joy and the clapping of hands,
the ministers were seized with agitated hearts.
Those betrayers of their master, having escaped with difficulty, were intent on securing the kingdom.
What enemy’s self-interest has ever been accomplished by ministers who merely bestow wealth? Then,
while the king’s business was underway and the sun was hanging low, Lakṣmaka addressed Khaśa,
who was clutching his waist-knot, asking, "What is this?"
He said: "Even a pot-bearer's wife can thwart what one intends to do;
how is it that I am absent when the Khaśas are opposing you?
Go now, therefore, to bring about their destruction and their reversal."
Having spoken thus, he released Ānanda and laughed with his other ministers.
By the king, who could see far ahead, [he was saved] from falling onto the path of the Viṣalāṭa.
The commencement of the *Deṅgapālagṛha* was conceived [as follows]:
"Therefore, the opening of the primary section was grasped simultaneously, by one who had previously woven a long snare of meanings for this very purpose. (KRT 8.1729cd–1730cd)
At that moment of agitation, the steward became free from confusion;
he realized that [the prince] had escaped like a trained bird and was now within reach.
He said to them: "This is no joke for me; when the task is ruined, there is no room for recklessness."
"What would happen even to Khaśa’s brother-in-law if this man were struck down and all his wealth destroyed?
By the unimpeded power of fortune, that brother-in-law of Khaśa,
having restrained everyone, summoned those sharp-edged [soldiers] from the front of the fortress.
The lives of the bandits reached the throat; the intellects of the ministers reached a state of doubt;
and the pleasures of the celestial women reached the peak of the mountain of sharpness.
He [the king], bound with a leather loincloth and a strip of cloth marked with his own name...

With arrows, he proclaimed his own mastery over all directions in battle, like that of a lord. That betel-box became a dagger for the application of hair and beard, which was used by those monks living off the king who desired to die.
Then, having ascertained their end,
he turned back against them as they quickly sought refuge in the camp of Koṣṭheśvara and others.
By means of his own dispatched soldiers, Lakṣmaṇa engaged with them one by one through strategic maneuvers.

Seeing his own tail curled up, Ṭikka pressed down his fingers out of fear. At that moment, he was guarded by the Khaśas, who were apprehensive of flight; during those days, he did not eat due to mental anguish.

The hero, weary of delay and eager for a contest with the fierce ones, remained there as a mendicant, diverting his mind with the dice-board. When the assembly of the fierce ones arrived at the courtyard of the palace with a desire to fight, [he waited].
As he rose, his small remaining fortune was exhausted. When a friend arrived while he, a lover, was gambling with his beloved, no agitation arose within him, as if he were rising to greet the guest.
Thinking, "What would be the use of killing so many even now?",
he abandoned his quiver and emerged, sword and scabbard in hand,
with hair no longer darkened by the long stream of thought that had flowed from him.
With the hems of his hero’s garments, it was like a fluttering banner of variegated cloth;
with the luster of his earrings— shaped like flawless conchs— swaying over his cheeks,
and with the radiance of sandalwood paste applied to his forehead, his smile was illuminated by the pride of his own majesty.
In their various and wonderful movements, they performed a reverse foot-stamping that seemed to illuminate the space with firebrands made from the blades of their swords,
their eyes,
and the cloths of their lips; with the bright edges of their washed lower lips firmly bound by the saffron-colored garments upon their lips.
With his playfully tossing manes bristling on his shoulders like those of a lion,

he moved about performing various wonderful circular dances (*maṇḍala*), characterized by swift, variegated, and steady steps, through the beautiful and abundant coordination of his eyes, mind, hands, and feet.
That entire populace, looking upward, [beheld] the conduct appropriate to propriety, the ornament of pride,
the constant exaltation of the manifestations of self-importance that was never transgressed,
and whose sudden fall remained unobserved.
He saw that monk wandering ahead of his enemies;
the prince, a scion of royalty and grandson of Madhu, a great hero born of a princess,
followed him even though he was the elder brother of Pālaka’s son, accompanied by Raktika.
As they entered through those houses with their uneven heights, which acted as obstacles,
Gārgika— who had taken refuge in a Buddhist monastery— blocked them alone with a shower of arrows.
As they fled, they were rendered invisible by the shafts discharged from his bow.
Like elephants driven by a headwind against hailstones,
he was repelled after a long time by the Khāśas with their evil-aimed stones; his limbs wounded and his bow broken, he turned away from the opposing warriors.

As he advanced along various winding paths, the soldiers entered his range of vision; they all came within the sight of the mendicants and others. Then, in an instant, they beheld one mendicant whose composure was evident, with a weapon held at his side.
A certain large soldier, seizing a spear, ran forward swiftly.
As he was about to strike with the spear, the monk, who is compassionate toward those who seek refuge, [intervened].

Having thrown [him down], he ran and seized his hair with an impetuous hand; and as he was about to fall, his life-breath still issuing forth, he struck him with a sword. While he was being struck, those two princes, full of blood, struck him once more.
When that [army] had been struck down by those undivided warriors who bore various weapons and were clad in armor, those three then fought against their opposing foes; and the enemies,
terrified by their weapons, became scattered.
Like trees from which swarms of bees have been driven out by hooded cobras living in their hollows,
they were unable to strike those enemies— the swordsmen, heroes, and others. Withdrawing, they then scattered showers of arrows at them from a distance.

As the lion-king among mendicants shattered the cage of arrows, showers of well-nourished stones were released by the Khaśas from the palace. As he ran, his body was mangled by that terrible rain of rocks.
The arrow, having plunged into the mass of liver and shattered his ribs,
quickly took three strides and fell upon the earth, scattering the quarters of the sky. Then, it removed the long-standing trembling of his enemies.
The maiden, pierced by the arrow through the path of her groin,
fell down at the edge of her husband’s feet, wounded yet barely alive.
But Raktika, pierced in his vital organs by that very same arrow, was overwhelmed with agony.
Though still alive, he sat upon the ground as if lifeless. Accompanied by those of noble lineage, the slain monk shone like a mountain peak broken by a thunderbolt, yet adorned with flowering trees.

In the midst of such a circle of kings, for the monk who was the very soul of King Harṣa, there arose no sense of humiliation; rather, his state of supreme honor reached its highest point. Even the Creator, though eternally thwarted by him, was made to feel his pride even unto death.
Having accepted his own defeat, he was surely rendered powerless by him who wields the unimpeded wheel.

What miserable wretch is there among those former great kings of formidable power? Yet, in his presence, they were nothing at all compared to him, whose noble final act [of renunciation] is so exalted.
While the enemy warriors, seized by their own boastfulness, were climbing up,
Kumāriya— though in that state and afflicted by pain— fought with his sword.
Even as he was rendered helpless by the blows, he continued to strike, thinking only, "I must fight."
"Struck many times at length by enemies who had realized the truth,
when he had collapsed, the fools were censured with the words, 'Enough with these blows! Thus,
when the mendicant was struck down, the enemy soldiers were repeatedly beaten by the Khaśas."
By some base swordsmen, he was struck while his blood flowed, nearly deprived of life by the unbearable pain of many wounds inflicted by unyielding weapons;
he had enjoyed a lifespan of thirty-nine years and nine months.

On the tenth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha in his sixth year, that king was slain. Those for whom this had been the cause of long-lasting upheaval and the reason for total destruction, being struck with wonder at his virtuous nature, praised him in this way.
For several *nālikās*, that skull did not relinquish its twitching of the eyes, the trembling of the eyebrows, and its smiling countenance,
as if it were still alive.
One [of the two halves] entered the sky, while the other remained upon the earth.
That body, the company of apsarases, and the earth and water— [all] insentient and inert—
the ministers brought the shaven heads of those three before the lord of the earth as he stood on the field of victory on the following day.
Just as the ocean, having witnessed its own wondrous nature in the manifestation of the glorious nectar, jewels, ivory, horses, and the moon, so too is this king;
displaying here and there marvelous qualities that are a wonder to the world.
The state of being an object of experience does not belong to anyone at all.
(Couplet) He did not feel pride, thinking, "My father’s enemy has been slain," nor did he rejoice, thinking, "This thorn in the side of the royal family has been destroyed. (KRT 8.1782ab–cd)

Seeing that the mendicant’s head was merely a pretext for his noble character, he thought: "My father did not become angry, thinking, 'This man has shaved my head'; for the strength of this man's disposition is to be inferred from his outward form, not from any distortion caused by hatred. (A pair of verses).
Its clarity is like that of crystal, not scorched by the light of the sun;
from his rise to eminence until he became a sovereign, this was manifest.

Alas! It is a tragedy that his own death has been witnessed here before the casting off of this body. Even those who were formerly known for their favor toward him, as well as the descendants of Aurva, now look on with indifference as he remains nothing but a skull.
Thus reflecting within himself upon that extraordinary nobility, the lord of the earth commanded that the enemy’s funeral rites be performed immediately;
and at night, even when his sleep was interrupted, he meditated upon the rise and fall of that foe.

He reflected again and again upon the manifold variety of the nature of existence. Even after a thousand years, people thought: "Surely there will never again be such a state of insecurity regarding inheritance in this land."

Having burnt away the thin grass, it spreads out the young shoots; having shown the day and increased its heat, it produces rain. When the workings of destiny touch upon such variety according to its fixed law, there is no confidence whatsoever in the certainty of anything. Having accomplished his task, the mind of the steadfast man, seeking rest, becomes steady.

Fate ordains the entrustment of the burden of long-term tasks to others. As long as the rider has not yet descended from the first horse— whose fatigue was induced by the long journey— and while the entire second horse is still being prepared for the ascent, the back of the mount is mounted by another who, having relieved the beast of its load and protected its seat, finds it easy to ascend and is thus unable to endure waiting any longer.
In this very way, when the kingdom had become free of enemies for a mere night,
a messenger entered before the king, mute with grief.
He was questioned by the agitated courtiers on the very day [of the king's victory].
The mendicant who had departed was one who brought peacelessness and inflicted a state of misery.
Long ago, two half-brothers, Salhaṇa and Loṭhana, were bound on Mount Lohara; they were those whom King Sussala had cast there.
When the elder brother had died, the servants of Koṭṭa forcibly seized the younger brother, Loṭhana; him,
who had been consecrated here today during the third watch of the night,
[the minister] addressed along with five proud sons of his son and brothers, all of whom were worthy of the kingdom.
Once he had been released from his bonds, he spoke to that lord in the treasury: "He would suffer,
he would become bewildered, he would cry out with arms outstretched, he would fall,
he would sleep with his bowels loosened, and then he would certainly reach a state of motionless vision."
The king, whose mind had been soothed by the swift alleviation of his long-standing distress, was—
as if crushed by the thunderbolt of the evil news falling upon him at that moment—
regarded with significant intent even by the guardians of the quarters.
The king did not abandon his former state through changes in appearance, conduct, or gestures; for indeed,
no other monarch had ever before been created by such a slaughter, which was irresistible from every side and could not be overcome by anyone else.

By his strength, the kingdom that had been lost by his father was once again secured; likewise, this [son] has destroyed his enemies and reclaimed his paternal station. Yet, both the fortress and the treasury were lost, and even the boy’s name was forgotten.
In that place, where there was but one heir— poor and friendless—
he brought about calamity for many years, destroying wealth and honor; for in that land, which delighted in misfortune, its sole protector had been slain.

This circle of vassals has arisen, endowed with allies, fortresses, and wealth, yet it is composed of six hostile elements and possesses a dissatisfied populace while being destitute of treasury. For a lord of the earth whose majesty has been proven by such a touchstone [of adversity], [this is no obstacle].
I know that even Rāghava, full of self-restraint, vies with him in fortitude;
for his father, weighing their virtues, regarded them as equal in power, whether in the granting of sovereignty or in exile.
Whether summoned for his consecration or dismissed to the forest,
not even the slightest alteration in his demeanor was observed by me.
[I saw him] together with his beloved younger brother in those lovely forest regions.
Having promised further prosperity, she declared that it should remain limited by a specific duration:
"In this collision of pleasure and pain experienced in a single moment,
there is a vast difference between the two due to such distinct variations in their respective conditions."
In order to demonstrate to people that power is certainly devoid of any substratum, Fate has equipped himself with a multitude of various instruments and cut him down.
O Lord of the Earth, who would not hold in high esteem the most wonderful deeds of this king that are about to be described,
given his abundance of prosperity?
By the king, an ocean of fortitude, the remainder of the task was to be understood in full detail.
Questioned, the messenger then related the news of the fortress:

"When Bhāgika had abandoned the fortress and departed for Maṇḍaleśvara, [the king] became one whose efforts were frustrated; his mind was intoxicated by wealth and pride, and he was devoid of affection."
Intent solely on adornment, food, and the enjoyment of women, and fierce with intoxication,

he conducted himself unworthily through his mode of life which caused his dependents to turn away from him. He was restrained by his maternal uncle, who felt compassion for his kin, from such acts as the uprooting of eyes.
The king did not perform any action capable of protecting those who had been bound.
Māyāvin, named Udayana, was a scribe with great ambitions;
and the chamberlain Māñika [acted] against the firmly rooted minister.

In the meantime, Indrākara, the son of Bhīmākara, was born; meanwhile, those who desired to seize him contemplated his death here and there out of hatred for his father. Yet, they were never able to kill him, as they never found an opportunity.
He descended from the watchtower for the sake of his mission. To ensure the king’s confidence, he sent such a message from Kashmir, where the means of subsistence were reduced to a mere pittance.
Having composed secret letters addressed to all the householders without exception,
they had previously made an agreement with the wife of the one destined for consecration; then,
having seen him emerge from the fortress at night, they released him from his fetters and set him rolling along.

They consecrated [him] before the temples of Siṃharāja, Svāmī, and Viṣṇu. (Tilaka) A certain woman named Śaradā, a wife of King Suśśala, remained there as a humble person, granting her consent to them. (KRT_8_1823)
Then, having warded off the bolts with iron machine-breakers dedicated to that task,
they plundered the treasury and its jewels and other wealth;
such great acts of violence were committed by those seven along with their servants.
That hostility toward the Caṇḍālas which had been abandoned through his generosity was now provoked again.

The inhabitants of the fortress were deprived of sleep by the clamor of kettledrums, trumpets, and other instruments; they then beheld the rolling [of the chariot], adorned with royal ornaments, as it moved along.

Illuminated by lamps, that assembly of the king’s ministers was filled with wonder by one whose noble attire was such as they had never seen before. Out of affection, the noble youth drew near to those standing at his side.
The two *ṭakkuras* named Carma and Pāsika, along with their armies, were from his own land; yet,
because their pride had been shattered by his resolve,
the remainder of the night— pale with the touch of moonbeams— passed away for them entirely.

Then in the morning, his love, made fierce by heat through the hearing of bad news, approached to obstruct the sun’s rays as they scorched him. When he reached the surface of the city gate, he was met by the enemy soldiers who had come forth.
"Seeing him turned away, I moved toward the presence of the Lord.
Having heard this, the King quickly dispatched Lulla, the minister of Lohara,
and Ānandavardhana, the gatekeeper of Udaya, [to fetch him].
For those two, being experts in the terrain and natives of no other land,
were capable of discerning the fortress by the signs of its small provisions, water sources, and weak points;
and having entered the city, they saw that their heads were being bowed down by those seeking gifts of affection.

Being led away by soldiers, they seized the mendicant and burned him. By the king’s command, he was mourned as he was being consumed by fire in his ancestral land by a crowd of people, mostly women, who were unrestrained.
In the season of summer, when the sun was fierce with its rising heat, the king,
though having no faith in success, dispatched Rilhaṇa.
He was resplendent with virtues such as heroism, devotion to his master, purposefulness, and disinterestedness.
For thus did he, desiring victory, come to have his undertakings rendered fruitless;
or rather, impelled by destiny which had granted him delusion,
that king was made to deliberate on manifestly improper counsel by treacherous ministers.
At that moment, fierce with the heat of summer, he tolerated his servants who had begun their tasks despite the distress caused by the enemies' difficult assaults upon the lowlands.
Only Udaya, the lord of Kampana, remained at Rajjoli.
All the ministers followed the doorkeeper once more;
others followed the king’s son as he mounted his horse amidst the tumultuous throng of ministers.
The length of that army, with all its equipment at the peak of excellence,
enveloped the quarters of the sky as it occupied the watchtowers and fortifications;
it proceeded to capture the besiegers by every possible means.
Lulla and the others, stationed at Koṭṭopānta in the city of Phulla,
caused their enemies— who were preoccupied with fear, dissension, and battle— to tremble.
When Tuṣṭa, the lord of the land, was captured, he gave his daughter to Loṭhana.
To him, the lord of many lands, who was known by the name Prāptapadmalekhā,
and who had arrived to provide assistance, the enemy host was countered at every moment in battle by the troops of that king named Śūra.
While those kingdoms were besieged, his mind swinging with fear, Loṭhana accepted both prostration before the king and punishment. In this world,
where the commencement of fruitless undertakings is difficult to endure, this much alone is achieved.
At this time, our withdrawal from this [conflict] is appropriate, lest we incur dishonor. In this season,
auspicious with the commencement of autumn, when our forces have gradually grown strong,
we shall then undertake a magnificent enterprise with every effort.
Thus, day after day, the king did not accept what was sent by Lakṣmaka;
and the other ministers, following the advice of Śākya and others, [remained silent].
Udayana, the chief minister, having praised him and offered much wealth—
To provide assistance to his lord, he even brought Somapāla; yet that man,
though bound by kinship, was excluded from the company of the twice-born, for his mind was greedy for wealth,
and he plotted against the king who was submerged in great calamity.
"If you grant many boons upon being stirred, what need have I for consideration of my kin?
Otherwise, I shall tell others deceitfully, 'I belong to you.
Thinking this to be a trick, the Soma-drinker approached him.
In this justification, there was some slight pretext for Sujji’s departure.
(Couplet) For when he was brought back from his inclination toward the life of a mendicant, he was dismissed by the king through the mouth of Somapāla. (KRT 8.1854)
The messenger followed him— who was seeking the wealth previously promised—
as a debtor follows a creditor to whom he owes a debt;
for at that time, [the king] knew him to be a mendicant who had been nearly destroyed by this [debt].
Displaying contempt by asking, "What is the point in allaying this calamity?",
he then gave nothing at all to the mendicant out of intoxication;
for he had heard that the king was useless and knew him to be filled with grief.
As long as he did not share in the calamity of the iron [weapon], there was fear; but having heard that he had arrived full of arrogance, the king once again became filled with wrath, thinking,
"I shall cause your rolling about to be joined back together."

Having spoken thus to the messenger, [he thought: "I shall cause gold to be given by Loṭhana, after telling you [this]"; and he intended to make Somapāla a tribute-bearer (balita) for the sake of achieving his own purpose, while rendering all others powerless.

Accompanied by a limited number of servants who set out with him unobserved in the midst of that army, he reached Vīramūlaka, which was equal to the moon [in splendor]. (Kulaka) [He went] to that place whose fame had been defiled by an unseemly rain of dust. (Kulaka)
Through his greed for enjoyments, he destroyed the expansive nature of his being.
Because of drinking water as white as frost and sugar,
that Kashmiri man was unable to abandon his soft and unctuous food, which was difficult to digest.
Unable to eat even parched barley flour and the like outside because it was mixed with husks,
he sought to enter Kaśmīra by whatever means possible.
The people of Kaśmīra, seeing no further purpose in their task and being parched by the summer heat, [departed].

Upon hearing that sudden crash, they fell into a state of agitation. While eating roasted meats and drinking the fragrant, captivating, light, and cool grape wine (*mārdvīka*) scented with flowers, [they stood] before the doorkeeper.
"We shall swiftly seize Sujji by the beard in battle and bring him back!"—
with such boasts did they display their self-importance.
They were joined by the Kaśmīrakas, the Mitas, the Khaśas, and the Saindhavakas.

Even though they exerted themselves, they were unable to march against him; for those who were full of pride, it was their conviction that they would grant the tribute to Jayasiṃha— the foremost among kings— as a boon to their rival.
Somapāla, slighted by the rolling of the dice which sought many gains,
displayed some favor toward the royal faction.

"While my father-in-law’s armies are occupied in the conflict with the enemy, why do you, relying on me who am prepared for their welfare, seek out a vulnerability? Thus was Sujji rebuked by him; yet Sujji, consistent with his own arrogance, replied:
Having donned his armor and disregarding everyone, he became the leader in seizing the king’s army;
then, struck by the great terror of a fever born of the intense heat of the month of Āṣāḍha,
Lakṣmaka rose up from his division and fled in the night.
Having dispatched messengers to report quickly that the camp had been destroyed,
some of those soldiers, desiring to kill Sujji, pursued him;
one group followed the king’s army, while the other followed the enemy.
They set out along a path as difficult as a chasm,
having abandoned the road through the air which was subject to their enemies;
near that [destination], they were beset by the perilous time known as Kāla.

On that day, the soldiers, together with people of various ranks, entered the villages whose names were not forgotten, having reached their respective lodgings. (Yugma) Even in the nearby villages of those who had followed them on the journey, they were recognized. (KRT 8.1877–1878ab)
Having eaten and drunk, they spent half the night there, free from fear from any quarter. Then,
in order to quickly inform their own enemies of his arrival, Sujji,
filled with agitation, approached and caused the sound of musical instruments to be made.
At the very end of the night,
the army, deprived of its support and leader, quickly fled from there by various mountain paths. Ministers were abandoned at dawn by those who robbed them of their variegated garments.
As if by earthquakes or by the melting of various minerals from crumbling cliffs, the armies were being swept away;
no one took up a weapon to protect them. At that time, not another was protected by anyone other than by their own selves, through whatever means possible.

Some, leaping and bounding over high places, with their crimson lips like garments and their red buttocks, attained a dexterity like that of monkeys. Others, having cast off their clothes, revealed their fair bodies blossoming like flowers.
Like fragments of yellow orpiment stone driven by the wind, they went forth.
With bodies as massive as mountains covered in groves of bamboo thick with piercing pain,
some advanced like young elephants emitting shrieks born of their labored breath.
What was the use of shouting mantras? There was no one there at all who fled like an animal with his composure overturned.
Then that fool, mounted upon the shoulder of his servant, ran forward as he went.
The doorkeeper was spotted from afar by some of the enemy warriors;
naked, yet adorned with armlets and earrings that flashed like rays of the sun,
he pursued them as they fled with all their might to fulfill their vow.
Struck by a stone hurled by a servant, he was dropped from his shoulder and wounded by the rock;
standing there with his body motionless, he was seized by those who possessed great speed. His frame was emaciated like that of a śārikā bird distressed by grief over its new captivity.

With his eyes narrowed like a serpent manifesting its venom, he thought: "Surely Sujji would inflict a further slaughter upon me, who am already bound and have robbed him of his wealth of honor. (Kṛt 8.1890cd–1891ab)

Having placed him upon their shoulders and stripped him of all his garments and ornaments, he was led away at the front by those shouting with derision. (Tilaka 8.1892) This courageous man, having covered his face with a cloth, was carried out. (Tilaka 8.1893)
Having said, "Like Bṛhadrāja," he gave him his own garments;
having clothed him in a cloak and mounted him upon a horse once more,
he steadied him with courage, consoling him with affectionate words.
Surrounded by Khaśas whose horses and sword-sheaths were stripped away,
the illustrious one then took him and went into the presence of Somapāla.
These [women], possessing the flickering grace of lightning sporting in the courtyard of the sky—
Whose fortunes remain stable? Only those who follow fortune itself.
Before whom [the king] was once fed at will like a servant with the thought that he was performing a service, and whose limbs were personally attended to with applications of saffron paste.
Within just five or six months,
he was perceived by the people as standing before Somapāla and the others in that very same manner, even though they were bowed down before him.
Lulla, whose face was darkened at the edges by white-gray hair,
was silenced by grief like a forest-dweller bound in the midst of a forest by his enemies.
Having accepted the insignia offered by Sujji, Somapāla— KRT_8_1899ab KRT_8_1899cd KRT_8_1900ab

Having seized Kaśmīra without resistance, he returned to his own kingdom. Having arrived from the presence of Loṭhana, he was entreated by the brave Māñika and others, who promised him abundant wealth, to release the warder.

For at that time, the people of Kaśmīra— though they were greedy and desirous of seizing the kingdom which was dependent upon the *pratīhāras*— did not hold in contempt the *ḍāmara* upstarts who followed the faction of the *pratīhāra* instructors. (KRT 8.1902–1903ab)

And although the king desired to give away abundant wealth, he did not do so. When his ministers, their pride shattered, had reached the city, and when the doorkeeper was defeated, the monarch did not lose his fortitude.
Those very elite troops with whom he formerly established a dual kingship as a mendicant,
and by whom Sussala was sustained when the kingdom was in turmoil—
those [troops] were then seized by the king, who suffered from the affliction of a cold fever.
Ten thousand of those warriors met their death.
Then, in that region, there was no place where even for a moment there was silence;
day and night there was the tumultuous wailing of kinsmen and the sound of funeral drums.
Exhausted by the heat of the summer sun, with all worldly activity brought to a standstill and his energy shattered,
that time became like a lost kingdom;
even the Kashmiris who had arrived from various distant regions [found themselves in such a state].
Lothartha, whose prosperity had greatly increased, arrived at the royal gate.
Having obtained this extraordinary royal splendor by a stroke of chance,
his unimpeded power of movement was like that of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera).

His brothers, kinsmen, servants, sons, and others were inseparable from him in their conduct, sharing his very nature and being undivided from him in both prosperity and adversity. Possessing great wealth,
he did not shower rain out of season, nor was he tight-fisted when it came to its proper distribution.
His worldly dealings, which had ceased through the ripening of his years, were no longer perceived.

(KRT 8.1912cd) Shade moves without restraint, while sunlight itself is accompanied by shade; thus, in hundreds of instances, suffering is distinct from happiness. Yet the state of happiness is distressed by its constant interpenetration with endless suffering. (KRT 8.1913ab–cd)

When such prosperity had been attained, and Māra had become both diminished and increased, Dilha, the son of the only son Loṭhana, passed away. Grieving for that [son], she whose heart was pierced by the stake of sorrow—

Then the wrestlers met their destruction, for they were fond of rolling on the ground. When his wife was thus deceased— she who shared his feelings and was preeminent in virtue— and likewise when his son had perished,
he perceived no further purpose in his royal fortune.
This was the manifestation of the lack of affection so easily found among kings,
or perhaps it was the deluding power of Fortune, that he did not recognize his own happiness again;
for even though he was penniless, he, knowing the proper time, acted likewise toward his father.

With thirty-six lakhs [of coins], the lord of the earth secured the liberation of Lakṣmaka. As he arrived on the road, where a shower of flowers was scattered by the people to celebrate the increase of his fortune, who could have known that his royal prosperity had been overturned?
Having forgotten the reputation of his former subjugation due to the power of his newfound fortune,
he once again became capable of both punishing and favoring others; yet,
with all his self-restraint and skill destroyed by the lure of wealth, he was rendered powerless.
Sujji accepted the office of minister without guile from King Loṭhana.
He gave him the daughter of his maternal uncle and removed his distrust;
he did this simultaneously with the pain caused by the king's current distress over the loss of his beloved wife.

The skillful [king] sent for the royal Padmaratha and brought him there to marry his daughter, named Somaladevī. Having thus established him with firm roots through these principal alliances, [he departed].
He attained freedom from debt for his assistance in the unimpeded seizure [of power].
And he contemplated an entry into Kaśmīra,
being urged by the new king who had entreated him many times through the mediation of the Ḍāmara and others.
Having thus formed an alliance with the kings of the border regions,
he then employed a policy of intrigue against his enemy,
being full of vigor.

There, at the commencement of that [work], the gatekeeper of the eastern gate, profound in intellect and possessing undiminished courage, attained a state worthy of praise among those who discern the essential from the trivial. For he, though having lost all his own possessions, was sought after by those seeking his welfare.
He was ever intent upon his duties as a lord through acts such as giving and honoring.
Residing in the place known as Vanaprastha, located near Lohara, he—
unwearied by incessant battles— brought about the disintegration of the enemy forces.
Having been cast a sidelong glance at with this intention— whether falsely or truly—
the King of Loṭhana, Māñikendra, Araka, and others felt fear.
Alas, the king, whose mind was set upon Sujja, [intended] for us, the Ākrikas, who were to be slain.
He knows that he suspected him because of that instigation; thus [they thought].
A son was born to King Sussala by his queen named Sahajā.
"We shall make Mallārjuna the king here in Lohara for your benefit."
Then the wise King Jayasiṃha suddenly directed his rolling [of the dice] as if out of affection for that [fortress]. Then,
King Jayasiṃha, desiring to turn that fortress into a women’s quarters, sent a message to them under a pretext.
Those who had no trust in him likewise disregarded his promise.
Then Loṭhana, perceiving that Mallārjuna had begun to act as a wheel-turner (a rebel),
imprisoned those former brothers and sons, as well as the wheel-turners themselves.
Feeling apprehension toward his imprisoned younger brother,
Vigraharāja, who was full of resentment, he employed a supreme stratagem.
The king, an expert in expedients, having formed an alliance with his paternal uncle under a pretext, [acted].
He hastened to reclaim the lost kingdom through various efforts.
Having dismissed Śūra, Loṭhana— whose reign was now unshakable due to Sujji’s exertions—
remained for some months without disturbance, subsisting on his regular stipend.
Sujji, the son of Padmaratha, had previously brought a maiden; hearing that her mother had arrived for the sake of her daughter’s marriage— still unespoused—
and that she was highly esteemed in this context by Tejaḥpāla and the others...

Accompanied by his ministers, he went forth to meet him at the city of Darpitapura. Then, Mallārjuna, having found an opportunity through Māñikā and others who had gone to the prison and released him from bondage, was consecrated in the kingdom of Koṭṭa by those who had united together.

The *ṭhakkuras*, brought as before, barred those servants of King Siṃha who had arrived at the base of the city gate and were seeking to enter. On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, in the sixth year of Loṭhana—

Just as he was united with sovereignty, so too was he swiftly separated from it. That fool, lacking in fortune, grieved for his unmarried daughter and his unspent wealth, both of which had come under the enjoyment of another.
Having wandered through places such as towers and other locations, he, whose power was lost,
obtained some remaining treasury by force from Sujji.
Having humiliated the servants of King Siṃha who had been summoned previously, Māṇika—
He brought King Mallārjuna to a state of unrivaled prowess. By that king, who was young in age and excessively lavish, the offering of betel with pearls instead of areca nuts was once performed.
The renunciation of *ghāṭaka* (robbery), *kuṭṭana* (torture), and so forth, out of a desire for the pleasures of the senses during the rainy season,
was declared by the knowers of reality to be always faulty.
The treasury of King Sussala, accumulated through the oppression of his subjects— KRT_8_1949ab.
Therefore, that prodigal man spent his wealth according to his own whims; for he,
whose conduct was like a tortoise, being heated by pride, cast aside virtuous men and nourished a host of courtesans, bards, rogues, libertines, servants, and the like.

The wealth of kings— whether it be that which destroys rivals, brings about welfare, and so forth, or that which is reduced to ashes by fire— is acquired through the oppression of the people. The riches of a ruler born of victory are those produced by the affliction of his subjects.
The treasury of Śaṅkaravarman, which had been plundered by the sons of slaves such as Utpala and others— who were like Yamas to their grandsons—
was enjoyed at will by Prabhākara and his ilk, who were like paramours to their own wives.
Women who had fallen under the power of the bodiless god (Kāma) gave wealth acquired through sin to Sugandhāditya, who was entitled to share in their enjoyments, as if he were a cripple.

For the sake of King Yaśaskara, she squandered his accumulated wealth; rendered helpless by the god of love, she embraced the people. Having obtained the wealth acquired by former kings, Pārśvagupta died.
A donor was born as the son of Jāyā through [the influence of] the exaltations and other such factors.
Saṃgrāmarāja, wealthy and like a bee at the lotus-face of Śrīlekhā,
was robbed by Vyaḍḍa, Sūha, and others, even though he possessed a fervent desire for intense acquisition.
The formidable sovereignty of the king, whose wisdom was destroyed by a lack of discernment,
was reduced to ashes;
for by his son, who was an unworthy vessel, the noble lady was made to taste the passion of a paramour.
The treasury of King Kalaśa was produced by the skill of the *kukalāka* [bird]; his wealth,
along with his houses, women, and sons,
was delivered to the fire by Harṣadeva, who possessed an insatiable thirst for acquisition.
By Candrāpīḍa, Uccala, Avantivarman, and others who were firm in righteousness,
the depletion of the treasury— which is consistent with justice— was never considered improper at any time.
Thieves, usurers, frontier kings, courtesans, pimps, and the like—
When the new Mallārjuna rose, they began to plunder his well-provisioned stores;
though he had frustrated their desires, the king grew weary and, having deceived them regarding his swords,
then dispatched Citraratha swiftly to attack.
Increased by an equal increment of two at each of the feet and tips of the doors,
and joined with an infinite number of neighboring units, he established his station in Phullapura.
Even though they were extensive, they could not prevail because of their reliance on the fortress.
In order to conquer the army of Mallārjuna in battle,

his followers ascended the fortress to sow dissension; however, that man named Saṃvardhana, who was a servant of his and held in high esteem by the king, was slain at night by the followers of Mallārjuna.

Even while remaining in their fortress— a place otherwise invincible in battle— the enemies fell into a state of subjection to fear when the Lord of Koṣṭha arrived there. Having bound a treaty and fulfilled his promise, he then released them.
To honor their mother, Mallārjuna went into her presence.
With a dress distinguished by widowhood yet radiant with former sovereignty,
she made Koṣṭheśvara and the others anxious and fickle-minded.
When she had departed from his presence after having gained his confidence,
Mallārjuna gave her hand, which he had accepted, to the gatekeeper.
Koṣṭhaka was drawn away by the passion of the queen’s eyes.
Under the pretext of a desire to see him, he ascended the fortress accompanied by a limited retinue.
Then Citraratha,
having descended, went into the presence of the lord of the earth together with him, bringing with him various gifts.
Then the king, having deliberated, employed the lord of the eastern gate— who was skilled in diplomacy—
to win back his enemies through policy.
When Skanda had departed for the vicinity of Padmaratha, even while he was rolling about, [the enemy forces] were overcome.
The newly crowned king obtained a slight extension of his reign;
he married that daughter of Padmaratha named Somā, and, having endured the long period of mourning,
he also wedded the daughter of Nāgapāla.

Therefore, those kings such as Somapāla and others, possessing hidden deceit, accepted wages in the capacity of servants from that one who was deluded by the sense of "I" (ego). Through the activities of poets, singers, chatterers, warriors, and bards— KRT_8_1976ab–KRT_8_1977ab.

Many rogues robbed him, yet they too were of royal lineage. From childhood, his wisdom was unripened; though seen crying out much, he was recognized by the foolish as one of skillful intent merely through the maturity of his speech.
Like a lamp blazing for an inauspicious rite, his face shone without [the presence of] harshness; yet, though he was of gentle appearance, no other [quality] was seen there that was not noble.
In this interval, the king seized Sujji, who was of formidable prowess.
Thinking, "Let it not be that even Mallārjuna has taken refuge here," the lord was more intent on expulsion than on admission;
at that moment, the doorkeeper displayed a certain degree of capability.

Bestowing upon Sujaya the garland of authority over Kampana and other regions, which had been sent by the King, he did so without the garland of royal duties; for, out of consideration for Somapāla who had come to his house dissatisfied, [he granted it].
Becoming gracious, he drew from his own hair-tuft with his left hand, out of delight, the garland and gave it to him,
who was already satisfied by its acquisition.

By means of a thickening rain, he caused the creepers to flourish through abundance. [Cakkalaka] Rilhaṇa abandoned his friendship for Bhartṛhari, who was blessed with prosperity, and displayed hostility toward Sujji upon the latter's accession. [Kṛt 8.1984cd–1985ab]
Honoring Sujji with a formal reception, the king had him enter;
he banished Dhanya and others from the country, yet not out of his own inclination, but because of the words of that [Sujji].
When the king, having committed an offense, found an opportunity and sought to kill him through assassins...
Koṣṭheśvara fled when he learned the news from his presence.
When the king arrived, having seized the lord of men, Koṣṭheśvara,
struck by a rift in his own faction, then departed for another land.
But Loṭhana, seizing some local chieftains (*ṭhakkura*s) on behalf of the Jina,
while residing in the place called Bappanīla, forcibly [attacked] Mallārjuna. There, indeed, his inconceivable prowess was witnessed.
Even though he had been defeated, he always struck at him where he was vulnerable;
he seized horses, plundered, and caused havoc in the markets and bazaars. He brought about the destruction of highways, fortifications, and other strategic points everywhere.
Then, requested by the one named Rājarāja, who was a *ḍāmara*,
he entered the kingdom of Krama in order to obtain the sovereignty of Kaśmīra. Having learned that [his rival] had been killed by Citraratha while nearby, he—
In that forest, he went once more to the land of Bappa-nīla.
While he repeatedly launched assaults even upon the watchtowers,
Mallārjuna, residing in the fortress, was unable to hold it back.
Having caused his nephew to bestow much wealth upon his paternal uncle,
Koṣṭheśvara, having prepared for his expedition, then entered into a treaty.
Having established his firm position at Lohara, he then took Loṭhana [under his control].
Desiring to seize [the king], he fell upon the land of Kaśmīra;
having leaped over the mountains, he set foot in the district of Kārkoṭa. Having descended onto a path that was not passable for others, he was [attacked] by other Dānavas.
Having emerged from his alliance with Nāvāpa, the swift-acting lord of the earth,
employing every effort, rendered him [Nāvāpa] struck down by his own rising [rebellion].
In the meantime, the chamberlain arrived, having escaped the oppression of Asta.

Prosperity does not belong to those of little merit, nor does there exist any permanence of life. Dwelling in their homes with all exits blocked by a fondness for clearing them away, and living without restraint, those whose intellects have been made light by prosperity do not, through their impulsive conduct, realize— alas!— the sudden descent of destiny.
Constantly driving people away from his house,
he did not realize that Death had fallen upon his back while he slept in comfort. For he,
having been feverish, now sleeps free from fever, his fever having been spat out.

Having realized this, he was not recognized; while still sleeping, he then passed away. When the king returned to the chamber where the wrestling match had taken place, there was neither that wrestler Arjuna, nor that chamber, nor that wrestling ground.
Mallārjuna slew Chadmodayana as he stood nearby; Koṣṭhaka, whom he had established in neutrality, grew angry with him. Then, having gathered his forces, he did not appease that distressed man.
He rushed forth in his anger with his army to attack, accompanied by his sons and grandsons;
though he was joined by horsemen and measured forces such as the *koṣṭhakas* and *mallakas*,
he crossed the *paroṣṇī* array and crushed that invincible host.

In those battles against the Khaśas, Saindhavas, and others, King Siṃhabhūbhṛt met his death; yet that king was not slain out of hatred. Having ascended to the summit of the fortress, he fell from the peak of his own pride.
His majesty shattered, he again occupied the inner apartment.

Having ceased his rolling about and remaining still, he once more became free from enmity. Because of that [treasure] which had not yet been delivered as a gift, that turbulent man fell into a state of conflict.
Having bound the officials, he caused customs duties to be collected as if he were a king;
by his own name, he had vermilion seals impressed upon the merchandise in the market town,
like the joining of two glass jars with lac.
In every moment, a breach of alliance arose between the two.
Having endured the harshness of empty words, the Lord of Lo-hara fell into a state of detachment.
He too led him away with unrestrained rivalries of beauty. Then,
having sent Skanda into the midst of that army with a great clamor,
he made it exceedingly joyful by seizing the finest horses and the most excellent weapons.
Having given [the two]— through uneven acts of forceful prowess in the future—
the foolish Koṣṭhaka thus brought about the easy destruction of his enemies.
Through the relationship of giving his daughter in marriage, he [secured] the father-in-law of the chief ministers.
In the meantime, the king thought of killing Māṇavaka; his passion was surging with the intensity of mature youth. For it was quite evident that he had been won over by his mother’s illicit affair.
At the time of his meal, those fierce men, having received a signal from the king, were given weapons and deprived him of his life as he was eating. Shaking his sword-blade,
wearing his hero’s band, and shouting loudly—
Plundering that army, he displayed various forms of martial prowess; yet,
alas, even Indrākara was not spared from the midst of his hostility,
for the king himself treated him with poison by means of a medicinal draught.

Then King Siṃha, from whom all enemies had been driven away by the gods, laid siege to Koṣṭhaka and dispatched Sujji for the sake of victory. He reached the vicinity of his destination in just one watch of the journey.
As long as he was agitated by the loss of his horses and thrown into confusion by the fortress,
Mallārjuna— distraught by internal divisions and unable to hold his ground—
abandoned the stronghold with its treasury and fled.
Deprived of his kingdom and being plundered on the roads by bandits,
he somehow protected the remainder of his treasury while looking toward his downfall;
having been fallen for eighteen years, he reached the eighth year of his exile.

On the second day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, while he was still in his kingdom, that donor cut off his own head— having been deprived of the nectar of the moon’s crest— and thus rendered himself one whose head was severed by a weapon. In this world, where even the Lord (Śiva) committed such an unworthy act toward one who had helped him, what other person could remain there with a double-tongued serpent at his side?
"Thinking 'these are pearls,' [the eye] is attached to water resting upon lotuses; thinking 'this is consciousness,' [the mind] is fixed upon inert matter.
Alas! That certain deluding power belonging to Śrī, which rests within her, flashes forth as that by which whatever is known at all [is perceived].
In the forests, some strike with wondrous weapons; others do so with their sense of smell, some with their sight, and others with their sense of taste.
There may indeed be certain malicious people in the houses of kings who attempt to cause harm through their speech alone;

yet they are unable to consume one who has taken refuge in the Lord, just as firewood placed before a *jyotīrasa* gem cannot burn it. However, if such a person were to follow behind him, those wicked ones, finding an opening, would reduce him to ashes, like the rays of the sun.
The lord of Kampana brought the fort of Harṣaṭa in Kāpila under his suzerainty; gathering a multitude of Koṭa servants with great efforts,
he delayed there while preparing a bed for that [territory] to be led back once more.

After a few days had passed there, while the king was still in a state of favor, those naturally wicked men— rogues whose poison was envy— brought about his defilement through secret incitements. (Tilaka)

What king could be more devoted to his own firm resolve in action than this ruler of the earth, who is made to dance like a child by rogues? In his childhood, he was granted a state of dullness by those who were mostly fools and well-liked by him.
Even when mature, one should not abandon the king's dark luster, as it is with a gem. For kings,
by the mere fact that another servant is unknown [to them], a calamity like a thunderbolt falls upon the innocent, bringing great suffering to the kingdom.
When a task to be accomplished has been resolved upon, one should employ female slaves like Lakṣmakā and others;
thus Sujji, having obtained the support of Prāyoji and Rāja, set out to conquer Lohara.

Then, when that man of wondrous deeds had accomplished his task, those wicked men struck him with the unfailing science of calumny, which was equal to the Brahma-weapon; yet they failed because of the king’s affectionate words, which betrayed no sign of agitation due to his profound composure.
The lord of Kampana did not perceive any turbidity [in him] upon his return;
for how could there be such suspicion toward one who is by nature free from malice,

In the meantime, Kamalīyā and the others made a certain kinsman their sole companion— a man who,

Through the watering of wickedness and slander, that tree quickly attained a hundred branches.

Having thus addressed the one who had heard [the truth], he then made that drinker of the jar (Kośapīthin) agree, saying "So be it," and approached Citraratha to slay him.
Even in this age of Kali, which is indeed turbid due to the weakness of the Dharma,
the power of the gods of the earth shines forth unbroken even today.
There is no one whatsoever whose full merit has not been exhausted by the Brahmins.
He displays fortitude through his skill in uprooting fallen wickedness. The virtuous one, terrifying the twice-born, attained the slaughter of the twice-born and the gods;
Citraratha, who treated Brahmins with contempt, was slain by a Brahmin alone.
His mind surely overcome by that deed incited by the twice-born, he brooded upon his own death,
casting away his life-breaths without cause. On another day, those Brahmins perished by the fire.
In that very contest of equal rivalry, he was left with his followers slain;
failing to reach Citraratha, who was endowed with vast strength,
the slayer spent many nights in vigilance, day and night.

For as he proceeded along a path bordered by the limitless countryside, he was both invisible and visible while amidst the throngs of people. At one point, with a speed that was harsh due to its marvelous steadiness, he [passed] swiftly.
Having descended from the ladder, he entered the king's palace. Then,
as he was lingering at the top of a pillar in the midst of the vassal lords, that man of fierce audacity struck him on the head with a dagger.

Like one about to die, his memory failing due to exhaustion, with eyes wandering, his vital energy departed. Realizing that he had been caused to be killed by the king, those who were devoid of courage—
Terrified, his followers did not abandon him even in that state.
Knowing him to be lifeless, the fierce [soldier] did not strike again;
seeing his brother had reached the second ladder, he restrained him.

"Even though his path was entirely free of obstacles, Citraratha did not flee; rather, he was struck down by the king. Thus he cried out loudly. "He has perished, along with the enjoyment of his kingdom consisting of roasted meat and other luxuries."
Then, out of fear, all those cowardly followers of Citraratha fled;
his elder brother, Loṭharatha, having escaped in terror,
sought refuge with a certain dancer, placing his breasts upon her face.
When Citraratha had been brought thus close by the king, the monarch himself comforted him, saying, "Do not fear; who has struck you?
While those present asked, "By whose order was the gatekeeper killed? and "Who was the slayer? Kṛtavarman spoke.
Searched by the soldiers, he declared, "It is I," and revealed himself.
Steady in his valor, which was praiseworthy for leaping over [the enemy], that hero struck down thirty or twenty warriors by his own fortitude; then, having been struck on the foot, he fell.
For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the evil-doers,
and for the sake of establishing righteousness, I manifest myself age after age.
Having obtained from his hand a letter containing the reasons for that task, he was written [therein].
The hope for the end of that [period] is purified by this verse:
Then Citraratha, afflicted by aversion, madness,
and dejection, became one whose healed wound reopened due to the piercing of the joint at his forehead.
Having spent five months in this way, his body emaciated and devoid of nourishment,
he lay tossing and turning daily upon the surface of his bed.
With Mallārjuna placed at the forefront, the city of Koṣṭhaka was on the verge of upheaval.
In the midst of that, he entered a mountain fortress thick with trees.
"Let me not cause delusion for the world, which, remembering its past calamities, fears a renewed state of dual sovereignty, by wandering about with the intent to devour my own kinsmen."
As if his limbs were tormented by the sudden onset of a storm from unseasonable clouds,
the people quickly fell into a state of weakened power due to the rise of a foreign enemy. Then, that tree-fortress, extending for many miles in every direction, [was besieged].
He hemmed him in with ministers who had surrounded the forests and villages on all sides;
while Sañjayapāla was binding the camp with Yavana troops.
They mimicked the enemy’s tremors, like trees rendered motionless by a windless state.
Even the mountain, though fortunate, had its ridges and slopes cast down by the falling rocks;
it was like a scent-averse elephant facing an enemy who is a rival for a female elephant.

Having encamped his army at Govāsa, as directed by Rilhaṇa, the king roamed through the forest like the sun among owls, causing his enemies to sink. Thus, by the undertakings of the king of fierce power, [the enemy] was paralyzed and submitted.
For three or four months, the Lord of the Treasury remained without the ability to move about,
having been driven into a hostile foreign land by neighboring kings;
his own faction was divided, and his efforts as the king’s servant were rendered futile.
Due to his foolishness, he was unskilled in understanding the conduct of kings;

having forgotten his offense, he desired to reconcile with the monarch whose foot had been severed. Knowing that reproach would follow from deceiving his lord who wished to remove his own wrath, he remained silent.
With single-minded devotion, Sañjayāla fulfilled that wish of his.
Even though he was thus distressed, he did not seize the enemy king, desiring instead to establish peace;
for among those born of the Earth and Hara, freedom from malice is no cause for wonder.
While delivering the king’s enemy with his own finger severed,
even as he cut it off, the monarch was unable to sever his own wrath.
With a cloth tied around his neck and carrying a sandal upon his head, he went forth.
Even after his meal, he was unable to make the king desist from his anger; for,
like a king himself, he had not accepted the insignia of the subordinate monarchs,
and he carried out every royal command with pride, offering his own counter-arguments.
The king heard that Mallārjuna had been bound and was being led through the middle of the marketplace. For prosperity follows upon the prosperity of those who are destined for success;
indeed, he was being carried on the shoulders of his attendants.
Unable to traverse the road due to the exhaustion of being footless,
he emerged from various places of danger and reached the village named Sāvarṇika, which was protected by Loha, with a guard stationed there.

The lord of the earth was put to death by the *ṭhakkura* named Jaggikā; meanwhile, he heard that his servant Priyaṅkara had arrived in his presence. Having somehow escaped from the fortress while his pursuers were nearly ready to capture him, he departed.

Once he has bound it, who then would have the power to transgress destiny? The Gaṅgā, which had been coiled within the belly of a single great seer as he lay upon the path of the sky, emerged with great difficulty; yet when swallowed by another who filled the hollows of the ocean, no one was capable of transgressing what was destined to be.
The gatekeeper of the eastern gate was appointed by the king of vast intellect to guard the vicinity as far as the boundary established at Jaggika;
for without him, there was no one else who could bear the burden of fortitude, profundity, and valor, nor possess such great wisdom.
For in times of crisis, the king does not tolerate the support of other ministers.
Having bypassed the obstructed paths with those receiving wages from both sides, he,
the lord of the earth, beheld that enemy standing in the darkness.
Though his resolve was empty, he maintained an appearance of steadfastness;
praising him as he arrived outside and having said this and that, he spoke again:
"He who holds in high regard devotion to his master, which is superior in every respect."
You, the foremost among the wise, were drawn away by those afflicted by greed;
without a companion such as you, who acted like a protective amulet,
I suffered loss through the many deceits of that wicked king during my youth in the kingdom.

It is indeed by necessity that the brilliance of kings becomes difficult to behold; like the end of winter on a day when the sun has set, they become impossible for the eyes of men to gaze upon. Yet, with the tips of their mandalas as red as blood, they shine beautifully at their rise.
Thus that king was as fruitless at his setting as the sun;
blessed was his advent, for it caused the women of the city to tremble—
just as the throngs of Apsarases are agitated by passion at both the fierce rising and the fierce setting of the sun.
Having gained entrance into society and achieved some degree of success like one of noble birth,
I have become as mature as a poet, yet I have reached the height of my folly. Now,
having become a guarantor of truth, may you establish peace within your own heart.
"By means of this one boon, you have not exceeded what was to be accomplished for me.
Having said this, he then touched a crystal in order to produce conviction.

He brought the *liṅga* together with its pedestal before the Lord of the Gate. [The gods] surely desire men to possess a superior disposition for fighting, rather than warriors who rain down spears, pikes, and javelins in the crush of a deceitful battle.
Having thus reflected and touched the Śiva-liṅga, he accepted the boon he desired; and he (the deity) spoke to him again:
"Unharmed, with his gaze drawn [toward you], he approached the presence of the king unscathed."
"Just as you have come to this state, so now he entreats you.
Hearing those words, which were struck by his wretchedness, all the kings stood paralyzed with shame,
like sprouts moistened by rain.
Then, O monk, that final moment, when remembered by those possessed of consciousness,
once again became the cause for the blossoming of a mind that was previously settled.
Mounted upon a vehicle carried by men, that shameless one was led away to his leaf-hut.
Thus, even while beholding the worlds he had protected, he remained unchanging;
like a beast on the path, rendered helpless by hunger, sleep, and other such needs,
he was dragged along by some [force] and was not touched by any conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Seeing him being led away by such guards, the people’s hearts became moist with compassion; they did not rejoice in the king, and they said:
"O King, toward this one who deserves pity, the eldest-born of your lineage..."
Such cruelty is not seen even in a man who has lost his father; who,
unless he were heartless as a sword, would dare to commit this act against one whose body is as lovely as a dark blue lotus and who is beyond reproach for suffering?
Then, their vision being devoid of any connection between what preceded and what followed, they forgot their destination and reproached the king on the road for this and that. Or rather,
how can any calculation be made regarding children, fools, and the like?
Even for the great, there is never constant one-pointedness of mind when listening to the gambling match, the dragging of Draupadī by her hair, and so forth; rather,
a greater anger toward the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra arises than that felt toward the Pāṇḍavas.
When the Kurus drank blood, when their heads were struck by broken thighs,

and when they heard of the enmity toward the Pāṇḍavas, that very same [hostility] was seen in them as well. No one who understands the higher and lower courses of actions exists without a middle course.

How could there be a lack of distinction from his own experience for a bystander in each of those cases? Carrying on his shoulder a clay vessel marked with a cut-off finger, mounted upon a draft animal, he arrived at the city in the evening.
On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, the lord of the earth established him,
accompanied by guards, within the ninth monastery in his eleventh year.
For five or six nights, he remained fasting and suffering.
Out of compassion, he went to the side of those who sought the touch of his feet.
To those who had petitioned him and received his promise,
he declared that Citraratha and Koṣṭhaka were to be executed solely for their treachery.
Then the king,

wishing to imprison five trusted men, including Rihlaṇa and others, who had departed from his own realm, had them seized. When all [his other ministers] had lost their vigor, the queen herself took up the burden of effort.

Then Rilhaṇa seized him with both arms, as a crocodile seizes a fish. Deprived of his weapons within the cage of that strong man's arms, he stood motionless, blinded by sleep as if paralyzed by a demon.
The wrathful Bhikṣurāja, a rival of Kularāja,
struck at the nape of his neck with a sword out of devotion to the king;
and the protector of the earth, striking him on the head with a battle-axe— KRT_8_2315–2316ab.
And that scion of royalty was struck down by the king out of anger;
with his vital organs pierced where they meet at the nape of the neck,
he writhed on the ground, drenched in blood.
By the mighty elephants led by Kamalīya, his brother Catuṣka was felled to the earth like a boulder from a mountain slope;
seeing their two masters thus struck down and bound, [the soldiers were overcome with distress].
A twice-born man named Mallaka rose up with a drawn sword;
striking at high and low among those who lived off the king,
he was not perceived by the monarch as he fell, creating a tumultuous uproar.
As he was slaying those various great warriors who were rushing toward him from the presence of the king,
the King of the Kula charged at that man of great splendor with his sword drawn.
Unable to strike back as his hand was falling too quickly,
that expert in physical training seemed to be blocked by a wall;
unable to retreat, to stand his ground, or even to strike, he was rendered helpless.

And he stood firm, having steadied the unscarred [Nanda] with many holds; while Padmarāja ran nearby, making a clamor with the sound of his arms as they were tossed up from the stamping of his feet, Nanda cast his gaze toward the wrestler.
Then, finding an opening, the king of the clan struck him in the chest;
as he was departing after striking, he crushed the thumb of that man's hand. While both of them were striking the king of the Bījas, who was dense with the heat of pride, Kṛt_8.2325ab–2326ab.
As he struck back, he then swiftly dealt a blow. Abandoning even those three assailants who had come within his range of vision,
he rushed toward the king who stood at the door of the four-pillared hall.
When the king had become his target, the lord of the clan, pursuing him with great haste,
rendered him powerless by wounding his hip bone.
Then, surrounded by all his warriors, he quickly [dispatched] those who were impotent and lame.

Having slain him, he lay upon the hero’s bed, with the flowing blood serving as its coverlet. Witnessed by his master who was still alive yet fallen into calamity, he— whose valor was praiseworthy and whose moment of death was not to be envied— was reckoned among the heroes.
When the servants in the outer quarters had fled, the one named Janakacandra, though a commoner, displayed supreme poverty-stricken fortitude;
unarmed, he seized a battle-axe from one of the king's servants.
For he, leading many [souls] to the presence of Yama by acting as the foremost messenger of war,
had an axe in his hand; and for him who was desirous of departing,
that axe entered [the moon], like a crescent moon seeking a share of the sun’s orb.
