When our husband was thus bound, we neither saw nor even heard that the virtuous and proud wife of Koṣṭhaka remained steadfast, saying: "May he,
being alive, obtain you once again as his husband."

Disregarding the words of his wives, he entered the fire. Purified by the feet of that Satī, whose fame is sung throughout the world, the Fire-god was cleansed of the sin incurred by his longing for the embrace of the wives of the Seven Sages.
She, the daughter of Vasantasena and sister of Dhanyodaya,
maintained her vow as the wife of a *ḍāmara* out of pride in her pure lineage, rather than out of a desire for wealth—
wealth which even women of the *lavana* caste might pursue despite widowhood.
He was a village official and head of a household who shared in the enjoyment of the slopes [of the mountain];
he was conceited, his dejection brought on by the delusion of his own intellect.
By her and by her two attendants, the enclosure was constructed high above Koṣṭhaka.
Though his wounds had healed, he was reduced to a mere mass of worms by certain misdeeds; devoid of life, within seven nights he became a carcass in the prison cell.
Then Citraratha, emaciated by wasting away, [beheld] the king who was defiled.
Upon hearing this, Mallārjuna became extremely distressed with fear.
His beloved wife, Sūryamatī— a virtuous woman who had been his only spouse—
had already become a guest of the other world, having previously served as the guarantor for his prosperity.

While his body was afflicted by a wasting disease, while his home had lost its possessions, and while his husband was clouded by discord, he did not find even the slightest pleasure. "Though I am guilty, no unpleasantness should come from the king to me while I am staying at a sacred ford."

Having reflected thus, he set out under the pretext of going to die before the Queen of the Gods. Then, from various locations, the king brought away the wealth of him whose splendor surpassed that of the Lord of Wealth— a wealth abounding in manifold riches.
By means of golden garments, armor, jewel-horses, weapons, and so forth,
each [king] displayed his own splendor, as if in competition, becoming greater and greater.
The royal tree, withered by the heat of the hostility toward iron and the heat of its own nature, [was restored].
He was nourished even by the sprinkling from the mountain stream of the Fortune of the Tall One (Tallakṣmī).

Even though the calamity had long since vanished, Śālva did not abandon Saubha— just as one accustomed to dwelling in the forest does not abandon his fear— just as he might have abandoned Śrī-Kalyāṇapura.
In whose palace the Fortune of Kings remained sleepless, as if turned into a captive, pale with anxiety and mingled with the rays of white parasols.

Having perceived that he had been employed by the king, that Vijaya, born of Bhava, slew the fierce one named Ānanda, and was himself slain by him. Thus did he spread his fame as one so distinguished for protecting his subjects.

The two servants of King Jayasiṃha, who were full of every kind of zeal and whose intentions were clearly manifest, remained at the sacred ford while Citraratha stood there, desiring to grasp his feet;
they were the very generators of passion for him.

Having won over the king with the payment of abundant bribes, Śṛṅgāra departed, his father having been defeated; he attained the status of sharing in the royal fortune and pleasures. He once again placed the gate, which had long remained open, back into its position at the time of sunrise.
Like a king on the opposite bank of a river during the rainy season,
Citraratha— his vital organs tormented for a long time by the inevitable consequences of his evil karma— became a mere memory eight months later.

Though he may bring laughter, he is not subject to corruption; though he may appear deformed, he is not to be rejected; though he may be foul-smelling and exceedingly dull-witted, his words are accepted. We praise that one of inconceivable and supreme excellence, by whose power he overcomes his former nature. He who, through formerly despised activities such as gambling and the like, attained the state of being desired.
In his youth, due to the unruly nature of that king of variegated mind,
he was constantly dismissed by the monarch who had recently attained imperial sovereignty;
thus, out of weariness, he would take betel leaves from him and go into the presence of Citraratha.

Through his messengers, he attained the status of a trusted authority by demonstrating his knowledge of various affairs; at the conclusion of those missions, he engaged the king’s servants and the overseers of the treasury. At that time, the royal court was devoid of all other exalted ministers.
Sajjaka’s son, Śṛṅgāra, attained the position of chief minister.
(Cakkalakam) Although he was ignorant and practiced false views, his misdeeds did not [fructify];
nor did his life-span [end prematurely], nor did his wealth diminish, because of his offering of vessels. (Kṛt 8.2360cd–2361)
Even though he considered himself fortunate through the enjoyment of women as his seat,
he attained the generosity of one who bestows grain,
since he provided a seat for his gurus by joining silver with his own precious metals.

Union with the Sovereign of the Gods, which exists [for him], is now appropriate for him. Even by kings who were not his inferiors, it was impossible to follow him. On the full moon of Āṣāḍha, the initial preparations involved an immense expenditure of wealth.
There, in Nandikṣetra, he was introduced by the foremost musicians, such as Cappa and others;
nourished by them over five or six years in accordance with the requirements of time,
he was recognized as being devoid of substance when it came to the role of a court jester, yet he was granted an official position.

By the power of his devotion to his master, his actions and duties were inconceivable. Even that serpent, whose neck-ornament was repeatedly known to break during the pulling of mountains by the hands of young women prepared for play, suffered defeat when commanded by the enemy of Tripura; yet, in some cases, he who wields power does not surpass another through the majesty of his master’s command.
Relying upon one another— both Rilhaṇa and Dhanya—
they embezzled the funds intended for the production of the *Janaka-śṛṅgāra* by means of bribery.
On one occasion, having bound Janaka along with his ornaments and pearls...

Śṛṅgāra released him along with his wife and sons from the drops of tears. At times, having become weary of that [pleasure], he caused it to be deprived of its dignity; for he sought sexual union only when requested by a woman who was harsh in her protection and whose breasts were exposed by the loosening of her garments.
With the waves of his ring fingers dancing from the friction of his thumbnails,
raising the tips of his left and right lips, his eyes curved,
and the furrows of his forehead deepened and lowered by the knitting of his brows; KRT_8_2371ab–KRT_8_2372ab.

Furthermore, one of them, having accomplished his purpose, mocked the world; [this was expressed with a *tilaka* verse]. One was perceived as being in a state of delirium, speaking with indistinct syllables and harsh words, with eyes closed, shouting loudly, and laughing while clapping his hands.

For those who have extracted the reality [of things] through the flash of refined ease, is the framework of discourse not sufficient for such [beings], even when it concerns a matter of laughter? For those who are mindless,
there is a lack of fitness at all times regarding every subject and every word.
He knew that for those whose lives are as light as grass, passion is not to be censured;
he was a lord of the earth whose intellect was unshakable and capable of cutting through everything,
and who, through his practice of dharma, had attained the preeminence of those adorned with merit.
Like one who has attained awakening, he performed a service toward his enemy by inflicting harm;
just as sandalwood brings relief to the limbs of one who has been burned by a forest fire.

He, whose intellect was pure, shared his wealth with his family members while still distributing honors appropriate for his gurus, sages, the lord of the twice-born, and others; he constructed temples for the host of deities beginning with Vijayeśa.

And by the distribution of ambrosia, the fortunate one attained a state equal to Mount Kailāsa. In the construction of monasteries, temples, groves, ponds, and irrigation channels, as well as in the restoration of what was decayed, his constant concern was for those devoted to such works.
Having once displayed acts of enmity toward his fellow students,
he— who is the very embodiment of cruelty— is thus described by the dull-witted.

By a single evil deed committed at one time, he has brought to an end his noble duties, which primarily consisted of nourishing the entire world, sustaining the seven oceans, and gratifying Brahmā and the other gods.

By that [act], she— who had attained lightness from the celestial river by touching the heap of bones of the lineage of Sagara’s sons— became indeed worthy of being buried with those very bones in the cremation ground. In the meantime, the Brahmin Śivaratha, who was surrounded by many attendants, died after binding his own throat with the noose of a *kāyastha*.

Having thus removed various thorns [from his path], the lord of the earth, devoted to benevolence, established his dominion free from obstacles; for the king’s efforts were primarily directed toward the removal of the coverings provided by his adversaries.
Like sunbeams released from a cloud, they attain sharpness;
yet this king, a jewel among monarchs,
has reached a state of charming maturity, just as a grapevine attains a ripeness of sweetness through its full development.
He continuously performed sacrifices with extensive sacrificial fees,
as well as marriages, pilgrimages, and other honored great festivals;
he shared his own resources with those who practice dharma through these rites.
Like the moon with its splendors [illuminating] the medicinal herbs of the principal mountains, he—
his mind undistracted— provided the necessary materials for the citizens' promised celebrations, such as the marriage of their sons and the consecration of their homes.
Having brought those who were mines of timber for the prosperity of the kings under his own control,
he renovated the entire city;
while those experts in reality were immersed in the worship of Hara, they were absorbed in royal affairs.
His state is watched with wonder, like that of a sage;
from morning until the end of the day, his activity is observed.
There is no task to which he has not gone, nor is there any where the wise do not exercise their supervision.
In the blinding darkness of the absence of inquiry, knowledge shone forth within,
like the flickering lightning of the cloud-glory of Jayāpīḍa.
Having bestowed his royal fortune upon him, as if it were a steady radiance of jewels—

The light of that which is variegated by the diversity of virtues has been made imperishable. By him— [the one] by whom the lords of villages, whose ancestral lineages are like the moon for the sake of [granting] agrahāras, were made masters of lands whose wealth of fields had been plundered.

The houses built by him for the learned were mansions with vast heights; they seemed to have the Seven Sages upon their roofs as if to witness his excellence. On the path that originates from creative genius and is first discovered by wisdom, he acted as a traveler.
Taking that caravan leader as their support, the wise remained free from fault;

for even while the noble king lay upon his bed, he was exceedingly dear to them. Indeed, the sound arising from the agitation of the water used for the ceremonial sprinkling of his royal insignia—though it was a natural occurrence—was most beloved by him.
Likewise, for one who is asleep and has set aside flutes, lutes, and other instruments,
his cherished state is the conceptualization of the speech of wise men who are free from malice;
such was the case during the time of kings such as Śrī Lalitāditya and Avantivarman.
That which was established through consecrations and other rites has now reached its conclusion;
for he ensured that a secure and stable arrangement was made for all monasteries and temples, which arise in their own due time.
The monastery first attained the foremost position among all foundations for the Ratnadevī, who had firmly ascended to the state of being her husband’s favorite. Then there was Rilhaṇa,
a kinsman to the multitude of virtues on the path of Dharma.
He became the forerunner of the entire succession of ministers;
pure in intellect, he [honored] those rich in austerity, those of attained excellence, and those advanced in dharma.
There was no one capable of abandoning even his palace of confidence;
for throughout his life, it remained never empty of virtuous deeds— chief among them the gift of a black antelope skin with two openings— and of marriages to the daughters of Dharma.
For all those who had maintained the sacred fires, the great-souled one’s rites proceeded without obstacle;
by him, having distributed all the requisites for sacrifice,
the fortunate ones enjoyed excellent enjoyments during that sacrificial session (*sattra*) which inspired wonder.
He whose sixty-four castes had minds untouched by false views; by whom,
during the reigns of the two Pravarasenas, the city was adorned with extensive monastic bridges and eminent groups of agrahāras.

In the first [city], in the preeminent capital of the lord of the earth, he attained a state of supreme renown, having caused the temple of Rilhaṇeśvara to be built, which inspired great wonder. [And] for the sake of his beloved Sussalā, who had departed to the other world, the wise [king]—*Kṛtin*—[erected a monument]. *Kṛt* 8.2409ab; *Kṛt* 8.2409cd; *Kṛt* 8.2410ab.

He had a monastery built at the site of the Bhaleraka water-shed. It became famous by the name of a cat who, having forgotten her natural instinct for self-preservation, followed [her master] in death when he died.
When her husband was clouded by jealousy,
his beloved play-cat remained far ahead of her in the region where she was acting like a human being.
From the day of their departure for the sacred ford, she maintained a constant cry.

Casting aside the food she had brought, she abandoned her life out of grief. While Diddā ascended to the highest pinnacle by the path of establishing her authority among the wives of the kings, Sussalā did so among the wives of the ministers.
The Śrīcaṅkuṇa monastery, which had reached the state of being nothing more than a name,
he now caused to be rebuilt through the construction of stone temples, residences, and other structures;
and by means of the installation of water-wheels, as well as works such as wells and schools for students.

The entire city wall of merit reached its full completion for her. By means of that monastery, which pervaded the entire sacrificial ground of the former royal lineage, the city was led to a state of visual delight.

Just as if by a sudden fall from her established position, that [fortune], wasted by consumption (yakṣman), quickly became a misfortune for Śrī Sureśvarī, acting as a messenger to a vast state of union with dissolution. Monasteries and agrahāras were established by the fortunate one named Ballabha.

They did not obtain even their desired names; for how can fame come without merit? Likewise, Kampanāpati, having established agrahāras and monasteries, always heard only his own name associated with them.
When the question was posed by the lord of Udayadvāra together with the hosts of Brahmapurī,
the bank of the Padmasaras lake attained splendor at the monastery (maṭha).
[Likewise] at Śrīdvāra, by the lord of the Śṛṅgāra-tantra, who was born of the Aja lineage...
By means of his own sinless self, through the construction of monasteries, gardens, ponds,
and other works such as bathing-halls, temples, Brahmapurīs,
and bridges, Alaṅkāra, the lord of the great treasury, adorned the earth.

Budha was born from the Moon for the sake of peace through medicinal herbs; he who was a poet became renowned for endowing the nature of a *dānava* with generosity. He served Nṛsiṃha and bestowed non-violence upon Hiraṇyakaśipu.
At the time of the Varāha festival, he gave a cow to a Vaiṣṇava who was unprecedented;
near the monastery of Bhaṭṭāraka,
the monastery of Śṛṅgārabhaṭṭa— like two full oceans— was free from infamy through its renown.
The minister of peace and war, Jaṭṭa by name, a man devoted to meritorious deeds, established the shrine of the Eight-formed Lord (Śiva) for the king of Dārvābhisāra.
Alas! Among all trees, the auspicious glory of the single Karavīra tree alone became the ground for the affection of the spring season.
The flower that spontaneously brings to fruition some indescribable emblem of the Enemy of Love (Śiva) appearing therein—
among all the ministers who have been granted a share of the king’s prosperity,
only the one called Bhuṭṭa, the younger brother of Jalha, deserves the highest pinnacle of excellence.
The Self-Existent One (Svayaṃbhū) manifests himself and personally accepts the worship;
whether it be at Jyeṣṭharudra for Vasiṣṭha, or at Bālakeśvara,
that place is free from impurity due to its monasteries, hermitages, and magnificent mansions.
By him, a city named Bhaṭṭapura was established there;
and in that city, Hara was also installed under the name Bhūteśvara.
And in the village of Maḍavāgra, Sāra— acting as a mirror for the confusion regarding the Dharma—

led the establishment of the Vaikuṇṭha monastery and other sites as his own place of residence; through Ratnādevī, he firmly secured these foundations, making them stable by binding them to his own purpose.

In Ratnapura, there is a lofty monastery with many doors that possesses the grace of a full necklace for the sake of those who have performed meritorious deeds. Mṛtyuñjaya shines here, as he dwells in houses washed with white plaster.
As if creating Śvetadvīpa in order to sever the people's attachment to impermanence;
once Gokula had been established by her, the founders of the cowherd settlements,
such as Śūravarmā and others, were counted as those who consumed even grass as their food.

In that place, which was filled with herds of cattle roaming at their unimpeded will and abounded in water reaching only a span in depth, Mukunda— whose body was free from all ailment and who was a temple of wondrous beauty and magnanimity— dwelt.
The horse [was given] by Viśvakarman; the Siddha was Govardhanadhara. Having constructed a monastery at Nandikṣetra, she established delightful [shrines] in Jayavana and other such places.
In Dārvābhisāra as well, she built a city named after herself, a temple of magnanimity for Urvīśundara, which rivaled the city of Indra;
she did so even with the intention of honoring those venerable elders who had passed away.

That queen, who was affectionate toward those who sought her protection, established various shrines. Then, having adorned every limb of the earth with ornaments, that bull among kings built for himself a monastery (maṭha) as a special mark of his devotion to the Lord of the Earth.

The vast land which was granted by the unassuming monarch has been designated by the learned as the preeminent place known by the name Siṃhapura. The grandson of the Lord of Kārapatha established the Sindhujan Brāhmaṇas there.

There he built the Niviḍas and Draviḍas, situated within the center of the ancient Siddhas; what need is there to praise his construction of monasteries and the like— he who once again established the entire Kaśmīra region, including its villages and cities?
This land, which by the tyranny of time had become like a desolate wilderness,
was once again joined with wealth, people, and dwellings, O King,
ever since you were initiated into the sacrifice of granting desired boons.

Even by those who were primarily artisans, monasteries and temples were generally constructed. When the king, free from envy, made available excellent treasuries, garments, jewels, and other riches for the common use of all, the citizens celebrated various great festivals.
When the rice crops were destroyed by unseasonable falls of frost and other calamities such as fires, the abundance of food there ceased for a moment;
and a marvel occurred when the speech of *rakṣas* was heard at night.
Having learned of the occurrence of portents such as comets, the king brought [the offender] into his presence.
Śuḍḍha by name, the younger brother of the Lord of the Granary, who had caused a widespread upheaval,
was brought into the king's presence through battles and secret punishments.
Having crushed kings such as Vikramarāja and others,
that monarch [established] Prayāga, Gulhaṇa, and other rulers in Vallāpura and other cities;
and like the noble Sun among kings, he established lords of subjects in Kānyakubja and other regions without decay.
He brought about the prosperity of the lands of the fortunate ones, free from pride. Once, while that [kingdom] was shining with constant splendors,
Yaśodhara, the king of Darada, fell into the poverty of life.
Although he was the immediate neighbor of the king, through his excessive service to that sovereign,
he fell into misfortune when the king’s disposition toward him changed;
for his own minister, named Viḍḍasiṃha, had treated him with deceit.
Having enjoyed the kingdom with his beloved while his son was still immature,
and having gradually brought the country under his control, he— while the child was king in name only—
desired to destroy him as soon as he wished to seize the earth for himself.
Another minister, having placed the son of Yaśodhara at the forefront, experienced a reversal of fortune along with him; meanwhile, the one named Paryuka experienced the opposite. (A pair of verses.)
Having placed the people of Kaśmīra behind him, he established a dual kingship there,
abandoning Sañjapāla and others who were capable of bearing the burden of all affairs;
his intellect was obstructed by the stupidity of another name through a lack of devotion to the gods.

Though he was a knower of mantras, the king accepted the role of consecrator for his own son, who was still immature, as the latter— imagining himself to possess the pride of authority through the assumption of all official powers— was being anointed with fragrant unguents and was moving about with vigor. 8.2461cd–2462ab.
Where are those who possess a majestic splendor due to the onset of unprecedented undertakings,
whose intellects are unshakable as they consume all things, and who understand what must be done?
Where is the common folk, who are mostly as foolish as children and have lost all sense of worldly conduct?
Fie on the perverse maturity of the self-will of kings! [A couplet.
(KRT 8.2463cd) Those who oppose others only when it serves their own ends desire the destruction of excessive power;
they do not seek to understand the internal state of the army, the disease, the fortress, the treasury, and so forth. (KRT 8.2464ab–cd)
Those immediately adjacent to the earth seize the mantra merely through formal procedure;
enemies with friendly faces should be considered as having already provided assistance.
In that undertaking begun by stratagem, there is the seizing of the enemy's assistance.
Where are those witless men, like cranes, who understand the context of affairs?
Like a tree growing on a riverbank, it falls due to the mutual conflict and destruction of its own banks;
it cannot be pulled out by the powerful, just as one cannot be swept away by the currents flowing through its midst.
When Paryuka was in a difficult situation and desired various bribes for his task,
Viḍḍasīha was slow to move even to seize the "milk-slaughter" (the reward).
Viḍḍasīha then entered into an alliance with Paryuka.
When the virtuous lord of Kaśmīra had departed as he had come, he harbored resentment. In that situation,
the tree of his long-standing wandering through all offices of authority became the very cause for the satisfaction of death through the impulse of passion.
Up to the beloved of Lakṣmaṇa, everyone held authority through a state of non-duality;
thereafter, however, it became divided a hundredfold like the water of a waterfall. Other ministers also shared in the majesty of their master by virtue of their counsel.
By some stroke of fate, they obtained a measure of relief at that time.
What praise can we bestow upon that compassionate ruler of the earth,
who placed the son of his deceased minister— though himself a child— in his father’s position?

A wondrous path was set in motion for the ministers by their servants; devoid of shame, they seized the fortune of their lord as if she were their own wife. Having offered the splendor of their deceased master to the ruler of the earth as a tribute—*Kṛtya-kalpataru* 8.2474ab–2475ab.
Indeed, having accomplished his task for the sake of the prosperity of his lineage,
when the treasury-guardian named Viśva had perished,
he was protected by another known as Sahaja; thus great is the value of companions.

Though entreated by the king, he did not accept an office of authority; rather, he rendered assistance to the intellect of the master’s son named Tiṣṭha. Even though those in power saw that his steadfastness was unshakable, they [could not prevail].
Fie upon the succession of servants who are promoted higher and higher!

The water from the triple-streamed Gaṅgā, which was used by the Creator for his ritual rinsing and which removed the fatigue from the feet of the Enemy of the Asuras when they were weary from traversing the worlds, was placed by Śambhu upon his own head. For even among the dull-witted, when a single person is appointed to a task, all others become helplessly devoted with deep respect through the contagion of following one another.

The tree of wicked conduct, having sprouted through the attainment of purification and the removal of latent impressions, was nourished by the water provided by Sāñji and Ādhakṛt; it gradually became ready to bear fruit.
After two or three years, he became full of wrath toward Viḍḍasīha.
He caused his messengers to roam about, longing for the unimpeded kingdom and other such things. Having taken refuge with a king who was a hero and whose resolve remained unshaken even from afar,
he lived together with his kinsmen by means of occupations such as agriculture and trade.
The King of Darada, who was subject to the intrigues of ministers related by blood, formed a league with the Ḍāmaras, including Laṅkāracakra and others.
(A *yugma*).
He too, being a friend, was the first to send word to the lord of the mountain fortress. (Kṛt 8.2483–2484ab)
A base man named Janakabhadra died while seeking to gain [the king's] favor.
Having observed him in various places— from Karṇāṭaka to Āḍhaka—
some people conceived a mind for malice toward him as he departed, while others felt only goodness.
Although he had thus undertaken such a vast enterprise,
the king, lacking the exertion to overcome indolence, neglected him as he was about to enter the hermitage, remaining unperturbed by the cold.

While the city was being ravaged by those who sought its destruction— those who had been nourished by the illustrious [king] but were now driven away, like a swarm of insects— the Lord of the Gate, Udayarāja, was dispatched by the ruler of the earth. He then gathered an army in the city of Śaṅkaravarman.
He heard that Loṭhana had arrived at the side of Alaṃkāracakra;
he also heard that the son of King Sussala, named Vigraharāja,
as well as Bhoja, born of Salhaṇa, had both come there with him.
Then, right there at the place of sacrifice, he quickly traversed for them in a single day a path that would have taken many days to cross.
Having achieved the binding together of the necks of his herd, he became subject to their will.

Then that *ḍāmara* fled, his movement thwarted by their assault. Subsequently, they took refuge in the fortress named Śiraḥśilā, situated within the Madhumatī river which possessed the splendor of pearls from the ocean.
The lord of the gate, wandering over the vast grounds, could not determine whether he was submerged in the thicket or situated within the fortress; then,
as he was reproached for attempting to climb this difficult fortification, he became apprehensive.
Even by fate, the power of the king could not be overcome.
When he was intent on rising up, all the bandits were crushed there;
like fish in a small pond when separated from their water by heavy rains, they met their end.
Then, by means of those secret transformations such as the *trillaka* and the rolling on the ground, Hari,
the Lord of the Earth, who was skilled in the arts of illusion, once again acted. Then,
as they ran about, the burning of cities, villages, and other places became impossible to remedy.
At every step, his own partisans sought to protect him as he fell into distress.
Wandering throughout the circle of the quarters, visible and invisible everywhere,
he became like a comet— the son of Brahmā— foreboding the end of a kalpa.

When his exhausted ministers pressed him to make peace due to the exigencies of the time, he regarded the entire earth as already lost to the kings of Maḍava by all the people. As the enemies advanced with no means of resistance remaining, [the situation became desperate].
In the meantime, having consulted together, the king dispatched Dhanya.
When the task was placed upon his shoulders, people who stood by felt shame;
then, the people spoke of this reversal as "the master of the gate."

"The monk Mallārjuna was indeed alone, while you three were together; alas, when united, you are difficult to overcome"—thus all the subjects reflected. O Lord of the Earth, the conduct of the king’s summons was like that of a gatekeeper.
Even while desiring his own success through his own lack of renown, he remained one whose efforts were directed toward the heart [of his purpose].

(KRT 8.2503cd) Indeed, he who does not succumb to folly when alone, nor resorts to indifference out of anger when the master’s business is at stake—even though that master is deeply dependent on him—such a minister, desiring the accomplishment of the goal through conduct free from ostentation, prevails; but this is not possible for a king of meager merit. (KRT 8.2504ab–2504cd)
When Pañcacandra had died, he placed his younger brother, named Ṣaṣṭhacandra, upon the royal throne; yet even he departed after his undertakings had begun,
along with Dvibāhuka and others who were foremost in their respective fields, together with singers.
The outsiders and other dependents of the king followed after Dhanya alone.
Then, [he established] the village of Tilagrāma in Koṭasindhutaṭa among the lands of Dhanya and others;
furthermore, the lord of the gate stationed at Draṅga [surveyed] the rear routes.

Free from the impetuosity of those eager for a headlong entry into battle, he conducted himself with a depth of courage that withered the fortitude of his enemies. He had the architectural layouts of the palace renovated by groups of artisans using axes and other tools.
Blessed was he who, on the banks of the Madhumatī, established forest tracts rivaling cities,
dense with trees and free from darkness, provided with dwellings;
and being capable, the lord made his camp rich in every luxury.
In that region, during the harsh winter season of heavy frost, by virtue of his store of merit,
the earth became fit for the king’s conquest, adorned as it was by the sun.
[He then issued] a dispatch of a multitude of world-wonders to the one desiring victory.
Even in a time when authority was eclipsed by a dual kingship, the king’s power was not diminished;
rather,
it reached its highest point during times of danger through his very exertion.

The king led his army to steadfastness, comforting those who remained by granting them gifts; meanwhile, he showed the signs of his own weariness from the long exile, manifesting through the wailing of the villagers oppressed by the burden of the expedition, which took the form of his practice of patience. (KRT 8.2513cd–2514)

Thus, even though they remained there for three or four months, those cruel garrisons, though besieging the forts, were unable to seize them. For, despite the siege of their supplies and reinforcements by those arrogant ones—*kṛt* 8.2515ab; *kṛt* 8.2515cd; *kṛt* 8.2516ab.
Nothing unpleasant or causing dejection had arisen at all.
Desiring to manifest their own power at the edge of the snowy season,
they stood like formidable mountains with joy sprouting forth.
Abandoning agriculture for the sake of the farmers and the recitation of the Vedas for the sake of the twice-born,
who were all agitated in the villages, he took up arms everywhere.
Waiting for the dissolution of the snow upon the mountain paths, [he advanced].

Desirous of victory, the Dāradas stood ready with their cavalry. The people trembled constantly, struck by fear at the onset of the royal army, which resembled a bed of black cotton-wool from a mass of mist.

Thus, because he failed to examine the ultimate strength of his opponent, the king began his endeavor in vain and fell into doubt regarding victory. This alone is some unique method of deception suited for those whose minds are steeped in cleverness.

O deluded one, by that very self through which they imagine their power to be unassailable, they would have their efforts thwarted even by an enemy who is but a mere child. Today, the enemy’s army, whose essence is mere rumor, might tremble;
yet his success will be frustrated by his own intellect blinded by anxiety.

One might quickly pierce it with arrows, strike it down with winged shafts, or surround it with a sudden assault; yet all this would be in vain through such well-known qualities and preparations. (8.2524ab) If the lotus were to become a source of fear for the elephant, then one should employ a daring effort with one's own limbs capable of enduring anxiety to uproot it entirely.
(8.2524cd) For by means of rolling about and other such actions, one might somehow escape from the grasp of the ears. (8.2525ab)

Having reached the city of Laṅkā, he perceived that the kingdom had already been conquered. Otherwise, how could his own followers have woven together a patched garment for him? As he rushed forward with unrestrained speed, the gatekeeper yielded the way.
Because they were incapable of resisting, he then abandoned the fortress;
and on the following day, he himself pursued those royal seedlings.
Koṭṭādri was situated within the waters, with its base narrow and its length extending behind.
He was seen by them like a crane distracted by the prey of a large fish;
observing him to be as powerless as a house for elephants devoid of elephants,
they abandoned all hope of victory and bore fear in their hearts.
Then, while they were saying, "The enemies must be harassed here with arrows made of stone and iron;
here is the protection of the waters, and here the defensive stones and machines must be guarded," that *ḍāmara*,
seizing them with fortitude, spoke thus.

He thought thus, seeking only his own protection and not being firmly resolved for battle. (A pair. Then, when the enemy force had launched its assault upon Tilagrāma and the bandit was incapable of retaliation, they fell into a state of exhaustion from anxiety.
Furthermore,

Loṭhana censured that [plan], which was characterized by a cleverness of wisdom both manifest and hidden, turbulent, filled with malicious intent, and unconcealed; whereas Bhoja, however, praised it as being "unassailable," saying, "Let no malice take root."

Having confined his uncle, he attended upon him constantly with feigned praise. When the uncle was averse to him, rolling on the ground and stubbornly refusing to submit, he thought that his consolations had achieved some measure of success in influencing his mind, and he remained thus in agreement with him.
Thinking, "The king might kill me," he would have abandoned them once they had departed;
yet, saying "Not us," he did not restrain his uncle from going.
While you, all of us, and the enemies were all hemmed in, the foes became fierce.
Having conceived a backstabbing enmity toward me, they remain steadfast in their efforts from some source;
whatever they may do shall succeed—therefore, abandon this one thing: me.
"Or else, having brought other men of greater beauty, I shall quickly remove your imprisonment"—
having said this to him,
he who had adopted a semblance of conciliation created a slight disturbance.
Saying to him, "I shall release you tonight or tomorrow," he,
whose courtesy was undiminished, deceived him at every moment;
just as enemies who remain far away and fail to act properly cause an obstruction to a sacrifice.
They passed their time of decline by means of food brought from external villages. Then, fearing an unfavorable outcome, they informed the king of an agreement, saying,
"An alliance should be made with those who are well-disposed toward Dhanya and the others."
Recognizing that a reconciliation with them through various such signs was impossible, the king ordered that fortifications,
watchtowers, and enclosures be constructed.
He also dispatched his kinsmen, who had attained great renown, to carry out the task.
They will abandon them in their own abodes, either because they have been bribed or due to a state of alarm;
and having become harsh, our undertakings will certainly lack excellence and reach no conclusion. Through reproaches for the failure of our actions, we shall fall into remorse among the people.
If Harṣadeva had not perceived this, he would have obtained a stream of milk after seven days of effort; having heard this, even another person is distressed.
Everyone has obtained what was destined to be obtained through their own auspicious and inauspicious deeds.
In this world, the failure to act is considered a transgression; yet here, even the three worlds are said to be within one's mouth.

While there are feet and wings, neither on earth nor in the sky can a winged ant move about like a tree-trunk in a pit; what would be the use of such a feat, for what certainty is there regarding the attainment of goals?
If Aruṇa had been born with two feet upon the body of Sahasrapād, even though he lacked thighs, what more could he have achieved? Therefore,
disregarding his status as a witness, let the entire fortress be besieged.
Let it proceed right there for both us and them throughout their full lifespans.
Like a tireless wind or a consuming fire, this [effort] generates persistence through its continuity; like water, it wears away even the great mountain ranges.
It engenders a resolve that is firm and never abandoned in undertakings, leading to the attainment of results in this world whose splendor is inconceivable at every moment.
Having heard the king’s cruel command, Dhanya and the others then abandoned that fortress wall and rampart and ascended it with speed. [The king wondered:
"How will they wage war? Or how will they hold their ground? KRT_8_2552ab–KRT_8_2553ab.

While those stationed in the fortress looked on with curiosity as he scattered arrows, he— being blessed— constructed that region, making it resemble a city with its dwellings, by pulling up the upward-pointing [shafts] from below and pressing them down firmly. (A *yugma*).
Then, with countless numbers never ceasing,
the destruction of the two armies proceeded at every moment; on the following day,
having seen the autumnal [omens], the son of Garga arrived.
He brought about the prosperity of the citizens of Saṃkrandana’s city by slaying warriors in battle. Alaṅkāra, who held the office of chief magistrate in the outer capital,
was invincible to human combatants and slew his adversaries in many ways.

How can those who roam the surface of the earth compete with the inhabitants of the mountains? (KRT 8.2558ab) Nevertheless, the infinite array of their military engines is beyond thought, even for the inconceivable.
(KRT 8.2558cd) Those stationed in fortresses are few, while the vast majority take refuge in the camps. (KRT 8.2559ab)
Therefore, even though they had slain many in the past, they were themselves wounded by a minor magical rite (*kṛtyā*).
With the doors and gates of their enemy’s fortress blocked and oppressed by two or three battles,
the stronghold thereafter became as if its eyes were closed in terror.

Observing Dhanya and the others, who were following the openings provided by the internal dissension among the protectors, those stationed in the fortress could find no cause for confidence. Crying out to one another for the sake of warding off sleep, they did not sleep at night.
But during the day, they saw the fortress silent and empty;
yet at night, it was filled with the sounds of the various watches' drums from those respective armies.
The sparrows dwelling in their hollows shrieked as if at the roar of clouds. The royal soldiers agitated them in every possible way, while the waters were obstructed by boats wandering day and night.

With their paths blocked, they suffered from the parching of thirst; but when their provisions were exhausted and no movement was possible, they fell into a state of dejection. Then, though hungry, they could only gaze upon the enjoyments suitable for the earth, which had been won by those who possess such enjoyments.
The heirs of the king, receiving poor food,

made a wish for the cessation of eating; let alone rivalry, having crossed that [barrier], those hungry ones even daily harbored a longing for the servants who partake in the enjoyments of the lord of the earth.
Then, he separated Bhoja— who had declared, "In our current military arrays, an improper act would be insufficient"— and placed him at the middle peak of the fortress,
because one was old and the other was the son of a courtesan.
Knowing his unfitness, he considered him alone worthy of a dual kingship;
"Without this man, enemies would not properly attack these two," thinking thus,
he gave that departure abroad a false reputation.
Desiring the destruction of the circle of her lover’s ornaments, she, like a fleeting woman,
became moist with intense affection due to her passion for his eyes;
through the power of her secret spell, she brought about a distinction between the outside and the inside.

Day after day, Sālhaṇa searched everywhere for the path to her ears. [Couplet] With a mind shrouded by the darkness of passion, he did not reveal this to her for fear of being discovered; however, he made his request known through an intermediary. [KRT 8.2573]

Patient, trained in equanimity, and finding joy in the steadfastness of loving-kindness, he, like a Bodhisattva, did not harbor anger even toward an offender. Though great, even the cause of death was treated with affection by him who was free from passion.
He was forgotten in his heart, like an elephant by a *śarabha* on its back.
Then Bhoja was dispatched from within the camp of his sleeping enemies; though he had already traveled a great distance, he was followed by the son of Alaṅkāra.

Whether out of a desire to harm or out of fear, his resolve shattered by agitation, he quickly turned back and was once again placed near his father, who was staying in the fortress. (Yugma) Having rebuked his son, [the father] said to him: "You shall go tomorrow at night. (KRT_8_2577–2578ab)
Saying to everyone, "He has gone," he placed the covered [coffin] aside on that day.
One man set out alone with no certain plan, thinking, "Two will depart tomorrow. Then, having been awakened during the night by Dhanya and the others, all the noble ones rose.

Then, at midnight, intending to depart, he looked out from the tower of the fortress upon all those in the camp who were awake, surrounded by kindled fires. Having illuminated the stronghold with fire, he went out through the main gate.
Even an ant would not escape being noticed by his enemies who were so intent upon him;
the houses, as if trembling with the flickering light of their flames, protected Sālhaṇi by forbidding him through the shaking of their heads out of fear of his rashness.
Unable to proceed quickly at that time of day,
that fierce one [the Daitya] descended into a chasm near the foot of a banyan tree,
accompanied by the lord of the Daityas named Kṣemarāja.

He sat upon a stone slab, which was like a raised dais yet situated in the middle of a chasm. Having ascended it merely as a seat, finding it sufficient for his purpose due to the fear of falling, both of them spent those five nights there without sleep.

Having secured their means of sustenance with balls of barley-meal held in their hands, they abandoned their excrement right there, like two birds leaving it from their nest. They remained there, their forms indistinct yet wonderful, as if they were merely sketched in outline.

Beholding the splendor in the enemy's camp, they were filled with wonder at its proximity. For them, relief was found through the heat of Jayasiṃha’s majesty-fire, which, though vast, caused a forgetfulness of the cold.
Then, on the sixth day, when there was nothing left for them to consume,
the clouds began to rain down frost like salt upon a wound; likewise,
their efforts at playing the lute of their teeth were rendered futile in that appropriate manner.
With hands and feet rendered numb by the onset of cold, they fell asleep; surely,
as they lay there thinking today, they were struck by hunger and the chill.
We shall fall upon the mountain ridge like two birds bound by a snare.
To whom shall we cry out, or by whom are we known, that he might rescue us?
Then, like two young elephants sunk in the midst of a mire, [we are lost].

Then, when the two were thus situated in that precarious position, the bandit entreated them at night; having hoisted them up with a rope, he placed them in an empty dwelling. Having provided remedies for the cold by means of kindling fires of straw, they remained there.

There, they forgot their suffering through sleep that had come after a long time. Even more than that, a calamity befell those two whose bodies were rolling about; though they were dear to the people, they did not even approach the mountain because it was harmful to their eyesight.

As the two of them ate barley, *kodrava* grain, cakes, and the like along with their husks, their limbs and garments took on a pallid hue due to their lack of nourishment. Their entire circle of ornaments was reduced to mere names, and all their food supplies were completely exhausted.

He accepted Holaka and Yaśaskara as equals through the gift of food. Then that *Ḍāmara*, agitated by hunger yet fearful of the division of his servants, agreed to sell those enemies of the king through messengers.

He did not abandon his mind, which was defiled by sin and terrified by the fear of unrighteousness and ill-repute, because of the excessive prevalence of difficult calamities that cause living beings to flee;
for by establishing the remnants of the enemy king, he protected himself.
Desiring to act with purity of reputation,
he [the king]— though his mind was obscured by the counsel of a servant named Udayana who clung to the straw of falsehood—
protected Sālhaṇi and Bhoja, yet he hastened to give those two [to the enemy].
Knowing that without him it would be improper to inflict punishment upon those two by the king,
he considered it appropriate to leave his own entire undertaking unimpeded;
and he [also] deliberated upon the calamity that might befall him due to the lack of food.
Then Dhanya and the others, though desiring to conclude a peace treaty, did not understand [the situation].
Consequently, some pretext arose for them to wish to depart;
how much more so when two shares had been promised to be given to those heirs?

For the sake of accomplishing the stakes of giving, bestowing gifts, and rising from court, the fortunate one led his rival toward prosperity; may auspiciousness be ordained for him. Binding the enemy with a continuous stream [of policy], serving him while concealing his own anger, and dealing with him like a great serpent by employing crooked maneuvers through deceitful conduct—[may he succeed].

That ground, fostering a devotion to appropriate duties, became the source of accomplishments even when they were fully manifested with intense and firm impetuosity. At that time, the servants of the king, their excellence diminished by the hardships arising from long sojourns abroad, fell into a slackening of their zeal.

Having obtained Satya, that minister is capable of gathering [the army], just as the source of a narrative, when well-structured, organizes a complex plot. Having learned that the alliance was firmly established, the soldiers turned their faces toward their own homes.

Disregarding their master’s courtesy, they stood firm in an instant. Having obtained food that had been sold by them, Lavaṇa was slow in his actions; meanwhile, Dhanya and the others, because their forces were small, found themselves in a state of peril.
With their eyes fixed upon the city gateways, hoping for his arrival,
that day scorched those suitors who had been denied him;
the night, with its creaking chariot wheels, passed with great difficulty through their minds.
Seeing no other course of action except the renunciation of life,
when a task accomplished with great effort has been ruined by the dullness of their intellect,
[they addressed] the Lord, who had disregarded the weight of their words out of self-importance.
Under the pretext of grieving for what is lost and mocking various [failed] strategies,
other ministers will surely render us miserable; for,
due to the immediate disparity in their military expeditions, they will destroy our very core.
Others said, "Not seeing the completion of their task, they may have done it"; yet others spoke thus:
"Having consulted with those enemies of the king, he has employed this illusion; now that bandit, having achieved his purpose, surely stands laughing at us."
As they were thus expanding their various intentions, some small and others great,
that night— having bestowed infinite rewards upon their bodies— faded away. (A Kulaka) Then,
at dawn, the ornament of the royal court, eager for bold action, [prepared to depart].
Having ascended the fortress of Ḍāmara, he brought him under his control through diplomacy and intimidation.
On that day, having endured a delay for the sake of traveling for a single day, he,
whose courtesy was exhausted, clearly said to him, "Go!"
Therefore, some proud men, when about to undertake a task capable of washing away their humiliation, must ensure that it does not result in the destruction of their reputation.

This is that very time which brings darkness to the eyes of all people; yet for the noble *kṣatriyas*, it is proficient in manifesting eternal light. The sword-blade, dark as a cloud and wondrous, though joined with the celestial nymphs [of the sky], clearly and impetuously bestows its attachment upon the orb of the sun. Indeed, on the battlefield of victory, kings abandon their bodies and attain nothing less than a single solar orb.

The orb of the fierce-rayed sun, as well as the desired circles of the breasts of celestial nymphs moist with love—none of these cause such agony as that arising from beds with surfaces intensely heated by constant friction; nor does the pain of the vital organs arise so much from life-breaths departing from their knots. Nor can one remain with a heart terrified by the cries of weeping kinsmen; indeed, this death is surely some rare ground for the attainment of happiness for the fortunate.

Your father has gone to heaven by paths dense with the canopies of sword-blades; your brothers, having wandered through the thorny forest of dagger-stalks, have attained a noble state. Having followed this path—crushed by your lineage—with impetuous and haughty conduct, you have [attained] the sunless region in the sky and the hearts of the radiant. That empire which was brought to you by fate but repeatedly maintained through weakness, and that which you acted like a child in an age suited for tranquility—even for that, [you are now reaping the fruit].
Now that atonement for him has been obtained, it was brought about by the Creator; let this [atonement] not become as difficult for you to perform as this kingdom was for one mute in his duties.
(8.2625cd) Even though the kingdom was attained, it was lost; time was spent by those who ate the leavings of others; and the condition of universal destruction became the cause [of his end].
(8.2626ab) What indeed was appropriate for a powerful king who lived as a beggar? But that which he accomplished at the end of his life is such that he remains preeminent over all. (8.2626cd)
Though thus incited, he, being devoid of passion, did not take up that vigor; for even when in contact with fire, wood lacking sap does not burn.
But he whose egoism was stilled became like a child whose sleep has been broken.
Agitated by rising fear, he wished to weep with his lower lip protruding. As those who had taken refuge with the king set out to take him away, delivered by the executioner,
they beheld him in such a state and, out of compassion and in order to instill courage, spoke to him.

Do not despair; for in the heart of a god, which is radiant with the rising of the moon of compassion, the blindness of the darkness of passion does not take root at will. He is an ocean of the nectar of goodness; he is a divine mountain of steadfastness.
He is a sandalwood tree that cuts through the torment of suffering for those who have sought refuge;
having perceived his holy and pure form, like the celestial river in autumn,
your mind will surely find firm composure within him.
Honoring without distinction those of your stainless lineage who preceded you,
your own conduct will lead you up from the ground of lightness that is shame;
for even toward others who have wronged you and are submerged in calamity, you feel compassion.
"Because it is the cause for testing his forbearance, he indeed knows those who have rendered him service.
Having spoken thus, Lolasthūlakūrca, delighted by them, emerged from his house with a long,
thick blanket draped over him, like a bull emerging from a cow-pen.

Seeing him approaching, unadorned, with withered and tattered garments and weapons, mounted upon a carriage, Dhanya felt a sense of shame and humility. He beheld his body, its long eyes motionless, its beard coarse and thick, and its form devoid of splendor.
Then he beheld [the enemy] like an owl that had emerged from its cave-dwelling.
The mountain, with those moving camps ignited by fire,
shone as if it had become a touchstone for the gold of the king’s majesty.
When the royal camp had departed, the sky violently released a shower of frost during the rainy season;
this cut through the subjects' doubt regarding the king’s immortality.
[For they thought: "If cold were to fall before its time, people would perish, submerged in an instant."
Like soldiers who have entered the interior of a flour-mill,
so in the nineteenth year, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna,
Loṭhana, then nearly sixty years of age, was once again imprisoned.
To honor the army that had returned from its long expedition,
the lord of the earth ascended once more to his lofty, detached palace.
Having gratified the army with gifts, honors, conversation, and glances as was appropriate, he dismissed it; then he looked upon Dhanya and the others who had arrived.
And once more, at the base of their pair of arms, he placed his hand quickly by means of his soldiers.
With his garment tucked up and his face covered by the edge of his robe,
his ear-lobes were devoid of ornaments; and with the coarse, white beard-hairs that had grown upon them,
his cheeks clearly revealed the emaciation caused by suffering.
From time to time, amidst the citizens who were vocal with various loud cries, he cast sidelong glances from his eyes,
whose pupils were dull and dejected; [he was one] who had been glanced upon by the side-long looks of the Goddess of Misfortune—
[looks] characterized by cowardice, wretchedness, fear, exhaustion, and hunger.
[He saw me] with trembling limbs and sleepless eyes, as if afflicted by the cold;
[he saw] the earth as if spinning, the mountains as if toppled, and the sky as if fallen; and he saw his own lips parched.
Let there be divine obstacles, or let fierce darkness prevail;
let the winds reach the vicinity of the royal palace and wither this [kingdom].
How can I stand before a king who causes harm to all?
He gazed at him as he moved from step to step, restraining his footsteps; [this is] an internal couplet.
Because he was surrounded by many people, he saw him only faintly visible; then, as he was being announced by the doorkeepers, he beheld him rolling upon the courtyard floor. [This is] a kulaka.

Having understood the signal conveyed by a gesture of the brow, he ascended that assembly hall, which was like a pond of lotuses agitated by the eyes of the spectators. Then, having been directed to a spot on the ground at his side by the king’s glance, he took his place.
Having knelt upon the ground,
he touched his head to the lotus-feet [of the King]. Grasping the forehead of that emperor— who was bowed low in agitation— with his two lotus-hands, [the King] raised up his head.
The touch of his hands, which held jewels and medicinal herbs, removed the fever of his mind; and,
cool as sandalwood,
it swiftly dispelled misfortune from his body through the power of the merit of that compassionate lord of the earth.

In an instant, he was touched in his heart by the expectation of confidence. "Do not fear"—this was the speech of one who was proud; "you shall attain happiness"—this was the word. His anger, as if broken by a lack of depth, does not now dwell within you.
When this is said, the disclosure of former enmities occurs;
in that moment, as if in a jest, [the thought arises]: "You are our kinsman.
Then, due to the power of one's own previously offered heat, there would be the utterance: "You have been afflicted."
Having reflected thus, the King looked at him but did not offer any word of encouragement.
[Tilaka] As he bowed his head to touch the feet in a gesture seeking safety, the King again made contact with his own feet upon the crowns of his [the enemy's] heads. [Kṛtyakalpataru 8.2660ab–cd]
Saying, "What fitness do I have for such hospitality?", he was forcibly made to accept betel offered by his own hand by his paternal uncle.
Smiling, he said to the gatekeeper who stood bowed at the entrance, "Are you weary? (8.2661–2662ab).
And with his left arm, he touched Dhanya, the sixth, and Praṣṭha.
Having discerned him through his skill, courtesy, profundity, humility, and other such qualities,
the king considered himself inferior to one who was thus endowed with the virtues of a sovereign.
Then, with his hands joined in humility, he sent his radiant paternal uncle— who was bowed with shame— to his home through the mouth of Dhanya, having first offered him comforting words.
He who had previously been intent on attacking him now cast his gaze upon the path of political statecraft.

That very expression on his face remained unchanged even upon the attainment of the fruit. Neither does the ocean undergo distress by the boiling of the submarine fire, nor does it lose its coolness by the waters of the Himalaya entering it;
so too, there is no one whose profound mind maintains a constant and equal disposition during both times of sorrow and moments of joy.

Through affection, steadfastness, and sincere courtesies appropriate for kinsmen, the king gradually removed the shame associated with the loss of manliness and the mere subsistence of life. Even though the kingdom was being ploughed by the two heirs alone, the king, who was skilled in counsel, [acted accordingly].
Bhoja, too, reflected inwardly upon the serpent’s fang;
desiring victory over his remaining enemies, he remained sleepless, having abandoned all agitation and haste out of fear of the exhaustion of travel.
Having emerged from the abyss and dwelling in an empty house,
Sālhaṇi did not hear any news regarding the conflict between his paternal uncles.
Seeing from behind the royal ornament that had come into the presence of Ḍāmarā, he then became filled with the suspicion of treachery;
and he gradually beheld it, its full extent difficult to discern due to the distance.
Then, on the road leading to the city, he saw a military camp with its rows of tents pitched;
because it was distant, he did not recognize it as his uncle’s. Thereupon, he observed the difference between that vehicle and the one belonging to Dhanya and Śaṣṭha.
And he thought: "What is the cause of this departure from the camp?
Who might this third man be, mounted on a carriage, between the two fortunate ones?
Being questioned by him, a certain commoner then spoke with joy:
The two of them, their bodies rolling and contending, went toward the city with their alliance firmly established.
Abandoning doubt and free from malice, he experienced fear and a state of alertness;
yet for a moment, that [fear] was cast aside by his affection for his kinsman.

When the army had departed, the river, joined by birds crying out in emptiness, was imagined by him to be weeping for them; "If only my loveliness would take pity on you, realizing that you are now here! he thought.
He thought that Dhanya and the others would lead [the army] back in due order,
and thus he awaited them. Hearing the resounding roar of his own retreating royal host as it returned to bring him back, he suspected at intervals that it was the sound of mountain torrents.

Then the world was born from the darkness bestowed by the clouds, as if its beauty had been afflicted by midnight and rendered barren by midday. From that time forth, the rain-clouds maintained their presence until the month of Rādha.

"I am one who deserves to be slain with confidence, unworthy, hostile to the Brahmins, and devoid of shame," thus reviling himself in the presence of the Bhojas, the bandit then sat down upon the earth, which was like a sacrificial ground marked out for the performance of a long-term soma-sacrifice amidst a mass of snow.
Out of regard for the agreement, Sālhaṇi suppressed his indignation and, as if consoling him, said to him: "There is no lack of generosity on your part in this matter. And he added:
"You have [acted] toward one who was distressed by the calamities of dependents, children, kinsmen, and so forth."
This was done there for the sake of protection; you ought not to reproach anyone for it.
If there had been a desire for malice there, there would have been no compassion shown toward me. Therefore, this state of dependence on others occurred in accordance with the exigencies of time.

We are not like those born of the lineage of King Harṣa; we are not to be executed, but rather restrained, as we abide by the duties of kingship. Our own reputation would suffer, as would theirs, and the king would be straying from the right path.
"Alas! While protecting me, you, the wise one, have forbidden [me] what remains.
To him who had spoken thus, he replied as if casting off the weight of shame, constantly praising him: "In all matters, you alone are my witness."
To him who said, "Abandon me this very moment," he replied,
"I shall do so at the end of the snowfall," and departed.
Knowing that you would not eat, the bandit would direct his wrath toward you.

There, Bhoja was told by someone that he had eaten the food of a sick man. Touching the food he had obtained after a long time, and reflecting that "these two [relatives] sold themselves for this," he considered the flesh of their bodies to have been consumed by those two.
The bandit, however, saying "I shall certainly send you away at the end of the snowy rains—either tomorrow or today," did not release him for two months. [He thought:
"Knowing that I am staying here, once the king has finished his preparations and the snow has ceased..."
Thinking, "He is selling me," Bhoja hastened to depart;
whatever pretext he produced for the purpose of stopping him,
the robber cut that down and rendered him guilty of an offense.
Born from Balahara, who was named Tejas, he was the son of Bhadramatṛ;
covered with a long woolen blanket and longing for childhood,
he spoke thus regarding his own splendor, which served as a touchstone for the excellence of various heroes.
In that army of the Sussala dynasty during the period of dual sovereignty, he attained the status of one who purifies the assembly.
Immediately thereafter, having been promoted by the king because of his trustworthiness toward his father,
he gradually assumed administrative authority over districts such as Evenaka.
When the king had turned his face away and the Naga Khūya had made the hermitage ground desolate,
one named Rājavadana, desiring to seize him, protected him. (A *cakkalaka*.)
Everyone suspected that the king’s lack of compassion toward his subjects was due to his own wretched state and his inability to maintain his position; thus, he made his pleas most fervently,
yet without the circle of ornaments upon his person.

Desiring a dual kingship, he did not then hand over the one born of royal lineage. (Couplet) Even though Udayana was far away, he brought him before his very eyes; yet, though he wished to seize him, he was unable to abandon him.

The king, having sent wealth to Bhoja to induce him to make a formal agreement, then dispatched the district governor Alaṃkāra. If you depart now, abandoning me who am prepared to go into his presence—
"I shall thus give up my very life," Bhoja spoke in a terrifying manner;
"I shall see you tomorrow at dawn"— saying only this,
he departed from the fortress during the fourth watch of the night without even saying goodbye.

Even during a heavy rain, he searched the paths with indignation; and by the end of the night, while he was still searching, he heard that [the prince] had departed. Then, having desisted from his futile pursuit, he followed him during the day.
He set out for the abode of the goddess Śāradā with a limited retinue; yet,
as if unable to remain before them due to his courtesy, he went on ahead of those two kinsmen who had traveled in the same caravan, leaving behind the wives of the kinsmen.

But he, though young, was unwell; thinking of the public scandal regarding himself, he pierced [the target] only five or six times. Having his desire frustrated in approaching the female elephant, he took refuge with the wives of others.
Desiring to join battle, he took a path along the honey-sweet bank.

[Tilaka] In some places it was formidable with the sprouts of the fangs of Death, possessing the sharp edges of needles made of solid stone; in other places it was darkened by the nooses of Time, which were like clouds obstructing the light.
In some places, it was formidable with masses of falling snow like arrays of elephants; elsewhere, its bodies were wounded by showers of arrows in the form of the hissing of waterfalls;
in other spots, the ground was drenched with blood made visible and clear by the pleasantly cool breeze.
In some places, with their vision obstructed by the sun’s heat and the light of the snow,
they clearly perceived the downward slope as an upward ascent;
though repeatedly thinking it was an ascent, they were actually on a descent.

Having traversed six or seven days on a path made difficult by the season of frost, he reached a village on the frontier of the kingdom of Darada. (A *kulaka*. His meanness and insignificance were destroyed by the abundance of offerings presented by the simple-minded villagers.

The lord of Dugdhaghāṭṭakoṭṭa, having bowed to him, led him to be honored. Viḍḍasiṃha, standing at a distance upon being informed of his arrival by the messenger, dispatched the royal reception ceremony, including the parasol, musical instruments, and other honors.

And that lord of the fortress, having been instructed by the king, ensured the increase of desired prosperity in the kingdom; he prevented the prince—who was the rightful heir from the royal lineage—from exercising ownership over his own treasury.
Then the Bhoja, acting like a king, arrived at the royal residence to pay his respects.
He was brought by the son of the king’s face (the messenger), who had approached to see him;

he was sent into the presence of the king by his father, who was entirely estranged from the monarch. By that [messenger], he was made known as being like a noose set at the tip of a fierce enemy’s bow.

Having instructed him with words appropriate to the gravity of the task, his trust, and the nature of their relationship, he sent him forth—neither accepting [the mission] as his own, nor yet abandoning it. "Am I a trusted confidant, or am I utterly estranged from the king? he wondered slowly.

"You shall know me," the king said to him through his messengers. Then, in order to demonstrate his firm resolve to the king under the pretext of the enemy of the Gotris (Viṣṇu), and while declaring his own faultlessness, he accepted the battle with the Nāgas and others.
Lacking the full assembly [of his forces], he gradually established stability, and then, in due course, equanimity;
thereafter, through his physical forms, he—hardened by fortitude—inflicted superiority upon them. Thus did that son of the Earth attain a firm footing for that unprecedented [king].
Just as the kinsmen of the Naga did not feel shame upon entering into servitude,
for he was adorned with virtues such as generosity, forbearance, steadfastness, and freedom from greed;
having approached him, they became like a sudden manifestation of prosperity that had been constantly practiced.
The stability of the earth, Śiva, and others who possess a support is no cause for wonder; however,
the vast display of this supportless one is truly worthy of praise.
Forming vast military arrays with thieves, forest-dwellers,
and herdsmen, he remained there after raiding the village, guarding against the Bhojas and others;
they abandoned their mutual rivalry and jealousy at the counsel of their ministers.

Then, either out of a fondness for plunder or because they disregarded political wisdom, other Dāmaras also desired to seize [the king]. At that time, their desire to plunder— which had been suppressed and destroyed by his suppression— reached a hundredfold intensity through their rolling about and binding [of the enemy].
Although Trillaka and Jayarāja were both raised by the king,
they did not at all perform penance, being rendered helpless by their obsession with the discus (*cakra*).
He was like a pit for owls, or like the destruction of diseases.

Like Pātāla to the Daityas, or the ocean to aquatic creatures, he was the refuge of all bandits; intense in his magic (*māyā*), he brought about a calamity by besieging the lord of Devasaras. (A *yugma*).

Then the twice-born, desiring the protection of the earth, sought to provoke him; they undertook a fast unto death at Vijayeśvara on behalf of the king. Though he was aware of the destruction wrought by the untimely bandits, they did not desist from their petition.
Then, out of courtesy, he became a follower in the king's assembly; while the king was preparing to depart, Jayarāja— who had been the elder among those whose enemies were defeated—
perished like a boil that had suddenly arisen.
The fortunate lord,
having achieved the isolation of the barbarians on one side, then set out for the kingdom of Maḍava in order to please the brahmins;
meanwhile, his own soldiers, led by Maṭhara, were incited to dissent by the ministers.

The ornaments forbidden by the twice-born were abandoned by the king from his presence. He was always intent on establishing the lawless bandits; thus he appeared with envy to them, fostering their very vices.

"Having brought about the destruction of the dual kingship, I shall uproot Trillaka," the king declared; having made this vow, he dismissed the Brahmins. Then Trillaka, becoming terrified, agitated them with various unpleasant things.
Like a disease that has not yet broken out and remains hidden within other ailments,
[the king] installed Yaśorāja, the younger brother of Jayarāja, as the ruler. Following his advice, the one named Rājakā attacked his rival.

He went to rescue that Devasaras, which was occupied by a haughty enemy; because his army was small, Sañjapāla’s victory remained uncertain. Then, having learned of the situation, Rilhaṇa arrived and engaged in a fierce battle.
He became the first guest of the sidelong glances of the Goddess of Victory. Then,
when that Nandana had swallowed the ocean of his enemies' foes,
the ocean of Sañjaya’s allies became fit for the removal of the water of insignificant enemies.
Even though the kings of his own land were conquered, Yaśorāja was unable to remain without a protector, like a child in an empty house. Therefore,
the king waited for the completion of the period of dual sovereignty.
Trillaka, through various deceptive maneuvers, caused a delay;

then, at the appropriate time, he cast out from his hidden ambush the "thorns" of the enemy circle— those who were like needles and arrows to his own side— scattering them in all directions like a porcupine.
Then Pārthīhari, who was the fourth son and the younger brother of Loṣṭaka,
having been imprisoned along with the king and his brother, escaped from the prison.
He was protected by that [king] in his own residence as his own son-in-law.

Accompanied by countless *ḍāmara* warriors, he was led into the forest retreat (*śamālā*). (Yugma) Upon hearing his roar like that of a *kurara* bird, the bandits who had been hidden became manifest, like *śaphara* fish dwelling in a lake. (Kṛt 8.2750ab–cd)
Then Gajaga, like a sixth moon, obstructed the haughty Rājavadana,
who was surging like the ocean at the time of universal dissolution, just as the mountain on the shore checks the sea.
As their masses waxed and waned, the two of them fought on.
Like two snow-capped mountain slopes with their frozen crevices in the heat of summer,
Jayacandra and his younger brother Śrīcandra were then distanced from the royal palace and deprived of their stipends.
Because of their knowledge, their restraint, and their lack of self-sufficiency, and out of affection for the burden-bearing task at hand,
they were apprehensive regarding the arrival of some misfortune from the King, who was worthy of respect and their elder brother.
Fled from the camp, the two brothers-in-law arrived before the king's face and became his rivals. Then,
by the countless Khāśakas who were travelers on the mountain paths, KRT_8_2756ab.

Seeking the wealth of the former kings, he plundered Bhūteśvara. With its strength destroyed by powerful forces, the entire kingdom— lacking a king, unprotected from the incursions of thieves, and fallen into a miserable state— reached a wretched condition.

Then the king, having ordered a fourfold battle against Udaya, the lord of Kampana, and Rilhaṇa, entered the city helpless. But Pārthvahari was difficult to subdue, like a great disease that cannot be cured by medicines.
The two armies were brought to a standstill and could not be struck down; at that moment,
even Rilhaṇa’s prowess became diminished as he waited for the right time or yielded to the wicked counsel of his own partisans.
But Viḍḍasiṃha, having learned of the king’s conduct regarding his meals,
dispatched many messengers to summon the lords of the earth in the northern region—
even those who were aware of the impudence of the wife of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera).
Even with mountain caves resounding with the songs of human maidens;
even by the coolness that counteracts the heat of the ocean of sands on one side;
and even by the breezes from the peaks that bring joy to the inhabitants of Uttarakuru.

The lords of the Mlecchas, fleeing from the mountain thickets of the Himalayas, took refuge in the various directions, obstructing the quarters with their horses as they pursued the camp of the lord of the Darads. While the king was thus arranging the assembly of the monarchs, the ruler of the Darads struck [his own camp].
Meanwhile, the neighboring kings from all directions approached the presence of Bhoja.

Seeing those who had come from Girivraja— whose speech was unfamiliar to him, yet whose affection was rooted in love like that of monkeys that have climbed up onto his shoulders— he was filled with joy.
Jayacandra and others, though sent from the king’s own mouth,
were Kiras and Kashmiris of royal lineage who sought his side;
as did those led by Balahara, both those stationed nearby and those dwelling afar.

Sālhaṇi nourished [him] with gold, attaining the highest state of a treasury-keeper. Then, because he was thoroughly crushed by the well-born [Bhoja], Niścedya-cakrika, along with Rājavadana, fell into a state of terror toward the ascetic Bhoja.
Because there was no further specific task remaining for either of them, their mutual lack of trust— which had quickly reached a state of high proficiency— dissolved. This occurred even though he,
with the exception of Darada, did not desire to march against the enemy.
Out of pride, he desired only those measured horses for assistance, thinking:
"If the enemies of this army were not capable of enduring its foremost display,
then either their equality would manifest, or there would again be a defeat that would shatter our strategic union."
"Therefore, for me who desires a single battle with a total mobilization of all forces,
the attainment of victory or defeat is considered to be separated by only a single day. When the Bhoja king spoke thus, he then laughed with a smile.

Leaving behind that army which had come seeking him, he led his small retinue away. (Tilaka 8.2774cd) At the end of the narrow pass, as they were proceeding with the escort he had granted them, that scion of royalty heard that the King of Darad had arrived. (Kṛt 8.2775ab–cd)
When he had turned back from his pursuit to re-enter the city, Balahara caused that army and its womenfolk to enter the fortress once more. Then,
seeing them slaughtered, the soldiers fled like deer bewildered by a whirlwind.
Gārgi, naturally steadfast and firm, did not waver from his composure.
All his own soldiers, as well as Nīlāśva and the formidable Dāmaras,
having formed a united front with their adversaries, advanced, eager to crush the enemy army.
Although he was thus situated in adversity, when entreated by his own people to set out, he spoke with a dejected face:
"I am not able to see the Lord.
He was not born into the lineage of Candrasūryavarman.

Having honored Bhoja— who was useful for subduing the Nāgas born of the Malla lineage— Viḍḍasīha, together with the king and his own vassals who were the very essence [of his forces], dispatched him forth for victory.
Then, as he proceeded through the throngs of barbarian hosts, driving his armies along,
there arose behind him, separated by only a short distance of travel,
a force of followers that stirred up agitation throughout the world.
Out of enthusiasm, Sālhaṇi considered the entire earth as already within his grasp;
for his army was formidable, having been emboldened by horses and by the subjugation of the Mleccha kings.

Then, at the place called Samudradhāra, he blocked that path. Resplendent with such supreme and invincible strength, he who possessed a face like a king considered the moon of the sixth day to be already between the teeth of Death.
