Then the earth, flooded by the lamps created by the rain-clouds of the monsoon,
became like a blooming blue lotus. In the vessel of the earth filled with the wine of water, the trees bore fruit.
He dispatched the illustrious Dhanya, who resembled a blooming blue lotus and was distinguished by his mere aim at the target,
along with the remaining forces, against the formidable sixth king, Jālandhara;
and then he sent forth that fortunate lord of Udayagiri as well.
With their paths blocked by the army, those two—
Śaineya and the son of Pavana— followed the track of Dhanañjaya, as if on the path of Arjuna himself,
across a vast expanse of ground filled with water and covered with large, dark clouds.
Like a flash of lightning woven [into the clouds], she appeared with a sound like a burst of light;
there the king became one whose splendor was free from reproach, whose retinue was exalted, and whose army was undivided.
Formerly, in the presence of the king, he was indifferent toward both the courage and the steadfastness of the people.
Now, another [trait] must not be cast upon him by the enemies, thinking "he is of royal lineage.
Trillaka, sending messengers with instructions, brought about the prosperity of Pārthvahari.

By the power of one of those two, he wished for the hand-to-hand combat [to end]; [this was] like a painting drawn without a wall, belonging to Balahara. Then, having observed such power on the part of the king as well in every respect—‖ (KRT 8.2793cd–2794ab) ‖—‖ (KRT 8.2794cd) ‖
Having divided his entire army here and there amidst the perils posed by the enemy, and having recognized a vulnerability that could not be remedied, he— whose misconduct was now laid bare—
long concealed [his true nature] with his own limbs, yet his behavior was like that of a fat cat.

He cast aside even the second thorn, which was difficult to overcome from without. [Tilaka] In the darkness where the mass of clouds causes blindness, and in the great wind of the heavy dust-storm, the great effort of the whisperer (the spy) became known through the division of his own side. [Kṛt 8.2796cd–2797ab]

There, in various dire straits, he acted as a destroyer of his lineage for the king; restless and sleepless, he pursued that which was meaningless while nourishing what was harmful. Then, in Śūrapura, together with many violent outlaws, he—

Filled by him, let the earth be observed as it is by the fullness of the rainy season. (Tilaka) Let the long-standing transformation of that [earth] as it moves toward the maiden be observed, like the crumbling of the embankment of a riverbank during the fullness of the rainy season. (KRT 8.2800ab–cd)

At the onset of the rainy season, that army appeared like the world emerging from the belly of the sleeping Upendra; it was as if the entire universe had gathered there. That force could not even be numbered by those who were capable of counting such a multitude.
Even though he was surrounded by very few warriors who were merely fit for maintenance,
Piñcadevadraṅgādhipa, with just that many followers, made the warriors of the South and the rivers his guests in battle. (A *yugma*).
With the circles of funeral pyres blazing on the riverbank reflected in the water of the stream,
it was as if the cremation rites were being performed even for those who had already died.
Thus, having forgotten death, he engaged in a single-day battle.
On another day, having somehow been brought back by his trusted men after his main force had been broken,
he gathered his troops everywhere within that empty city;
in two or three days, he considered the city easy to capture.

He caused his desire for the Padma kingdom to slacken out of fear of Yaśorāja and Kampanādhipa, who were stationed at his back; such a feat was not accomplished by his servants when even one of them was dissatisfied.
In the *ḍāmara* kingdom of Hulla,
which was subject to another's will, such a calamity as that which arose on all sides for the son of Sussala was never seen even during the dual rule of Sussala himself.

Then, disregarding the four [elements], King Rilaṇa dispatched a foot-soldier to remove that [disease] which was like a goitre on the neck. Having set out to destroy it, he was bound by those who were devoid of tranquility.
Advancing to slay the Saṃśaptakas, as if for Prāgjyotiṣa, Pārtha rushed forward against his enemies,
turning back and felling them;
with his face turned toward the lotus-like enemy, he was like an elephant casting down the bees clinging to its back.
Exhausted by battle, he spent the three watches of the night at Rāmaśeṣa,
which was consecrated by the roar of the enemy host as they were cast into the roaring tributary stream.

As he was entering that auspicious city in the forenoon, Sogra arrived and, having approached with his forces filling the quarters of the horizon, blocked him once again; like a hawk swooping down, he fell upon the enemy foot-soldiers who had come against him.

Like a jackal devouring goats that it has seen and lost, he swallowed them up before his eyes. At his onset, which was like that of a windstorm, Rilhaṇa was abandoned by his foot-soldiers, just as a tree sheds its leaves in winter.

As he watched them fleeing, they felt no shame for their cowardice. For one who has reached the ultimate limit of detachment from the body, what is appropriate is beyond reproach. Then, having approached him, Rilhaṇa was entreated by his own trusted friends and spoke.

The smile [of the Lord] is a reminder of his devotion to his master, attaining equality with the Creator of beings. Alas! Even though there is no difference between one creature and another, if the Lord [shows favor only to some], then fie upon the life of that servant who, despite being in the state of service, has failed in his duty!
The lake of his face, which had become a vessel for the dark lotuses of his beard,
turned as pale as a white water-lily due to old age, as he approached the feet of the king;
and while those [lotuses] withered, they became radiant with the bees of his knitted brows.
How could it not be mocked by the unbroken play of Fortune?
(This pair of verses) This path, which is to be avoided by cowards, is certainly not for the steadfast:
that one becomes averse to happiness due to the fear of even a slight exertion. (KRT 8.2822)

Just as there is a fear born of cold when one is merely wearing a garment, and then, upon bathing in the waters of a sacred ford, there is the attainment of the pleasant joy of delight comparable to the experience of Brahman;
so too, for those who cast off their bodies in battle, there is first a state of agitation at the onset, followed by the supreme bliss known as *kaivalya* and thereafter final liberation.
Having spoken thus, he alone plunged into the enemy host.
Seizing arrows whose whistling sounds were muffled by the breath of Indra’s horse,
and blazing with the green hue of the lapis lazuli on his golden hilt,
he attained a surging intensity upon the stage of battle as he brandished his sword.
As he struck down swords with his sword, the lives [of his enemies] rose up from the earth under the guise of a net and clung to him like grass clinging to a *tṛṇamaṇi* gem;
even those who had counted their enemies as negligible followed him into battle.
Having become the target for animals, even their very lives became as straw to them.
Having entered the mouth of Death, he emerged through certain passages,
like water entering the ear-cavities of a fish with its mouth closed.

Constantly making retreats for the sake of exhausting his fatigue, he emerged with his strength largely depleted; yet, having gained momentum, he became formidable to the enemy. Then, a fourfold force with abundant troops fell upon him from the rear.
When they perceived that enemy army— which was like a serpent with two mouths— as having arrived to assist their own side,
their agitation did not merely cause them to dance excessively like peacocks; rather, it was as if they were dancing for joy.
Alternating their formations, they displayed front and rear to one another in battle,
like the Mandara mountain and the shore of the ocean during the churning of the sea;
as they whirled repeatedly between those two [combatants] who were as immovable as stakes, they vomited forth [fire].
Like a weaver [driving his loom], Bhāsa, impelled by the speed of his horse,
received that enemy of a single army,
just as the rising growth on a riverbank receives the weight of water from a single island.
By him, playing with fierce speed, the army of the enemy was made to have its weapons and earrings disarrayed, rendered incapable of acting like men;
the frontal globes of the elephants of his foes became pale with terror and drenched with sweat.
I know that while doing so, he consecrated the king once again in his kingdoms.
And that earthly lion (Hariscandra) and [the other] remained alert toward one another at every moment of the night,
like two sorcerers and a vetāla seeking each other's vulnerabilities.

Having called upon the soldiers of the king as witnesses for those who had come to his aid, on another day he set out after Trillaka and the others, who had abandoned their purity and were fleeing through the forest paths toward the enemy.
On the third day, Sañjapāla went into the presence of Rilhaṇa;
tormented by the king’s majesty, he was completely withered away by those two.

Like a tree at the edge of a forest consumed by woodworms, he was wasted away by his two pure and white [sons]. Like a funeral pyre, finding no peace through futile battles, even the fourfold army was gradually brought to a state of diminished fervor by the rising [of the enemy].

With horses bearing proud golden armor— possessing the strength of Darada— he descended from the mountain caves toward the battlefield. The regions overrun by the Turuṣka people fell under his control.

The entire earth was perceived by apprehensive people as if it were overrun by barbarians. When even the two door-panels were separated from him by the mere distance of a step, that man without a companion encountered their swords before him in a display of reckless courage.
He, the enemy of his foes, led that army clad in armor blazing like gold,
just as a mountain with its waterfalls leads a forest fire with its rows of flickering flames;
having shaken off Jayacandra and the others who had blocked his advance.
Arrogant due to their great strength, they plunged into the forest.
With thirty thousand horses and twenty thousand steeds,
the son of Garga received them with speed and brought them under his control.
His enemies witnessed that superhuman prowess of his,
as he displayed, before each one of them, what seemed like a universal form.
In an instant, they fled, their faces cast down toward the tips of their horses' manes.
The base men plunged into the mountains like *kimpuruṣas*. This defeat has arisen from ignorance of the terrain and from exhaustion;
tomorrow, placing us at your head, you shall recover your victory.

Thus addressed at night by Rājavadana, Jayacandra, and the others, the givers of their wives said "So be it," speaking falsely as they prepared to flee. [Yugma] Having sent Dhanya and the lord of the gate far away, the powerful Balahara—
Desiring to deceive him by blocking his western routes,
he then formed the intention to station the king of Darada together with his army at Tāramūlaka.

Then, while those intoxicated and blinded bandits were intent on their purpose, Sālhaṇi resolved that the entire kingdom was already conquered and took heart. Even though victory was not yet certain, he then set out accompanied by his endless host of vassal lords.
Thinking, "I am capable; I shall become [so]," he rose up.
When the moon, rivaling the friend of the lotuses (the sun), rises with its body divided into fragments by the elephants' ichor that destroys the lotuses, those who possess a lovely luster would die;
the heat would be abandoned by the sun-stones that share in that beauty; and at the time of calamity, both good and evil may occur beyond all expectation.
That which consists of constant indifference toward a monk even when he is in distress due to his fierce nature;
and [indifference] toward the heads of those who betray their sovereign because of their kinship with Tikka and others;
and that which, through lack of affection, increases a wonder unique to no other—[this is the mark of a true king].

Then, at that moment of calamity, those two whose faces were like the king of serpents, though their efforts were applied with difficulty as if upon the very crest of trust, surprisingly became filled with wonder and intense devotion due to their dedication to their own purpose. (Tilaka)
Seeing that calamity brought about by another, which he himself ought to have managed, the king felt as much regret as a poet who sees his intended meaning spoiled by another;
he then prepared to win over his own enemy as an ally.
"Abandoning the face of royalty, serve me," he said.
"Wait for your son who has arrived, the one who robs you of your splendor and strength;
why do you treat him like a guard treats a man mounted upon a carriage?"

Having thus instructed him and dismissed him, he left that elephant, who was like the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), because it had been embraced by a goat— a result ordained by fate. Everyone proceeds toward what is pleasant or unpleasant solely out of intent for their own purpose.
But in the case of affection, enmity, and so forth, one perceives nothing at all.

The pair of tusks of the elephant, whose luster is surpassed by the light [of the moon], is censured as being the frontal globes of the beloved elephant, due to the bees' perception that they are the taste of nectar; the lotus is censured as being the dwelling place of the enemy, the cock; and here, there is no pleasure for the moon, for it is not the nourisher of the lotus, nor are the bees its enemies, for they do not cause it harm.
Then,
desiring the welfare of the king, he began a lifelong enmity with that Balahara in order to overthrow his foundation.
"Since he has thus broken your tributary princes while remaining unbroken himself,
this king will slay you along with your followers," so said the king to his own men with a face like that of a lion.
Then the two leaders of the Kampana army, who had brought the kings of Darad and Rajanaka [as captives], [were addressed].
Both Prakhyāta, Kṣemavaktra,
and Matta rushed toward him; Ojas by name and Koṭṭeśa, trembling with fear, spoke in secret to the minister,
and their words were laughed at by Bhoja, who understood the inner truth.

Then, although obstructed at the front by that army which was like crystal, the sun-like King Siddhārtha shone forth; alas, he fell upon the fuel of his enemies. He was already emaciated by the consumption disease (yakṣmā) of evil thoughts regarding the misfortunes of the kings.
He attained a state resembling the waning moon during the dark fortnight.

When the lord—who had been the protector of his rear—was stricken by disease and at the forefront of battle, and when the position itself, though worthy of being attacked, had become shattered by fear; ||| KRT_8_2871cd–KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872ab–KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_2872cd ||| KRT_8_28

Then, abandoning all those who were dependent on food and thus deprived of strength, they fled on the following day, plunging into the mountains with the monkeys. [Yugma] Having seen that we are highly esteemed, we shall return again tomorrow morning. [KRT_8_2873cd–2874ab]
Having spoken thus and made his request, he went with Sālhaṇi and those [others].
Due to his helplessness, he who had previously been a treasury-drinker became a cowherd for them. Having failed in his purpose, he fell into a state of agitation, as if sinking into a pit.
It was as if blazing and filled with blood flowing from every head at once;
it resembled the stones of a staircase descending through clear water;
and it was like the sky, known to be equal to the earth, having fallen down.
As he was departing, his face became imperceptible due to shame;
and he reflected: "Fie on us, who, though we are constantly born in such abundance, remain ignorant of ourselves even upon seeing the king, and fail to recognize the nature of mortals!"
For great poets whose reality is manifested through the maturity of their inspired genius, there is no other way [to describe it] when describing the fire of such majesty.
If the sparks of the king’s crest-fire did not exist upon the earth, [how could this be so]?
Why have we come here to show such lack of fortitude even at the mere setting down of a foot?
In this tumultuous scene where the blood of heroes has been drunk by many mouths,
would these parched throats not manifest [their thirst] were it not for the fever of its flames?

What need is there for that blindness caused by the columns of smoke for one whose eyes are wide open? It is merely a state of confusion regarding the discernment of what is the path and what is not the path.
On the other bank of the Madhumatī, having abandoned those who dwell in Darada—*Kṛtyakalpataru* 8.2882ab–2883ab.
Then, concealed by the curtain of waves, he dwelt upon the bank of that lake.

Gradually, his fatigue from being uprooted was removed by them, who— driven by a desire for revenge that was growing as they waited for him to arrive there— led him into their own camp to make peace with him.
For they desired to live off the king—who showers countless benefits—by means of the trade of protecting him, through their skill in policy.
"This is not the time for war; the arrival of winter is near."

In the month of Madhu, we shall again undertake this supreme enterprise. If you have the patience to bide your time now, O Bhūṭa, we will place you within the treasury of the powerful Trillaka along the royal highway.

Having said this to the king, Rājavadana relied upon them; thus, by means of a stratagem, he intended to have that lowest of men bound within his own kingdom. For even the cunning of those residing in the royal city was surpassed by them.
The length of the summer days seemed as long as the days of separation;
thus Balahara reproached him for his delay,
saying, "I have placed my arrows [at your disposal]," while snapping the tips of his *vaṭa*-grass arrows.
Out of sheer enthusiasm, he did not even notice that firewood was being brought,
nor did he take account of the approaching royal army;
for he was suddenly distracted by news of the fleeing Dravidian and Bhoja kings.
That it did not shatter was surely due to the perfection of its fortitude. That which remains with its form unbroken even when the support of its outward display is shattered—
who other than a superhuman being could achieve such a feat, remaining undaunted by battle?
Then,
out of consideration for the time, the two lords of the gates, Saṃdhiman and Sūdhana, joined him there with some delay, in the hope that the Bhoja king might return.

Therefore, that Alaṅkāracakra came with Sālhaṇi to lead her away; she was requested [as a bride] by coming as a kinswoman and offering a dowry. Having understood that even in this pursuit, the assemblies were intent on hostility, [he departed].
Seeing him prepared for death at the front of the bridge on the path,
accompanied by servants who were mostly young men,
the army of King Darada became deeply distressed and fell into a state of wretchedness.
Dispersing the conflict with her arms, the river, carrying away the [enemy] force,
seemed to mock the army of Darada with the splashing sounds of her surging waves.
[The air was filled] with the neighing of his own harem-females and with the resentful cries of the Mleccha kings.
Then, terrified of the carnage, Viḍḍasaha abandoned him;
with his vanguard having broken the bridge-guards, he then reached the further shore,
putting those [enemies] to flight while filling the quarters with the sounds of his trumpets.
Since the army was powerless and he himself desired peace,
Viḍḍasīha brought a messenger and spoke thus to the king:
"By your master’s superhuman power, let it be so."
Out of a sense of rivalry with their neighboring neighbors, the two fishermen engaged in contests;
their intentions being utterly untrustworthy, they went to the presence of Yama, each claiming,
"I am Jayarāja," while in heaven they were both proclaimers of the other's power.
By that divine power, even defeat became victory for me;
for a traveler, falling into a ford after the collapse of the riverbank is an elevation.
Then, having stayed for some time in the city in front [of him], he entered his own [city].
On that very day, without realizing that Bhoja was approaching, he— though possessing a face like a king— departed for Yama’s realm, where ill-repute serves as a radiant garland of welcome,
having entered into a treaty with Dvāreśa and Dhanya.
Turning back that horse which had arrived— the leader of the wise—
they took it and approached the presence of the lord of the earth.
Though they had been excluded [from the assembly] due to pride or delusion, or perhaps through lack of discernment, [they now returned].
While the king’s kinsman was enjoying his meals with indifference,
Rilhaṇa did not turn back, even though he had been summoned repeatedly by his lord, who was filled with impetuous longing;
for he had not yet completely eliminated his enemies.
In the presence of the Lord, he was unable to stand;
for like a cook desiring the master's favor, he could not remain anywhere to eat.
By him, in battle, the two daughters of the Earth and Hara were split in two.
Possessing the form of the Lord of Magadha, he became incapable of action as if by Bhīma.
By him, the earth was made into a mere clod in battle, as if it were his mother’s womb;
like a serpent in the Khāṇḍava forest, he entered [the earth] pierced by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva.
Contracting his fourfold [limbs] into a difficult-to-pierce enclosure of three *lakā*s,
he— free from pride— slid into the shell of his own body like a tortoise.
Having accomplished his task entirely through the king’s valor alone, he...

The king’s side went toward the binding of the bandage of light from his toenails. Thus, although the calamity had been dried up by the king’s exploits, its sprouts were once again made manifest through the fault of the minister’s intellect.
Since Rājavadana was worthy of punishment but had been gratified by his gift, the king received him again as he approached fearlessly; then, having accepted a bribe,
he reinstated him.
"In the place called Dinnāgrāma, in the settlement of the Khāśakas"—
thus Āyāsya spoke to him, saying,
"If the gatekeeper had not followed me, he would have departed from my range with only a limited retinue."
Trembling like a boat being carried away by the current of a reckless torrent,
he was brought to steadiness by Trillaka through the casting out of the rope of policy;
yet he reflected upon the king’s helplessness in the face of the surge of calamity.

He who again adopted that instability and lack of priority was a fool. Even though he was being established in composure by his ministers through ornaments and other means, he did not abandon his crookedness, like one of unsubdued self whose grasp is difficult to overcome.
Disregarding him as a physician disregards an unripened abscess, the king set about lancing his enemies, those adversaries who were like boils that had reached maturity.

"You must come here later when our own land trembles," having said this to the Bhoja king, Alaṅkāracakra departed, intent on an invasion. That bandit named Jayānandavāḍa [attacked] the city of Ānandavāḍa.
The enemies as well, exalted by their prowess and following the path of royal tradition, pursued him. Standing at the front was the ornament of the royal household, accompanied by only a small force;
he appeared to them like a sandbank on the ocean, surrounded by those chariots which were like the waters of the sea.

He, however, being alone, provoked among the people the apprehension of a disturbance caused by the sacrificial rites of Rāma, as he engaged in combat with many. He made the right side of the demons agitated by their confusion at his impetuous onset.
He went to the battle, immediately crushing the enemy's pride as he flowed forth;
like a wind swiftly driving a heap of cotton, he quickly scattered that formidable army of his foes— what more need be said?
The son of Ānandavāḍa abandoned that [elephant] for the sake of a morsel for the flocks of vultures, herons, and other birds; having slain it in battle with that arrow,
he [did so] while the Bhoja king was desiring to rise up and wishing to seize it.
The analogy of the hunter chasing the *krakara* bird through the mud increased [in its application].
Just as a *krakara* bird, lacking the strength to pull itself out, exhausts itself while running in the mud, so too the hunter,
falling into the mud, pursues it day after day.
In this manner, during the height of his audacity, Bhoja constantly fell into despondency;

and the king, wishing to capture him, repeatedly suffered from a delusion of mind. While Bhoja remained stationed in the village of Dinnāgra, that king, though possessing a face like that of a god, [fell into despair]. (A *yugma*).
Furthermore, what [could equal] the Lord’s statement that "thieves and outcasts are better"? Then those fierce robbers,
their ranks broken, again tied up the maiden— who was even more beautiful than before— with knots, she whom they had repeatedly sought for her heroic splendor.

They were not only unable to withstand the gatekeeper who had arrived; rather, with their efforts rendered futile by impossible battles, they caused him distress. Then, for the sake of protecting them and for the sake of rousing others, he advanced.
Having fastened his girdle with a circle of ornaments that were drawn [into place], that Sālhaṇi,
wishing to go to their side the following day, repeatedly urged his horse;
then, when his army was exhausted and he had reached the hermitage, he was noticed at the gate by the gatekeeper.

As if unaware of their deceptive stratagem, he entered into an agreement with them; under some pretext, he went aside to a place situated obliquely at the base of a tree. While he remained there, from a distance, there arose a cry of distress from somewhere unknown.
Hearing this, the Bhoja king, becoming somewhat agitated,
spoke; though being ridiculed by his own men, he ceased from that groundless agitation out of fear, yet he did not prepare his horses.

Then, his circle of ornaments scattered, Daśagrāma quickly fled before him, crying out, "Where is the prince? and thus escaped. Thereupon, a great sound of musical instruments arose from the midst of the village.
At the onset of night, amidst the unobserved clamor of the army and the roar of the troops in the midst of darkness, Bhoja fled; meanwhile,
Alaṅkāracakra prepared for battle against those tasks to be performed the following day.
The fire given by the gatekeeper, illuminating the path through the mountain,
became a source of harm to them, whose very selves had already been destroyed by darkness.
Forgiveful toward the gatekeeper, they waited for an alliance with the Bhoja king.
Then, having heard that news of his defeat, those Ḍāmaras departed.
Not abandoning the bonds of affection for his children and kin, that steadfast man, by taking refuge with Dhīroccala,
waged an inauspicious battle against the circle of Bhoja ornaments.
Even there, Bhoja was not satisfied with the pleasure of food and other such things.
His prowess was born from the fire of Bāṇa during the burning of Tripura, and his birth was from the submarine fire (*vaḍavāgni*) during the churning of the ocean.
Indeed, having encountered Mount Mandara, there was no longer any friendship with happiness for the lord of the serpents.
Having arrived on the ground of his own domain to dispel hunger, thirst, and fatigue—
Bhoja further desired to bind him with the sons of Alaṅkāra;
however, intending to do this or that according to his father’s counsel or his own intellect, he departed after making his plans and reached another territory.

Then, having determined his course of action, Balahara, who was skilled in affairs, returned once more to the village granted by Dinnā, indifferent toward other pleasures. Meanwhile, the gatekeeper Hitoddhāra, though capable, remained there with his mind set on [the king's] welfare.
Because of an eye disease, his exertion was broken; why then was he suddenly struck down? He who wished to give [the kingdom] to Bhoja instead gave it to his son Ḍāmara.
Having been defeated by Parmāṇḍi, Gulhaṇa, and Rājāja, [he met his end].

When the application of punishment was carried out due to the king's fierce hostility toward disease, the gatekeeper entered there helplessly after first employing conciliation. At that moment of assault, he who was capable of bearing the burden met his destruction.
Druma, named Āmaya, and the sixth moon, Gargaja, were also emaciated by disease. There,
their two younger brothers, having taken up an excess of that very malady,
brought the earth to a state of misery through afflictions such as Skanda and others.
Trillaka, increasing his discord with other powerful men and intent on conflict,
did not accept even the king’s conciliation.
When the sixth doorkeeper had reached the end of his life due to illness, [the king approached] the one before him.
Appointed by the king, the fortunate man set out for Tāramūlaka.
Bhoja, having fallen from his position, might fall into the power of other powerful men;
once he has regained his standing and crossed over [the danger], he may become difficult to displace from his country or residence.

Having reflected thus, the king, desiring to win him over through means such as conciliation (*sāma*), undertook that mission with little agitation. (Yugma) That misconduct, arising from the king’s ignorance of the sun’s adversity, [afflicted] the monarch. (KRT_8_2961ab)
Like a female serpent whose tail has been severed and dragged away, she recoiled because her efforts were thwarted;
and perceiving that the powerful king was like a lion’s mouth while the monarch was weak,
both his inner circle and his outer subjects underwent a gradual transformation.

Alas! Vulnerable points are always easy to find, just as in the case of the policy of punishment (*daṇḍanīti*), which is like a path leading to the chasm of the underworld. Having entered its interior through many expanding openings, one may suffer a fall due to unforeseeable constraints, or else, having been abandoned by the king, that person whose wealth is exhausted might depart from here seeking a patron.
Having spoken thus, Balahara caused him to carry out that task.
Observing that this illusion had gained a foothold within the royal faction, he,
through his skill in statecraft, devised other stratagems to employ.
Seeing that Māyā had gained free rein within the royal faction, that fortunate man, performing his coming and going with difficulty, became an object of ridicule for the people;
there was no end to the royal business that was constantly turning back upon him.
He encountered [him] like the rope of a water-wheel on a well-drawing machine.
Even though he possessed sharpness, when the task whirled around like a wheel,

Having thus resolved, Bhoja, as if desiring to devour them at the end of the night—

Saying, "We shall commit this rash act," he led away Bala and Hara together. [Tilaka 8.3154cd] Out of courtesy, that king, mindful of his noble lineage, did not provide food for these vassal lords who had come for his sake. [Kṛt 8.3155ab–cd]
Likewise, not knowing his own lack of consensus, the ministers,
devoid of confidence because of him, considered the ruin of their policy to have already occurred.
Even when there was the quivering of fish caused by the violent flapping of the birds' wings, they did not perceive it.
As they rushed forward, their perception of the enemy was clouded by confusion;
on the opposite bank, those stationed there, satisfied with their own stratagems,
perceived no one other than the wheels [of the chariots] as being possessed of the onset of battle.
The father of the monkey who was the messenger of Marut and Kakutstha,
having crossed the ocean, provided those messengers with the means for crossing over the rivers.
Resorting to the trees on the shore, which were filled with the whistling sounds of birds suffering from feverish heat, they spent that night thus; at the end of the night,
[they beheld] the delusion of a golden lotus upon the crest of the mountain.
As long as the rays of the rising sun did not sever the darkness,
so long did the nocturnal water of the plants— not yet opened from their bud-like eyes— seem to flow out, as if out of grief at the sight of the cakravāka birds separated from their mates.
Having emerged from the grove of trees while still wearing his modest robes,
he hurried the war-horses forward, touching their heads with his feet;
he warded off the heroic sons of the Immortals who desired to obstruct him with mere glances from his eyes.
Rendering the warriors fleeing in all directions devoid of their luster, a youth of handsome appearance wielding a battle-axe approached them face-to-face;
mounted upon a carriage, he was seen by them as he reached the riverbank. (A *kulaka*.)
Seeing him, whom they had never seen before, with his locks anointed with sandalwood paste and his body smeared with saffron, they thought, "This is Bhoja.
Having passed the night, [he departed], infatuating that king’s face.
And having quickly taken leave of him in the morning, he appeared before him in that manner.
As the chariot with its yoked horses entered the water and the steeds galloped toward the far shore,
Dhanya and the others approached him joyfully and surrounded him.
Then a tumultuous sound arose from the two camps:
on one side it was loud with lamentation, and on the other, filled with joy.
Hearing that noise, those who had rushed from all directions with the intent of battle [were struck with fear].
Seeing him joined by others, [the king] struck him on the head with *ḍāmara* drums; yet,
his reception began with words of welcome and other honors,
wherein the natural order of things— such as the distribution of non-destitute, pure grain and so forth— was not abandoned.
As he was floating upon this earth, which is possessed of stability,
that blessed man, praising it in this manner, was addressed [by the Earth]:
"O Prince, this earth is possessed of stability."
While you were praising him, that blessed one spoke thus:
"Among all cows, your cow excels by dwelling in a state of changelessness;
her milk is superior to the milk of the Ocean of Milk, which is afflicted by transformation."
For whom, like a male cuckoo,
has it become possible to emerge from the midst of the base and plunge into the company of your own kin,
now that the path of virtuous conduct has been first struck down by you?
"It is no wonder that we are traveling; if this were our final journey, it would be even more so"—
with such words of exultation pouring forth,
he was led away by those who praised the horse as it surged with waves of victory.
Then some of the Lāvanyas went along, shouting and crying out at him as he was being led away by his own kinsmen, like crows toward a cuckoo. Thus,
in his twenty-first year, on the tenth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha...
The king received him, who appeared to be about thirty-three years of age;
the queen welcomed him— who had offered his salutations— as if he were her own dear son returned from afar,
and she provided food for him and his weary attendants.
Beholding him, whose multitude of virtues was consistent with the lunar dynasty,
she thought her eyes were deceived, as if she had never seen him before.
She was captivated by his natural virtues, such as gentleness and sweetness.
He regarded his pure conduct as the very essence of the lord of men.
The complexion of the face is the gateway to the state of the mind, and the brilliance of the home is the radiance of domestic fortune;
for women, conduct is the indicator of their husband’s true character.
No one, out of courtesy, spoke to him as he approached the presence of the king— eager to depart yet manifesting the fatigue of his journey by the waning of the day. Then,
the ministers, whose neutrality had been somehow obstructed by their disagreements, [acted].

That lord of men instructed him until the end of his life; he was thereafter devoted to [his service]. When the king said, "Enter my presence," those words—which served as a prelude—produced a sensation like the piercing of a probe within the hollows of his ears.
Then,
having recovered as if from a vital wound struck long ago,
he observed that their steadfastness remained centered within them, yet there was a supreme trembling of the lips due to courtesy.

For him who wished to cast off his life-breaths and spoke harshly, those whose heads were bowed in humility brought about a change from dullness through their consolations. And though he was unaffectionate in his conduct, they addressed him with words that were just and eloquent.
He thought that no one could defeat him with a counter-argument.
Then, as if demonstrating his own subjection to the Lord dwelling within his heart,
the fortunate hero spoke affectionately, illuminating [the space] with the rays of light from his teeth.

How can there be delusion in you regarding matters that follow their natural course, even though you know the manual of royal duties established in right conduct? Could that be called peace where there is no prospect of an alliance being made?

"How did you not consider beforehand that one departs without having acted? Knowing that your sovereign was a king easily accessible to his subjects, radiant with courage, and devoted to the practice of the dharma of kinsmen— "

Neither his hypocrisy, pride, arrogance, nor the stability of his malicious speech can compare to the clarity of the mirror of his devotion; what beauty is there even in his sighs? That prosperity which he derives from subsistence upon others is not equal to the attainment of universal sovereignty.
Does that light which is reflected from a burning lamp become itself ablaze?

That state of being dedicated to assemblies for the discussion of *nirvāṇa* found among the abodes of the tranquil ones belongs to that royal sage who is followed by a multitude of followers in his assembly.

Thus, for you whose supreme bliss is almost as easily attained as reaching your own home, what need is there for other mountains once your glory has been perfected by these sites? No others are counted as deluded, for they have not been born from the waters of their own pits that are rendered dark by the serpents and subject to time.
In the summer heat, they embrace sandalwood trees that are cool; even in the month of Māgha, they enter a hole that is neither cold nor warm.
Whatever impropriety there may be toward the king’s life-sustaining resources—the queen and the princes—that very impropriety is, for them, propriety itself.

Like water that has lost its heat and become cool after being boiled, your undertaking will once again turn bitter through remorse. Thus, having failed to reject her capable speech despite its power, [you have acted wrongly].
Slow-moving Manthara stood there, his vigor dulled; he remained for the sake of setting out.
Then, seeing on all sides the local inhabitants composing hymns of praise along the path, his mind became firmly resolved upon the excellence of his duty already undertaken.

Under the guise of the dust trampled by the feet of the infantry, the surface of the earth appeared as if it were joined together with the sky. Bhoja reflected: "I wonder if I shall ever reach that king?"
I hope that his audience with the Lord is not hindered by deceitful flatterers; for who among masters, when their abode is obstructed from within by parasites,
finds an opportunity to manifest their true virtues?
"By providing cooling remedies, I shall become beloved by the ocean tormented by the submarine fire"— thinking thus,

he did not perceive the city's agitation or other disturbances due to the numbness caused by such reflections, as if the outpouring of the river from the snowy mountains had been swallowed by a *timi* fish.
Because the horses of the army were held back, the king’s residence was not far away. He was neither too tall nor too thin, his face darkened by the rays of the sun;
he was as fair as the pericarp of a lotus, with a body that appeared relaxed and loose.
He had a hump-backed protuberance on his shoulders and a broad chest;
his beard was not too long, and the prominence of his cheeks and throat was clearly defined.
He possessed a prominent nose and lips like the ripe *bimba* fruit, with wide and well-proportioned nostrils.
Glancing sideways—[he saw] one who walked with a steady and slow gait;
whose head was covered by a well-arranged cloth turban and [smeared with] sandalwood paste; and marked by a crescent-shaped line, pale as the moon, kissing the parting of his hair.
Mounted upon his horse and surrounded by ministers standing on the palace roof,
the king gazed at him as he approached. (Kulaka)

Then, questioned by the king with eyes wide with joy, he ascended the crowded assembly hall while the people craned their necks in curiosity. Having touched the feet of the king seated before him, he sat down after taking hold of the king's hand with his own.

He presented a cow-shaped dagger with its handle bound in his hand before the king’s seat. Then, placing his hand— with its snake-like vine and two fingers extended— at the edge of the king’s chin, the monarch spoke:

"You were not seized in a state of conflict, nor are you being bound even now. Therefore, my dear friend, why do we take up this weapon that has been offered by you? He then informed the king: "O Lord, regarding the bearing of weapons..."

The protection of one's master is the cause of one's own preservation. When the Lord— the master of the seven rivers— is guarded by the fire of his own majesty, even the opportunity for one’s own weapon to be used is seen to be rare.
"Even in another world, the refuge is taking shelter at the feet of the Lord;
what need is there for other means of protection in this world?
The King said to him: "Now you have shown a bond of rivalry with my own courage."

"Like a debater who has fulfilled his duty, there is no further task remaining for me. O Bhoja, I have now spoken out of a sense of courtesy toward my lord; nothing that I have said was intended as mere flattery."
What evil have you not contemplated? What unpleasant thing have you not done? Let it be understood that whatever has remained unaccomplished has not yet reached manifestation.
Why have you not been born into the lineage of the Mallas as a cause [for their downfall]?
We, who possess only the eyes of flesh, knew you previously to be of another lineage; yet,
O King, whenever we have entertained a desire for that which is displeasing to you,
at those times the earth has become increasingly vast.
As long as the brilliant luster of poets shines forth through their inspired genius,
such majesty of yours has been manifest before us;
it was never abandoned by me, whether on the crest of a mountain, in a ravine, or even in a cave.
In the groves of the snowy mountain, there is a fever born of your majesty.

From that time forth, O Lord, my devotion to bowing has been perfected; yet, because I remain at a distance, I am unable to perform the salutations required at dawn and twilight, as I am seeking refuge [in you].

Now, whatever was indeed performed by the wicked out of a desire for non-distinction [with you] was merely for the sake of manifesting their own flickering nature, and not out of a grasp for a physical form. Through our connection with you, we are now to be looked upon as kings throughout these quarters.

Due to contact with the waters of the Gaṅgā, the reputation of being a glass jar has spread upon the earth even today; it shines forth in every direction under the name of Śāhi. The multitude of those born into the kṣatriya caste, descended from his lineage, is infinite.

"When you were entrusted [to us], from the very moment we were joined with the mountain king (Pārvatīya-bhūbhṛt), we became inclined toward dejection, with faces turned away by the consumption of poor food.
Such are these [words]; or rather, the Lord himself is the authority.

Having spoken thus, he again grasped the feet of the king with his head. Then the king, whose turban had slipped off due to the agitation of his prostration, covered the head of the one who had risen with the cloth from his own head.
He took up the sword that had been placed upon his lap and, consoling it, set it down;
and with an unfathomable depth of composure, he spoke to the one who had forbidden him:
"I have given these away; you may either keep them or honor them."
"You must not turn away from taking up the sword; you must carry out my command.
Since his command was never in vain, he [the King] followed that instruction.
That knower of time, having followed the King and paid homage, placed the two swords upon his lap.
Then, at that moment, he became a vessel for the king’s freedom from restraint, his lack of pride, and his consoling words, like one who has long served him.
O King, that fortunate and virtuous man who has entered elsewhere and paid his respects to his own deity—
without having heard of your virtues—
regards neither his life nor his wealth today as worthy of account, remaining instead free from all perturbation.
"Therefore, O King, let due honor be considered even for the sake of your master.
"Even so, what is being said would not find a place on the ground of possibility," the king replied, "since this is what we are considering in this matter."
After engaging for a moment in various conversations with Bhoja, the lord of the people then went to the inner apartments of Queen Raḍḍā;
having offered his salutations and beheld her, who was radiant with virtues such as benevolence...

He considered that royal *pārijāta* tree to be joined with a *kalpalatā* creeper. "O Queen, this man has come here because he is worthy of honor due to his kindness and kinship; he excels even among my sons," the king said to his wife.
Then, for the sake of honoring them, that treasury of kindness, accompanied by Bhoja,
entered the inner chambers even with his wives who had borne the weight of their duties. There,
the skillful queen addressed Bhoja, who had arrived together with the king.
"You have just now become a trusted confidant of the king," [he said] with a smile.
With a face of bashful smiles, she gave her response to her husband’s words of welcome by bowing;
even while pointing out the Bhoja king, she spoke.

Noble son, do not forget that you have rejected the counsel of a trusted friend. For one who takes pride as his sole refuge, the cultivation of affection for kinsmen is like water offered daily by a former benefactor that does not touch him once he has grown old.
It is fitting for those like you to conquer the lotuses of your own kinsmen; otherwise,
for us who are sinking under the hardship of our duties, the preservation of our high status could not be achieved without his arrival,
yet he has not returned here.
While protecting the shore at Uddīpa, let there be a plant rooted in its body;
surely, like a creeper following the fall of a great tree,
the life-breaths are considered to follow the path of the husband.
"Act in such a way that there shall be no other state for me who am to be protected," the king said to her,
O Queen, you who are the witness to all that ought to be done:
"Even you do not consider my conduct toward him to be otherwise."

Even though he had subdued both Duṣṭa and Sujiṃmallārjuna, my mind has not yet attained freedom from distress or reached a state free from remorse. Then, at the king’s request, he remained in that most excellent abode together with his followers.

Bhoja thought that Rājadhanya could not achieve a firm standing elsewhere; for he reflected that the propitiation of a sovereign is impossible to accomplish through those who remain far away, lack a protector, and are seldom seen.

The king appointed protectors and made [the city] secure. "By this means, O King, no worship of the gods need be performed. Having understood her intention, the pleased king then gave her a residence.

He resided within the royal capital, which was filled with every kind of necessity. The king, too, attended upon by his own people and others who were overflowing with affection and a sense of kinship, attained a delight there as if he had been settled there for a long time.

Upon seeing the extraordinary sight of his rapid enjoyment of pleasures, the king also remembered him as if he were his own beloved son; and by means of messengers, he brought him to his side. Out of respect for his kinsman, the king took hold of him by the right side while he was eating.
He never refrained from giving food and other things that were tasted for their flavor; likewise,
he bore an unfeigned affection such that he was fondled by his young children there just like a kinsman.
Just as he clearly adopted that very course of action,
so too the king, along with his retinue, felt an irreproachable confidence. He pointed out those who were close to him, yet internally divided and split into two factions.
The king cast off both his own world-weariness and the abundance of his enemies within the assembly hall through an unartificial composure of his faculties.

He was neither dull-witted, nor arrogant, nor did he practice the "heron's vow" (hypocrisy). Regarding the king’s errors of negligence, omissions, or excesses in his affairs, he paid no heed, just as a poet pays no heed to the flaws in the work of a great poet.
He did not boast of his own prowess or recount the sacrifices he had performed;
nor, when questioned about his past deeds, did he speak of them with elaboration.
[Instead,] through flatteries such as the lord’s kinship with him in terms of equality and other such qualities...
With showers of views perceived by the wise, he spoke so that there might be no further rebirth;
likewise, even when touched [by worldly things], his disposition was not shallow,
such that the wicked, the jesters, the malicious, and others were unable to fathom him.

In moments that were fragile, having ended with disturbances such as the loss of light, he felt no apprehension whatsoever as he went to his dwelling. Just as the king’s grip became looser through his confidence, so it was.
In that very same way,
he did not run about restlessly like a stallion; always remaining at the forefront in other matters,
his path was blocked from entering the inner apartments or the secret chambers of counsel, even though he was not forbidden.
Having himself respectfully requested the means for attaining [the goal] through formal petition, he,
whose mind was constantly filled with doubt, cast aside his dependence on others. At that time, when [the opportunity] was not yet [right], he remained under the protection of those who guarded it.

Not even the events of his dreams remained unknown to the king. He did not report the mutual reproaches of the ministers and the women of the inner apartments, nor did he mention his forgetfulness, treating them as if they were the result of an evil dream.
Even though he was conscious, his voice echoed through the assemblies of ill-natured jesters;
though it vibrated within him, he spoke of the insignificance of those rogues.
Thus, having understood the matter through the conduct of that man of pure character—
The king, feeling affection, bestowed upon them a love even greater than that for his own sons.
By King Siṃha, this new bridge has been established for the protection of the lineage— a bridge difficult to cross for the sovereigns of the Kali age.
Thus, with all his afflictions dispelled, Trilaka then reflected upon the king’s well-being even amidst the fire;
for at that time, he had fled along the path of the snowless mountain.

Deceit is difficult for a living being to overcome; as he hung there, lost in thought, [the horse] remained bound. While the wise one was waiting for even a moment during the journey, the running began by Sañjayapāla without hesitation.
That hero, whose base was small, together with many formidable armies from the celestial lake, established his position against the sun;
for that region was entirely open to the entry of his adversaries.
He perceived that the external warriors were devoid of substance and did not advance out of pride.
The followers of Trillaka, though lacking arrows for the battle,
engaged with him and did not fail in their manliness.
Accompanied by an army beyond measure,
Lava fought with fury against Dāmara as he rushed there with a total mobilization;
those inhabitants of Devasaras were filled with plundered wealth.
Then all [the troops], fleeing from Sañjayapāla, abandoned him;
for when the world was everywhere submerged by the distress of the enemy’s continuous rain,
only the soldiers stationed at the headquarters remained, lofty like the principal mountain ranges.
Those who had long endured the wrath of their enemies, being exceedingly fierce themselves,
slew many others in various battles and were themselves slain there.
When all [the warriors] were wounded in battle, they sought refuge within their own circles.

Among those heroes there, even Mārtāṇḍa was covered with numerous wounds. Gayāpāla, who had slain three horses along with his driver, shone in battle; due to his skill, he remained unobserved as a foot-soldier.
The infant, his younger brother, was startled by the first sight of that [city]; he filled the heroes with amazement, for they had witnessed countless great battles.
The right arm of the Lord of Kampana did not perform that feat which his left arm achieved;
for the sun merely scorches great elephants, while the moon can break their tusks. As he galloped on horseback, the weapon flashed from his single swinging arm.
Like a forest fire accompanied by smoke and a staff, he stood as if mounted upon a winged mountain.
In that tumultuous conflict with the enemy, his horse— its path no longer steady— once again threw him from its back amidst the gashes of arrow wounds.
Afflicted by the impact of the earth’s hardness beneath his armor,
he lost consciousness while being carried out from the midst of his enemies by his two sons.
When the entire camp had perished on all sides, he remained within the courtyard of the sun.
Having cast out that hostile witness, the two of them then departed from there.
The king set out with vast forces toward him who was stationed there;
although he was quickly reached by such a multitude, [the enemy] formed a formidable, compact mass.
When the protector of the earth had reached the field of victory,
Sañjapāla, his bonds severed, set fire to the dwellings of the Lavanaya.
Even though he was in such a state, while the king’s brows were knit in anger, [he remained there].
No longer poor, he found food easily available in the series of mountain valleys;
yet, though free from rivals and excluded from worldly possessions,
he became a vessel for the reproach of servants whose cleverness was only evident in times of calamity.
Then, his hand-branches severed by the wrath of the Earth, he [the king],

the eldest of whom was named Gulhaṇa.
Then the illustrious Śobha consecrated his son, that bull among kings,

When the queen departed to consecrate her son, the kings made her feet— already reddened by lac— as crimson as rubies with the rays from the red gems upon their heads. There, once he was consecrated, [he restored] the earth that had been parched by a fierce drought.
As if sprinkling water for the sake of consecrating her into the state of a queen, the cloud-like [army] poured forth; then,
once again eager to cause a upheaval, Rājavadana,

Accompanied by his nephew Nāgabhrātṛvya, Gārgi entered [the enemy lines]; he then destroyed the advancing armies on the narrow path. Thereupon, Gārgi remained for several days with his face withered by humiliation.
In the battle, he bound Loṣṭhaka— the foremost of the sons of Nāgabhrātṛ.
Having entered with speed that place which was unassailable by others due to its inaccessibility,

Nevertheless, Rājavadana did not lose his courage;
he neither made a truce nor grew angry, for it was impossible to force him to withdraw. Day after day, the king’s forces fell away, diminished by their own ranks.
From Jayacandra’s mouth, he constantly drank in misfortunes.
Then the lord of the earth, extending his boundless nails and arms as if within the very midst of battle, struck him down with sharp weapons hidden and placed [within his grasp].

Siṃhadeva, the upholder of his lineage, had established [the following]: a pair of verses (Kṛt 8.3317cd).

Having turned betel-leaf into a triple protection against disease,
as it were, his own son bestowed upon him a sweet embrace that restored his very life.

That lord of the earth, whose long-standing resolve is to uplift his subjects, must be protected even at the cost of his own life; for at every step he is submerged in calamity. Even when he is sleepless due to illness, those desiring his welfare [should attend] to him because of their close association.

At that final moment, the grateful king did not depart from his side. For the minister who cherished his subjects, there arose for a brief instant a transformation of his true nature, becoming a bestower of life upon the people.
When those subjects who had experienced suffering due to the deaths of kings beginning with Māndhātṛ attained happiness at that time,
there arose for the new king a kingdom that had been overwhelmed by the calamities of dual rule.
That assistance which is unimpeded is [the work] of Time, which fears all obstacles. Indeed, by its power, who is there that does not forget the sequence of what was done before and after?
The capacity of the Earth lies in the act of bearing [the world], while the fitness of the Conqueror of Mura (Viṣṇu) lay in his state as the Boar for the purpose of uprooting it.

Having become the city magistrate when Sūjjena had been executed, he put an end to the long-standing disorder of the country. He abolished the irregular practice of using *dīnāras* in transactions for purchases.
Having restrained him, he was set to work on tasks that would cause his downfall, free from all hesitation. When there was a violation of the virtue of a married woman,
the king’s application of punishment was halted by him after due deliberation.
Having become entirely devoted to the welfare of the people, he once again brought about their oppression by obtaining the office of city magistrate;
and while remaining in his married household life, he was surrounded by bound female dancers.
He forcibly punished many who were being accused of association;
what indeed is the use of reflecting upon trifles like husks?
No other person was his equal in the ground of non-malice and non-greed.
Although he followed the custom of the times by taking up the roles of a mendicant and a wrestler,
he did not abandon those two who were devoted to their master’s welfare, nor did he kill them.

Even at the time of his greatest prosperity, there was never a lack of generosity in him who had not diminished his own giving; yet at his death, his wealth was not sufficient even for the rites of consecration. What more need be said of the king’s sufficiency in gratitude? (Kṛt 8.3341–3342ab)
He who, like life itself, shared out those things brought to him among his dependents; he who,
for the sake of his beloved named Vijja— who was a guest from another world— constructed monasteries for the wealthy community of monks known as the Vijjas, was a truly blessed man.

For one who has departed to the next world, what application did he make for the fulfillment of his emanation, established as it was by his own steadfastness? (Yugmam) Through the dwellings of those whose merit was increased by the attainment of righteousness in kingship, KRT_8_3345ab.
Even those whose sole occupation was war, when engaged in meritorious deeds,
[acted] because of the abundance of food for their enemies due to their taking refuge in the Turkish lands;
for them, nothing other than cruelty had been learned for the sake of maintaining their birthplace.
While King Sussala was intent on his livelihood by opposing their means of subsistence, those who had taken refuge in Kashmir during times of conflict—
born in that lineage of Kṣatriyas— were the younger brother of Kamaliya.

The scion of royalty known as Saṅgi established his own foundation by means of his own name. Once the Bāṇaliṅga had been installed by him on the sandy bank of the Vitastā, those whose minds were liberated through immersion in the waters of the celestial river (the Gaṅgā) were born there.
And having beheld his monastery, adorned by those whose wealth is asceticism,
one turns away from the curiosity of seeking to behold the world of Rudra. [This occurs] when,
at Loṭane, one establishes others and bestows wealth upon the meritorious.
In those days, that man of pure intellect was not yet overcome by passion.
Udaya’s beloved, named Cintā, adorned the sandy banks of the Vitastā with her amorous play, O Lord of Kampanā.
Under the pretext of five palaces, the hand residing in that monastery was,
as it were, raised up by Dharma with its five fingers extended high;
this was the minister of peace and war named Maṅkhaka, who was like a brother to Alaṃkāra.
By his establishment of monasteries, he became the foremost of Samaṭha through his prestige;
by his works such as the restoration of monasteries, agrahāras, temples, and dilapidated structures,
his younger brother named Sumanas equaled Rilhaṇa.
Having built a monastery at Bhūteśvara,
he also caused water from the Kanakavāhinī and the Vitastā to flow into Trigrāmī;
and in the region known as Kaśyapāgāra, there was the river Nīlabhūḥ.
As if out of a desire to conquer, the Ganges flowed toward the eastern direction; there,
for the sake of crossing over cattle and other livestock, he constructed a bridge, thereby performing a stainless deed capable of ferrying him across the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

In the city, he who had a temple bearing his own name and the mark of the bull built, and by whom a monastery was established as a refuge for a multitude of those who had fallen away from wearing matted hair;
he was the one who fashioned the Mammeśvara [liṅga] out of pure, refined gold.
Likewise, [he visited] Somatīrtha, whose vicinity was illuminated by the gardens of the waters. Here,
among the kings of his lineage who were rich in the height of their dynasty and other virtues,
there arose a sense of envy among the ministers who were seizing their wealth, lives, and other possessions.
Whether out of anger, lack of habituation, false attribution, or envy, even Indra, the lord of the Vasus,
caused King Māndhātṛ to fall from heaven.
With an unswerving mind, he daily elevated his servants who possessed the loftiness of their duties.
Seeing the increase in the majesty of his own lineage, the king was delighted.
Rilhaṇa, a wise servant of King Kalaśa,
performed the consecration of golden parasols as a token of his affection.
In Rurukeśvarī, where Śiva and Śivā are united, there is a golden leaf;
together with the bell, it attains the friendship of the ritual offering (*āhāra*) and the nightly vigil (*ārātrika*) accompanied by lamps.
The auspicious couple, Śiva and Pārvatī, are the beloved son-in-law and daughter of the Himālaya, their kinsman.
Under the guise of a golden parasol, Mount Meru has arrived to cover their heads.
It was with reference to them that the Self-born Brahmā, while making an effort to fashion the limbs of Gaurī’s beloved [Śiva], was consumed by me.
It was established here that both [the umbrella and the discus] were present; for, under the guise of a golden umbrella, the fire of Śiva’s eye moved upward.

And there, a great golden umbrella fashioned by Rilhaṇa now shines brilliantly, fixed above the temple of the beloved of Rukmiṇī, reaching to the clouds. Then, the discus—lost due to its master’s stumble caused by drinking blood—arrived as if it had come to behold its own beautiful form, like the sun itself.

At the sacred ford (tīrtha), where the preceptor is the powerful conqueror of Manmatha (Śiva) whose banner bears the bird (Garuḍa), the Lord’s golden parasol—its excellence consisting of the very essence of ritual action—is resplendent. For one [form], it reaches the pollen of the lotuses of the Gaṅgā, which quivers with the hissing of the serpent on the crest; for the other, it has the luster of a mass of lightning situated beside clouds resting at the edge of the hair.
In the city of the golden shell of Brahmā’s egg, it is crushed by the parasol-flower; in the likeness of the ocean, it is offered as a long-lasting oblation within the dense cloud.

The golden parasol, which served as a cover for the two oceans— the source of excellent jewels— was adorned by the dark hue of the enemy of Kaiṭabha (Viṣṇu), who wears the moon upon his crown as an ornament. Four sons, noble in their virtues and skillful, were born to King Lohara and Queen Raḍḍādevī.
Like Lakṣmaṇa with Rāghava, Aparāditya, sharing an undivided affection, grew up under Gulhaṇa while residing at Lohara. Indeed, the child Jayāpīḍa was [raised] by King Lalitāditya.

Protected as Śatrughna was by Bharata, [the kingdom] proceeded on its course. From that sun among kings, who was beautiful to behold and worthy of homage, there arose a fifth mountain of the earth— glorious and righteous— like the rising morning sun.

Ah! Lālityāditya moistens even the walls with his playful movements—movements that, though fickle since childhood, have become harmonious through the abundance of his faith. His fair face, with its copper-red lips, has been treated with protective collyrium.
His speech, though indistinct due to childhood, yet pregnant with greatness, appeared like golden lotuses marked by bees and sunlight;
its utterances were as if moistened with nectar, like those of the ocean being churned.

Born of a noble lineage, that prince, even in his childhood, manifested through his majestic presence the unfolding of his future destiny. Though he had not yet abandoned his ornaments, his crest-lock was like the plumage of a peacock, which— by the grace of its slightly curved tail— seems unable to endure the touch of water.
Having drunk the water of the pond, he proceeds with his movements turned toward the majesty of the state described; such is the nature of that person of excellent complexion.

(KRT 8.3379cd) The four royal fortunes, together with the splendor of the lotus, became his daughters—Menilā, Rājalakṣmī, Padmaśrī, and Kamalā—all of whom were distinguished by their virtuous conduct. (KRT 8.3380ab–cd)
With those ever-delightful children, who were like pleasure-gardens for diversion,
the two of them shone faultlessly like the rainy season and the spring.
In this region purified by sacred fords and shrines, they spent their wealth on acts of charity.

All prosperities had become the very fortune of Queen Raḍḍā. Accompanied by her, that queen of the earth shone like the Goddess of Royal Splendor (Rājalakṣmī) amidst the vassal kings and ministers during the royal processions.
In the land of Satī, multitudes of pilgrims abandon their other holy sites at the mere mention of her immersion;
they immediately feel a longing to touch the form of Satī while she is intent on bathing. During festivals in this wondrous land, people are always eager to see her when she emerges from the rain.
Since she is followed by clouds like the rainy season,
she has surely set out for the holy bathing places of kings to perform ablutions.

Out of envy for those holy fords, the sky would appear as if raining down divine waters; yet, out of eagerness for the sacred sites, that lady of delicate limbs did not perceive the cloud-scraping mountains nor the river-eroding banks,
for she found the path difficult to traverse.
By her, who was steadfast through many religious foundations and restorations of ancient sites,
it is a marvel that the city of Dvārakā was crossed by this clever woman even though she was lame.
Even today, under the guise of the splendor of the overflowing ocean of milk, [she remains].

Emerging from a white stone as bright as the moon, appearing as if born from nectar, Rudreśvara— the glorious Rudra who removes the affliction of poverty through the tears of Upamanyu— is the ornament of Kashmir.
She extracted the very essence of the world’s beauty, along with its pure golden core;
and by her, the restoration of the palace of tranquility was accomplished,
even while the king was transformed by the fire of his anger toward his subjects, as if toward his own servants.
Like the ocean, the refuge of the Udanvatī river, or like the Himalayas, the refuge of the Haimavatī;
while the king’s favor remained steadfast, the punishment and reward of even other monarchs were instantly and uninterruptedly carried out according to his will.

By her, the king Bhūbhṛt, the son of Somapāla, was brought by the proud Queen Menilādevī to a state of great magnificence through marriage. Ah, the character of one's majesty— whose experience is easily acquired in the land of his birth— does not, for the most part, deviate from its true nature.

The discus of the Sun, which had undertaken the vow of rolling through fire and darkness, cut through even that darkness arising from it. For the king, whose excellent realm was graced by jewels, there arose a firm guarantee for the cleansing of the world’s wondrous empire.
When Queen Menilādevī was married,
even the father-in-law, casting aside his opposition, became a sincere bestower of the kingdom upon the groom.
[The king’s] younger brother [defeated] King Prājidhara in battle by force.

Standing before one struck down by enemies, Ghaṭotkaca—exerting himself to settle the score for his enmity and crying out with intense passion—took refuge in *Raḍḍā*. Having attained this, he reached a wondrous and supreme royal splendor. (A *kulaka*) Kṛtivarman’s *Raḍḍā*: *“O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā!”* The *Raḍḍā* of Ghaṭotkaca: *“O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā!”* The *Raḍḍā* of Rāvaṇa: *“O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā!”* The *Raḍḍā* of Śatrughna: *“O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā!”* The *Raḍḍā* of Arjuna: *“O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā!”* The *Raḍḍā* of Rāma: *“O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā!”* The *Raḍḍā* of Nala: *“O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā!
