O Mother Raḍḍā!”* The *Raḍḍā* of Brahmā: *“O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā!”* The *Raḍḍā* of Indra: *“O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā!”* The *Raḍḍā* of Yama: *“O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā!”* The *Raḍḍā* of Varuṇa: *“O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā! O Mother Raḍḍā!”* The *Ra

Having secured the assistance of the ministers, he caused King Pañcavaṭa— the betrayer of his brother and the one who had expelled King Prajji from his kingdom— to fall from his royal power; for he was unable to overcome him due to the king’s majesty, which was overflowing with the waters of abundant charity.
The dark river Khaḍgavallī, which fell within the range of his enemies,
produced the infamy of the second lord of Uraśā by means of its own [darkness]. Through the power of the gods, he seized the exceedingly formidable city of Agramati.
Then, many lords of armies— shaken by the moonlight that wards off both cold and heat— attained such widespread fame. Twenty-two years passed from the king's accession to the throne.
In exactly twenty-five years since he attained sovereignty,
such a sight as this has never been seen elsewhere by the merit of the subjects; may you remain for years exceeding a kalpa, possessing a beauty that is the very ripening of virtue.

Even water, by its flowing nature, gradually becomes like stone as it dries; and a stone oozes water when the excess of fluidity arises. Since time possesses a sovereign power whose majesty is unimpeded, who could remain stable in their natural state on this path fashioned by the Creator’s power—a path so wondrous?
When more than five hundred and twenty-five years of the Kali age had passed...
In Kaśmīra there was a king named Gonanda, who served the descendants of Pṛthu.
His son was Dāmodara, and his wife was Yaśomatī. Gonanda’s son was also [named] Gonanda; he then surpassed all other monarchs.
There was a king named Lava, whose name signified his noble lineage and his favor toward the thirty-five unknown [sages]; from him came his son, Kuśa.

His two sons and grandsons were known as Khagendra and Surendra; then there was Godhara, born of another family, whose son was Suvarṇa. Janaka was born from him, and his son was Śacīnara, the son of Śacī.

Then Aśoka became the king; he was born from the king’s paternal cousin. From him was born Jalauka; after him came Dāmodara, whose lineage was uncertain. Then there were three [lines] equal [in status], beginning with Huṣka and others, who were born of Turuṣka descent.
Then Abhimanyu was the third; then Gonanda, Vibhīṣaṇa, Rājendrajit, and Rāvaṇa followed in succession. After him came another Vibhīṣaṇa, Siddha, and then Utpalākṣa.
After that, there arose Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakuśa.
The king was Vasukuśa; his son was the famous Trikoṭiha.
From Bakā, Kṣitinanda was born, and Vasunanda was his son.

From that king came Naranya, and from him Goptā Gokarṇaka; from that lord of men was born his son Narendrāditya Andhayudhiṣṭhira. His [throne] was overthrown by servants who were born of another lineage.

The king was Pratāpāditya, and his son was Jalauka. When those two were born [and] had departed, Vijaya, born of another family, arose. When Jayendra’s son was the prince, that minister became the one who made peace.
Then, by Śrī Meghavāhana, the son of Bhūpāditya and grandson of Yudhiṣṭhira, [this was] proclaimed in the lineage of the Gauṇandas.
Then Pravarasena, the son of Atramāṇa, obtained the earth;
his son was Yudhiṣṭhira, who had Hiraṇya as his rival in battle.
From him were born, in succession, King Narendra-āditya and King Raṇa-āditya;
their son was King Vikrama-āditya,
and Bāla-āditya was the son of Raṇa-āditya.
Then came Durlabhavardhana, the son-in-law of Bālāditya;
his son was Durlabhaka, from whom Candrāpīḍa was born. Tārāpīḍa was his younger brother, and Muktāpīḍa was his younger brother as well.
There were two kings, Kuvalayāpīḍa and Dvaimātura;
Vajrāditya was the son of King Muktāpīḍa, and his two sons were Pṛthivyāpīḍa and Saṃgrāmāpīḍa, after whom [the lineage] continued as kings.
Jayāpīḍa and his minister Jajja were his sons, followed in succession by Lalitāpīḍa and Saṃgrāmāpīḍa. Then there was the eldest son, Śrī Cippaṭajayāpīḍa, who was born of Kalyapālī.
Having killed him through sorcery,
his maternal uncles— Sāṃmata and the others— who had not yet obtained the kingdom,
installed Jayāpīḍa’s son, Ajitāpīḍa, on that throne.
From Saṃgrāmāpīḍa was born he named Anaṅgāpīḍa.
Then Utpalāpīḍa, the son of Asyājita and Apīḍanandana, uprooted him. Thereupon, Avantivarman, having been restrained by the heroic minister Śūra—
The son of Sukhavarman,
the heroic Śaṅkaravarman, established sovereignty over Naptopala; and Gopāla was his son.

His brother, named Saṃkaṭa, was seized on the street and killed; their mother, known as Sugandhā, then destroyed that king. Then the foot-soldiers of Pārtha, the great-grandson of Śūravarma, [attacked].
Then, in due order, they made Nirjitavarman [the ruler] of that [lineage].
Cakravarman and Śūravarmā were the sons of Nirjitavarman.
Having been appointed many times to the kingdom, Śambhuvardhana established his authority.
In the interval after he had obtained the kingdom, a minister assassinated that king.
After Cakravarman had passed away, the wicked son of Pārtha [reigned] in due order;
then Unmattāvantivarman was [king], and his son was Śūravarmā.

When [Yaśodharman] was deposed from the kingdom, the minister Yaśaskara established him in the kingdom with the assistance of the twice-born. His grandson was Varṇaṭa, and his son was Vakrāṅghisaṃgrāma; he remained in the kingdom after having expelled that [Varṇaṭa].

Anātya, known as Parvagupta, obtained the kingdom through treachery. His son was Kṣemagupta, and then his son Abhimanyu; while he was still a child and being protected by his mother, his son Nandigupta [ruled].
Then,
when his grandson Bhīmagupta had been slain by her through cruel deeds under the name of Diddā,
Saṃgrāmarāja himself was made king at the end of his nephew's reign.
From him were born two sons, Harirāja and Anantadeva.
Then Kalaśa was the son of Ananta, and his two sons were the kings [who ruled] in succession.
Although both were named Utkarṣa and Harṣa, they deposed the king.
Then the two kings [Bhoja and Jayasiṃha] forcibly seized Harṣadeva,
his son, from the arrogant stride [of power]. Born from the one named Malla— the grandson of Jasurāja, who was the son of Bhrātṛpāla’s son Diddā— he attained sovereignty through excessive greed.
Then, after those servants who had slain him through treachery,
there was a king named Raḍḍa, known by another name as Śaṅkharāja, who reigned for only a moment. When he was killed by Garga, Salha, the son of a different mother, also came to power.
The powerful brother of that King Uccala,
named Sussala— the Mallika and uterine sibling of Uccala— having slain him, seized the kingdom.
When he was torn away from the throne by disaffected servants, [another] king was installed.
For six months, the grandson of King Harṣa, known as Bhikṣācara,

remained [in power] after having once again exiled Sussala, who had regained the throne; but he was eventually slain when, through the treachery of the Lavanyas, the kingdom was won in a dual sovereignty.
Having slain that king,
who was a wandering beggar despite his complete beauty, Jayasiṃha— the son of King Sussala and a sovereign of incomparable prowess— now dwells gladdening the earth.
Like the Godāvarī river rushing forward with its seven mouths and tumultuous waves,
this *Rājatarangiṇī* now enters the midst of the ocean of the illustrious King Śrīkānti’s noble lineage to find rest.
